Growing up in a low-income, predominantly African-American, Asian and Latino community in West Oakland is what made me who I am today. Everyone knew each other and said hello on the street, we all respected each other and everyone watched out for each other, no one cared what race you were or where you came from in the end, or especially how much money you made or how wealthy you were. With the amazing submersion in culture and a more raw, more real side of American history and community came its own territory and set of downsides, of course. Poverty and constant unnecessary death from gang violence were an unfortunate reality that everyone strived to break free from. For me Oakland is a mecca for culture, music, art and education that I lovingly call home, but also a hotbed for hatred and violence caused by misundertanding, frustration and greed.
It doesn't matter where you're from who you are or what you look like, We Are Chicago is relatable to anyone who's ever felt like they were outside of their element in their own town. To anyone who remembers the awkward years of school, or felt like they didn't fit in with the routines of others. Where the influences that drove you become bad ones, and negative elements start to move in. The life of living in a city.
We Are Chicago has a very Do-It-Yourself feel, a kind of approach collaborated on by community members and leaders as opposed to long-time game developer vets. It doesn't have the fanciest graphics and can even feel slightly stiff in the animations department but what We Are Chicago lacks in technical modernization it more than makes up for in genuine heart for its subject matter and its outright addictive storytelling.
I have to admit I was slightly thrown off by Aaron's role as a silent protagonist. With voiced dialogue for all of the cast it was hard to figure at first that I was my own silent character, and not one of the friends we're first introduced to. It had a positive effect in the end, however, giving me more room for creativity in imagining just what this character is like and how he speaks or even better, putting myself in his shoes and his position. You really feel immersed in the role of a youth struggling to beat the bad elements closing in around him.
It takes a look at a part of America with a serious eye that's hardly, if ever, looked at in the gaming demographic. Something this demographic shamefully laughs or brushes off when presented with a picture of reality, and something these developers have done a great job of accurately portraying without the hype or the flashy and violent packaging other games with an urban city setting have. This is something anyone with an open-mind should be able to seriously appreciate.
That doesn't mean We Are Chicago has no violence, it's actually centered around gun violence but not in a positive or attractive light. Instead of embracing or promoting it as we're used to videogames doing the developers have shed some light on the very real consequences of income disparity and in turn, the violece and strife it causes all the way down to the youth of our communities. It's all incredibly eye-opening and sobering, and it has a very positive end-message and goal. As the creators state, "In addition, Culture Shock Games is incorporating content into the game to benefit two Chicago non-profits and donating a portion of proceeds to support All Stars Project of Chicago, and Reclaim Our Kids, who are empowering at-risk youth in underprivileged communities of Chicago." This is an experience that's good entertainment for the mind, and has a positive effect on our communities, and overall for our currently sick country.
In the unfortunate period of American history we're currently in where close-minded intentions are emboldened, We Are Chicago couldn't have come at a better time to put real topics in the spotlight. I sincerely hope to see this become a successful trend in the gaming media in the days to come.

That being said, it was by far too short. In the last scene, I thought "Oh goodness, right in the feels..." Shortly after that, the credits rolled and I silently raged. The ending seems extremely rushed and half done. I found it annoying that I had to use certain animations in the campaign; ladders, crawling through holes in walls, etc. The multiplayer seems to be dead at the moment, could be that I am writing this review at two am.  I found only about six servers, and only one server had players. Five to be exact.
Pros:
Fun and interesting storyline
Guns, guns, guns and C4
Sprinting and reloading at the same time
Cons:
Lack in variations of weapons
Extremely short storyline
Unnecessary animations
Few players in multiplayer
If you could buy the game at $5 or less, I would buy it again.
Nobody's ever going to accuse this game of having serious depth... but it's definitely a roaring good time for the time you spend with it.

This game is a remake of 1997's Sub Culture except set in space, which to me is a great thing because SC is one of those great games from the Windows 95 era which does not play correctly on modern Windows, and which I very, very much enjoyed.  If you are familiar with SC, you already know exactly how RG plays in virtually every way.  For those unfamiliar with SC, Rebel Galaxy sets you in your stock ship into the open world of a system, and after buying a jump drive for your ship, you can jump to other equally-large systems.  Each system is randomised in structure and naming for the most part, but the story and factions remain the same from one playthrough to the next.  You space-truck goods for funds with buy and sell prices varying from one station to the next, you pick up goods in the wild along the way through various means such as space mining or salvaging, you fight pirates, you buy new ships and new components, and you repeat this for 90% of the gameplay.  The campaign itself is unreasonably short, so the majority of the gameplay comes from the commerce grind to earn the credits required to upgrade enough to progress and do it again.  Fortunately, I like the commerce aspect very much (it is why I bought the game (see:  fondness for SC)), but it definitely can be a point that drives players away, especially since it is advertised as some sort of space dog fighting game when it by no means plays out like that.
This leads me to my slew of complaints about the game:
-The combat is broadside in style, like old real-world ships.   I read in a blurb from the developer that they were apparently very into the Assassin's Creed:  Black Flag ship combat, and chose to use it for RG in spite of it being entirely anachronistic in the context of fictional space combat.  The idea that your ship has to ignore what is going on in three of four visual sectors in favour of lining up torpedoes on one side only while much faster ships zip around you and shoot homing missiles blindly and successfully is nonsense.  RG's gimmick is that your turrets auto-fire on nearby targets for you while you aim torpedoes, but this is absurd for space combat, and it gets to a point where you are just better off slicing everything into pieces with mining lasers as you spam homing missiles, damn the financial expense.  You get in, channel-pewpew, and get out, forever, not bothering with the gimmick of inefficient torpedoes and uncontrolled turrets that the developers want you to use for some stupid reason.  The combat system is my largest complaint about RG, because you spend so much time putting up with it.
-Also on combat, do not bother to do escort missions, ever.  There are better ways to earn cash than getting frustrated as your papier-mâché escort target flies face first into enemy fleets, leaving you with a "mission failed" screen as though you could stop the inevitable.  The escort targets do not level up with you as you upgrade your ship, but enemies do, so very early in the game escort missions become literally impossible when your Mk1 escort target has to survive against anything higher than Mk2 enemies which completely ignore you and all focus the soft target.  I have no idea how the Cofax side story ends, because I never bothered to chat with her until well after I bought Mk5 gear for my Deep Horizon (giant cargo ship from the Merchant's Guild), so her Battlewagon gets one-shotted by mission hostiles.
-Relating to Cofax, there is another dumb gimmick in this game called Warp Pairing.  It is poorly explained, and even more poorly implemented.  It is kind of like locking yourself to the escort target so that you do not have to manually fly around them during the escort, except that it is broken in the following ways:  Your paired target may just fly around in circles or back and forth between arbitrary points indefinitely with no way to fix this, your paired target may break the pair for no reason whatsoever, your paired target may break warp speed for no reason whatsoever, and my personal favourite, you when pairing may under the AI's control repeatedly crash into and kill your paired target.  This feature does not work, but fortunately, it is not required for any part of the campaign.  Just abandon the mission if you get it in a sidequest.
-Warp itself is also broken to an extent.  The game tells you to not worry about manually breaking warp because you will be pulled out of it automatically when you close in on an object, but time and time again I crashed into planets, space stations, other ships, my objectives, and space debris because of the warp failing to break until I broke my ship's face on something else.  When I was lucky, I just flew right through and past my objective.  I would also often be pulled out of warp when NOWHERE near an object.
-There are other poorly-implemented, one-off features which seem to have been included only partially done and forgotten about mid-development.  The "hacking" is one such feature; I would wager that the overwhelming majority of all players only hacked exactly 10 times for the achievement before never bothering with it again since it is kind of a waste of time.  Mercs are another such feature who, like escort targets, do not level up with you and quickly become obsolete or liabilities.  Many of the stations' "features" also fall into this category, like bartenders and news boards.
-Due to the broadside combat fetish, this game's camera will go crazy fairly often.  Fly past anything and the camera may forcibly turn to the side, and continue to jerk back at what it thinks is an object of interest while you try to put the camera back to facing forward.  This is greatly irritating.
-Diplomacy is impossible in RG--you either are neutral or higher with the Militia, or you are neutral or higher with the Red Devil.  As soon as you get the other faction to neutral, the faction which you were allied with (no matter how high that the reputation was) INSTANTLY becomes hostile.  This happens even if you only do missions which would raise one reputation without lowering the other, making any attempts at diplomacy completely meaningless other than for the two achievements.  There is no reason for this to happen, but the developers do not want you living a grey life even though a bartender in the game specifically indicates that this is possible.  No, you get black or white.  For a game which emphasises freedom, not being able to play both sides seems like an exceptionally arbitrary restriction.
-Some ships which you can buy are wide, and they take up way too much of the screen at all times if you use them (see:  Deep Horizon).  There is no first person perspective, either (which seems like a travesty for a game set in space), meaning that your only options are limited visibility due to a locked camera or getting a thinner ship, which may not be ideal for you.  You also cannot customise the ships visually, such as with paint, which seems like a huge missed opportunity to me since you spend the entire game looking at it with the locked camera.
-The soundtrack is both the best and the worst.  Swamp rock, space western setting is very appealing to me (Borderlands, Cowboy Bebop's hard luck background, that kind of thing), but the songs with lyrics get very old, very fast.  Do yourself a favour and delete all of the music files which do not end in "inst", because you will absolutely come to hate the soundtrack if you do not.  On the other hand, the instrumentals work perfectly for the unglamourous space western setting.  You also have the option of including your own soundtrack, but your music will most likely not be mastered at the volumes that the default music is, so you will find disconnects where your music is inconsistent in volume, resulting in too-quiet or too-loud music.  This is especially noticeable when you merge RG's music with your own.

One of my favorite pirate titles. I originally got the game Pirates of the Carribean for the xbox, which has almost nothing to do with the movies, and thought it was a buggy heap of bizarre russian translation. But then after playing it for a bit, I found out that it was a decent pirate game that plays like a third person adventure of Sid Meir's Pirates.
Over the years, the translations have gotten better, the possibilities and content keeps slowly increasing, same with quests and quest variation. The game has become much more playable. It does take a bit of google searching certain quests for clarification as a heads up.
The game still has a few bugs where I have ctd, and a few annoying game design choices. An example, collect all the amulets in the game early and go out of the way to check for indian traders outside town. At one point deep into the game you are going to have a 1 year time limit and the quest will randomly choose 3 of those 24 amulets to go fetch about 6 months into that time limit. Also the game doesn't autosave except before boarding a ship and only if you have that option selected. So this game can be a harsh lesson in patience or a new found diligence to manual saving.
I see a lot of people complain that the beginning is too hard. But just remember this. If you are being chased by a ton of pirates on the world map. Let them catch you. Then just use the battle phase to run away and shoot some knipples. Chances are you are going to be way faster than them and now you get cannon and accuracy experience. Those crappy shots you take do count toward your experience and it is all about accumulation for when you move up to a class 4 ship.

If you want to play a multiplayer shooter, grab one of the more mainstream offerings that still has a community.

Hatred is a isometric shooter that was made to stir up controversy. Did it do what it was made to do? Yes it did. It got attention. Publicity. "No publicity is bad publicity" is the saying that fits this game well.
It's gaining a hype train because "OH NO! IT'S TOO VIOLENT". Ahhhh to be honest, It's not as violent as I thought. It's the context people flipped out over. Really, Virtual violence is nothing to get disgusted over. It's not real and whoever thinks a game like this will turn people into killers is more brain dead than the AI in this game can be.
So how's the game? It's okay. To put it as blunt as possible, it's repetitive. Is that a bad thing with this game? Well if you're like me, you gotta deal with frustrating things VERY often. That repetitive nature of shooting people can help relieve stress. Because DEATH, KILL, DESTROY, SWAG!
It's a well working game. More optimized since it's release. Yes. Bought this game before and refuded because of a horrible experience with the game. This game still isn't all too amazing however. So let me list the problems with this game.
The story is literally just filler, the protagonist sucks as a character, forgettable ambiant music, cars control like wild go karts, the "Challenge" people talk about isn't actual challenge, "NOW THAT'S EDGY" all over the place and with the stuff going on around there, I can pretty much hear the developer go "TEE HEE! THAT OFFENDS PEOPLE~" like the herp derp 666 symbolism all over the place. To me, It's just overused. Though I gotta say, that blatant "HURR DURR SATAN WAS HERE" stuff did get people all booty tickled. I salute to that at least.
So that challenge I was talking about. It's consistant in "bad" games where it's challenge comes from how many things are thrown at you rather than... an actual challenge. The downtown level is a perfect example of this. Too many things going on that it's hard to keep your respawns. Not that I can't beat it. I got close. It's just not a fair challenge and challenge junkies like me want something better.
I'm not expecting 3D Ninja Gaiden levels of fair challenge but at least something that doesn't seem like they ran out of ideas.
Now for some good stuff.
The game is actually VERY pretty to look at. Here's what makes the game fun too. It's the beauty of the distruction and death. I'm not saying that as some sort of edgy poem either. Graphics in this game are very pretty and when shooting up places, it looks spectacular to see things fall and crumble.
Gameplay may be repetitive but damn is it fun to see the massive genocide through. Seeing how many you can put down. And yes, the civilians aren't defenceless either. They WILL shoot back with guns they pick up from dead cops.
So in the end, I would recommend this game. If you're looking for virtual stress relief, this game is for you. It may be dumb. It may be edgy but it's fun. A good game to play after a stressful day, week or month. Mod support is here too. So that's a huge plus.

I had lots of fun beating Beyond Earth. It plays a lot like a full conversion mod for Civilization V, but to say that's all it is betrays the beautiful restructuring of game mechanics that this version posseses. The game feels more dynamic (thanks to a tech web, as opposed to a tech tree), making each playthrough a completely different game. While Civilization V (and its predecessors) was completely addicting, Beyond Earth makes each game a radically different experience, something that Civ 5 did way better than any of the other installments of the franchise.
That being said, I wasn't particularly fond of the glitches. I've heard a few people mention them before, but when I sat down and played through Beyond Earth, I found them to be quite bothersome. None were game-breaking, but often they were reptitive annoyances that are completely circumventable... once you learn what they are. The achievement counters also seem to be off, as I found myself occassionally getting two points for certain things when one normally ought to receive only one... Not that I'm complaing about that though!
And the achievements are indeed a stellar part of this game. Civilization V was the first game to add them, and they often felt very grind-y and unneccessary. Beyond Earth slimmed most of those bad ones out, leaving in just a few for those gamers dedicated enough to endure the small bits of grind and reach 100% completion.
At $49.99 currently, Beyond Earth has quite a hefty price tag. I'd personally wait until a 50% off or more sale, just to feel like you had no doubt that buying this game was money well spent. If you can get it for that price or less, it's simply a steal.

Great sandbox universe game.  It has a storyline with optional side activities to do as much or as little as you want, along the way.  Mercenary missions, trade missions, bounty hunting, mining.
The combat gives lots of choices for playstyle, with different weapon types, with different strengths and weaknesses.  More strategy than twitch skill required, alongside a soft progression system that has some give to it, if you're good enough to fight ahead of the curve, or not, if you'd rather not.  It is more arcade than sim, with a 2D map, but I don't find myself missing the vertical axis, really.  It works fine without it, though I can see how that might bug some players.
Initially, you start off in one solar system, and it feels small, but once I was able to afford the jump drive, I realized there was a whole lot more to the game than I'd first thought - and it's all very polished and professional. Well worth the $20.

Overall, I have found the game very disappointing. There are a number of reasons for which I say this, but I will attempt to summarize those that I feel are the most important.
- First and foremost, the complete lack of unit variety. The supposed reasoning behind the low variety of units is the Affinity system, however I find that the Affinity system of upgrading units is labor intensive and hinders my play of the game. I find that I must unnecessarily divert large amounts of time and resources to gain Affinity, all for a moderate boost to unit performance coupled with a change in unit appearance. Units between civs have no variety, which leads me to...
- Boring, cookie-cutter civs. The different civilizations have little to make them unique beyond some minor buffs. The buffs themselves are reminiscient of the buffs found in Civ 5, however there are no Unique Units, Abilities, or Buildings to really change things up; the civ you choose to play as influences your play style in a very minor way. Better, more varied civs is needed, not to mention simply more of them. Diplomacy and interaction between civs is boring, stale, and just another window to close while you get back to killing aliens.
- Boring, stale, worlds. Every time I play, I feel like I am playing the same map. There is very little map variety, or at least it feels that way to me.
These are the major points that ruin my enjoyment of the game. There are more, but they are more minor and far more opinionated. The points outlined above I feel I can reasonably claim are failings on the part of the dev team and not something that can simply be dismissed as 'my opinion.'

The best works of science fiction are the ones that hold a mirror up to our wold to break down and explore radical ideas, and how they might impact human society in this imagined future.  It is the percieved distance between this imagined world and our own that allows commentary and criticsim of our modern world to be sharper and more focused.  With this in mind, Sid Meier's Civilization:  Beyond Earth is a massive missed opportunity.
The spectre of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri looms large over this release, but where SMAC took human philosophy blended it with a wild imagination, an extremely hostile frontier and some downright brilliant writing, SMC:BE is tame, pedestrian and boring.
The futurism here just isn't creative enough, the frontier feels dead and laissez-faire, and clicking next turn feels hollow and unrewarding.  There are just no chances being taken here, and the result is a lumpy, bland future-esque skin for CIV V, but where CIV V was refined and improved over time, SMC:BE still feels like the bland, next-turn click-fest.
The idea of landing on a Precambrian-era planet is interesting, but the alien variety is nonexistant and samey, and the Factions the same - the Developers recently blamed the boringness of the factions on lack of historical familiarity, but that's a huge cop-out:  SMAC managed to make each faction unique and engaging, and thanks to the strength of the writing, instantly recognizable.
The one thing they did manage to get right is the tech web, which is a fascinating look at progressive research.   However, compared once again to SMAC, the techs themselves feel fairly bland, and the options they unlock usually limited to +1 to one production or other.
This game needs help.  There's apparently a 2.0 patch coming out, and hopefully this addresses the problems in this game in much the way the first major CIV V patch did, but the game feels bland and lifeless as it stands right now, which is especially disappointing considering its' fine pedigree.

I'm amazed this game hasn't gotten more press than it has- I found it on a Steam sale for $1.99 completely at random.  It's quite short (replay value = 0) and has serious flaws, but for the price it's absolutely worth it
Pro: The world is both unique and starkly beautiful.   The monochrome graphics add a wonderful atmosphere, and the way the trees and shrubs move in the breeze is beautiful.  Sound is very well done and essential. (play this game with headphones)  The day/night mechanism works well.  The weapons are fun- having to deal woth the long reload times of flintlocks while being swarmed by enemies is a nice touch.  Stealth, when it works, is really useful- there's a huge difficulty bump in about a third of the way in and the only way I found to survive the ambush was to run and quitely snipe the enemy one by one.
Cons: This is tough- it's clearly a work of love by a few people without a huge budget.  That said, they couldn't get everything they wanted, and it needs polish.   It's labeled as survival horror, but it's really not scary at all.  In fact, the nighttime enemies are laughable- the skeletons especially look like they're drunk.   The story is decent, but it's obvious the authors had more they just couldn't add.
The real problem is the core exploration mechanic- it just doesn't work well.  You have a map, which by default lists the positions of almost every object on the map before you explore an inch.  It makes the visual and sound cues worthless- just walk to the marker.  Strangely, the markers disappear when you find the item and there's no way to put your own markers down, which is a major issue when you have to revisit them.
The devs do have an option to turn off the map markers, but that adds more problems.  The story is told by meeting wraiths at nighttime, but without markers for them it's nearly impossible to learn everything.  The wraiths can be seen at a distance, but the shadows can't, and worse the shadows only appear once certain conditions are met.  They appear near significant events (murders) but the markers for those vanish when you visit them (and you can't place your own)  Without turning on markers for them, you have to search a couple of acres of territory over and over for the one guy you need to talk to.  I tried to play it without map markers only using sound cues (and listen) but it's just too damn frustrating
All that said, ignore the cons and buy the game.  It's a unique take on the genre and hopefully the devs will manage to write the sequel it obviously needs.

This game officially holds a special place in my heart, and it's incredibly difficult to get there.  I am an avid fan of war games across a multitude of genre's.  So when I found this absolute gem of a game I was excitedly horrified.  And I am more than greatful for it.
This War of Mine in a word is breathtaking.  The art is incredibly surreal, the music invokes a feeling rarely conveyed properly in gaming; a heavy sense of dismay with an incredibly trifling dash of hope.  The characters themselves look haggard, almost blank, which after reading the bio on each of them...can't say I blame them.
This is an easy enough game to pick up and go with, but soon enough you realise that there is no time for luxury.  Making the abode barely livable just to keep the inhabitants safe from illness, using rat cages so they can get a "decent" meal at some point.  Desperately hoping you can get the supplies to make it to tomorrow let alone next week...  This game has just the right balance of keeping the player on the edge of their seat and at the same time hoplessly sitting back realising that the lack of wood, medicine, or food is beginning to have a major impact on the characters.
Then there is the moral dillema's.  I told myself on my first few playthroughs that I would stay as true to myself and the decisions I'd feel I'd make as possible.  After too long however I found myself making choices that I could only pray I would never have to make in this life time.  I remember an old couple whom I walked in to and was telling myself I would only take wood from.  I had a good amount of both food and medicine at home, but the fuel for both the stove and the heater were running low.  The husband pleaded not to take her medicine for she was ill and I kept telling myself I wouldn't, and I didn't...but the feeling of misery lingered in my mind.
So absolute kudo's to 11bit studios for daring to create an aboslute masterpiece of a game that this is.  I truly thank you for this entertaining yet sobering experience.

I had taken interest in Betrayer a few years back but only now did I end up picking it up and playing it.
Sadly, the gameplay quickly proved to be very repetitive, the loop was go around the map collecting items, then do the same in the otherword (a sort of ghost dimension) and finally talk to characters about said items to move on to the next area, were we'd do it all over again.
From the forums I learned that only in the current patch (1.9) did the items become marked on the map, before requiring the use of a listen mechanic (which I never used) to find said items. I honestly don’t know if the listen mechanic would have made the game better or simply more frustrating having to cross the large maps constantly pressing the listen key to find the items.
Combat felt frustrating and broken, perhaps it was my poor skill but my shots seemed to always graze the enemies without hitting them, stealth was no better as I’d hear enemies enrage and run straight at me before I’d even seen them or while I was trying to sneak, even worse every enemy had a ranged attack with undodgeable projectiles combined with every weapon having a long reload time and even a chance to glance doing zero damage made it painful to fight long group of enemies, making pikaboo and AI exploiting tactics the default strategies, that is until I found melee.
When combining the melee attack with a few of the items that gave it bonus damage made it 1 shot kill practically every enemy in the game, so for over half of my time in Betrayer combat simply revolved around me running from enemy to enemy to melee hit them before they had time to shoot their ranged attack which made all the weapon progression in the game totally irrelevant.
Still, I would have been willing to forgive these shortcomings had the story gripped me from the start and motivated me through until the end, but alas it did not. Every new character I met felt like the previous one, down to how their lines were written making them devoid of any kind of personality, I have almost completed the game but feel little interest to return to it to see it’s conclusion which is really the biggest fault I could put on the game.
I wished I had better things to say about the game, I felt it had  a lot of potential, perhaps with some more polish on the combat system and a revision on the writing it would have been a game I would recommend. But as it is, I’m afraid I’d have to suggest that you spend your time elsewhere.

First off I would like to commend 11Bit studios on creating such a unique slant to the war - game genre, though I don't think this title can be or should be placed into said category, its more of a strategy title.
This ‘game’ has thoroughly enthralled me over the better course of two weeks and find myself completing or ‘surviving’ over half of the 12 ‘missions’
With that, I think that there are a few things lacking:
Longevity - each ‘story’ is very similar, you can essentially do everything, interact with everything, and see everything with in two ‘stories’ on my 6th ‘story’ it turned into more of a grind to reach survival, and mashing end turn or ‘stay inside button' for day 42 through 45.
Speed of AI - very slow, too much time is spent waiting for water to be distilled, counseling of characters that get ‘depressed’ characters going up/down ladders, characters completing tasks, ‘loading’ of the nights ‘events’ at the beginning of the next day is also slow, as well as the loading of each scavenging map, the fast forward button was created way back in the day by JVC, yet none available here.
Too much repetition - really the only excitement and break in the monotony of scavenging resources is directing a character to shoot or backstab an unwitting NPC. Would be nice to have some add ons, another set of new ‘stories’ with new maps perhaps?
Too little interaction with in world - Im starving but cant kill any little protein bags (rats) running around under my feet? (Other than setting traps in my building) I also can't scavenge a working TV for its parts? Or bring it back for morale boost.
Glitches - If you make food at the stove, and leave it there ‘overnight’ you can not utilize the following day, it will show that there is ‘cooked’ food, but if you try to feed it to another character or use, it gets ‘stuck’ in a loop, and you will need to complete the day to progress and to ‘break’ the loop, if you build another stove that one will glitch as well, and you will not be able to cook any food.
Garage glitch - (actually useful, but I don't think intended) If you manage to steal items from the ‘son’ and make it without getting killed, you can return the following day and the ‘son’ is not guarding the first room, he’s backed up into the fathers room. You are free to scavenge and remove multiple useful items. Booty gets restocked daily as long as son/father stays alive.
If son dies, and father remains alive the third scavenging location inside of the basement ‘kitchen’ restocks daily.
Church glitch - essentially same as above, remove items from scavenge area that Patrick is guarding, make it out alive, return the next day and Patrick is backed up into the second room
Patrick can also die, as long as the Father upstairs stays alive, the first scavenge point that Patrick was guarding restocks.
Again, a very engaging experience, and great ‘darksy artsy’ feel overall, just needs to be expanded, perhaps different struggles as a civilian WW2, WW3? And why just survive getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you daily? How about the ability if you play your ‘cards’ right to thrive and build a community. A community with capabilities to expand into other areas of the neighborhood rebuilding the infrastructure as you go and having the ability to play beyond the 45th day, if you so desire

If you love Bioshock, you'll love Bioshock 2. The game is pretty much the same with the first one, only now you're not a lone Survivor in an Underwater city, now you're a Big Daddy. Goes by the name of "Subject Delta". You were a prototype model of Big Daddy paired with a single little sister, until her real "mother" Sofia lamb, found her and separates you from her. you were hypnotized by Lamb to kill yourself, and somehow years later you're still alive and awake, and now on a quest to find the girl to save yourself.
The mechanic of the game is similiar to the first Bioshock, weapons in your right hand, and plasmids in your left hand, only now you can actually use both weapons and plasmids in the same time as both hands are shown in the screen. Of course it's better now because you can use your creativity to combine your plasmids with the usage of weapons. Also, because you're now a Big Daddy, you can adopt  little sisters and make them harvest ADAMs for you. You're a big monstrous creature and it's seems like the combat is much easier than the first game (Especially when you're in a fight with another Big daddies, it's much easier) but not until you meet the Big Sisters, that's a real challenge.
If you've finished the first game, the game's story is original and complex, and for the plot-twist it's unpredictable and amazing. Here in Bioshock 2, the story is less complicated than the first game, but the story is more emotional which is good.
Overall, i love the game, the mechanic is an improvement from the first game, and the story is good. Recommended if you've finished or at least played the first game, if you haven't i suggest you to play it first so you can feel the vibe of Bioshock.

This game is very enjoyable, if you're looking for something to play for about an hour a day! The game is perfect for practicing your MTG skills, or just playing if you can't play in real life. It's 100% free to get everything in it, and it is your choice if you want to buy into speeding up the collection process by using money... But it is by no means required.
The game has improved a lot! The game used to be littered with bugs, but so many of them have been fixed. Although there are a few still and the game is still not perfect, it is definitely moving towards something much better. They are also updating it as new sets come out, with no sign of stopping -- the current cards in it are very similar to standard format today, without Dragons of Tarkir included. When the next set shifts in, Kaladesh, it will be basically standard -- although, Magic Duels is done in a more... Learning based format? The one thing I don't enjoy is that they have removed some cards from the sets in order to balance the gameplay apparently, putting in some older cards to take their place in the 'starter box'. The result is a game that is unbalanced anyways, honestly. I think that they should just include everything that is in say, Standard, when Kaladesh rotates in, and I hope they move towards something like that. The rule of only maxing out at  1 mythic, 2 rares, 3 uncommons, and 4 commons.. For copies of a card in a deck or collection is sort of weird, but I think that can balance things a little better in my opinion. It's nice to see players having to use cards that don't see much play because of the rule and really diversifies gameplay.
All in all, I reccomend the game, for sure. Just expect a few bugs here and there if you're getting it. Starting off may be a little difficult too using starter cards against possibly people with great decks just on a losing streak -- but that is just luck. Things will get better.
----------------------------
Edit: Wizards of the Coast has now dropped this game to develop an MMORPG in its place. Honestly, I really loved playing this game, but as soon as I heard there were never going to be any more cards, I stopped playing and haven't played since.

First of all, I love Civ games. I have been playing Civilization since the original. I have 770 hours played on Civ V. Also, I didn't start playing BE assuming it was going to be exactly the same as Civ V. Just like when Civ V came out, there is a lot of pushback from people who don't like Civilization changing. BE does many things well, but it does things differently than Civ V.
Pros:
- Tech "web" makes game progression much more interesting. Tech is much less linear and you can specialize if you want to.
- Aliens are done well. I feel like they updated this part of Alpha Centauri well. Miasma tiles play an important tactical role in combat, and Harmony players can use them to their advantage.
- Unit upgrades aren't tied directly to tech. I think this makes the game more interesting, as you have to choose between techs that will upgrade your troops and others that might unlock more buildings, etc. Units can also be upgraded outside the tech tree through quests, and you there is a degree of customization to the upgrades.
- Espionage is improved from Civ V with more stuff for spies to do. You can even have spies add to a project that helps your cities instead of spying.
- Lots of choices for tile improvements, with powerful ones costing upkeep. Tech allows customization of improvements as well.
- Setting is cool, although the game could use a few more terrain palettes for variety.
Cons:
- There aren't enough 'civilizations' to play as. This is inherent in the setting, as they have to make up every sponsor instead of just drawing from history. But there does feel like a lack of variety over Civ V.
- Stations aren't done well. These serve a similar purpose to city-states, but they only function as trading partners. However, they always seem to disappear, either from neglect (they just seem to die out), or from other people attacking them. There is no way to enter into diplomacy with them, so you can't defend them from other players.
- The game is a little too easy to play against the AI. The non-linearity of the tech web allows you to upgrade your units faster than the AI does. Since they balanced trade routes, this isn't quite as bad.
Overall, it is a great game. Is it as good as Civ V? Currently, probably not. There are still updating it, with much needed balancing being done (e.g., wonders have been much improved). But that doesn't mean you shouldn't play it. If you haven't played Civ V yet, by all means, I would say play that instead. But if you want something new, this is a great addition to the Civilization series.

Looked into this during a free weekend and purchased it after in the corresponding sale.
I did not know much about the X series so far, besides that it is a space sim sandbox and that whenever a new sequel comes out, it is usually bug-ridden and then patched up by the developers afterwards. Since 4 years have passed since release, I thought I could give it a try, probably all the rough stuff should be ironed out by now.
From what I have seen until now the game was perfectly playable without encountering any noticeable bugs. The campaign introduces you to most of the key game elements, so getting into it was far easier than I thought. You still need to be willing to look up online how certain things work exactly though, as it is a fairly complex game. Also sometimes it feels that the tutorial instructions were written by someone who knows the game / the series all to well and did not consider the perspective of a total newcomer with 0 knowledge about the game.
Once you figure out how to do everything you get more and more fluent in controlling your ship and ordering other ships around etc. Sometimes the game is still unnessecary complicated: To repair the hull of your own ship, for example, you need to dock first, and then find and manually walk up to the egineer on the station to ask him for a repair, while you can do a lot of other things like selling goods etc. by simply calling the NPC from afar.
If you are willing to look past those control issues, you can roam around in a space sandbox with a lot of possibilities, running missions, trading, exploring, upgrade your ship, scan space for hidden goods and lost trade containers, board capital ships, hire personnel, build up a fleet, construct stations for further trade and production.....
I can't say however how the game compares to the previous iterations in the series, a lot of reviews were negative due to the fact that you can only pilot a single ship & only command the others, where you could all fly them yourself in the previous parts. Also I read that the economic simulation is not as detailed as it was before & apparently a lot of features and quality-of-life improvements that I started with were not present at launch, which makes the huge amount of negative reviews understandable.
Overall I would recommend the game to anyone that is interested in playing a complex space economy sim, and is willing to invest some time online to look things up on the net until you know your way around in the game. If you are coming from the previous X games I would approach with care and read some of the more recent negative reviews, to see if the aspects you care about are still the same as in the previous X games.

Initial Impressions:
- Factions don't feel particularly diverse. There are minor differences in starting bonuses, but stylistically they're very similar and there aren't really the special units from older Civ games.
- The tech web is a confusing mess. Not necessarily functionally, but because they've shoehorned in name-changes everywhere they possibly could. Culture is now affinity, for example and the names of each affinity are silly: is purity pure human or pure environment? Why is supremacy economical when it conjures images of, y'know, domination? They didn't bother to change the logo, mind. It's still an open book. Not very advanced.
- Paths to victory feel very muddy. In earlier Civs you knew you were making progress toward your goal, but it feels like a whole lot of guesswork, here. I went heavy on the military front, for example. Seeing that I was haemmorhaging energy (money), I got every improvement, tech and building that would improve that. I still had to sell all except one of my military units just to break even. On the easiest difficulty. What the heck? In earlier games I could take stock, see what I did wrong, and either improve it or learn for the next try. In this one, I've got no idea what I've done wrong, and I've got no idea how I'm stacking up against other Civilisations.
- And you know that 'one more turn' thrill? You know how a neighbour does something unexpected and you spend the next 50 turns trying to compete/mop up? Gone. The music is soaring, but my heartrate didn't do the same even once.
+ Outposts are a good idea. I remember on III boxing in my continental neighbours with new pop-up cities, and although you couldn't do that in V thanks to happiness (which is also renamed. Seriously, happiness is happiness), your opponents had no issue with it. This feels like the most logical way of doing things.
I can't recommend the game as is. But I will play plenty more and come back with a more balanced view.

This is the game that burned me the most.  Forget Spore.  Forget numerous MMOs that were going to be the WoW killers.  This game was created by a company that had three previous games to build onto and expand upon.  Release was always a buggy mess as I learned buying the original X3.  However, under the bugs was a great game.
Those that say the game has improved are ignorant of what makes X a great series.  It isn't pretty graphics.  It isn't abstract ships that exist for scenery.  It isn't the lack of bugs or free updates.
You are allowed to command one ship.  You can't change that ship.  You can't rename the ship.  It has a co-pilot who is memorable for all the wrong reasons.  You can't replace her.  In fact, there seems very little to make your experience unique.
The ships around you aren't doing real things.  They are abstract.  The ships in previous X series were going somewhere, with something.  If you killed all the ships going into a factory, it would lose supply and stop working.  The Universe was alive and breathing where affecting the system had consequence.
X Rebirth has problems with its structure.  No number of updates will change that.  They can get rid of all the failed console port code, the shoddy, repetitive, meaningless first person mode and even the models that looked worse than Oblivion.  The bones still remain and those are the bones of a game that ignored what makes X a great series.

When I purchased Betrayer, I got it on sale and only paid a little over $2.00 for it. I honestly wish I could go back and pay full price for it, as the creators of this game gave me over 20 hours of gameplay. But what is Betrayer exactly?
It's a first person shooter/exploration/horror game, set in the 1600s. The premise is simple, in that you end up as a nameless pilgrim who washes up on shore after a shipwreck. Disregarding an ominous message, you end up battling the undead with bows, crossbows, pistols, muskets, tomahawks and small explosives. Your only other human contact is a mysterious woman dressed in red, so you need to find out what is going on and hopefully escape with your life.
The gameplay is very solid and plays better with a Steam controller, although the keyboard and mouse setup works fine as well. No problems here. Graphically the game is great looking, whether you keep the default black and white noir setup or saturate it with color. One thing to note is that there is no music outside of the title screen, as the rest of the game relies heavily on sound, whether it is the wind blowing to help you with stealth kills or the moans and groans of the undead as they charge at you.
One thing that can be a little frustrating is that the game, while open ended in each of its seven main areas, doesn't provide a direct linear explanation of the story or your overall objective. The story must be pieced together from clues and notes that you find along your journey, along with conversations you have with undead spirits, that you can somehow speak with despite no explanation as to why. So you know, the main objective of the game is to remove the corruption from the areas that have it so you can move onto the next map, although not every map has corruption within it.
Currently there are map markers which point to the clues, notes, corrupted totems, and treasure, but these can be disabled if you wish. However leaving them on does not detract from the gameplay. These items should definately be sought out as not only will it improve your understanding of the story, but through the treasures you find (along with loot from defeated enemies) you can upgrade your arsenal of weapons along with ammo upgrades. Some people say this turns the game into basically a 'walking simulator' but it's no different then any other sandbox styled title where you need to travel to your objective.
There is a lot to be had here and for the price it's an absolute steal. I give this game a musket blasting, crossbow shooting, undead killing recommendation.

The game has improved a lot! The game used to be littered with bugs, but so many of them have been fixed. Although there are a few still and the game is still not perfect, it is definitely moving towards something much better. They are also updating it as new sets come out, with no sign of stopping -- the current cards in it are very similar to standard format today, without Dragons of Tarkir included. When the next set shifts in, Kaladesh, it will be basically standard -- although, Magic Duels is done in a more... Learning based format? The one thing I don't enjoy is that they have removed some cards from the sets in order to balance the gameplay apparently, putting in some older cards to take their place in the 'starter box'. The result is a game that is unbalanced anyways, honestly. I think that they should just include everything that is in say, Standard, when Kaladesh rotates in, and I hope they move towards something like that. The rule of only maxing out at  1 mythic, 2 rares, 3 uncommons, and 4 commons.. For copies of a card in a deck or collection is sort of weird, but I think that can balance things a little better in my opinion. It's nice to see players having to use cards that don't see much play because of the rule and really diversifies gameplay.
All in all, I reccomend the game, for sure. Just expect a few bugs here and there if you're getting it. Starting off may be a little difficult too using starter cards against possibly people with great decks just on a losing streak -- but that is just luck. Things will get better.

Let me start by admitting something. I bought betrayer alongside other games during a sale, and then uninstalled it after less than an hour, finding it confusing and dying to a group of enemies frequently. It was only because I needed more playtime to get trading cards that I reinstalled and played it a bit more. I am very glad that I did.
Betrayer is a very well done suspense game, a murder mystery or sets of murder mysteries if you like. It is more disconcerting and more eerie than it is terrifying. There is a great sense of foreboding in the game helped by a very interesting and pretty black and white, with red hints, pallet.
Each area of the game has a certain story to it, whether it be the burning of a woman falsely accused of being a witch or a father’s desire to do anything to preserve his family’s honour. You investigate, reading notes, finding clues and discovering what’s happened to the inhabitants. Sometimes you fight Spanish conquistadors, sometimes humanoid ash creatures and sometimes skeletal opposition.
Like a lot of games you start off with very mediocre weapons, can only carry a very small amount of ammunition, water (health) and bombs and so it can start off tricky. But using the stealth system and then eventually gaining better equipment means it becomes more manageable later on. The weapons are interesting (crossbows, bows, muskets and pistols) and thematic, muskets hit hard but have an agonising reload time, for instance.
Yet the decent combat, takes a backseat to the story, the mystery of the New World settlements and what happened to them. This isn’t a game that holds your hand, with an unclear sense of what you should be doing prevalent throughout the game; it’s what put me off originally and some of the negative reviews reference the lack of direction. I think that this works for this game and with a new patch if you want to you can see where most (not all) of the places and items of note are on the map.
For the price, especially on sale, this is an absolute steal. An atmospheric story telling game of mystery, discovery and a not in your face sense of horror. The ending divides opinion a bit, I won’t spoilt it but it is short/abrupt. Betrayer isn’t really a traditional shooter and its lack of an obvious sense of direction isn’t for everyone. For those that like mystery, suspense, a story that you discover rather than are told, I can’t recommend Betrayer enough.

First of all, during my entire playthrough I experienced ZERO crashes. I'm not saying that these other people are lying, but just know that it is certainly possible to play the game completely through without any hiccups.
As for how they handled the remaster, I think the things they added make the world look better overall. Environments are more dense, some models have been touched up, and everything looks really nice. The director's commentary is nice and provides some cool insight on the development process, but it can get a little repetitive and you can probably find it on YouTube. They also added a museum where you can see some early character models and read about the creation process, which is pretty neat. However, one MAJOR gripe I have with this remaster is the sound mixing. It sounded as if there were no walls in the play space. If an enemy spoke and they were in the next room, they would sound like they were on my shoulder. The sound would not be muffled or drowned out in any way. I don't remember that happening in the original, so that's a big negative.
The game itself is fantastic and, in my biased opinion, still holds up to this day. There's nothing I can add that you probably haven't heard already. I'll be cliche and say, "If you haven't played this game already, what are you waiting for?!?"
Negatives? The hacking is probably the only thing that I'll say has aged poorly. You do it ALOT and it is tedious if you have the right upgrades. Also, it is my personal opinion that you get WAY too powerful by the end of the game. I played on hard and the beginning was tough for sure, but by the end, nothing can put up a decent fight. Maybe that's the point, so take that with a grain of salt.
All in all, this is the best way to play through the first Bioshock. If the sound mixing was better it would be perfect, but alas, that should not stop you from checking this one out.

Before the infestation of Steam with "indie games" and "walking simulators" since the last two years. There were a really good real indie games. Like this one.
It's a first-person exploration survival horror game.

No, this game is way better than Resident Evil VII.
The tag "Atmospheric" means something when it comes to this game. It has very nice visual style. The game by default is in "noir" visual style: black and white with red for the enemies. But you can change the color settings, as you want it. Perfect combination between "art game" and  real "survival horror game".
The story is surprisingly good and very original. It's scary but not gory like in the Resident Evil. More mystical ghost type of horror story. You, the main character, are a shipwreck survival, who wakes up on the coast of colonial Virginia. What happen, where are all of the colonists and who is the cute girl in the red dress? There are several huge areas to explore and solve this mystery.
Some may say that the game suffers because there aren't voice acting. When it comes to talk with the NPCs there are only text menus. It's indie game after all. But for me, this perfectly fits with all the spooky ghosts which populates the game. A ghost don't speak with a voice, it talks directly into your head. Only a text can bring that feeling.
The gameplay is solid. I don't know how other to say it. It reminds me about the first survival horror games like "Alone in the dark" and "Resident Evil". The game don't "lead you" or "hold your hand" and show you what to do. You are doing all the exploration as you like and by yourself. The fights are heavy and difficult even against one enemy. There is a stealth mechanic for silent kills and avoiding multiple enemies. The stealth mechanic includes a gameplay mechanic option to mask of your steps with the sound of the wind. To fight properly you must to use all of the items and weapons you can find. You can't really "die" in this game. If your Hp hit 0% you are "kissing" the ground, pass out and the lovely girl in red dress, drags you back to the nearest settlement. But you are losing all of the items and weapons. To get them back you must go back on your "dying place" and if you die again before getting them you will lose them like in the hardcore RPG "Dark Souls". Also, there is very nice "sound" gameplay mechanic. You are using your hearing to navigate- finding points of interest or hidden objects. There are very nice and helpful option settings to make the game more "friendly"(easy) for certain players. Like removing the Dark Souls "items backpack drop" when you die. Or putting a visual "sound" indicator on your compas for people with hearing disabilities.
For this money is a steal. I mean, there are so many "triple A"  $60 games with less content.
On several times in this review I compare this game with the classical exploration  survival horror games mostly the Resident Evil and its "VII" first-person part. Honestly to say, Betrayer is several times way better than REVII. It perfectly nails all the "parts" inside the game. The fights and the stealth, all optional. It's your decision, how to engage the enemies. The exploration part "is/was"(read about this below) perfect. The map size, they are not too huge to lost in them. Or too small to make the game feel linear, like in the REVII. The perfect size for exploring. Again, it's your decision to engage the heavily infested with enemies settlers post with the current weapons or to search for better weapons and money.  Perfect combination of art-game, survival horror classics and hardcore elements.
BUT.... But there is one tiny unpleasant going to awful... problem. The last update: [1.9]. This update adds all of the objects and points of interest (a.k.a the quest places) on your game map. And I mean directly on your map... by default.... There are not hidden. There is no setting option to disable them. The only way to hide them, temporary, is from the game map itself. But they will be still there to tempt you and spoil your play. By this, the entire exploration part of this game goes to hell. Everything is based on exploration. And the non linear narrative of this game became broken. I don't know why the developers did this. Maybe they received too many complaints from "gamers" about "difficulty exploration". The game is now, just a stupid generic walking simulator for hypsters and other casuals with no knowledge about video games. No challenge at all.
I highly recommend this game. It was extremely good on the previous updates. But until the developers fix this "map problem", I recommend to not start playing it. This is a really awful game spoiler.

I want so badly to like this game. And I do, on the surface. But out of the many, MANY games I've played (not even just counting pirate games), this has to be one of the most stressful, painfully frustrating games I've ever played. After putting 22 hours into this game, I still felt like I was in a tutorial, and just got sick of it. I'll just put this into pros and cons:
Pros (I'll start off as optimistic as I can):
- Cool weapons; also accurate for the time unlike some pirate games
- I think this is the best pirate game I own GRAPHICS-WISE, yet also the one I run at highest FPS out of all of them! Sid Meier's Pirates and Blood & Gold: Caribbean have slightly worse graphics tbh, yet I get about 10-20 FPS more on this game, averaging at 70-80, even in large battes and highly populated areas. Hats off to whoever optimized this game, you did the one thing AC4:BF could not!
- Acceleration, otherwise the game would be so slow it'd be unplayable. And I don't mean slow as in FPS, I mean the ships crawl like turtles unless you have it as 6x-8x speed. No idea why the devs intentionally had ships sail in real time by default, since every other pirate game I've played has already figured out that it's way too boring.
- There are surely other good parts of this game, but none of them are apparent to me after my 22hrs playing, meaning they're too much of a pain to get to in the first place.
Cons:
- The English translation is HORRIBLE! Run-on sentences, uncapitalization, misused phrases that don't make sense, etc... literally one of the lines is "hello I need an information". It's so weird too, because it's just stuff the player says, most of the NPCs have near-perfect English, as if they're uneducated like they would be in that time. At least 40% of the dialogue looks like it was written by a 9 year old.
- The average player, including myself, will spend AT LEAST 4 hours... ON THE FIRST ISLAND! You don't even get a ship until you get a TON of money, and you have no choice but to do a lot of quests (some are okay) and steal from houses! And even if you find anything good, you have to sell it all just to get all of the supplies necessary to leave the island once you get a ship! On top of that, once you've sold all the things you'd rather keep, you ALSO have to sell most of your cargo! For at least 2 hours I was thinking, WHEN CAN I GET OFF THIS DAMNED ROCK?! I thought this was a pirate game, where's my damned ship already! There is also no tutorials, no manual, nothing. I've had to write discussion posts pleading for help at least 15 times before I even bought my ship. It's ridiculous. I only started getting a hang of the game maybe 10 hours in, and I'm usually good at getting into a new game.
- Bad combat system. Your crew gets in the way during a boarding, even on a huge ship, and they get killed off by the eliter troops, leaving you surrounded by 20 angry pirates. The worst thing is, if you die, you restart at that boarding, and unless you win, it's impossible to abort: basically, save every time you do something major, or you could get stuck very easily with a ship that's too good for you, and dying over and over will get you nowhere, so you'll have to restart. Over my 22 hour playtime, I've gotten trapped like this two times, totalling to about a 3 hour set back each -- and I do NOT like redoing things.
- Little to no gear upgrading. In my 22 hour playtime, not ONCE have I seen another sword or pistol or armor besides the ones I had in a store. All I got once was an arquebus from a special quest, but then I got stuck and had no choice but to go to a previous save, about a 3 hour setback. Damnit was I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I never saw the quest again.
- Map navigation. You can't go anywhere without 5 pirate ships after you, and they usually outsail me, and you can't avoid fighting with them. Also, most quests give half the days I need to get to where I need to be, and if I'm just 2 days late, the quest not only fails, but my reputation with the quest's nation becomes HOSTILE! How the ♥♥♥♥ does missing a single shipment of cargo make a whole nation think I'm their enemy? That'd be like a kid having his homework in a day late, and then he gets expelled. Then if you wanna build the rep back with that nation, either THEY'LL be trying to kill you, or a governor for that nation will give you another quest -- that's twice as difficult! Speaking of difficult...
- The EASIEST DIFFICULTY is what I've been playing on. If this is the easiest difficulty, then whoever plays the hardest difficulty will quite literally throw his computer out their window in rage and proceed to punch their tv multiple times... in the first 2 hours.
- No cheats. I'm no cheater in most games, but this game needs it. This game also needs modding, which it can't be yet. All I need is a few extra pesos and maybe I could get somewhere in this game. If I could just have a large ship and crew, some good weapons, and enough cargo, maybe I'd actually continue playing this game. But for now, this game is just such a piece of crap.
TL;DR: There's a part of me that just wants to play this game, thinking "maybe things will be different today?" but they never are. I want so badly to just have fun with this game, but alas, it's quite impossible. For this reason, this is the first game I am not recommending, which is so sad since this game has so much potential, and I've played many stupider games than this one, but this is the first on steam that I've truly needed to dis-recommend. For these reasons, keep your $20 in your wallet. If you want to ignore this review completely and buy the game anyway, I beg that you at least wait until a sale and spend only a few dollars on it, else you'll very likely be missing that $20 shortly.

My first 3 to 5 hours were not good.  I had trouble and restarted from scratch a few times. I finally goofed up and restarted from my existing save and noticed that I got to bring in my XP, keys, recipes, etc.  Through persistence, I learned that I could level and level until Chuck was as powerful as my weak♥♥♥♥♥♥needed him to be.  You can think of it as an integrated handicapping system.
Anyhow, once I got Chuck leveled up to around the 10th level, I was able to pursue the campaign.  I still am not done, only being about mid-way through it.  But I am having a good time, especially by arming the people that I rescue with automatic rifles, shotguns, and a load of firepower.
I have also found that the ninja suit (DLC item) makes the game a lot more comfortable.  You are largely invisible to the zombies which allows you to do stuff like look at your phone and plan.  The ninja suit has made me a lot happier with the game by taking a bit of the stress out of the game.
If you are not familar with the series, there are a lot of mission timers running all the time.  You have to find a rare drug once every 24 hours.  Missions disappear if you don't get to them - it is really bad if that mission is a plot mission.  Travel distances become obstacles to overcome by finding shortcuts and by making the best time.  Sometimes, it would just be more fun to go on a zombie slaughter, but the time constraints and resource management really make that something that is better to avoid.  Anyhow, you've got important stuff to do and the zombies are really just an obstacle.
Speaking of the undead, it is really quite a technical achievement - you can enter some large open areas and there are THOUSANDS of zombies moving about.  If you stop and watch them, they are all doing something and the game doesn't bog down or stutter - the optimization is evident.
Anyhow, I liked this one well enough to invest in DR3.  Far from done, but even if I cannot finish it, I've had a good time.  Thanks, Capcom!

The Gist:
Set in a post WW III America, occupied by North Korean, this game came out in the heyday of CoD: Modernwarfare. Though it rang many of the bells of the direct competitor, it also fell short in many regards the former did. Ultimately a severely mediocre game which did not manage to dethrone any other game.
The Pros:
-Good graphics and a good visual presentation over all.
-A not too overused setting (at the time anyways).
-The multiplayer acutally set itself aside quite well from its competition.
The Cons:
-First the worst: the movement in this game feels terrible. Described as "floaty" and "unresponsive" by reviewers, when it first came out, it displays all that can go wrong with a CoD-esque game. You move at a literal snail's pace - try to sprint and your unathletic avatar give up after five meters.
-On top of the former, in all the ingame cutscenes (and there are plenty, dragging out the expierence) you move even slower, forced to endure unskippable, cammy at best but mostly boring text.
-Some sad technical shortcomings, FOV is very narrow, some sound bugs.
-The story meanders between shallow and melodramatic, a short and unsatisfying bore.
-Though interesting at the time, the multiplayer is dead now.
-There is an unjustified amount of expensive DLC, splitting the community (not that there is anything like that anymore).
Game is fun!.. BUT need to be able to go back to the last galaxy before the end of the main quest line is done.

I've spent a silly amount of time on this series since my youth.
Basically, you build a theme park. That's the entire game. You can either do the scenarios, which are questionably balanced and take forever, or you can build a sandbox scenario to build the theme park of your dreams. Or, you could turn this into a murder simulator and make death-coasters and drown people. You can also download a theme park made by someone with a lot of time and bask in the glory that is RCT-Obsession. The coaster builder is amazingly robust, allowing for a lot of customization. With patience, you can sit down and build the roller coaster of your dreams.
If you're going to get one of the three currently-released games, I vote this one. RCT1 on Steam has no sandbox mode, and you can't download the trainer/patch needed to make it work because you need an unpatched version of the game to do so. Also, you can just download and add in every single RCT1 scenario into RCT2, so there really isn't much of a reason to pick up the first game, unless you want to hear the theme music or something. If you're nitpicky, there are a select few advantages that RCT1 has over RCT2 - more path and ground options that make building some styles of scenic buildings easier, some coasters have different trains that allow for a bit more creative freedom, and some coasters have a tad more flexibility in the kind of track you can place. However, these differences are seriously negligible because you can bend RCT2 to your will with trainers and custom scenery. And, yeah, I vouch for the use of a trainer with the RCT games, unless you're playing scenarios, because it unlocks the true potential of the sandbox here. RCT3 can't handle big parks, or tons of people wandering around a park, and also has an iffy engine that might just ruin your entire park because everything starts to float for no good reason. RCT2 has aged amazingly well, still plays great, and has a robust community that has implemented all sorts of incredible custom content that you can install and use in your park.
The only downside here is the scenario play is totally lackluster compared to RCT1. As I said earlier you can install all the parks from RCT1 and play them within RCT2, but there is no real progression because everything is unlocked, so you're mostly just playing them for fun. You have to reference something to do them in the proper order, if that is something that you would want to pursue. The RCT2 scenarios, while some have cool scenery or landscape, and some have some awesome pre-built coasters, are not very fun to play overall. They range from incredibly-long and dull, to insanely difficult and nearly impossible to beat without sheer luck.
The game runs fine and doesn't have many compatibility problems with modern systems, which is a relief. Avoid alt-tabbing and you shouldn't encounter any crashes.

Beyond the 100+ hours I've put in on Steam and the 71% achievements earned, I've played this since it launched on Impulse, Stardock's failed online game distribution client and Steam competitor. I easily had close to 200 hours there and a full 100% achievement completion on that version. I bought the full priced collector's edition at launch, bought it again on Steam, and bought the 2nd collector's edition for the Rebellion expansion. Even with all those purchases, I'm pretty sure my price per hour is hilariously low (if I'm remembering the prices I paid right, it's somewhere around 60 cents an hour!). This is one of the best spaceship fleet combat games ever, and the surrounding strategy elements are great too. It was dubbed a RT4X when it came out, meaning it combined RTS and 4X gameplay, and while I think it's lighter on the 4X part of it than some would like, it still combines them well and is a ton of fun to play. The end game can bog down if you're going for a goal of wiping out the other side(s), but you can change things up and set several different win conditions to keep it moving faster and avoid that. A map editor, a random map feature, and a great stock of premade maps keeps you busy for a long, long time. 3 factions with 2 variants each also make for some good replayability. One flaw I do have to mention, though: there's no campaign mode. I was surprised by this when I first started playing, but once I got into it, I no longer noticed it's lack. That said, there does seem to be an interesting story behind this world as told via the opening cinematic that I'd love to explore in a sequel. Finally, I have to say that visually it holds up wonderfully. It's still beautiful and you can zoom in and out seamlessly from individual fighters to multiple solar systems. I can't recommend this game enough!

Just an amazing "game."  And I put "game" in quotes like that since it's not really a game, more an interactive story something like the old "Choose Your Own Adventure" kids' books.  Sort of.  Kind of.  But different.
Don't let that put you off, though.  It *is* essentially a 'walking' adventure, but the concept is deliciously new and engaging.  I would strongly suggest playing the Demo first, for a few reasons.  First, the demo is kind of a preview of what TSP is actually like to play.  If you hate the demo then you'll likely hate the game.  The Narrator is the same, and the sense of humour and satirical tone are pretty consistent.  Second, the demo is not a preview of the game itself.  When you finish the demo you'll be at around the same place you will be when you start the actual TSP.  Third, the demo is hilarious even by itself (though TSP is hilarious in its own right).  I will warn you that  there are a few (very few) spelling errors in the captions if you have them turned on.
And it changes.  Things don't always stay the same (mainly the narrator's comments).  If you go back through the same area a number of times, what the Narrator has to say is at times slightly different. Or maybe notably different.  Personally, I'd recommend NOT trying to 'Beat the Game' as fast as possible.  Do strange things.  Go where the Narrator *doesn't* tell you to go.  His commentary when you do the 'wrong' thing is quite funny sometimes.
SO, what's this game about, you ask?  It's rather like the comment from "The Matrix:" Nobody can explain TSP, you have to see it for yourself.  It is a short game, though in theory you could keep playing indefinitely, since the end is never really the end is never really the end.  It is plot-driven, sort of, in a way, and the graphics may be a bit low-quality compared to the shiny expensive games out there.  But you'll likely not care.
I really really really recommend TSP.  Seriously.  I spend most of My time playing games in a completely different genre (turn-based strategy, eg. Civilization or Pandora).  I still loved this.  93/93.

I can see why some might enjoy this game but I didn't enjoy it.
Aspects that were okay:
+some entertaining boss battles
+some attractive characters
Aspects that I didn't like:
-time limits for everything * (largely a matter of personal preference)
-low weapon durability (weapons break easily)
-slow movement speed **
-escort quests for NPCs can be a pain in the a$$ ***
-bland characters and storylines (not much backstory is given for characters)
-difficulty suddenly jumps towards the end (challenges are good but a curve > a spike)
clarification:
*the time limits are easy to meet but they can ruin the fun for players who like freedom
**no sprint mode and vehicles are slow as well
***escort quests are annoying due to NPC programming (pathing, decision-making, etc.)
TLDR: I can't recommend this game to anyone who thinks the above points would bother them.
These points of contention can be subjective and if they wouldn't bother you, then you might still enjoy the game. I personally don't enjoy time limits, as they psychologically make everything feel like a chore (e.g. there's a big difference between having to finish a book by 3 o'clock tomorrow for a college assignment and being able to read a book at your own leisure). The weapon durability also felt like Zelda where your Deku Stick breaks after you get in a few whacks (I love Zelda but that kind of breakability doesn't feel right in a game like this). Feel free to disagree, but ad hominem attacks will be deleted. Present a legitimate argument and I will show you respect in return.

Black The Fall is a game developed by Sand Sailor Studio and published by Square Enix under their indie company name Square Enix Collective
Black The Fall was an interesting game to play especially when it came to the ending which I won't spoil in this review, however, this game is far from perfect and could do with some polishing here and there
The world of Black The Fall is beautifully done and terrifying at the same time and reminds me pretty much of Playdead's sombre and terrifying; Inside. Everything's beautifully and stylishly detailed and is a real treat for history buffs who will definitely have a good time spotting the various historical references the game makes. However, I did notice some janky animations here and there, but overall, the world Sand Sailor Studio created is believable and wonderfully sombre
The gameplay of Black The Fall mixes platforming with puzzle solving, and even thoug some of the puzzles are not that hard, they're not too easy either. The game doesn't hold your hand at all, so you'll need to learn the ropes, which can mean dying a few times...
The game also throws in more than a few mechanics into the mix while also constantly reshuffling the way the player is supposed to use these said mechanics, which made the game not fall into the usual boring platforming genre
Black The Fall was a definite surprise! I personally loved the minimalism of the game’s bleak aesthetics and I think the developers nailed perfectly the oppressive atmosphere of a totalitarian regime
I can understand the game's mixed reception as to it's short length, janky animations and somewhat eazy-ish puzzles especially towards the end. But the game took an interesting twist to what the game is based on and the totalitarian regime that once was in history. I recommend getting Black The Fall either when it's on sale, with a permanent price drop or given to you for free and I think you won't be dissapointed!
