I just finished it. Being a Romanian myself (yes, I bought the game partly to support Romanian indie game developers) I was intrested to see how a game would fit into the world of the totalitarian regime that we used to live in (although in the game is slightly exagerrated). I am not disappointed - the world is nicely built, the game looks great, but I feel the characters / textures are a bit on the low quality side, as if no anti-aliasing was applied.
From the first few screens you'll be slaped in the face with the utter resemblance between this game and Oddworld. Heck, it's even about the same thing - "normal" being trying to escape from a factory; I was suprised the guards didn't sneer when they shoot you, just like the slugs in Oddword. However, it quickly turns to "puzzle platforming" so the resemblance fades away. That being said - I'm not a bit expert on puzzle platformers, so this game made me scratch my head a few times (read: puzzles are sometimes hard). The controls are a bit clunky in the beginning (keyboard player here) and it feels like the character is not responding properly at times, but you get used pretty quicly.
Warning - the finale is tear jerking, especially for someone who lived the days of the Romanian revolution 27 years ago. As a nitpick, I find the voice acting of the crowd a bit weird, missing the usual crowd murmurs, shouts and whisles. as if everything was happening inside inside a recording studio not in a crowded plaza.
4/5, I highly recommend it!

developed by
, a Romanian game development team and it was published on Steam this year on 11th of July by
.
The developer has been working on the game since 2014, when it was successfully funded over Kickstarter.
The game has a lot of common features with inside; it is a monochromatic side-scrolling puzzle-platformer, where your unknown protagonist is dropped in a massive industrialised world full of traps with almost no context or explanations.
, an interpretation of a Romanian communist dystopia, filled with more or less obvious metaphors and symbols, where hundreds of malnourished people are forced to work, supervised by obese overseers and security cameras that will trigger machineguns at your smallest mistake.
Early on you'll be able to acquire a laser pointer from one of the overseers, that can be used to trigger the elevator, to take control of other workers or just to open doors.
Alongside your trusty pointer, you'll acquire a new friend; a robotic bug, that will help you solve many puzzles. Your new friend will follow your along your journey, but you can also control him with the laser pointer.
Most of the puzzles only have one solution, and you must find it using your trusty laser and a hand of help from your new friend, the robot bug. Failing to find the solution to the puzzle will likely result in your death, fortunately the game's checkpoint system is very forgiving and you won't lose much progress. The puzzles are not mind-bending, more of a trial and error style and if you manage to get stuck it's mostly because you're missing something, often something with which you an interact. Anyways there is always a sense of satisfaction when you finally work out the solution, and you're able to push forward, further and further away from the factory.
The achievements can be easily unlocked in a single playtrough; four of them are unlocked for reaching certain points in the game, while five of them are unlocked by finding hidden safe places where civilians have gathered, and the last achievement is unlocked by sitting on the very first bicycle untill the ticker counts down to 9000.

This review comes from the perspective of someone who didn't play this game when it's hype was going strong about a decade ago and who has managed to avoid being fully spoiled on all plot details. I also did not experience the crashing issues that some seem to be having, so I can't speak to that matter (I think it may have crashed once, and it might have even been caused by Steam when it happened).
+ The remastered version does a decent job of bringing the game's graphics up to something close to current gen or at least the generation prior. Graphics and the underwater atmosphere were a major selling point of this game when it first came out and, although not nearly as attention grabing as it might have been back in the day, you still very much get the sense of being in an underwater city, complete with glimpses of flora and fauna and the occassional leak. I found very few things that broke that immersion. Sounds and occasional but strategically-placed music tracks are also used to excellent effect.
+ The plot is the sort where you walk into a post-apcolyptic world (on a smaller scale than, say, Fallout) and must attempt to piece together what happened, in this case with the assistance of a "mission control"-type guide who claims to need your help to escape. The famous plot twist with Andew Ryan is suitably impactful and should be cause for thought days after finishing the game (if you managed to avoid being spoiled on the plot for this long, anyway).
- The final boss fight and the ending were both a little weak and didn't feel all that well thought out. Sadly, the earlier plot twist was far more interesting. It's also possible to lose interest mid-game before the big reveal due to some uneven pacing without much happening.
+The idea of plasmids as unlockable special abilities was interesting and allowed a certain degree of character customization, although there could have been some tweaking done here as certain abilties definitely seemed far more useful than others.
- I would not recommend playing through the harder difficulties unless you are deadset on getting achivements...it's the type of game that adds "challenge" by upping enemy damage and by making them bullet sponges...rather than feel challenged you will feel cheated when you get one-shot after shooting a splicer in the head, from behind, and sometimes multiple times.
OVERALL RATING:  I was pretty satisfied once I finished this game, although I wish the ending was a little less anti-climatic. Overall, I give it 8.0 out of 10.0 (B-)

Avoid this game. The Sea Dogs/Age of Pirates games are fantastic. This however, was developed by masochists with no families or jobs.
First of all, you have a tutorial that takes around 6-8 hours with a guide, I say with a guide because without a walkthrough you will find yourself emerging from the tutorial island with no money and a trashy ship. A certain quest needs to be started early on, and then finished right before you buy your first ship, so you can have enough money to do much of anything. Also, be sure to do quests in order, and in a timely fashion, should you fail to do so, you will hurt yourself for the early game.
The tutorial island doesn't teach you anything, it just holds you back and forces a challenging scenario like in Age of Pirates 2 CoAS. However, once you emerge from said island... it doesn't get any easier.
Your ship is crap. Rats eat most of your weapons and cargo. Pirates are not only much more plentiful than previous games, but incredibly aggressive. The later quests put you on a time limit, and suffer from the tutorial islands' godawful style of playing things in order, on time. Miss a mission and you miss a companion or useful weapon. Take to long doing what you want, and you can FAIL the main campaign.
This isn't an open world sailing game at all. Somehow the developers managed to turn what was an open ended sandbox, morrowind-esque sid meier' Pirates! clone into a game where you have to figure out what the developers are forcing you to do. Really, its not much different than something like Myst at the end of the day.
Basically, this is by far the worst in the series. Is it worth ten dollars? Not really. Go to
and spend twenty dollars to get Age of Pirates 2 City of Abandoned Ships. Far superior, and with the Gentleman of Fortune mod, infinately replayable. Or, head over to Pirates Ahoy! forums and learn about your options regarding Sea Dogs 2: Pirates of the Carribbean, which is old, but excellent, and with the New Horizons mod, easily the best in the series.
TL;DR: Developers are the descendents of people who where given a potatoe, and a rifle with one bullet, and told to charge across a river and die. Only masochists should waste their time here. Go get Age of Pirates 2 City of Abandoned Ships instead.

First off; let me just say it is NOT NECESSARY TO GET ARRESTED AND LOOSE ALL STUFF AT THE BEGINNING.
This game would be a great game of piracy, and/or mercantilism - whatever would be your cup of tea. While it has a certain degree of railroading, it is also possible to play it sandbox and just sail around being a jolly roger in search of bounty and glory.
There's just a few things that irritates and one thing that makes the game near unplayable.
Let me just first underline that the sea battles, while a challenge, are well executed, give an air of realism, and that you actually can sail around the world in first or third person view - rather than reverting to a map mode.
And that despite now being more than 10 years old the graphics still hold up, and it is in my opinion the nicest open-world pirate game available (Next to Sid Meyer's Pirate Gold - not the 2004 edit, the 90s ones - and I need not say that the graphics of those games have not aged well..). There was a time when I would just set my ship to sail along the coast, and have the game run in the background while I did stuff IRL.
Also - you not only hire a crew - you have a range of specialists - which is cool. This is a feature in other pirate games as well, but they are mostly third person strategic affairs - which this is not.
Also, rare in our time, the game is a challenge. No quest markers, you actually need to take notes - morrowind style, and this is a concious choice made by the developers. Which I find a nice change from the incredible hand-holding of Bethesda and their ilk. !This and that quest marker in your ♥♥♥♥ing face! However, this could be better executed, and choosing to have rhetorics as a character specialty is a waste of your real-life energy.
Which brings me to the negatives:
The game is developed by russians, the translation is so-so, which makes for some interesting and usually incredibly rude dialogue. These dialogues are usually also just with 2 options. Some insulting line, or an opt-out - also usually an insult. This I can take, we are pirates after all.
Worse are the controls. You'd better select fencing as a speciality, because that is a nightmare. These horrible keys also affect the sea battles, but not so adversely. The range of actions are at the same time quite extensive, which is streneous. There is way to train your fighting skills, only through actual fighting, which can of course provoke the guards of the area, which will get you killed. This is the only game which I would consider selecting the easiest option, or even cheating. It is extremely unforgiving.
The game lacks a tutorial - but there are some online. They also suffer from bad translation and individualized experience of those who wrote them, so use them IN COMBINATION, with a critical eye. I also suspect certain quests need to be executed in a certain order, or you will not gain access to other quests - which can break your save (at the start of the game). I was fortunate in this regard, but there were 2 quests I was never offered because the order in which I talked to certain people. So be very aware (especially because of the abscence of quest markers). Also, note that it is NOT NECESSARY TO GET ARRESTED AND LOOSE ALL STUFF AT THE BEGINNING. Just be patient and ask around.
There is no built-in edit capability, although a fix has been made. Also there are no mods for this game as far as I am aware. While the graphics hold, the selection of ship types are sufficient, I imagine some would love to mod clothes, armor and generally stuff. This would be exceptionally hard.
Finally, and what I consider a game-breaker is the way the game starts. A tutorial of sorts I guess, but it is incredibly lengthy (took me a day first time, and the tutorial walk-throughs are essential for this), and it ends up in a scene where I have to face down 2 pirates that both have more health, more strength and better fencing skills than me, and they can also fire their guns. So you can imagine how well that turns out.. So I haven't made it off the island.
How do I know the sea battles are nice, how can I know that sailing into the sunset is a beautiful experience in this game? Once I had a ripped edition of this game, where the entire island was cut out of the game. Yeah - why do I have to suffer through it? Why did the game designers make the game this way?
So if you consider yourself A REAL ♥♥♥♥ING HARDCORE SEADOG, then you are welcome to try it, and pass the island, and you will be rewarded by a great game. But you may save yourself some time and convert the game files to be cheat compatible, 'cause you can't get past the pirates. It is impossible.

Yup, you’re looking at a depressing monochromatic art palette, the only other dominant colours being yellow and red, for fiery explosions and blood respectively. The dark visuals excellently portray just how dark and sinister the game theme is, though at times can be more of a hindrance as NPCs and objects start to merge into the background. You’ll often at times struggle to notice minute details in the game world, such as the dude pointing a 12 gauge shotgun at you who you just ran past. The black and white style is not for everyone, but it’s done with intention.
I need to say this right off the bat, the soundtrack is AMAZING and fits perfectly with Hatred. You know that sort of game where you start it up for the first time, hear the menu music and think ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ did this game just speak to me??”, well this is that sort of soundtrack you can expect.
The score is dark, moody and twisted, with the opening menu music letting you know exactly what’s in store for you. The music throughout the campaign entails a great sense of progression, as earlier levels quietly spew out depressing music with creepy undertones, then gradually getting more upbeat and chaotic as the final levels release bombastic crescendos as you pass the point of no return in your genocide crusade, with the grand finale blasting you with organ church-esque music as you reflect on your blood-ridden journey.
The soundtrack has been extremely well thought and I can’t stress how well it ties in with the game theme and level design. For those interested, the talent behind the music also composes for The Witcher series (fantastic score in those!).
There really isn’t much to the controls. You can run around gunning down anyone in your path, switch to a slower and slightly cumbersome fine-aim mode, or karate-kick people and throw grenades. Let it be known that the controls aren’t as fluid as you would like and you will encounter problems like getting stuck in doorways or having difficulty judging line of sight to your target. The controls definitely need a while to get used to, and even still it’s far from perfect.
Surprisingly, there is much more depth and strategy involved than you would think. Sure, during earlier segments you feel like the Terminator as it seems no one is capable of bringing you down, until you encounter SWAT and the army, who will hunt you, flank you and kill you. Hatred is brutally hard, and you will die, restart, and die many times until you formulate strategies, know when to retreat and how to set up killzones.
You can perform executions on people in order to regain health, which shows a graphic animation of your character shooting/stabbing or stamping on the hapless individual in question. The animations get dull after the 50th time so thankfully you can switch it off, however sadly that turns off all the cool and cheesy one –liners the character spews out.
There are only a handful of levels in the campaign, with each getting progressively more and more difficult. Each map is heavily populated by hundreds of NPCs going about their daily lives, and it’s up to you to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥up and lay waste to anything that moves. You generally have to kill a certain number of innocent people and defeat waves of various law enforcement agencies before being allowed to progress to the next map. You get a limited number of respawns which can be increased by doing minor side missions.
Hatred does push the envelope and offers players REAL destructible environments that dynamically alter gameplay. Trapped in a room with low health whilst SWAT is closing in through the front door? Just blow a huge effin' hole in the back wall and escape from there! Spotted a cheeky patrol of officers cleverly hiding in the room next to you? Shoot holes in the walls with your high calibre machinegun allowing you to target the officers in the other room!
This is true destructible environment and not predetermined “I can destroy this glowing wall but not this wall that looks exactly the same but isn't glowing.”
Hatred unfortunately bares inconsistent frame rates during the campaign, much less so during survival mode. Personally it’s not a huge issue with me as it’s never dipped below the uncomfortable realms of the minus 20 mark. Still, if you’re a 60fps freak than you need to check to see if your specs are on par with Hatred’s requirements.
The answer is sadly, no. I could blabber on all day about how the media brainwashes you to think a certain way, but if you’re a mature adult you already know that by now. The fact is if you’ve played GTA, Fallout and many other games, you’ve already committed mass murder. Also no one seems to mind that GTA has an unskippable interactive torture scene, whereas Hatred just has you kill and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Nothing to see here, move along.
Also the developers Destructive Creations should be applauded for their marketing the game. They never lied about what their game was about and never tried to sugar coat anything in order for people to buy. They offered a game where you play a mass murderer and can destroy the environment and nothing more. No promise of XX hours, day 1 DLC and the normal♥♥♥♥♥♥♥AAA companies do now days. This is gaming in its purest form and does exactly what it says on the tin.
Hatred is a Sick twisted arcadey game, make no mistake, but it's nothing you haven't done before in a violent video game. Whilst it’s extremely short, has quirky controls and some performance issues, it’s a brilliant game to blow off some steam after a long stressful day at work.

This game brings back lots of childhood memories. All that time spent creating parks and in particular, tons of wild roller coasters. This game is still great even after all these years. I've played this for much longer than my Steam time shows. I've played 1, 2, and 3, and I have to say this and 1 are close in which is my favorite. The gameplay is simple yet fun, I'd recommend picking it up if you can, it's a great way to spend a couple of hours at a time trying to beat yet another scenario.
There's lots of variety in parks and ride in here. Although honestly the two expansion packs didn't add much original stuff, just rethemed rides and lame scenarios that somewhat force you into a box regarding park design. You can also create your own scenarios or download ones that others have made. I'd also recommend adding the UCES expansion, a community expansion that added tons of scenery, a bunch of scenarios, and a few new rides. It might be a little hard to find now as the official site no longer exists, but there are alternate downloads around for it. Just a word of warning, the first time you run a UCES scenario, it will usually crash the game. This is normal as the first time you run the scenario any custom content used in it must be installed. The next time you select the scenario it should run just fine.
If you want to make your own scenarios, you can also pick up some custom rides and themeing that are out there. Amazing Earl and Buggy are two people to look up. There is also a pack that contains almost all the scenarios from RCT1 and its expansions which have been remade for RCT2. Just google "RCT1 scenarios for RCT2" and that should get you something.
Pros:
+Great variety of rides available, including lots of roller coasters
+Various scenario objectives and scenarios for lots of variety
+Low system requirements will run on pretty much any computer
+Lots of extra community content (if you know where to find it)
+Fun way to spend a few hours
Cons (These are mostly nitpicky):
-Scenario editor is fairly limited, making a park that has pre-built rides is a bit round-a-bout and not the best way
-Expansions don't offer much in terms of new rides, just a bunch of rethemeing
-Scenario selection screen can get cluttered/hard to navigate if you have lots of scenarios installed
-No career/progression. All scenarios are available from the start unlike 1 & 3.
A final note, some people may have issues running this on newer machines. I have a 64 bit Windows system, and I have no problem running it at all. A demo can probably be found online, install that and run it before buying to check that it will work on your system.
Overall 10/10, a classic that still stands the test of time.

Wow, I did it! I actually said I don't recommend this game. In my books, Beyond Earth is a 6.5 out of 10 and not worth the time invested to play it. I've put a ton of time in to try and like it, but it just doesn't add anything to the previous editions of Civ.
When was the last time you never built industrial production buildings because they are noisy and ugly and a detriment to a cutural / artistic society? When was the time you never built financial institutions because your society was driven by technological innovation? Tell me the time you never actually built buildings because you were a nomatic race (units had building functions).
Despite what faction you are, despite what Civ game you play, or any of the options you select in any of the Civ games, building you city feels exactly the same. In fact, you could actually fill your queue with the exact same production no matter what options or factions you selected, and the game would essentially unfold in the same fashion.
In Beyond Earth, there really isn't anything that I think was really well done. The tech tree is different, but none of the techs actually change gameplay with the exception of adding spying in one tech (and that just makes it manditory to get Computing ASAP).
There is so much they could have done in this game, but really it's just another Civ game. Beyond Earth is only worth buying if you're new to Civ games or a dedicated fan who can never get enough Civ.

OVERVIEW
This is an epic game that makes you become a citizen trying to survive the harsh war. You will make decisions that will help or hender your chances of survival. Will you live by a moral? Will you kill the poor elderly people that have lots of food and meds? That is for you to decide.
BREAK DOWN
Decisions: The way the choices you make affect the game is amazing. For example, if you steal something, people will say, "It was either them or us." or "Has this war turned us into looters." It is amazing. But thats not all, helping people out when they knock also has good and bad outcomes.
Moral: The character dynamic for morale is great. (From what I can tell) The more you steal, the more you kill, and the more of your people die, the more peoples sadness increases. They can even get to a point of depression.
Survival: Foods, meds, bandages, materials. Those are the basic things required for your survival. Without food, people will starve and die, without bandages injuries can get lethal, without meds illnesses can get lethal, and without materials you wont be able to make anything. You actually feel stress while managing your stuff.
Other: The graphics are great, the 2-D is an amazing fit for this game, the controls are great once you get use to them, and the character skills are also well planned and well thought out.
ALL IN ALL
All in all, this game is phenominal! All the different aspects are put together to make the perfect combination. This game is an easy 9.5/10 for it's amazing story and in depth roleplaying. Aswell as it's ability to be played for hours on end. I recomend this game to whoever is in to Survival RPGs and has tons of time to spare.

I recently finished Bioshock for the first time. I decided to go with the remastered version mainly because of the updated visuals. I had heard a lot of great things about this game, some even calling it the greatest video game of all time. Now, having played the game I fully agree, Bioshock is no doubt one of the best games I've ever played.
The story, which is mainly told in the form of audio diaries, is unlike anything I've experienced before. It's dark and disturbing yet beautiful and euphoric. The voice acting and audio are second to none and the visuals holds up well for a 10 year old game with updated graphics. The gameplay is so much fun and extremely satisfying with many different weapons and ways to approach an objective. Honestly it's hard to describe just how good this game is, I can simply urge everyone to try this game in order to understand just what I mean. It's really a must-buy.
The only couple of complaints I have with the game is that sometimes when attempting to listen to an audio diary, there's a little too much sound around you which leads to some of the monologues in the diary becoming hard to hear. I also encountered a bug in which, without going to much into detail as it's story related, a splicer I was supposed to photograph spawned and then dissapeared. Simply reloading an older save solved the problem but apparently this bug has been present ever since the original release and one could have hoped that they'd have fixed it in a remastered version.
Nevertheless, Bioshock is a wonderful game showcasing that video games actually can be a work of art. 10/10
On a sidenote, the game ran wonderfully on my rig (i5-6400 and gtx 1060 6GB). I always had a stable 150-200 fps during gameplay and >400 fps during cutscenes

Sadly, a great initial entry title in a franchise does not always ensue a worthy successor; Bioshock 2 is one such example.
PROS:
- Though still capped, the physics engine seems to render higher than FPS (found in the original Bioshock), rendering combat a relatively easier experience.  However in the eyes of PC veteran who are used to seeing 60+ FPS, Bioshock is still subpar.
- Character models are more realistic (compared to the semi-cartoonish ones from the original Bioshock), which is fitting for a supposedly dark, confined of a horror environment.
- Certain creative, though not necessarily improved weapons.
- The last few levels are original; they do not feel repetitive compared to the final levels of the original BS.
CONS:
- Sound is largely broken in this game.  Apparently this only happened after Patch 1.4 (ie Minerva's Den), but was never fixed in current version of 1.5.  Sound effects of weapons are muffled at best.  Various vending machines refuse to produce respective sound effects on a random basis.  Background announcements stutters and fades without apparent reasons.  Scene-triggered background music loops infinitely despite said scence being long over.  These audio glitches severely breaks the immersion the game attempts to create.
- Main game was shorter.  It took me 32 hours to finish the main game, then 8 hours to finish Minvera's Den DLC.  In comparison, the original BS took me 43.
- In-comprehensive key mapping for the PC version.  I had to manually edit a .INI file just to bind a key to refill EVE.  Imagine playing Diablo, but without a hotkey to replenish Mana.  You get the idea.  To me, this is simply lack of care for the PC crowd.
- Random crashes, sometimes post (thankfully not during) saving.
Bioshock will likely remain as one of the best games I've played in the past 2 decades; unfortunately its sequel leaves much to be desired.

This was my first Hitman game. I bought it imagining I'd get something like Dishonored or Deus Ex where you use your abilities to create a route to success. But now I think that deep down this is really a puzzle game, where you find a pre-written route that the devs put there for you rather than inventing your own.
Allow me an example:
I need to get on the roof of a hotel. There's a manhole down to sewers on the left, the main entrance in the middle, and a guarded gateway on the right. When I approach those things various light up to use: the ladder down to the sewers, the door into the lobby, the repair guy I could maybe mug for his uniform, etc.
But on the far left there's a fence blocking an alley, with bins next to it at a convenient height for clambering over the fence, and a fire escape up the side of the building on the far side of the fence, and none of it is guarded. So, I approach the bins to climb the fence, only I can't -- there's no "press E to climb on this" lighting up when I get close. If this game had physics based bottom-up gameplay like Dishonoured, I would use the jump/climb buttons to get over anything within my height capability. But it's a top down scripted game, so I can't climb a thing if the level designer didn't see fit to put a "climbable"flag on that thing.
In its way this is like an old school point and click puzzle adventure. You have to guess and experiment to find (one of the) answer(s) the devs envisaged. I'm not a fan of that so I'll give it thumbs down, but anybody who is and also likes stealth/assassin games might like it quite a lot. Apart from being fundamentally not my kind of game, it seems quite polished.

Bioshock 2 is viewed as the black sheep of the "Shock" franchise, created as a cheap cash-in sequel by a different development team that crafted the first Bioshock.  But beyond the initial impressions from fans and critics lies a very competent game, that in some spots actually outshines the original.
-The story is just as good, if not better, than the original.  Most people disliked the story because it didn't add much depth to the mythos of Rapture, but the story in Bioshock 2 is much more personal and is more about the citizens of Rapture than the city itself.
-The gameplay is vastly improved.  Plasmids and Guns are duel wielded, making combining them in combat much easier.
-Mechanics are streamlined, not simplified.  Gene tonics no longer have a type and can just be equipped, assuming you have the slots.  Hacking is now done in real time on a simplified  mini-game.  Even the research mechanic is reworked to use a video-camera that gives you more research points depending on how well you combo your plasmids/weapons.  There are also new weapons and plasmids that are fun to use and don't feel gimmicky.
-The art design is top notch.  The level designers have fun showing what rapture would look like with 10 more years of rust and decay.
-More moral decisions beyond "Save/Kill Little Sister".  The game also uses your decisions to inform the last act of the game and the ending.
-Final "boss" fight is much better than the one in the first game.
-The first hour of the game stinks. Period.  After you get into the first real level, the game begins to open up and let you start having fun.
-Some of the new characters have to be hand waved into existence, especially since they were supposed to be around before the first game but are clearly never mentioned in the first game.
-Levels are much more linear and not as large as in the first game. There are few sidepaths, but mostly you'll be running from point A to B without backtracking.
-There are a few new enemies but I would have liked more enemy variety.
-You can use little sisters to gather Adam, but you have to protect them as they do it.  Most people hated the escort mission from the first game, so it's something to be aware of.   I personally enjoyed this part of the game due to the multitude of alternate amunition that makes setting up traps fun.
-It's clear that there were some significant rewrites late in development, some characters introduced at the start of the game are simply left out of the rest of the game's plot.
-The FoV is very low and requires ini-rebinding to reset it every time you launch the game.  The problem is going into ironsights also resets the FoV, making you have to press your bound key to reset your FoV every time.
-Occasional issues with audio cutting out if there were too many sounds are playing at once.

Ignore people saying the game is a cheap cash in: the gameplay is better and arguably so is the story.  Although there are fewer levels than in the original, the game actually took me more hours to beat than the first game: around 14 hours.  It’s also interesting that a lot of the story beats and themes end up being used in Bioshock Infinite (although I’m sure Ken Levine hates to admit it).
Minerva's Den is also an excellent add-on to the base game, and lasts around 3 hours.  I'd recommend playing through Bioshock 2 on hard mode if you've played many shooters before, the difficulty curve stays pretty good throughout the entire base game.  Minerva's Den is a bit harder on the same difficulty however, so keep that in mind.

This is the 4th game of the Putt-Putt series by Humonguous Entertainment.
Target audience is children up to pre-school or kindergarten (3-6), or for those that played this as a child back in the mid 90's and wish to go on a nostalgia trip, or for people like me that played a Putt-Putt game befored but never experienced certain ones (this game for example).
This is the first Putt-Putt game where puzzles change in each playthrough at the start of the game, whether it's finding Pep in the Medieval time or lost in the desert in the Western time, getting your history report from a dinosaur's feet or from a king, recover your calculator locked in a chest in a ghost town or from a wizard who uses it to make gold from stone, or your lunchbox from a prospector or from a future museum of ancient artifacts. (Just to name a few examples I've experienced while playing the game a few times and getting the card drops.) I'm under the belief you'll find one item in a random time zone with a fixed problem and solution, but not possible to find two in one location.
However, some of the puzzles that lead up to the items are "click it again to instantly solve it" instead of using an item (Saves the Zoo has this, but with only one puzzle that you already worked up to prior) that I fear the developers were having a hard time making creative ideas to solutions, especially with a lot of possible combination of problems, but thankfully there's very low quantity of that.
This does introduce history very roughly to children, like very basic stuff to possibly get them interested while at the same time not overwhelm them, or possibly be interested in sci-fi with the Future time zone and the whole time travel concept. Although, this game isn't good for making history reports as it doesn't offer much facts, let alone information, of the Dinosaurs, Medieval, and Western eras. (In other words, not good for homework or education, but still fun.)
Beyond the main story and such, like all H.E. games there's silly stuff to click in the background that any child, those that are a child in heart, easily ammused, or very good at improve for entertainment that they may enjoy.
It takes roughly 30 minutes to go through the game, depending on what playthrough you get and if you don't scene skip (esc if possible), but again this is more for children so it could be longer for them, if they don't get easily distracted by the background sillyness they stumble upon in which cause would be even longer.
Feel free to get this in a bundle (Putt-Putt or H.E. bundles) if you enjoyed these games as a kid and wish to relive them, or have kids of your own and they enjoyed one of the Putt-Putt games.

Heads up, this review is LONG. There will be a TL;DR at the bottom.
This game is a gem, covered in a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you've read negative reviews for the game I hate to say that most of them are very much accurate. This game is very unwieldy, hard to learn, harder to master, and really doesn't teach you anything. The closest this game has to a tutorial is essentially a few hours of being stuck on one island doing small quests to make enough money to buy a small ship. Unfortunately, this means you likely won't know if you want to keep the game or not until after the refund period has passed.
So before I go on, you need to be absolutely sure you want the game before you buy it, because you won't be able to refund it.
Now that that is out of the way, I want to address all the things I love about this game:
It is, for the most part, a sandbox game very similar to that of Mount & Blade. You can do what you want and do it over a big area (the entire West Indies). There is a "main" quest, but you could completely ignore it if you didn't want to do it, as you'll still witness almost all the game has to offer without it. However, there are certain events and areas you'll miss if you skip the main quest, so you should get to it eventually.
As for the actual gameplay, it is phenomenal. I love Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag for its amazing naval combat, and I can honestly say this game does it better. The naval fights are very action-packed and intense, bigger ships have more cannons that deal more damage and fire farther, you have different ammunition to choose from, and you can even get into large battles at the sea. Furthermore, if you choose to board instead of sinking a ship outright, you've got even more fighting in store. I can only praise the naval combat, I really can't think of anything wrong with it.
The regular combat is a bit different, especially since there is no tutorial to actually teach you how to swing your sword (unless I missed it or something). It is not nearly as straightforward as the naval combat, and if you don't know what you're doing, you'll easily die to the first enemy you encounter. However it is very fun and intense, and some fights can go on for quite a while depending on how strong your opponent is along with healing items. You won't just be cutting through enemies like you would be in Mount & Blade, each fight can easily end with a sword through your chest and a man marking your grave.
On to the more guided sections of the game, there are a plethora of quests you can take on to fill your coffers when you aren't strong enough to go raiding fleets for gold and silver cargo. Most quests consist of you seeking out a specific ship or some gang of bandits, but many quests are much deeper, especially once you get into the main questline. A lot of effort was clearly put into these quests to make fun and engaging gameplay, and there are really only a few quests I haven't liked. I'm sure I haven't even done all of them yet in 120 hours of gameplay.
As for getting strong enough to take on these flotillas bearing gold and silver, you start out as a weak, inexperienced man who is merely a virgin to Caribbean life. This game uses a dynamic levelling system, where your skills get better as you use them, rather than just increasing whenever you level up. You must improve your skills if you want to get anywhere, as when you start out you'll barely be able to take on the smallest of ships and weakest of dueling opponents.
There are lots of other things to do, but I feel I've covered all my bases for the sake of this review. Now on to the negatives:
To start off, the game is Russian, and this is an English translation of it, and sometimes that translation is really bad. The quests I haven't liked have been quests I flat out couldn't understand due to terrible translation, and I've even come across some segments of dialogue that are still in Russian.
Speaking of quests, you HAVE to pay attention to dialogue. A lot of times your character will simply omit important information in the quest journal, so if you weren't paying attention you could easily get stuck and end up failing the quest. This is especially true with the main questline, so make sure you are paying attention to the dialogue.
While I have been praising this game for the gameplay, I need to further emphasize how unwieldy the game is and how it completely fails to teach you the mechanics of the gameplay going in. You are very much alone in figuring out how to play, so I recommend you check out guides for the game. I myself have been frequenting the forums to find out a lot of things that the game should really be explaining. This is a dealbreaker for a lot of people, and that is something I can perfectly understand. If you aren't willing to take the time to learn how to play the game, then this game is definitely not worth the purchase.
Along with the unwieldy controls and lack of tutorial, this game is very unforgiving. If you die, you are dead, and you better have saved recently. I highly recommend to keep as many saves as possible, and NEVER overwrite a save file. If you get into a really tight spot and you don't have an earlier save you can revert to, you'll likely have to end up starting over. Which means you have to go through the awful, hours long "tutorial" again.
I understand that the negative aspects of the game seem to outweigh the positive ones, and that's where a lot of the negative reviews for this game come from, but I have to say the opposite is true. This has quickly become one of my favorite games, but when I started out I was extremely frustrated with it. All I can really say is give the game time. If you are planning on buying this game you can't expect to be able to get a refund, once you get it you're in for the long haul.
TL;DR: This game is like eating at an excessively fancy restaurant. The menu is confusing and you have to wait a long time for your food to show up, but once it does you've got a 5-star meal. The game is really fun if you can just figure it out and really get into it.

It fulfills a niche, but I couldn't get into this game. Everything feels janky and odd, and some characters just feel waaaay too oppressive to have any fun playing against. When someone is a hyper-mobile healer with heavy CC, defense abilities, aoe heals, and decent damage... Well, you're not going to have a time. Some characters are just outright better than others, and others are just unnecessarily complex. 2 paragraphs for a skill just to say 'charge forward, do x damage and stun for x.x seconds' is kind of ridiculous once talents are mixed in, and it all just gets kind of complex for something so fast-paced. The idea of everything being skillbased with even basic attacks being skillshots is cool and all, but sometimes your bullets feel janky or the physics just don't move how you expect. Definitely something you need to get used to, but you'll miss a lot of shots just misjudging how fast your attacks are and how they'll move as you and your opponent move. Not only that but matchmaking doesn't especially shine either, especially since the default is 2v2 in a game clearly geared more towards 3v3.

The game is boasting that it's from 2012. Well it was completed that year but don't be fooled! The game can be traced back to Pirates of the Caribbean (2003) a. k. a. Corsairs 2 or Sea Dogs 2 and manages to look and feel much worse. TEHO in essence is a stand-alone DLC for Corsairs 3 a. k. a. Sea Dogs: Caribbean Tales (2006) which also was a huge step back compared to PotC. The developers tried to make a joke with game's abbreviation: PO:TEHO (PO standing for Pirates Odyssey) which looks like a transliterated russian word "fun" but it only makes them look even worse 'cause this game is anything but fun.
The first quest is atrocious. I couldn't leave the starting island for 6 bloody hours! And that's after playing the previous 2 games for at least a thousand hours. In PotC you can complete a similar tutorial and learn all the basics in 5 minutes or skip it and learn the game as you go. In TEHO they make backtracking a key game mechanic. You will be going the same paths for hours in a series of lazy uninspired fetch quests.
Naval battles are ridiculously brutal. You start with such low stats that it may take a couple of hours to capture the weakest ship. And let's not forget about "glitched" ships that you can only sink by aiming manually or by boarding. I'm pretty sure that it was easier to become a real pirate than play this game. It kicks in after about 100 hours once you reach decent skill points in Navigation and Cannons and becomes more playable but those hours will chase you in nightmares.
Music is a huge disappointment. I still listen PotC soundtrack sometimes but TEHO's music is the most generic and annoying thing I've heard in years.
Overall TEHO is a bug infested mess with hugely reduced playability to make it more "realistic" - yeah, good luck making it to another island in time while the wind is blowing in opposite direction. Also you could choose a female playable character in Corsairs 3. In SD: TEHO you can't, which is a pity 'cause you're stuck looking at guy's rear for many hours.

Ok, I have to mention it early : I was really into the previous title, Age of pirates 2 : city of abandoned ships. I spent hours on it. This game is based on the same engine, with the same gameplay which I already mastered, so I was not stopped by its inherent difficulty. For all the good time spent on AOP, I felt compelled to share a review on this game :
.
Yes, it has a really steep learning curve ; but the (very) long tutorial and main quests are really more informative than the previous title.
n°1 flaw : Yet... understanding the basics of the game is not enough. Even with that, you will die. Die from your choices. Die from a stupid mistake in battle. Losing is not a bad thing, but the game is unbalanced (land combat mostly) and not flexible at all in that regard. It's not
losing is dying. No prison. You will not be marooned. You will not be rescued.
1) But this series is unique, and this is the most complete opus : a good pirate simulation, the hardcore one. It's a really engaging rpg in the style of
, you sail through the caribbean on a global map from port to port, you trade, you can sail for one nation, you can be a pirate, a smuggler, explore islands for treasure or derelict... You have lots of possibilities, lots of random generated mini quests,
2) The sailing is sloooow, but you can speed time. It's probably one of the most realistic sailing and naval fighting experience, even if the controls are arcadey. You have strategic options, you can give orders to your fleet. It in as unforgiving as the rest, but very rewarding when you master it.
3) You have a real crew, you have to take care of it and your officers. You won't do anything by yourself. It's very good at managing a ship and making you feel like a captain.
4) The storilyne is there and compelling enough for this type of game, it gives a good sense of purpose.
Well... This series was released at a time when pirate games were out of fashion. It has long been the only option for this quite realistic experience. It is clumsy, assembled with glue and nails on top of it, but it is really
. Now, things are moving, we have better productions coming. But it is still dear to my heart. and for the price, I suggest you give it a try!

Homefront's multiplayer, seems primed to be just another also-ran right from the get-go. With only two core game modes (Team Deathmatch and Capture and Hold) playable in two variations, the options are few. The loadout screen will be instantly familiar to anyone who has played a Call of Duty game in the past few years, and the online conflicts play out between the KPA and the US Army (rather than the ragtag freedom fighters from the campaign), so the intriguing setting is little more than window dressing. Though its inspirations are obvious, Homefront does a good job of appropriating tried-and-true mechanics. Earning experience, leveling up, increasing your arsenal, and unlocking new infantry abilities (read: perks) is satisfying, and the maps allow a decent range of viable battlefield strategies.

But you start the game having to complete 6 quests before you can buy your ship.  The quests aren't always straightforward, and it's the only way to make the money required to buy your ship.  If you complete all of them, you'll have 60,000 pesos, far more than enough to buy your ship, provision it, and hire a crew and navigator (necessary because you don't have the sailing skill to manage your starting ship).  If you miss a quest or two, you might come up short of cash.
The various quests range from fairly simple to overly fiddly, and if you make some wrong decisions you can fail a quest or get paid a lot less.  Expect to save and load often, but do not overwrite a save, always save in a new slot... otherwise the game can get unstable (according to the developers).  You can add an explanation to the name of the save game, which is quite helpful, and you can delete older saves when they're no longer needed, but keep saves at strategic points "just in case".
You'll have to sail to another island, do a few quests there, then sail back to the original island before the "sandbox" version of the game is unlocked.  Once it's unlocked, the game is a lot more fun.  All the starting quests function as a sort of extended tutorial, so you really need to do them anyway.
There are guides and walkthroughs to help you with the quests, not only the initial ones but quests later in the game.  These are essential reading.  Some of these are better than others, so keep reading.
You may find yourself starting a new game a few times until you learn your way through.  That's ok, the quests are a lot easier the second or third time through and figuring out the optimum path through the quests can be a lot of fun.
One major drawback is that there is no README file or manual with the English version of the game.  I've written a guide that should provide all the information you need, so check it out, and I've posted more information on the forums, including my own walkthroughs of the initial quests.
Even with all the problems, I'm really enjoying the game.  Even if I do use colorful language fairly often. :D
-------
Ok, time for an update.
I've finally finished the sandbox portion of the game.  The timer on the saved game says I've got almost 160 hours at this point, with 530 hours total in Sea Dogs because I started a lot of games.  This is the first time I've finished the sandbox.
It turns out the tutorial quests, before you get to the sandbox, are really necessary.  You do a bit of everything that's in the rest of the game, and it prepares you for the sandbox.  But it would be nice if these were spread out a bit more and you got your ship a lot earlier.
The sandbox is pure open play.  You can do pretty much whatever you want.  You have 3 game months to earn 1 million pesos.  It gives you time to level up your character, build up your skills, find a good set of officers, and hopefully find a good ship or two.  The sandbox is a lot of fun, and it's exactly what I was looking for in a pirate game.
The tutorial is one game, the sandbox is another, and now I'm starting the story quests, and there are 3, possibly with some branch paths as well.  This will be 3 more games, and playing the story quest is different from playing the sandbox.  You'll see what I mean when you get there.
By this time, I've "won" the sandbox and there's not much left to do there except start a new game.  The balance is just about perfect.
I've been told that the story quests are very good, with lots of depth.  I really didn't know what the game was about until I got to this point.  Some of the forum posts about the story line quests made it sound like something I didn't really want to do, but I'm quite looking forward to this now.  Getting to know the game makes a big difference.
I don't use colorful language any more, since I've learned to save the game at strategic spots.  :)

Now I see why people didn't really like Homefront. Don't get me wrong, it's NOT a bad game, but it's a disappointing one, especially when you see how much THQ advertised and promoted this game. So what's brought this game down? The singleplayer. First, it's awefully short; you can beat it in 4 hours. But the story, wow, there's such a cool background and the characters are totally relatable. And that's what annoyed me the most. It has such a good premise that you wonder why isn't it any longer. And the gameplay. It's like a typical military shooter. The problem is that it holds your hand WAY TOO MUCH. For example, you'll have to take out certain enemies, and there's an icon on it saying "SHOOT". Well, what else would I do? Blow a kiss to it? The problems of the singleplayer outweighed it's benefits.
Multiplayer fares better. The PC servers are still up, and there's at least one full server on afternoons. It's like a combination of Battlefield and COD. You can use points in-game to purchase things like armor and even vehicles. Maps are quite good too. Ground Control, the main mode, has you capturing certain points, like Domination in Battlefield, only that you can move up to a certain area if one team dominates it, like in the Rush mode in Battlefield.
In summary, Homefront is full-priced game with budget-game quality. Buy it when it's on sale.

Is there anything I could recommend for Homefront? The sound track is good, and the game is mercifully short.
Bad things however are aplenty ranging from a dead story  to bad and broken mechanics.
Story
Firstly the story while a novel one for video games Starts out well paced, but never seems to tell  or have a clear objective till the last level. I didn't even discover my character was a pilot until a good portion into the game. The demonization of the North koreans is well done but then they go and undermine what they had accomplished. They  recreate the nazi's then in the middle of the game you sympathise with them during a shooting with some crazy conservative nutjobs. Showing that the only thing more evil than the nazi's are white republicans. Pretty much in 4 hours (game length) you come to hate the monsters then feel sorry for them, then are left with no decent villians and pretty much no reason to fight  other than Murica. Ending it on a bland note. other than the 3rd best thing in the game. THE MAIN CHARACTER DIES.  Great setup but poor delivery.
Characters
Main Character
What you thought this would be you? don't be ridiculous you are just a pilot that does everything but pilot. No this is none other than Captain A-hole. I honestly got done with the game like 10 minutes ago and I have forgotten all of the characters but this guy. You can expect him to simply shout and yell at you and everyone else in the game to do whatever. He feels no compassion for anyone, only rage and vengeance. the second you are suppossed to regroup he will begin yelling at you  to group up as you search for any gun other than the smg. He continues to do this every 20 seconds. It is one of the most irratating things I've seen designed into a video game. Thankfully at the end he finishes his annoying life so I can feel at least some satisfaction out of this game.
The Player Character
You are a Pilot. you are captured by north koreans then broken out by freedom fighters. You are also, apparently, the one and only pilot in this colorado town. You are faceless, and the only time anyone ever talks to you is to make you do labor.
Essentially you play as Sam in the lord of the Rings. Your job, as the ultimate sidekick, is to do all of the things nobody else wants to do. Operate a self driving car that seems to not be able to target vehicles ( but one does it at the end of the game just fine) you operate the sniper rifle as Capt. A-hole walks you through. Here's a question, why doesn't Capt. A-hole do it? He knows what to look for, why train a pilot to snipe on a very important mission. You use the missle launchers and it is always your job to kill everyone with a rocket/EMP launcher, Sniper, Mounted gunners, Jeeps, APC's helicopters, Tanks and whatever they feel like throwing you into. You do in fact operate a helicopter. once. For about 15 minutes. in that time you do get to reinact Mission Impossible for absolutely no reason. You fly through a tunnel because the game won't let you fly over the hill.
On the last level (as a capable pilot) you get to run around with guns and shoot, instead of pilot, cuz that makez zenz. There are dozens of helicopters around and they use you as a foot soldier.
Gameplay
It's like call of duty but all of the controls are a little wobblybubbly feel. never really got used to it. All of the guns shoot really fast and bad guys can take you down with a lucky quick burst. Also don't expect anyone to cover you or kill bad guys. In fact just assume that every grenade thrown will land in your back pocket while being shot at by every concievable person in Colorado. Usually games like these will take away your team mates to show you how much more difficult a situation is with out them. when this game does it, I couldn't tell a difference.
Guns
They suck I found 2 that I liked, the m16 because it's semi auto without a scope, and the m249 because no one knows how to suppress (or really kill anyone) in this game so that's another role I had to fullfill. With all of the special gear and forced sniper sections, screw your 2 gun rule. Guns are random and there are practically no good ammo pick ups till the last level (Practically infinite Lmg ammo) Then you have the issue of not 1 or 2 or even 3 m4 types. You have 4. and you have the ACR on top of that. What is the best part you may ask? None of the ammo is cross compatible. so if you find that beloved m16, you have to find another m16 to restock on ammo. Honestly I blame this on the Captain A-hole. You are a pilot. How are you supposed to know what ammo goes where?
Forced gameplay
At the end of the day this is really what kills and makes this game drag. You have quite literally all of the downsides of a quicktime event without being told it's even happening. I died multiple times because I had not moved fast enough or I shot a dude during a mandatory stealth mission after I was ordered to but the event hadn't triggered because, apparently, Captain A-hole wasn't finished talking. there is also the game being stupid about where you are going during the piloting mission I accidently crossed the road while following some plot related vehicles. The game immediately jumped on my case about getting back on course.
Glitches
Oh the glitches, love being killed by invisible helicopters, events that don't trigger, or just general bullcrap? Then this is the game for you. Love being yelled at by capt. A-hole  while he orders you to kill  the 11th rocket trooper? Then this is the game for you. Do you love watching people that take interesting concepts and use them as toilet paper? Then this is the game for you. For everyone else there is really any other game.

Beyond Earth pretty much has none of the feel or intellectually pleasing aesthetics of that game.  It looks like a reskinned CivV (and is nice looking as far as that goes) but the gameplay lacks the kind of depth you typically see with the previous Civ titles.  As complex as the tech web, Affinities and Virtues are, they don't appear to set you on any particular "path" of gameplay and seem a bit superfluous.  Overall, I think they had a decent idea with this game, but it just wasn't implemented well.  Meanwhile, I'll still dream of the day they release SMACII and get it right.

Turns out, this is one of the most fun semi-casual games I've played in a long time. At first, the controls (especially the broadside firing mechanism) can be a bit unintuitive, but it only take a bit of playing to get used to it. Also, while the graphics are 3D, the player ship only moves in 2D (as in: your "height" is fixed). Initially that bothered me, but now I actually like it. It makes the game a bit more arcade-y, without dumbing it down too much (combat can still be extremely challenging).
In summary: unconditional recommendation to give this game a try.

Originally left a negative review, changing it after 10 additional hours of play.
So unlike most other games, Dead Rising 2 is not about completing the main storyline or going up against the bosses the first time you play through. Its literally about grinding for PP (exp) by killing zombies, completing rescue missions (side quests) and various other activities to level your character. As Chuck levels up, his inventory space, speed, atk strength, and other attributes grow and you acquire more combo cards to fashion new weapons. Personally, I like the nail gloves as they seem to have good crowd control, damage and PP gains.
During your 2nd playthrough assuming you have enough cash and stats, can you start going up against the bosses since at around lvl20 you gain the ability to roll and dodge attacks. My only complain is that these abilities aren't built into the character at the start because its very confusing to play this game after playing so many others where progression is generally linear (Even Dead Rising 3 has linear progression in that you can defeat the bosses the first time you go up against them but here in Dead Rising 2 you will probably waste a lot of time wondering what the hell you're doing wrong until you realize there's no way to beat msot of the bosses on your first play through).
Overall I enjoyed the game since I do like grinding for xp. The graphics look very good in 4k, I'd say akin to some iPad games I played in the early 2010s so honestly that won't bother newcomers to the series. But again liek me you'll fine yourself frustrated with a character who moves slow as molasses and can't dodge and is constantly grappling with zombies at the beginning. It takes a lot of patience, trial and error (if you die you'll be sent to your last manual save and the save points are very few and far between if you don't know where to look or get lost in the map). And the map is very large and well designed, the developers capture a good portion of Las Vegas pretty well.
Each playthrough lasts about 6-8 hours (the game takes place across 72 hours of ingame time). I'd say you can complete the game within 16-24 hours (about 3 playthroughs and optional freeroam playthroughs thereafter if you plan on getting achievements or maxing out your character).
I remember my friends not shutting up about Dead Rising 2 when it came out when I was a teen and honestly, I can say that this has aged well even for someone for hasn't played it until now.

This is an okay game. The gameplay isn't very exciting and it doesn't go anywhere or do anything interesting. The enemy bullets don't stand out enough from the background and the game seems random to the point where you can luck out with decent pickups at the start and go far or lose all your lives as soon as you start.

OVERVIEW
This is an epic game that makes you become a citizen trying to survive the harsh war. You will make decisions that will help or hender your chances of survival. Will you live by a moral? Will you kill the poor elderly people that have lots of food and meds? That is for you to decide.
BREAK DOWN
Decisions: The way the choices you make affect the game is amazing. For example, if you steal something, people will say, "It was either them or us." or "Has this war turned us into looters." It is amazing. But thats not all, helping people out when they knock also has good and bad outcomes.
Moral: The character dynamic for morale is great. (From what I can tell) The more you steal, the more you kill, and the more of your people die, the more peoples sadness increases. They can even get to a point of depression.
Survival: Foods, meds, bandages, materials. Those are the basic things required for your survival. Without food, people will starve and die, without bandages injuries can get lethal, without meds illnesses can get lethal, and without materials you wont be able to make anything. You actually feel stress while managing your stuff.
Other: The graphics are great, the 2-D is an amazing fit for this game, the controls are great once you get use to them, and the character skills are also well planned and well thought out.
ALL IN ALL
All in all, this game is phenominal! All the different aspects are put together to make the perfect combination. This game is an easy 9.5/10 for it's amazing story and in depth roleplaying. Aswell as it's ability to be played for hours on end. I recomend this game to whoever is in to Survival RPGs and has tons of time to spare.

This game was such a cool surprise! I had previously played other puzzle platformers, so I knew beforehand what I was getting into. Nevertheless, Black The Fall managed to grab and hold my attention. I found myself glued to the screen and butting my head against the puzzles again and again.
I loved the minimalism of the game’s bleak aesthetics. I think it nailed perfectly the oppressive atmosphere of a totalitarian regime. The levels are peppered with subtle clues that flesh out the story and speak volumes about the developers’ attention to detail.
As far as I’m concerned, the cleverness of the puzzles is by far the game’s main strength. New mechanics are always well introduced and the difficulty never strays past tough-but-fair territory and into overwhelmingly frustrating. It felt like the puzzles really rewarded paying attention and thinking creatively. There were quite a few challenges – brilliant in both design and execution – that led to extremely satisfying moments once I managed to solve them.

Long story short, I had great fun while playing this game and I really recommend giving Black The Fall a chance if gripping atmosphere and innovative puzzles are your cup of tea.

The first thing everybody's going to notice is the atmosphere, by which I mean everything art and story related. The world of Black: The Fall is rich and terryfing at the same time. Everything's beautifully and stylishly detailed, a real treat for history buffs who will definetly have a good time spotting the various historical references the game makes,
Gameplay-wise we're talking about a solid puzzle adventure with intricate, hard but rewarding puzzles. The game doesn't hold your hand so every bit of progress you make in this dystopian universe is as satisfying as it can be. The game throws in more than a few mechanics in the mix while also constantly reshuffling the way the player is supposed to use these said mechanics.
A lot of people have pointed out similarities to other titles. As someone who played both Limbo and Inside (the most commonly quoted titles) I can definetly say that Black: The Fall is its own game and some parts of the game possibly offer what I believe to be some extremely memorable, vivid and cinematic moments.
I recommend this wholeheartedly and am eager to see what the devs come up with next.

Game Grade: A-
Shorthand Review: Battle against hordes of murderous splicers in the decaying, or more accurately, the decayed city of rapture.  Bioshock 2 will force you to choose between your survival or your morals.
Detailed Review:
Personally, Bioshock is my favorite series.  You can ask any one of my friends and they will reluctantly agree.  If you have not played the first Bioshock, then I highly recommend that you play it first.  They must be played in order to understand everything.  Bioshock 2 has just about everything the first one had, but I do not want to compare them too much.  There are different endings you can achieve depending on how you play the campaign.  Also, the storyline (which will not be spoiled) is the 'at the end of your seat' game play we all enjoy.  The map tends to be large which gives you countless options on new places to explore.  Bioshock 2 is a wonderfully gripping sequal.
The first detail I would like to talk about is the replay value.  If you have read some of my other reviews, then you would know I talk about this a lot.  Replay value, to me, really makes a game worth your money.  As you may know, Bioshock is known to have different endings which rely on choices you make in the game.  There are multiple decisions you need to make throughout the game.  Some of those decisions are more difficult than the others.  To really get your money's worth out of this game, you should play to get every ending.  This will require many hours of game play, but each time you play it will seem like a brand new game.  There is also another game mode you can play called the 'Protector Trials'.  I am going to put this the best way I can.  Its hard.
Another point I would like to make on Bioshock 2 is the storyline.  Bioshock 2 is considered a "weak" sequel to many people.  Although it is not as good as the first, it was a necessary sequal to the series.  Bioshock 2 focuses on the desperate power grab for the keys to Rapture.  I don't really want to spoil anything so I will leave it at that.
Finally, I would like to address the map.  You can expect as much exploration in Bioshock 2 as the first Bioshock (a lot).  There are many secondary objectives and secret rooms just waiting to be found.  You can almost here their faint sceams.. "Find me.  Please... find me."  This is another reason why I think it has great replay value.  By exploring the map to the fullest, you will be greatly rewarded in more ways than one.  One thing that you should not expect to change in this game is potential exploration.  The map is a maze and you are the mouse.
Overall, the game is enjoyable with countless hours of possible game play.  Although it may not be as good as the first, it is still a clear Bioshock game.  There is still a 'horror' factor involved with the murderous splicers (as in the first game).  This game is definitely worth the time and money as long as you pay attention and find the cules.  I hope this review helped anyone thinking about buying this game.  If this did not help, then let me know by posting a comment.
I made the overall review a bit short to help people out with the common problem of crashing.  To “fix” the game crashing and you losing your progress, save the game every couple of minutes.  The beginning is the main place the game will crash.  Once you get about 15 minutes into the game, the crashing should not be a problem.  If you need more help on how to fix it, then post a comment and I will do my best to help you out.

tl;dr: A bunch of great ideas with poor execution: the game. This game isn't really worth the $20 asking price. Campaign is three hours long on a good day, and the mulitplayer is a bland, unpopulated experience. For the same price you can buy battlefield 3 or 4 on Origin, which outclass this game in just about every aspect. Don't waste your time here.
What it does right: I was hyped as hell when this first showed up, and the amount of advertisement and weird♥♥♥♥♥♥they did at E3 that year really made me want to buy it. The setting is a great idea. I wish more shooters would stray away from the modern military shooter that we're so used to by now and do things like this. However, when the reviews started coming out I'd figure I'd try it once it dropped in price... four years later.
The mechanics work, I guess. It's nothing special, other than maybe getting to use the Goliath to shoot rockets at enemies that are giving you a hard time. None of the guns feel bad to use, and they have a good amount of punch on enemies, but at the same time they do feel kinda flimsy. For a shooter that came out in 2011, it works. It's nothing special but it's not like the mechanics of the game are terrible.
A few of the set pieces were pretty cool, but those were a mix between laughable and alright. None of it felt particularly epic, but again, it served its purpose.
What it does wrong: Oh boy where to start. I guess we can start with the singleplayer. It's overly linear. I don't mean the good kind of linear like Metro 2033 or Killzone. I mean straight out of call of duty corridoor nose-leading. If you go in any direction other than which one the game wants you to go, you'll run face first into an invisible wall. It doesn't matter if you just passed through that open door ten seconds ago, you go one way and one way only. And you can tell the designating fighting zones from the talking corridors by the random stacks of chest-high cover littered around. It's painfully obvious that this game doesn't really want you to go out on your own or do anything other than move from cover to cover shooting bad guys. There is no variety to any of it.
The graphics also haven't aged well. I don't think they were even that great at the time. I think Half Life 2 looks better and it came out seven years before. The color scheme is bland and uninteresting, and you can't interact with anything other than picking up guns. Even your teammates have to open doors for you like this was a ps2 ww2 shooter.
The campaign is, in its entirety, maybe three hours long if you stop to look at the scenery once in a while. I beat it in two and a half. It isn't even a good three hours either. I was actually kinda thankful it wasn't longer, otherwise I might not have gotten through it. None of your npc companions are even remotely interesting and they don't bother to characterize any of them beyond very basic traits. You have no reason to be invested in any of it, as they just sling you into the action three minutes into it with barely any explanation. This doesn't change the further you get into it, either. Only after following these rebels for an hour and a half or so do they finally tell me in the form of an off-hand comment that they needed me to fly a helicopter for them. You think they would have taken the time to brief the pilot on that important detail, or at least asked if he could fly a helicopter and wasn't just a jet pilot or something.
The most motivation you get is the objective marker. No overall reason behind it, or important motive, just follow the arrow. Sure, I want to liberate the home of the free just as much as anyone, but blindly following the first couple of idiots that almost kill me in a car crash doesn't seem like it's the most solid of motivations.
And another thing, I'm getting really tired of silent protagonists. It worked in games like Dead Space because Isaac was completely alone, and didn't need to talk to anyone most of the time, but here? There are usually three other people that need to be interacted with in combat situations. Games like Far Cry 3 and Spec Ops: The Line have completely destroyed the notion that video game protagonists are better silent. I have no interest in Jacobs like I did Jason. Being invested in your character as a person goes a long way into being better invested in the game overall. This game did nothing towards this and ended up being bland and forgettable.
One last little rant before I get to the multiplayer: North Korea? Really? The only reason anyone ever gives them any respect is because they're allies with China. Never would a tiny, economically weak nation like North Korea ever be able to hold as much land as we are led to believe, or be able to invade and occupy the nation with the world's strongest military, even while under economic collapse.  The logistics of such things are simply impossible for North Korea, even if they did have the military size they say they do, which is most likely a lie. As much as I give battlefield 4's singleplayer♥♥♥♥♥♥ it at least had a believable scenario. Plus North Korean soldiers using Colt, Bushmaster, and Kriss USA firearms (All American-based firearm companies if you didn't know)? Did they even bother to do any research into this matter?
Now for the Multiplayer: They tried to add some unique features like battlepoints to build up like killstreaks, using this money to spawn into vehicles and use special weapons. I like this better than cod's killstreak system, since it allows you to buy things even if you're not doing that well, but I still don't like it that much. First, just about every class gets a rocket launcher, and you can buy it after one kill. This is not good game design. Vehicles are pretty much useless beyond a quick kill or two if you find a group of enemies that knows what they're doing. Vehicles are pretty much instant kills on infantry too, so that's annoying, and you can't even use environmental ques to tell where they are like you might in battlefield, where you might hear it coming or see it firing on the minimap. I think it did show up on the minimap, but I never saw it before one killed me.
It's got the standard setup for multiplayer unlocking systems. Get kills and unlock guns. I didn't play enough to unlock anything, but I never felt like using anything other than the first class was really necessary. I didn't see much variety in the enemies either, but then again the killcam gives you absolutely no information other than where the person who killed you was at. Since just about every class gets a rocket launcher, and sniping is pretty pointless on smaller maps imo, there didn't seem to be much variety to be had. I played a few games and there wasn't much exciting going on. The maps are too big for there to be large chunks of action, and I doubt that's ever going to change with the player counts as they are. Other games do everything so much better.
Overall, this game is nothing but all of the stereotypical elements of first person shooters from 2011. It seems like a lazy attempt to pull away customers from cod's fanbase, and even then, it doesn't do anything better than call of duty, it just imitates it in a different setting. If this game had come out on the ps2 seven years before, then I think it might have been a lot better received. As it is now, that's kinda what it feels like: a generic ww2 shooter from the ps2 made for a later generation. There's nothing special about it other than its setting. The multiplayer is bland, the singleplayer is forgettable, and the entire thing is nothing but a cynical attempt at checkboxing fps elements to try to bring in the cod crowd.
If you read this far and are still thinking about buying the game, please don't. I can not in good conscience recommend this game to anyone when battlefield 4, an infinitely better experience, is the exact same price. Buy that game for a much better fps experience.
