Yet again, the fact that Steam reviews don't have a "Meh" button, is really unfortunate.
At first, I didn't like the game - death was frequent and random and the camera was terrible. I even got a Steam refund, thinking that the game was horribly ported, but I found myself missing the combat and feel of the game, so I bought it again... on sale mind you.
Having a lot more time in the game now, I can give a clearer opinion on the good, the bad and the plain outright moronic.
You control a capital ship and you shoot at other capital ships with a combination of turrets and broadside guns. While there are also smaller ships in the way of fighters, gunships and bombers, you can't control them or even deploy them. If you want an idea of how ship combat works and have played SPAZ2, then you pretty much know. I'm not sure who plagiarised who, but someone did. I can't seem to find anyone else who has raised this point, which is strange, as the similarities are uncanny. Anyway, the good points and the bad.
First the good stuff. The graphics on the ships are nice - very nice. Everything else? Not so much. I'm not sure why space is so bright in video games, but I don't like it. The planets look pretty bad in particular, but luckily they are just obstacles to go around and the level of interaction with them stops right there. Another good point is the feel of the ships.
Another good thing is how the combat feels. At least most of the time anyway. Flying around in a big ship with turrets and lining up broadsides is pretty neat, though I tend to stick with turret heavy ships and let the game do the aiming, as broadsides don't seem particularly useful most of the time with the speed of combat as it is.
So the bad stuff. This is tough, as I don't know where to start. Ah wait, I know.
"Space" is kind of a strange word to be using in this game. You are on a 2D plane. There is no up and there is no down. This might as well have been a boat game rather than a spaceship game - it would have made more sense. It's not too much of a bad thing, I guess, as full 360 movement isn't always done well, but then come the obstacles. Flying through asteroid or junk fields is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ especially when you graduate to the bigger ships. Squeezing in between spaces can be awkward. Even worse is when you are "warping". See, when you aren't in combat, you will, after a time, automatically start going at "sublight" speed, in which your ship will go faster than it normally can. Any ship, or rock, or piece of space junk and this faster speed will cut out. Let me tell you: "space" is full of crap in this game. I dare you to fly any sort of straight line in this game without running into a junk field, asteroid field, ice field or random pirates who happen to be sitting in your flight path. It's so bad that it feels cramped and clunky. It's really bizarre.
Another issue that I find annoying is to do with the fighters. Remember I told you that the game is on a 2D plane, right? Well that doesn't apply to fighters. They have full 3D movement, so targetting them can be really hard, especially with the broadsides. Turrets can handle them but they seem infinately more powerful than capital ships when even in small groups, which I find pointless. Also, you'd better pray that you don't encounter fighters of a higher rank than you because they can outrun and outgun you. When the only thing to do is to cut your ship's engines and wait for your inevitable death as you can't fight and can't run, then you know something is seriously wrong.
The largest issue, however, is unibutton. If you've played any game ported from a console, you'll know what I'm talking about. Some games call it a context button while others call it an action button. I call it a lazy porting button: used for control pads with limited buttons and annoys us PC gamers with keyboards. This button is responsible for your warp and will automatically light up when you can warp... it's also your tractor beam, your speed increase button and hailing button. When you are near cargo, have hails going off and simply just want to go to warp, you might aswell just blow your brains out instead of waiting for the inevitable frustration triggered aneurysm. Devs: this is the PC. I have dozens of buttons which I'm not using, is it really so much to ask that I be able to map different actions to them?
The game can feel good though it does get repetitive after a time and the issues are just mind bogglingly dumb. A minor issue (in terms of the game not my hearing) is that the menu sound and music is so much louder than the actualy game that I have to keep turning the volume down when I exit.
This game is ok if it's on a sale, you will get some gameplay out of it and I do feel that it's better value for money than Space Pirates and Lego 2. Don't expect it to last, though.

The Good:
*Combat, while limited by the "age of sail" mentality and 3rd person view, is quite entertaining.
*Piracy, through force or "persuasion". Nothing more entertaining or profitable than stealing from the trader you are escorting.
*Exploration can be quite captivating thanks to being set in space.
The Bad:
*Obvious console port with minimal mouse utility in menus.
*Nausiating edge scroll turret aiming and disorienting auto tracking.
*Semi-fixed distance 3rd person view which can only be changed in menu, not on the fly.
*3D mining from a 2D plane can be frustrating as nodes can be difficult to aim at depending on turret configuration.
*RPG elements are minimal involving buying upgrades for one's ship, mostly linear, and fulfilling quests to receive mutually exclusive bonuses.
*Inability to scroll through one's weapons, can only select weapon groups be it ballistic, flak, laser, or the various missile types, making it impossible to see beneath one's ship to personally aim at fighters.
The Ugly:
*Trading, I swear the comerce AI is programed to to drop the prices wherever you go making it nearly impossible to make money through trading outside of special events such as Famine.
*Diplomacy, nearly non-existant beyound scaring off weaker enemies (kinda pointless) or dumping one's cargo to appease pirates (rarely worth it), and no way to improve relations beyound fulfilling quests for the five main factions (takes too long) or responding to distress signals (can be risky early on), and no way to improve relations with the minor factions.
*The Grell, ugly♥♥♥♥♥fish ♥♥♥♥ers with frankly overpowered ships who swim in schools, avoid at all costs until very late game.
Despite the overwhelming negativity presented above, I still enjoy the game and would recommend it, so long as it's on sale.

Despite those steps backward, things like combat and trading have been improved (I love getting favors from opponents in need) and the revival of the Alpha Centaur aesthetic is beautiful with modern visuals. This War of Mine is an excellent concept and is, for the most part, a good game. That being said, it is incredibly repetative.
You play a group of civilians hiding in a decrepit shelter, trying to survive the duration of a war. By day, you build things to improve your shelter, eat, grow vegetables, catch animals for meat etc.; by night, you send a member of your party out to scavange or trade for supplies from nearby locations so that you might live another day. Supplies are scarce and carrying capacity is severly limited, so you will constatly have to reassess your priorities as your situation changes.
On my first playthrough I had no idea what I was doing. I prioritised the wrong things at the wrong times and on top of that, proceeded to make poor use of them. Each day was a struggle and I eventally ran out of luck on day 33.
On my second playthrough, I had a much better idea of what I needed and when. The first ~25 days passed without even a hint of trouble. I scavenged, traded and stockpiled, all the while planning for the inevitable hardships I experienced on my first run. Despite this, my intially prosperous group of survivors were all at death's door by day 28, with a highly inauspicious future.
At the time of writing this review I am reluctant to begin a third playthrough. The first ~25 days are without challenge and feel like a chore. You eat, you sleep, you scavenge, you repeat. Once winter sets in, surviving becomes significantly harder, with any small misfortune potentially spelling disaster for your entire group. I would like to beat this game, and I am not usally one to shy away from a challenge. However I really don't feel I can summon the enthusiasm to grind through the hours of repetative gameplay required to reach said challenge. This game just doesn't offer enough overall depth to keep me coming back for more.
TL;DR
Good concept. Enjoyable for the first 2-3 playthroughs but gets old very quickly. Overall the gameplay lacks depth. I would recommend picking this game up in a sale.

You know those games where the AI ​​programming can translate into the failure to understand the basic principles of math and funny? This is one of those games. The first ground of frustration you'll have it when there will be clear that the most powerful enemies in the game are not the capital ship of any class they belong. The only opponents that you will still have to look at are the small (or large) interceptor groups. These aircrafts are the only ones that can be moved in a three dimensional space, then eluding the most of your turrets (normally located in the upper part of the hull). They shoot almost continuously, surpassing the cast limits theoretically imposed by their weapons. But in this game when mentioning the limits, they mean just those imposed to you. Because whatever happens, the AI continue to cheat. The missiles at their disposal are endless. Useless to try to set any kind of strategy. The only work that is always the same. Remain as much as possible to the edge of the battle, dividing the enemy troops and then destroy them gradually. So if you can not resist the temptation to buy this title, expect a generator of missions that does not take into account your points of damage or defense (missions reported as low risk where it will be easy to explode), an AI that uses cheating, and be prepared repeating the same mission several times. There is only one real challenge, which is to figure out after how many hours of play you will want to move on.
Maybe someone will think that I could have written that it is a shame because this game has the potentialities. But I do not think that's true. The strength of this game should be the gameplay, that if it were not limited by the reality of the facts, it would be pure adrenaline. Instead it is frustrating the most of the time. The game's soundtrack is undoubtedly the only note of color that distinguishes this title from many others. For the rest in terms of concept, I can not define Rebel Galaxy as innovative and original even.

At first glance the game does seem drastically different than Civilization 5. There seems to be quite a lot of negative reviews but I personally find it to be a very pleasant addition to the Civilization series. I started playing the civilization games way back when I was in middle school and Civilization 3 had just came out.
Here was my experience of this futuristic take on the civilization series:
At first I had a hard time trying to get focus on the game and understand what was going on. I played very on and off for a few days and stopped playing for about a week. I later resumed playing the game again and took the same approach I did to learning civilization 3. Once I understood the new mechanics and got a handle on the terrain, resources, improvements, and the daunting orbital aspect ( which actually turned out to be very simple to understand and is a fantastic element I have come to enjoy. Especially because you can create resources ;D ) so on and so forth of the intricate elements of the game. Once I played through one game, all the way (win or lose and I actually lost this one though it was close haha I started my first game on Vostok difficulty) I honestly have not been able to stop playing it. A lot of the nuisances that were present in civ 4 and civ 5 such as battling happiness and upgrading military units to compete with higher level ai (these are just a couple).
I really like how the virtues truly give you the ability to customize your sponsor (civilization). When the virtue tree has 2 bonuses branching to a higher tier bonus, you no longer need both of those bonuses to grab that higher tier and only need to pick one.
The way units upgrade is a really cool approach as too. Again, it gives you full customization of your nation. Even when behind you can still put up a fight, albeit a struggle, but it is doable and winnable. It also gives hope to being able to win a game when quite a ways behind. The instant upgrade of all units once the upgrade has been earned (affinity level reached a certain level for a particular unit) is a very nice adaptation. I remember in civ 5 losing games becuase I had no money to upgrade units and continue to fund new units.
Ultimately, I found this game to be very challenging, rewarding, and so many different ways to play the game and enjoy! I highly reccomend this game for someone willing to put in the time it takes to learn a game. Even if you are a civilization veteran, approach this game with some new eyes and it is all the more rewarding.

Back when it was about to release I was really excited to play this game, everything about it seemed, to me, what I wanted Dead Rising to be.
Ranging from the gameplay, the atmosphere, to the pure sheer absurdity of the whole, idea, of the game.
Now back then I "binged" playing this, and for what I remember I must have finished the game in two weeks time, spending most of it replaying the main campaign, and forgetting some side story missions to level up my character.
After that, I forgot about the game.
Off the record came, and went for me, I play it but I just couldn't "feel" the same way.
It had to do with me, not so much with the game.
But on pc, I decided to give it a try, see if the original was as good as I remembered it.
Turns out it is, but god, am I grateful in a way to now have the capacity to try and express clearly what I resent about this game.
For starters the story its pure absurdity, if you were expecting a good story for one reason or another, don't even expect the same "quality" from the first game, I like Chuck as a protagonist, I enjoy his personality, even if its a little dry, and generally there are a couple of good characters, both heroes, and villains, to enjoy.
But sadly the problem that I have with this game its that similarly to the first game it tries to become something a bit more complex than it can be.
In the last game I found it to be more tolerable because the narrative of that game where the encounters that you had while playing it, really the significant changes to the overarching story didn't happened until the last, crucial moments, so even if I dislike them, there were few.
This time around however right from the start the game tries to introduce a whole plot of conspiracies, filled with a series of cheesy characters, that, again, when looked alone, at their design, and personalities, it's enjoyable to have, and meet them.
But they're placed in a narrative that tries to take itself so seriously at times, that in often cases the charisma of this beings gets "sucked" dry.
Now that I really think about it, that's kinda the main complaint that I have with Dead Rising 2.
The first Dead Rising was a game grounded in realism in a lot of different aspects, in my opinion that game dealt with horror, whilst the subsequent releases don't, it explored aspects or betrayal, social critique, and psychological terror.
I enjoyed it tremendously in that sense because a lot of it got contrasted by the pure sheer absurdity of the gameplay.
But the game wasn't really "overblown" or exaggerated in any way, you couldn't craft a freezing ray, or make toy fists that shoot lighting like you could in the next couple of games.
The hilarity came from just the whole idea of the situation you were in, it was hilarious to just experiment around all the different items, weapons, and generally, objects, that you could use to hurt, heal, or escape, different situations, and, or enemies.
Even the skills that you earned while rescuing survivors, while brutal, and a bit "over the top" at times, remained believable in the illusion that that game created.
And the missions, while difficult, where in a way a bit more clear in their objectives, and often times it wasn't as much as the progression the one that was hidden as secrets, as much as it was just the actual special items, weapons, or areas that were.
To explain what I mean by that:
In this Dead Rising 2 the mission structure its incredibly similar to the last, to not say it's almost the same, you rescue survivors, bring them from around the massive map into your shelter, then depending on your actions, you get different types of endings.
The problem is that there are certain missions that are hidden, literally, unless you pick up a guide and read through it, there will simply be some items, weapons, and endings, that you won't be able to obtain.
It is an incredible flaw, and a frustrating one at that.
Then there's other survivors that require certain things from you, now this is handled for the most part in an enjoyable way up until you began noticing some of them require you to complete absurd request that are difficult to accomplish within the time limit you're given to complete each activity, and "trigger" each "main" quest.
At one point I had two missions that I wanted to complete, but along the way I ran into a group of survivors, a mission that was unmarked, and hidden, in order for them to come with me into the shelter however, I needed to first play rounds of poker with them, and beat, every single one of them.
After about an hour or so I couldn't beat them, got flustered because the timer for the other two missions was about to finish, and I simply end up murdering them all.
It wasn't even satisfying, it was just frustrating, and it made me wondered why even bother...
It wasn't however until I reached the conclusion that some "combo cards" couldn't be obtained unless I played through some hidden quests, when I decided to quit the game.
In this game you get the ability to obtain combo cards, either by interacting with objects around the map, rescuing survivors, leveling up, or murdering psychopaths.
You would think that you can just check the weapon combinations online, and you can, but if you do, without actually having the "combo card" you're only able to perform some attacks with the combo weapons that you get.
Now this is probably the biggest adition to the game, and one of the most enjoyable aspects that I found before, and now from it.
The combo weapons range from just believable combinations, such as "taping" together a fireaxe with a hammer, to completely crazy ones like combining a flashlight, and jewelry, forming a lightsaber.
This is yet another example of what I mean when I say this game doesn't really know if it wants to be completely insane, or completely "realistic" within the given, obvious, context in which the game takes place.
It's as if the developers forgot completely that in order to add, and recreate a lot of the systems of the original Dead Rising, they had to change some of the other crucial aspects of the game, (like the freaking timers).
So there are times in which I feel the game wants to make me as powerful as possible, a living creature of pure brutality that it's incapable of getting hit by a slow zombie.
But then there are other times when as I am swaying my paddlesaw, a zombie barely touches me, and makes me drop my freaking weapon.
Then you need to consider a lot of the new systems that have been added aren't only too insane for the foundations of the original gameplay design, but they're simply too complex.
There are magazines now that you need to obtain in order to get bonuses, it isn't a requirement, and frankly I find them redundant, half of the times I would just ignore them because the "buffs" that they provided weren't really too benefitial.
But then you have some cases, some incredibly specific cases, in which it is imperative for you to get them.
That hidden poker mission that I was talking a while ago, apparently if you get a specific set of magazines, they can give you a buff that improves the probabilities of you encountering better cards, and pairs in the midst of the game...
But you know, even after saying all of this negative things about the game, in the midst of every single one of them I can't help but to feel I enjoyed the game, back then and now, even if I quitted this time around.
I like the combo system, even if it kinda invalidates a lot of the other weapons/items that you get.
I enjoy the fact that there are secrets spread across the game, even if some of them are immensley cryptic, and lock progression, endings, and "combo cards" behind them.
I also enjoy thoroughly the characters, and some of the things that you need to accomplish to finish certain missions.
But it is like that with this game, kinda like a love, and hate, relationship, on one side I love it, on another, I hate it...

This War of Mine is a game set in a war torn city representing the 1992-1996 siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian war. As a group of citizens trying to survive the harsh reality of war, you are forced to do some things that you may not want to do. This game is a true gem, showing the depressing parts of war, which very few games have been able to capture thus far. This War of Mine forces you to create a mental connection to these characters that you're trying to keep alive, and when one dies you feel like a part of yourself has died with them. It's a game that I was personally scared to pick up, but when I did it was very worth it. I would rate it 9/10, the only point being lost was how steep the learning curve is for combat and how the ai sometimes acts. Other than that, it's a very well tailored game, one that should be a common experience among gamers across the world.

Sins of a Solar Empire is a 4X Strategy game. It contains diplomacy, research, expansion and combat like most other 4X space games, with the notable difference that SoSE is not turn based.
It does not offer a campagin or scenarios, but mulltiplayer matches over the internet or LAN. Skirmishes versus AI are also possible. A multitude of options permit the player to influence gameplay by changing sproduction, income and movement speeds, including pirates and other random encounters and changing the victory conditions.
SoSE will have you juggle between strengthenig your economy, researching better weapons and fending off your opponent. Macro management, or "making the right calls" is a very important part of the game, but micro management, unit positioning and ability/energy management can still have a strong effect on the outcome of any battle.

If you are a fan of turn based games like Master of Orion or Endless Legend and want to try something different, or if you are a fan of RTS games like Star Craft or Supreme Commander and want to go "bigger" (Supreme Commander Fans know what I am talking about :p), then SoSE is for you.
I find this game really fun, its a good way to pass the time, and the pixel art is really good. : D

Fun gameplay and good story. Really enjoyed playing this game even with its ups and downs.
Pros
- The main story as well as the tape recordings give more information on rapture and some of the characters from the previous Bioshock game.
- New main story villains, they can get a bit annoying
- New enemies added alongside some old ones.
- Upgraded plasmids give new abilities besides a damage upgrade.
- You now use Big Daddy weapons (Drill, Rivet gun, etc...)
- More ingame choices (Six possible endings)
- You can now carry little sisters and have them harvest adam.
- Big Daddy dash ability, loved this feature. Beware it costs fuel.
- Hacking things ingame felt easier compared to the first game.
- New soundtrack alongside some copy paste soundtrack from the original game. (This is a pro because it didn't really bother me that much)
- The Good ending.
Cons
- Your melee weapon (Drill) costs fuel, you can still smack enemies with it but i found looking for fuel annoying.
- The only way to feel like a real big daddy is to play on "Easy" mode since you can get easily killed by splicers in the other modes which breaks immersion in the game. Easy mode basically makes you harder to kill and enemies weaker which did the trick.
- Your Big Daddy footsteps now sound weaker compared to the first game. Maybe 2K thought players would get annoyed with hearing big footsteps the whole game.
- Some of the ingame weapons sound weak due to the latest patch; people have made a fix for this, but the fix crashed my game when i tried it, so i just got used to the regular sounds.
- The game does tend to crash at random times so save your game often.
- The "Save and quit" corrupts the save files for some unknown reason, you can still use the regular "Save".
7.5/10

Sea Dogs: To Each His Own, a game of pirates and adventure! And steep learning-curves and frustration! I was originally going to give this game a positive review, but after much consideration I cannot bring myself to; This game is not something anyone can pick up and enjoy, no it is quite the opposite. You have to already know how to play an Akella Corsair game to get any enjoyment out of Sea Dogs: TEHO. Though I personally enjoy it, there isn't much good I can say about it.
---------------------------------------------
Exploration: By far the biggest draw factor for me. Even after playing it's predeccessor for 1000 hours+, I still find exploring in this game series to be rather exciting, even if at times it is somewhat repetitive.
Naval Combat: In my original review of SD:TEHO, I complained at length about the combat. There is still a lot of negative things to be said about the naval combat in this game, but when a battle goes right, my good god does it go right; With that said, I must point out that the difficulty sways from ridiculously easy to ludicrously difficult, to outright impossible to win and lose. The problem with naval combat lies not so much with the A.I, but rather the weather and damage systems. Weather plays a massive role in this game, as it often decides the outcome of most battles, on a good day a sloop can take on a frigate and the adjacent lugger, on a bad day you'd be lucky if you can even move close enough to fire at them, due to there being no wind, or the wind blowing in the opposite direction, leaving everyone's ships dead in the water. In regards to damage: Most of the time your ship's cannons won't do any damage, and their cannons destroy your sails and crew whilst miraculously doing no damage to your hull, and when that happens in most cases the only way to "lose" or "win" is to reload your last autosave or pray they board you.
Roleplaying: Where as in previous installments it was possible to roleplay as a pirate, or a officer serving one of main powers in the Caribbean, however in this game it is no longer the case. You play the role of a rogueish French nobleman in a relatively linear narrative with very few choices throughout the story, not much is offered for roleplaying, however with that said the story in of itself is fairly good. I hope that in the foreseeable future this may be rectified.
Learning Curve: Like I said at the beginning: You need to know how to play a game from the Corsair franchise to even begin playing this game. Keep a guide and a map of the Caribbean handy, otherwise you'll be dead in the water, not knowing where anything is, what to do or how to make it off of the first island.
Quests: There is very little variety in quests, a lot of your time will be wasted by doing fetch and escort missions to earn money.
---------------------------------------------
By all means buy this game *if* you are a fan of previous Corsair games like AoP2, but to new players that are interested in acquiring this game: Do not buy it. Spare yourself the headaches and tears and buy Age of Pirates 2: City of Abandoned Ships from Good Old Games, far superior and easier to get into and enjoy.

Ok I'm gonna be honest: This game is really rough around the edges and can sometimes be quite frustrating. I've spent immeasurable hours playing Pirates of the Carribean (basically sea dogs 2) and I still needed to check the guides in the forum and on pirates ahoy to get my head around some of the basic controls and to understand what to look for in quests.
However, once you get through all that, it's a really rewarding experience. Sure they've recycled the lighthouse from POTC and sure the translation is sometimes abysmal and the graphics are pretty much the same as in POTC (a 2003 game), however that is to be expected from a £13 game.
The quests don't guide you as much as you'd like but this is what makes the game even more rewarding for me. Combat is unforgiving and if you haven't saved in a while you WILL regret it. Think of it like dark souls in that manner but simpler, without the gore and you create the checkpoints. This does mean that you might have to revert to multiple previous checkpoints depending how much you messed up. The tutorial is quite long and not as descriptive as a tutorial should be, definitely something that needs to be patched.
Other than that, once you get through those snags, the carribean is your oyster. All those (albeit copy/paste) reviews here on steam still tell the truth. This is a really good game if you like the whole pirate/RPG genre, the fact that I have played 45.9 hours in one week is quite indicative. I wholeheartedly recommend it for the price, would pay £30 if it were decently translated and had a better tutorial, would pay £50 if they also included graphics that were 2008-2010 standard (of course without sacrificing smoothness of play).

Very OLD Akella Pirates game player here when "dinosaurs ruled the earth".
I basically played the entire game in Russian before it was released in English offline.
The game series has been around since 2000.  Developed by Akella.  This is actually the SIXTH game in the series.  Sea Dogs, POTC (Sea Dogs Modification, SD2, the bad disney production), Age of Pirates (AoP) , Tortuga - Two Treasures, AoP2:COAS (City of Abandoned Ships) , and POTEHO (SDTEHO). Black Mark Studios has most of the original modders and designs from the original games.  SDTEHO has MANY of the same landmarks as COAS and similar quests.  Personally, I am partial to COAS for many reasons, but predominantly the freedom to do whatever the hell you want very early.
There are several other distinct subset series mods as well both from Russian (Ukraine), and the the generated POTC Build Mod, Gentlemen of Fortune and "Eras" mods.  The one that is most notable is the "Gentlemen of Fortune" (GoF) + Eras which makes the game even more massive in terms of gameplay, but "cryptic" terms of controls and difficulty.
In order to enjoy THIS game, a player has to be willing "take the pain up the bunghole", at least initially anyway.
It is rogue style, you die, you are DEAD.
You will die.
You will get frustrated.
You will get angry.
You will probably curse at your computer.
You will probably curse at Akella / BlackMark Studio developers.
You might even curse in Russian if you know the language.
Save your game, OFTEN.
I do mean A LOT.
You may even have to revert to an earlier stage because you missed something critical.
If you do not and end up on the main screen staring and saying "WTF!" because you just lost 10 hours of gameplay, it is YOUR fault.
I REALLY mean that.
This game can be incredibly unforgiving at times.
I was part of the design production team of the original English release of AoP2:  COAS, but passed on the English translation of SDTEHO, because even the updated Storm Engine is not aging well and problems with the original English release.  Currently the translation to English is absolutely insanely laughable at times, but most of us left that understand the game engine are probably not going to fix this game in the series this time round as Akella still has not learned their lessons.  Additionally, the entire source is not available inside the game anyway as it is ENCRYPTED.  Thanks Akella.
There are quests on this particular game that will give you more game rage that you have ever experienced in previous series.  "The Gambit" comes to mind, sailing in "real time" and even with time compression is laborious.  Most people have not seen the endings of the later games due to difficulty or just throw up their hands and go, "I quit".
"Silly gamers, SDTEHO is not for kids..."
Basically the gameplay provides a very solid RGP single player experience, but the controls are still ARCHAIC, graphics are aging (lack of intiial DirectX 9 support is UNACCEPTABLE this is 2016!), hit detection is average, and this game WILL NOT HOLD YOUR HAND.
There are no "arrows" to guide you.
You need to WRITE DOWN things in order to remember them.
You need to do some research on how to do things, because the game will not tell you how to do them even with the extra long tutorial.
There are a lot of game mechanic concepts that have to be understood UPFRONT.
Combat can be unfair and brutish for the unprepared.
Landmarks and graphics are RECYCLED from all previous games (with some small expanded list of new areas and features such as ships decks).
Items are GREATLY expanded, which magic and alchemy all over the place.
It adds a new twist to the game series.
There are NO FULL VOICE OVERS (that are unrelated to dialogue), so get used to it, or move on.
Failure to read dialogue can result in game failure, and some things are ONLY said ONCE!

An accurate simulation of what would happen if you handed a bunch of 11 year olds the keys to some high powered cars and told them to just flatten the accelerator into the first corner with all the forethought and finesse their pre-teen brains can muster. Do you like either going in a straight line or getting sweaty palms because there is a 1 degree bend in the road and the car behind you had the brake pedal listed as an optional extra that the owner was too much of a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to fork out for? Then this is the game for you!

Story
You strand with a ship on some Island during the times of colonisation, but something is wrong with the Spanish soldiers stationed there and all the inhabitants are dead. The only friendly person is the maid in red, who cannot remember her past and in some mysterious dark side of the world, skeletons and ghosts are haunting the Island. Can you escape the Island? The story is mostly told by Ghosts and Notes, though nobody in the game is voiced, meaning that you will have to read a lot. Though the story seems very deep and is, I did not really follow it, because of the reading close until the end and do not feel like I missed anything between start to finish.
Gameplay
In first person you run around and try to progress while fighting the mysterious creatures. You have a weapon arsenal of bows, crossbows, pistols, rifles and Tomahawks, which all have their advantages and disadvantages; though the tomahawk is in my opinion not balanced and the best (one shots nearly everything). Whenever you find a bell in the area you can use it to enter the dark world where there are different enemies, but also ghosts of the dead that might be able to give you important information. Sadly, you can simply use your listening ability to hear where the next objective is. This makes thinking unnecessary and you might just run from a to b like a dummy just to do the same thing in the next stage of the game again.
Graphics
The graphics make this game so unique. The world around you is only black, white, black and red which give the game such a sad or depressed filter. At first I thought it was great, but after several hours you do not want to be in that world doing the same stuff over and over.
It really is a good game and I sometimes did enjoy playing it, but the repetitive gameplay and the sad world can bring you down. I personally did not enjoy it most of the time, but I can understand the people that do. At some point I only continued so that the game would be over sooner, so If someone says he wants the game and thinks it is cool, buy it, 5€ is no big deal, especially during sales, but I thought so as well at first, so do not have to high expectations, because I at the end cannot recommend it for the fun I had playing it.

You know those games where the AI ​​programming can translate into the failure to understand the basic principles of math and funny? This is one of those games. The first ground of frustration you'll have it when there will be clear that the most powerful enemies in the game are not the capital ship of any class they belong. The only opponents that you will still have to look at are the small (or large) interceptor groups. These aircrafts are the only ones that can be moved in a three dimensional space, then eluding the most of your turrets (normally located in the upper part of the hull). They shoot almost continuously, surpassing the cast limits theoretically imposed by their weapons. But in this game when mentioning the limits, they mean just those imposed to you. Because whatever happens, the AI continue to cheat. The missiles at their disposal are endless. Useless to try to set any kind of strategy. The only work that is always the same. Remain as much as possible to the edge of the battle, dividing the enemy troops and then destroy them gradually. So if you can not resist the temptation to buy this title, expect a generator of missions that does not take into account your points of damage or defense (missions reported as low risk where it will be easy to explode), an AI that uses cheating, and be prepared repeating the same mission several times. There is only one real challenge, which is to figure out after how many hours of play you will want to move on.
Maybe someone will think that I could have written that it is a shame because this game has the potentialities. But I do not think that's true. The strength of this game should be the gameplay, that if it were not limited by the reality of the facts, it would be pure adrenaline. Instead it is frustrating the most of the time. The game's soundtrack is undoubtedly the only note of color that distinguishes this title from many others. For the rest in terms of concept, I can not define Rebel Galaxy as innovative and original even.

This game is both oddly addictive and frustrating.  Hours of play go by without me noticing, but every time something annoys - combat mechanics, navigation, etc.
The good:
Right out of the gate, you can do stuff.  You’re not limping around with crappy, starter equipment very long. The first couple missions are just challenging enough, and give you a decent reward to do some upgrades.  There’s no dishonor in running away from fights until you get good enough equipment to fight back.
It’s really is immersive, and I love that you can play your own custom soundtrack which enhances that. I haven’t done much with the main story yet, having too much fun tooling around the galaxy doing side missions and exploring stuff.
Equipment upgrades don’t depreciate, so you can sell them back for the same as the purchase price.  This is great when you’re starting out and just figuring out the game mechanics.  It eliminates those costly newbie mistakes that handicap you as you advance.
The annoying:
Some of the mechanics clunky.  For example: When mining, you blow up the asteroid then have to go hunting for what pops out using the pulse feature, boost your way to the loot (being careful not to overshoot it), then painstakingly angle into the sweet spot that will auto trigger your tractor beam. I’d really like to be able to target stuff manually and then grab it.
I have to agree with other reviews about the lack of Y axis. It is really frustrating, particularly in a big firefight when you have a swarm of nimble enemy fighters attacking you at all angles, disappearing along the vertical just as you go to nail them and all you can do swing from side to side, waiting for them to get back to the horizontal
Difficulty ratings are a crap shoot as far as accuracy.  I’ve gotten my tail kicked on a “low” risk mission and blown right through a “high” risk mission.
Misc:
The game doesn’t recognize my Xbox 360 wireless controller (which works with other Steam games), but does recognize my old Logitech F310 USB gamepad.  I find that handles the game better than K&M.

X Rebirth is a great space (fight/trade/build) game that suffered from a rough start, but the developer Egosoft stood by it and actually listened to the fans' feedback.
I purchased the complete/collector edition, including all the DLC, after the 4.0 release.  I am glad I waited because it sounds like it had a very negative start when released.
It is quite a bit different than the previous X titles, so it offended a lot of the loyal fan base.  Egosoft has a small but loyal community and I think X Rebirth is a lot more user friendly to people wanting to join that community.  I have tried all the X titles, but mostly X3 Terran Conflict and X3 Albion Prelude.  I find X Rebirth to be the least complicated out of all of them (after the 4.0 release).
They also made X Rebirth a lot more immersive.  You can actually walk around stations, talk to people, and hire employees, so the universe does not feel so automated like the previous X games.  However, walking around the stations can get a little bit repeative at times; a lot of the stations look the same, and the character graphics feel a bit out-dated or retro.  It kind of reminds me of the retro graphics of 1999's System Shock 2 (which is an amazing game by the way).
When I bought X Rebirth, I never played the vanilla version.  I immediately went into the Steam Workshop and downloaded some of the top rated mods of all time.  A big one that I love is the updated 4.0 Capital Ship Bridge mod.  In my opinion, it should belong in the vanilla version by default.
There were still some bugs that I came across in the post-4.0 version of X Rebirth, but the game seems stable otherwise and I was able to find fixes or work arounds from the forums.  They updated the user interface for 4.0 which I believe is very good thing based on videos I have watched that showed the previous versions.
After 4.0, the game is a lot of fun and it probably will give you a good idea what the future X4 game will be like, although that game is expected to return to the solid roots of the previous X3 and older games.
If I had to compare this to Sierra's Space Quest series (1986-1995), I would say X Rebirth is mostly similar to Space Quest 3.  If you get the Capital Ship Bridge mod, then it can actually feel a lot like Space Quest 5 at times.

Long version:
So with this "2.0" patch thing announced It seems like what they’re doing here is similar to what CA did with "Total War: Rome 2".
They realized the initial release was so poorly received that they have no chance of selling DLC for any more cash grabs. So they released some freebies while patching up the game to the point where people actually will want to play it, and buy DLCs.
I’m really not sure it will work here with BE though. There just isn’t that much to work with...
As it is, I wouldn’t call Civ BE a "Beta" or "unfinished" as many here claim.
From what have I played of it both on PC and Mac, I didn't get any game-breaking bugs, crashes or freezes.
It seemed pretty stable over multiple platforms, and that’s what Betas are usually aimed at ensuring.
So, it works. the question is "how" it works.
The real problems were (and still are):
- lackluster design of the thing
Copypasted so hard from Civ V it feels strongly like just an overpriced Civ V expansion.
While most old fans, and yours truly expected it to actually bring a fresh breeze from Alpha Centauri, which was a real sci-fi strategy hit back in a day.
- bland faction leaders, with so little differences they all feel the same, with nonexistent diplomacy
- limited alien types and environments
- boring tech tree.. err "web" with random stuff slapped here and there
That’s not something Beta testing, user feedback or "2.0" can fix, unless the developers just start over from scratch, which rarely happens, if ever.
So, if Firaxis actually patch up Civ BE real HARD free of charge as well as offers me DLC pass for Civ BE for free, then MAYBE I will consider us even.
Until then, sorry guys, no moneys for you, stepping my foot on it.

I have a confession to make: I've really never enjoyed any X title. This is despite me purchasing just about every X game (is this how you say it? Seems weird) that EgoSoft has released. My entry to the series was X3. I purchased a boxed copy waaay back in the day. Loved the graphics, but couldn't figure the game out to save my life. Then I ended up purchasing it again on Steam, played it for about an hour, then buggered off.
The only X game I've put any work into was X: Beyond The Frontier. I think that may be their first game, but don't hold me to it. Anyway, I picked up all the orignal X games and X2 during a sale. For X: Beyond The Frontier I decided to start from the beginning to see if I could get into the series. I put 18hrs in and the game was starting to shape up, but my ADHD kicked in and I moved on to the next shinny game I'd purchased.
I ended up picking up X3: Terrian Conflict and Albion Prelude a year or two later. I had decided I'd really delve into the series and was determined to enjoy the titles. I never played more than maybe an hour between the both. They are just such a slow burn of a game. The menus are confusing. The game takes a lot of effort to delve into. I see the greatness, I just can't get into it. Which is why I always end up purchasing EgoSoft's titles. I love space trading sim games. If they could get past the slow burn and confusing menus I'd be all in. Then steps in X Rebirth.
The X community (still feels weird) hated the game. It was linear. There wasn't as much freedom. The game was a buggy mess. To me those first two complaints sounded like a positive. The open ended, do whatever man I don't care, here's a lot of stuff to learn but we don't care to teach it to you nature of the X games was the runner's wall I could never get over.  So I bid my time and waited for the game to get enough bug fixes to be playable.
And here I am! November 2017 and I just purchased this game. OMG what a mess! Let me start by saying I've only put about an hour into it so far, but initial impressions are not good. The game takes quite a while to load. I went into the graphics settings, as I do with all my games when I first start them, and enabled V-sync. I have a Nvidia 970; so most games older than a couple years tear when running on my 1080p monitor. The game went blank, then a loading screen for about 45 seconds, then it came back but with V-sync still off... Okay... I clicked it again, then waited 30 seconds, then the V-sync option turned on, then the screen went blank, then a loading screen for 45 seconds, then the settings menu reappeared with V-sync off still; so I clicked it again and the game crashed.
Not a great impression. The game was still technically running under Task Manager, but the window was gone. I stopped the process and rebooted. Went into Geforce Experience and it had the game listed with recommended graphics options. But guess what?? YUP, Geforce couldn't set the recommended settings. They had to be configured in-game. So I reloaded the game, went to setting, and magically was able to get everything set with only a few loading screens showing up.
Now that my graphics are set I hit New Game ... and ... proceeded to wait ... for about 5 minutes. Holy Hell man! There are still glitches in this game. When you leave the cockpit the game skips or stutters the animations. The voice acting kept stopping mid sentance. The menus are still confusing and esoteric and now have the sad problem of not containing every option. Some stuff is just binded to the keyboard and you just have to memorize them.
The game told me to go to a spacestation, but it actually wanted me to enter a highway. It took about 10 minutes for me to realize entering a highway is not autopilot. I kept popping out of the highway! There was no real help the game gives you to learn how to play. Once I learned how to pilot a highway, the game began, and for the next 30 minutes all you do is enter and exit highways. It's exactly like the older X games, but now with a more frustrating navigation scheme. Gone are the days of time dilation replaced with some style of Enduro for the Atari 2600
So in conclusion, I may still play this game, but so far it's not winning me over. Yet again I supported EgoSoft for yet another title I did not enjoy. Maybe I'll one day learn my lesson... We'll just have to wait until X4 comes out and I'll let you know ;)

A nice atmosperic puzzle game about the communism era under the Soviets, although the game itself is set in an alternate reality of that era. The game has more depth to it if you talk with the devs (which I did back in 2016) or get some interviews with them, since the explanations about what you experience in the game will make a lot more sense. Many of these puzzles refer to living and working in the communist era. Sometimes you need patience or stay in line or go back and forth a lot to actually move forward and at all times you have to hide, even when you're exposed wide open to the threat.
The visuals are good, the sounds are very industrial and the atmospheric background music fits well into each of the scenes. While some might complain the lack of details in the graphics between the puzzles, there are some scenes presenting you with some serious problems of that world. Many of these might be exaggerated, yet there's a little truth hidden in each of them.
The gameplay is a bit of a mixed feeling: I like the evolution of having first nothing at hands, then the designator and later the little robotic critter. However the last one got me stuck in two riddles due to not knowing how to actually reach the solution (although I knew what the solution was). Then there was another puzzle that got me stuck due to the controls not being entirely clear in that scene (a ride with the bus). It's a tough game design decision to limit the control related hints and go without text entirely, so I have some respect for it, since it worked out for 95% of the puzzles without hints. All other puzzles were quite good although I usually don't play puzzle games anymore. I like the 2.5D setup of the scenes, as it reminds me of Pandemonium (a Jump'n'Run game from the mid 90's) and adds layers to the puzzles, allowing for more complex puzzle setups in certain scenes. Many puzzles are trial and error puzzles, where the character just gets killed if you do it wrong. It can be frustrating at times, if preparations for the solution takes a minute or two and you need to start over again. My gameplay time of 3 hours is average, yet I would've expected a bit more content after finishing the game.
Nonetheless I liked the game despite the mixed experience regarding the gameplay. If you have been living in the Soviet Union, it might be worth just to experience the scenes and compare it with your own memories of that era.

It's an RTS with almost no micromanagement, in space, in real time, with lots of glittery fighter swarms and pew pew lasers. The races are all interesting and play fairly differently from eachother... seriously, it's hard not to recommend this game, it fills a niche that desperately needs filling.

Everyone spams you with quests and I think you just suddenly win if you make enough friends or something? It's weird, I hate it.), or if you're only interested in vs players (which I know nothing about), I'd pass on this game entirely, even though it looks and sounds really good on paper.
The game is paced so unbelievably poorly that I, almost without exception, regret the time spent after I'm done playing... and it's entirely because of the poor AI, it's too smart where it shouldn't be (you have to level up your ships with combat, but enemies run away from any fight they can't easily win) or too stupid where it should be smarter (space stations aren't considered at all when they're sizing up if they can win a fight), and difficulties do nothing more than tell the computer how much to cheat, and then after a point I guess the AI just decides that you've won, because it never attacks you ever again... but it also doesn't hit the surrender button, and sense it's always running away from you the game becomes just hours and hours of bombing planets wondering if anything is going to happen.
Spoiler alert, no, nothing is going to happen, the moment you max out your fleet you might as well quit. They don't even put up defenses, it just takes forever to kill them all and then you're done.
Not to mention the achievements are some of the lamest busywork tasks I think I've ever seen, "win as [race] researching each and every tech in only [this tree] and nothing else ever", what? That doesn't make any sense, why are there 9 copies of this achievement? This isn't a reason not to buy the game, it just annoys me.
A friend of mine has all the DLC, and so long as he hosts I'm able to play with all the DLC. We haven't exactly tested it exhaustively, but none of the above problems appear to be fixed or even improved by them.

For all of you who don't know it yet: this is the fifth game in the Sea Dogs series (originally named "Корсары").
The previous games are titled as follows:
Sea Dogs 1: "Sea Dogs: An Epic Adventure At Sea" (2000)
Sea Dogs 2: "Pirates of the Caribbean" (2003)
Sea Dogs 3: "Age of Pirates: Caribbean Tales" (2005)
Sea Dogs 4: "Age of Pirates: City of Abandoned Ships" (2009)
Back in the day, "Pirates of the Caribbean" (which got the license of the Disney film) was my favourite pirate game of all time. I had played the classics "Pirates!", "Sea Legends", "Big Sea", "1869: History Experience" and many many more before that, but "Pirates of the Caribbean" was the one to keep me entertained for... well... years, actually. It just had everything: sailing, naval battle, exploration of many different areas of the isles on foot, trading, raiding forts and much more. The soundtrack was absolutely enchanting and while the game had a bit of a console feel to it (and a few bugs), it was just amazing. The two "Age of Pirates" games were great as well, but they had no real main story (at least not to the extent of the predecessor) - instead you could create your own character and just be free in the caribbean. Sounded nice on paper, but playing the game felt a bit redundant.
(My REAL problem with those games was the atrocious StarForce copy protection on the disks. I just don't like rootkits on my PC, so I installed them both exactly once and when I grew tired of them, I uninstalled them, never to turn back to them again. "Better go back to Sea Dogs 2", I thought for many years.)
It's been SEVEN YEARS since the last instalment in the series and now there's finally a brand-new game! And thankfully, it offers everything the great "Sea Dogs 2/Pirates of the Caribbean" offered. Here, we FINALLY have the good old feeling of being back in the caribbean. There's only one character to choose, just as in Sea Dogs 2, and it's great because it comes with a strong story hook (no pun intended).
Of course, the game's engine feels exactly like the one from 2003.
Yeah, the voice acting is borderline silly. And yes, apart from SOME(!) high-res textures, the graphics seem like they are from 2006 or something.
And yes, instead of video sequences that tell the story, you get most of the exposition by dialog boxes (almost like in those anime visual novels).
HOWEVER: This really *IS* what the perfect pirate game should feel like. It's a bit wonky, yes, but it's worth every second of your time, without a doubt. Here's why:
Want to sail your ship from island to island with the possibility of switching to real-time every second? You can!
Want to buy and sell ships, freight, loot and other items, equipping the best weapons and armor to improve your stats? Then do that!
Want to explore all the different islands on foot and discover exciting areas? This game has that, and it's gorgeous!
Want to engage in exciting naval battles with the option of boarding enemy ships, attacking the enemy sailors with swords and guns, advancing to the captain's quarters in order to finish him and take over the ship? That's what this game is best at!! :)
Want to raid cities/forts the same way - by attacking them with your fleet and then finishing them off with swords and guns? Heeeell yeah, go for it!!
Up until now, this game hasn't had all that much of attention (let alone media coverage), which is an absolute shame because it clearly deserves it! These developers DESERVE to finally have real success with their creation! So even if it's a pirate game: don't pirate it! Support these guys!!
If you've ever thought "A pirate I was meant to be, trim the sails and roam the sea...", THIS is the perfect game for you!

First some most usefull hints for newplayers :
Check the keys config first, tutorial is weak on explaining those.
R key : time acceleration x 2, press again to return to normal, cant be key-mapped so dont override.
+ / - : time acceleration/decceleration (up to 8 on sea mode, 3 on land, 2.5 on map, and down to 0.5 everywhere), cant be key-mapped. Decceleration is usefull for hard sword fights.
Fencing mode to feint : SHIFT key (default) + LMB = group attack, + MMB : feint + counterattack, + RMB = feint, can be key-mapped in config.
Normal attack mode : LMB : slash, MMB : heavy attack, RMB : pierce
SPACE : block (default mapping)
E : draw/hide weapon (default mapping)
Q : fire pistol (default mapping)
Enter : action menu key (some people completly miss it to open worldmap when in sea mode ie), use arrow keys to navigate within action menu, left/right for choice of actions, up/down to select ships (when on sea mode).
F2 : all purpose game menus (like the inventory menu -> items)
on world map TAB : free camera map scrolling

Even though the game couldnt get past the main menu I would still like to post a review of my thoughts on this hidden gem.
Sea Dogs: To Each His Own is a smart, sprawling sequel that wisely places an emphasis on freedom and fun. BlackMark Studio take on the Golden Age of Piracy begins in 1715, and is presented with a much-appreciated lighter tone that isn’t afraid to make fun of itself in the name of an entertaining journey.
Sailing across the massive expanse of The Caribbean, exploring gorgeous and unique islands, and getting yourself into all sorts of swashbuckling trouble provide some of the most rewarding and memorable stretches of gameplay I’ve experienced all year.
Even after putting in well over 50 hours with the Xbox 360, Xbox One, Wii U, PC, PlayStation 3, and PlayStation 4 versions, I’m still discovering new islands to explore.
No matter which console you decide to play Sea Dogs: To Each His Own on, you can rest easy knowing that it’s one of the best looking games of 2016. The current-gen versions build upon the gorgeous unity engine by showcasing well-lit, tropical locales and the amazing water effects on the open seas. And on next gen, the experience is even more impressive thanks to minimal loading and maximum draw distances that seem to go on for miles.
The way the camera zooms out when your ship reaches its maximum speed, the speakers bombard you with the sounds of the wind, and the sunset turns blood-orange, is simply amazing. The PS4 and Xbox One versions are nearly identical,Which in turn means there both♥♥♥♥♥♥compaired to the PC version.
The amazing world of Sea Dogs: To Each His Own has kept me gladly occupied for longer than any other game in the series, even though its story isn’t the strongest. At no point in my dozens of hours was I ever at a loss for something to do. Simply sailing wherever the wind takes me and seeing what sort of trouble I can get into is a complete joy.
Beyond the underwhelming main campaign, Sea Dogs: To Each His Own delivers a world brimming with gorgeous places to go, amazing secrets to discover, and nefarious pirates to stab.
All and all the game would be an amazing experience to have on steam if I could get past the main menu. 11/2 Do not buy this piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥

I had this game on my wishlist for quite some time and I honestly couldn't bring myself to buy it. I do enjoy spacey-shootey things, but that whole 'it's kinda like naval warfare' gameplay was not really convincing me. So it was on sale several times, and every time I saw that 'game on sale' email I was like 'yay' and then 'oh, rebel galaxy, hm'. Finally, a few days ago I was so bored that I thought I'd give it a try, keeping in mind the lenient return policy, so what could go wrong?
Well, for starters, I was wrong. This game is more fun you than I could have ever imagined, especially for that price.
But let's begin with the cons, since that is always what I like to read first. While the graphics are really nice, the character models are sub-par. Then again, they might have invented cloning in that universe, so it might be perfectly natural to have a gazillion space stations with the same bartender. or he's working more than other people. Bartending doesn't pay much, after all, so yay for realism.
It also is a bit  of a grind to get started, no way of cheating your way to a better ship. While that is not necessarily a con, it does mean that you spend your first few hours desperately trying to find a station that buys yourt goods for the highest price, or you do missions which dont pay that much in the beginning.
My last issue, if you can call my ♥♥♥♥♥ing that, would be that I truly and honestly miss a way to see which turret is placed where on the ship, because you might end up buying something super duper heavy hitting laser gizmo thing, and then you wonder why you never see it firing. Well, you might just ended up placing it underneath your ship, and since not many enemies go there (they better not, the buggers), it's not of much use there.
Now, the whole game is so much fun, I ended up playing it till VERY late at night, something I rarely do, simply forgetting the time. Want to be a fighter for good? a pirate? merchant? all of these? well you can, nothing is ever set in stone and you can more or less do what you want. trading is done well, a stations have fluid demands and you can't just always buy and sell at the same stations. 'Events' kind of help you plan a little, but not in a gamebreaking way. . So that keeps it interesting. Fights are fun and not always easy even with good weapons, sometimes you might need to run from them and come back later when you geared up. Special drops sometimes give you that edge you need, some special weapon or gear you cant buy, also a nice touch. The whole ship/speed/damage/defense whatchamacallit is easy enough to understand, but complex enough to keep it fun.
But while the game as a whole simply works and is super entertaining, the soundtrack is the real selling point here. You constantly feel like you are part of the firefly 'verse' and boy, they just nailed it with it. Also, if you don't like it, though you are clearly weird if you dont, they let you use your own music to listen to while you blast huge dreadnoughtships to smithereens.
Rebel Galaxy is one of those few examples of bought for ten bucks, would have gladly paid fifty.

A nice simple idea reasonably well executed.
I encountered a few physics glitches that occasionally caused stuttering, sometimes severe, once requiring killing the process. Overall though it played fine which is good enough for me - getting games which allow such open game play bug free is no easy task. As it was most of the problems I saw were in part a result of scenes that I'd made unnecessarily complex, usually by mistake.
Level design is adequate though I would have liked to see more use made of some of the features such as switches & rotating platforms.
Difficulty ranges from easy to requiring some thought. I took four hours to finish the game, but have a tendency to play slowly & I also avoided using hints, so there's maybe 2-3 hours in the game for most players. Although some of the levels presented a challenge there seemed to be fewer of these compared to the easy; I'd have much preferred a more uniform spread of difficulty.
Level difficulty also seems to be more or les random. There is certainly no clear linear progression of increasing challenge. I feel this should have been addressed during testing simply by reordering the levels somewhat.
That all said, if none of the above issues existed I'd have expected to pay two or three times as much for this game as is being asked. The full price is more than fair for the fun offered in exchange by this simple physics sandbox puzzle game.

After reading reviews about this game being successor to the freelancer classic, I bought the game. The first few hours of game was quite disappointing as the 2D flight mode and the lukeworm story can hardly convince me that this game is even comparable to freelancer. After 5 hours, however, the game became a little more interesting as weapons and ships are unlocked and some of the missions are quite interesting. I have to admit the graphics are good, not superb, but comparable to the freelance --- a shame on its own as the freelancer was a game almost two decades old. The combat system was not inspiring but acceptable and admittedly quite fun to play. Just as I thought the game is getting better, it quickly revealed to me that this is no more than a freelancer game in its core repacked with better graphics and a toned down 2D flight mode. The game soon degenerates into a struggling effort to complete repetitive missions to gain enough money to upgrade ships and components that are ridiculously expensive and are so for no other apparent reasons than to compel the player to complete those stupid missions. So far I think it is unrealistic to make enough money to buy any of those higher level weapons and ships with trade alone. The difficulty associated with some of these missions are also questionable as some missions would see you quickly swarmed by a horde of overpowered enemies ships while other missions give ridiculously high reward for the simpler tasks.
In conclusions, I believe this is a game suitable, in fact I would use the word ideal, for killing your excessive pastime at a moderate price. However, to comment that this game may even aspire to be of the equal to freelancer is a severe overstatement.

BUY THIS GAME! Really, it's one of a kind, this is an AMAZING game that will entertain you for hundreds of hours. It is a huge space trading simulator with gorgeous scenery, engaging storyline, puzzling situations, deep immersion, with several "game modes" from campaign to chain quests and freeplay.
You will probably want to know why I would recommend this game if it has such a low score, right? Well, it launched at 2013 with lots of bugs, but now, 4 years later, it is at 4.10 with a 4.22 beta version almost out, so the developers care and fix stuff. So, one reason is gone now - initial version was buggy, but there's more to it. It is in the same universe as previous Egosoft games - X2, X3, etc. - so people expected pretty much an overhaul of previous games, but this one was VERY different taking on a new approach (initially it would not even be in the X Universe, they would begin a new franchise but due to the bad repercussion of this decision they backtracked from it) -- so it received a huge influx of bad scores because people did not like being able to pilot just one ship, not liking the "highway" structures, being unable to release build spots when they destroyed stations and some other stuff pertaining to the kind of simulation.
But do these complaints have merits? I don't think so. Having just one ship allows for a better plot to be developed, with that ship receiving a lot of credit for being "special", and the NPCs mentioning it and relating to other events. Also, even though you do not pilot them directly, you can command other ships and arrange them in fleets even. The simulation is different and "fixes" a lot of the problems with the simulation in previous X games, and the fact that now you can enter stations and walk on it in third person and interact with NPCs adds a whole new dimension to the immersion and experience of the game. In fact, I find myself unable to get immersed on other games after being so used to this aspect of X: Rebirth.
And the experience, ah, the experience. X: Rebirth is a delicious game, where you can stop doing all other stuff and then land on one of your capital ships in one extreme of the galaxy, then ordering it to go to the other extreme just to appreciate the trip and scenery from the panoramic bridge... I did that half a dozen times to "wait" for some trading operations to be completed (remember, this is a simulation, things take time and you can get close and see the trade happening, with ships docking to stations and cargo being transported from them) and to be entertained at the same time. What's more, the music is soothing and relaxing (when not im combat) and for me it has even therapeutic value, I get calmer and less anxious after playing the game.
The game even changed my mind: I bought it for the campaign, I liked playing on a rail, I wouldn't care about the freeplay modes. That changed when I finished the campaign, after the cinematic ending the game throws you right back at where you were and you can continue it indefinitely. I took a shot at it and went 80+ hours after the ending... So I got quite addicted to it, you can say.
Of course, even now, the game is not perfect. There are some minor rough edges and being a simulation, there is a good amount of small operations which means grinding. But just as in real life where you buy stuff to diminish manual labor, you can use mods in X: Rebirth to decrease the amount of micromanagement and automate tasks; and this game has an EXCELLENT documentation, support and resources for modding, so there are TONS of mods to enhance your game.
To be frank the worst thing in the game for me are things that get in the way of the story:

Primal Carnage is a rather bland multiplayer game and I really don't recommend you trying this game out.
In Primal Carnage you play either as humans or dinosaurs and you fight it out on maps where you have objectives on each side. Like escaping with a helicopter for humans and for Dinosaurs you have to stop the humans from escaping.
It might sound good on paper, but once you start playing you find that the game is rather bland in almost every aspect.
I've played more with humans and not with dinosaurs, because I find that the dinosaurs are rather hard to control and to master, unlike the humans where you just point a gun and shoot.
I honestly thought the game was rather fun at first. It's also has a really active community, nothing amazing, but it's not dead even with a new game available on steam. But the more I played the more I noticed big flaws in gameplay mechanics.
First of all the hit detection for the weapons feels off. I felt most of my times I missed my target completely. The only really accurate gun is the Pathfinders shotgun who can take out enemies in just a few hits (not the bigger dinosaurs). The same goes for dinosaurs, I found that most of the dinosaurs also have terrible hit detection and even when I got up close it felt like I did no damage what so ever.
I also experienced some lag even though my internet connection is fine and I can play all my multiplayer games without a problem and I don't know why this game is acting up.
Graphically the game is also not really amazing, at points it actually looks downright ugly.
Like most Multiplayer games, I also think that Primal Carnage could benefit from an XP system to keep you playing. I get that MP games don't need that to be fun, but I think this could greatly benefit from an XP system.
Some of the map designs are outright awful, it feels like most of these maps were made to tailor for one side as some of the objectives are closer to spawns and it's sometimes harder to capture them since you kill an enemy and it respawns in a few seconds and comes back and kills you since he doesn't have to travel a big distance. Now I don't want them to walk from the start of the map to the end of the map, but some distance from the objective could be nice.
In general I can only recommend Primal Carnage on a very very big discount and check it out only if you're interested in it. I had some fun, but I'd rather spend my time playing other games, so I'm shelving this, not to mention that Primal Carnage Extinction exists which is a newer version of this game. Now I don't know if that's good, but it's a better idea to get that than this.
Final Rating:
5/10
Pros:
+ Fun Gameplay
+ Some classes are fun to use
Cons:
- Hit detection is flawed
- Map Designs are flawed
- Get's Boring after a while

First off:

Now then . . .
I'm a sucker for any meta, 4th wall breaking game. This being no exceptions. I dare even call it the best in it's field, whatever field that would be. The amount of content for such a simple concept is surprising.
For those who don't know, this game follows a "Choose-your-adventure" type deal, which branching paths. Each path leads to a different outcome, or ending. Some are as simple as closing a door, while others require you to push a button for 4 hours. Some of them are just funny jokes, while others make you question the game's story. Is the narrator in control of the story? Is Stanley crazy? Is this just a game with pre-determined outcomes (yeah, but in the game it's more meaningful)? It's an odd journey that gets more and more confusing the more endings you find. Even without that, there's also a ton of secrets and hidden dialogue you will miss first time through. Heck, the achievements are a game on their own.
The Narrator, Kevan Brighting, makes this game. The way he acts toward the player, the things he say, the way he speaks is just amazing. It's like Glados from Portal, they are just a delight to listen to (even though they insult you).
That being said, it leads me to the point that determines my final rating: Is this a game?
"Of course it is? How can it not be? You can move around, interact with things, how is this not a game?" most would say. But, it's very similar to a visual novel, but you just move the character instead of text saying he moved. Once you've watched a video with all the endings, there isnt much more to it. There are secrets, but they dont lead to anything other than more narrator dialogue. This isnt a bad thing, but it really shows how little of a "game" this is. And for $15 thats a bad thing to be.
I didnt get this for 15 bucks, I only paid $4, almost 1/5 it's original amount. It is 100% worth that price. But $15? That's a little too much. However, like I said at the beginning, if you dont know what happens PLEASE BUY IT. I promise you the experience of playing it is well worth $15. But if you already do, I can't say there any reason to buy it. And the fact that it's almost 5 years old at this point (there's even an achievement for that!) I can't imagine many people still don't know about it's existence. But I really wish I could have played this first hand and gotten the experience of the humor myself, without knowing everything there is to know about it (because I loved it so much without even playing it).
And if you're still iffy on buying it, please check out the FREE demo, which is an experience of it's own and has virtually nothing to do with the main game (making it an awful demo, but an amazing demo).
I'm done praising this game, thanks for reading.

1st of all I'll start by saying that I'm Romanian, so I'm biased about the feeling and atmosphere of the game. I've bought the game because I loved Inside and Limbo and wanted to support our fellow devs. What I got was a good sidescroller puzzle if you're not familiar with comunist history of Romania, and a piece of art if you were born and raised under the regime.
Technical stuff is pretty straightforward, nice minimalistic graphics and very well done atmosphere, decent and "opressive" music and sounds, polished and good controls. The overall game is very good, especially if you liked abovementioned Limbo/Inside titles.
Now, for the feeling, this is really something that will bring back memories. There are many references to our history and in the end of the game you'll have a nice surprise ( Spoiler alert:
)
The stores in the game are actual name of stores  from our comunist era, but written in reverse. The names are actual foods like Lapte = Milk or Carne = Meat, those were considered very high valuable commodities in the last years of communist regime, and very scarce and hard to find. Most of the people were real hungy and I remember dreaming of a chicken steak sometimes.
There's a silhouette of a fairy wheel at some point which reminds me of the one of the few entertainments we had as kids, back in the days.
The workers looking at a VCR in the underground, the crowded bus, the "Export" labeled boxes ...all are part of our painful history, and most of the people playing the game, won't get it. :)
And those are just several of the many many references across all chapters. It brings back memories, melancoly and sadness, but I guess we, romanians, are well versed in living with those feelings.
10/10 from me, probably an 6-7-8/10 for a foreigner.

While visual and gameplay comparisons with last year's excellent INSIDE are almost inevitable, Black The Fall succeeds in creating a world all its own and a satisfying experience.
The game builds its dystopian fiction from failed communism taken to extreme totalitarianism, ominous architecture surveyed by deadly armed cameras, an impoverished land left to abandon, and overfed commanders controlling hordes of brainwashed masses that scream at the sight of the Statue of Liberty.
Your unidentified character walks forward through factories and treacherous platforms, resolute yet nonchalant, after breaking away from his enslaved group. Avoid the red lights and fat middle managers. Point lasers to manipulate obedient slave workers and enable machinery. Find and reactivate a helpful mechanical companion.
Other areas may be a little too punishing due to finicky controls. Solving certain puzzles almost invariably requires getting caught by every possible danger as the only way to figure out how to avoid them next time. Respawn.
Timing is everything in a few scenes to the point where it becomes disheartening to figure out on which pixel the game expects the action performed, and getting the precise execution right. Respawn.
Black The Fall is definitely worth a trip through its inglorious and disturbing vision of a world gone wrong. It may not be as polished or surprising as its near-perfect rival INSIDE but it follows nicely in its footsteps, while bringing enough diversity, an evocative mood and very decent gameplay.
