As promised a long time ago, but unfortunately forgotten in the meantime, I hereby update my review. Apparently, the solution for me consisted in simply using DX9 instead of DX10. After this change, no more crashes have occurred. Therefore, I also changed my review to 'recommended' instead of 'not recommended'. I shall leave my original review below for reference.
______________________________________________________________________
I regret to say, stay away from this game. While the game itself is awesome, it is not really enjoyable unless by 'enjoyable' you understand piling up random crashes. I have actually finished the game because in my first playthrough, it would only occasionally crash (at random), but the crashes got more frequent until it became impossible for me to even reach the main menu. Now, if I were the only one to have encountered this issue, I could still recommend the game to you, but the internet, including the Steam forums, is full of people with all kinds of OS's and hardware setups who have encountered -- and continue to do so -- the same issue. It is not fun to play a game, regardless of how good it may be, if you need to worry all the time that it may crash any second. By the way, none of the suggested solutions I have found (and there are quite a few) have helped.
Once again, it pains me not to be able to recommend a great game (with respect to the artwork and the gameplay) like this, but I need to make clear one more time: the technical issues spoil the fun completely.
Update:
I may finally have found the solution to the crashes. Apparently, though I need to retry this with the DLC, the crashing issues are simply caused by the auto-save's tendency to get corrupted. If this happens, not only will the game crash, but it will also prevent you from getting to the main menu.
So far, the following procedure has proved reliable:
(1) When going to a new level, the game will automatically create an auto-save file. Wait for it to finish this, a message will be displayed, reading, 'Game saved.'
(2) Press Esc in order to go to the menu.
(3) Create a manual save file.
(4) Press Esc again and delete the auto-save file.
I kept doing this throughout my latest playthrough and had no crashes after deleting the auto-save file for the first time.
The next step will be to test this on the DLC Minerva's Den. An update will follow soon. If the method described above should prove applicable to the DLC as well, I am going to change my review to a recommendation.

A pretty solid twin stick shooter. Controls are very responsive and Not Important (our anti-hero) is relatively easy to control.

The graphics and art style are very nice and most buildings and objects in the game are destructible, which shows off the quality physics engine.
People whine about the subject matter while others just roll their eyes at how edgy the game presents itself. The thing is... The game knows it's being edgy and runs with it. Just watch the trailers.
Can you take anything Not Important says seriously? I sure can't. Does this game make me want to shoot people? Absolutely not.
It's a blast to play and great stress relief. You'd be lying if you said you don't shoot civilians for fun and stress relief in games like GTA or Saints' Row. Hatred is exactly that, expect without any real restrictions on your fun.
My only cons are that civilian character models are very limited, so expect to see the same faces everywhere you go. The weapon and environment variety is also lacking. Lastly, the AI for civilians is pretty stupid. They will constantly run towards you, run into fires, and can somehow sense where you are through walls before you even start shooting, which really breaks the immersion.

First, let me say that I have played X2 - X3 with all the expansions. My issues were similar to other players who are mostly casual game players. The learning curve was a bit too steep for me, and it was taking me a very long time to get things done. I read all the reviews to X-Rebirth and was reluctant to purchase another game I may not even play for more than a few hours. However, when I learned they were doing a VR version, I just had to give in and take a close look.
I curently use Homido V2 with my iphone and my Xbox gamepad connected to my gaming PC. I am able to play a few VR games with fairly good quality graphics. (Ultra Chess VR, Magician's Gambit, Everspace, and Space Rift).
I decided to perchase the X-reburth VR version and Unfortunately at first,  it wouldn't work with my setup, So, I purchased the non VR version and decided to check it out in case I was able to play the VR in the future. (I was able to play in VR - cool stuff!)
Having said all that, I gave it a shot in the Free Play mode, since that's the type of mode I love to play. At first, I was completely lost and had no clue what I was doing, although the gamepad support was excellent - just a matter of getting used to the accelerator and the firing. I kept firing instead of accelerating.
I watched a short Youtube video on the super basic stuff and before I knew it was flying around and landing on different space stations and finding stuff in lockers, boxes, and cases. I even was able to land on large ships! How cool is that?
Then eventually I made it to the travel lanes.
It was Grand Theft Auto V all over again but in space. In Grand Theft Auto I played many hours before getting on with any missions and had to do about a million taxi rides to make money. In X-Rebirth i'm scavenging the space stations and large ships to find free hidden gems and scraps to sell for credits.
Eventually, I will get to the real trading and missions, but at least i'm moving around and doing stuff. A lot more fun I think. At least, I will be ready when I can play the VR version.
I have no complaints, although there is a redundancy in the spacestations and ships you board and move around in, and will get old pretty fast after I do several hundred hours of exploring, but this keeps the games overhead and size to a minimum and leaves room for the other features in the game.
The graphics are adequate although not as realistic as Grand Theft Auto V, but I am very happy the way the game has been made so far and hope they continue to improve it.
Finally, this is an X game I can actually play for more than two hours or less. I have done 7 hours alrready as I write this review.
Update:
After close to 100 hours of game play, here are my game tips for those just starting out.
If you want to speed up the game a bit then subscribe to the extensions in the workshop to this game, just be careful and read the author notes - not all extensions are compatible with each other. Also use the SETA . Keep in mind SETA may not always be available when you are near your own ships or near serious action.  Getting the jump drive helps but you need to have some experience with the maps feature, and getting the jump drive from a mission may not be that easy.
1.) You should first work on upgrading your ship. It will make life easier for you. Check the YouTube videos on how to upgrade the skunk.
2.) The easiest way to get credits is to do the missions until you can buy trade ships, although I found myself doing missions anyway to keep up with the credit hungry stations you build if you get that far in the game.
3.) I found the easiest missions to do was the transport missions, you are basically doing taxi rides, although these don’t pay much. The destroy minefields mission pays much better, but you may get some damage to your ship. The Kill missions pay really well but requires you to destroy a capitol ship. You need to know what parts of the ship to destroy to save time and servive the mission. I haven’t tried the others missions so I can’t comment on them.
4.) if you are doing trading then get the trade updates for each sector you find - Best is to watch a YouTube video on trading to get the specifics on the trading feature of the game. Purchase the XL ship that can transport anything not just energy, bulk, or containers. The Home of Light DLC has a shipyard with the ship I’m talking about in Sector 8 or near that area. There may be another shipyard in another system with the same ship.
5.) the stations require a lot of credits and can get complicated when expanding, you have to make sure you placed the manager and all the needed personnel. Each station may also require a specific specialist to get the station to function at its best. There is quite a bit to know when it Comes to building stations especially if your doing it on your own and not part of a mission. The build missions pay well and gives you a location to build. I haven’t tried a build mission yet.
6.) You will need at least close to a million credits to begin your trading empire with some loss added to your experience - this includes plenty of military protection.  You can slowly build your way up with a lot less credits. It all depends on your style of play and how much time Your willing to take to build yourself up. A couple hundred thousands credits can get you a trading ship to start. You just have to remember that the more cargo lifter drones you have the quicker the trading goes at the stations, and the more construction drones you have the quicker the repairs on your traiding ship if it gets damaged, and so on.
I have not had the chance to try the mining aspect of this game yet so I can’t comment on that.
7.) Two million credits will give you a great start with plenty of trading ships and several stations as well as all the destroyers and fighters you need to protect your empire.
8.) For the more advanced player, I highly recommend renaming all Your ships. Your trading ships should all have unique names or something to tell them apart. It makes it easier to locate the ship when they are being attacked. Or if your trading ship is carrying more than 10 million worth of cargo and you want to personally escort them. Also, learn how to assign ship control to stations, battleships, and commanders. This keeps everything in groups and easier to manage.
For eaxample: say you want an army of fighter and battleships to escort you to a major battle field. It’s easier to have a few commanders to give orders to than to each and every ship on your squadron.
And, assigning a battle ship or fighters to a defense officer gives them the resources needed to protect your empire. There is probably more to all This since it’s something I recently learned how to do.
Each player will require a different amount of credits depending on how they play the game. Best is to read the forums on the best places to start constructing your own stations if your not doing the build missions.
YouTube and the forums are the best places to speed up the learning curve.
Enjoy the game.

Betrayer is a first person adventure game mainly in black, white, and red which sets in 17th century. You'll arrive in a land lacking of people and you'll have to find out what happened in that place. Although the game starts in black, white, and red, it can be adjusted to color, although imo, it's easier to play it in default color.
This game's bgm gives off eerie vibe with some environmental sfxs such as rustling grass and breezing winds. Some sfxs can surprise you with its sudden noise, especially when it's combined with the eerie graphics. Personally, i think that this game's music is one of the best part of the game.
Although the game doesn't have an AAA style graphics, the black, white, and red color gives of an eerie atmosphere perfectly. However, i have to admit that the graphics look weird after you change the default color to a more colorful setting. The in game text might be quite small, although it's still readable.
The game has a separate story in each area, although the story in the last few areas stay connected with each other. The game mainly tells about betrayals which are done by the people living in the area, which are resulting in death. There are also some clues which are written in a piece of paper about anything that happened in the area. This game doesn't have a fixed ending which makes you to have to interpret the ending and some part of the story by yourself.
You'll arrive in a land with no people and all you have in your hand is a bow. The game will start teaching you a few controls, although it missed some controls, such as the sniper mode which is initiated with right click. Although the game teaches you some of the game controls, i ended up forgetting most of it.
You can do stealth kills in this game which can be either done from close or afar. There are some items which can help you to not getting noticed by your enemies and there is also a wind which will help you to blend in with the surroundings.
In this game, you'll mainly collect some things in the area and kill some enemies. Most of the area requires you to do the same thing which can make the game quite boring.
The game environment is very gloom and dark, which sometimes can surprise you when something shows out of nowhere. The battle sfx can also surprise you, although you'll get used with it in no time.
Because you'll mainly use long ranged weapons in this game, ammos can be quite costly. I didn't know that you can get some ammo by dying, which will help me to upgrade my weapon instead of spending the cash for ammo. Some of the ammo that you are using will also remains the area, although sometimes the ammo will stuck in some places which makes you have to rebuy the ammo.
I experienced some frame skips in this game. It's quite annoying, especially when you want to snipe the enemies from afar. The mouse also runs slowly and i'll get more frame skips if i try to make it faster. The game also loads very slowly when it's transitioning from and to areas. The game lags after i'm alt tabbing and it will be not responding if i'm alt tabbing for too long. The weapon can also fire randomly by itself when you change maps.
There are 5 kinds of weapons in the game, which are crossbows, shortbows, longbows, guns, and muskets. All of them have their own strengths and weaknesses which can be covered with charms, tomahawk (mid range single targeted weapon), explosives (mid range area targeted weapon), and melee attacks (which is mainly used for stealth kills). The charms can give you some buffs, such as health boost and movement speed boost. There are 3 unique weapons for each type of weapons which can be considered as ultimate weapons. All of them has different stats which can be chosen based on your play types.
This game is focused on two worlds, this world and the other world, where the spirits resides. You'll have to travel between both worlds to uncover the mystery in the land you are in.
Lastly, you can adjust this game difficulty with 3 difficulty settings in the options, with normal being the default.
Pros:
- 5 different type of weapons
- 15 unique weapons
- 3 difficulty settings
- Great atmosphere
Cons:
- You'll do almost the same thing in every maps
- Frame skips
- Loads very slow

CONS:

If you're a fan of being an elite soldier fight for freedom and destroying evil dictators don't buy this game.
Don't get me wrong it's a good game just not for everyone.
Story: The game takes place in the fictional city of Vysena in the republic of Vysenac during a civil war and follows a group of civilians trying to survive. The game itself is the tales of the survival of these civilians and seems to lack a clear straight forward narrative, but some key events will occur no matter what. One example is when two children walk up to your 'little patch of heaven', asking for medicine to treat their sick mother. The Game does have an ending but it can only be achived by surviving the whole war.
Graphics: The game looks good, if you're a fan of ruined buildings, black, grey, abandoned tanks and other depressing stuff. The art style seems to resemble a very well done pencil drawing with the only colours being different shades of grey. In short the game looks good with a high resolution.
Gameplay: The gameplay consitis of two phases; day and night. During the day you allocate food and medicine, let people sleep, craft items like beds or weapons and make sure not to use up all your supplies. The night is the ONLY period of time when you can go and scavenge for supplies outside of your 'safe haven', (this is because snipers pervent you from leaving during the day). You decide who will scavenge, who will guard the base and who gets to sleep, your 'safe haven' can and will get raided. Weither or not the raid gets well for the raiders is determined by who's on guard and if they have a weapon. When scavenging you search rubble and bins, and use tools to open doors or clear debris. If there hostiles nearby you can try and sneak past them which involves hding in dark areas, and moving carefully. When it comes to combat you will either run up to them and beat the living hell out of them, or you take cover and shoot them. If you sneak up behind an enemy you can preform a sneak attack, but unless the character you're playing as has combat experience, it won't be an instant kill. Stealth is highly recommended in my opinion, but if you do attack someone kill them quickly and after they're dead either run or hide. This is beacuse killing someone makes lots of noise, this will attract enemys. But know that any wounds a character suffers will need to be bandaged and left to heal.
Edit: as of update 1.3 to the game You can now create your own scenario's. You can pick how many locations you can loot (minimum of 13), certain features about these areas, when the game will end, when, for how long and the severtiy of winter is. You can also choose the characters you get at the start, the difficulty and it allows you to create your own characters.
Final verdict: The game is well made and is good if you like a dark, depressing and somewhat realistic, look into the life of civilians during a war. I sum it up as a zombie apocalypse without the Zombies. The only problem I face is a lack of a manual save & the fact it only auto-saves when you return to your 'safe haven', overall i give it a 9.5/10.

I could only imagine if EA were to acquire the license to make Jurassic Park games and work some of that Battlefront magic to do an upscale Jurassic Park FPS. One can dream… until then, the next best thing is Primal Carnage.
The concept is simple… the game pits a team of player controlled dinosaurs against a team of player controlled humans, and they battle it out in a deathmatch.
Firstly, I want to praise the game for the art and sound design alone. The dinosaur models and the maps look great for an indie game, real impeccable direction here. The dinosaurs look very similar to a well-known blockbuster dinosaur franchise; right down to the different sounds the dino’s make, but are just different enough to avoid litigation.
The game is filled with intense action and frightful moments. Nothing is quite as heart-pounding as trying to outrun a tyrannosaurus rex that’s only a couple of footsteps behind you, breathing down your neck and you escape by the skin of your teeth; or how about you’re grouped up with a few of your teammates, cornered by raptors that dart in and out of the surrounding foliage, picking you off one at a time. Then there are scenes of just pure chaos! You never really know how each match will unfold, but every time it’s an exhaustive experience. There are some people that can binge play it like any other FPS, but for me I can only handle so many matches in one sitting.
Although there are only three modes, I feel like the game makes the most out of either of them, and of course there is the unspoken roleplay experience which there is several servers for that too.
The game will also decide who will become a dinosaur or human, and the most popular servers do a switch halfway through a session so that everyone gets a shot at either side. Sometimes if the teams are unbalanced, you can request to switch or the game will “auto-balance” the teams.
There are a total of 6 playable dinosaurs and 5 humans, all of which are balanced so that each character has a specific role to play, but the game also lends itself to loners who just want to kill.
Now, IMO, Primal Carnage is one of the better looking indie games I’ve come across and it has a very high level of fit and finish, but it’s not a perfect game… Like just about all indie games on Steam, even though it looks good, PC still seems like a half-baked idea. Of course PC isn’t without it’s blemishes as an indie game. The devs did cut corners in content, offering us only THREE modes (Deathmatch, Get to the Chopper, Capture the Egg) to play and only 6 dinosaurs (Including Spinosaurus, only available at certain stages in certain modes it seems)! There’s also no single player, no story mode, no NPCs or AI, and you must have an internet connection to play.
The other thing about PC is that there usually is only a handful of servers available, and only a couple have a decent ping. The best servers tend to only run the Docks map and the Utility Base map. The player base is also mixed, so new players will be thrown to the wolves right off the bat, and many of those wolves take FULL advantage of any exploit they can. This is a frustrating situation that was never addressed, like implementing some kind of rank system so that new players can enjoy the game with similarly skilled players, and not tossed into a deathmatch with players that have over 1,000 hours logged.
PC uses the Unreal engine, so the gameplay is very quick and very twitchy. It doesn’t need much to run it at a respectable resolution. For the first two years I’ve played PC, I did so on a computer with a GTX 555 and i-5 Processor with 8-gigs of RAM, and it performed decently even on high graphic settings. The game is a bit buggy, so expect it to crash from time to time.
To wrap up, Primal Carnage is one of the unsung heroes of Steam that just never met its true potential – or at least for me it is, anyway. It’s a prime example of what Steam should be used for. It’s  great fun, great bang for the buck.

this game has a lot of potential, but it's too hesitant to embrace its ridiculousness. it's sitting between literally showing what the player's avatar is doing and showing what they imagine they're doing. we get to turn into flying plane-totems, but we can't see our bullets. we can get thrown into the air by powerups, but we can barely jump.
just picked this up. i've been tracking it since greenlight, and i thought it was a great concept, but now that i've played, i'm going to have to say the implementation's not great (at the moment). in fact, if nothing changes, i'll probably never play it again. i'm still giving it a positive review because it's in early access, i think it's an excellent concept, and it could be an incredible game, but it just needs some work.
my major issue with the game is that it is inconsistent. the main, underlying idea is that you're a group of people pretending to be airplanes, but there's the question of how that actually works out: for instance, on the less literal side, the game fits into a kind of pretend-magic system, where the player becomes a member of the cult of the wind, and sees their imagined dogfights as reality. on this side of things are several of the powerups: for instance, we can turn into totemic airplanes for a short duration, collect speed bursts, and get catapulted up into the air. we hear plane sounds, gunfire, and plane crashes, but we experience the joke of the game through our character models: they remind us that we're still just people running about pretending to be planes.
on the more literal side (cf. the game's description in the store), we as players see the real world, and we're not inside our characters heads. they're stuck off in their own worlds, playing a game that we can't see, so we just witness what they're physically doing. they're running around, jumping to no great heights (there's a little bit of floatiness, but nothing much), miming bullet fire, and are just generally limited by human capabilities.
now, the game could go either way; we could either see a game that's very literal about the player perspective, where we no longer turn into airplanes or get shields, or we could see a game that actually puts us in the head of a cultist. right now, the player can
but they cannot see their bullets fly. they can get thrown forty feet into the air, but they can't jump more than a normal person. the player is limited also by the fuel resource; if you run out (without resupplying at randomly-selected powerups), you die. i hope the game fits into the second idea, because i won't be playing a game where people pretend to be airplanes: i could do that at my house. i want to be inside someone's head when they turn into an airplane and fly around.

Before I begin I would like to point out I made this video on day one when it was very much early access with a very limited map and other features range.
So when I first saw this game I wasn't quite sure what to expect from it; I thought the concept was very interesting and I liked the cult story behind it where these people basically worship old recked airplanes. If you want to find out a little more in regards to the features then you should check out this guide:
Visually the game has a very basic simple cartoony visual style. This isn't necessarily a bad thing and helps it to fit in with the Art Deco style the developers were trying to adopt, the Art Deco style is indisputable with the various stereotypical Art Deco looks around the map(s). The clean look of the game helps you focus on the targets such as enemy fighters or flags. Graphics could generally be improved with increased polygon counts on various items around the maps.
Upon reading the guide for the game I was expecting the weapon noises to sound like people saying "pew pew pew" as we all did when we were kids. I was dissapointed to hear that the sounds are actually just ordinary stock shooting sounds not made with a human voice at all. I think this is something that has been overlooked and could possibly have removed some of the anticipated charm
Unfortunately on release the game only has one and a half maps. I say 1.5 because there is a finished and prototype map. The prototype map looks like something quickly thrown together just to get something else shipped with the game upon release. I find it odd that if the game has a map editor they couldn't get a few more maps finished before releasing it on Steam.
Temple of the Wind is the finished map and is quite pleasing on the eye. Generally it doesn't give you a feel of a cult setting, it seems far too nice, but due to it being a deserted temple you can get the impression that all isn't quite what it seems. It has 3 different levels to it all of which are accessible via staircases/elevators or jumping or with various speed / jump upgrades.
Sky-Top Prototype is a half finished map with no textures. It works with a capture the flag game mode where there is a neutral flag at one end that both teams have to run / jump their way to and then bring it back to the base. It still needs some work but I imagine the devs are working on this as I type.
There is a nice selection of weapons and upgrades that can be picked up from various "kites" within the maps. These provide power ups such as extra jumping abilities or extra speed from quicker or more powerful weapons and one really insane rail gun. I think the weapons are fairly nicely balanced and I look forward to finding all the ways to counter each weapon / upgrade!
There appears to only be one / two game mode(s) so far in Cult of the Wind and this is Capture the Flag combined with deathmatch. Neither is seperate from the other so technically I feel there is only one game mode thus far.
It is possible to seperate the two game modes during server set up by inflating the amount of flags you require and reducing the amount of kills needed to win and wice versa. This isn't a perfect set up and it would be nice to see some more game modes in the near future.
From my experience so far there isn't too many people playing the game just yet, but of course it is brand new and this will probably change quite soon, at least I hope so. I have managed to get into a server with just me and my friend but also both of us got into a server with other people without any issues which was very reassuring. It is definitely a game designed to be played with multiple people in the server all shooting at each other.
As I mentioned at the beginning this review was written on day one with only 2 hours experience of gameplay. I'm sure there will be many more updates coming out soon. I will recommend this game based on the anticipation of what is to come in the future. I think if you are going to buy the game try to get some of your friends on board too! The game is looking good and I hope more maps come out in the very near future!
If you would like to see visuals of how the game looks and some of the gameplay features that are not shown in the trailer I have a video on YouTube which may help you.

It took me a while to get used to this game, but what swayed me was at least it has the modern elements of making it an enjoyable game.
What's good (in comparison to Blood Money for single player only as I have not played Contracts mode):
+Graphics
+Sound
+Voice acting
+detail in environments
+Able to switch from dual to single silverballers instantly as well as apply silencer
+More combat abilities (with good animations) to kill (e.g. simple choke from behind, using objects like hammers or knifes for instant kills, hand to hand combat (instead of pushing or headbutting ppl in Blood Money)
+dragging bodies looks realistic and you can dump two bodies instead of one in hiding spots
+instinct allows you to mark enemies in slow time and then execute them in normal speed so it looks badass
+weapon sounds are good
+good variety of handguns and assault rifles
+the impact you feel when you headshot someone is nice.
+Long single player
debatable whether it should be in the game:
Instinct mode allows you to see through walls which I thought was a little unfair and just unecessarily unrealistic in a hitman game
what I didn't like
-Total change in execution of missions, as it's story-driven. One level continues after another story-line wise. Didn't feel like a hitman since the levels you experience are tied to the main story. No more independent missions just to kill a target for money.
-Targets for assassination feel just spontaneous, because of the previous point that it's story driven
-enemies can see you quite easily (although I suppose that's adding to realism)
-no instant save system, only checkpoints which are found and activated manually throughout a level. Loading a checkpoint results in all enemies respawning again even after killing them
-don't get to pick out arsenal of weapons before each mission
-As the game is story-driven, from what I can remember the majority of missions involves you infiltrating places you're not suppose to be in so there's no being a hitman in a public place full of civilians to get the job done. You can't be detected. So that's what i meant about being like a spy rather than a hitman
-disguises are almost useless as anyone else of the same disguise can see through it unless you use your instinct meter (which is filled up by completing objectives, subduing or killing people, etc.)
-hand to hand combat: you press the SPACE BAR and some combination of A,S,Q,D (can't remember which keys it could be, but in the area of the keyboard) in quickly succession, but the keys that pop up on a person's body so that you can fight them are small and in white so it was difficult to get it right on one try.
-all those negative points above just forced me to end up shooting my way through almost all levels, as reloading and restarting for a stealthier approach was frustrating. I don't have much interest in watching all walkthroughs to get a really good score before actually playing the levels for the first time. so there's probably a bunch of clever ways to kill targets, but i don't want to go find out.
overall score: 7.5/10

A desperately artsy survival horror that ends up being neither survival nor horror, but rather a depressing graveyard of unrefined ideas.
Around 90% of the time you'll spend slogging through the forest from one map marker to another fetching assorted junk to read some bland 17th century felony reports as a reward and then backtracking for more markers until the plot decides to just drop it at some point and roll out the credits.
The other 10% is dedicated to awkwardly paced abrupt combat encounters, most of which are all about slowly kiting around in the open or side-stepping behind a tree and hoping for the best, while trying to use a severely limited assortment of unwieldy “realistic” killing tools against small groups and waves of repetitive enemies with Diabloesque AI, dodgy unpredictable hitboxes and rng-based deflections.
There is a rather rudimentary stealth system to serve as an alternative, but in practice it is only applicable to make your gameplay time 3-4 times longer than it has to be, while in most really challenging encounters where a stealthy approach would be desirable the combat is script-forced on you anyway.
Overall while being an obviously budget-crippled and mechanistic but passable and at some points rather enjoyable and suspenseful experience Betrayer is very hard to recommend gameplay-wise. Especially so since its plot is pretty hard to get invested in while both the protagonist and the Maiden in Red have all the personality of a windows system cursor and a 90’s chat bot.

Despite running on a 10 year old engine this game still looks amazing.
The deep story, role playing rivals even with Assasin's Creed IV. A milestone in sea games.
I was thoroughly impressed with the first Sea Dogs title, their sequels - Pirates of the Caribbean, Age of Pirates/Age of Pirates 2 City of Abandoned Ships which makes this game, the logical continuation of that tradition from Akella to make these games (although now they just earn money as a publisher since they own the rights to the game).
On a technical level this is the same Age of Pirates with numerous additions. Think of it as the Warband of Mount & Blade.
The story got much better since the first Age of Pirates. Continuing with the good tradition of CAS (Age of Pirates 2) story and quests got a special spotlight, many of them are randomly generated.
You play Charles de Maure, a french aristocrat who came to the New World to help his brother. Eventually you get entangled in politics, earning a revenue all the time to fight off scurvy and... boredom in the sea. This is a slow game.
Relationships with factions, bounties on your head, pirating, bribing - all of it is improved and refined to make a believable experience.
Unlike more arcade games this one is hard. It plays by the logic of a 15 year old mentality.
Life in the sea is hard, sailing is slow, authenticity to the maximum. This isn't for everyone.
I consider this a great expansion if you loved the previous games. It is hard to get in if you never played anything like this before. Learning the ropes may proove difficult since the game doesn't like to hold your hand at all.
Like a newborn baby you'll try to hold on to every possible hook on getting your sailor life easier.
The tutorial exists though. If you were looking for such an experience than this is the closest you'll get in he forseeable future.
Since there's no English version yet (reportedly coming this summer) everything will be in Russian. Thus, this can only be recommended to those passionate about naval adventures, and a realistic RPG/simulation of sailing. If you watched Pirates of the Caribbean a  million times - this is for you.
To those who stay, take care of CTD's and freezes. The age of exploration is nigh. Save often! Don't use quick saves or time compression as it provokes crashes.
TL:DR try it but don't buy DLC's except Caleuche.

Long Story Short: It's alright, but feels like a bland reskin. It lacks the chatacter of its predecesor without adding enough to counter that. I'd only reccomend it during a sale. 6-6.5/10, so a good game. It's by no means bad.
Long Story: I felt I was overall  a little dissapointed with Civ: B.E. I'd still liked it, and it was pretty good, but dissapointing.
When I got into the game I really expected an entirely new experience. What I got felt like a reskinned Civ V. No real improvements from the previous game. And where there were improvrements there tended to be a little something that pushed them back. Sure, there were more trade routes. But at times they felt tedious to handle. The quests are refreshing the first time around, and a little dull the second game onwards, as there's typically one choice that's the right awnser. Health can go from infuriatingly difficult to manage and teetering around -5 to breezing through at +15 with one policy upgrade. The policies have nice improvements but I never feel the dedication to take one all the way and max it out any more.
The leaders are a huge step back, in my opinion. While they have a diverse cast, and feature some interesting combinations (save for the utterly ridiculous Kavithan Protectorate - It's going to take more than the world can dish out to get Pakistan and India buddybuddy), the characters themselves feel lifeless. I loved how animated and colorful the leaders were in Civ V. They felt a little more talkitive, and they were very lively feeling. It was interesting to encounter a new character, because I always enjoyed seeing what actions they would do in greeting and in what setting they stood. In Civ: BE I get a bunch of quiet, curt, and dismissive handwaves, and the leaders seem almost mute at times. I don'tfeel a big difference from leader to leader. I almost always think of them less by person or personality, and more by their nation's color scheme. And when I play as them, I almost forget who I'm playing as at times. The AI rarely feel aggressive, either. I missed seeing notifications that some unknown warmonger was taking capital after capital. I never feel remotely threatened by the AI. I actually was attacked by one AI, who moved his army out to the empty space between our civs. We fired at each other a couple times, and after several turns of rather boring combat he surrendered and GAVE me a city. He was never once threatened in any way, and had at least twice my unit count. But he just sat there and waited, and then gave up and gave me a city (which I gave back, it was a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ city anyways)
While the civilizations don't offer much in the way of differentiation, I enjoyed the affinities. The different unit groups for each one were good. And while I mostly used Purity, I enjoyed what time I spent as the other affinities. I really liked being able to float the majority of my forces across the ocean and shell my opponent's capital into submission. But this wore thin along with the rest of the game about halfway through a session where'The Drag' hits. early game is exciting, but no other part really meets up to that.
The music was good, but once again I missed the music that each seperate civ had in Civ V. the different themes brought more fresh air into the game.
All in all, I give it a pretty mixed review. It was a fun game, sure, but it is still outshone by Civ V. If you REALLY feel you need to experience this game, go ahead. But I'd advise to keep playing Civ V for a while, let the inevitable (and infuriating)  DLC come out to improve on the game, wait for a sale, and nab it then. Civ V still has the replayability to keep me going for 'one more turn', where Civ: BE really lacks that.

Takes the fun/addictive elements of freeform space sims while avoiding the over-complexity of some of these titles (such as the X-series). As usual you start with an underequipped ship and earn money for better weapons/systems, new ships, and even mercenary support if you want it. You can earn money via missions (randomly generated and storyline), trading, mining, piracy or bounty hunting; it's up to you if you want to stay the right side of the law or if you aim to misbehave. It's worth noting that your starting ship is a corvette and the ship classes only get bigger from there on (right up to massive dreadnoughts). Because you're always commanding a large ship, combat is very different from a fighter-focused space sim and as others have pointed out it the 2D movement gives a 'naval battle in space' feel to it (though faster paced); it actually works pretty well, making the battles very fun to play - which is a good thing, because there is a lot of combat in this game.
Visually this has a beautiful-looking universe, some spectular space battles and a wide variety of nice ship designs (from Serenity-style rustbuckets to more conventional-looking starships). I like the fact that the different ships cater to different playstyles -  bigger isn't necessarily better as there are other factors like speed, manouverabilty and weapon placement, so instead of a linear progression to the 'best' ship, people will find their own favorite ships along the way.
There are some aspects of the game that could do with some improvement such as the scaling of encounters and missions - the actual difficulty of missions doesn't always seem to match the stated risk level. Also it's quite possible to get into fights where the only chance of survival is to run, especially at the beginning of the game; though this is not a bad thing in itself, the fact that the game pops up a combat tutorial note on your first fight (even if you're totally outmatched) could confuse new players into thinking they should always be able to win their first battle. I can see why the single checkpoint-type save is controversial, but personally I'm fine with a single save AS LONG AS there is some backup in case of corrupt saves - fortunately haven't had a corrupted save yet, but would be pretty peeved if this happened after hours of play.
The hillbilly rock soundtrack does help create that 'wild frontier' Firefly vibe, but it also starts to get a bit old after about 10 hours - fortunately there is an option to stream your own music - this is a great feature that allows you to select different music sources for different situations (ambient, combat, idle, station etc).
Overall this is probably the most enjoyable space game I've played since Freelancer.

I knew that he had probably been killed, but we needed the supplies, and I didn't want to give up on Bruno. I set out with a knife; the only weapon we had left, and traveled to the building. All was quiet. I jumped up some rocks to get to the first floor, and headed towards the door in front of me. I opened it, and was aghast at what I saw. A man standing there with a pistol, with blood in a pool around his feet. His wounds looked even worse than Marko's. He raised the gun saying, "You can't do it man." As there was no other choice, I ran forward with the knife. He threw several weak punches at me before I struck him down with the knife. He convulsed once, and lay still. Shaking in mixed grief and shock for my actions, I wandered in a daze throughout the house, collecting what I could find. I managed to grab a bandage for Marko. While I was looting upstairs, I found the body of Bruno, clutching a knife. Close by, the bodies of two older people lay, covered in blood. Realization of what Bruno had done struck me like a thunderbolt. He had killed the two older people, and had lethally wounded the man who had tried to protect them. I grabbed what I could and left quickly. I never wanted to go there again. I don't know if my life is worth living anymore if I take the lives of others..." -Boris

Technical problems:
Trade routes have an arbitrary and obscure value determination.  Trade routes are still clunky to renew. Aesthetic problems:
You don't love the planet, you don't love the leaders.  You don't even love your own civ.  You cannot care less about what's going on.  The alien taming is a novelty, not enjoyable.
Health dominates the entirety of the virtues decision tree, strategically speaking.  There is nothing but Prosperity into Colonist into health virtues.

There are no subcity elements to contend with.  No sustainability problems.  No corruption or empire contentment.  The affinities actually have no natural animosity for each other, the A.I.s just act like they do.
Sci-fi is cool.  4X is cool.  And Civilization maintains its certain style of branding that comes through in the tone of things, in the character designs, in the  look-and-feel of the advanced gameplay elements - the "wow cool" of the components that comes from the designers' enthusiasm. If you're a fan of being an elite soldier fight for freedom and destroying evil dictators don't buy this game.
Don't get me wrong it's a good game just not for everyone.
Story: The game takes place in the fictional city of Vysena in the republic of Vysenac during a civil war and follows a group of civilians trying to survive. The game itself is the tales of the survival of these civilians and seems to lack a clear straight forward narrative, but some key events will occur no matter what. One example is when two children walk up to your 'little patch of heaven', asking for medicine to treat their sick mother. The Game does have an ending but it can only be achived by surviving the whole war.
Graphics: The game looks good, if you're a fan of ruined buildings, black, grey, abandoned tanks and other depressing stuff. The art style seems to resemble a very well done pencil drawing with the only colours being different shades of grey. In short the game looks good with a high resolution.
Gameplay: The gameplay consitis of two phases; day and night. During the day you allocate food and medicine, let people sleep, craft items like beds or weapons and make sure not to use up all your supplies. The night is the ONLY period of time when you can go and scavenge for supplies outside of your 'safe haven', (this is because snipers pervent you from leaving during the day). You decide who will scavenge, who will guard the base and who gets to sleep, your 'safe haven' can and will get raided. Weither or not the raid gets well for the raiders is determined by who's on guard and if they have a weapon. When scavenging you search rubble and bins, and use tools to open doors or clear debris. If there hostiles nearby you can try and sneak past them which involves hding in dark areas, and moving carefully. When it comes to combat you will either run up to them and beat the living hell out of them, or you take cover and shoot them. If you sneak up behind an enemy you can preform a sneak attack, but unless the character you're playing as has combat experience, it won't be an instant kill. Stealth is highly recommended in my opinion, but if you do attack someone kill them quickly and after they're dead either run or hide. This is beacuse killing someone makes lots of noise, this will attract enemys. But know that any wounds a character suffers will need to be bandaged and left to heal.
Edit: as of update 1.3 to the game You can now create your own scenario's. You can pick how many locations you can loot (minimum of 13), certain features about these areas, when the game will end, when, for how long and the severtiy of winter is. You can also choose the characters you get at the start, the difficulty and it allows you to create your own characters.
Final verdict: The game is well made and is good if you like a dark, depressing and somewhat realistic, look into the life of civilians during a war. I sum it up as a zombie apocalypse without the Zombies. The only problem I face is a lack of a manual save & the fact it only auto-saves when you return to your 'safe haven', overall i give it a 9.5/10.

For an in-depth review, tune into the video below:
Otherwise, here’s a summarized write up.
Inspired by the Romanian’s Communist regime that ended in 1989, Black the Fall focuses solely on the tale of an unnamed machinist trying to escape the facility. The story is likely only going to appeal to a specific set of people. Whilst playing, we witness many scenes that play out as a form of symbolism to the real-life conditions during Romania’s Communist regime (eg. Poor working conditions and abusive authority) but that’s really the extent of the narrative.
There are no memorable characters, no spoken dialogue and no distinct personalities. Essentially if you aren’t interested in how this parallels to Romania’s past, then you’ll likely find no compelling factor in the story.
BTF is a slide scrolling puzzler where the objective of each puzzle is to get from the left to the right side of the screen. It’s easier to understand the puzzles if you separate between the ones inside the facility (section 1) to those outside of it (section 2).
Both sections include simple platforming, avoiding getting seen by enemies and interacting with brightly lit switches that do things like opening doors. At times, you’ll platform your way to the objective but very early in the game puzzles start to focus on a laser pointer you come across that allows you to control nearby workers to activate switches you can’t reach. You can also manually control the pointer to point toward light-sensitive panels to activate things in the environment.
Section 1 puzzles for the most part are pretty simple, since most of them take place in a small area with very few items to interact with and therefore very little experimentation. There are some puzzles in section 1 that are bigger in scale but these are few and far between. Besides the simple straightforward puzzles using the laser pointer, you also have a few interesting ones that surprise you now and again with how ‘neat’ they are. I say that because you’re not going to think it was anything more than mildly clever in terms of its difficulty.
Even the interesting puzzles in section 1 can still be seen as rather simple. An example is a puzzle that requires you to listen for nearby environmental hazards and move forward in the dark using you sense of hearing. Not particularly difficult but a ‘neat’ addition nonetheless.
In section 2, puzzles change because you also get a new robot companion. This time, you can use your laser pointer to direct him to specific areas, effectively giving you 2 players to control. Puzzles here are more complex by comparison because of the increased scale allowing for more interactable items per puzzle and, with it, more experimentation.
Also, this is where the game introduces puzzles that require the robot’s help and since the robot’s moveset is more diverse than just moving left and right (it can swim while you cannot), it makes for more creative puzzle design. It’s clear that section 2 has the more challenging puzzles but even then, they were never difficult enough for me to feel stumped or to force me to pause for minutes on end.
Ultimately when looking at all the puzzles as a whole I would say most of them are simple to decent in difficulty. From that category, only about 25 percent of them are ‘neat’ or an interesting twist to make you go ‘huh, never thought of that’. The rest are either just really easy which is a problem in terms of value since the game already doesn’t have a lot of puzzles to begin with.
1) decent presentation – nice minimalistic visuals for character designs and nice sound effects. BGM takes a more ambient role.
2) some puzzles are genuinely an interesting execution of mechanics
1) most puzzles are simple – gets better in section 2 but they still don’t pose a significant enough challenge
2) the story is likely only to be appreciated by a small set of people – no conventional narrative to enjoy.
Black the fall is a short game, but above all else, it is a puzzler that doesn’t sport a lot of difficult challenges. Most are simple to decent at best with about a quarter of that portion being interesting in a unexpected manner. Taking that into consideration with the fact that most people aren’t going to be invested in the Communist setting, it’s difficult to justify the value proposition. As such, I’m going to recommend that you wait for a sale on this one, probably till it’s about 10 dollars. And that’s pretty much it for the review.

Black the Fall is a game about a cog in the machine finally trying to escape from a communist regime. In order to do so, you must avoid both sentry bots and human guards alike. This is accomplished through puzzle solving and careful timing.
Generally, I really like the dark aesthetic of the game. Particularly that, even with the futuristic aspects like robots and control vests, the game feels like an slightly aged version of 80s communism, all cement and wire and Lenin posters. Honestly, it kinda feels like a jab at Russia. What I think this game did particularly well with visual design though is visibility. In some games with a darker look, it can be difficult to distinguish what’s where in the level. That’s fine if that’s what your going for, but when that’s not on purpose it kinda sucks. Another thing I liked about this game is the use of the three dimensional perspective and scale. The game itself in linear, meaning you can only move forward or backward, but the levels are built with depth. Actually, one of the nice things the devs improved from the pre-alpha build to the press build was the tracking when the perspective shifted. In the alpha build, sometimes the lines didn’t follow the curves, so you had to either jump around the corner or fall off the edge, but they’ve fixed that in this build which is nice.
As for the actual mechanics, it’s mostly basic puzzle solving. There are certain items you can interact with which are marked by those flashing yellow and red lights. Usually, to get past cameras and guards it has to do with careful timing and hiding in plain sight. Luckily the vision of the guards and cameras is marked with a clear red circle around the pool of light so there’s not a lot of questioning whether or not the enemies can see you. That changes a little later in the game with the bigger bots, and those can be harder to deal with. The biggest problem I have with those is knowing when you are far enough away to avoid detection. There’s also an important mechanic using a mind control device you get from one of the guards that you can use to control other works and make them do what you want. I was happy to see that in the press build they had that feature working on the controller, because in the pre-alpha build the pointer wouldn’t work but it’s totally functional now. The pointer also becomes important later in the game with the introduction of your adorable robot insect-dog companion, who is guided by the pointer, but more on him in a second. The last thing I wanted to say about mechanics was that, even when the game introduces previously unused abilities, there’s always a sign near by to tell you what’s up, which was particularly helpful in one section of the game where the section was completely blacked out and you had to listen for the steam jets to dodge around.
As for the companion robot, he’s cute. The trickiest thing about him is that he can move in three dimensions, which is important because if he stands directly in your way you knock him off to the side. That particularly sucks when you use him to block steam jets and knock him out of the way. You can also use him as a climbing tool by changing him into a stand, which is a feature helpful in a few other situations as well. The nice thing is that, unlike most puzzle games that involve two characters, you don’t have to worry about trapping your friend in a previous room as he is able to navigate through the environment on his own.
On the whole, I really enjoyed this game, and would like to see more from it.

Another day, another preview. Black The Fall strikes home in the most literal way imaginable, since I don’t get to write very often about Romanian indie games. This particular title is sufficient proof that Romanians can create self-sustaining projects and not just provide textures or quality assurance for big gaming companies. Debutante developer Sand Sailor Studio has been working on Black The Fall since 2014 and the game has changed drastically over the years. It witnessed a successful Kickstarter campaign and the support of Square Enix, during the final phase of development. Right now, it’s less than a month away from the retail release on Steam along with PS4 and Xbox One versions as well.
The press build I had the opportunity to test out, offered 14 short chapters that could be regarded more as elaborate scenes, connected to one another. Black The Fall focuses on a dystopian scenario in which communism somehow managed to survive and thrive in Romania even after 1989. The game tells the story of an aging machinist that has had enough of his miserable life and wishes to escape the clutches of a totalitarian regime which has turned his home country into an industrially repressive hellscape.
Black The Fall is filled with more or less obvious metaphors and symbols. Malnourished workers supervised by obese overseers and security cameras equipped with machineguns, are noteworthy examples. It’s all very bleak, inside the factories as well as outside of them. The land and water seem contaminated while the goods produced by the laborers are going straight to export, lining the pockets of their “masters”. Living and working in such conditions is no more than a painfully slow death sentence.
It might appear far-fetched but the truth is that the Socialist Republic of Romania was a regional economic power while also managing to pay-off its entire foreign debt at the expense of internal prosperity. Nicolae Ceaușescu’s few and fixed ideas were increasingly depriving Romanians of even the most basic necessities or commodities, near the end of his 24-year long rule. And it’s always the upper class (or “nomenklatura” as it was called in the Eastern Bloc) which doesn’t suffer from any austerity measures. This ain’t exactly the idyllic picture envisioned by the several European philosophers who never lived long enough to get a taste of their own “medicine”. So much for class struggle…
Unity Engine assets may have been used since the project’s inception, yet the 2014 visuals are a far cry from what you’ll get to play in 2017’s Black The Fall. Pure black & white has since then been replaced by a much wider selection of shades and colors along with increased complexity of the game world and objects within it. You may compare this title’s visual style to that of Deadlight, This War Of Mine or the more recent INSIDE. I’m pleased Black The Fall departed from the far too simplistic looks which were closer to LIMBO (a game which has far too many clones, as it is).
Performance-wise, I had no trouble running the game in my monitor’s native resolution (3840x2160) and constant 60 frames per second. Standard Unity Engine behavior and I could hardly complain about the results. The in-game Settings tab shall hopefully contain sufficient options, for most players to maintain a preferred ratio between stability and level of detail. Even with the relatively limited time frame and number of accessible levels, I still managed to take 50 screenshots through the Steam Overlay.
Black The Fall features a lot of set pieces along with propaganda material and direct references to local or international symbols of communism. No matter how you perceive this political ideology, you can’t deny that it has left a profound mark (or scar, if you will) upon humanity and its ever shifting history. “A lie told enough becomes the truth”, right, Lenin? Well, the game I’m previewing today is most certainly not lying about its looks in the Steam Store Page. What you see in those official screenshots, is also what you'll be playing.
The soundtrack is decent enough, but there’s always room for improvement and the sound effects are in ample supply. Not exactly voice acting, yet the seemingly indistinct grumbles emitted by the fat guards are in fact, a handful of words in Romanian. Overall, the OST is neither mind-blowing nor as dull as in countless other side scrollers found on Steam. They are certainly not the kind of repetitive sounds that might force players to mute them and listen to their own songs.
Black The Fall is first and foremost an atmospheric side scroller. The silent protagonist shall have to use his wits, if he ever wishes to survive his escape attempts. The State has many weapons at its disposal, from the already mentioned guards and turrets and even cleverly masked traps along with giant AI-controlled robots. How do I know that we’re dealing with “Artificial Intelligence”? Well, after you’ll notice far too many human guards that have passed out drunk, you’ll understand that the massive machinery that’s hunting you, is basically shooting at almost anything that moves. In a certain case, crows, which you’ll be using as a distraction to pass by one such robotic menace.
Using the environment to your advantage, is just one way of advancing through the game. Another involves platforming (no side scroller without this feature, right?) and the last but definitely not least, represents the use of a laser beam which reminded me of the visible signal triangulation within Rocketbirds 2. With the help of this laser, you shall manipulate fellow workers, distract guards and also control a small friendly robot, in later stages. So if you felt that the journey ahead will be both dangerous and you’ll long for company, at least half of your worries can be laid to rest.
From the puzzle sections I could already experience, Black The Fall is not difficult to understand or play, but you will have to be cautious during the segments that require stealth and finesse. Subtitles need to be included in some capacity (or at least closed captions), since there is a level through which players must travel across a corridor in total darkness and also pay close attention to the steam pipe noises. A trap that represents instant death, unless you avoid it.
And you’d have to hear it in the first place, before you’d have even slim chances of success. I always appreciated the inclusion of English subtitles in any film or video game made by English-speaking countries. You have to be aware of potential deaf customers and cater to their specific needs. So that pitch black level section needs a visual cue of some sort, for those few players that cannot hear at all.
Even if I won’t give it a final rating, I am pleased by what I managed to play so far in Black The Fall. I have no information related to price tag or the future inclusion of Steam Achievements & Trading Cards but I hope the developer understands the need to include those as well, for Steam players and collectors.
The game itself, is most certainly a different take on communism and the foes you face in this case, are far more cruel than mercenaries or zombies will ever be. The official screenshots show a glimpse into even more schocking scenes, which were still unreachable in the press build. I’m looking forward to playing and completing the storyline in Black The Fall as soon it is made available.

I only played the single player on the game so just a few comments on the game.  Single player is incredibly short but also very fun.  With the backstory to the game there probably could have been a lot more added but even with what little campaing there was it was very enjoyable.
The story was great in my opinion.  Not the typical you are a military super soldier and you go to whatever country and kill a bunch of terrorists.  No you are fighting for the USA that's been invaded by a united North/South Korea.  The story worked for me because of the setting and enviroment that the Devs created.  There was some incredibly gruesome scenes as well a touch of realism as people are going to do what they feel is best for their survival and it wasn't just everyone against the invaders.
Loved the setting and enviroments that you play through in the game.  Some of the areas are semi generic cover based shooting but some of the locations do evoke some sense of feeling in the game whether pity or anger at whats happening.  The only complaint is that as a FPS the areas are very linear and would have been nice to explore some of them a little more freely maybe open up more paths to achieve the goal.
The game also varied the pacing in the levels for the most part as well.  In some levels it was a constant frenzy of action while others were a little slower with small burts of action to break up the tension.  Again it worked for me because if it was just all 100% constant action shooting every enemy you came across it would get bland fast.
Good deal of weapons in the game, mostly automatic weapons, would have been nice to get some more variety in pistol/shotguns or other weapons instead of just from dozens of different assult rifles.  I also liked that there wasn't just a ton of ammo laying around everywhere to collect.  I was switching between a variety of weapons to keep my ammo up as when I'd get a new weapon there wasn't always ammo for it and I'd be on the lookout for me next weapon or playing a little more conservatively to make what ammo I had count.
Only complaint would be that the character model gets caught up on really odd pieces of terrain and you can't tell if you should be able to get past an area or not.  Sometimes there looks to be a path but you get caught on something.
It's good.

As an idle diversion this was alright. If you're bored and it's on sale and you just wanna mindlessly destroy enemies, go for it.
If you're going for something for story content, innovative gameplay or a new experience I'd suggest running away as fast as you can.
I bought this title on sale for five dollars US, for five bucks I'd say it was worth it, I enjoyed it *JUST* enough to warrant it. For full price? I'd probably be pretty mad I bought it.
My take on things:
The Story:
The story's background is so impossible you'd be more likely to encounter Santa astride a Unicorn than the scenario depicted in this game.
The characters are tired stereotypes and overacted, sometimes hilarious so.
The writers seemed to really want me to have an emotional response to this game and the events in it. If their goal was annoying me, they succeeded. If the intent was making me feel something for their poorly written characters they utterly failed.
It was also extremely predictable, so many moments meant to be surprising weren't in the slightest.
The Gameplay:
It's a retextured Call of Duty, and it somehow managed to actually be worse than call of duty. This includes the "shocking" moments and first-person moments of your character being tossed about and blown around.
It works off the exact same mechanics as Call of Duty, enemies endlessly spawn until the player advances to a certain point.
All engagements play out almost exactly the same and get exceptionally boring.
There's a complete lack of bullet penetration, shooting at an enemy behind plywood or a plastic traffic pylon results in absolutely nothing.
I can recall years ago when this game was coming out a trailer touting that "this game will be different" and something close to "we won't have you killing hordes of enemies, we want to avoid kill-fatigue in games like Call of Duty where you just kill people on automatic and don't even think about it after a certain point". It was a blatant lie, I'd be hard pressed to point out a game with more generic enemies packed into small areas than this one.
At the end of the day I've played worse, but not many.
If you want a game wherein America is the one getting invaded and you don't mind an RTS I'd highly suggest World in Conflict as a viable and fun alternative. Much better writing, much more plausible story.

Homefront started out on a good foot. Within the first 5 minutes I was confronted with the possibility that North Korea could end up invading a country (in this case America). This got me hooked on what was to come, but the journey ahead that I received did not live up to this expectation. I can happily recommend this game for its idea and trying to run with it, but unfortunately there are a few factors that limit this recommendation to only getting this game if it is on sale ($5 or less, in my personal opinion).
First of all, the visuals are great. The sounds (gunshots, music, voice-acting, etc.) were fine too. However, certain character animations and the almost genre-standard 'invisible barriers' made it hard for me to immerse myself into the game.
Then again, I feel like it's not the type of game that needs you to be immersed in. The story is decent and the gunplay itself is fine, so apart from a few minor things that I disliked, overall the game is okay. I felt that it was too short (clocking in at just over 3 hours for me), and after the opening of the game, the "shock-factor" of the invasion rubbed off. But in the end I played it for a bit of fun, and that's what I got :)
So if you're okay with a short experience (the MP is very limited now due to the game's age) and a few minor technical issues that can be looked past, then maybe you'll be okay with this game. You should have some fun if you're a fan of first-person shooters, but just don't expect a compelling story that lasts for a good amount of time.
Enjoy :)

+Tons of weapons! When you start fighting hordes of enemies there could be ranging from 2 different guns to about 15 which allow unique firefights.
+Great story line (We'll look more at this later.) I love "alternate universe" storylines where what-if's become the "this actually happened". Its really neat because it throws you into a world you don't recognize and forces you to try to grasp at things that just aren't there anymore.

Why? Well, simply put, this game is not optimized for pc. Yesyes #pcmasterrace whatever, but this game was made for consoles like the xbox and ps, that is obvious. Keybindings are weird, moving and looking obviously needed a controller, aiming/shooting/running,crouching; pretty much anything that requires specific actions and attention are lacking.
IE: Shooting down the sights..., dear god the sight aiming... (I won't even discuss sniping because it was better to shoot from the hip with them more than half the time). So You look down the sights, line up a head shot, or even a bloody body shot. 10m away, easy right? hahah yeah no. Yes them. THAT is your ai friends, who shoot at walls, corner you so you can't continue (ie:fallout, you know what I mean), and just are generally the most ridiculous things ever.
Also, they are whiney as hell and keep yelling the same thing over and over like they have one script for the area you are in. Next area? Cool they'll say something new! Over, and over, and over again; while shooting at a wall.

OH, except for will direct ALL attention to you as soon as you enter the area, even if you haven't shot anything or looked at them or done anything to attract attention (including sneaking into the area and hiding behind crates. Be prepared for unlimited grenades to be thrown at you.)
I can talk about damage and how you need a "few" head shots to kill a basic enemy with a m16 (decent gun in the game fyi), but with their little subs they can put you down in seconds flat, even if you can't see them, THEY SEE YOU >.> Oh and they like throwing grenades at you; not just the enemies but your friendlies too. Always a good time when they throw grenades at you, while you're searching for hidden things, when no enemies are around, while yelling at you to hurry up every 2 seconds.
**ALMOST DONE I SWEAR**

I'm greatly enjoying this game. Love the handling - reminds me of PGR.
Runs really smooth with my HD 7870. I'd go as far as to claim that this is the best looking Racing Game available at this moment - since Need for Speed Rivals has been crippled to 30fps and Forza 5 has been downgraded to accomodate to the Xbox One's lacklustre performance ;P
My only gripe with GRID 2 so far is its businessmodel and pricing - there should have been no pre-order incentives to begin with - since there is no shortage of supply or shipping cost when it comes to digital distribution. I shouldn't be paying more just because I choose to buy the game during the week of its release rather than paying ahead of release... I simply like to be able to access the stuff I buy immediately once I put my money on the table. In addition I'm not a big fan of microtransactions only devalue the initial purchase and make people hold out for Sales and Collectors Editions... which I did. Aside from being rather pervasively integrated into this game - most of the car-pacs seem to be variations on the cars you can unlock in the game - thus don't seem to affect the balance of the game.
The one DLC that does offer something interesting (Destruction Derby) comes at no additional cost.
It appears that some Tier 3 cars which you should be able to win in career mode are locked away behind some nasty difficultiy spike - but thankfully you are able to switch difficultiy in the options at any time during your career which negates the frustration.
I'm having a blast with this game so far - the WSR is a brilliant idea and provides a lot of diversity and motivation. There's a distinct Street Race Action-Movie feel to the game and its events which make it very cohesive - though its gritty Sepia tone and Hollywood Soundtrack may not be for everyone... but this is more down to personal preference and subjecitve perception. The Car demolition and aggressive AI work really well and add an additional layer to the challenge.
I'm not missing the Cockpit View all that much, since I don't use it for racing - In other games I mostly use it  to check out the interiors - it kinda adds to the feel of driving a real car. Maybe with the arrival of Occulus Rift the Cockpit View will become relevant once again?
All in all I can recommend this game to anyone looking for a challenging Racing Game.

Late to the party, but thaks to Humbe Bundle I am discovering this amazing classic.
You're trapped in a mega mall, with thousands of zombies. Almost every object you find can be used as a weapon, and as you play you earn crafting recipes to combine multiple items into a unique special weapon. The plot is the right kind of cheesy (and takes a welcome back seat while you go rescue people and♥♥♥♥♥♥around with different weapons), with all sorts of ridiculous characters making up a cast of survivors you can rescue, and there' a quest system that revolves around a three day time limit that pretty almost guarantees multiple playthroughs are needed to find everything.
The graphics are impressive for a port of a 2012 console game, with proper hordes of zombies with hundreds in any area. The mall setting works great for a non linear zombie game, with all sorts of useful stores to loot (for useful, cool, or just plain weird weapons as well as a variety of stupid costumes, and that sweet Zombrex the main character's infected young daughter needs every 24 hours to stay alive), and a familliar environment to navigate (I would wager most people have been to a mall at least once in their lifetime, even down to small details like the restrooms being a savepoint.
I get some small performance issues in the particularly large crowds of zombies, especially in big open areas, but it is nowhere near enough to be a gameplay hindrance (it barely reaches "mildly annoying" on my scale of agitation), but part of that likely has to do with the fact that this computer is not exactly new (nvidia gtx 550 ti with 4g VRAM, an i3-2120 processor at  3.3 ghz, and 6 GB of RAM), but overall the game looks and plays wonderfully.
It also has 2 player co-op and a 4 player game mode, for those who like human interaction (I'm unsure of the quality on multiplayer, as I have not tried it).
