Civ 5 is an awesome game, definitely worthy of the franchise. One of the very few things I very much dislike about the Civilization games is how you are bound to going forward in time. You can chose to start from a later age but you can't chose to stay in one age longer, except if you play marathon or epic (which I usually do) but you're still unable to achieve pretty much anything in, for instance, the archaic age, even though, playing as Babylon, I should be able to have a history-worthy empire at that time (But it's impossible) which makes civ really unrealistic - as if you can't have a big empire with lots of cities 1500 BC. Another thing that bothers me about the original game is how you're always bound to the empires of this world, and always one ruler who somehow lives for 7000 years... It would be cool if you could just make your own culture and empire, not really bound by any of the empires in the actual world so you could more realistically rewrite history.
I heard many people complaining that this game is "just like an expansion of Civ 5". I compeltely disagree, the game is different. I played Civ 3 and its gameplay is still similar to Civ 5. It's just a weird conclusion, this game is different and it feels different to me. What I really like about it is how there are these factions that represent more developed alliances that relate to those of the present world, and that you're not really connected to history at all so many of the problems I had with the Civ games, that I mentioned above, fall away. Nevertheless, the game isn't perfect. As I played it, it seemed rather unfinished - just slightly. There could've been a lot more features and fun things in the game, more expanding on how the other nations react to you and one another, especially concerning how to deal with alien life (I really liked how they did the thing with symbiosis with alien life though) and there should be more ways to win the game, and more immersion in the world (this does count for most civ games, though. Lacks immersion. Civ 3 had this cool thing with your palace expanding if your people get happier or something. I don't know why they ever got rid of that. That's the kind of stuff that really catches my eye and gets me immersed.)
Other than all that, I'm just a big fan of sci-fi. I love history, but history is written and rewriting it is awkward (americans in mesopotamia with the pyramids and the porcelain tower??) unless you would take away all the pre-determined things (like set culture, wonders. As I said, it would be awesome if we could design our own culture. Sort of like how "Gods and Kings" adressed religion, but very much expanded upon). Sci-Fi, like High Fantasy, however, is completely free of that. This setting, the whole emotional opening cinematic, the whole idea... It just blows my mind. This setting and theme comes very close to my ideal of the future of mankind. I said ♥♥♥♥ yes many times while starting off the game.
A bummer: After playing this game for 6 hours straight I was nearing the end of the game. It was a pretty big letdown. I was very close to finishing the satelity thingy for the alien buddies victory, but someone else was ahead of me. ( a freakin NPC, I know I suck.) and the ending was very anti climatic. I loaded an earlier save later on and did it again, this time with me winning but I was still underwhelmed. The original Civ games had underwhelming endings too, I must say, but this just felt like much of the 6 hours weren't  well spent. Again, this does count for Civ 5 too, but not to such extend.
Alright, so let me wrap this up. I am a crappy Civ player that only plays against NPC's and sometimes a friend of mine. I am a casual player and this was my impression of the game. I'd give it a 7/10.
You don't have to take my word for it though.
It had some amusing parts, but there really isn't very much content and it gets old fast.

*This War of Mine: my thoughts*
So I recently picked up the game _This War of Mine_ during a Steam sale, and man is it well done.  The basic premise is that you play as a group of survivors in a recently war torn city.  Rather than fleeing, you are trying to make it by though any means necessary, scavenging, looting, and in extreme situations you may need to injure or kill other survivors, bandits, or soldiers.
The words to describe how it plays are difficult to find. Because of the theme, it's not a game you "enjoy", in that it makes to feel good.  In many ways it elicit many negative emotions, as it is a game that simulates surviving the horrors of war.  I think it does this very well.  In many other survival games, it is presented in the "we will do anything to survive" mind frame, without any real consequences for choosing the more extreme options.  In many cases, the extreme options often lead to extreme rewards, incentivizing you to do just that with few, if any, drawbacks.  This game, however, doesn't just let you get away easy with playing like a psychopath.  It's not just about surviving.  It's about surviving, and being able to live with yourself afterwards.
This War of Mine takes a look into the minds of your characters, their personalities, and the complex interactions between them and what they choose to do.  I remember on my first attempt, playing through as if it were just another survival game (i.e. playing like a psychopath), and choosing to sneak around, hide, and then kill someone so I could raid his house unhindered.  Not only was my best scavenger severely injured (injury is very difficult to deal with) in the fight, he carried the horror of what he'd done home with him.  The mood infected the whole household, making everyone Sad, and even one person seriously Depressed.  They eventually recovered enough to function, but it continued to scar them for as long as I continued playing.
The mood system is extremely nuanced as well.  Every character is unique, with some recovering from different types of trauma better or worse than others.  Arica, a streetsmart carburglar, is much less affected by stealing from people, though it matters what type of people she steals from as well.  Stealing from a group of bandits is treated differently than stealing from an old elderly couple.
That is what really stuck out for me about this game; the way they present a nuanced and horrific situation as complexly as it deserves to be.  Some games I play to have fun with, but it's game like this that I choose to play because they make me think.

Alright, here is the lowdown.
I had been anticipating this game since it had been announced. I also had played a bit of alpha centauri, so I was interested to see where this game would go.
The Good:
- Some of the issues with 1UPT have been solved. I am still not a fan, but floating units helps you siege cities easier, which as somebody who has 500+ hours in civ (playing emperor/immortal)  I appreciate this greatly. This effect comes in more late game.
- Cities don't get built instantly, which is great. I think we can all agree that it is annoying when you are 1 tile away from a settler who makes a city right before you get to him, and now suddenly, you have to come back with an army. Instead, they have an outpost, which is far easier to assault. This prevents the computer and other players from making low-risk, high reward cities all the time. They have to actually consider where they are building this outpost and defending it.
- The Tech web is very unique, and doesn't really force you into one direction. (although skipping out on spy tech at the beginning is truly shooting yourself in the foot)
- This game has FAR MORE depth than civ V did at release, and still more depth than CiV V after Gods and kings.
- Aliens are interesting in that they can be passive, or aggressive depending on how you deal with them. (This could use some more fine tuning. (Simply having Green, Light Green, Orange, and Red as aggression markers is not enough, give us more tiers, we need to be informed of exactly how much they feel aggressive to be able to act accordingly)
-Tier bonuses within the Virtue tree allow you to go accross the tree as oppose to just choosing one, and being forced to stick with it.
- The spy system is far more relevant than in Civ V, and cannot be ignored completely. This could be improved further though. (They could give you more choices of what to do)
- The three different ideologies are awesome, they all go in their own path and have their own playstyle. Unfortunately, in Multiplayer I inherit the Ideologies of my allies, which makes no sense to me. I think there should be an option to turn this off at least.
- Runs almost as well as Civ V.
- The technology announcer is a woman, unfortunately this means Civ Guy's voice is gone. So you don't get to hear him tell you "You have discovered COMPASS" Kinda sad, hehe, but I love the woman's voice even better.
The Bad
-Totally uninspired maps. It seems like the concern here was that players wouldn't be able to understand that a land is fertile unless it is a green grass land. Come on Firaxis, I think we are smarter than that, or else I don't think Civ would appeal to us.
- The landscape is completely like a re-colored Civ V, and is far too afraid to venture into sci-fi at all. It tries to hard to provide us with an easy way to understand the game from the first time we pick it up, and make us feel at home. Unfortunately this causes the land to look incredibly bland, and the color pallet is horrid, it is green, purple, and brown.
- Both of these issues come from the conservative approach that they seem to have take for this game, Make it easy, simple to understand. They were afraid to take risks, FAR too afraid. Look at alpha centauri, they were bold when they made that game, that game had personality; which leads me to my next point.
- I play this game, and I don't really see any type of personality to it. It is a blank slate, just  a video game on a screen, no story, no basic theme. They tried to give you the idea that you lead your own future, but instead it just feels like they didn't give the game any spirit. (Maybe adding more themes for each ideology, and unique buildings would give you more of a feeling that your nation has become unique. ( A good example of this is Civ V, when you played civ you feel like nations strive for glory, and we look at the accomplishments of civilizations. In Civ BE it feels like you like land on a planet, and they tell you. OK, go tell your story. (that's it...)
- Teching up in the beginning is VERY SLOW. It pick ups rather fast once you get to the mid late game. But at the beginning, MY GOD, it is slow. I usually play standard on CIV V, but this feels 3 to 4 times as slow when it comes to teching. Maybe the way the game was designed required this, I myself am not sure if I buy this.
- The 1 UPT, although somewhat improved, is still an issue. This issue could be solved if they allowed siege units to fire above hills/forests. I guess they forget how to do that on the way over to Alpha Centauri... Seriously, I understand the distinction between Realism, and gameplay. But let my damn artillery fire 3 tiles away, even if it is for reduced damage. This will open up options for people, maybe let you have elongated sieges. Whether this is for gameplay purposes, or realism purposes, i don't get why artillery fire only 2 hexes away in the beginning.
-Religion is gone. I for one understand why this isn't in the game YET. But it needs to make a re-appearance, this was an aspect of the game that gave Civ V depth. This may have been cut because of the 1/3 rule they have at firaxis. From game to game,they removed 1/3rd of the freatures, and replace 1/3rd. They are so afraid to overburden us with features, but guess what Firaxis? If you want us to stay fans of your game, you have to add a bit of depth(as our mastery increases), or else your fans get tired of your games.
- The map packs aren't distinct, i can't really even remember which one looks like when looking at the map list. I know they have to consider balance when making maps, but these maps have very little to nothing unique about them. At least change up the color pallet, make us feel like we are on a different planet. I just feel like we are on a different version of the same planet every single time I play.
- The wonders make no sense, and aren't even drawn out. It's like they expect you to fill in the colors with your mind. Just have one of your awesome artists draw up something futuristic and awesome. We don't need to fill in every single part of the game with our imagination, give us a base idea or image to work with. Not the quickly drawn up blueprint of a wonder that wasn't even explained properly.
- There is very little Alien diversity. I think there are about 4 aliens, and they are the same 4 in every single map. (2 water aliens for a total of 6) Still, it isn't enough, they should vary, they should be part of the equation when you start the game.
The suggestions
- Give us an intro for each victory, that would be awesome, and help build the "story" that Firaxis wants to help build in our minds.
-Give us more uniqueness for each Ideology.
- Provide us with more ideologies in the long run.
- Bring back religion, and add some depth to it if possible. (Find a way to make it work.)
-Please...Please, please... re-work the maps, they look terribly boring, the color pallet is horrid, and they are the opposite of inspiring.
-Bring some scifi into this, give us farmable deserts, habitable mountains, ocean cities, floating cities. Give us something original, ANYTHING. Make us dream of the future. I believe Firaxis can achieve this while keeping the game balanced.
- Bring randomized aliens into the game. Have a type of alien species that spawn randomly at the beginning of the game. Depending on what it is, you can adjust your strategy.
- Extend the benefits and possibilities that you have when you go beyond level 13 of an affinity. Let it change our civilization even more, and maybe give more benefits.
All in all, the game is good, pretty good, but not great. It needs something more, and it needs to be daring.

Excellent game... took some tinkering to get it running properly. The only real problem I had was frequent stuttering eventhough I was holding steady 60 fps. To fix this:
1.) right click on start menu (I use Windows 10) and search %appdata%, open that folder.
2.) navigate to: %APPDATA%\BioshockHD\Bioshock\
3.) Open Bioshock.ini
4.) Under [Engine.RenderConfig], change "TextureDetail" to Medium or Low, (don't forget to save the file)... Medium worked fine for me... no more stuttering!

Disclaimer: I've played one of the three currently available "attractions."
I really like the idea behind this game. You're at an amusement park and each "attraction" is a mini-game of sorts. The developer has done a decent job of keeping the game updated, so I can only imagine how big this game could end up getting. I do feel like it would've benefited as being an Early Access title rather than getting a full release with only a few of these mini games to play, but at least it's still relatively cheap.
So far what I've seen is a lot of cheap jump scares. It's nice to see that in a game that's also pretty and has great atmosphere, no one seems to be doing those cheap jump scares anymore unless it's a 2D platformer or something. And the fact that the developer can create multiple different atmospheres you can jump between is pretty damn cool. But don't expect this game to be a psychological horror game, because it's not, it's more of a thriller. There are a few puzzles too, which weren't necessarily easy, but they weren't necessarily intensly difficult either.
Also I should point out again that this game is GORGEOUS. The dev built this on Unreal 4 and it really makes this game pop. The engine really helped with making the atmospheres feel believable if at times disjointed, at least in Black Hole. The audio was great, although I had trouble with music stopping sometimes if I left the area and then there would be no sound. Some of the effects for the scary portions are so strange that they're scary because you don't know what the hell they are...and for me that's good, but it may not work for you.
Would I recommend you buy this now? Probably not. Would I recommend you buy this when more attractions are available? Probably. And maybe even then buy it on sale. It currently costs $8 and it's a little steep for maybe 3-4 hours of playtime, but of course there will be more later. Give it a try though, you might be surprised.

A space fighter/flight game is an itch that has gone unscratched for a very long time and for a very simple reason; They’re not terribly user friendly to start with. They're mostly varying flavors of spreadsheets and menus.
Rebel Galaxy avoids this problem by... not being a very complicated game. It’s stuck on a single flight platform which completely omits the need for severe flight tactics, and is instead comparable to Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag’s style of naval combat, down to the similarly used “Broadside” cannons. After that, it’s a matter of strategically placing some of your turrets as they autofire at your enemies while you control one, usually some type of rapidfire thing to cut through your enemies.
Enemy ships, usually the small fighters, tend to have access to the 3D plane which is not as much of a problem as you might expect as it usually just means you need to plan your position to open fire. Again, your guns can shoot them depending on placement.
Meanwhile it has a sort of MMO-like questing style of clearing enemies, shipping goods, defending traders, as well as a story mode. I actually have a lot of fun just ignoring the main quest (As you do), running around making ALL the money, upgrading my ship, and having a giggle when my main quest’s risk rating reads “Very Low”.
As an aside; The music is wonderful and it took considerable resistance not to name my ship “Serenity”. It’s got a couple hours of full length (~3 minute) songs that will change in space stations or open battles which helps mix it up a bit.
If I had a complaint, it’s probably that there’s not too much to do mid flight. Mid transit, there’s not a lot of popups when you’re fighting thousands of whatever-unit-of-distance it’s using. It amounts to three things interrupting your warp speed: Distress Signals, Ambushes, and Asteroid Fields/Nebulas. When you put aside all of the controversial themes of this game it's basically a Postal-esque slightly isometric shooter. The plot of this game is minimal - you just go around and shoot random people/cops/SWAT/soldiers with the final purpose to blow it all up to hell in some atomic power plant. I think that if developers decided to make this a zombie/alien/bad guys (terrorists, soldiers of some oppresive country) shooting game it wouldn't be controversial at all.
Let's get to pros of this shooter:
- game is quite smooth, it plays well
- shooting mechanics are ok for such a game
- some levels have really good design - sewers, train, the town with a politician and power plant - level of details is admirable
- really, power plant level is nice to look at
- survival mode prolongs gameplay time
- graphics style is nice imo, we have black, white, shades of gray and I think red and blue
And some cons:
- weapon rooster is small - pistol, shotgun, assault rifle (ak47 look-alike), bazooka, flame thrower, m16 (I think), submachine gun, uzi, three throwable objects (HE grenade, molotov, flashbang) and heavy machine gun mounted on some vehicles
- some weapons are useless - shotgun, flashbang, pistol
- some enemies are too strong - SWAT and soldiers can take a lot of bullets
- healing system is plainly stupid - it's the same as in Space Marine game - to replenish health you need to finish enemies lying on the ground. It would be nice to just have some random medkits or stimulants
- game on higher difficulty levels is really hard (this is a con to me, it may no be to others)
- long loading times
To sum up - it's hard to give either a thumb up or thumb down here. This is not a good game because it lacks some polishing here and there as well as it lacks any plot at all. On the other hand this is not a bad game because I had fun when playing this game as a shooter and some of the levels were pretty in design. I've bought it in some bundle and it was a good offer then. If you like such isometric shooters then go ahead and grab it, there is a big chance you will enjoy it. If you would just like to try it then maybe just pass this one, there is really nothing special to it.

X Rebirth is a different game from any of the X3 series, (which I've played, and modded, a lot).  But it's also worse in many aspects.  I'll recommend it, but with caveats - that you know and understand what you're buying...
Good:
The graphics engine is a big upgrade from X3, and as a tech demo and foundation for future projects, it's what you'd expect going forward - (the main reason for its existence).
Which feeds into the improved atmosphere of the game's setting.
More equipment upgrades (tiered) for the player ship.
Can own a fleet of combat and trade ships (like X2/3 series)
Remote (direct) trading in basic goods/missiles etc. works, even if limited to the zone you are in - (the financial 'cost/penalty' isn't that great).
More common NPC combat compared to vanilla X3 (all games).
Neutral:
Unlike X3, (but like XBTF) this game revolves around 1 player flown ship.  This makes X Rebirth a completely different game to X2/3 - but also means it needs to be judged on what it adds, as much as takes away...
Bad:
Complexity for complexity's sake, without the gameply depth it should enable.
Upgrades for the player ship are very limited, making it a very short-term gameplay element.  This makes the single ship far too limiting for gameplay development in a game of this size and potential scope. Additional random weapon mods only do so much.
Walking in stations adds very little to gameplay beyond repetitive scouring for goods,  getting crew and talking to black marketeers. (Either add something more meaningful to overall gameplay, or remove it, IMO, atm, it's a chore to do it in person rather than remotely - the exploration could definitely be improved.)
The UI feels clunky on PC (obviously designed mainly with console use in mind).
Due to lack of depth, direct (even if remote for the zone) trading can't afford to be too profitable...
Trading with owned freighters feels clunky, and the distinction between different types of freight is definitely a complexity the game didn't really need, but again, trading cannot afford to be too profitable, so...  The ratio of viable trades vs number of goods is usually far too low, especially early on.  Separating direct and indirect trading makes both more shallow.
(Auto) Ship commands/fleet controls are too basic/non-existent even compared to vanilla X3R, let alone modded X3AP.
Ugly:
Bugs.  (Apparently altering the R key to NOT fire missiles, (don't want it being confused with the long range scan), was enough to cause it to eventually disable all firing/launching/scanning.)
Not knowing how much a trader will buy something from me (directly) in advance, (even as they tell me the selling price), until after I've bought it and have it in my inventory.
The Bigger Picture:
The X3 series had a fundamental game that not just worked, but had so much potential, that it still never came close to reaching, even after all the mods X3AP has today.  And this is the problem I see with X Rebirth:  So much of what has changed may have added some capability in the short term, but severely limited its potential in the long term, especially for modding.
For example: The only four true limitations in X3, globally, are the 480 sector map (not sector size, which is more limited by your computer power), (though there were two sectors it never liked for me, so it was more a 478 maximum effective sector map), the effective 120 overall weapon slots, (30xS/M/L/XL) (that could have any number of weapons per slot) that the AI could also use, (there were a couple extra that only the player could access),  the effects/appearance the weapons could have, and the fact that stations and complexes were not modular and therefore had fixed goods to trade.
The amount of different ships in the game, (that the player and NPC's could also fly), overall weapon numbers, shield sizes and numbers of trade goods in X3 were only truly limited by application.
Not only that, but apart from adding ships, chanigng all of this was fairly simple (just tome consuming) due to basic individual xml files.  The additional complexity of X Rebirth in this manner makes adding and changing it far harder and even more time consuming.  The problem, is that some of these limitations (weapon slots/upgrade slots) by not be easy to add to in the numbers X3 had, and therefore it potential simply may not be as great, not just for future games, but modding aswell.
Most of the mods so far have been to make the game easier to USE, rather than adding gameplay, (though some have, of course, but it's been almost 4 years already...)

So, I finally finished playing X:Rebirth. I tried it two or three times, then abandoned because of bugs and ugly interface, and then tried again. And now, when I finished it, I can say only one thing: better play X3:Terran Conflict instead. Because it’s just plain better. Because X:R has only fraction of X3:TC’s content. X:R feels like endless X3:TC middlegame – the time, when you sold your starting fighter, bought powerful corvette and flying around to scrape up money for some basic capital ship. Despite the fact that corevette is given for free from the start, and both fighters and capships in the game are both useless and unplayable.
Fighters are easily destroyed because they have stupid AI and you outclass them. Capships are easily destroyed because they have exposed destructible turrets and you have remote guided torpedoes with effectively unlimited range. Combat is broken and requires neither skill nor money investment. Boarding is laughably easy and requires, at most, 2-3 millions in the beginning – just sell your free starting freighter. Money gain from boarding is enormous, since here, unlike X3:TC, you can repair ship hull and even weapons(!) for free. This, in turn, completely wreaks economy and makes station building (in which devs invested a lot of efforts) useless in the first place.
I really don’t understand people who invested 200+ hours in this game. In Terran conflict you had really required lot of resource so make strong economy to build a lot of ships, to supply those ships with weapons. And there was story missions like “pay 2 billion (NOT million) credits and we will give you your own sector”. There was purpose in strong economy. Here you can get any amount of fully equipped ships just by taking assassination missions and boarding – and the worst that it will be not just cheaper, it will be FASTER. And now we slowly come to the cherry on this pie of a broken glass…
Bugs and (more importantly) bad interface decisions. There were a lot of complains about that in the first days after release. Now there is not that much. Because the worst, game-breaking ones were cleared. Non-game-breaking ones… Just read
, no point to list them all here. After you read the link above – maybe you will be able to play smoothly. I, on the other side, spent maybe a third of my 70 hours playing time on finding those workarounds manually via google and Steam discussions. And there still were some I had to guess myself – e.g. appeared that the starting freighter has 60k of container space, 60k energy space and 10k fuel space. Game just said "130k", so I spent half of the hour waiting for my half-empty freighter to start picking valuable containers, in stealing which I put so much efforts.
So in the end – IDK. Maybe if you really into all this station/economy building stuff, and if you read all manuals about avoiding bugs, and don’t mind saving often into different slots – just in case – you might (just might) enjoy X:R. But not me. I went through main campaign, captured a collection of destroyers, and turned
into a state of a brick by wreaking all weapons and engines. And when I flied third sector (during campaign it’s not available from the start) I understood that I just bored. There is nothing more here for me. There are some DLC, additional sectors – i don't care. There is nothing NEW waiting for me there. I better go play X3:TC again. And that’s what I recommend to everybody else.
P.S. In the end of campaign you have to board Xenon (hostile robots that tried to eradicate humans for centuries) stations. There you can find crates with random wares. The ones that infest usual stations, and purpose of which is to contain a loot you can take and sell for little amount of money – like in Diablo. Think of it – human-eradicating robots built enormous station and put a crate of human alcohol there. I don’t know how can anyone defend this game with such stuff in it.

This is one of those games that had a catestrophic launch, completely broken, and nobody thought it could ever recover.  The team at Egosoft made a commitment to fix it, and they really did.  Unfortunatley, many players jaded by the initial launch are so angry about the initial launch they can never give the game a fair chance.
This is really one of the best space sandbox games that you will find.  Such a massive universe to explore.  So many different ways to play.  A few tedious and repetitive tasks, but there are plenty of mods to help eleviate that.  You can log hundreds of hours (obviously since I'm at almost 800) and still find new ways to enjoy this game.  Operate a fleet of traders, battle fleet hunting down bad guys, build a pirate fleet and destroy and loot merchant ships, setup your ship like a sniper with guided missles, or build an empire of space stations, or try to do it all.  This is as open ended as a space game can practically be.
There is only one significant flaw that still exists, and there is really no way to fix it.  One of the best parts of a space game is customizing ships, different ships, etc.  Do you want to fly a tricked out fighter, heavily armored destoryer, or man the bridge of your carrier?  You get one ship in this game, the skunk.  You can customize to an extent, but you just get that one ship.  Some mods allow you to sit in your capital ships and use them like a bridge/headquarters, but it's still limited.
Buy this game and keep an open mind when playing it.  It is not X3 (the predecessor).  It is an ambitious game that had a rocky start that really clawed it's way back.

I eagerly bought this game, thinking it would surpass or, at least, match its predecessor, but, to my surprise, the game performed poorly. Civilization is a game of immersion. Each playthrough has its own story, characters, and events that bring the game to life. However, there are too many features that were omitted or altered to Beyond Earth's detriment. For example, the art of Civilization V is simple yet elegant, and it provides a meaningful insight into the game. Whenever I build the Great Wall of China wonder, I get to see an image of the Chinese imperial soldiers, standing on the wall and guarding their country from foreign threats. Whenever I build a Beyond Earth wonder, I see....a schematic. The schematic is so bland, so insipid, so flat that it sucks out the joy and pride I feel when finishing a wonder within the game. Overall, I strongly disliked the stylistic choice of design for the buildings and wonders. They are cold and lifeless.
Furthermore, aside from aesthetics, there are inherent flaws that prevent the game from being enjoyable. Conquering cities is far too discouraging due to the penalties to health, especially in the early game. I understand that, in the early game, one should focus on establishing an infrastructure, but, in the real world, factions and civilizations have waged wars since the earliest days. I would truly appreciate it if early warmonging was less penalized, so that one could realistically wage war and not fall so behind in science and culture. I would recommend giving cities the power to simultaneously produce units and buildings, so that a warmonging faction might suffer from not creating workers but may still produce buildings to pick up the pace.
As a final note, the inability to create my own maps hinders the game. I usually like to play in small maps with several nations in order to force the players to expand at least once throughout the game, but, in Beyond Earth, the game automatically truncates the amount of factions to one that it deems appropriate for the map size. Even if the designers remedied this issue, the World Builder has still not been implemented. Firaxis is releasing a new game, called Starships, and the World Builder is yet to be seen. Ultimately, Firaxis needs to address many of this game's flagrant problems prior to even considering releasing another game.

Before playing this game, I played the full unroasted BioShock series and absolutely loved all three games, their atmosphere, their graphics and story. The remaster of the first BioShock put me in awe in the first 5 mins. Unfortunately, I was let down by utterly horrible cutscenes, poor mouse smoothing and a massive lack of customizability in the graphics settings.
Let’s start with the graphics settings. Most titles that are released to focus on better graphics (such as almost any remaster) have extensive graphics settings to cater for all types of pcs and to satisfy all pc master race lords with the satisfaction of saying they can run on all ultra-settings, Bioshock did not live up to these standards. It had no texter quality settings, shader quality settings or shadow quality settings. None. I may make the settings sound minimal and that’s because they really are with the only settings there that I found at all necessary being the fov and AA settings. The fact that I was running at 140fps and couldn't do anything to improve the basic game quality had me kicking myself.
The mouse smoothing was a basic issue that, as far as I can tell is due to a poorly done pc port. Not much more to be said on that, was just a bit of a peeve.
I loved the BioShock series and I had played the original game all the way through 4 times and i figured the remaster would at least have enough charm to give the game the replay value that it had already. A huge part of a games immersion can come from the cetaceans and it can be a fine line between boring and captivating. Bioshock remastered cutscenes were simply hard to look at and I ended up quitting the game before the scene with the first little sister had finished as there we two thick back bars on the top and bottom of the screen taking up near 40% of the overall image and just to kick it in, I could pause and see the full image but could not remove these massive eye sores. This ruined the games replay value for me.
Simply put, this game was ruined by 2 little bars and some missing settings and it kills me that all it to was those simple things to make me never want to play this wonderful game again.
If anyone at 2K ever sees this please get those two bars fixed because that’s all it will take to make this game great again.

Improved from early on, Duels offers a good introduction to Magic and it's rules while offering a free to play experience and an ever expanding card pool. While currently there are only two sets available (Origins and Battle for Zendikar) it's an inexpensive, especially compared to paper magic, way for players of games like hearthstone to sample and enjoy a much more complex and rewarding experience.
The downside however, is the somewhat clunky interface - Magic was not designed specifically for a PC or mobile experience, so compared to games like Hearthstone its many phases can take much longer than they would in an offline game - and rather poor experience with the AI.
The AI seems to almost always play variations of the same blue/white deck full of tempo cards, and while it is good at extending the length of games, it isn't particularly challenging, especially once a player has worked through enough coins to amass a sizeable collection.
The online experience is better, although again its a mixed bag with things like searching the library/graveyard being much faster and smoother than a table top Magic experience, while things like navigating phases and responding to opponents actions at the correct points in the stack can feel wonky and require much more attention than in an offline environment.
The ranked experience is pretty similar to other online card games, where you are given a rank (in this case a number) and are normally automatically matched up with other players within 5 or so levels of the same rank. There are instances when players with a wider spread are matched, but this is likely due to lower player count at those times rather than something with the matchmaking algorithm.
It is a free to play game after all, and with that comes grinding in game currency, in this case coins. Recently the amount of coins granted for doing in game things was greatly increased, and at the new level the experience is improved. Each pack costs 150 coins and each player is capped at earning 400 coins per day, with a mission (currently of between 50 and 100 coins) available, as well as 30 coins per win in online matchmaking and a bonus of 20 coins for the first win in online matchmaking.  This means with 1 online matchmaking game and a couple games against the 'hard' AI (at 15 coins each per win) you can earn something like a pack a day only playing 3-4 games.
At the moment to a player semi dedicated to playing regularly it shouldn't be hard to keep up with grinding playsets without trouble once you have the current cards, but for a new or more casual player, especially as sets are added, it will likely require some packs to be purchased with real money to be competitive or have access to all the strategies in the game.
Overall Duels is a great game in a pretty package, for free. If you have the time, money, and inclination to play paper magic, do it, Duels just doesn't (and isn't likely intended to) compete with that. But for anyone looking for their Magic fix without spending thousands of dollars on paper Magic decks and touranments, or just to explore a more complex and interactive game coming from Hearthstone or other online card games in a free to play environment, this game does that and does it well.

Rebel Galaxy, a game developed by two guys in an apartment somewhere.  It has you, the protagonist/antagonist, piloting a myriad of ships on a 2D plane while searing holes through smaller ships buzzing around you.  It's a simple game with beautiful visuals and a non-complex playstyle.  It takes a few minutes to get the controls down, but once that's done, it becomes second nature.
It's the choose your own adventure book of the space World.  Want to be a militia-supporting pilot that tries to do the right thing?  Ok.  Prefer to be a pirate that melts the armor of miners and traders?  Ok.  Want to be a miner or trader?  Ok.  Bounty hunter?  Done.
It has capital ships to fight/pilot, an array of modules/weapons to upgrade and many missions to accept and complete.  There is a propensity for the missions to get shallow, but the combat is fun enough to continue.  The desire for me to have the biggest, baddest ship in the Galaxy continues to drive me.  If I find myself getting a little weary from the missions, I go mine, or trade.  I find myself thinking about how I want to build my next ship.  Do I want an array of beam lasers?  Or do I want to build a missile boat?
The game does have a storyline arc, but I'm not fully through it yet, so it's difficult for me to comment on it.  I am intrigued though, because I want to see where it goes.  Since that's the case, it has sufficiently pulled me in enough for me to continue.
The music is terrific, and the game offers the ability to point toward your own local set of music based on triggers.  Want your collection of dubstep to play during a battle, but have a desire to have your atmospheric collection to drone on when you're just flying around?  Totally doable.
For the price, even at full cost, it's my opinion that the game is worth it.  It's a fun time sink that allows me to drop the "why so serious?" facade and just play a fun game involving lasers and explosions while making my own choices.

Basically Assassin's Creed: Black Flag meets Starfleet Command. This is not a simulation - it's more arcadey than even Starpoint Gemini, but it's better for it. If you like any combat based on firing arcs and positioning at your optimal range, or managing shield, weapon, and barrier cooldowns, you'd feel right at home. The combat in this game and the variety of ships, weapons, strategies available, and the tradeoffs you make between them is stellar. You can even build your ship dedicated to ramming stuff. Just don't expect anything from the story. Ships are constrained on a 2D plane with fighters and gunships having some leeway on vertical positioning.
Your best time with the game would probably be the beginning, flying a hunk-o-junk trying to find your feet, running away from the big fish. It's a game that oozes identity. Do pick it up if you like this genre.
One minus is that weapons and systems are tiered, so after you've seen all the varieties (which there are a lot of), the only way up is bigger numbers. Also, unlike some other games like X3, there's almost no variation between star systems, like alien installations or anomalies and so on, so the endgame can get rather repetitive.
There are a large number of ships to choose from, but many of them seem sub-par; small ships do piddling damage, huge ships are sitting duck to swarms of smaller ships and cannot defend escorts effectively. The best ships are ones that can punch way above their weight class - and IMO that's generally the Barracuda and eventually the Minotaur, but they obviously only shine once you max them out. You do get 100% trade-in for anything you buy and that's a huge plus - you can experiment with crazy combinations at no cost.
When I played at launch, escort missions later in the game were an absolute nightmare. Ships would path into asteroid fields and get stuck for an hour, or the tiny destroyer(s) you need to protect would trade broadsides with dreadnoughts like it's going out of season. You can't even reach them in the fastest ship before they blow up. There were a large series of patches addressing such things - hopefully the silly escort AI / pathfinding are gone by now.

A brief summary of Betrayer:
This game is an excellent buy, especially for the price. Steeped in mystery and leaving much to the imagination, you are cast into a dreamlike version of the New World. This game is delighfully macabre, and offers increasing variations of challenge.
Despite what others may say about the game quickly losing flavor, I find that the various difficulty options give the game a little more depth. The game is somewhat strange to get used to at first, but you will quickly find yourself discovering exactly what you need to do next completely by accident. There is also an option to drop loot much like you do in Dark Souls when you die, making the game capable of greater difficulty on the hardest setting. The game explains very little, and some areas of the game will prey on your most primal fears as you creep through shadows and forests to find hidden clues and treasures, all the while wondering what might pop out at you next. The combat does offer a challenge at higher difficulty levels, and you will often feel panic set in as you are unexpectedly discovered by enemies, some that tactfully blend in with the environment.
The game does play pretty quickly, but has decent replay value with the several difficuly options and the option to switch to full color mode as well (although I personally love the gritty black and white texture because it reminds me of old horror films). Honestly, for a $5.00 game, I was very satisfied with my purchase, and I think Blackpowder will come out with more great games in the future with a little support.

Grid 2 is about the role of your driver in the formation and proliferation of World Series Racing, an international racing series that encompasses several racing disciplines across a wide range of car types. While this structure makes sense in the context of the narrative it has the unfortunate side effect of wearing out each location's welcome. Each region has three or four primary race location with varying routes through each. While the tracks themselves are technically different they share sections and landmarks from tracks that you previously raced in. Spreading a dozen races across three locations where you encounter some of the same sections across various routes does not leave the impression that variety is this game's strong suit despite a track list that would indicate otherwise. Grid 2's greatest innovation is it's LiveRoute system. Basically track designs are modular and with LiveRoutes these sections of track are loaded on the fly completely randomizing the track and forcing players to react to each change since the mini map is unavailable. Each section of track comes together seamlessly without creating any awkward or impossible turns though some sections of track can be repeated several time throughout an event which really detracts from the novelty of the feature.
Vehicles embody the characteristics of their real world counterparts but sliding and drifting are much easier and emphasized but Grid 2 is devoid of the turbo boosts and jumps that characterize pure arcade racers. Ultimately it's a system that is extremely enjoyable. Muscle cars roar and and corner like hippos sprinting around a KY jelly covered skating rink. Tuners slide around like asthmatic mosquitoes as their turbos hiss and wheeze while track cars warp across the asphalt and slice through corners like razors through the wrists of a My Chemical Romance fan. Unfortunately the car count is on the small side, encompassing less than fifty of the most elite performance vehicles from the past and present. Well I should say the most elite races not to wear Porsche, Ferrari or Lamborghini badges. Customization is also limited to changing wheels and adding garish liveries to your machines. Copious sponsor stickers also spoil your vehicle's aesthetics while offering an opportunity to complete objectives that earn WSR more fans.
Togue events, Checkpoint races, Overtake events, Endurance races, Drift events, elimination races, and head to head races round out the event types. These events do an admirable job of keeping the main campaign from becoming stale. Likewise strong AI ensures that you have to work a bit for victories. You opponents can be really aggressive and full damage means that trying to play bumper cars in the corners can end your race or severely hamper your car's performance. Ricocheting off of your opponents in the first turn and holding the lead isn't as viable a strategy in Grid as it is other racing games.
Car models are appropriately detailed though they lack cockpit views. Matte, gloss, metallic and pearlescent paint are convincingly rendered and the damage models are unrivaled. Hoods, bumpers, fenders, spoilers and trunk lids can be smashed off and tires can even rupture. Geometry wrinkles and deforms after impacts in a rather convincing manner. As great as all of this is what really stands out are the tracks... Sparks from overhead subway rails shower the streets of Chicago and papers blow over the roadway, mists hover over the pavement in California as leaves blow around. Dubai's glorious skyscrapers and yachts dot the landscape. In short the tracks seem alive... It's a nice departure from the often drab and dead cityscapes that many games have you race through. The sound is also solid. Races are mostly scored with a symphony of pistons pumping like drums, turbos whistling like woodwinds and tires squealing like the string section. Exhausts howl, echoing off of mountain sides and tunnels and the echoing of your opponent’s vehicle seconds off of your lead can be intense.

Hoo HOO! Now this one is excellent. 2D platformer that is styled after Genesis games, or at least the way that people remember them after many Sonic hacks. Hero isn't slow, he can charge shots and shoot, runs around, collects the sparks which work as money to open chests that will either have active or passive item. Heh, I found it fancy to find out that health is actually floating point or so after getting one of damage type resistance items. You also can't get Game Over, there are no lives to count, you just lose half of sparks on death.
But well, despite all the excellent visuals and music that makes me feel jolly this one does feel amateur. And talking of music, most tracks feel a bit samey. I am sure that Genesis games had more varied tracks in games most often. But yea, amateur. For example, difficulty is a bit all over the place. Then I feel that game would benefit from this little trick that indie devs use of "for 2 or so frames after seemingly falling off ledge you can still jump normally", albeit I had trouble only at a start of a game. I wish that double jump ability would reset everytime I interacted with bounce pads. Or that the duration of high jump powerup would reset everytime I went back into lazor that gives it, before the powerup runs out by itself.
And then depth devs tried to give it some depth that I don't think work out that much. Well, there is day-night cycle. This one is nice, combined with ability to select any level which sometimes get random effect in them, bad or good. Night or day impacts behavior of enemies, which miniboss you fight in first levels and some other things. This one is nice, albeit night should be darker, haha. Not sure about items however. Passive resistance ones are fine. But then there are passive ability stuff "shoot shadows when you jump, recharge in 20 seconds" that were kinda there. Kinda not good enough and then you can't control when to activate them. Perhaps they were good at boss fights when you spam everything you've got but then enemies have temporary invincibility after getting hit so I am sure it wasn't so excellent there. Could go without bosses having those.
Active items that heal health are fine too. Can't say for heads that give additional ability. I actually spend my time holding attack button all time in order to charge it up beforehand, which somehow led me to occasional confusion of "which of these two buttons to press to jump". I know, silly, but somehow I was confused this way in the game. And having third button to think about for head abilities while you keep charging... Yea, didn't find many use. You also don't need them much in platforming sections, just in boss ones. Sometimes.
Plus, some randomization that I didn't care about.
But hey, I suggest you to beat this game anyway. It's jolly, OK?! And good. You will enjoy collecting and platforming over challenges. I am surprised that dev got the levels size just right, big mazes but not to the point where I was getting impatient.
Dev should add very cheap OST DLC so I could keep it in my Steam library.

The Stanley Parable is only a brief game, but comes with a fair amount of replayability owing to the mass of endings and easter eggs that can be found within it - and believe me, they're worth looking for. The game has a dry and snarky sense of humour, and ranges from laugh-out-loud funny to weird to existential musing to outright dark and depressing at times. The idea is simple but very effectively handled (a series of choices, to follow the narrator or not, to behave or not, to go left or right, take the red door or the blue door) and provides quality entertainment throughout its gameplay. The narrator's delight/amusement/exasperation/anger at your actions is what really drives the whole thing, and is very cleverly delivered.
I've gotten 3hrs' play out of it, and could go back for more if I wanted to get all the achievements - I got it on sale and have been absolutely delighted by it, but for the sheer entertainment value the full price wouldn't be a letdown either.

One thing I want to discuss in this review that I consider of highest priority is the state of the game’s community.  I saw many reviews claiming the game to be dead.  I disagree.  In my personal, albeit admittedly limited experience, I have been able to find active servers to play on.  In the evenings one can expect to find about 20-40 players online at any given time, often populating 1-3 of the seven or so servers.  Usually there is one crowded server with 20+ players in it and a smaller server that may have 2-10 players online, giving both the option of playing on a crowded or a less crowded server.  I must also stress that the servers populating are ones running game modes in spirit of the creators, not the RP servers that have engulfed the game’s successor.  There is only one RP server and it typically has 0-5 players online.
Regarding gameplay, I’m a fairly new player to the series.  I scarcely played PCE and purchased PC just a couple days ago because many friends of mine suggested it was a better game.  So far I have enjoyed the gameplay.  There are two game modes that see frequent play, Team Deathmatch and Get to the Chopper, both of which I enjoy.  Mechanically, the game feels fluid and the physics and movement are well-designed, both for third-person dinosaur and first-person human play.  I’ve had no lag issues at all and hits register when they should do so.  The game has a very high skill ceiling, which admittedly has been tough as someone so new to the franchise entirely but it also encourages and entertains me by my desire to improve my own skill.  Even if I have rage-logged once or twice, I wouldn’t want this any other way.
The entire basis of the game is humans versus dinosaurs, always in a team setting.  Of course I love playing as the dinosaurs, but I was also pleasantly surprised to find I didn’t dislike playing the human side.  It’s typical for me in games like these to heavily favor playing the animal side, but in Primal Carnage this isn’t the case.  The different humans you can choose from playing are comical, charismatic, and enjoyable to play with a wide array of weapons, each with its own set of strengths and weaknesses.  None seem particularly unbalanced or overpowered, and in general the dinosaur versus human establishment doesn’t feel one-sided.  Both sides are fun to play.
Some of the maps are somewhat occluded, misty, and dark, giving good places to hide and ambush, whereas others are open and sunny so there’s good map variety.  They are also well sized, not being too big or too small.  A good balance of sneaking around and finding action has been struck by adequate map size.
The graphics and sound of the game are adequate, but nothing particularly fancy.  I can’t comment too much on regard to optimization or graphics settings.  My computer handles the game fine on max settings with an Intel I7, 8GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce 980M card.  The dinosaur models aren’t the greatest, but it isn’t a particular point of grievance for me.  There are nice skins which I wish were unlockable in-game, but they’re only by purchase.
To conclude, the game’s community is not dead.  It’s just small.  Gameplay is enjoyable and both sides are fun to play with good maps.  Graphics and models are adequate, though I wish I could earn skins in-game through play.  Sometimes small communities can be more fun than big ones, and I haven’t had trouble finding a place to play against others which is the main point I want to stress here.  I recommend playing.

Minor spoiler warning, because you simply can't talk about this game without at least slightly giving away something.
Having played a few similar meta games, I had this recommended to me by various people. I was excited to try it out because if it was executed as well as I had hoped then it would have been a great game, but honestly I'm not impressed.
It is so deeply unsatisfying to me, because there's no real storyline to play. There isn't a "true ending", just many many many little endings which are all accesible instantly, so you don't feel like you're progressing at all by playing the game. You don't get anywhere or unlock anything, you just learn about this sort of weird meta story thing, but it's not one I was impressed by at an hour in.
SPOILER WARNING! SPOILER WARNING ABOUT THE NATURE OF THE GAME:
It might have been interesting if you could eventually break out of the cycle that the game puts you in, which is dying and then coming back to life to go and find a new ending, but you can't. Which apparently is the point of the game. Which is annoying. It also doesn't feel that clever to me, and the humour gets really dull after a bit. There's also too many parts where you just have to stand there for minutes listening to the narrator, awaiting your inevitable restart. I also don't actually like the narrator's voice so I'm not entertained at all in the sections where I'm just waiting.
I might be completely wrong, and it may well be that you need more than an hour to truly start to enjoy this game, but trekking through the same parts over and over again just to get back got me so bored that I couldn't be bothered to keep going. I do not recommend this game.

I first saw this game around the time it came out, but not on Steam. I had seen some guy on YouTube advertise this game and explain some of the things about it and how it would require some really strong system specs.
Years later I finally bought the game, by then
had come out, and my first impressions of it were lackluster. Missing was the excitment and gone was the joy. It felt like the game was on a very loose ball-joint, one that turns too fast and isn't big enough to fit securely in its socket. It kind of rocks around and tries to stay in place only to tilt and annoy you in that miniscule unnessecary kind of way.
that's how it feels to me.
So to get down to it, this game is bassically Jurassic Park meets TF2, and as you might guess, the game is unbalanced, everyone will tell you that; you will actually see reviews that point this out because it is painfully true. The Dinosaurs will wreck you everytime, unless you can co-ordinate and work together, the humans could hold a decent
, humans who go on the offense last long enough before being swarmed by four Raptors and a Carno.
The gameplay is great for both sides, I'm aware the balancing issue I broguht up has painted the gameplay in a negative light but that's just the way of the game. Gameplay-wise it's to be expected from a game like this. The human side has various classes to pick from; the Commando and Tracker classes standing out in my mind as heavy hitters, but don't take my word for it. The aim with the human team is to bassically survive, kill Dinosaurs, and depending on the game mode, hold the point and await evac (that gamemode usually comes special with a Spinosaurus.)
Playing the Dinosaurs (which everyone seems to prefer, again, balancing) is unique. Roaring, depending on the Dino you are in control of, allows for some unique attributes to be contributed to your team (Pteranodon lets all Dino's see humans through walls, Rex and Spino grant damage boost, for example.) This faction hits hard and is almost always guarunteed to win. That doesn't nessecarily mean it's not fun.
They do get stuck and are a hassle to control at time, it's also very easy to make a mistake and become a Fossile of you don't know what you're doing.
Graphically it's nothing flashy like
or cartoony like
, it has its own style and look to it. It looks amazing on its highest settings and the textures on the Dinos stand out beautifully, the colors and patterns are like-wise gorgeous.
DLC is nothing more than skins.

this game is still primarily a versus game, from what I've heard, the
has become more of a roleplay game, I should note that I ahven't played or touched

Finally, it comes down to the truth of this game; it has long since been abandonded by the developers. Lukewarm Media apparently went bankrupt and thus responsibility for the development of this game was handed to Circle Five Studios and Pub Games, however, they chose to leave this game to Fossilize, while they worked on... need I say it..?
.
Although this review has been primarily mixed to negative. I will end it on a positive note by saying that; despite the games flaws, problems and development history, there is fun to be had with this game. Playing as the humans can be very unfair at times, but if you know what you're doing it can be fun to play almost as much as it is playing as the Dinosaurs. The community is almost non-existent and I'm sure Extinction does some things better with this game, but

couldn't have flourished.

Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is a game that takes the weapons, environments, and game mechanics from Half-Life 2 and puts them into a PvP multiplayer game. If you couldn't tell by the title of the name, Half-Life 2: Deathmatch puts you into the boots of either a Rebel or a Combine soldier and you fight the opposing team to the death. All of the weapons from Half-Life 2 are in this game, including the Gravity Gun. So, yes, you can pick up a toilet and launch it at your enemy to kill them. You will start with a set of weapons usually consisting of a pistol, SMG, stunstick, and Gravity Gun. You will have to go searching for your other weapons including the shotgun, crossbow, magnum, and AR 2.  You can also pick up the weapon that your dead foe was using when they died. If they dropped a weapon you already have, it will be given as ammo for that weapon. Ammo, health, and suit chargers will also be scattered throughout the map. Be sure pick up those as you go. (Using health and suit chargers may leave you out in the open, so be careful of enemies.) The core character mechanics from Half-Life 2 also make a return, the only difference being that your character moves a little faster. That means that shooting while sprinting is still a thing. While it may be a bit cheap, it's still a game mechanic to be exploited. That also means that the game is a lot more fast-paced and frantic then most multiplayer FPS games on the market such as Call of Duty or Battlefield. (Note: I don't hate these two game series. So, shut up.) The maps in this game are based off of areas in Half-Life 2. While most aren't ripped straight from the game, I feel like maps like Lockdown is ripped right from Nova Prospekt, a level in Half-Life 2. There's also tons of people still playing this game. Though most servers may have bots, that shouldn't stop you from enjoying this game. Overall, Half-Life 2: Deathmatch is a really fun multiplayer game. It's currently only $14.99 on Steam. You also don't need a very powerful computer to run it. So, go check it out.

This is NOT quite the same as previous X3 titles. I do not mention earlier incarnations then X3 as I have not yet fired them up.
I can appreciate some of the criticism when comparing against X3(x): inability to pilot more than just the one craft; the annoyance of the highways instead of jump gates; the incessant comments made by the co-pilot, Yisha, and the repetitive comments made by the other NPCs.
However, when taken on face value, it is far from the shoddy effort that a large proportion of the gming community made it out to be.  Had it arrived with a different name, and title, most of the negativity from the gaming nerds would be misplaced.
There are oodles of effective mods available which enhance the overall experience; numerous additions which can alter the gameplay, or provide upgrades or changes to characters, the universe, the (single, playable) ship and the game mechanics itself, removing a lot of the tedium of having to repetitively locate traders, mission characters, scanning of stations and so on.
The game universe is large enough to travel around in. 3rd-party mods can increase this size drastically - although in most cases at the cost of interacting with the main story missions. So post main-mission only.
One of the major failings of this universe is that, in every system there are a limited number of build sites available and complex structures that were possible in previous X incarnations are not possible here.  Supplying the stations follows similar characteristics as previously using cargo-carrying craft as supply ships - I have even used the (captured) gigantic Xenon L. There is a lot of granular control over what can be produced at stations, one can limit production, control of station facilities, etc and, once again, with mods this can be further enhanced.
Yes, one may criticise this for being far from what was offered in previous titles but, if taken on its own merits it is still an enjoyable spacing experience.
The inclusion of the extra DLC should have been part of the original game package and not afterthoughts but what's done is done and we make the best of things and move on.

Magic Duels is a great game for beginners and casual magic players, but that’s about it. If you want to play seriously, this game is not for you. The game has some major flaws that have yet to be addressed. The biggest problem is the quest mechanic. It is meant to encourage players to play every day, but the challenges are repetitive and do not count all your progress. For example if the quest is to win 2 duels with a R/B deck, the game will not recognize your victory if you built your deck using the deck builder. This means you must you use the awful deck wizard to build a deck to complete the quest. The game also doesn’t recognize a victory with a R/B deck in two headed giant mode. This issue has yet to be solved and could be easily fixed. Another fundamental flaw of the game is when a player concedes. If you are playing online and your opponent concedes, quits, or otherwise disconnected, the game forces you to play an AI. So many things to say, but I'll try to keep it short. Starting with the good.
The game seems like an inspirational piece as it take a few cues from Sonic (3/Knuckles/Advance series), Ristar (some of the graphics and controls), Gunstar Heroes (self explanitory if you get to this one part of the game), and Kirby (Misc and one specific boss).
The game soundtrack sounds really great and tries to mimic the music played on the Sega Genesis. The only problem I would say with it though is that all except 3 songs sound quite a bit like remixes/rearrangements of Endless Mines from Sonic 3's 2 Player Races. They're not horrible as I like Endless Mines, but think they should've had a bit more variety.
I do like how the music is different in the level whether it's day or night. Nice touch on that.
The levels are amazing. I thought it was cool that there were alternate route everywhere you can go just like Ristar and Sonic... but it went way beyond that it seems.
All of the levels (except the final one for reasons) feel like a giant level where you can go or end up anywhere, but you never really get lost as each path leads to the end. Quite stunning actually. Even greater how the levels are completely different whether you play them day or night. And I could be wrong, but it looks like there's 3 level layouts per levels (Day/Night/Other).
The stars were also somewhat a nice touch as at first I was worried that I might run out if I don't pick up every single one, but there's enough out there that you shouldn't be too worried about running into a chest and unable to open them.
The bosses were somewhat unique with some being really easy, while others being really hard, and a few where you need to look for those specific patterns to even attack or damage the boss. Not sure what else I can say other than they didn't feel like any were reskinned of another.
Onto the bad of the game (one of them just a preference to me maybe?)
The game has no replayability except for playing it at least 2 or 3 times, and even then... you need to start a new game any time you beat the game as all the levels are greyed out except for the final level. This I think is really bad as it kind of makes the level select screen pointless after you beat the game.
Other than seeing the 3 layouts of each level and then of course seeing every boss and maybe certain alternative routes... there isn't more to do in the game. Not really a horrible thing, but it sure isn't a good thing either.
A lot of the sounds of enemies sounds like it was ripped right out of Sonic 1 2 and 3. While I did mention the capturing of the Genesis sounds, I don't know if this was intentional, but they really sound way too much like the sounds from the Sonic games. Like the spitting fire sounds or the bumping balls sounding like... the bumpers from Sonic 3 and many more.
Doesn't make the game bad, but it kind of messes with the originality of the levels a little. Just a little.

Games that are developed by just one person always deserve special praise and this is one of them. Blink the Bulb is a clear homage to the Sega Genesis and is very faithful to the limitations of that system. The vibrant graphics in particular are very appealing and give each level a unique charm.
A strong point of this game is the level design. Each level is fairly large and offers many different paths to the end. Levels also change depending on the day/night system, which adds even more to replayability. The combat is fairly straightforward and mostly involves charging up shots to shoot at enemies. Getting past regular enemies is pretty easy, but the bosses at the end of each level provide a decent challenge. There is also an inventory system and I appreciated the variety of passive bonuses that can be accumulated throughout the game.
For a free game the standard of quality is remarkably good - if it came out 25 years ago I am sure it would be considered a classic. My first playthrough took a little over an hour, which may be short by today's standards, but very suitable for an old-fashioned game like this. As someone who grew up with a Genesis this was a real treat to play. I hope the developer will have more games coming in the future.

It's a weird feeling to finally finish this episodic game that I started playing a couple of years ago. Not only because it's a sad feeling to finish a game you've been coming back to and exploring for so long, but also because I would argue that TDM is, despite some minor flaws, one of the most artistically fulfilling and aesthetically original games I've ever played.
First of all, the design of the game is obviously the thing that everybody will mention. But the cardboard-and-clay-style is worth mentioning at length. Because TDM's highly unique style is not just a gimmick, it also enhances every inch of the games dream-focused plotline, making it a game that is both otherworldy beautiful and right-out dreadful and terrifying.
However, sometimes the game is a bit off - some dialogue and plotting can feel a bit lacking, as well as some minor bugs breaking the immersion somewhat.
A few puzzles can also feel a bit too obtuse and unforgiving, which is a shame, considering that TDM also packs some of the absolutely BEST puzzles I've seen in a recent adventure game. At it's best, TDM uses it's ominous dream logic and creates some immensly satisfying brain teasers that are both perfect within the story and interesting and fun to solve.

All in all, TDM is a game that starts out as something I figured for a clichéed dream story, but soon evolves into a literal existential nightmare, filled with twists and turns that will haunt you for a long time to come. Highly recommended.

The Dream Machine is an old-school point ‘n’ click that really likes its long-winded musings about the nature of human existence. Although its philosophical nature and clay animation style may classify it as an “artsy” game, its adventure game bits also hide some interesting moments.
It is difficult to review The Dream Machine, because while it starts as a seemingly normal adventure game, eventually it transforms into a naval-gazing exploration laced in existentialist metaphors.
Said adventure game bits bring us back to the golden age of point ‘n’ clicks, not just with the classic handmade clay animation but also with the tedious pixel hunting and some decent dose of moon logic. These early, plot-focused chapters introduce our protagonist, Victor, who recently moved to a new apartment building with his pregnant wife, but soon discovers that an evil machine is feeding on the dreams of all tenants.
From there, our job is to enter the dreams of everyone in the apartment, and as the story goes, the writing style detaches itself more and more from reality (and sanity), shedding many adventure game bits to end in a series of philosophical monologues on human existence.
It is easy to dismiss the game as an art project, especially in later chapters where the graphical filters go on a rampage. Still, its uniqueness will have a lasting impression on anyone (assuming the game does not crash on them), and considering it is one of the primary goals of art, we can say that The Dream Machine is a rather successful project.

I didn't encounter hardly any technical issues or bugs like almost every other review mentions. There were no issues with textures or sound or anything like other reviews mention. However, the game crashed 3 times in total. I saved fairly often, so I only ever lost 20 minutes of my time at the most, which was annoying, but it wasn't the end of the world.
My problems with the game are actually related to the game itself rather than any technical issues. The difficulty curve in this game is kind of ridiculous on the normal difficulty. I didn't play on any other difficulty so I can't speak for them. The first half of the game is pretty easy. Enemies weren't bullet sponges, ammo wasn't scarce, and hacking was really easy. Then after you beat Sander Cohen (which is a relatively easy boss fight), the game became pretty difficult. Suddenly, ammunition became incredibly scarce. There were a few times where I was left with nothing but my plasmids, and maybe some liquid nitrogen in my chemical thrower, since I rarely used that ammo type. And the enemies seem to take more and more ammo to kill (although it might just seem that way because of the sudden lack of ammunition). And hacking suddenly became monumentally hard in the later parts of the game. Granted, I didn't know that you could freeze a machine before hacking it in order to slow down the flow rate. Since I didn't know that (and I'm not entirely sure if the game ever tells you that or if it's something that you're just supposed to find out), I had a lot of trouble with the machines where you have to replace the first tile very quickly, or else you'll get trapped in by alarms. This happened even with the tonics that reduce the amount of alarms in each machine. The strange thing was, despite the second half of the game being pretty difficult, the final boss fight was pretty easy, and only took a few minutes.
Overall, despite the difficulty curve making some parts of the game less enjoyable (especially the Hephaestus level, that one really wasn't much fun at all), Bioshock is still a fantastic game that holds up today, and if you've managed to not hear any spoilers in the 10 years that this game has been out, you will probably be surprised by the twist. If you aren't plagued by constant crashes and other bugs, it can be a very enjoyable experience, and I look forward to playing the other games in this series.

I'll say it right from the start: this game is basically a flash game with good graphics. If you think your money's worth shouldn't be going in the looks of a game, don't buy it at full price.
I say that because Hatred in itself is very simple, both in what the player can do and the enviroment: you run around and shoot people, some shoot you, you have a variety of around 8 weapons total, plus 3 types of grenades. You can steal cars and army vans with miniguns, make some things explode and that's pretty much it. The game also has 7 levels plus 3 levels in another game mode, so overall there isn't enough to it to justify the price. It will keep you entertained for a bunch of hours and it has replayability value if you want to kick back and kill some people to pass time, but if you're looking for something to excite you and fascinate you this isn't it.
What really sets it apart is the presentation: the artstyle is BEAUTIFUL, both in the game and in the Steam items (the cards make for some gorgeous wallpapers). It's not complex nor original, but it really is pleasing to look at and goes perfectly with what the story's about. The graphic is technically well done too, especially for an indie game. Kickass music and voice acting to boot.
The serious bad things of this videogame are in its programming: it crashes, it slows down, it screws up the aspect ratio, materials go through other materials... none of this happens frequently, but enough for them to be something more than accidents. Also the UI will work against you in certain situations, not to mention some in-game items will get in your way despite nothing setting them apart from items you can go through.
Oh, and if you didn't get it by now: it's a game were killing people is the main objective. Everything revolves around it, so if you're stuck in a parallel dimension where Doom and GTA never happened you may want to stay away from it. That said, the people you kill are hardly "people", they just stand around and repeat the same, boring exclamations over and over ("Jesus Christ!", "He's got a gun!" etc), so no worries (and kinda boring too).
I recommend it because it does offer something new, both in substance and presentation, and it is a fun time-killer when you're in the mood. I only suggest to buy it when the price goes down.
