This game has excellent atmosphere and a fantastic combat system that manages to feel very impactful. Muskets and pistols are superbly implemented and their reload mechanics make changing weapons a necessity at times, and the other items you can carry around give you plenty of options. When you fire off those gunpowder weapons you really feel it and you have to make strategic decisions about when it might be safe to reload which adds some depth to combat.
The great atmosphere is brought about by good sound design and a beautifully haunting aesthetic. The mostly grayscale world, with smatterings of red really works to amp up the semblance of mystery, it gets the mind wondering “why is it like this? What could possibly be the cause? When will I finally lift this accursed grey?” This impetus pushes you on ever deeper into the forest, discovering clues and interacting with all sorts of nasties in order to try and uncover the ultimate answer.
Unfortunately, that's where the positives end. The game felt a little bit too long to me in truth, I feel the game could have used one or two fewer areas as it does get repetitive, and it felt like near the end even the developer was getting tired of writing stories as the things to find became more about gold and items and less about story, although that was welcome by that point as I just wanted to conclude the story by then.
It did redeem itself a little, but I still feel the story and the ending were underwhelming. I was intrigued at times, but overall I think it could have been a lot better. While the combat was full of impact, the story most certainly fell flat.
That said, I do still recommend this game, it is very cheap and if you're after something a little bit different the combat and the aesthetic alone are elements worth seeing, and the story passable enough to keep going until the end.

Ah, Bioshock 2. The scrawny, overlooked middle child of the Bioshock franchise. Neither the adrenaline-soaked action of Infinite, nor the dark, atmospheric journey of discovery of the original. Now that I've played it I can see why it was a let down for many.
Here is an example of when worlds collide for the worst. The ability to wield the power of the Sith in one hand and the power of the Terminator in the other does not suit the dreary tromp through Rapture's half flooded tunnels. It's an action game in a horror setting, where the action overwhelms any sense of dread, knowing that whatever pops around the corner will find themselves just another red smear on the soggy carpet in the blink of an eye.
Writing is far weaker than the original. Sofia Lamb is a little more than Andrew Ryan, except she was found in the clearance aisle of Villains R Us. Like Ryan, she calls out your actions throughout the game, but never succeeds in getting under your skin. Minor villains come and go with no significant buildup nor payoff. The moral choice system is back, too. Just as useless as it was in the first game.
Speaking of mechanics, playing as a Big Daddy turns the 'Little Sister Escort' level from the original game into a game mechanic, again with the ability to save or harvest them once their Adam collecting is done. The 'save or harvest' aka 'good or evil' mechanic was already pretty gimmiky in the original game and even more so now. Any player who pays any amount of attention to escorting Little Sisters will be positively swimming in Adam, without a single harvest.
All in all, though, Bioshock 2 is still a worthy game, despite feeling more 'DLC' than 'sequel'. It does an admirable job of expanding upon the lore of the original game and fielded some new mechanics that would be refined and put to greater use in Infinite. Had it not need to follow in the footsteps of the original Bioshock it likely would have fared far better than it did.
On the note of Bioshock Infinite, the similarities between Bioschocks 2 and Infinite are quite noticeable. Beyond the mechanics there's the father-daughter team, with the daughter as a support character, going up against a deluded tyrant insane with the goal of utopia. There's the insane religious dudes, the frustrated minority, sick of discrimination, and the painting of the protagonist as the harbinger of doom to a close-knit society. Get the feeling that, like Subject Delta, this game is a prototype. At least it's a fun one.

This is compounded by the fact that you can only save at specific locations in the game, so sometimes dying to a boss means several loading screens and minutes of travel time before you can try again.
Speaking of those save points, they're in a game where the clock is constantly ticking.  Taking time to save means you're losing time to rescue survivors or defeat optional bosses.
But if you can get past those things you find a pretty satisfying zombie beat em up with a solid B movie storyline.

Honestly man, this game is okay. I wish steam had an option for neutral on if I recommend it because it really depends on the person.
I think Egosoft tried to make an offshoot game from the X Series about what happened in Albion and how it affected the nearby systems, but it just wasn't ready to be recieved by the fans. I remember buying this game about 2 months after it came out. I got home and put the install disk inside my pc and after I finished downloading it, the game booted up. Simple enough right? Well, after about 5 seconds into the loading screen, the game crashed. 3 times after that aswell. Finally, I started it again and it worked.
I started the campaign as I had seen so many others do on YouTube and I quickly saw how unfinished this game was. At the end of the day, no game is actually finished, but this was far from being ready to be released. I played a couple hours but I uninstalled because it just plain wasn't fun. Not even the 2 DLC releases that came out enticed me to replay this game.
Then 4.0 came out. 4.0 truly made X Rebirth a brand new game in my opinion. Hundreds of bugs were squashed, the factions were corrected, speech and subtitle issues were corrected, and the game was optimized a hell of a lot better. This game finally became playable so I dumped a whole lot of my free time into it. Like all the other X games though, mods enhanced this game further and made it more enjoyable. The mod I'm referring to is CWIR because it just adds a whole new experience to this game. Anyways, there are still annoyance features that are in this game, like the difficult to understand U.I, and the annoying voice acting. There's also the lack of speech asset variety and lack of ship variety as well.
This game is not all bad stuff either. The graphics are really nice for an X Game, and there are mods that just add to the already beautiful ship/station design. The fights can get really intense and when you have a massive fleet fighting another, it's just awesome to see. There are missiles flying, small ships flying around shooting up other small ships, and capital ships just going at each other is what I enjoy seeing in this game. The stations are also really nice as well. A really big thing that I enjoyed was the fact that you can walk around on the stations! That was something that I don't think we've seen since the first X Game (I do not own because it's a little too old for me lol). There are some station varieties and the modular system for stations and ships work really well in your favor because it does actually affect economies and your ship's performance.
Either way, this game right now is something I'd recommend, but marginally. What I like to keep in mind is, positives come and go, but negatives will just pile up. That's what happened to this game. People focused too much on the pile of negatives and completely disregarded the positives.

This really is a unique game, controls are incredibly simple as you just use the mouse, click where you want to go, double click if you're in a hurry, I found this game to be a mix of xcom base building and abes oddworld, but I will expand. Your hideout is a wrecked shelter in need of repairs, you can scavenge this place early on to start off and gain resources, everything is a factor to your survival, you need water, food, and heating, you can build apparatus to help achieve this, but you always need to balance your limited resources, and rest, because you are up against the clock and bang...the suns down and now you need to go out and hunt for those precious supplies. Now you need to balance again, do I sleep, guard against a potential raid to me, scavenge and what do I take with me if I go out scavenging? A weapon, bandage for someone in need or a crowbar to break in, each item taking up space you could otherwise use for more scavenging?!
The amount of diversity and choice in this game is amazing, you can come back one night a hero, the other a monster, or not come back at all, you're group continues regardless, the question now is do you have what it takes to survive the war? I fully recommend this addictive game that will continue to surprise and astound you.

War Child is a great charity and I am more than willing to pay a little overpriced to help the cause.  There are a few things that could be improved upon, combat is basically just clicking, now this works most of the time because its trying to be short and brutal. First of all, I will just say I recommend this game for those who don't like reading long reviews. I thumbs it up, and I think you should try it.
However, there are some issues. Glitcheness is one of them; being a raptor can be annoying. The jump button only works every few seconds, you can't jump quite as often as a ratpr should. So naturally ... you fall down holes a lot.
The other issue is balancing. This is a hilariously unbalanced game. There is just no fighting players playing as Tyrannosaurs, especially when there are three of them. Do not waste your ammo on them. They rarely die; they run if they get too close to death and go heal somewhere. This is a team game, you are playing to help your team win. Shoot the little ones. Group up where the Tyrannosaurs can't get you and shoot the smaller dinosaurs to get the kills.
As a dinosaur player, do not bother being a Rex. I know it's awesome, and the only species anyone really cares about in this game, but when the player hides under a roof or in an alleyway, there's nothing you can do but pout your big dinosaur face off. Besides, everyone aggressively clicks their mouse over the Rex hoping to be it and the chances are you won't get to play as his/her lordship.
My advice would be to be that guy.
That guy that lets his teammates get what they want and instead plays strategically. Let the silly children play as a Rex and be the dinosaur that runs in and disrupts the enemy so that they flee cover and are left vulnerable to the one-hit killing Tyrannosaurs.
I also advise playing as the Pathfinder as a human. Damage against the Rex is as abysmal as everything else but shooting a raptor head on and murdering it straight up with the shotgun is such a "Booyah" moment. XD Blinding them with the flares is also handy when a motherlovin Rex is stomping after you and you're screaming your face off, running for your little shotgunner life.
If you've read this far, then good on you, and I hope you enjoy the game if you do indeed buy it.

This is a really fantastic point & click adventure game for fans of the genre. The whole thing is built up of clay figures and backgrounds, spruced up further with bits of paper, moss, fabric, twigs, leaves, and other materials, which gives it a unique and kind of nostalgic look, reminding you of classic claymation. Amazingly, it's built up in Flash. I've experienced the occasional glitch where dialogue text repeatedly pops up, sometimes white screens where the game apparently crashes, and some bad slowdown on certain heavily layered graphics, but mostly it's extremely stable.
You play as Victor Neff, a young guy who just moved into a new apartment with his pregnant girlfriend, and discover something crazy. I'll avoid saying more than that, as the story takes many surprising turns. It took a bit of playing for me to gauge what kind of story the game was going for - the static clay figures look a little grotesque, and I was expecting a more cartoonish plot. Instead, the game gets quite serious, even dark at points, and tells a fairly mature tale. A good deal of it reminded me of I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream, another excellent adventure game.
It's a very challenging adventure game. A few times now, I've had to look up online help to get further. The game lets you switch hints from the main character on or off, but even switched on, it can get very difficult to figure out. Still, never unfairly so.
If you miss point and click adventuring, this game should provide you with a great many hours of gameplay.

Sins Of A Solar Empire: Rebellion is one of the best RTS games of all time. It's easily the best game Stardock has ever made, and probably will ever make (if Galactic Civilizations III is any indication). It's a naval macromanagement game with surprising depth, excellent balance, and some of the best mods I've ever seen. The DLC packs (other than the soundtrack, which I don't have and can't vouch for) add new mechanics to the gameplay are essentially micro-expansions. There's no campaign mode, no unforgivable microtransaction store or online-only singleplayer (as of 9/28/2016), no extraneous and unnecessary social media connectivity, and overall no pointless filler or mobile game BS to speak of. At worst, it's a solid RTS that harkens back to a time when game companies actually sold games. Entire games. Fun ones. And at best it's a classic that deserves its place alongside Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 and Starcraft: Brood War as one of the staples of its genre.

The Dream Machine is a very complex game. The point and click controls and puzzle solving may lead one to believe, at first glance, that this game is a standard, by the numbers adventure game with a stop-motion aesthetic. But much like the apartment in which this game takes place, there is a lot more lying underneath the surface, waiting to be discovered.
The story is deep, thought-provoking and highly engaging, albeit very surreal and a touch depressing towards the end. This game is one that requires a lot of thought and a lot of patience, because starting around the second chapter, most of the time you will spend playing this game will involve backtracking, and if you are clueless about what is going on, the game can become somewhat tedious and frustrating. All in all, however, the cleverness and surreal gameplay should be enough to keep things interesting.
Mild Spoilers: This game contains a lot of claymation gore and a bittersweet ending.  Do not play if either of these things upset you.

The original Bioshock was both a fun video game and daring art piece. When it released in 2007, Bioshock was unqiue to the blockbuster market. Few titles were attempting to blend FPS and RPG together, fewer were experimenting with lofty political satire. Contrast this with today, where Bioshock clones are produced annually.  Irrational Games transformed a novel idea into a deserved mainstay of modern gaming. Anyone with interest in the medium should give Bioshock a try.
However, I would avoid this "remaster." A contractor studio named Blind Squirrel Games did a poor job updating Bioshock for modern hardware. The biggest issue is that Bioshock Remastered lacks basic stability. Based on countless reports from the Steam forums (as well as personal experience), this version is prone to eating saves, breaking game logic, and simply crashing. It is not worth risking these headaches when every purchase of Bioshock Remastered comes bundled with a serviceable copy of the original.
---
GPU - GTX 1070 (SLI Disabled)
CPU - i7 6700k
RAM - 16GBs
Storage - NVMe SSD
OS - Windows 10
Resolution - 5120 x 2880 (Nvidia DSR)
16x Anisotropic Filtering
100 FOV
Default Mouse Cursor Scale
Fullscreen
Vertical Sync - OFF
Antialiasing - OFF
Distortion - OFF (Enabling can cause crashing)
Real-Time Reflections - ON
Water Ripple - ON
Maintain UI Aspect Ratio - OFF
Before playing, I couldn't Reshade 3.0 to work. Injecting a sharpening filter caused Bioshock to immediately crash on launch. The stock antialiasing failed to cover a large portion of rendered objects, so I alternatively downsampled the resolution from 5K to forcibly eliminate jagged edges. It took 90 minutes to diagnose and repair a conflict involving the use of Nvidia DSR and a third party program on my PC. I would experience excruciating input lag unless I deliberately killed an essential app on my PC before every launch.
Throughout playing Bioshock Remastered, I suffered crippling microstutter at various points. No modifications to the settings alleviated the problem, even if I lowered values in the .ini files themselves.  Unlike other vocal users, my game only ever crashed twice.

On the cusp of finishing the DLC for Dead Rising 3 and starting Dead Rising 4, I want to say Dead Rising 2 is the best of the series. The gameplay is miles ahead of the first game, between the much larger world with much more activities, and the core mechanics of the game being based around making combination weapons and vehicles to gain PP from using special weapons to kill - versus taking photographs and getting the occasional extra points based on standard weapons or melee kills, in the first game. While the graphics are better in some ways than the original, the texture quality is also worse. That seems to be the weird case in 3 as well - the graphics overall are better, but the texture quality is muddied by crappy Instagram-inspired post processing like desaturation and constant solar flares, for some examples.
Compared to Frank and Nick, one of which is kind of a jackass and the other is a doormat, Chuck was the only protagonist in the series who felt relatable, too.
Other than that, Dead Rising 2 isn't that much better than 1 or 3, but I feel it slightly edges them out by a few percent, despite having most of the same weapons as the third game. For example, the blam bow in DR3 is kind of disappointing, although it was cool they changed it up with fireworks instead of dynamite.
One thing's for sure though - if you want to mindlessly slaughter hordes of zombies, you're better off with 3, as the maintenance tunnels and plazas of DR2 won't offer the gigantic crowds to get you up to 100,000 kills quickly. Not to mention DR2 is still unstable and abandoned, and they never released Case Zero on PC. The game will also crash if you kill too many zombies at once, how awesome!

Man, this game is depressing, but in a good way - if that's possible.  In a market flooded with violent shoot-em-ups which glorify war and massacre, it's good to have a game that highlights the awful reality of conflict.  It's like a wake-up call to those of us who think blood and gore is so much fun.  After all, what harm can a violent video game cause, right?  Desensitisation, that's what.
Full of life-threatening decisions, despair, and bleak hope, this game really hits the emotions.  I never thought I'd see a game that so unashamedly exposes the true horror of war.  It really hits you hard when you see your people starving, or dying of their wounds.  The most thought-provoking game I've ever known of.
A brave move by the game studio as well.  It would have been all too easy to produce another tired cliche of a war game, but they've taken things in another direction.  This truly is survival horror.  There are no zombies, or monsters to worry about here.  Just the most dangerous beast of them all - mankind.
If you want a gritty game that's not afraid to really put you in the thick of things, you can do no better than this.  This remarkable game touches you, haunts you, and makes you think.  Now tell me, how many other games can boast that?
Despite it's depressive nature, you'll want to play this again and again.  I know I'll be back for another run-through as soon as I've cheered myself up a little.  You find yourself really caring what happens to your group of survivors, finding it gut-wrenching when something bad happens.  It's like losing your best friend,   When my first character died, I really felt down.  When they all died, I felt so sad I could have cried.
The game market is full of half-realised titles that simply don't deliver the goods.  This does in a way you'll not easily forget.  It's great to see someone put thoughts like this into the common person's head.  Only when we truly realise the disgrace of war that we'll want it to stop.
Can't recommend highly enough.  Just play it!

I have always been leery of space sims, hearing of the \'horror\' stories of EVE online and the sorts. That is, until my friend introduced me to this.
It literally took me five minutes of listening to the soundtrack and watching him play the game for me to get hooked. It was one of the few games on Steam I purchased at full price, and I was not disappointed.
Despite its Indie tag, it doesn\'t feel like an indie game. The visuals are spectacular, the campaign is entirely voice-acted (even the alien species), and the combat is great.
I don\'t think I need to explain the plot or setting in detail. You\'re in space. You\'re finding ancient♥♥♥♥♥♥ Uhh... Untrustworthy aliens/Australians. That\'s all you need to know.
This game does the RPG-style building-up of your equipment very well. You start with a dinky little ship with a laser. After you\'ve completed a few missions and/or saved/looted some traders, you can buy better lasers. But wait! Your ship\'s too small for any more lasers, and you\'re finding it difficult to deal with pirates/police! Well, now you\'ve got to get a bigger ship that can withstand more damage and wield more lasers. You complete a few missions and save/loot some more traders...
The game gets progressively difficult in a way that takes you out of your comfort zone. You can continue to do missions in your current system where enemies aren\'t hard to beat, but the reward is significantly smaller than that in more difficult systems. Additionally, you can only get better upgrades to your ship in harder systems. Frequently, you\'ll find yourself battling against a superior opponent, only to either destroy them or escape at the skin of your teeth.
The difficulty does peak at some point though. Enemies don\'t seem to get much harder or meatier just as you\'re able to get MK6 weaponry (last tier), while you can still acquire better ships and better equipment. Once you\'ve got the money to afford a Blackgate ship, the game is practically over.
The trading system is not as powerful as simply completing missions, but I overheard that the trading system used to be busted, allowing players to make millions within an hour by only trading. Either way, you can still make a hefty sum from researching how each \'event\' changes commodity prices (such as when a planet/station\'s at \'War\', the price of Ammunition goes up).
If you\'re looking for a great singleplayer game that\'ll most likely last your 10-20 hours, this is the perfect game, ESPECIALLY for an Indie game. It\'s not confusing, combat\'s satisfying, the soundtrack is rockin\', and... just, everything is there.

Hard to believe, but this game is even more unintuitive than previous generations of the X-Series; this time not just because of hugh menu options, but also an extraordinary buggy interface.  Clicking/selecting objects is nearly impossible, and once you do, you quickly find there are different, discreet areas where you must click to get certain functionality.  Example, docking with a merchant ship....it is not enough for you to select the ship to get a docking option, instead you must find an obscure docking click spot  to dock your ship.  Even flying into the docking bay will not give you the option of docking.
The tutorials are not instructional, only frustrate.  You get instructions via your co-pilot/technician on task, but absolutely no hint on what keyboard keys are required to enact her suggestions other than a quick, nearly invisible message that flashes on the screen and then vanishes before you notice it, and even if you were to catch it, is too terse to explain anything about game play.
Also, be aware, you will only be allowed to fly the biggest piece of garbage in the known universe, the aptly named Skunk.  You cannot take control of other ships you own, which, needless to say is a let down.
While being able to dock and enter different ships and stations seems like a critical and needed new feature, it falls flat.  Every docking station is exactly the same, and you are not allowed to go anywhere on stations or ship other than the 100% generic docking bay.  Seriously Ego, if you were going to so nerf this experience, why even bother to introduce it.
The biggest problem with the earlier versions of the was every ship, not under your control, was determined to crash into other ships, causing their instant destruction; the likelihood of such an event seemed to be proportional to the cost of a ship.  That problem has sort of been fix, but in an unacceptable manner.  Ship collisions still occrr but now they just don't cause damage.  I am not joking.  I spent five minutes taking my Skunk and bouncing it inside my merchant ships docking bay, causing no damage to either ship (I was frustrate because I could not find the stupid docking click target).
There might be a great game underneath this garbage interface.  A more patient player might discover a beautiful gem and laugh at my lack of lack of garbage stamina.  But this learning curve, coupled with pointless compromises on the original game, has crushed any motivation for my continual time investment.

So. Guys, this game is awesome! Just put a little effort in it. Yes, you need to install mods to fully enjoy it (imho), but why not? =) Thanks to the community who made this game just amazing! But if there would be no game, there would be no mods for it, right? So thanks to Egosoft for making this game and I hope they understand what they've done wrong and will fix everything in the next one! So my arguments.
As others write, Pros:
- It's friendly for new players of the series, since it has a tutorial not only about how to move, but also about trading, ship commanding and etc (in the campaign). This helps a lot, I never watched any of guides about this game (except for long range scan :3), you don't need them! Well, if you are not a newbie in the space simulation game. if you are, there are official tutorials with ingame links to the videos on how to do everything.
- Has highways. Yes, its a plus, since you can move quickly in the sector you are in. And when you get a good engine or just a capital ship, you can move even without them. Also, you can get a jump drive for Skunk, so it will be even faster.
- So everyone say that game has only one ship. Well, yes, in the beggining. But you can dock into a capital and give it orders. With mods installed you can have a capital ship bridge, where you can freely move and watch what is going on through windows. And you have a 3rd person camera view, so technically you're on a ship yourself, can move it and attack enemies, right? So here you go, you just got a lot of other ships to control! Also, there are some mods to replace the Skunk and even start as a capital ship, you can check them out. But I think they are bugged as hell =D Never tried, sorry creators, maybe I'm wrong.
- Graphics! Yes, yes, you heard it right, graphics! Why does everyone complain about graphics? This is a SPACE game, so SPACE looks AMAZING! I never saw something like that in other games. You have a lot of sightseeing in different sectors and it's really eye candy! Ships are awesome, they have a very good design! Stations are just perfect outside! You can even see a lot of small and cool details on them, with something moving and something happening! Battles with all this pew-pewing and stuff are even better! Yes, the characters look like s**t, but you don't even need to visit them unless you need to repair your ship (this takes like 1 minute to do), other things you do just by communicating with a station. So about station indoors - they actually look good, all those fountaines and etc, but it's repetitive, yes. At least they made some difference in them depending on your location. But it doesn't help =D Anyway, you don't need to spend a lot of time on them, so there are more pros than cons here.
- Live economy. So in order to build or produce something you need materials. And other people need materials to provide you with your materials. And then for example, there are other people who need something to provide food for those people who are making you your materials... you got it =D So this is actually a huge system and it works. And for example, sometimes you need to wait for a lot to build your ship, since there is a chain of events for this to happen. And traders or miners can also be attacked by pirates or another enemy faction.
- Skills system. You can see the change between the one star skilled captain or another officer and those who have 5 of them. And it's really cool. Especially when you can take out bigger ships with your high skilled crew which has a smaller ship and fewer turrets. Not always, but it's fun to watch and test =) You can run away anytime, if your engines are ok :3
- So overall - you build your own empire, you fight your enemies, you explore the unknown! And there are places to explore! :3
Cons:
- For me, there are too few weapons to mount on your ships. And no fitting. So you can't place anything you want on another place, or hide something like shield somewhere. You only choose how many turrets and shields you need and that's all. You don't have other engines to choose for NPC ships, nor other modules. And you can't place something on a ship yourself, it's all automated. Would be cool to see something like in Mechwarrior Online, where you have some unchangeable stuff, but other things you can mount youself where you want, depending on your mechs (ships) resources.
- A.I. sometimes a bit dumb. Sometimes they don't listen to commands, I don't know why. Or they listen, but execute them badly. Like if you mark a place on a map where they need to go and it's a very long journey, they sometimes don't use their boost and this will take them forever to accomplish. Most of the time you can help them with that by giving a new order, stop it, and then go back to the previous one.
- Also another thing about A.I. I don't actually know if this is a real problem. But after finishing campaign if I attack any of the stations controlled by PMC they don't send ships to assist. Maybe they don't have them or maybe it's a campaign problem - I don't know. I never played freeplay for now, I need to check this out. But there is no challenge and that's bad. Yeah, the station itself sometimes has a good defence and you can lose some of your ships, but if they are doomed, why are they not sending any reinforcements? So it doesn't feel like WAR and can be very dissappointing if you start a game in a freeplay mode. Will check this out and update review later. Also, maybe it's a mod making this.
- As far as I know, you can't mine ore yourself (or trade everything station produces). I love mining in EVE. So... yeah =D I mean, you have a mining laser, but you don't have any drones to pick up ores and you can't place ore somehow in your inventory, you use other ships for that. So it's better to order them to mine (or trade) without you.
- U.I. Yes, it's bad. Well, updates changed it a bit, but it's still bad. To command your ships and stations, you need to do a lot of stuff and push a lot of buttons. And same for all other menus. At least you can silence everyone you are talking to with mods, otherwise it will take much longer and will get you on your nerves. Why can't you just pick everyone on the map with your cursor and give them orders, like in strategy games? This would be better for such gameplay. You just pick a sector and drag select everyone, or just click someone to give them orders. Hope this will be the main idea in X4. So you can do everything with a cursor or a gamepad. Same for the 3rd person view, why do you control it with a numpad? oO Why not mouse? oO Engine is so tough to do that? Can't you change it somehow? Please? =)
So, yeah, maybe I forgot about something and will update my review. But overall the game is GOOD! It's made out of good motives by it's creators with a good attention to the detail. It's not X4! And yes, there are still some problems, but I enjoy it anyway and you need to try it too! Just don't forget about mods :3 If you feel that you need help with trading - use mods. If you feel you have problems with highways - use mods (get rid of them for example). You have mods for almost every aspect of the game and you can make it much better without any problems. And you will enjoy it too!

Dead Rising 1 was a cool little game around the time it was released that displayed what's possible with improved processing power and an overall hardware boost. At its core the game was about escorting survivors to safety and completing missions within alloted time in a mall playground where pretty much everything could be used as a weapon.
Dead Rising 2 is the type of follow-up that doesn't rock the boat too much and adds incrementally to the formula. Now rather than just a sandbox with a large amount of weapons, you can participate in various activities throughout Fortune City.  Most are slots, gambling, and various related games. It's fine if you like wasting time, but I've never been a fan of mini-games, and there is no time to waste. As stated in my Dead Rising 1 review, you have a sandbox playground predicated on timed missions leaving little room to mess around in unless you're aiming for the bad ending or doing a subsequent playthrough.
Granted, there's not a lot to do anyway other than slots and other gambling related activities. Most of the interaction is in picking up different weapons and killing zombies, which means there's a lot to see and kill but nothing beyond that. The real fun and reward is in time management and juggling optional survivors with finishing the mainline quests in time.
New to the series is the ability to create new weapons by mixing two together; albeit with the restriction that you must obtain the card for the recipe first. Meaning that you can't get creative; you can only mix and form what the developers have allowed. It's a fine feature but, like the gambling and slots, it just gets a shrug from me. It's a nice addition but nothing amazing.
New to the series is the addition of co-op. I tried it out a bit; it was *alright*. It's just another hand to help you complete the game, but as most of the game is escort missions its really just a lot of walking around. The person I played it with didn't find it enjoyable, and I can understand why. In my view its not a "co-op experience", its more like co-op in Sonic 2: something included that doesn't really add anything or do much other than fulfill an obligatory game mode. I'm not saying its bad, I'm just saying it doesn't add anything or do much other than make the game easier. It's not a "co op game"; one that you buy specifically for the co-op. It's more an aside; and as an aside it does its job fine, but it will make the game easier so do take note of that.
Worth noting is how much better the survivor AI is. My god is it better. They won't get stuck in every horde and...its just night and day. You don't have to desperately clear waves of zombies in front of you lest the survivors get stuck. It *does* make things a bit easier but, man, if its this or DR1 pathing of some of the survivors this everyday please.
Like Disgaea 2 or Crazy Taxi 2 its more of the same; if you enjoyed the previous title you'll enjoy this one. And there's nothing wrong with that.
Worth noting is this ridiculous "zombie rights activists" subplot introduced early on and then abandoned. Great writers.

God I so want to recommend this game but I just can't.  As a veteran of Wing Commander, Privateer, and numerous other space exploration games, as well as the X series, which I thoroughly enjoyed, this game is visually beautiful, but that is about as far as it goes.  It is a game without purpose, it is a game without growth, and a game full of trivial time wasters.
I could go into detail, but lets just keep it simple.  The stations on the outside are huge with lots of intracacies.  The stations on the inside are empty feeling, full of useless things to do, and the sparse characters that populate the stations are time wasters.  Basically the X universe is populated with total morons.  There are mini-games throughout, such as disabling a ship's security, or trying to converse intelligently with the morons, but again, these are purposeless distractions.
In terms of flying the ship, it is actually decent to control and there are some (highlight the word "some") options for your ship.  But, there really aren't that many, and instead you find yourself playing endless enemy crunching which, again seems to have no purpose in the universe, except maybe to hope to find some missing piece that will give your ship a 10% boost in some... thing...
There is very little guidance in the game, but being a vet gamer, this is usually no problem for me.  But the problem in this game is there are missions that are really only understandable (not even talking solvable yet) if you go to the web and look up what the hell they want you to do.  And then you have to fly to the corners of the universe tracking down what is essentially crap.  Then the whole build station, manage station stuff is like going into the mind of some programmer who had zero clue how to make it user friendly and... oh my god... manageable.
So here is the bottomline.  You're stuck in one ship, although you can loosely command and build a fleet of mediocre ships.   In this one ship, you can upgrade your engines a little, you can upgrade your weapons even less, you can upgrade your special systems even less than that, and then you can go out and bore yourself in a beautiful universe.  It's rare I pay full price for a game, but I tried... I really did, and I even bought the expansions in hope of something better.

This review is coming from someone who purchased rct3 before purchasing rct2.  Those of you that own rct3 and are considering purchasing rct2, this review should help.  So I will list pros and cons about rct2 compared to rct3

- The peeps (AI) form sizeable queue lines for your rides, making you feel like your ride is popular

CON'S:

- You can't ride your rollercoasters

- No nighttime phase (some would consider that a pro)

Soooo...Homefront, homefront. This is kinda an odd game to speak, I mean it's not a very good game but nor is it bad. Originally as many recall this game was developed by THQ before they went bankrupt, after which they sold the rights to the developers of Crysis and the game was back on steam (after the companus bankrupcy it was removed from steam for some odd reason)
So, Homefront takes place in the far future where the leader of North Korea is dead, his son took over and somehow managed to unify the North and South Korea (wishful thinking much?), then they somehow take over Japan and China. While this is going on the US is being kicked around like a Juarez ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, going bankrupt and losing it's major wars in the middle east (Oh hey, George Bushes worst dream came true, America no longer having a big♥♥♥♥♥♥, being hit by a deadly bird flu an etc. All this leaves America crippled and North Korea rolls in an takes ground, an it's up to the glorious resistance to save America an all it's Apple pie/Burger king eating citizens from the evil Korean cooking.
Now, if you read trough this synopsis and haven't blown your brains out, then congrats you're the small part of us squishy humans that likes using their brain thingies.
Yes, this script reads like something a basement dwelling paranoid whackjob would write and then put on youtube, because it is. The script for this game was writen by John Millius, the same clown who wrote Red Dawn -frankly, you'd think after THAT stink burger someone would take away his writing pen-, and he pretty much brings the same jingoism here as he did in Red Dawn. To make it short, in Miliuse's eyes anyone who isn't American is apperantly a equivilent of a Nazi, because as in Red Dawn, the Koreans in this game do everything except twirlling moustache's or having swastikas. It's clear they are trying to make you hate these guys with every cheap way possible, which just comes off as juvenile and laughable (or maybe I really don't care 'cause I'm not American an the plot to this game is seven layer cakes of stupid)
Anyway, let's forget the stupid plot and speak about the gameplay itself. Aaaan...there isn't much to say really, the game is your standart Modern Military shooter, if you played enough CoD you pretty much got this in the bag. The game can be clocked out in four hours tops (if you don't die that often) and after that there's an abrupt end for the upcoming sequel (which I honestly wanna see, it kinda seems more promising than this game.) The weapons are standart, the characters are all bland as hell, you are silent and actually don't have the ability to open doors for some unknow reason.
Honestly, I'd say the real best part of this game is the multiplayer itself. It has 32 players limit, it def feels more like a Bad Company 2 or something Battlefield esque, rather than CoD arena/twitch reflexes shooting. There's some fun maps and mods, and it really feels like you're on a battle.
Now, can I recommend this game?  Well, I'd say you should only buy it on sales and just for the multiplayer itself, because the single player isn't really worth it.

Once there was a storm off the coast of a little town, and hundreds of fish got washed up onto the beach. A little girl came from the town and started throwing the fish back into the sea. A man walked up to her, however, and said: "Why are you trying to save them? Surely you must know that you can't make a difference here." The girl looked up at him with a gasping fish in her hands, and simply said: "Yes, but for this fish, I've made all the difference in the world."

The walking may seem cumbersome if one is expecting typical smooth motions of a point-and-click but remember it's the process of this type of animation.
ETA: Finally finished this game. FINALLY. Toward the end, it was more of a chore than it should have been. The story collapses as you get into the side quests of various dreams. I felt as though the integration and use of those elements could have been better, more smoothly executed. The artwork also kind of suffers at the end, as well; a bit disappointing as that's what initially drew me in.
The puzzles were great; I enjoyed those quite a bit (just not in the last chapter). There is unexpected "nudity" and disturbing content toward and at the very end. If you're a woman, more than likely the ending is offensive on some level. If you're a man, creeped out. Regardless, a very wtf moment for everyone.
The story would've done fine w/o that oddball inclusion. There is also "gore." I'm putting quotations around the terms as this is claymation and you'd have to admit to limitations in creating that kind of element using that particular medium.
Having said all of that, there is another disturbing moment but one that you kind of feel coming throughout the game. It made me truly question my motives in the game and I enjoyed that opportunity to briefly reflect on that. All in all, I'd still give a thumbs-up for the artistry and puzzles.

I like the idea of this game, 4X mixed with RTS. But I just don't like this game, I wonder why.
I hate double DRM, but it's not the reason.
This game lacks a complete tutorial or campaign/story mode, but well it's OK, I normally only play a few campaign battles in RTS games, then only play skirmish once a while.
As a 4X game, SOSE don't give you much time for planning. This game has a big tech tree, and in 4X games I usually take a few minutes to think about which tech direction I want to go at the beginning, but the realtime gameplay just doesn't let me. Well if you played a lot it could become as easy as muscle memory but still, if it is a 4X game, player should have some time for planning.
Star development and ecnomics are simplified a lot compared to other 4X games. More like RTS: Build mining drones, improve the population, build factories, build defence platforms. And then, build as many ships as you can.
Diplomacy seems totally broken. AI hates you at the beginning if you are a different faction. In most 4X games when you meet alien ship, the first thing is a greeting, but here when your fleet meet theirs, they just start firing at each other AUTOMATICALLY, and it hurts relationship. You have to research technology to communicate with AI, before that you may already at war, and even when you finished that technology and offer AI pacts and trades, they just laugh at you and refuse. The only thing you can do to improve relationship is complete their missions, which are usually to attack others, so there is actually no peace play. (If you don't complete them, relationship also gets worse) And AIs just gradually become friendly with each other, because they don't do missions.
As a RTS game, SOSE's battle is very slow paced. It could take a minute to move from one star system to another, with normal game speed setting. And you can only move through certain lanes. So it could take minutes to send reinforcement, and when your fleet gets there the battle is already over.
The fleet battles themselves also looks boring: you move fleets into a star system that has enemies there, and ships just automatically move to each other and start firing. You can control ship movement and manually choose target, but it doesn't help that much: Ship maneuver is super slow compared to projectiles and lasers attack range, you always fight in open space, and often get surrounded at the point you enter a star system. You can't see formations in traditional RTS games here, it's mostly just numbers and rock-paper-scissors that matters: You get more ships, you win. One ship type is stronger against another, you build right things, you win. Furthermore, you upgrade to more advanced tech and get more big ships, you win. Once the battle starts, you can only retreat your fleet, or watch the result. That's good if this is a pure 4X turn based game, but RTS elements are added in, and doesn't work as expected.
The graphics isn't bad, it's quite good considering this is released some years ago. Problem is, you don't have chances to really see details like the screenshots above, if you're playing normally. You would take half your time watching the star map. Clicking on systems to build ships and upgrades. And another half, controlling your fleets moving from here to there, (and this can also be done in the star map interface) and micromanaging fleet battles. Even when you zoom into a star system to control your ships, they look as small as ants. Ship attack range is super long compared to their size, when you zoom in until you can see details, you can't do anything but only watching.
Combining 4X and RTS looks like a good idea, but the 2 elements turn out to be conflicted with each other in many aspects. I think this game did its best, but I don't see it solves all the problems. It's like they put a simplified RTS and a simplified 4X together, and I can't enjoy either of them.

With lasers, ropes, and rockets at your disposal, it is really up to the player to shape and re-arrange the world as you see fit to create your own way forward.
My only gripe with the game are some of the lazy achievements that require the player to use the rocket 1000 times and find 1000 boring stones (yes, the protagonist collects boring stones). The former is the least useful tool and I topped at about 350 uses after getting the rest of the achievements, and the latter usually amount to about 30 stones per level, of which there are 6. Do the math and you will see how many times you have to beat the game to get to a 1000 stones, assuming you collect all of them every time. This is really a minor issue though, only worth mentioning because everything else is spot on.
So, get your explorer hat on and set out to get your pants back, because the fate of the world may very well depend on it.

As many reviews have already stated this game is like the love child of Sid Meier's Pirates and Freelancer, it's neither one or the other but has emulated some of the features from both games and merged these into an interesting hybrid.
The 2D naval style fighting makes it less complicated than a 3D counterpart but don\'t let that fool you that it's less of a challenge. The variety of ships, weapons and modules give it enough diversity to keep you playing for that next upgrade but without bombarding you with sheets of complicated stats. The soundtrack isn't going to be everyone\'s taste but I think it's awesome and really suits the pace of the game.
Yes it's a bit clichéd, the main story is short and it's quite simplified compared to others in the genre but that's the beauty of it - it isn't trying to copy a successful franchise and then failing miserably; it has it's own spin on space rpg that's different whilst being familiar at the same time.

Betrayer tries so hard to be unique that it forgets about gameplay along the way.
The game tries to be unique by coloring everything black white and occasionally red and replacing the common mini maps arrows with a "play-button" and moaning sounds.
The idea is solid, but the story is lackluster and combat is VERY repetitive since there are not many different enemy types and all of them do the same in combination with glitched hitboxes. On a positive side: Salvaging your amo is a cool concept.
The constant ringing sound makes you feel like you have a tinitus and rappidly shifts from "unique" to "incredibly annoying".
Overall it is a very lackluster game that hides its gameplay issues behind the "art"-tag. People who've played Mad World have seen that this artstyle can be implemented for much more than "being a  special snowflake".
Overall it could be fun experience despite it's flaws, but sadly combat and questing are EXTREMELY repetitive.
There are worse ways to spent your time, but also better ways to spent your money.

First impression is good.
---a pretty cut and dry story, \"message from shady family member, going on a quest to find them\", is the first thing you are given, as well as some decent voice over. It gets a little interesting as things progress, but I\'m not spoiling ;3
---the beginning ship is faily appelling visual wise and it dosen\'t look like a hunk of junk (although without some stratigic use of credits, it IS a hunk of junk later on).
---Battles are navel style, making placement stratagy and situational awareness a must. The music is AWESOME, changing in intensity when you are cornered into a battle.
---Travel music can get a little repetative if you avoid battle, but still enough to keep you going. Space Detail is good, even on the lowest setting (what I\'m run when I start any game)
---the combat is fairly fast paced, flashy, and deadly.
There are a few negatives, and they are all understandable.
---Minor lack of info in intro tutorial.
There is a small tutorial on how to fly, switch guns, warp, and dock. However, unless I compleatly missed the info box, there was nothing about the system map (press M in game) and setting custom way points. a little thing, but the map will show you any station in the system, even thoue youhave not visited. you can also see the currnt prices for goods if you have visited the station, cutting down on aimless wonder and making it easier to get a good deal on your goods (and keep you from getting your illegal goods confenscated)
---No True vertical movement.
this one is a very minor one. your ship moves on a flat plane of travel, adding to the Navy Ship feeling and making combat less hectic than having to worry about moving up and down to get in position or get out of deadly situations. other large ships are also stuck on this flat plane, making your broadside attacks useful. However, the tiny fighter craft are not bound to this and can loop around your ship and pepper you with shots and missiles. unless you practice with your turrents, they will be exceedingly irritating and will make it diffucult to battle without getting half your hull blow to bits. this adds to the starting difficulty, and I love it, but I know a few people will have an issue with this, so I\'m marking it as a negative (but for me, it is a positive)
Other than that, get the game, become a space cowboy, and grow into the scorge of the galaxy. 10/10 would buy again.

Ok, let's begin this, shall we?
Gameplay-wise, this game kinda reminds me Portal. No, you don't shoot portals. The developers give you an ability that can easily break the game. And surely, it does. But it's also hell of a fun, and you do it more often than you should!
The ability in question is the fact that you can cut and manipulate almost anything around you. Seriously, you can cut buildings, pathways, you can get stuck or cut the very platform you're standing on, if you're standing on one. It's fun. If you ever tried Red Faction, you will love this kind of freedom in messing with props and the whole map. If you haven't... well, you're going to have fun either. Worth mentioning the physics of the whole game, well managed.
Graphically, this game is GOOD. It feels hand-drawn, it looks hand-drawn, it's nice to look at, the proportions of the characters kinda reminds the Psychonauts style. It's just very nice.
Songs are good as well, each piece comes from a different indie band, so you'll also discover some bands you really never heard of, likely.
So, it's worth buying? Maybe not at full price. If discounted, HELL DO IT. It's a light game that doesn't look, doesn't feel and doesn't play like a light game, specs-wise. 10/10.

This is NOT an action packed game. Combat is NOT the solution to your problems. This is NOT a happy game.
If you don't have any gripes the above statements, a really good game may lie ahead of you. The basic mechanics of the game are Point and Click. In addition to hit points, your characters have hunger, sickness, and emotional life bars. Any of which can ultimately kill them. After having gotten emotionally attached to your characters, you WILL lose a character or two or more. Deal with it. The end screen will loosen a tear or two, even in the most detached players.
That said, the game will take you on an amazingly in depth journey about living and surviving in an urban war zone. You have a shelter and the whole city to explore in a side-scrolling perspective, make moral desissions and deal with the psycological repercussions they have on your characters. At the end, all you want to say is:
♥♥♥♥ THE WAR

I love this game, people seem to forget. It's a BASE GAME. Has anyone remembered the previous Civilization base games? They lacked in depth and were boring, this base game has just as much, maybe even more content compared to the Civ V base game. They have brought back things like caravans/caravels, ideologies (affinities), and more from Gods & Kings and Brave new World. The graphics are stunning and the game really makes your economy a crucial part of your game, your civ relies on diplomacy and trade routes to keep and create a great economy. You are now able to exchange things for favors, these favors can be later traded in for energy, cities, and can influence other people to make peace and go to war. Overall, Beyond Earth is an amazing game, with much more content and adds much more enjoyable content in this installation of the Sid Meier: Civilivation series.

This game seems to take a lot of flak for being different to earlier games in the series, but having now finished the story campaign, I will definitely be playing again. Sure, it's different, and the no-kill stealthy escape levels are unsettling to get used to for veteran players, but this game is so rich! It's worth playing just to hear some of the hilarious things that the NPCs say.
Pros:
++ Functional and logical AI. No more getting seen by one guard and then being attacked by some other random guard on the other side of the map who doesn't know you from a bar of soap.
++ Effective sneaking (at a balanced speed, allowing you to actually stealth-attack a moving target from behind).
++ Great NPC dialogue - overhearing average people on the phone to their friends and family is a really good touch. Also, hilarious in-jokes for those who stop to listen.
+ Achievements that force you to explore and re-play levels with different styles (with even more in-jokes).
+ The entire disguise mechanic now works in a balanced way.
+ Variety of locations and level size/style.
+ Nice hand-to-hand combat mechanics.
+ The ability to hide until everyone has calmed down.
+ Little side-stories that reveal themselves if you look and listen closely (most notably the "trip to Hawaii").
+ NPC comments can be affected by your play style on earlier levels.
Cons:
- Bloom.
- Too many different keys in the PC version - every action is controlled by a different button, and that's unnecessary.
- Irritating inventory slots that don't allow you to carry a knife and a bottle at the same time.
- Enemy movement is sometimes affected by getting close enough to trigger dialogue (which is okay, but...) and when the level is restarted from a checkpoint, the guards may be in their "second positions" making life harder.
-- Does not include the line "I need to use the bathroom".

Wow, first off, I'm only bothering to add a positive review because I just realized the review rating right now is like 53%! Holy shnikes!
I understand, though. Really, after playing Civ 5 with all the DLC, Civ BE is kind of underwhelming. I think the biggest reason it comes short though is because of the limited number of factions. Only 8! If you want to play with more than 8, you either have to mod up (especially a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for multiplayer or nigh impossible for non-Windows users), or overlap different players with the same "sponsor." Yes, the game does make it possible to do this and changes the color for the players using the same team, but, it's kind of a turn off to me to have to keep track of purple Brasil and green Brasil...
On the plus side though, and overall I do give this game a thumbs up (when it's on sale!), it does add a number of cool things ..... the Affinity branches and the technology web (that's right web... not tree) come to mind. The way units upgrade across the board as you increase Affinity levels is kind of cool. Being able to pick your upgrade bonuses and even mix Affinity branches up a little bit is kind of cool. Barbarians (aliens) are now much more interesting and can actually change hostility toward individual civs. And purely for flavor, the sci-fi battles and multiple terrain textures (desert / fungal / terran planets) are fun.
So, for Civ 5 + DLC fans, Civ BE right now is indeed not worth the big $. You'll miss nukes. You'll miss 20+ unique factions. However, if you enjoy sci-fi flare, it's worth it on sale. Being an avid Civ fan, I was curious and had a few extra bucks, so I went for it.  I wasn't disappointed, but I wasn't excited either, until I noticed that Beyond Earth is actually a game of subtle nuance. I do "recommend" it with a caveat: At the current price of 50-60 dollars, I would not recommend it, ... I recommend that you wait until the price comes down a bit and more mods become available through the modding community.
The game can be easily modified to your liking and/or playing style. Check out the Steam Workshop for all the latest Mods for Beyond Earth. The Workshop makes it very easy to install the various mods available for Beyond Earth simply by "subscribing" to them and ticking off which mods you want to use from the main game menu.
For more in-depth discussions about Strategy and Tips for Beyond Earth, go to the CivFanatics forums here:
Civilization: Beyond Earth is very slick and polished in appearance, and is full of wonderful art and graphics, yet, in the beginning, the gameplay feels like Civilization 5 on an alien world, with the addition of "Affinities", "Virtues" and Orbital Satellites and other features altering the game mechanics.
At face value, Civilization: Beyond Earth appears to be an elaborate full conversion type of Mod put together by a skilled game modification team, only this team got paid for their work. It is most definitely NOT a successor to Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri or Alien Crossfire. It does have a reference to the Progenitors through some rare ruins found on the planet, and the Contact Victory, but that is the extent of any similarity to the earlier games.
What many may have missed though, is that Beyond Earth has a lot of subtle elements and nuances at play within the game. This is why I think it deserves a second look.
The Wonders are presented in an "understated" way, that is, there are no flashy "Wonder Movies", only a brief dialogue about the Wonder and it's effects. Personally, I could care less about the absence of this type of eye candy and tend to focus more the actual benefits each Wonder bestows upon my chosen faction.
In the very beginning of the game, during set up, you are asked which planet type in which star system you are colonizing. Real star system names and planetary types are used for flavor. I tend to prefer Huge maps with Epic or Marathon game lengths. It is through these choices that enabled me to discover what others
have overlooked in Standard or smaller map sizes with shorter and faster game lengths.

You can choose to focus on only one Affinity or a combination of Affinities, which in turn will unlock more combat unit types. Affinity levels also grant bonus enhancements for your chosen faction in the areas of Industry, Food, Energy, and/or Culture.

At first glance, it appears to have a similar structure to what you find in Civilization V, but it works in a very different way. All of the Virtues are unlocked from turn 0, and you are best advised to
progress through them in a linear fashion, ie; fill out the Might Virtue, then the Prosperity, and so on. The best way to progress through the Virtues is using a combination of all 4 with a goal of completing the "Synergy" bonuses along the X and Y axis of the Virtues grid.
The Technology "Tree" has been replaced with a "Web" which takes some getting used to, ... okay, change is not always bad.
At first glance, it appears to have no clear direction to follow and no linear progression. If you do not have a clear idea how to aproach the Web, be assured, the
does and will leave you in the dust if you don't understand how it works with the Affinities and Virtues. Pick an Affinity to follow first and use that to guide you through the Technology Web, ... then it begins to make sense.

This effect is a no-brainer. A faction that is all chummy with you in the beginning, can become not so friendly later in the game due to their chosen Affinity development path. This is why there are factions. Each Leader thinks they know best about how to colonize an alien world.
The Harmony Affinity views the Alien Lifeforms as something to be understood and preserved, If you seek to destroy the Alien Lifeforms, a faction that has chosen Harmony will become hostile toward you.

If you make a "promise" like not settling cities near a faction, or attacking the Alien lifeforms, and break that "promise", they will remember it. Conversely, if you make a "promise" and keep that "promise" for a certain number of turns, they will remember that too. Promises have a Diplomatic effect.
are not as useless as they might appear to be at first. If you have gained some favors with a faction, you can extract promises from them in turn, and generally, they will keep them. Promises such as
, or
, etc., can be useful. Go to war against that faction and any "favors" you may have had with them are gone.
Believe it or not, unlike the Barbarians in Civilization games, the Alien Lifeforms can be made into "allies", ... of a sort. You can gain the ability to become immune to the pervasive "maisma" and "befriend" the alien life to the point that they will not attack your cities and instead attack the factions that have followed Affinities and practices detrimental to them.
It is not a blatant alliance, yet it is a subtle and somewhat helpful "understanding" with the alien life on the planet and they will, in certain circumstances, attack whichever faction is attacking you.
Another feature is the ability to launch satellites, all kinds of satellites. At first glance, this feature may seem somewhat weak and boring, until you go to war with another faction. Then Orbital Laser platforms, TacNet, and Phasal Transporter satellites can turn the tide in confilcts.
Quests is another marginally interesting feature. Most often thay are minor quests given after constructing a certain building type, thereby creating a "decision point" for the player:
There are a few major quests that follow a short story and contain multiple "decision points" for the player to follow.

Here's my short review for 'Betrayer'. I got the game for $1 on sale and found it to have very high value for that price. At a higher price I think that the value drops considerably. However, for $1 I got more than 12 hours of gameplay out of Betrayer which is on par with some triple A titles that cost up to 40x times more.
At the time of writing this game is getting a little old. However, that isn't to say that the graphics aren't remotely good. When I first played Betrayer a few years ago, it was one of the nicest looking games I had seen in a long time. Making good use of tesselation and post processing even just with DirectX 9. The colour palette was really interesting and I liked the art style a lot.
In 2017 the game still looks really nice. If you want to play in full colour, which I absolutely recommend as it can make the game feel a lot more 'alive' and enjoyable choose the following settings in the options menu:
I think the above settings give the game the most realistic colour output. Playing in colour for me was far more entertaining and enjoyable than playing entirely in black and white. Because the 'otherworld' sections are always in black and white no matter what, playing in colour outside of the otherworld - and in black and white in the otherworld made for a good balance.
Sealth is pretty fun. You can augment your stealthiness with some charms available for buy or just found in the world. The maps are pretty huge, albeit very sparsely populated with both enemies and things to pick up. It really feels like the developer(s) just threw things here-and-there without much direction or reason. Running everywhere can get a bit tedious and none of the fights in the first part of the game are all that hard. Only the very hard to see enemies that make very soft whistling sounds are much of a challenge.
To put it very short and sweet. It's a fun game for about 10 hours and it's very cheap. I personally liked the story. I'd get it on sale for a dollar like I did and enjoy it for what it is. Expecting it to stand up to some ridiculously high margin of quality like triple A titles is just ludicrious. Betrayer plays like a game developer's first try at releasing a game and for what it is, it's really quite good.

I have played hundreds of hours of prior 'x' games and after 50+ hours (mainly offline) play, I have enjoyed nearly all this game has thrown at me. For me, I dont know if I could go back to the old 'x' games now as I have loved a number of new features/graphics.
It is single player only. You fly and improve your own spaceship (enhance its weapons, engine and shields) and build an empire of owned trading/fighting armada ships that are a mix of small figters to large capital ships and space stations, the likes of which are operated by captains, pilots etc that you can order about but not so much control directly. This is in a large 'sandbox' (and there is an optional campaign which I am part way through) universe. Exploring that universe has been a big part of the fun. I have the two extra DLC's and estimate I may have explored 1/3 to 1/2 so far in 50+ hours.  I have enjoyed the fighting aspects and am looking forward to bringing more ships into later larger fights. I especially like the (new to x games) methods of travel - you can boost for a while over large distance, coupled with use of 'gates' between areas. There are also 'highways' which are like fast boosts but only go in one direction. I am not a  massive fan but do not see them as any kind of barrier to my own enjoyment of the game.
The game (engine) has run well on i5 4690cpu and 1070 card, 16gb ram. I have setting on high/max on 1920x1200 monitor. I have had no crashes other than a crazy one when changing the V Sync setting from the main menu! Was a worrying start but thankfully the game has had no problems since. Graphics are good (excluding inside of stations) and sound/music good/great except the music can sometimes get repetative if you are sat in one place whilst looking through maps/your empire.
Do not be put off by the overall bad score (which from what I could see was mainly from a bad initial game release) - instead try out the demo and see for yourself if the game could be what you are after.
The above being said, there are still elements of the game that you may wish to avoid by using steam mods. In particular any mod that results in more time flying and less time running around inside space stations which imo detract from the best parts of the game. There is a great list of mods in the forums of Egosoft. The interface also takes some time to get used to (but as I did, it was not as if it is slow, just not user friendly, at least at first).  I also had to look up how to do things like set up a station, even though I was in effect doing the tutorial for it, because the game does not explain every intricacy. There are good guides and videos on the web to show you these things.
When I first saw this game come out (years ago) I saw it was flawed and bugged both myself (from old demo) and  from peoples posts. I am so glad I noticed it again and gave it a second chance, even at the full price I paid £40. A couple of weeks later I am not too disappointed the game is now something like 70% off.
Anyway I am off now to explore/build/fight some more and mainly took the time on this review to help even out what I think is the dumb score the game ended up with. Based on my current experience and imo this (Version 4.1 and with mods) deserves closer to a 90% score.

You just moved into a new appartment with your pregnant wife and you soon realise that something's not right. What starts out as a bit of a detective story slowly turns into something more sinister. You are definitely no hero but you are trying to do the right thing even if that has sometimes unintended consequences.
In my opinion, the last part of the story is the weakest and it would have been better if the game had ended with the 5th part but YMMV. But up to that part it is interesting and darker than usual in adventure games. This is not a happy story, not suitable for children (there's death and other rather disturbing things).

Hard but not unfair. This is no game for newbies to the genre. The individual chapters are not linear for the most part, you can "work" on several puzzles at the same time and sometimes there are several ways you can solve a puzzle.
There is no in-game help, no hints besides what other people tell you and no hotspot viewer, although the latter is not too important since there is no pixel hunting in this game. I never got stuck because I overlooked something. I did get stuck a few times, though, and twice so severely that I had to stop playing to sleep over it. For the last three chapters, there are no walkthroughs available, so be advised, if you get frustrated easily this is probably not the game for you.
The puzzles in chapter 5 are outstanding. Very mild spoiler:
Very simple, just point and click. You drag items from your inventory (appears at the top of the screen) to where you want to use them. I would have liked the option to double click exits to move through screens or at least to run faster. Instead, you move with one speed through the screens which slows the game down considerably in some areas, especially chapter 5 which requires you to run around a lot.
I liked this game quite a bit. A lot of work went into the backgrounds and it shows. The puzzles are hard and you often have several to solve at once, the developers did a very good job here. The finale to the story was a bit weak, in my opinion, but the overall story is captivating. The game is well worth its full price if you look at my game time but there are frequent sales as well.

I had this game on CD-rom when I was a kid, and it still works on my old computer, but now that it's on steam, I can play it much easier and have just as much fun as I did when I was younger.

*This is a review of the full game*
Beautiful and emotional point-and-click adventure with some of the best and most charming dialogue I have seen in recent years. The game is filled to the brim with creative puzzles that are sometimes almost too clever for their own good. It starts out a little bit sluggish but becomes very exciting as soon as the plot starts to kick in. Visually the game is stunning, especially the environments deserve notable praise. The characters, in my opinion, maybe looked a bit too crude to be immediately likeable, but they quickly grow on the player emotionally as the story progresses. The dialogue is immersive and well-written, rich with both clever comedy and emotional baggage. The sound quality is a tad crude but is well-implented and extremely effective in serving its purpose.
The game has classic point-and-click gameplay but also succeeds in providing uniquely creative and smart puzzles that are sometimes so clever that players will probably overlook the solutions that are right under their noses.
Chapters 1 to 4 get a five-star rating from me. Well-designed puzzles and enough balance in difficulty and effort not to be slowed down quite too much. There's a beautiful build-up in tension of the story during these first four chapters and there have been moments where I felt the game really reached out and spoke to me emotionally. It would be an understatement to say that a lot of big corporately financed AAA game studios could learn a thing or two from Anders Gustafsson's magnificent writing and narrative design.
Chapter 5
Although this chapter is probably the richest in content and length, this is where the quality of gamedesign goes subtly downhill, with some areas (like Mr. Willard's dream) being very uncommunicative to the player as to which actions to pursue next. For me, this led to frustrating hours sluggishly walking from screen to screen trying to solve puzzles that were already finished for the time being. This is also the first chapter where the game becomes a bit less linear and expects the player to backtrack between different dreams, without explicitly communicating it to the player, which seemed a bit counterintuitive at the time.
Chapter 6
From a gameplay perspective, there is just way, way too much backtracking in this chapter (coming from a person who loves backtracking-heavy genres such as metroidvania games). The game demands that the player revisits the same characters over and over and make them repeat the same things in different words over and over only to receive the tiniest of breadcrumbs leading to the next clue. Once you've finally got all the 'breadcrumbs' you have to put them in a certain order in a very far-off place, without having any clear indication as a player whether your setup is correct or not, leading to potentially endless hours of backtracking. At this point, regardless of my emotional and time investments so far, I would have put this game down if it weren't for the "Quick Travel" option and a walkthrough by my side.
In retrospect, this whole chapter kind of irked and confused me. The story abruptly becomes more abstract and philosophical. By the time I had reached the finale of the game, I had become so out of touch with the game world's inherent logic and 'reality' that I couldn't tell whether aborting a duplicate fetus with an adult mind was a good or a bad thing to do in regards to the context of the story and characters. The ending also striked me as rather dark and sad, and I hope that the rumours of a possible alternate, happier ending are true. Ultimately, I might just have been a bit worn out at this point and felt that the same charm and beauty of the first four chapters seemed a bit absent in the final chapter.
Final verdict:
Despite the disappointment I felt with the final chapter, I would not have wanted to miss out on this gem of a game. Anyone with a disposition for visually beautiful and unique games with deeply emotional narratives should not miss this one!
