I'm going to be painfully honest with you here... this is not a very good football game.  Sure it has potential to become something in the future, but as of right now, I just cannot recommend spending $16 dollars on this game.  I hate Madden, I hate the NFL, I wanted to be able to love this game, especially since this game being good would be great for the sports video game market... but this game is basically boiled down to the on-field action (no season, franchise, stat tracking... all the things you want from a sports game), and the on-field action isn't very good.  If you want to buy this game just to spite Madden or to expand the competition, I totally respect that, but I think the average sports gamer is going to find this game lacking in too many areas to really enjoy it.
Playing defense is a nightmare... the controls are slippery and unintuitive... it took me 3 quarters of a game to figure out that RT was the tackle button, and even after that I wasn't entirely sure that RT was the tackle button.  The pre-snap controls are equally as baffling (RB/LB to cycle players?  Y to call a timeout?  Why???).  Most of us have been Maddenized by this point, why not just make the control scheme similar?  Be different in presentation, be different in how the game feels on the field, but please don't make me learn an entirely new control scheme - especially not  one that makes zero sense.  I was ready to throw my laptop through the window after the 3rd time I got called for delay of game for accidentally calling at timeout that I didn't have (again, WHY MAP IT TO THE Y BUTTON????)  Of course, the first time I got called for it was after I kicked off, and the delay of game triggered the other team to have to kick to me... so that was an unexpected glitch in my favor :)
Offensively, I enjoyed the presnap motion, I feel like they nailed that pretty well... I am a big CFL fan, and all the pre-snap movement is something I really enjoy... it's just hard to see your outside receivers, so expect to get nailed with the occasional offsides.  The passing game feels okay... there's some animations missing that could make it better, but for the most part it feels competent... running after the catch is a decent amount of fun.  DB AI is not the best though, so you are not going to see much resembling a contested catch/battle for the football.  Basically, if the DB is going to knock it down, the ball is either going to hit him in the back of the head, or he's going to stand in front of your WR and jump straight up and down a few times... and maybe pick off a pass here and there.  The running game is fairly non-existent from what I can tell.  My biggest gripe offensively lies in the QB within the pocket game... He feels like he's about 100 years old shuffling around until either a DL hurls his body into him, or the DL decide not to rush and you can finally get him outside of the pocket.  After years of playing newere football games, it doesn't feel very good.
All in all, I just can't recommend this game to the average football fan.  Maybe CFL fans who are harder core than I am will like it, but I see most people begrudgingly accepting their football video game fate (ie, it's Madden or nothing).  If you're comitted to trying to build a brand other than Madden, than by all means, buy the game and hope the developer continues to support this series, because you can see some glimmers of potential (one of those "everyone's got to start somewhere" kind of things).  Me?  I'm going to refund it, because $16 is just too much for me to drop on the hope that this will some day turn into an awesome series.  If/when it gets there, I'll be more than happy to buy it, but my video game budget is currently too limited to purchase a game that I don't enjoy and that I'm not going to play.

Betrayer could best be described; and as others have already listed, a stealth based mystery game that relies on exploration as a means of driving the story forward. It takes place during the colinzation of the new world in 1604 by charters set out by both the Engilsh and Spanish Empires.
You begin the game shipwrecked on the beach, further inland you run into the only "living" human you will to talk to the entire game; a Maiden in Red, she has no memeory of what happend to cause the various settlements you find throughout the game to be full of the Pompeii esque remains of the Colinists and why no one living seems to remain. Unraveling the secret past of the Maiden in Red and of the former Colonies as well as its inhabitants is up to you.
The game does have combat; and while nothing too eather shattering, is more than adaquate for what the game sets out to do. The game gives you variuos choices weapons that all play distinctly different from eachother and have their own pros and cons. For instance the bows (silent, faster to fire) and black powder weapons (stronger, but load and long reload). The differences in the weapons do warrant some thought before rushing into fights when wandering the map, however during other times the games brings the enemies to you making it more a questions of what is able to ill the fastest.  You also get charms that buff your chracter as well as throwables in the form explosives and tomahawks. I really didn't use the latter much.
The story is progressed forward by the players ability to ring a bell and transfer from the normal white washed world to a extremely dark "spirit world". Within the spirit world you will meet key wraiths, as well as secondary shadows of the former colonits whose spirits that are still bound to the world for one reason or another. It is here that you will you will unravel most of the mysteries of the New World Colonies.  From the first wraiths you encounter in any given area you will usually be given a short incomplete narrative. It is then up to you to  fill in the gaps using clues you find in the living world in order to refresh the wraiths memories and finish their stories.
This is where I major give major cudos to who ever wrote the various stories of the wraiths you enounter in game. What might at beginning the  sound like a story of somone consoling  a perons who just lost their father slowly begins to warp with each new clue you uncover and present to the wraiths.This continues until  the story evolves into someone being murdered and another executed. By the conlcusion of each investigation the original phrase thrown out by the wraith will have usually taken on a whole new context and meaning. Writing of this nature is not always an easy feat, and is something I'd like to see more of in the video game realm.
Would I recommend this game? Not necessarily to everyone, if you enjoy mystery, interesting writing, and something different, then yes this game is probably for you and you would like it. If I were to apply a number rating for those who care, I would give this game a very solid 7 maybe a shaky 8.
*You do get the shovel eventually. Yes you will have to backtack to dig up some of the things you find earlier in the game.
*Stealth is slightly less useful in the spirit world, but still applicable.
*Pick up everything you can in the map before entering the spirit world in any area, in my opinion this is the best way to get everything done in the quickest way possible.

I played this game at launch, and it was pretty bad. GFWL was a nightmare, there was constant crashing, multiplayer was a buggy mess, and the actual campaign was severely lacking. I probably would have given it an overall rating of 4.8/10. A slightly below average game.
When it was updated recently, I gave it another try. I do applaud 2K for releasing the massive patch so long after the game was released. For current owners, they got the Minerva's Den DLC for free, GFWL was removed, Steam achievements were added, several bugs were fixed, and multiplayer was much better. Still not perfect though. Lots of lag and no proper anti-cheat in multiplayer, and lots of crashing in single player.
Anyway, on to the main game. The biggest problem I had with the story was that it felt the exact same as the first one. The villain, Sofia Lamb supposedly had entirely different point of view than Andrew Ryan of the original game, but it didn't feel like that because the way she carried out her actions and the way she talked/presented herself was the exact same as Ryan. Some of the endings were a little cliche, the writing for Eleanor had some really cheesy and mediocre moments, and the overall story just didn't feel right. Like, it was all based around this relationship between Eleanor and you, a big daddy. And you're not even her actual father or anything haha. It was just strange. Cool idea, but I think it could have been written better.
I do think a few of the added moral choices were a great touch, how a few main characters fates were all dependent on you. Soundtrack was also fantastic. And while the multiplayer is completely unnecessary, when it worked, sometimes it was pretty fun. The whole background was kinda cool, how it all takes place when Rapture goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ But of course, there's a stupid levelling system tacked onto it which can kill interest quick. Had to grind for so long to get the last few achievements.
Gameplay wise, there was definitely an improvement. Instead of having all the different types of tonics, they were just grouped under one general selection. Dual wielding was great, and many of the weapons were a lot of fun to use. However, just like the first one, the movement is clunky, the FOV is awful and the guns still felt sluggish. Graphics are ugly for a 2010 game, and environments were practically identical to the original. Enemy variety was essentially the same, and the constant Big Sister fights were just annoyingly tedious and stupid.
I guess I'd give BioShock 2 a flat 6.0/10. It's a decent game. There are definitely improvements from the original, and a few great ideas. However, throughout the campaign, it just really felt like 2K was beating a dead horse. Get it on a sale.
As far as the Minerva's Den DLC goes, it gets universal praise everywhere I see it. I really didn't think it was that special to be honest. The story was decent and the pacing was good, but the gameplay just felt like more of the same. I'd give it 5.5/10, it's an above average add-on.

This review is for the full game.
This is a really well-done "point and click" adventure game. It was put together in stages over several years, and it has the resulting depth and breadth that other games of this type rarely do. The handmade visual style is unlike anything I've seen in this type of game, and has a vivid, reach-out-and-you-can-touch-it solidness to it.
One thing worth stating upfront is that THIS GAME IS NOT FOR KIDS. I mention this because I'm a fan of the Amanita Design games that have a similar 2-D approach, like Machinarium, Botanicula and Samorost 3. Those have some spooky elements, but mostly they're kid-friendly as well as having challenging puzzles for adults. Dream Machine goes WAY farther into a dark, grisly, sometimes horror-tinged realm -- and I think it is exclusively for adults.
The plusses of the game are many. I was surprised that the creators were able to sustain long-form storytelling over the entire series. Every little element in the early chapters is of-a-piece and builds toward the puzzles as well as enhancing the story over the full course of the game. It's extremely cohesive and cumulative in how it unfolds.
The puzzles and Zork-like adventure aspects of this game are very satisfying. There are only a few puzzles that require structural analytic thinking (like trying to figure out how to arrange transistors in a box to get the right amount of current). Rather, most of the puzzles require direct observation of the locations and situations, with logical solutions that reward you for paying attention. You will need to retrace your steps sometimes to really LOOK at things, but the game designers don't hide anything in obscure places. Everything you need is upfront, as long as you're paying attention and thinking things through.
I love it when games like this have that sense of FAIR PLAY, where they give you JUST ENOUGH but NOT TOO MUCH to figure things out. Dream Machine strikes that balance very well. Some of the puzzles might require you, aptly enough, to sleep on them for a bit, but that's about all. (I got stuck once due to my misunderstanding of how a laser beam was directed at a wall, so I looked for a walkthrough, but saw too much and felt like a jerk for spoiling the fun for myself. After that, I was happy to solve the rest of the game on my own, even though I almost got stuck later -- something to do with a character asking me to make a sandwich....)
On the NEGATIVE side: The aspect of the game I found most irksome was the text. Though well-written and sometimes very witty (as with the phone calls to God scene), the constant click, click,click of the dialogue between characters approach tedium at times. The designers seem to have learned to keep things brisk over the course of the game, and I felt like dialogue wasn't *quite* as obnoxious in the latter chapters. Since the game doesn't have any voice-over acting, but just text, at least you can click through as fast as you like. Still, I wish they had given you an option to get a single-screen display of all the dialogue on the 2nd pass, instead of having to click-click-click-click-click each time.
All in all, this is one of the most surprisingly ambitious and "Wow I can't believe how much game is packed into this game" experiences I've had with a low-cost, 2-D, indie game purchase. No regrets, it was worth the time and money, and I felt like I got to experience an original, well-constructed, creative-risk-taking story in the process.
This game deserves a good-spelling recommendation because it reflects my driving in the real world since I can't even get past the first turn.

I usually don't do reviews but X Rebirth sure needs one, looking at all those butthurt people giving this game a thumb down.
I didn't buy the game at release, so I never saw all those horrible bugs everyone is talking about.
Now, the game is good.
It looks nice and It has a really great atmosphere of being in actual space travelling around between space stations. All those vehicles flying around the stations like on highways making the stations look awesome. As long as you don't enter one of these stations. The NPCs look awfull and the stations are dead inside. Luckily you don't really need to enter stations often in X:R 4.1.
I would love the feature of entering stations, if it was properly developed but it feels pretty unfinished at this state.
Some people say the atmosphere in X3 and X2 was far better but I don't get that. Sectors in X3 feel like the stations in X:R, dead. Of course X3 is an old game, so that's no wonder. I really like the sector design in X:R, with the galaxy split up in systems, sectors and zones, connected through Jumpgates, Super-Highways and Highways. Some people don't like the highways but these are mostly the X3 fanboys ^^
About the game itself, it's complex. Not as complex as X3 but that's not particularly bad. You will need guidance and like 10-15 hours to get into the game and actually play it but it's totally worth it. Don't even try to learn the game by the campaign, the campaign is no real tutorial, even though it claims to be one. Check out youtube or steam for guides to get started.
As I already said, the game isn't as complex as X3. There are less ship types and you can't chose from different weapons to equip to these ships, they are presets. However, this game was never designed to be like X3 or to be X4, it's Rebirth. They tried to bring X into another direction while still keeping the core elements of X: trade, fight, build, think. And as of 4.1, this succeeded. It's more open to new players than the previous X's that were for genre lovers only. Only thing I really miss, where are the borons? :(
Some people also mentioned the voice acting and yes, it's terrible. The dialogues are always the same and sometimes it sounds more like a parody of previous X games but you get used to it, as the game isn't about a good story but about making your own stories. (Btw, the X Lore is pretty good stuff, if you like science fiction stories you should check out the history behind the games)
All in all, it's a good game. There a still some bugs and flaws but if you can ignore such things and concentrate on the real gameplay, you will like it. If you are more into using your buildt up economy to go into a war, then you should pick up some mods, as the vanilla game doesn't really allows a full scale war. Also, if something annoys you, like scanning the stations for hours, there are mods for everything annoying in the game, so defiantly check out the workshop ^^
Before you decide to buy the game at full price, you should watch some 4.0+ gameplay on youtube to see if it's worth for you. Also buy the DLCs, they double the universe size and add tons of awesome stuff :P
Thank you Egosoft for not giving up this game at release!

I've been following The Dream Machine ever since it first entered development several years ago, and it's been an absolute trip to finally be able to finish the entire story.  One of the most impressive things you'll notice about this game right off the bat is, as advertised, the fact that the whole thing is done in claymation.  Anybody who's done any sort of claymation knows how much effort something like that would take, so this needs to be respected.  The background music further adds to the ambiance, making the whole game even more of a mind trip.  The game's style alone should be enough to earn it the attention it deserves.
However, the true focus of this adventure is on the story, where you will enter the dreams of your neighbors from your apartment building.  While the concept of entering dreams is nothing new, this game offers a unique perspective on the whole idea in ways that I prefer not to spoil.  All I will say is that it is a creative adventure with intuitive puzzles that tie in fittingly with the plot.  In short: buy this game, it's totally worth the money, and the creators deserve all the support they can get.

Slowly in XT we got our first big ship and got to fly all other ships. X2 saw everything expand. Then came X3... the worst of all X games... it got rid of docking sequences, it got rid of♥♥♥♥♥♥pits, it introduced some very unnature nebulars that made stations transparant and didnt hide backgrounds as they should have done. It did more to destroy the immersion of the X series than any other game before or since.
But X3 did introduce capital ships for the player just as it pretty much destroyed the trading game that had made X stand out from the original Elite games for so long.
I was never fan of the X3 series despite testing it heavily for Egosoft and they are my least played X games until X Rebirth which I am now replaying so that may change.  Todays X Rebirth is a vast improvement over the original release of X Rebirth, that is for sure.
Now comes X Rebirth....
Like all X games, Egosoft did a terrible job on the campaign, the missions are really badly explained as usual, players would credit Egosoft for making bugs and ask for fixes when in reality, those where design features, designed to work that badly, not bugs.
Seriously I am not kidding.
This time X Rebirth has the dubious honour of having the worst Campaign for any X game I have ever see. The coding of the campaign is to be blunt terrible. You cannot dress this up...it is terrible.
X fans expect campaigns to be badly written and badly explained when Egosoft make them. So for most of us, this was not news. I actually helped test X3 and worked my♥♥♥♥♥off to make it the most stable game Egosoft had ever made. I got my name in the manual and everything. Yet at release it was still a buggy mess. So I had wasted my time.
Which is why most experienced fans jump straight in to sand box where terrible campaigns dont exist and you just have the pure joy of the real X feeling.
THAT is the game your actually buying, the sand box game without the campaign.
X Rebirth fixed many of the issues X3 caused and makes X feel all new and shiney again after years of the old out dated sector design being the defacto standard.
Sure I loved the old factories and I hate the new ones. I consider the old factories to be something that added quite a bit to the game and I dont see anything in X Rebirth that comes close to replacing it.
Which is why I am mostly flying around shooting stuff this time around instead of trading like I normally would. X is the not trading game it used to be anymore.
But it is a very good space game if you have the patience to learn to play it on your own. Remember Egosoft dont explain things very well. So working stuff out for your self is important.
Even in the days of manuals, Egosofts manuals where never that helpful.
With V4 X Rebirth also runs very smoothly now, very few issues outside of that horrendous campaign.
I personally would give you this advice, the same adice I have given to all potential customers of all X games..... If your impatient and need instant satisfaction then dont buy an X game, it will annoy the hell out of you.
But if you are patient and like a challenge, can be bothered to work your way up to the good stuff and look out for opportunities.... Then you should definately buy X Rebirth. Expect to get 1000s of hours out of it.
Its not X2, but its definately not X3 either and thats got to be an improvement in my book.

If you're here because you're in the mood for a science fiction RTS, or Sins is on sale, let me dispense with the formalities and tell you straight out that this is one of the best, most intuitive and fun space RTS games ever.
It's hard to believe it came out in 2008 -- the visuals have aged extraordinarily well, the UI is easy to navigate and easy to get used to, the units are responsive, and the research trees are deep, powerful and varied.
There's no homogeneity here -- each race has unique ships with unique abilities and playstyles, and they each have research trees that emphasize their strengths. Certain lines of research are proprietary, meaning another race doesn't have an analog or way of replicating it, but you can be sure they have their own singular perks.
The races also have different approaches to economy, space travel and fleet logistics. While the backbone of a dangerous Advent fleet is the Illuminator vessel with its devastating beam weapon, amplified by the synergistic effects of Advent's carrier capital ships, the heart of the TEC fleet is the JRM Missle frigate, protected by a front line of heavily-armored warships. Likewise, the Vasari appropriately feel more alien than the other two races, but they have proprietary stardrive tech that lets them cross vast distances quickly, and the ability to ramp up their economy quickly.
With the updates (included), each race is further split into two factions each, providing a choice of six different races/ractions you can select from and fight. Additional updates added powerful starbases and more powerful defensive units, in addition to other features that have made the game deeper and more enjoyable.
I've been playing Sins since it was released, and probably have a few hundred hours of play time aside from the 95 hours or so I've got on Steam. If you give Sins of a Solar Empire a chance, you'll get more than your money's worth -- and you'll certainly have some late nights as you tell yourself, "Just one more planet, one more capital ship, one more battle..."

Egosoft has put more than its fair share of work investing in free updates for this game. The previous installments got updates as well. None of the X games are 'dead' and even Terran Conflict , Albion Prelude and X Rebirth still get love from the Devs. There are not many Developers around who are that dedicated to their polishing their games. They listen to their playerbase as well.
So in short, this game is worth it yes. Read on for the full review, and download the worthwile mods from the workshop.
The careful observer will notice that the factories 'unlike in X3' have animations that show the manufacturing of the goods. These manufacturing modules can be hacked and destroyed they are not just eye candy.
The modular choice for the trade ships feels very realistic and less is more IMHO. One does not need to memorize 500 different ships from 5 different factions, although the factory-complexes now make the trading a bit less easy as you will need to find where to trade what instead of having separate stations that each manufacture one commodity. Also, the anmiations and the use of unmanned vehicles for the unloading and loading of cargo by the trade ships, and their defense drones is very well done. The Specialized drones you fly launched from your corvette class ship is are spot on as well.
Unlike others who prefer the older X3 series (Reunion, Terran Conflict and Albion Prelude) I like the detail that was put into this one which is a lot more polished and it is clearly visible. A lot of fans of the old series hate this game because they expected X4 and it is quite a big difference for one as you can fly only one ship. I modified the game as well to get rid of the 'Highways'. For those who have this game from Egosoft directly of from GOG, there are 3 other ships that can be flown. - Look for the skunk overhaul mod on the egosoft forums or on Google.
If you can look past the remaining few bugs, and the still horrible voice acting and dialogue choices, (save often and turn off the speech in audio options) the game is very enjoyable.
This game has a pretty high learning curve and you will need to read the manual and get used to the quirky menu sets. Some tasks (like scanning for trade offers on stations) can be tedious, but there are mods for that.
Unlike the hands on Elite Dangerous, this is more a mogul game where the pace can be slow or fast, and there is enough to keep you busy like stations to build and ships to capture, build and manage, and it doesn't really become a micromanagement nightmare.
The flight envelope is not really what I would like it to be and is a very dumbed down WASD and two trigger affair, that cannot be compared to Elite Dangerous or even I-War 2, but I have been able to mod it sufficiently to my liking even with flight assist of and newtonian flight.
Version 4.00 is very stable and does not crash at all. Version 4.10 features TrackIR and Egosoft is working on a VR version of X-Rebirth. I am actually looking forward to the VR version of X-Rebirth to play next to ED and Empire Of The Dying Sun.
This is not the X-Rebirth that first came out. This is now a very polished game for people who wish to take their time and are more into management than dogfighting.
I'll be keeping an eye open for X4, but X-Rebirth VR will be on my purchase list. Please let us not wait too long.

Civ Beyond Earth offers a different branch from the normal CIV games. The game builds on a lot of aspects from CIV V and dumbs down a few. I've played the game repeatedly and beat it on all affinities except Purity (in the process). However the game lacks in its replay-ability and it feels sort of hollow after so many rounds of playing. May be so spoilers toward how AI act  in this review. Current state is a 7/10, and would buy if on sale.
Early Game:
Game is absolutely awesome in the beginning and you feel like you are on uncharted grounds that you must conquer or become one with. The aliens (bugs) in the game are a true threat and very commonly there is always one CIV waging a war against the bugs in the game causing more initial tension in the game promoting some early game warfare with astronaut suits and weaponized rovers between CIVs that adore the bugs and CIVs that want to kill them.
Mid Game:
Starts to get boring because all your doing is just hoarding buildings/wonders/victory quests. Diplomacy is not existent at this stage and if you want war just do it and there are little consequences except being condemned (but no one cares about that). What is good are the stations (city-states) were quests ask you to destroy certain stations because of their beliefs/practices or stations just don't like each other and want you to kill either off. The war against the bugs sorta dies in this stage because your units start simply overpowering the aliens and their is no sense of true danger. Unless your fighting siege worms or krakens but it's meh.
Late Game
Tensions rise!!! And alliances form, sorta  mainly tensions rise... You get these godly über units that are specific to your affinity choice which makes war fun when the two top dogs start slugging it out. The AI is most aggressive at this point and wars sprout everywhere commonly dividing the CIVs into three factions based on the affinities. However the AI have little room for diplomacy no matter what and wars commonly cary on until one or the other is wiped out. The bugs are just pests at this point and get one bagged from the weakest units in an army. Harmony affinity CIVs do little to protect the aliens and the aliens do little to join with Harmony Affinity CIVs effectively getting rid of the purpose of going harmony. Leading to Supremacy and Purity becoming the most war like and best because of their major production buffs. Than victories vary from going back home and helping humanity, killing off humanity and seduce all into supremacy, or becoming one with the planet. Each victory requiring a massive amount of settlers, or war units, or going turtle mode.
CIV AI
The CIV AI is real basic and they feel overly predictable. It's few instances were a supposedly friendly AI because of trade actually declares war on you for hostilities toward other CIVs or the Bugs. Therefore the CIV AI feels kinda blah and kinda easy to push around with little consequences.
Diplomacy
Nothing like CIV V and this game did horrible on diplomacy IMO.
Aliens or the Bugs
Fun at first and mid game but die late game and the bugs don't side with harmony CIVs making them a simply annoyance to all.
Affinity
Supremacy: You incorporate chips and metal into your people effectively making them cyborgs but ridding yourself of humanity and being and CIV all about numbers and results but no emotion. Essentially a robot CIV get nasty buffs toward production and science and get cool sounding uber units with the best ranged unit in game. Black and yellow color scheme that looks good. Basically go back home and commit mass extermination of the human race. Most radical and few AI choose this. Will constantly be at war late game.
Purity: Keep humanity pure and keep our culture and heritage alive and save earth if possible. 49er colors and feels the most familiar out of all the affinities. Victory goes back and saves earth. Cool uber units and has production and growth buffs with some culture. War is so so
Harmony:
Best melee units in game and sweet looking über units that rain hell and have the fastest healing rates, especially if there is miasma in game. They get buffs toward health, food, culture, a little to science. Greenish and bluish color schemes. They fall in the middle and choose to abandon earth and become one with their current planet keeping their humanity but embracing the minds of the native aliens and the planet. Kinda turtles it late game

I'm writing this about the entire game. In fact, if I was writing this about the first 2 chapters, I woud've been hopeful. "So much potential", I'd write, "such an interesting premise!" But no, the full game, after 7 years in development, is an utter mess that gets more teious and boring to play the further it goes.
First two chapters establish the premise of a strange horror mystery dream thriller sci-fi tale with not particularly good writing, but one that fits the mood and stop motion looks. Game doesn't really have a very strong focus on puzzle solving, moves at consistant pace and establishes an intersting setup.
Chapter 3 is where things start falling apart. Game enforces more teidous walking back and forth, asks for obscure puzzle solutions and doesn't present a particularly interesting story, but at least it moves the premise forward. Chapter 4, on the other hand, feels like a step back in the right direction and apart from more poorly designed puzzles at times, feels like the concept developing and game design of the game evolving.
And then Chapter 5 happens and everything comes to a grinding halt. Game stumbles and falls flat on its face, pace killed completely, initial setup almost all but forgotten, tone sent completely off the hinges. And if you manage to suffer from Chapter 5, you're greeted not with a return to form, initial promise fullfilled and game logically concluded, but with a mess of self-discovery, pseudo-psychological "smart" sequences, scene borrowed from Kubrik and an ending quote from Radiohead. I suppose, it's easy to forget what you were doing in the first place in 7 years of making of the game, but maybe doing something almost seemingly unrelated to anything before, isn't a good answer.
It's not a particularly fun adventure game, with really tedious "puzzles" starting in the last chapters. It's not a good story, because the storyline falls apart somewhere after midpoint and it's not particularly well written. And it's very definitely not worth time it requires to suffer through it all. Which is a shame, really, because it had "such an amazing premise".

In my opinion this is the best instalment in the Deadrising franchise. I first played this on the Xbox 360 when it released in 2010 and enjoyed the game very much albeit from a few frame rate issues and mid-long loading times.

Deadrising 2 is a ton of fun to play and rewards the player for taking risks as well as creating ridiculous item combinations to beat back the zombie menace.
Couple cons with this game though:
-AI is not very smart. They move slower than you so you'll be normally waiting at an area door for them to catch up and they frequently get grabbed by zombies. They aren't too bad if you know how to manage them though ensuring they stay away from big clusters of zombies and enemy humans looking for a fight. (Try not to give them guns, they might get infinite ammo but they tend to shoot each other or you quite frequently)

There are guides online to achieve controller support with this game but if you're comfortable using M+K then just stick with that. The difference isn't major and you can be more accurate with guns.
Overall I would give this game a solid 8/10. There's a good 20-30 hours of content as well as repeatability and plenty of well created achievements to aim for.

This review isn't going to be as dramatic as the others.. but here's what I thought of it.
Once you understand the game concepts it loses almost all of it's replay value. The thing I found most unbelievable was that only 1 person in the group could scavenge at night. I do not think that this function should be risk-free, but you should be able to send out party members at the end of the day.
I also found the moral choices to be lacking when compared to the reviews I had read about the games' realism. In my experience, it was just as dangerous to attack the hospital or church as it is the hotel or school. There are very few times when taking advantage of NPC characters is worth the mood hit that was caused from it.
Items in the game are completely non-realistic. A water filter should be able to give more than 4 'units' of water (whatever the 'units' are, it's too little). You should not be able to grow 8 vegetables in 3 days or distil moonshine as easily as presented, and catching rats in your home would be almost unthinkable when given the situation you find yourself in. Usually I would just give it all a pass, however this games calling card is its' realism.. so make it realistic.
This game is fun, and well worth the 13 dollars I paid.
However, it's grossly overrated and did not live up to the standards that others praised it for.

-Disguises don't work well at all which doesn't really make sense either way that people are suspicious of you from 10 feet away or more even when you turn your back or have a disguise with a mask. Basically I got the same vibe others did, the game borrows alot from splinter cell. A QTE melee event that goes a little too fast on higher difficulties which makes me not want to melee an enemy without a weapon & 'mark and execute' slow mo kill from the Splinter Cell Conviction. I don't need such theatrics.
-Forgettable music
-Level design, the levels are for some reason very linear for the most part. So much so I don't find much enjoyment at all, by the time I start getting into it there is a load screen (although its fast), it breaks immersion for areas to be split off like this with one way to get to them, and it renders everything you did prior consequence free. ie susipious guards, dead bodies, blood splatters, blown disguise etc
-Lack of subtletly, there is no option to turn of lights, close doors, and way too many areas to dispose corpses off.
-Equipment, or lack there of. You can't carry more than one type of pistol or throwable weapon. There is no equipment selection, no map and combined with mostly very linear levels it makes for a tactically dead game. You just sort of improvise as you go, I get that was sort of the case before but there is no choice but to play that way this time & it alot less interesting when you have so little routes to take in such cramped levels.
+They put in a proper cover system, I don't rely on it but its a little easier to move in and out of  corner and move between cover. I don't want to pop out of cover to pick off guys one by one because that to me is more of a 'soldier' type of gameplay but I appreciate the choice to.
+I liked the story for the most part to be honest, I don't get why people seem to think Hitman is emotionless, hes shown emotion before its just never gotten in the way of his ability to perform. ie he can turn it off at the first sign of danger. He also never displays fear as someone made for killing would. The way he talks to the child though put me off at first, he got a fathery instinct pretty quickly.
+But generally speaking the controls are easier because you don't have to use everything with the one activate button. They seperate 'disguises', 'drag corpse' & 'human shield', you can always do your hand to hand attack even when you have a melee weapons equiped.
+Cut scenes & Patrick Bateson
+The visuals, perhaps they could have spent more time refining the maps, ie make them larger and add more routes with atleast a few more assassinations instead of dumping 18+ possible assassinations into so few missions. They went overboard on providing replayability only to put way to much focus on other kinds of missions that I don't find anywhere near as interesting, the "jason bourne' comparison comes to mind of being on the run rather than being the predator. I liked some of it but mostly it felt odd to see the game lose its edge, comparisons to previous games are inevitable, afterall Hitman series is unique and Bloodmoney set the bar so high.
What do I think overall?
Its scores low on the 'planning' element without larger maps and your own in-game map display, too much emphasis on 'unlocking abilities', ie perks (hint to the developers, they do not fit this type of game), scores middle to low on the 'staging accidents/assassination & map design', scores high on 'style' & 'cinematics' but that isn't the core of Hitman. I would rate it 6/10 as a game in its own right, and perhaps 1 point lower as a Hitman game for its unusual choice of focus in gameplay design and some elements that don't work well for Hitman, like adding in instinct to overcome the useless disguises and too many non-assassination small linear levels. I prefer not to recommend to fans because of expecations the series has set up. As a story it delivers some great cutscenes, with impressive visuals that run well on older machines, but it doesn't interest me & I doubt I will play another if I hear it follows this one.

I know what you're going to say, "16.1 Hours played? That's not enough for a review." you're right I'm still trucking through the game and honestly I'm going to voice my opinion anyway.
Take my review with a grain of salt as I entirely agree with xXDragonSlayerPrincessXx's review
This game is HEAVILY escort based as the primary way to level up is to retrieve survivors and bring them back to the safe house, however it's such a pain when one of your survivors gets snagged by a zombie and you realize that they've been left a little behind so you have to wait for them to catch up. Staying still makes zombies group on you and going to free that one survivor so they tag along a little faster kind of causes you to get tangled up into their mess.
Boss battles will kick you in the teeth pretty hard, especially that the game doesn't give you much warning that it's a boss fight. Players may find that some Psychopaths move quick and can rough them up pretty quickly, and some you have to "cheese" out and pray that they get stuck. I.E: the motorcycle boss fight, you can't drive your bike into him and he takes damage like a brick wall. I had to get him stuck on the fountain area and whittle him down with a flame thrower.
The game also will treat the player quite unfairly when you're up against armed enemies as guns will almost ALWAYS hit you even if you're moving out of the line of fire, every bullet hits if you don't dodge perfectly and even then rolling to dodge isn't unlocked off the bat. This becomes a huge problem when the game hits the point where there are four snipers in the main street and you not only have to deal with Big Earl and Friends but the zombies in the plaza as well. Imagine getting grabbed then sniped at only to take damage from both enemies, falling down just to get up and have a few seconds of time to get out of the way only to get popped and dropped again by Big Earl.
These are just some of the issues, combat feels a little clunky as your character can't just spam attacks. A swing and a miss is.. well a swing and a miss, it's as if you swung your bat to crack a head missed and react far too late to prepare the next swing and instead what you get is grabbed. Did I mentioned timed missions? You're given waypoints to do things however everything is timed, and you've got to know where you're going as getting lost costs valuable seconds and honestly the map doesn't really help. There are "short cuts" to travel the map but they're out of the way and it'll waste your time and you won't be able to complete all the objectives not at-least on your first run.
DO NOT MISS STORY OBJECTIVES. You'll have to start over. That's what I had to do, and on the second round I knew what I was doing however at a certain point I was still struggling to keep up with all the objectives and the little time given to do them, new missions pop up at the worst times and may even become a hindering thing.
All in all, if you want to buy this game, buy it on sale. Full price is.. asking for a bit much.

Gettin' Jiggy wit It" is a 1998 single by American actor and rapper Will Smith, released as the third cut from his debut solo album Big Willie Style (1997). The song is based around a sample of "He's the Greatest Dancer" by Sister Sledge. The chorus is sampled from "Sang and Dance" by The Bar-Kays. Released in January 1998, the song was Smith's second hit produced by Poke & Tone, who replaced his long-time partner Jazzy Jeff, though the record-scratching techniques of Jazzy Jeff can be heard in the song.
The song spent three weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100 chart from March 14, 1998. It also won a Grammy Award in 1999 for the Best Rap Solo Performance. It was ranked the 68th greatest song of the 1990s by VH1. However, it was ranked at #19 on the list of AOL Radio's 100 Worst Songs Ever in 2010. The song was included in Pitchfork Media's 2010 list of "the seven worst U.S. No. 1 singles of the 90s"

: Passing mechanics have changed, meaning the ball is dropped less in catchable situations. The player still needs to see the ball, but some frustrating missed opportunities have been reduced.
TL;DR - budget indie title that has a good (and importantly,
) basis for a gridiron football game with some polish issues and limited to single matches/games (no season).
The foundations of a good football game are here. The selection of plays allows for varied offensive options, with competent AI to execute them and defensive AI that performs defensive schemes well.
The AI is very competent. On the offense, they form the pocket well, run their routes, and aren't supermen catching the ball (they have to see the ball coming). Defensively, AI reacts to motion before the snap, sticks with their men, reacts in zone coverage, and does a good job of deflecting passes fairly.
Art assets are nice. Player models are decently modelled and there's a good variety in stadium design and details. There's also a lot of off-field characters, like the guys moving the chains and camermen on carts moving about. Varied weather effects are also nice to see.
Good character. There's some humour to be found in the game and the motion captured animations of the players make the game more than robotic. Players celebrate or taunt when they deflect passes or score a touchdown, and show frustration when missing a field goal. The animations are a little jittery, but it's good to see an indie developer try to add character rather than it being a purely mechanical game.
Challenging! There's a good variance in difficulty. In my first game, I was defeated quite badly, but as I gained confidence in the gameplay, I started to get better results, though I'm still having some tough losses.
Limited to single games. If you're into your franchise or season modes, you'll not find it here. Personally, I enjoy pick-up playing pick-up games, but I know some will feel this is lacking.
Lighting. While the art assets are nice, lighting is a bit bland, which makes the visuals look worse than they actually are. A comparison I'd make would be racing simulators like rFactor, where the models are nice, but the simplistic lighting lets it down a little.
Lack of polish in some areas. Certain assets, like menu icons and button prompts are fairly low res. While not a serious issue, it lowers the overall visual aesthetic of the game. Not a big issue, but you'll be aware you're playing a budget title.
Canadian Football 17 is a competent game with a lot of fun to be had, albeit limited in scope. The important thing here is the mechanics of the game are good, so the football itself is fun to play. There's a good foundation to build upon for updates or sequels, so for those seeking a career or franchise mode, there is at least a good game to build upon. If playing the game for the sake of playing isn't enough for you, then you'll want to sit this one out. I'm personally having a lot of fun playing the single matches, but I understand this won't be enough for some.
NB - there is also a play designer, though I haven't looked at this yet. The plays that are in the playbook as standard are competent and varied enough for a casual player like me, though I may delve in to it later.

A heavily cinematic approach to the Hitman series, a fresh take not that many people were fond of, but ultimately does enough justice to its origins and I personally believe it to be a huge improvement, at least for one installment.
What I mean by this is it's fun for a change/for a while to have Agent 47 taking action into his own hands and watching him deal with new challenges regarding human actions and emotions and a bit of character growth. Even if somewhat cliché'd.
Whether you're into action, stealth or both, despite having partitioned stages rather than big sandbox-y environments, you'll be going from cover to cover getting past your enemies through a fair share of creative or classic accidental and/or stealth kills or action-packed firefights.
There's also an interesting online mode to create or play contracts. Basically the creator of the contract plays a specific stage in a determined way and other players will have to try to redo the creators' steps or figure out a new way to achieve the same or better results in order complete said contract. It's fun for a while, whether playing new contracts or beating highscores, adds a few more gameplay hours at the very least.
On the downside, there are a few glitchy bits in mechanics and disguises not being very effective, as well as a score system in the main campaign which kinda penalizes your playstyle.
All in all, a most entertaining experience and in my opinion the best Hitman game so far.
I'd definitely recommend this game to any fans of the genre or the franchise, take it for what it is and not for what it allegedly should have been.

At the very beggining it comes clear that something has gone terribly wrong with both the english and the spanish settlements on the neighbourhood. Only friendly person with whom protogonist begins to cope is mysterious lady dressed in red.
Betrayer merits highly on visual level - graphical desing is astonashing. I really loved how wind waved the trees and I could see every sprig shivering in gallantic spruces. The immersion is fulfilled because there is no background music and you can literally hear the wind blowing. I also loved how the color scheme could be set from full color -setting to default which shows only red colors and leaves everything else black and white.
Gameplay in Betrayer works like in any typical fps. While the weapon arsenal is unusual and exotic I found fighting too simple. The enemy AI is not worst possible, but majority of melee enemies just rush at you from long distance which makes it easy to take them down with bow or gun depending on hostiles' strenght. While the gunpowder doesn't grow in trees I had no difficulties to survive.
The game's biggest advandage lies in its horror feature and I admit having rather unconfortable moments when wandering in wilderness in night time/mode. The enemies lurking in there are more gruesome and surely got me scared a couple of times. However like in other action horror hybrids it is easy to get used to these dangers. Any boogieman or -woman can be killed and thus usually every new type of enemy may get one scared only a couple of times before killing them becomes a routine.
If I could give this rating somewhere between good and bad I did. Betrayer has some features like already mentioned colour settings which I would gladly see in other games too. On the other hand either fighting nor freightning features last long enough which makes gameplay to flatten much too quick and even the story sorted out to be medicore after promising start.
Eventually it is a price tag which lift's my thumb up - even higher if it's on sale.

Very cool game. Different than anything I've ever played before. It's basically a first-person exploration game with a bit of horror thrown in. You're shipwrecked on an island and have to explore to find clues as to why the island inhabitants disappeared.
The game takes place in colonial times so you use bows, flintlocks, and matchlock weapons. Weapons have realistic, multistage reloading procedures that can be interuppted and then resumed from the last step completed.
Headphones are an absolute must for this game. You find the various clues and treasure by pressing a button to "listen" which will provide directional "humming" sounds to lead you to it. There is a mechanic so that headphones aren't necessary in that a white box will appear on the left and right of your overhead compass that fade in and out to point you towards your objective. However, this takes a lot away from the atmosphere and spookiness of the game.
Once in-game, there are two settings I strongly encourage you use. Firstly, turn up color saturation to give color to the world. The black/white with red highlights scheme looks cool for a few minutes but the game ultimately looks much better in color. Besides, the "otherworld" is already in black/white. Secondly, check the box titled [Otherworld Gain]. I like the deep black of the default otherworld but it was just too difficult for me to navigate.

Fear Equation is a spectacular mix of resource/crew management, turn-based tactics and strategy, and creepiness.  But breaking it down into its elements is like pulling apart the rose, petal by petal.  What really makes it is that it confines you to the stark, dark confined of a single train car, but through visual and aural cues, radio transmissions, and that trust, trusty monochrome monitor, creates a vivid, much larger, imagined world around you. I think the documentation could be fleshed out a little more, as I'm still not quite sure how some things work, but the discovery process is a blast.

Fear Equation is a micro-managment turn based game. You are a conductor on a train that is one of the only sanctuaries of a fog that's covered the city. This fog is dangerous, and manifests itself into the nightmares people have. Your job is to get as many people out in your train as possible. The premise is simple, but while playing you will discover there are a LOT of moving parts. There's a lot to read, learn, and keep track of. Each passenger you pick up has their own opinions about you, their fellow passengers, and even the fog. Keeping them docile is important. You have to make sure they don't hate you or they will revolt. Also make sure they don't like you too much, or they will kill everyone who hates you. Outside the train is just as dangerous. There is the military that will shoot anything that moves and the fearless, who believe they are allies to the fog. You encounter these when you send passengers out for supplies.
As difficult as the game might sound, there is a lot of options for customizing your train ride out of the fog. You can mix and match different perks that help or hurt you, and you can make custom passengers with their own skills. As an added bonus, you can hook Twitch chat up to the game and make the viewers passengers on the train.
So together, it's a really fun game although difficult at first. There is a lot of  options to make it easier if you want as well.

Tiny and Big can be completed in below two hours, excluding 100% completion. As it is a short game, it's also desrving of a short review, however, a positive one.
Even when overlooking the bizzare and unique style this game has and the somewhat simple gameplay, this game is extremely unique. It is reminiscent of Double Fine influences, and plays very smoothly. in comparison to another physics based game I recently completed (Human Fall Flat) the game controls in a much simpler way, and works like a 3D platformer.
The controls are quite responsive, the gameplay is easy to grasp (a combination between a platform puzzler and Metal Gear Risng, I'd say) and the overall style is unique and the story, although short, is humorous and intriguing.
While it is kind of disappointing to say the game is no more than 90 minutes if you're here strictly to finish it (not to  100% completion), I am actually glad the game is so short. Just as you feel like the game has nothing more to offer you and might get repetitive, it just ends, giving you the boss battle to test your skills (I had to repeat it around 15 times, and all under 10 minutes, so it's mildly challenging).

If you're the kind of guy that likes physics and enjoy a good level design, you'd love Tiny and Big.

How refreshing it is to play a true stealth game!  No HUD indicators to tell you how well hidden you are, no tagging enemies so you can see them through walls, none of that - just you, tensely stalking your prey, staying out of sight, using the occasional gust of wind to mask your footsteps, figuring out when to make the first strike.
I have a lot of respect for Betrayer, it doesn't promise much, but what it does promise it delivers excellently.  I found the stealth gameplay to be very enjoyable, and while sneaking around is white-knuckle tense, it ramps up to 11 when full-scale combat breaks out.  One of my most memorable moments in gaming was fighting a group of posessed Spaniards in a small town, frantically trying to hide behind the houses as I took forever to reload my muskett, feeling the pressure to make every shot count in this deadly game of cat and mouse.
The story, or rather, stories, were also very enjoyable.  In each area of this game you will find clues - a blood splatter, a broken arrow, a sole boot - and then you'll be able to enter the "otherworld" and present these clues to the spirits of the dead.  With each new clue, they'll remember a bit more of what happened to them while alive, and as you show them more clues and corroberate accounts, you'll piece together the stories of these dead colonists - some stories have pretty clever twists that will leave you shocked or appalled.
Atmosphere in this game is spot-on too, the washed out colors of the world, combined with the eerie ambient noises, and lack of music, really put you on edge the whole time.  The Otherworld is worse, everything is dark, and a gray fog severly limits your line of sight, the open forrests suddenly feel claustrophobic and you find yourself fearing what you might unknowningly run into.  And let me tell you, you never get used to seeing a whispy white-eyed ghost materialize in front of you.
Great game, definitely recommend it!

A fun adventure that will leave you wanting more.
The length of the game is its one glaring flaw. I took my sweet time exploring (though I didn't find every single thing). Even over an hour on the first level alone! And I still finished the game in an all too short 3.7hrs according to Steam. It really stinks too because this game is spectacular otherwise. Gameplay rules the day and this delivers it superbly. You have three tools to get you through this unique 3D platformer; A laser that cuts through pretty much anything in the destructible environments. A grappling hook to move chunks of the world around with (you can manually push as well). And a sticky rocket to get chunks well out of your way. The freedom these seemingly simple tools give you is astounding. Unfortunately the first level is the only one that fully gives you that feeling as the rest of the game is more linear. But boy oh boy, I have not felt that in some time. You're free to make your own solutions to your problems. Get to places you "shouldn't" be able to get to. And find all sorts of silly ways to kill yourself along the way.
The atmosphere and art/sound direction is top notch as well. Weird world, good art, interesting sound effects, wacky energetic music. Its got it all. And the controls felt just fine on keyboard and mouse to me (only had to lower mouse sensitivity). I had one or two camera angle issues when near an edge but none more than average for the genre. Ran well too. It all just comes together with the spectacular gameplay and makes for a very unique gaming adventure. It's really a shame there isn't more to experience. I find it odd it hasn't gotten more attention or even a sequel. I'd gladly pay double+ the retail for modding tools or a 10hr campaign. Its that fun. But I got to take what I got.
A big big thumbs up. But be very aware it can be beaten in a mere 2hrs. And barely much longer even if you stop and smell the roses. An achievement hound could probably get 6+. Keep an eye on it though, a very under the radar game that is really worth the few hours you do get. Recommended!

Betrayer is a game marked by absence. There is no soundtrack to speak of and its color palette is limited to shades of white, black, and red. That emptiness is chilling, but does also serve to enhance what is there. The normally ambient sounds of the breeze and rustling in the distance are given even greater purpose as they are the means of hiding your movements from enemies while tracking theirs. The player is left constantly shifting between being the hunter and the hunted, a feeling that is heightened by a selection of weapons centered around bows and 16th century firearms. And despite incidental noises being the only sounds the game provides, the tension of always listening for the next encounter means actionless stretches are not tedious.
However, the desolate landscape and the fight for survival are secondary to the mystery of the game. The plot unfolds largely through documents left behind by the colonists and the game does a surprisingly good job of switching between those grounded stories and an overarching narrative while elegantly tying them together. Betrayer doesn't force any motivations, or any personal details for that matter, on the player character which makes it odd, then, that the only other living person in the area isn't given them either. The enigmatic Maiden in Red remains so guarded - or just naturally passionless - that it's difficult to connect with her, which leaves it equally difficult to invest emotionally in the situation at hand. While this disposition does make sense for her character, it seems like an important opportunity was missed. It's moments like these that cause Betrayer's sense of restraint to feel a bit less than intentional. Maybe the game was designed to emphasize only the most essential elements or maybe it was left unfinished. Whichever case it is, the important parts are here: an immersive world with an intriguing story to tell.

Pros:
- Comic book art style
- Unique laser cutter and grappling hook mechanics
- Quirky
- Short (doesn't overstay its welcome)
- Silly story
Cons:
- Stiff platforming (think Kingdom Hearts 1)
- Lots of accidental deaths
Tiny and Big at its best can be a delightful and fresh action platformer. It's weird in a good way which helps to drive the player to progress to see how much weirder it will get. The laser cutter mechanic is unique and fun to use.
The downside with this game is mainly its physics. It's a decent physics engine (don't get me wrong). But with an action platformer that depends so much on its physics mechanic, it's to be expected that there will be a lot of cheap accidental deaths. This can cause a great deal of frustration. To remedy this, the developers allowed for a near instant respawn (though you may be placed a few paces back). Another thing is the platforming. It's not terrible but it just feels stiff and imprecise which also allows for frustrating accidental deaths.
All in all, I appreciate what the developers tried to create with this indie title. It would be extremely difficult to implement these unique ideas without all of the associated hiccups.
If you're into action platformers and you're looking for one that's different from the norm. Check out Tiny and Big. Get it on sale.

Everything about it is worse than even X2, which was released in 2003. Gameplay is clunky; interiors, characters, all look like they came from 2001; even the backdrops of planets and stars look less amazing; the voice acting is actually worse; the music isn't as good as it used to, and one mini-game has a stereotypical techno-ish soundtrack that loops every 3 seconds, and not even properly, so it skips.
X3 had 100, 150 sectors. This game basically has 4 different backdrops. FOUR. Four very large maps, but pointlessly large, they could've stuffed it all into a smaller space.
Getting from place to place is no longer by jump gates, but you fly through 'highways'. No longer do you immediately get where you want to go, but you must 'drive' down these highways for 10, 20 seconds, longer. Combat is no longer smooth and dramatic and certainly no sexy battles going on here. Trading requires more douching around. You can now walk in stations, but they all look the same. You can talk to people... well no, you can't talk to people. You can click on them and get them to show their wares or hire them or whatever, and on occasion you can engage in 'small talk' if they blurt something out loud about one of 4 subjects. The poor production values and slow (even for the X series!) gameplay ruin the story mode, I was not invested in any way.
Old games like X2 and Freelancer, budget games like Darkstar One, even recent games like No Man's Sky or that one space level from Call of Battlefield do it so much better.

Hatred
Isometric shooter
Destructive Creations
Destructive Creations
is an isometric shooter developed and published by Destructive Creations, and has become famous due to the violent nature of the game.
The story isn't deep and neither serious, paying homage to multiple exploitation movies of the 80s. You play as the Antagonist, a man who hates humanity and decides to commit mass murder until he dies. The dialogue is mostly said by the Antagonist, and is either painfully dumb or hilariously cheesy. This game is not meant to be taken seriously.
Using the Unreal Engine 4, the game looks good and has great destruction. Unfortunately, the performance is very poor, the environments look bland due to the black-and-white style and the NPCs are not much varied.
You go around and shoot people. The end.
All joking aside, your goal is to go to points of interest and kill everyone that you find in the surprisingly huge levels. You can use three weapons at a time (ranging from pistols to flamethrowers) and three types of grenade as well as gasoline tanks and whatnot scattered around the environment. You can also drive some vehicles, but they usually destroy after a few shots. If a person falls to the ground and doesn't die, you can execute him/her in order to regain health. The animations tend to get repetitive and annoying, but you can disable them in the options. The A.I. isn't even all that smart, with civilians casually strolling by while you are stomping someone's head on the ground.
The concept is repetitive, and if what you have read might keep you entertained, than buy this game. Otherwise it's not for you.
The game is challenging thanks to the high number of police officers. You will mostly likely die because of explosions, getting run over by a car or simply not executing someone. The order difficulties tend to make the make more entertaining, while still not being too frustrating and impossible.
Most of the sound effects are fine, but the music isn't all that memorable. The voice acting is cheesy and the music lends itself to the nature of the game, with a hard-rock soundtrack that fits the gameplay but isn't all that great outside of it.
A total of 7 levels, 42 achievements, mod support and possible DLC make this a game playable once or twice in its current state. There are some secrets in the areas that you explore, but nothing worthile.
Much ado about nothing. This game will be forgotten in a few months and we will all look back and laugh at how everyone overreacted. The game is a good time-waster, not that different from something like 1997's Postal or going on a mindless rampage in GTA. If you like the genre, you'll have a blast playing this.

Mr. Bree is a hardcore platformer. It is generally easy to pick up, but it gets progressively harder as you go on with a ton of traps ready to kill you at any time.
Mr Bree balances the hardcore nature of the gameplay with very generous checkpoints. This is nice for players who might be a little intimidated by a harder platform game as you can easily make progress even after dying a lot.
I highly recommend this game as it was quite fun. With the game time above I was able to complete the game and also spend a lot of time in hardcore mode, which is truly brutal towards the end. There are tons of achievements and you can also collect items inside the levels to unlock more levels. For the money it was well worth it, as it's a great game with a reasonable amount of content.
One small gripe I do have about the game is the changing color scheme within the levels. The color scheme of a level will change after you die about 5 times, and this will repeat in going through certain colors or weather effects. This would be a cool effect if it didn't dramatically change how the screen looks. The red color was quite annoying as it was very difficult to see. Of course I could just suicide my character until the color scheme changed, but I feel it is something the developers should look into and consider changing.
The 2 boss fights in the game are ok, but don't feel too fun because of their boring mechanics that are reused between both of them. I feel more time and creativity could go into them to make them more interesting, or just remove them in favor of hard platforming.
These are my only complaints, and this game was still pretty great and I'm glad I purchased it. If you're a fan of challenging 2D platformers, this should be a no brainer for you.

I never expected to play another FPS as good as "Half-Life 2". HL2, like it or not, is one of the gold standards by which games are measured (shooters in particular). I thought if I were lucky, I might happen in to another two or three games that could hope to approach the hallowed shrine that is HL2. Not beat it, of course. But if I could play something else that came close... well, that would be great. Something innovative, engaging, grossly absorbing. Something that was simultaneously interactive and cinematic. Something that would punish, but bring me back for more on all fronts: great graphics, interesting gameplay and a compelling story. "Bioshock" delivers.
It seems appropriate to confirm something mentioned in other reviews: the crashes. Yes, they happen. On occasion, I was ejected from the game and dumped back to the desktop. When that happened, I was always able to load back in from my previous save and continue play. Those instances were infrequent: during my play-through, the client crashed a handful of times. With one exception, the crashes seemed to occur shortly after loading or saving. First one happened about ten hours in. It's more irritant than anything else, but still comes as a surprise when a product so seasoned and polished could still be plagued by random crashes.
The remastered version sacrifices none of the gameplay or style that made it such a signature experience. While not as breathtaking as some titles released more recently, this is still a gorgeous game that has the added benefit of running on an older or less powerful rig. This version also includes three 'challenge rooms' that each offer a unique, stand-alone scenario. The events in those challenges are not connected to the main story: they are strictly tests of the players knowledge and ability.
10/10, two thumbs up; I cannot recommend this game highly enough. Would you kindly play this game? It's a classic in every sense of the word. Not just as an FPS, not even as a game, but for storytelling in any medium. Finally, HL2 has something to keep it company in that lonely bracket at the top tier of entertainment. Very much looking forward to the next installment in the franchise.
Tangential thought: HL2 = 1984; Bioshock = A Clockwork Orange?

Short Review:
*starts game with three men*
*7 weeks later*
*ends game with three women*
10/10
Medium Review:
Pros:
-Unique: lets players experience the civilians' perspective during war rather than soldiers or fighters
-great system where you have to craft, scavenge and manage your own supplies, fortify your shelter and plan your night missions well in order to sustain as many of your survivors as possible
-high replayability value; events, challenges and loots are all randomized so gameplay will always be new and interesting
-neat cast of characters; I enjoyed that each had different personalities and reactions to certain events (eg. Pavle wants to share remaining food, Bruno wants it all for himself etc)
-presents you thought-provoking challenges where they test your morals and values (steal from others to help your friends? give away your remaining rations to help a neighbor?)
-if a character dies, he/she stays dead. I list this as a pro because it really adds to the tension of the game, knowing that dying in-game can't be remedied by reloading and your every move has consequences. it makes all the dangerous night missions that much more intense
-artsy graphics and a sad, melodious soundtrack that suits the game well (eg. when the remainder of the group find out one of their members have died)
-the characters' reactions and interactions. I really enjoyed seeing the characters react when someone died. Themaying things like "Yesterday he was with us...and now he's gone" really adds to the sorrowful feel of the game. I also enjoyed seeing the characters talkign to one another when trying to cheer one another up; it was heartwarming in a way to see this group of survivors supporting one another. I'm glad the devs made the characters more realistic and relatable through this.
-you can find and loot your friends' dead bodies. RIP.
-all proceeds of the game's DLC go to charity: is that admirable or what?
-Best of all - I'm in the game (sort of, lol. shame that Marko died first in my first playthrough)
-Really makes you feel like you're in a story of survival, where anyone could die in any manner and you'll want to see your favorite characters pull through.
Cons:
-no tutorial
-combat can be hard to grasp for new players (I lost three survivors because of this and it really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off) though admittedly this is realistic as civilians would likely have a hard time taking down trained soldiers
-there's a weird game bug where sometimes your character refuses to go back into hiding after backstabbing a hostile. this nearly got me killed.
-no save point at night. if you quit the game midway in the day or night, you start the whole day all over again.
Still 10/10
- Would love a sequel
Long Review:
So I was left with Anton and Arica after Katia, Bruno and Pavle all died in horrible ways. It was the beginning of winter, it was frightfully cold and Arica was terminally ill. In a fit of desperation I stole from the hospital to try and save her life, which sucked cause the city hospital's done a lot for my survivors.
Anton got the meds for Arica, and even sacrificed his last hot meal for her. There wasn't much dialogue but I imagine their conversation went along the lines of "Here Arica, you should eat something", and "I'm not going to make it...it's too cold".
But Arica was recovering and I was hopeful that maybe she would survive. Perhaps she could get through this.
And then the very next morning both of them had frozen to death and I was like wtf.
10/10 best war game out there

It seems to be complicated at first in terms of many manuals, but after a couple of hours, it's rather repeating to do the same things: get up to assign orders and work, scavenge, set destination, call it a day and then get up bla bla. Let me explain why that is.
It lacks stories and that is the biggest issue making it repeating. Yes it has a clear main story: you're the engineer in charge of train and your main goal is to get as many survivors as possible to escape from the fog and reach the final destination. But the problem is the journey to that final revelation. Honestly I don't mind going through same game phases such as lottery, orders, work, and guard but it's a pain to do them in a dull way as the game moves on. Basically there is no story-based events like side quests, hazards, or accidents when going through all of the game phases. You just set where you wanna go and manage the resourses, inculding passengers, fuel tanks, food supplies, etc. Don't get me wrong. I love micromanaging but not in a boring way. So what I do is to make sure my passengers that I assign to scavenge stay alive when they are searching that area. Also build defense against the fog attacks at the last game phase. That's it, that's the main part of the game. If you're a fan of strategy board games, you might enjoy reading intriguing narritives on your quest cards. In this game, nothing; only random fog attacks and dispute of passengers with no stories or narritives.
It's not a bad game though, but definetly need to put depth in it. Give it a try, but do it on sale since it's not worth $15.

Pros:
- Comic book art style
- Unique laser cutter and grappling hook mechanics
- Quirky
- Short (doesn't overstay its welcome)
- Silly story
Cons:
- Stiff platforming (think Kingdom Hearts 1)
- Lots of accidental deaths
Tiny and Big at its best can be a delightful and fresh action platformer. It's weird in a good way which helps to drive the player to progress to see how much weirder it will get. The laser cutter mechanic is unique and fun to use.
The downside with this game is mainly its physics. It's a decent physics engine (don't get me wrong). But with an action platformer that depends so much on its physics mechanic, it's to be expected that there will be a lot of cheap accidental deaths. This can cause a great deal of frustration. To remedy this, the developers allowed for a near instant respawn (though you may be placed a few paces back). Another thing is the platforming. It's not terrible but it just feels stiff and imprecise which also allows for frustrating accidental deaths.
All in all, I appreciate what the developers tried to create with this indie title. It would be extremely difficult to implement these unique ideas without all of the associated hiccups.
If you're into action platformers and you're looking for one that's different from the norm. Check out Tiny and Big. Get it on sale.

Fear Equation is excellent - one of the finest roguelikes I've ever played, and an early contender of one of my Top 10 Games of 2016. The biggest thing worthy of praise is the depth of this game - I still feel like I've barely scratched the surface. Between micro-managing supply raids, fuel consumption calculation, monitoring radio chatter, social engineering in the carriages, tense diplomacy between factions, monitoring dreams, and power management, this game is huge. If you like deep strategic games, you should get this.
It's also a spectacular example of story-telling and atmosphere - throughout the game, you stand in 3 spots in 1 room, and the world feels big and epic and real. You feel terrified for the fate of little blobs on a radar. You feel scared because people you never see might not like you - or like you a bit too much.
It works brilliantly as a train simulator. It's a great roguelike. It's a fantastic real-time strategic action game. This game is better at multiple genres than many games dedicated to just one genre are.
I cannot recommend this highly enough.
