Betrayer is a game marked by absence. There is no soundtrack to speak of and its color palette is limited to shades of white, black, and red. That emptiness is chilling, but does also serve to enhance what is there. The normally ambient sounds of the breeze and rustling in the distance are given even greater purpose as they are the means of hiding your movements from enemies while tracking theirs. The player is left constantly shifting between being the hunter and the hunted, a feeling that is heightened by a selection of weapons centered around bows and 16th century firearms. And despite incidental noises being the only sounds the game provides, the tension of always listening for the next encounter means actionless stretches are not tedious.
However, the desolate landscape and the fight for survival are secondary to the mystery of the game. The plot unfolds largely through documents left behind by the colonists and the game does a surprisingly good job of switching between those grounded stories and an overarching narrative while elegantly tying them together. Betrayer doesn't force any motivations, or any personal details for that matter, on the player character which makes it odd, then, that the only other living person in the area isn't given them either. The enigmatic Maiden in Red remains so guarded - or just naturally passionless - that it's difficult to connect with her, which leaves it equally difficult to invest emotionally in the situation at hand. While this disposition does make sense for her character, it seems like an important opportunity was missed. It's moments like these that cause Betrayer's sense of restraint to feel a bit less than intentional. Maybe the game was designed to emphasize only the most essential elements or maybe it was left unfinished. Whichever case it is, the important parts are here: an immersive world with an intriguing story to tell.

First off let me be clear that Fear Equation is an interesting idea, but I’m just not happy with its execution. I wish there was a better system in steam then just yay or nay? Because this game kind of leans closer to the middle then being outright bad.
That said it has some problems that need to be ironed out but can, and probably will, be fixed.
1.	Mrjihun pointed out the save problem has been explained. Thanks Mrjihun!
2.	After the fog attacks give me a summary of the damage that occurred. Lack of information isn’t just damaging to gameplay, it’s also boring in a game that is all about information and the decisions you make.
3.	Fuel needs to be much more common because a “Hail Mary” should be a last resort when the random number generator really messed you up, not something you do regularly.
4.	I understand the limitation to only sending five passengers out at once to scavenge for both technical and story based reasons. That said what I don’t understand is the mission team not bringing everyone you meet onboard the train, or as the “driver” my having the option to revisit a location to grab supplies they skipped out on the first trip. I admit I may have missed key details about how missions work but I remind you of the tutorial problem for any error on my part with this criticism.
5.	The game feels generally vague and brief about everything it tries to explain. That said at the same time much of what I little I actually do feels like it’s largely out of my hands, and decided by the random number generator.
This game like previous Screwfly Studios games is all about information and decisions. The problem is the information I am given regularly doesn’t feel exciting or interesting, which the same goes for the defences/upgrades I am building, or the passengers I am managing. The first exciting thing to have happened to me was when the train was attacked by the fog, but a lack of details about what happened made it very anti-climactic. The next exciting thing was reaching a town after six long days of skipping time, ended up being significantly less interesting then searching a house in Zafehouse diaries, when it should have been at least as interesting.
I suspect it gets better when you have a larger train population so you can actually get faction intrigue. But the trip to get there is too boring and devoid of interesting things for me to do to be worthwhile. However considering Zafehouse Diaries again, I didn’t particularly enjoy that game when it was first released either but the developers made significant strides to improve it afterwards. So this review maybe entirely useless in six months, but for now I can’t recommend this game.

Decided to finish the game and delete my old review (which I made after playing 40 min) and write a new one after beating it.
PROS:
* Pretty good graphics for a game that was released in 2010, environment looks good, zombies look pretty good. Sometimes I'd get a distorted line in the middle of my screens during cutscenes but this might just be problems with my PC, I'm not sure.
* Time limits on missions or whatever they're called are both good and bad. I just wanted to get through the game as quickly as possible after 3-4h(the ammount of escort missions which I hate were reduced by the time limit) of escorting survivors all over the place. Also helps you finishing the game in a timely fashion, this might be a pro if you are one of those ppl that never end up finishing a game because there's too much stuff to do, but it's a con if you REALLY want to do exactly everything.
* Tons of different crazy weapons to use if that's what you're interested in, I'm not so it didn't do much for me unfortunately but I'll still leave this as a pro because it's a big selling point of the game and it delivers on that point.
* Great music during psycho fights and top notch cheesy one-liners by Chuck after the fights are over
CONS:
* The only time you  get something resembling checkpoints is after finishing a case(maybe giving zombrex to Katey triggers this as well, can't remember) where the game asks you if you want to save, rescuing survivors or going back to the safehouse does not give you a checkpoint, doesn't autosave, this has to be done manually. Forgetting to do this can be extremely punishing and has forced me to redo 30 minutes of progress 2-3 times. I can't see the point of not having some form of autosaves or always prompting a "would you like to save?" after rescuing survivors, this is bad game design imo.
* Combat is ok but not good by any means, it feels clunky and there's very little variation unless you're constantly creating different types of weapons. If the combat was more fluid and not so damn clunky I could overlook the fact that there's very little variation, but this isn't the case.
* Some weird hitboxes during the fights with psychos(been swinging at psychos that should well be in range but they don't take damage, they might just be invulnerable doing certain animations but I see no reason for this and there are no clear indicators for when they're invulnerable if this is the case)
* I absolutely hate escort missions and this game consists of a lot of them and is one of the best if not the best way to earn PP and lvl up, this leads to you doing a lot of running around with survivors tailing you constantly getting grabbed by zombies and delaying the escort mission even further. Also, forgot to save? Gotta do it again. Gotta give capcom some cred for not having any escort missions after the mutated zombies show up though.
* Options menu is really starved, seems to only contain what was available on the console version + the extreme minimum that's required for pc, I'm not sure if this is because the game is 7 years old or if capcom is just too ♥♥♥♥ing lazy to bother with implementing a bigger options menu but since Dead Rising 3 is locked at 30fps it's probably the 2nd option, because ♥♥♥♥ PC plebs. If you're porting to PC don't be lazy, capcom.
* Story wasn't very enjoyable, although if you're playing this game you're probably not playing it for the story.
Some additional whining:
Some things don't feel very thought through, for example not being able to swap weapons while in a dialouge or on the walkietalkie thing, while this is realistic, this isn't meant to be a realistic game in that fashion. Accidently picking stuff up while trying to open doors because there's♥♥♥♥♥♥placed next to them, this is I'm guessing to create a more realistic environment but accidently picking up trashbins, dropping my weapon and losing half my health while trying to open a door because the "open" prompt changed to "pick up useless ♥♥♥♥ing item" because a zombie bumps into me is really annoying. Grouping tons of stuff together when there's space to spread it out is dumb and is prominent throughout the game. The snacks next to the garbage bags outside the safehouse is a prime example of this.
I didn't really enjoy fighting any of the psychos and ended up cheesing every fight with tons of food in my inventory and 2-3 melee weapons. I was going to put this in the CONs section but it was most likely my stupid approach that caused the fights to feel like every fight consisted of only: Swing, get hit, eat food. This was repeated untill the fight was over.
To conclude: When I played the game I went between 2 modes: "Meh" or "I really don't enjoy this game". I definetly do not recommend the game at the full 18.99€ price tag but if it ever shows up at 5€ or less on a steam sale you could pick it up to keep yourself distracted for 10+ hours.

A very boring, uninteresting game that left me highly disappointed as well as angered by its terrible mechanics and design.
Betrayer was a game that I good expectations for back when it was in early access and I bought into the beta for 13.49 usd (the game was originally 14.99 on steam when I bought it.)
The game, at the time, seemed promising. It was taking on an interesting art directive. This following description of the beginning of the game is still accurate in the final product.
You enter into a blighted land that's void of color with the exception of the color red. While you proceed inland, a woman fires an arrow at a post with a note attached. Telling you to leave this land for it is cursed and lest you desire to be trapped here too, you should make haste away from the land. Building up atmosphere, you look around you and the winds howl, the trees and leaves rustle violently creating a very ominous feeling of living in a corrupt land driven mad. You continue down the winding path only to be stopped by another arrow hitting a post near you. It tells you to take the bow near you and arrows. The creatures who dwell in the lands are spirits of people who once lived there, now insane, they skulk the lands, only to be thrown into a murderous frenzy should they see any living soul who wanders this place.
You will need to kill them. She tells you to aim for their heads and use the wind to mask the noise of your arrow, and your kill. Now. For starters. This is one of the first problems i've encountered in this game. The mechanic of using the wind to mask your... ANYTHING. Doesn't work, ever. It doesn't mask footsteps, even if you're crouched and hardly moving. It doesn't mask arrows, grenades, crossbow arrows, musketshots, thrown handaxes, pistol shots. It's a faulty mechanic that doesn't exist at all. The wind is just wind, it has absolutely no gameplay value except contributing to atmopshere.
And then we get into the next part. A lot of the weapons in this game accordingly have a low reflect chance. Meaning if you shoot an enemy or throw a projectile at them, it has a "small" chance of reflecting. At least that's what it says on paper. But in reality, the reflection rates in this game are stupidly high. It's pretty common for enemies to reflect your attacks. Your arrows, your bullets, and sometimes even handaxes.
And that's where we get into the next part of the bad enemy design/weapon design as well as player mechanics. In this game, you'll take a lot of damage from enemies from one blow. Though alternatively, assuming you're aiming for the head, all enemies die very quickly, usually in 1 or 2 blows to the head, and about 4 or 5 if you're fighting a captain demon (except grenades one-shot everything including boss-like monsters).
So anyways. You'll quickly assume in this game you're supposed to play it very stealthily. Avoiding conflict, sneaking around foes. Attack only when you absolutely have to-except that's not how it works at all. For some reason, all of the enemies in this game seem to have pin-point knowledge of where you are. I've had many times where enemies are charging at me from far down the field and I have no clue how they saw me, heard me. And this is inconsistent too, sometimes you'll just have enemies who know exactly where you are from a little over half a football fields distance, and then enemies who'll not know you're extremely close to them, at nearly pick-pocketing distance.
I think the worse part is that all the enemies in this game will simply just charge you. They'll run up to you and get in your face and quickly kill you. Which is stupid, you have sometimes freaking squadrons of men just charging at you. And for how slow the reload times are for guns, and the deflect chance on arrows. You'll be standing there like an idiot constantly firing arrow's they'll just deflect or reloading a gun while they hack your bloody limbs off.
though it doesn't stop there, it gets better. It's an entirely liable strategy to lead a mob of enemies to a barrel of water and then iterally stand next to a barrel full of water (because barrels of water replenish all of your health and give you 3-4 potions that replenish your health by 40 points out of 100 total health) and just strafe around and reload your guns/fire them and shoot arrows and then pick them up and fire them again at the enemies until they all die while you keep drinking from a barrel of water. This is literally the only strategy I could find that was functional to actually take over a few stronghold positions in the game. The difficulty is otherwise impossible for the mechanics of the weapons you're using.
So i'm going to halt there and go back to the atmosphere.
So in this game after you leave the tutorial area. You enter the world and proceed up a path to a abandoned village full of people turned to ashen figures. You won't find much in the village save for a bell. You'll place a bell on its bellpost and you'll ring it. Once you do this, a loud sound resounds from the bell and you enter the dark world, the place where demons wander. And the game sets the tone for what they want of the dark world. A shadowy place where unspoken horrors echo deep within the blackened foggy haze, you will hear screams in the fog, but you and a courageous foot will have to proceed forward into the haze. But i'm getting ahead of myself.
You'll pick up a dismembered eye, ear, and tongue in the village. To allow you to see, hear, and talk to spirits in the dark world. This is assumingly, where your investigation begins. To figure out what happened to the people here who lived here before these lands became cursed.
But i'm going to ruin everything for you right now, because there's absoultely ♥♥♥♥ing nothing. I streamed this game for several hours on twitch.tv and I can tell you that there seems to be absolutely no story here. Nothing is explained, everything you meet and talk to is just people who died painfully normal deaths in the real world in the time period it takes place. And for that I mean being killed in a battle with natives, a person was killed so the killer wouldn't be found out as a traitor, natural death from disease, suicide from depression over a loss, there's even a person who commited suicide by accident because they didn't know how guns work and accidentally shot themselves in the head.
Nothing contributes to whatever story there is in this game, it's just fetch quests, and you have these incredibly boring conversations. That basically sound like this.
"I don't know who I am."
"Were you killed by this gun?"
"Yes."
"You are Alvar Thompson."
"Oh yeah, I am."
"What happened?"
"Oh, my son died and I got really depressed so I killed myself."
"Okay."
"Yup."
And that's it. Sometimes there's "more" to the story, and it's just more fetch quests and finding out why they're dead. The best part is that after you find out everything there is to learn about someone. You report to the girl who was firing arrows at the post back at the village (She's only there in this land cause she's looking for her twin sister.) and then you just give the like, murder weapon or a memento of the person who died, as a gift to her. And you get 4 options and none of which contribute to the story. And you learn nothing about her.
I've hit my character limit, so i've deleted a lot of text to type this and the below. I will post a video review of this game in the future wrapping up my points about this game.
Anyways, this game is riff raff and you should stay away from it. Even at 4.99 usd, this game is a waste of money. The atmosphere and gameplay as well as story are all bullocks and a waste of time.
Sorry for my incomplete review, but I hope to some degree that the text provided will help you in your decision in buying this product. Thank you for reading my review.

Betrayer is a unique FPS game that focuses on mystery and intrigue.
The review will be represented with a simplistic "Pros/Cons/Neutral" format.
Pros:
* Beautiful visuals. (Monochrome can be turned off and fiddled around with)
* Sound design is just magnificent. The immersion that it introduces is astounding.
* Great mysteries.
* The spiritrealm type of thing is a breath of fresh air.
* Collecting the collectibles help you do mysteries and collecting stuff can be therapeutic thanks to the scenery and the simplicity.
* Extremely low price, seeing as it's even been on the Groupees 50 cent bundle. Very easy to trade for as well.
* Very good controls.
Neutral:
* Your hand will not be held. (Take it how you will)
* Combat is fairly simplistic.
* The stealth system is very easy once you get used to it.
Cons:
* Difficult to see whether you've been detected by the enemies, only a sound queue to notify you.
* Enemies don't respawn after clearing a cluster, meaning you have to play the game again at least once to get all of the achievements.
Overall:
7.5/10

Sins of a Solar Empire has consumed many hours of my time, all of it worth it. Before I started playing some of the many mods available, the vanilla version was very simple to get involved in and the learning curve wasn't to harsh. I eventually found Sins to be addicting and devoted many hours to playing.
I eventually moved onto mods. Specifically: Sins of a Galactic Empire; one of several Star Wars mods available, but the one I found suited to my kind of "fun."
Some Features:
- Large Matches, up to 8 players, either with friends, other players, or AI (with varying types of AI difficulty sets)
- Different victory conditions for those who like to switch it up or like to change up how to win their game
- 3 vanilla factions to choose from, 2 sub-culture for each faction for different types of playthroughs
- Active mod community with varying amounts of mods that range from Halo to Star Wars to Star Trek
While this may be a dated game, a new DLC was recently released which was a nice surprise to find. So if you ever tire yourself of vanilla, you can certainly utilize the new DLC
You will lose some games and you will spend hours upon hours in some, it all depends on the challenge you set yourself up for.

This was one of the most fun space-based games I played in recent history... and I own/have played a LOT of space games.
This is not exactly "space" sim as much as naval ship arcade-based action RPG, but it has the atmosphere, characters, and ship variety to keep things fresh.
I clocked my 52.5 hours in a single play-through from start to finish, and yes, I did play this game for fun, so I did not rush past areas or just hop from mission to mission. I hunted for bounties, stopped raids, broke blockades, and... well... PLAY the damn game instead of just trying to get it over with.
The game's unique take on broad-side combat, old-school battleship-style A la WWII, makes for a refreshing space experience that made me wonder why other space combat games did not adopt a similar format long ago.
This is NOT an X3-equivalent space empire building sim, nor is it a hardcore rogue-like. It's simple a great single-player adventure with great combat mechanics and above-average story progression with TONS of polish and character. This is better than most AAA titles today.
For the money, it's a steal at full price. On sale it's a MUST GET.

+ Unique claymation graphics
+ Interesting and varied settings
+ Brilliant and mostly logical puzzles (Yes, even in the dreams)
+ Seamless transition between chapters
+ Writing gradually improves
- Main character is too much of a blank slate
- Glitches
- Game crashes without warning
- Unsatisfying ending
- Game window can't be minimized
- No inventory shortcuts, even for things like keys that you use often (you always have to click and drag)
* Lots of horror elements, so the squeamish or easily spooked should take note
Good news: if you buy this game now, you won't have to wait years for its completion anymore.There's no need to worry if you're just picking it up: the transition from chapter to chapter is impressively seamless given the long development time. The exact same environments can be used without any jarring shift in graphics thanks to the claymation, too. I bought it early on and waited for it to be finished before starting, which is good because the game never offers a recap of what came before.
Let's start with the obvious: The Dream Machine looks incredible, even with the annoying black bars at the sides of the screen. A tremendous amount of love went into making this, and it shows. Plus thanks to the premise, the setting of each chapter changes drastically, which keeps things memorable and fresh from start to finish even if the worlds you explore lack the fullblown surrealism of actual dreams.
The downside of the beautiful claymation is that it's difficult to see which objects you can interact with or not. There's no button to highlight all the hotspots you can check out, so your only option is to move your mouse along the screen and wait for things to light up. Worse is when a smaller component of a whole is what you need to find. Let's say you're supposed to click on the handle of a bicycle. If you scroll over the bike the entire object will light up, which disguises the fact that the handle yields a totally different interaction when clicked. It's needlessly frustrating, especially when the problem could so easily be circumvented by the main character giving a hint like "the handles on the bike are loose."
Speaking of the main character, he's really not a strong lead. Victor has no job, no ambitions, and no apparent hobbies other than perhaps music (which you would never know if not for the guitar in his apartment). You can choose to play him as someone mostly kind and helpful, or be a complete jerk at every available opportunity. If this had noticeable consequences on Victor's behaviour in the scripted sections it might be interesting, but they seem to play out the same regardless. Even Victor's descriptions of the things you click on lack personality: "There's nothing remarkable about it." "It's a chair." "I used this X to Y."
Chapter 6 makes a last-ditch effort to provide him with a blandly generic backstory. By the end of the final chapter I didn't have a clear idea of who Victor *was*, which detracted significantly from the ending―an ending which seems to offer an obvious opportunity for a final, meaningful choice if he is indeed a player surrogate, but instead shuttles you down a predetermined path.
The game's main plot is tidily written. It fully embraces the fantastical aspects of its story, playing out largely like a mystery/horror with unpredictable twists. The silly, stilted dialogue of Chapter 1 fades away in lieu of genuinely fascinating concepts and characters who are, if a little one-note, still a memorable addition to the worlds you explore.
There are occasional lapses where Victor re-explains something he just told someonne in a different interaction, or  where one of his previous actions is mysteriously ignored. For example, at one point you set an angry mob on a character who rages at you for the betrayal; go back in a few minutes and he'll politely welcome you into his home as a friend. In another instance you spend quite a lot of time talking to a group of men who have been searching endlessly for a certain place, often to the point of madness. Once you find it, you can backtrack to talk to them...but there's no way to tell them about what you've found. Little details like this would have made the world so much more convincing.
The ending is certainly not the worst I've seen, but it was too abrupt to emotionally resonate with me. It took maybe ten minutes then boom, game over. After a night of racing to the story's conclusion I was left feeling underwhelmed. (It didn't help that the game crashed right in the middle of the climactic scene.)
TL: DR: The flaws are minor, but there were enough of them to taint my enjoyment of a game that's otherwise beautiful, original, and set in a compelling world. I'd say you should definitely still give it a shot if you like adventure games; just remember it's not a perfect experience.

I dunno where all the hate is coming from regarding this game. Sure there are a few issues here and there but overall it is fun. Although many have compared it to civ 5 and argued civ 5 is better, i disagree. This game is similar to civ 5 but different enough that it has its own personality (i.e. affinity levels are how you level up your units), quests for you to do (which is new) and instead of trying to use characters based on earth history (albeit loosely) like civ 5, this game starts you on a new planet.
Sure that path you choose (i.e. affinity) means that pretty early on you have to decide which affinity your going to major in (as this determines which resources you will need the most). Its still engaging. In my opinion this is no different than when I played civ 5 and had historical expansionist leaders nearby to me (i had to formulate a strategy early on to decide whether i was going to woo one or some of my neighbours or go full on military myself and quash my neighbours).
This game requires similar decisions as people with similar affinity will be warmer towards you and more hostile towards you if your not. So all in all i don't find it detrimental that early on i need to pick an affinity. In general though the comparison to civ 5 (which is also a great game, but has been around for years and has had expansions and other dlc content added on over time) is not a fair comparison content wise. Civ 5 has been out for awhile and they released content that expanded the game...beyond earth just came out and people are comparing to civ 5 as it is now (not as it was when it came out..which was still damn good).
The graphics are amazing, it plays similarly to other civ games so if you have any experience with previous civ games you should be good to go after a few games. New fans to the series will face the daunting task of anyone coming into any civ games (using the civilopedia and advisors often to find out WTF is going on.
I haven't played this game as much as some of the negative reviewers simply because i have bought a lot of games lol..what can i say i love games. All in all this game lived up to my expectations from viewing the early gameplay videos and developer videos. I read the reviews before i bought it and they recommended it too.
overall i am satisfied with this game and have already preordered starships (as this game although a standalone will have some cross over play features with starships).
final opinion...its a great 4x strat game, buy it if you like 4x strat games as there is a lot here to do, and its fun and has a good deal of depth.

Sins of a Solar Empire is without a doubt my favorite 4X game; it's even one of my favorite games of all time.
The learning curve is admittedly rather steep, but once you learn the game it becomes very clear that this is an absolute masterpiece of a game. Assembling fleets of fighters, frigates, and support cruisers led by capital ships and then sending them into hostile territory- where you face enemy ships and their static defenses such as turrets and mine-fields- is thrilling every single time.
There is infinite replayability here. From playing 1v1 with a friend (or co-op) to all-out warfare (economic or militarily) with a handful of players, there's plenty of ways to play. You can customize and tinker with income rates, build speeds, victory conditions, etc.
If you're a fan of 4X or just strategy/tactical games in general, or even if you enjoy really cool sci-fi settings, definitely check this out.
Also, I've played hundreds of hours of this game, so my Steam "time played" is not indicative of my actual familiarity with Sins. Do yourself a favor and check this game out- it's amazing.

I am split about this game.  I enjoyed many of the missions, but as beautiful as the world they place you in is, it is very linear.  You are forced down very narrow paths with at most the ability to walk around the left side of a vehicle/box/house versus the right side.  Throughout the game you have the challenge of discovering little bits of news papers as background story but I found that while looking for them, almost always after a firefight, you miss out in the NPC dialog as they continue on with the mission ahead of you.  Speaking of which, the running mechanic is to me far too slow.  Walking crouching feel correct, but running feels like I have a 200 Lbs pack on my back.  There is a prown / crawling position, but that got used twice, once in the opening mission as a demo, and once later.  The mission types are wonderfully varied, from heli pilot / gunner, hummer gunner, sniper, rpg gunner, grenade launcher missions, in addition to the standard fps mode but they only appear forthe most part once each (minus the fps missions).  Which brings me to my biggest problem with the game, it's very short.  It took me only 7 hours to finish and it could have been faster if I wasn't overly aggressive running and gunning and dying in many of the FPS missions as I was, in addition, if I avoid the side news paper hunting element of the game
I could have easily taken another hour off the total time.  Over all a good game, but only at a discount.  Side note, I did not play the multiplayer part of the game.

Honestly, I don't care much for Super Meat Boy and the sub-genre it helped spawn. I don't fault the way those games are designed, it's just a personal preference. Short & brutally hard games just aren't my thing. I still managed to get most of the way through Mr. Bree+. I guess I should explain why.
Relatively-speaking, this is a pretty easy game. The deaths are constant, but the checkpoints are frequent. The music is also really good. Porcine protags are few and far between, so this game gets points for that. At the moment the only other game I can think of is Muchi Muchi Pork. This is a 2D shooter about pig-girls who ride flying bicycles, while fighting evil*. Anyway, this is a game that's actually rather pleasant, despite Bree's aptitude for exploding. His constant internal monologuing makes him a bit pretentious as well, so half the time I feel like his deaths are deserving.
There are a decent amount of stages, the rare collectible, and the controls are suitable enough. There's even a hardcore difficulty and you're constantly challenged to beat your best times. However, Mr. Bree+ is held back from potential greatness due to a number of issues:
Poor frame-rate - It goes without saying that a platformer should be 60 fps. Mr. Bree+ is 30? Less than 30? More than 30? Whatever, it's not good enough. This lack of frames translates to missed jumps, which results in shredded pork** Flying objects are also more difficult to dodge, which is the reason why I didn't beat the other boss. There are two of them, one at the end of the forest, the other at the end of the slaughterhouse.
BIG hit-box - The difference between Mr. Bree and Mr. Breesket can sometimes be attributed to his large hit-box. It's kinda hilarious really, because even sharp objects that touch his cape will kill him. I figure that this game can be improved, if it accounted for bacon-saving close shaves.
The lousy boss-fights - The thing about bosses, is that any issues with the game tend to culminate at these exact moments. This evil warthog is beaten by dropping a box on his head a few times. Getting there is a pain. Before he each attack he has a little code-word, which clues you in on what he's going to do next. The thing is, you won't know the first time around, which leads to guaranteed deaths. This might have been alleviated if the hit-box and frame-rate were improved. The other (slaughterhouse) boss forces you to dodge flying spikes while wall-sliding. It was at this point I surrended.
In my opinion, both bosses could have been dumped in exchange for some new stages, or a better finale. Maybe Bree could attempt to escape giant meat-grinder/tank, or parachute from a butcher's flying fortress while dodging buzz-saws, I don't know. Fixing the frame-rate/hit-box issues is probably a lot simpler, and would leave me less of an excuse for being a quitter.
Mr. Bree+ isn't a bad game. Even for a guy like myself who thinks spikes should belong in pits and not walls, ceilings, or in the atmosphere. Aside from a frustrating finale it's a decent enough game to jump through. Give it a go, you might not regret it.
*If you guessed that Muchi Muchi Pork is a Japanese game. Congrats!....You don't get a prize.
**Mmm...shredded pork.

A disappointment. As an avid Civ player, I would not have needed much but I tried the free trial for a weekend and just could not get myself to want this game after many hours of play. There are some interesting new twists, but in general the flaws overwhelm them;
1. Visual confusion - in the main map you cannot see what type of unit is on a tile if the tile is improved. Several times during a big battle I had to just guess and attack the wrong one.  The tech tree is eually confused. Most everything is a shade of white or grey so you really figure out whether a path gets you new units, buildings, or other traits very well.  Finally the planet itself (and even the factions) are hard to figure out due to jumble of colors and constrasts. In general, after hours of scrolling, hovering, view mode switching and struggling, I just wanted out.
2. Theme confusion - after the great intro video, the entire story line is trial-and-error.  Alien bugs, are they dangerous or should you leave them alone? Alien planet features good or bad?  Game makes all of this trial and error, leading to early death several times.  Civ is not Don't Starve. The commitment to a world is too long to have a single bad choice doesn't lead to immediate death by trial and error.
3. Alpha Centauri - was just so good, that all I could think of was how much I wanted to go back and play that instead of this visually confusing assault on the eyesa and brain.
Really sad result, but keep trying folks - Civ is still the best strategy game out there!

I have to say, Fear Equation is my favorite of Screwfly's games. It blends the people management from Zafehouse: Diaries and the mission systemd from Deadnaut, without being super sophisticated. The learning curve is small, and you get the hang of things very quickly. It is very difficult, even with some of the easier engineers (engineers are the person you play as). I was a little hesitant at the beginning worrying that it would be too complicated and I would want to stop, but worked through my first few days on the train, got the hang of it, and was sucked into it for hours (And then died, customized the passengers as my friends, and started again.)
As usual with Screwfly games there is a cool customization feature, where you can create your friends, family, and yourself as the engineer of the train and see them all show up. When creating a passenger it is pretty simple and straightforward, and includes ways to increase stats like choosing their occupation. There is also a pretty wide variety of portraits the game comes with for faces of your custom passengers, or if you're really into it you can put your friends' actual faces into the game folder and use it in-game. Lastly on the custom passengers there is a three question sheet that determines what faction that passenger will usually be in, and how influenciual they will be to other passengers in their carriage.
You can also customize you engineer, the portraits are the same and you can choose different atributes for your engineer that will make the game easier/harder.
I would recommend this game to most everyone, and I hope you enjoy playing.

The style of graphics remind me a quirky comic book. Though at first it was unusual to my eye, very soon I got used to it and started taking it for granted.
The soundtrack is worthy of notice. Someone from the team did an amazing job in finding and compiling the songs into one wholesome soundtrack, but despite the variety of artists, the songs clung to each other with their sound, as if though one single person/band wrote them. Mostly instrumental, they have a jazzy incline with a little bit of "dirty" garage sound. And notice how the tapes are drawn in the gameplay! Anyway, the music is a huge plus.
I loved the introductory game console tutorial, which organically fit into the "main" game, not breaking the continuity, not creating any LND (although, that rarely happens to me) – it just made sense and supported the wholesomeness. To be honest, first 5-10 minutes of the game I was grumbling out loud – whether it was a feeling of being obliged to remain sceptical or just my typical "Why do I have to do stuff?" attitude (-that applies not just to video games – it is practically my life's motto, if you may ask). I didn't like that the radio kept telling me what to do. Now, on the other hand, that I think of it – the radio and its lines were, too, organically written into the game, and I just keep wondering and admiring the game's crafted continuous harmony. But in another 10 minutes I was so engaged with the gameplay, I started having fun (not counting highly dynamic scenes). And finally. (For the next sentence you'll need the proper context.) "Cutting stuff to pieces" – isn't that the dream?
Gibberish audible talk of the characters shows an original approach. Plus, ears don't get tired from hearing repeating "phrases" over and over. I've had opposite experience, so Tiny & Big obviously wins here.
One little thing that I didn't quite like has to do with speech bubbles. There were two kinds of them: the ones that waited for the player's mouse-click and the ones that didn't and were simply timed. With the latter, I had a problem as I couldn't read the texts, even though short, fast enough and they went on, while I continued to miss pieces of dialogue. Part of that problem was their sudden appearance, but not sudden enough that I could realize the start of dialogue and pay attention to it. Since I also had to continue to play the game, I had to ask the next sitting person to read it to me out loud. Well, yeah, highly dynamic games are not my thing as I get easily overwhelmed. If you don't have problems with reading, it won't bother you at all.
In conclusion I will say this: Go buy the game and play it if you still haven't! My compliments to the team.

Repetative, Boring, Unrewarding.
Well there's a lot to choose from. The game is essentially Scrabble with RPG elements. You fight generic halloween enemies; the bigger your word, the more damage you do. The main problem is the difficulty curve is too steep. In most RPG's, you have an idea of what you're up against and can prepare accordingly. In Letter Quest, you are railroaded through levels which exponentially increase in difficulty. The result is that you reach a point where you must grind to continue. Unfortunatley, the majority of upgrades are tiny and even insignificant, which means you have to grind longer. For example: For 500 gems (you get 100-200 per level) you can increase your damage by 5%. To increase your damage by 50%, you need to get at least 5,000 gems (again at 100-200 per level) and only spend them on damage. But you only start with 225 health and most enemy attacks do somewhere between 20-30. The point is that terrible pacing puts Letter Quest at a massive disadvantage. It was already at the bottom of my backlog, but forced grinding puts it on my wall of shame.
Believe it or not, the grinding isn't actually the worst part, that title is reserved for how damn repetative this game is. Every single fight is the same thing with different damage variables. You put up bigger numbers than their numbers and boom! You win. At the very least, enemy damage should also have been based off of randomly generated scrabble boards, rather than giving every single monster consistent damage. It makes the game boring, especially when you realize it's impossible to defeat a particular monster without more grinding. Sometimes you even bust out the anagram machine and realize that even when you consistently use the longest possible word or the word worth the most damage, you still can't possibly beat the monster until you increase your damage or health.
The entire game is an unrewarding slog. You fight monsters to get better gear to fight tougher monsters to get better gear to fight tougher monster to get better gear.
Save your money and play scrabble instead.

‘Letter Quest: Grimm’s Journey Remastered’ for Steam has you steer a small grim reaper through hordes of ghosts and barbarian bunnies on the search for a good slice of pizza.  The gameplay is all about grabbing letters from a 3x5 grid of scrabble tiles worth various points to spell words to empower each swing of your scythe.  It’s a well-implemented RPG with branching paths, a store to upgrade your weapons and potions, stackable books with their own experience meters, temporary status buffs and hangman-style treasure chests.  There’s four ranks of difficulty for the main forty levels and an endless mode.
Tailoring my attack is fun, but I’d also have enjoyed more story.  Many ranked challenges have limits on words or time.  Harder enemies can poison your tiles and change your letters and heal themselves and enchant your tiles to eat their neighbors.  They might be immune unless you use a corner tile of the letter grid or take eight times more damage if hit by one of the crystal tiles that appear in your rows.  It’s a 2D game made in Unity, which I hear is challenging.  The unmastered version lacks the catchy music but also runs on mobile devices.

This is a wonderful example of a single simple gameplay concept developed and executed perfectly, making for a game that is quick and easy to learn, but addictive and very satisfying to master. The letter arrays may be random, but if you have a flair for anagrams and an ability to think creatively you can surprise yourself with the the solutions you'll find to maximise your damage into each of the game's dastardly foes.
Whilst you consider what words you can even make, bear in mind the extra constraints. Perhaps an enemy only takes damage from words that are 5 letters or less, or takes double damage from a word beginning with a vowel, or ending in an E, perhaps you have a side quest encouraging you to play palindromes, or words with double letters, or you just want to get the achievement for playing the word 'bacon'.
Then there's the charming art style, the cute character descriptions, the neat little references to other letter tile games, and all the other touches that show how much love went into this game and you have something that works as both a quick time killer and an enjoyable longer session, with and endless mode to guarantee you won't run out of ghosts to kill.
If you like scrabble, boggle, crosswords, or just the idea of slaying a zombie by spelling the word ♥♥♥♥♥♥ then this is well worth picking up. 5 stars, highly recommended.

Most things from BioShock apply to BioShock 2, so I'll do the rundown on changes.
2 Quick discalimers:
1-It crashes, a lot, and seemingly for no reason. It doesn't autosave as much as I wanted it to, so save often!
2-The scarier moments from BioShock are pretty much gone (make of that what you will), so if you're not a horror fan, you'll probably enjoy this a bit more than BioShock, but it's still pretty bloody.
So you're a Big Daddy by the name of 'Subject Delta', but you can still use Plasmids and such, because your a prototype. Your little sister, now a grown-up sister, needs your help after you get ressurected. The story is above average, but overall weaker than BioShock. Similar progression to BioShock as well, semi-linear missions but plenty of exploring for cakes and ammo. We've also got some new characters to go with our new areas too. Another change I like is the visual style. Set 8 years after BioShock, Rapture's leak problem has got a little...bigger...to say the least. The art deco style has been preserved, but there's odd glowing underwater plants and stuff, and the sequences where you get to wander around on the ocean floor are really beautiful. I spent the first 10-ish minutes going 'Whoa, everything's so pretty!'.
Gameplay is largely the same, except now we can dual wield Plasmids and Weapons, a much needed improvement, and a full new host of weapons as well. Plasmids are largely the same, but some changes and additions, usual sequel things. I also found I was using a greater variety of weapons and Plasmids than BioShock, where I was often just using Electro-Bolt and the Machine Gun, Gene tonics are more streamlined, so you only have 1 HUGE set of Gene Tonics, which is rather nice as in BioShock, I was often thinking 'gawd, I need more combat tonic slots!'. Hacking isn't total♥♥♥♥♥♥anymore, just a kinda Quicktime event, but you can still screw up, and you can also hack from a distance, hooray! Enemies are largely the same, two new types of Big Daddy and one new Splicer is all I've seen so far. So pretty solid all round, nothing too different from the original, but some much needed changes.
However, BioShock 2 does have a fair swathe of problems. The story isn't as good as before, which is a real weakness. The main antagonist has the most annoying voice ever, and she's always around, but the other characters are fine. As a Big Daddy, when you get to a Little Sister, you have two options: 1-'Adopt' her, take her to a corpse, gather some ADAM as you munch through half your health and Ammo after fighting a butt-ton of Splicers, then do it again, and finally send her to a vent, and I don't think you even get rewards unlike BioShock. Or, 2-Kill her on the spot, 120 ADAM, bam, no fuss, lots of mess, but no uneccesary usage of Health kits.
On the note of Health and EVE Hypos: You can only carry 5 of each, but First Aid Kits fully heal you. I found I was often low of health. And it annoys me how you can eat, drink and smoke through your steel diving helmet, unless Subject Delta can absorb nutrients through Osmosis or something.
When you are dealing with Little Sisters, there's a chance it can summon a Big Sister, a kind of Mini-Boss. They're kind of annoying, but not a huge♥♥♥♥♥♥to deal, and you are given proper warning. But please, ONLY spawn one if we're being evil and harvesting them, NOT protecting them with our lives and finally freeing them from their torment.
The other two problems are more technical. I found the Audio was very quiet, everything was quite distant most of the time, which is really annoying, especially when sound is so important. The other problem is buttons. Although being able to dual wield is nice, there's a lot of extra keys, and it can get a bit cluttered. Due to too many keys, there's no manual way to reload EVE, which is a real pain in the middle of a fight, so you have to zap yourself to 0, then reload, which is about as fast as the original.
But overall, BioShock 2 is still solid. It's kind of like Portal and Portal 2. They're both good games, but BioShock is superior to BioShock 2. The story is less tight than before, and there's some dangling threads here and there. BioShock 2 also has the morality element present, but it's handled a lot better, a bit more grey. And I genuinelly felt sad with the ending I got.

Graphics and interface

Graphics are horrible, user interface is horrible, the game is slow even on a brand new machine, which is simply ridiculous for this type of game.
Game play
The game uses the same horrible game mechanics as Civ V. The game is simplified over Civ IV, uses hexes and 1 unit per tile rule. This alone leads to unsolvable problems: The map gets clogged by units and worker micro is a nightmare.

The research circles are a neat idea, but it doesn´t matter what you research. In fact, it doesn´t matter what you do at all, since most AI´s can´t expand past 3 cities, and this is a problem, since infinite city sprawl (ICS), a problem solved in Civ IV  is back in Civ V and Civ BE.
The fore mentioned problem with endless reconfirmation of trade routes I consider so serious as to pronounce the game unplayable until fixed. Civ V players are supposedly "used" to this from Civ V, but these players also complain and for real Civ vets, this is simply unacceptable and unplayable. Galactic lore
The sci-fi theme of alien planet colonization is interesting and the content is interesting. many lore and flavour texts from classic sci-fi novels such as Isaac Asimov are a plus.

A solid start, with poor design choices made early on.
First, let me say that I bought into the hype when this was released. I couldn't WAIT to get my hands on it. On deliery day it was the greatest dissapointment ever. Multiplayer just simply lacks the people, mechanics or environments to make this my go-to (or even regularly played) multiplayer game. Enjoy getting stopped in the middle of a driveway stuck on something invisible? Enjoy taking a rocket to the face seconds after you ducked behind cover? Absolutely love getting killed before the 'you've been hit' red marks show on your screen? Then this game is your multiplayer paradise... assuming there are anyone populating the servers.
With that aside... single player. Holy Smokes this SP tells you a story. There are scripted tunnels of cinematic moments that are meant to evoke emotion, and they do (almost, more on this later). The gameplay is fairly linier, you go forward in a straight line, no room to wiggle or backtrack to get something. Nope, forward it is. However nice the story is, it is objective based. For instance, one of the opening gun fights you're trapped in a gas station trying to clear out the enemies so you can make an escape. I huddled in the station taking stock of things, and sniped out the enemies out by the pumps, turned around to look at something, and BAM! enemies respawned out front. I took my time in that gas station, and after 45+ enemies, I realized they were respawning... But once you move past their spawn points, they stop spawning there. Cool effect to move you along in the story, annoying as heck if you're looking for the hidden objects.
Now, the cinematic lock down sections. I get it, you're trying to tell a story. Thank you for attempting to inject story into a genre that lacks it. However, if you're going to lock me in a bus for the first 3 minutes of the game... make it a cinematic I can skip. Please. For the love of all things sacred. Let me skip watching people being executed on the streets.

This is a nifty little platformer with a few hours worth of entertainment and mild frustration. You are a pig...walking on 2 legs for whatever reason and everything around you is going to gut you. There are spikes, arrows, traps etc. Every level introduces new elements. There is also 1 puzzle piece per level which you can collect to unlock a sort of prologue.
The character will frequently share his thoughts with you if you enable it in the options although you will often miss it, because the game is quite demanding. It calls itself "hardcore" I think, but it's not Super Meatboy level insane. It plays a lot slower and more determined, although some passages seem to be only manageable by pure luck (arrows so fast you can barely see them) and those are extremely annoying. Luckily though the game handles pretty decently. Your character moves when you tell him to and stops when you tell him to, even in mid air, which took some getting used to. He just stops dead when you release the button.
You can also get 5 special powers. The first of which is how to jump (lol that was kinda funny). The game gets increasingly more complex (1st of 3 official "chapters"). It also looks kinda neat and is challenging, but mostly fair, as you get a multitude of check points during each level. The only real gripe I got with it is the setting. You're in a forest and that's it apparently (with exception of the slaughterhouse prologue you can gradually unlock). Also when you die the screen often changes colour (I think this is to simulate daylight and night time?).
Hands down the best thing about this is the beautiful and soothing sound track though. Whoever composed it is a genius and deserves your money. If it were purchaseable I'd buy it. It is eerily enchanting and ominous.

I loved this sidescroller, it takes its inspiration on Super Meat Boy and that's not a bad thing, it's really fun to get through the 45 main levels through trial and error and will highly recommend it for $3 to any platformer lover.
It took me nearly 5h to finish the game main stages and its rather unforgiving final boss, however I then decided to play some of my other games and didn't finish to unlock the 15 secret levels of The Slaughterhouse, if you are a hardcore player you will need to collect special puzzle pieces hidden through the main levels to have access to it, 3 pieces = 1 stage of Slaughterhouse.

It has good controls, although sometimes very sensitive near the ledges (reminded me of Super Mario for the NES), I played the game with an Xbox 360 game pad and had a blast, it has a good learning curve and doesn't punish you when you die since you are just teleported to your last checkpoint stone on the level.
I loved the visual look of the game, a nice touch was that every time you die you respawn and the time of the day has moved forward and on sun down all is really reddish and a little harder to distinguish some elements, I rather play during night, morning or day but I enjoyed this nonetheless, if I was stuck on some area and things got reddish I just committed suicide a few times until night had fallen.
The story is quite bizarre, you get a better grip of the story by looking at the trailer than by the game's cinematics. You are a pig who wakes up in the forest with amnesia and are trying to get back home, as you progress you collect some golden puzzle pieces that actually unlock a bit of your memory and grant you a few more abilities (jump, run, double jump, etc) and this is what drives the game forward until you get back home and battle the game's final boss, an classic boss that you will need to memorize all his attack patterns to beat, meaning that you might die (A LOT) in the process.
The music is so so, you pretty much only have a couple of tracks but fortunately the tunes aren't that bad or otherwise this game would have become very nightmarish very soon, I played around 15 levels a day and finished it in 3 sittings and wasn't bothered by the score at any time (except maybe with my 249 attempts to beat the boss).

Supposedly a good multiplayer experience. But if you, like me, just like to experience a good single player campaign, don't bother. Even if you are a John Milius fan (this is not the expected "Call of Duty meets Red Dawn").
On the pro side (which is more of a "not completely distgusting" side) you get some distinctive characters (well, you'll be able to distinguish between the philosophical positions of Rianna and Connor. And you'll recognize Hopper because he's the Korean kid. Let's not overdo it with character depth), you get a "Go Wolverines" banner, the story is kinda sorta engaging, the 4 hours needed to complete it are kinda sorta acceptable and the cliffhanger ending qualifies as "it was probably pretty cool when Milius described it to the designers".
What really kills it is the implementation in the game: The flow is generally interrupted by barriers of the invisible (ah, okay, I am not supposed to go explore a bit, yes?) and visible kind (it is annoying to see the NPCs hurdle them and not being able to oneself), the events are badly timed (ah, to get rid of the enemy Goliath, I need to press this button exactly now?) and the mix of required interaction and watching pre-scripted scenes is badly balanced. All of that ruins the immersion feeling.
So: No reason to play this for single player fans. Go watch any version of Red Dawn instead, at least these movies won't bother you with bad interaction design. And while you are at it, check out Tomorrow When The War Began.
P.S.: Does anyone know what Primary Weapons System paid to get their Diablo into that game? I like long-stroke piston guns like the next guy, but seeing this rather obscure thing as a standard weapon in the game was kinda distracting.

Overall, a visually beautiful, slower-paced game that reqiures you to manage the resources on the train, assign passengers to carriages based on their factions to prevent internal conflicts, and build defenses against the fog. Once you reach a destination, you can send passengers out to search for items/food/fuel, either through a random lottery or by rigging the lottery to send your stronger passengers.
It's not a reactive game, like Deadnaut, instead you plan ahead and then watch it executed. Personally I prefer this style, but I tend to like management games anyway.
For few tips from my few hours playing:
*Pressing TAB skips to the next phase (Lottery, Orders, Work, Guard), and also helps you fall asleep quicker after you've clicked on the bed.
*If the train is moving don't bother doing the lottery, just keep an eye on which day you're planning on arriving at the next town and only use the lottery then. Just TAB passed it to Orders.
*Don't allocate too many orders. I was confused at first, but the greyed-out boxes in each carriage page are the orders they are working on. Too many ongoing orders increases your chaos level, so stick to one or two until they're done.
*When scavaging, you attract less fog if the engine is off. Turn the engine off by taking the throttle down to zero (to the left). But beware: if you run out of battery power when scavaging you might find some of your passengers that weren't scavaging have died.
*Increasing the power to a carriage seems to make them work faster/more efficiently.

Hitman: Absolution is a stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix. It is the fifth installment in the Hitman series, and runs on IO Interactive '​s proprietary Glacier 2 game engine. Before release, the developers stated that Absolution would be easier to play and more accessible, while still retaining hardcore aspects of the franchise.
The game was released on 20 November 2012 (which is in the 47th week of the year in reference to the protagonist, Agent 47) for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360.
Hitman: Absolution was met with a polarized reception. Most positive comments were concerning the game's graphics, environments and locations, and the varied gameplay options. However, many critics disliked the game for not "feeling" like a Hitman game. As of March 2013, the game has sold over 3.6 million copies.
The game is played from a third-person perspective and takes place primarily in the United States, mainly around the city of Chicago, Illinois, and the fictional town of Hope in South Dakota. The player controls Agent 47, a master hitman. Gameplay is very similar to past Hitman games; as such, it is a stealth game that incorporates action gunplay.Players choose how to complete each level, taking branching paths to get to a target or location.Players may use pistols, bottles or bricks, assault rifles, shotguns, fiber-wire, or steel pipes, against enemies if opting for the action oriented approach, or avoid enemies all together, not being seen, using disguises, blending in the environment, and only attacking the set target(s), if using the stealth oriented approach.
In the aftermath of Hitman: Blood Money, Diana Burnwood, Agent 47's handler with the International Contract Agency, suddenly goes rogue, carrying out a catastrophic sabotage that includes publicly exposing the Agency. The Agency reforms under Agent Benjamin Travis; Travis assigns 47 to kill Diana and bring Victoria, a teenage girl in her care, to the Agency. Shooting and wounding Diana in her home in Chicago, 47, rather than executing her, comforts the dying Diana, who gives him a letter and asks him to keep Victoria safe from the Agency.

After about an hour of playing this game I can safetly say I know how the game is going to progress.
So what is Fear Equation? Fear Equation is a horror game set aboard a train, what role do you play? You are the engineer! Or well I guess the guy who runs the entire train aswell, you are given certain areas to view things and interact such as the notebook which is where you will decide who does what via a lottery (Which I believe you can rig so only certain people get chosen) and upgrades, Defence building and Dream Logs. There is a computer which you do all the scavenging from and listening to comms. The front is where you man the train and decide where to go, if you stop the train and turn of the Throttle the battery will drain and if it runs out the entire train will go dark and depending on how long it's out for will depend on how many people disapear and never return, you however are completely safe. The back of the train is where you sleep and hope everything will be Okay!
---Gameplay---
One part you have to study dream logs and then counter possible threats depending on how many people are having said things in their dreams with defences such as barricades, heat etc, you have no other control over what they do. You can increase power to their carridges though I haven't found a use or problem for doing so as the tutorial seemed to just stop abruptly which in a sense is good as what's scary about a game when you know how to do everything. On the computer you will do scavenging which is similar to Dreadnaught except you only plan what they do and how long and then sit back and watch, make sure you have enough time as if the fog rolls in and they are in there then people will start disapearing and never been again. You use resources from that time in the next day where you build the defences and upgrades etc.
--Is it Scary?--
I'd say there's more tension than actual horror in this game, there are some creepy scenes you will see at night through visions of sorts but nothing that will make you jump out for your seat (Though I haven't died or hopefully not seen all the scenes yet).
--Custom Game--
This is a mode where you can choose from either preset cards with their own settings or create your own Engineer with custom or preset profile picture, you decide how hard or how easy the game will be, think the fog gets dense to fast? Choose the slow fog modifier. Think getting upgrades for something is too hard? Get it full upgraded. Think upgrading make the game to easy? Block the ability to upgrade. You can choose multiple ones to properly define your experience.
--Conclusion--
I'd say for the Current price it's worth it, there's a lot of content and even custom which I haven't checked out yet but I will and update this review later. I give it a 9.5/10 For being a very unique and fun experience.

Betrayer is a fun FPS adventure game that definitely stands apart from other games. There isn't really many RPG elements so I wouldn't go in expecting such, but it is still a compelling little story type game. It is set in a world with two variations, light and dark, during colonial times. The backstory and messages scattered across the map are in no way dull and do not detract from the main story like in some games and the main storyline seems interesting enough.
The only issues I currently have with the game are the enemies with their extreme ranged accuracy, enemies having really wide detection ranges, no voice acting whatsoever (which is okay still), and not much in terms of customization of anything (which is also okay because it seems like more of a story game anyways).
It does a lot of things well though, such as the animations, the sounds, the graphics, and just the individual character of the game. I would say it is worth picking up because it really does have an interesting style that will keep you occupied for awhile.

X: Rebirth is a mixed bag, there were some major issues with the game at launch which is part of the reason I waited until later to purchase, that and all the negative reviews.  As it turns out the vast majority of the negative reviews are actually longtime franchise fans that didn't like the new game formula, X: Rebirth on it's own(now that most of the big bugs have been ironed out) is a pretty solid game.  I bought the game on sale, but if not for all the bad reviews I would have paid full price, the game is worth the $30 tag for sure.
Good:  I'll be brief at first and go into details further down
-Interiors for ships and stations add to the experience
-Harpoints to target on ships/stations to take out weapons, engines, etc.
-Nice variety of stations
-Plenty of side missions to do
-Complex enough design to allow more options, simple enough that you only need a couple "how to" videos to learn everything
-Crew: nice to be able to feel like you're working with people
-Ability to "command" your fleet
Bad:
-Interiors aren't that flushed out
-AI pathing and behavior
-System to increase Crew members' skills is extremely repetitive
-Complex enough that the game doesn't necessarily show you how to do everything
-Unable to pilot other ships besides SKUNK
-Fleet commands are extremely limited
MORE DETAILS:
Interiors - This feature makes it into both the good and bad category, and for good reason.  The addition of interiors to an X Universe game is huge and can be quite enjoyable to those looking for a bit more out of their game.  Being able to look around the inside of your ship(s) along with the inside of stations you visit can allow a player to immerse themselves into the game more easily.  This feature could have been one of the shining examples of the new direction for X: Rebirth, but the development fell short.  While it was a great step in the right direction, it seems the developers wanted to force you to visit these interiors whether you liked it or not.  Patches since launch have allowed much of the "on-station" tasks to be performed while in the sector instead but at launch you were forced to go onto stations just to recruit new crew members, which is a pretty huge part of the game in X: Rebirth.
Ways to Improve:
- Take away requirements to visit stations that are repetitive
- Add actual vendor stores instead of random people standing around the station
- Addition of "Recruiters" which will track down the crew you need
I will add more to this later when I have more time, all in all there are definitely some glaring issues with X: Rebirth but I feel it was a risk worth taking for Egosoft and I hope to see them continue with the concepts explored in this game, even it not for the "main" iterations to the series.  The game has a ton to do and will be able to keep you busy for hours if you like building a trade empire.  The story has a decent build up but then just falls apart at the end and feels like it was rushed.  I wouldn't put the main story into either bad or good because it functions great as a tutorial and is fairly rewarding, but the ending could have been much bettter.

This is the game that I was hoping Elite: Dangerous would be.
The only thing that made me hesitate to try it out was the 2D space combat... It sounds lame for a SPACE game to only allow 2D flight, right? Well yeah, but you forget about that pretty quickly because it's FUN.
Rebel Galaxy said, "You know what, Elite can have their flawless space flight simulation, we're going to do everything else better." And they did. And all those other things are what make the game fun to play.
The ships all play differently, between speed, maneuverability and varied weapon slots (broudsides, turrets, cargo space) several play styles are opened up. And the cost of the ships and their upgrades scales well with what you get out of them, and the missions you will be able to undertake with them.
Missions that take longer or are higher difficulty always pay more, so no guess-work there. Actually, I found that the best reward/risk ratio was on the escort missions, probably due to the "dreaded escort mission" stigma, but they work fine. The escortee flies around in an area until you put their ship on auto-follow and follow them, so they and you can't get lost.
Combat is fun. And it get's hard! Side quests are fun and some are pretty funny. Trading makes sense and offers a somewhat viable alternative to combat to make money, though I found that combat was more fun and I would use trade as a supplement. You can easily do both with the same ship.
Trade starts to get lucrative especially when you start to go between systems, the different systems have different supply and demand needs, and so do (to a lesser extent) the planets within them. So you can make money trading within-system but finding the best trade routes involves finding the best planet to buy in one system and the best planet in another system to sell to. Again, this is pretty consistent and doesn't randomly change. There are events that will affect supply and demand but it's clear when one is going on, and it's laid out in plain English what the effects of the events will be.
Worth playing.

The review is for the game version 4.00. Latest updates as well as community mods have finally turned the game into a fun and enjoyable experience.
X-Rebirth is an open-world space game with such features as trading, empire management and ship combat. The core aspects of the game are:
- Attention to details. Ships and stations are no longer simple meshes, floating in space, but complex organisms, consisting of multiple components, affecting functionality. You can cripple ship by destroying engines or sabotage station production module with a drone.
- Immersion. Seamless world allows to experience mind-bogglingly big space as it was defined once by Douglas Adams. At the same time space has never felt more alive with mass traffic flying around stations and huge cargo ships transporting wares across sectors. Player can even talk to individual NPCs aboard stations and ships.
- Real economy. Everything is driven by the law of supply and demand. Destroying even a single mining drone can cause problems in multiple production chains and stagnate economy of an entire sector.
- Freedom. Become a bounty hunter, engage in fleet battles or create self-sustaining complexes. The game is a sandbox and provides all the necessary tools for the player to chose his role.
While X-Rebirth is set in the same universe as previous X titles, fundamentally it is a completely different game with a separate list of features and a new scalable game engine. The game has a number of pros and cons with most notorious being:
Pros:
- Game stability. As of 4.00 I have not experienced any game crashes even on modded setups.
- Automation. Assign ships to station manager and he will decide whether to send them trading, minining or patrolling.
- Dogfights. Without upgrades fighting small craft presents a real challenge as enemy fighters will actively boost and manouver.
- Trading. Player no longer has to issue manual commands to dock and buy/sell wares, but only find trade offers and confirm them. His trade ships will carry out trading automatically, while player can search for other trade oppurtunities or do missions.
- Graphics. While graphics in the game are simple in comparison with modern titles, ship and station models are aesthetically pleasing.
- Modding support. The game has received Steam workshop support and is easily modifiable via XML scripts.
Cons:
- Game performance. Although X-Rebirth is a CPU intensive game with the amount of simulation taking place, I get around 30 FPS(3770k+gtx680) in busy areas and during big battles. Upcoming patch 4.1 seems to improve this situation and provides performance increase of 25% on average for me.
- UI. User interface has always been a problem spot for X games, and unfortunately X-Rebirth is not an exception. Although, there have been improvements with mass broadcast commands, adjusting  properties of individual components still takes too many clicks.
- NPC models. In comparison with any modern game are simply bad. The good part is you do not have to seem them that often with mods like TAF and ability to remote call NPCs.
- Audio cues. Voice lines are repetetive and disrupt gameplay. Mod SilenceYouAll is mandatory to play the game and keep sanity.
- Plot. The biggest issue with plot is it tries to bridge various pieces without logically explaining  connections between them. However, X-Rebirth's main focus is to provide open-world sandbox experience, so plot is more of an extended tutorial rather than a thrilling story.
- AI. Game AI has lots of room for improvement as oftentimes ships show undesired behaviour. Combat ships with long range weapons tend to close distance, pathing issues in asteroid fields and innefficiency of trade ships. Patch 4.1 and mods like MICT improve on some of AI aspects.
- Balance of the game. Game's balance is far from perfect and a lot of things are either useless or OP. The good thing balance is easy to adjust to your liking via XML patches and in fact there is a number of mods already on Steam workshop.
- Various features making game better/more interesting:
* Absense of automated traders. Implemented in YAT mod.
* Inability to manually specify logistic chains. Implemented in MitchTech Logistics mod.
* Player HQ. There is no mod that adds proper player HQ, however there are several mods for player      shipyards.
* Destructible stations. Again, a number of mods to enable station destruction.
* NPC building stations. Due to real economy station destruction and construction has not been implemented in stock game. However, mod CWIR adds a whole strategy layer to the game and makes NPCs fight in faction wars, capture new sectors and
build stations there.
* Customizable ships. Unlike in old X games it is not possible to change ship loadout and swap turrets.
* Limited number of ships. There is a number of ship packs available on workshop.
* Player is limited to only one ship. This ship is however is highly detailed with 3d cockpit and interiour.  Player also can  modify various options of the ship like engines, shields and weapons. Alternatively, thanks to capital ship bridge mod it is possible to command your empire from the bridge of your personal destroyer and never fly Skunk.
All in all, X-Rebirth is a mixture of both astounding momements and utter frustration. And it is not easy to make a definitive conclusion of this game using only binary mark system of Steam reviews. However, having invested a lot of time and effort into this game I am certain that the game is fun and you can enjoy it, thus I am chosing the recommend option. However, as with other X games I can not recommend this game to everyone but those who:
- Enjoy space games
- Enjoy economy tycoons
- Do not mind to use mods

XRebirth - one of the toughest game to describe... The launch was crappy, the game was clearly not finished, annoying, arcade-like and many other things that would make other company go bancrupt. But not Egosoft - this guys are famous for working on their release for years, not abandoning their creation. So after few patches (and  few years) the game is finally quite good.
Now, it aint space simulator like ED or Evochron but more like 4x empire building space simulator. You have quite engaging space battles, the universe is one of the most alive universe You will ever see in any game (Not empty like in ED) - here you have populated systems, where space ships are trading wares and it looks like a very busy highway in USA...
You can build your empire slowly by doing multiple missions, upgrading your ship to merceneary or fighter while building factories, warehouses and changing economy of the system.
The whole world is multiple systems connected by highways with empty space between them, there is a lot to do but learning curve is quite steep - as this game is a complex economical simulator not just a sim with random numbers. Here economy is really working, and it depends from your actions.
So after bumpy start I really can recommend this game in its current state. There will be VR incoming and new patch (hopefully soon) so more reasons to buy it...
