3 hours of trying to figure out if I'm the titular Betrayer
The Basics: 16th century First person mystery/exploration
Previous Time Spent: none
Expectation of learning Curve: low
Why I bought this: I've read a decent number of reviews, and been told specifically to get into it by a close friend. Additionally, this seemed inspired by the lost Roanoke Colony, which seemed novel
First Impressions: Betrayer has a striking look achieved by the use of monochrome and red. It also is a great game to play with the headphones on, and just get blown away by the sensory experience. You definitely feel transported to a different place. Wind blows around, moving the trees, and terrifying apparitions attack. There's a sense of danger and a great mystery hook.

My 3 Hours with the Game:You begin shipwrecked on the shores of the new world, wandering to a colony that has clearly failed. As mentioned previously, the use of color is great, and there's a very real sense of being in another time and place. There's great use of sound, such as rushing wind, and the combat is tense, frightening, and novel. Betrayer didn't need to be a first person shooter in order to accomplish the atmospheric storytelling,  but the combat wasn't unwelcome either.
I hit some initial technical frustrations with the game, involving odd controls, but after a bit of internet digging, I was able to solve this. I appreciated the fact that in spite of being a game that leads you from waypoint to waypoint, I was able to actually get stuck in the plot early on, requiring some more sleuthing, and use of the listening power (which I had previously ignored). I spent most of my time seeking out clues, following them, talking to ghosts and uncovering tantalizing clues to the doom that fell over this colony, which seemed to have multiple factors, from the geopolitical to the fantastical.
My highlight:The first time I rang the bell in the first fort, and found myself in the night world, able to speak to ghosts and presented with more fantastical enemies. The sounds were effective and quite frightening, and the realization that I could go through and deal with the corruption that had begun blighting the land was heartening. (Plus, who doesn't want to fight skeletons under black skies with a slowly reloading musket?)
My verdict: I'd strongly recommend giving this a shot(but maybe on a steam sale). The atmosphere is great, and the sense of danger inherent in fighting well armed monsters with a bow, musket or other 17th century weapon feels very real. There's a great frantic sense to reloading a musket while being charged by a squad of Spanish Soldiers (who seem like revenants or ghouls). Additionally, the story is fairly interesting, however I did get a bit of a sense of repetition after hitting hour 3, as much of the gameplay involves searching for waypoints on the map, clearing them, learning clues and talking to ghosts before preceding.
-Jon

This is the first word game I've played on Steam, but surely it must rank among the better exponents. So much so that I'm going to have to avoid waxing lyrical in this review! I'll be talking like a pompous arts student next (disclaimer: I was one).
The trailers are spot on, and give a good idea of how Letter Quest looks and plays out. The story is essentially non-existent, but there are lots of levels to get your teeth stuck into and the UI is particularly clean and polished. The 3x5 grid works well, and there's relatively little extraneous information cluttering the screen. You don't need to have swallowed a dictionary at birth to proceed, either; I'm no literary savant, and I got on just fine. Some of the levels even have special conditions that limit you in certain ways, such as including monsters that only suffer damage from four-letter words.
The progression feels fairly natural, and this is where the RPG elements come to the fore. Each level (30 in all) has four 'stars' attached to it: one for beating the level, another that's a time trial, one special condition star and the final crystal star. The crystal stars are as hard as nails in comparison, so you'll need to inject some beef into your damage, armour and other stats before you can feasibly hope to complete them, regardless of how vast your vocabulary is. In this way, Letter Quest doesn't really hold your hand, and you create your own level of difficulty and balance depending on when you try to attain certain stars - both a good and bad thing, I suppose.
By and large, you're encouraged to go for the heftier words for gem bonuses and general damage, but it's far from necessary to channel Shakespeare in order to beat the story mode. The separate Endless Mode is more of the same, albeit with predetermined stats; the decision-making here revolves around which temporary items you buy from the merchant, and how lucky you get with certain monsters and letter combinations. Occasionally, you'll find yourself up the creek without a paddle in both modes - no shame in getting beaten and retrying. This game is tough, at times.
All in all, Letter Quest is a substantial game with a good dictionary, a cute and pleasing aesthetic and enough content and difficulty to keep you hooked for some time. I can see myself coming back to it, despite the repetitve music making me want to gouge my ears out at times. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go and look up the definition of 'loquacious'.

Bioshock 2 is the same, and I think better than Bioshock 1 in almost every way that matters.

TLDR: An enjoyable follow-up to the first game continues the story of Rapture with a new protagonist, a new conflicted (kind of) big boss and more gene splicing action. This time around you have some moral decision making to do, and your actions affect the game’s ending.
If you’ve played the first Bioshock game, you’ll remember that in the mid 1900’s the world’s top minds secretly worked together to build the underwater city of Rapture, and created what they thought was the ultimate utopia, free of government and religion. Instead they were ruled by the free market and meritocracy, so everyone makes money based on being good at something. In Bioshock 2, you learn that the pressures of this “perfect world” started to get to the citizens (especially the poor), and a psychiatrist was brought in to help people deal with the stresses of pure competition. Unfortunately, the psychiatrist Sofia Lamb had her own agenda, and saw the opportunity to create a true Utopia in Rapture through the use of Adam.
Adam is a genetic material that can be used to create “plasmids” for artificial evolution through gene splicing. It doesn’t just give people super powers though, apparently it can be used to transfer the memories of the users to certain prepared users (Little Sisters). Little Sisters are orphaned girls who have been kidnapped and turned into walking “Adam factories” who can later be harvested for their gooey Adam. The Little Sisters are guarded by Big Daddies, brainwashed people in armored diving gear who are psychically linked to their Little Sisters and guard them from any threat.
In Bioshock 2, you play a Big Daddy, though the gameplay is nearly the same as in the first game (where you were a human). It’s still a First Person Shooter and the weapons are mostly the same as well. There’s been a refinement to the plasmid system where you’re basically dual wielding now (plasmid in one hand and gun in the other). In the first game you had to switch between gun and plasmid. A big change is that because you’re a Big Daddy, you do a bunch of mini escort missions where you guard Little Sisters as they gather their Adam. Just like in the first game, you have a huge variety of weapon ammo types and plasmid types to help you survive, though you might notice that the game is more difficult this time around. It seems like you take more damage in Bioshock 2 than in the first game.
Pros:
+The story is good though it’s a little difficult to figure out what the deal is with Sofia Lamb. How did she turn into such a ♥♥♥♥♥?
+The game takes what is good about the first game and adds to it. I kind of liked the hacking mini game in the first game better though. There are more weapon types, more plasmids, and more enemies. The mini bosses in the first game were the Big Daddies, who are back, but now you have the Big Sisters to deal with as well and they’re twice as powerful.
+The game has 6 different endings depending on the moral choices you make throughout, but they’re actually very close to each other. I’ve probably only seen 3 of them because I usually play games as a “good person” and had to go out of my way to make evil decisions.
Cons:
-People have told me that Bioshock 2 is the weakest in the Bioshock series and I can see their point. There really isn’t much more innovation and it’s kind of like a continuation of the first game in terms of technical improvement. Like with Saints Row 4, where people said it was almost a really long DLC for Saints Row 3.
-There were some technical issues for me related to graphics. It seems to be a common occurrence based on what I found when googling for solutions. To keep the game from crashing, I had to change the display to Direct X 9.
Overall, if you liked the first Bioshock, you’ll probably like Bioshock 2, though maybe not quite as much. The game takes about 10 hours to beat and is more than worth your time.  8.5/10

You are stuck in a 2D plane in a 3d space, however. This isn't a true 3 dimensional exploration game, and I respect the developer's decision to do this. This is a great game to stream to your TV, sit on the couch with a controller, and drink some brews while cruising at light speed through the galaxy.

You are a pig named Mr. Bree. You've been through something terrible that you don't quite remember and all you want to do is get home to see your family. Thus, you begin your platforming adventure through the forest.
First, the good: The art style is very nice and the music is pretty good as well. Checkpoints are provided for most levels, so you can pass even the harder levels without too much difficulty. These can be turned off when you unlock hardcore mode. There are collectibles to find that unlock extra levels and the rest of the story. The level design is nice for the most part.
The bad: The game is riddled with bugs. The game crashes and freezes randomly, has poor controller support, and environments that blend together and make it hard to distinguish foreground and background. Wall jumping feels janky and the controls in general do not feel tight enough to be in a 'hardcore-style' platformer. There's also a mechanic where the time of day changes each time you die in a level. Some of the lighting schemes for certain times of day render traps and pitfalls nearly invisible, making levels that you are already having trouble with even harder simply because you can't see anything.
For $2.99, I didn't expect a lot from the game. It feels like there is a decent platformer hiding somewhere beneath the bugs and issues and I think I could recommend it if some things got fixed. As it is, I'd rather just play Super Meat Boy.

This was one of many games I bought during a Steam summer sale and can I say how glad I am that I did? The Dream Machine has easily become one of my favorite games, if only because of the obvious love and care the creators have given in crafting it. And it really is craftmanship! It's a beautiful game, with every little detail telling a story. It really stands out from your run of the mill point and click game. I was hooked immediately by the unique and intriguing visuals, and the fascinating story and puzzles kept me playing. The music and sound design are top notch, immersing you in whichever dream world you're occupying. It's challenging, but not impossibly so, quirky with a delicious dark undertone, funny in all the right places, and full of things you never knew you wanted to see. From a ship poulated by a dozen versions of you to an apartment where time and space are determined by the photographs you find and rearrange within it, each new dream is like a whole new experience, with different and unique characters, new locations that are a feast for the eyes, and new puzzles and mechanics that keep that classic point n click gameplay feeling fresh and new. There's so much more I could rave about but I guess it's one of those things where I gotta say "you just HAVE to try it!" I just gotta find out how to give the developers more of my money since I got it on sale! Can't wait for Chapter 6!!

Reminiscent of Super Meat Boy in its ambience and brutal traps, this little platformer proves itself worthy of those who enjoy a short but fun challenge. This, coupled with an astonishing soundtrack, make this game a must for the genre-lovers considering its current price.
The only downside is the current lack of workshop content; it would be nice to see user-created levels in the near future to lengthen even more the game experience.
Note that at the time of writing this review, I've roughly completed about 1/3 of the game. In no way does my playtime reflect the actual duration of this game. Considering the levels get more and more complicated (NOTE: The difficulty curve in this game is pretty good), I assume it will last between 2:30 and 3:30 hours.
EDIT: I am about to finish this game, only about 10 levels left including a couple special levels, and still lots of achievements to earn. I'd say my estimation of a little more than 2:30h was kind of accurate. The difficulty in the final levels is still a bit challenging, though I find that I may struggle with a level but then complete the next one in just one go. However, the game is still as fresh as when I bought it, and I am enjoying every second of frustration and satisfaction of it.
I regret the $60 impulse purchase to this day.

This game starts out alot like other games in the genre, learn to walk, jump and run to name a few. The levels become ever more devious as you progress but are never hard for the wrong reasons. The music is very good and sets the mood nicely for each set of levels. The scenery and backgrounds for each level are beautifully done and are pleasant on the eyes. The hero moves at a slow pace to begin with but before long you are running for your life from traps and ducking and dodging with the best of em. In each level a collectible can be found and in alot of cases, a new power is needed so collecting it must be done later. All in all the game offers value at and above the current price. It has its charm and challenges and will have you cursing every god you can name at times but as always, overcoming the challenges is its own reward. For what the game is and offers, it executes perfectly in every aspect and any platformer fan out there should rise to the challenge.

Bought this game a few months back then on a sale once. The devs really listen to the community on the subreddit and it continually improves each update, whether it be graphic wise or gameplay wise. It was a good move for them to finally bring it out as a F2P game. The game used to get stagnant at times, especially in ranked games where you pretty much pair up/fight against the same people over and over depending on your server and/or timezone due to the lack of players, but that will probably change now.
The game has a lot of champions for each kind of playstyle. Definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants some action, especially when it comes to clutch 1v1 situations. It really gets your adrenaline pumping through you.
Also, as a side note. Support champions in this game aren't just healers that stay behind the attacking champion. They actually are one of the strongest champions in the game that can easily go toe-to-toe with an offensive champion. Poloma for example can heal a ton while dishing out damage at the same time. Perfect for those juicy 1v1 situations. I highly encourage people to try them out. Like I said above, there are different champions that offer different playstyles, so try to find the one for you.

Its different then the past X-games. But I like X-Rebirth as much as the X3 series.  Its true, you can "fly" only one ship but you can have a massive fleet from small rangers, medium freighers, till large and extra large capital ships (those capital ships can be longer then 1000m).  With a simple mod - capital ship bridge - can you land your skunk on a the capital ship you own and give the captain orders.  I like to play this way ==> 90% of my playtime is standing around on the bridge from my main capital ship from my fleet, ordering personnel around, remote managing my trade empire, remote managing everything to be hounest, while in the meantime the captital ship i'm on is flying around in the universe.  When the Capital ship i'm on ill run to my skunk so that i can enter battle together with my capital ship.
Its true, you don't fly the ship yourself anymore, but i still feel completely in command when ill stand around on my capital ship, givinfg orders to the captain, defence officers, engineers..
On top of that, you can build space station sthat are km's and km's long, You can be a trader, pirate, etc.. You can be and do whatever you want.  Space is gorgeous, and everytime you think you start to master the game a whole new lot of possibilities come clear to you and a whole new segment from the game opens up.
While the game is easyer to learn then its predecessor it still can have a very steep learning curve for people new to the Space-X4-genre.

I've never had this much fun looking for underpants before, and that's something I do every day. I don't normally have to topple ruins or cleave mountains or send boulders rocketing into space to find them though, so that's something. Really the accomplishment of Tiny and Big is taking a simple set of mechanics, and not only crafting an entertaining journey to use them on, but giving you all kinds of chaos you can cause with them. It's a game that knows it's fun, wants you to enjoy it to the fullest, and does a really good job of letting you do just that.
The oddly monochromatic Tiny is on the trail of an heirloom of his grandpa's, taken by the dastardly and equally monochromatic Big. His quest leads him to a mysterious desert full of ruins that very quickly take on a life of their own. As he hunts Big and his treasure, the hidden history of the world begins to emerge from the sands, and the adventure becomes a battle against a primal and terrifying force of nature. And yes, the heirloom in question is a pair of grungy underpants.
The entire game is steeped in this sort of punky, irreverant humor, starting with the art style. The thick lines, limited color palette, and simple faces evoke the underground comics of yesteryear, complete with impact text that pops up 60s Batman style whenever something dramatic happens. And once you start exploring the towering and mysterious ruins, you'll feel like you're skipping across the pages of Krazy Kat or SCUD's bizarre wastelands. It's a fantastic look, supported by some goofy dialogue and an impressively jazzy soundtrack that can be expanded by finding hidden cassette tapes.
What works even better than the aesthetic, though, is the puzzling. You have no weapons and no fancy abilities to move around, just three tools that let you wreak havoc on the environment. The first is a hook that lets you grab an object and drag it around, and we're not just talking little barrels or whatever. You can topple towering pillars and pull enormous gates open with this thing, despite Tiny's name-appropriate stature. You also have a rocket you can stick to things to help scoot them across the ground, or more often send them careening into the horizon.
But the real star of the show is your laser, which lets you slice anything in the world. As long as you're close enough and your beam can reach all the way across whatever it is, you can chop it up. Pillars, walkways, bridges, walls, cliffs, buildings, you name it, you can destroy it. This is used to fantastic effect in challenging you to cross gaps, descend shafts, or scale sheer walls. But there are plenty of other places you can get to by cleverly carving stones into your own bridges or ramps, and the wide open levels encourage exploration with collectible stones, the aforementioned cassettes, secret minigames, and special scenes that expand the backstory of the world.
Once I had a feel for the game I was unstoppable, slicing pillars into bridges and hacking cliffs into scalable ramps wherever I went. But I would still stop every few minutes to carve up a statue or a wall, just because I could. The tools in Tiny and Big are just so much fun to play with, you could easily spend 20 minutes just ruining a level by chopping it to bits and giggling the whole time. It even understands this, and gives you achievements for going bonkers with your powers and destorying artifacts and landmarks. It's silly and entertaining all the way through, not just in the way it's presented but in how it's designed.
Reclaiming your underpants won't take much more than two hours, but those are some of the best two hours to be had in a third-person puzzler. Plus there are secrets and par scores to challenge for each of the game's six levels, along with over fifty achievements for doing all sorts of funky things. Considering how unique it is in look, feel, and gameplay, there's really no excuse for missing out on this one. Tiny and Big is an absolute gem, the kind of funky, one-of-a-kind gem that more games should aspire to be.

Played a few times now.
I have played civ 3, 4 and revolution but missed out 5. So playing this version was quite a shock at first as there are a lot of features adapted from civ 5.
Once I got my head round that I really started to enjoy the game. It makes a real good change from the usual theme of its previous series (how many times can the same game be released with the same content? If the next civ wasn't this one you could name 90% of the building techs and units before you even play it!) by giving an entire new lease of life.
Main Pros are the new Tech web means you can research any line you wish, alowing you to adapt to the flow of the game rather then researching everything. In fact I havent played any games that let me come close to researching everything yet as there is so much!
There are also different ways to win the game which you can adapt to depending on how your game is going. This adds a lot of variety to the game.
Unit upgrading now no longer requires tech but instead requires afinity. You get the affinity from techs or decisions you make but is typically suited to your play style.
Most noticable change (other then the fact your on an alien world and not earth) is that every new building you construct (only the first time) you get a decision a few turns later which gives the building a boost (i.e you could make the building add +1 food or +1 culture) which would apply to all citys that build it.
Ever thought they got the leader specials wrong? In this one you select everything your self. the leaders you play as still have 1 unique bonus each which all seem balanced although I havent tried them all yet. But you get to also choose your landing ship (mainly map revealing bonuses) and also your cargo (your cargo gives an initial bonus when you start the game and even includes starting the game with a worker) All of which really allows you to suit your bonuses around your style of play and not the other way around.
Now for the Cons although I haven't found many atall.
There are no unique units to the leaders anymore however there are units that require high levels of affinity to unlock which usually results in only following one line of unique units.
No more great persons although there are still great generals and some ways to get free techs but no more instabuilds.
Initialy takes some getting used to as some civ veterans might find their old tactics flop here.
All in all I love this game and although I like to play them all this is my new favorite and I hope you enjoy it too! 10/10

For example, if you were at Blackwater and dressed as a security guard, you would get spotted nearly instantly by other security guards, but if dressed like a plumber, no one would notice you. Disguises seemed to not even work most of the time as you were spotted as soon as you walked around a corner.  The absolute most frustrating part for me was the fact that the game FORCES you to kill certain non-target characters to proceed, but then penalizes you for killing non-target characters. So I used to give this a negative review for various game-mechanic issues, but now I give a positive review because of some new features. Making your own characters was a great step.
Pros:
-Make your own characters: You can now create your own character to play in the game. Makes it much more fun in my opinion.
-Graphics. TWOM has a very particular and atmospheric art style. The greyed out, sketchbook effects and general grim overcast gives an excellent feel for a place that is truly a desperate and dangerous situation to be caught in.
-Choices. The choices are everything in this game. Being a bad person, by killing and stealing, will make it easier to survive. It all depends how many other people you're willing to sacrifice for your own survival. But when one of your favourite characters is dying of illness, or needs bandages, or is literally starving to death, you might be surprised how far you'll go to save them.
-Environments. I really like how the game has the areas you scavenge. All of them keep up wonderfully with creating an immersive, grim and desperate atmosphere.
Cons:
-Luck. A lot of the time, survival can turn on pure luck alone. Getting a bad raid in your refuge, or too many people getting sick/wounded, and you can get crippled and everyone die a slow and painful death.
-Guns. I think they should review guns. If I walk up to someone and shoot him with a shotgun, he really shouldn't be able to be up and still fighting. I'd support one-hit kills with rifles and shotguns.
-Scav. Only one person can scavenge per night. At the beginning it makes sense, but once you have four characters, it starts to feel gamey because the only reason only 1 person goes out is because the game won't let you send more.
Overall, a great and immersive game, with wonderful visual design. You won't find many other games like this around, which in itself, is also quite appealing.

Agent 47 doesn't begin Hitman: Absolution with amnesia, but the six years that have passed since we last took control of him in Blood Money do seem to have dulled his creators' recollections of what made him so popular in the first place. Hitman: Absolution is a slick, responsive and mechanically confident game - and on occasions it's one of the most satisfying stealth games in a year that already includes Dishonored - but a range of compromises to Hitman tradition mean it's still going to rub some people up the wrong way.
Hitman is a simple concept: someone gives you a target, or targets, and you take them out. The genius of it is the way the designers let you do that. It's not just about deciding whether to sneak past people or get into a gun-fight - it's about slowly tracking the movements of people through large environments and observing the ways you can manipulate them and their surroundings to bring about their downfall. Perhaps you place explosives where you know they'll wander, or maybe you arrive just in time to nudge them over a railing into a deserted alleyway, and often you do all this dressed in borrowed clothes that conceal your identity from all but the most detailed investigation.
Hitman: Absolution includes all of that stuff, and on the higher difficulty levels it leaves you to figure a lot of it out on your own. You sneak or roam in disguise through police stations, courthouses, dilapidated mob-run hotels, maize-covered farmland, factories and science labs, teasing out details about your target from overheard conversations and useful objects left on shelves or in poorly guarded rooms. Then you formulate a plan and try to pull it off. If you're new to the series or just a bit rusty, you might begin by simply trying to find a few moments alone with your target and your trusty fibre wire, but before long you're on the lookout for more elaborate and creative executions: self-immolation, industrial accidents, tainted drugs and the sudden, unexpected failure of previously reliable overhead rigging.
Feeling your way into these unusual scenarios is surprisingly comfortable thanks to robust controls and clear rules about how things work. Movement and cover systems match the fluent standards of modern third-person games, crowds and guards only find you suspicious if you're behaving that way, disguises don't work on people wearing the same get-up, and crates, cupboards and dumpsters can hold two bodies, one of which can be you. A new Instinct system (heavily regulated on higher difficulties) allows Agent 47 to see the movements of NPCs and targets through walls and highlights interactive objects in the environment, while allowing you to briefly evade detection by people who would otherwise see through your disguise. It refills when you perform actions that the game's scoring system considers admirable, like hiding bodies from sight.
The scoring system - how nice to play a big game in 2012 that gives you a score at the end of each level, by the way - encourages creative solutions and sort of discourages extracurricular murder, although it's a mischievous companion, and many of the optional objectives in your notebook hint at ways you might consider dispatching your target's entourage as well as him or her. It's impossible to complete all these tasks in a single play-through - you can't exactly wear every available disguise in a level and play through it only dressed in your agency suit, for example - and they can be ignored if you prefer to remain utterly undetected and only lay hands on your assigned victim.
There are plenty of times in Hitman: Absolution when all these systems come together in ghoulishly delicious harmony. Stalking through a cornfield dressed as a scarecrow, picking off machine-gun-toting goons and then stringing yourself up on a wooden frame to hide in plain sight; dropping a heavy piano lid on the head of a musically curious henchman without anyone noticing; distracting policemen by leaving a cash-filled safe open in a busted drug den; or turning the tools of several mad scientists' trade against them in gruesomely hilarious ways. Played as a kind of grimly amusing series of cautionary tales where you skulk through the shadows implementing the caution, Absolution is enormous fun.

Pros
+ The game is massive and from my understanding the systems are randomly generated, so you'll never hit the same systems on a different playthrough. It is probably not as large as other space-sims, however.
+ There's lots of things to do, which checks off most of the traditional space-sim tropes: Mining, Trading, Bounty Hunting to name a few as well as a good variety of side missions which cover your basic 'go to point A and blow stuff up' runs to things like 'Go to station B and run/break a blockade to deliver goods'. I've played for 30+ hours in a game which cost me a third of the amount a AAA game does.
+ The games events and economy, while basic, are a living thing. They'll play out whether you're there or not. If a station is hit by a crime wave, it will remain until someone goes and cleans it up, whether it's you or the AI militia. Trade convoys cross the system and deliver goods, which effects the prices you buy and sell for. If pirates (or you!) happen to cross paths with them on their trip the items will never get there, which may cause their stock to drop and their sell prices to rise.
+ The soundtrack is awesome and makes the game very reminiscent of Firefly. It fits the game incredibly well and makes battles against enemy cap-ships all the sweeter
+ Broadside combat is excellent, and remarkably fun. No longer do you just point at an enemy and click - your shields and armor are seperated in to quadrants and you constantly have to think about the best maneuvers to maximise damage while protecting your vulnerable sides. You can even direct-control the turrets on your ship, as well as deploying flak, EMP's, Mines or missiles.
+ Good variety of ships and weapons. Yeah, they're all cap-ships but that's the name of the game. You're not just some no-name rookie making your name running your fighter from a carrier. You captain corvettes, frigates, destroyers, cruisers and even dreadnaughts fitted out with machine guns, missile launchers, pulse lasers, beam lasers, flak cannons and your beastly broadside weapons.
+ In almost every regard the game is top-notch: the aesthetics are excellent, the controls are excellent, the sound design is immersive, the world is immense and the gameplay is, most importantly, fun.
+ The best custom soundtrack integration I've seen in a recent game, you get to pick which tracks play in combat, stations, while cruising... hell - there's even an option to mix your tracks with the original soundtrack.
+ Piracy pays in this game - one of my favourite pass-times in this game is responding to merchant distress calls with a few tons of high-price cargo in my posession. Save the merchants, sell the cargo to them at a premium and then threaten them to hand back what I just sold them for free. It's a brilliant way of making some extra cash.
+ 1:1 sell ratio on your equipment and ships, so there's never any risk of being stuck with expensive gear you decide you don't like.
Cons:
- Missions can become a little repetative after a while, although if you begin to feel like this you'll realise it's because you've played the game for a decent stretch of time
- Travelling across a system can take a little too long sometimes, even with engine upgrades I'm never feeling like I'm moving fast enough while in warp
- Difficulty can spike without warning, usually when you equip your first bit of next-tier tech: there's a reason even the bartenders tell you to upgrade shields and armor before weapons.
- Voice acting is 'just' OK. The npc voice pool is shallow and some of the emotional delivery is pretty bland.
- The dialogue options really don't serve a purpose. it boils down to 'Option one to be a coward and drop your cargo', 'Option two to politely refuse and lose a faction point', 'Option three to be a badass renegade, 'Option 4 to be a badass renegade and ♥♥♥♥ off this faction' all of which provoke the most pitiful and monotonous responses. If you want to be a badass renegade, be prepared to hear 'I hope you like the cold, Cutter' without an ounce of anger or fear behind it 9/10 times.
- This game could have really benefited from a sort of 'infamy system', which, depending on your net-worth, loadout, faction standing or how much ♥♥♥ you tend to kick provided a little more of an emotional response from your attackers. No matter what you do, say or how many of those pirate jack-offs you just disintegrated, they will always give you the same responses - 'drop your cargo or die', 'no? ok, now you will die'. They even say it if you've literally just wiped out all their health and their ship is about to explode.
- While the soundtrack is awesome, it's short and the tracks cycle every time the situation changes - it's rare you'll hear one all the way through. I don't think there's more than 10 tracks in total and some of those are instrumental versions of the others. It begins to grate a little around the 9 hour mark - thank god for custom soundtracks. The 'Sons of the North' and 'These Savage Lands' Albums by The Black Spiders fit the game incredibly well IMO and have saved me from getting sick of the original soundtrack.
- Once you finish the story, get yourself a dreadnaught and kit it out with 6th Tier tech there isn't really any motivation to continue. The story missions aren't particularly exciting enough to play again so your only goal after that really is to make money that you can't spend on anything. It's unlikely you'll feel motivated enough to commit to a second playthrough due to the 1:1 sell ratio on your equipment. If you have a Blackgate with Mark 6 Beam Turrets, Beam Broadsides and Defense tech then you can literally sell it 1:1, which lets you switch to any other ship you may have missed. The only way to screw yourself out of money late-game is either by trading like an idiot, fighting like an idiot or recruiting mercs who are idiots.
Unsure:
+/- Yes, it's been said countless times: there's no Y axis of movement. However with broadside combat I believe the game is better off for it. This game would be frustrating levels of fiddly control-wise trying to move up and down, while trying to maintain target lock with your broadsides/control lateral movement while aiming your turrets, while trying to line up your secondaries and maneuvre your ship to keep your target on your strongest side.
Summary:
There's a lot more they could have done with the "Negotiate" part of the game (they put that part of the tagline in quotations? has no-one else mentioned that?), it can get a little bit same-y and repetative after long stretches and it could do with more ship and loadout options but in the end the game is pure space-cowbow fun. My interest only began to waver at the end when I suddenly realised I had enough money to cover buying everything in the game and completing station missions, trading, mining or pirating were not only no-longer a challenge in my mile-long Dreadnaught, but also no longer pushing me towards any kind of goal. This is, however, over 30 hours in while most AAA titles struggle to hold my interest for more than 8 hours.
If you love Firefly and the space-sim genre but are put off by the overly-complex nature of some of them then give this a shot, it's the one you've been waiting for. Even if games like X and ED are your bread and butter, buy this as a sort 'tune out and have mindless fun' kind of game to sink a few hours in to. Despite it's lackluster story and character performances as well as a few missed opportunities in gameplay design, primarily it's a game where you're expected to have fun blowing ♥♥♥♥ up and besides Jahovas Witnesses, who doesn't like that?

Grid 2 is a blast to play, at first. That being said it is an outdated game that fails to live up to the hype or pedigree of its predecessor. While the controls are extremely tight (xbox360 controller) the game never truly finds its identity. With a familiar focus on youtube, much like the recent entries in the DiRT series, and a strong single player story experience, the first few hours are a gem. However, soon the driving becomes stale, pushed by the idea that every turn can be expertly drifted. Drifting is not easy and requires a delicate balance of countersteer and throttle managment, but once you've got it down it becomes second nature. You will be drifting alot. You will also be learning many of the turns very quickly. Tracks are built on just a few maps, with a few variations of the lap. There is notably a new race type where the lap changes on the fly. Its a really cool concept, but the variation is so low, after one of these races, you'll generally know map very well. Grid 2 also lacks any difficulty settings other than AI. The enviornments are gorgeous, however the cars look about as good as Need for Speed Shift 2.  The car list is populated by stellar choices, but it is very small considering what Gran Turismo and Forza have been offering for years. I also found myself unable to attach myself to any of the vehicles. Being unable to customize any performance acspects of the cars, I ended up using a car for a short time then moving on, never to return to my previous choice. While Grid 2 definitely finds itself in the middle of the sim/arcade racer spectrum, that is also my biggest gripe. Drifting is fun, but it is not the end all of racing. Maybe I've been spoiled by other racing games in the past, but I've come to expect more. More cars, more customization, more tracks, more difficulty settings, more fun. The ironic part is that the "story" is brilliantly done, and truly gives the player a sense of progression, which is very new to the racing genre.  Also worth noting is the inclusion of split screen, which is almost unheard of in pc gaming now.

I am surprised by how high quality of a game this is, (you still might be able to get it on sale for $4 at groupees)
-Feels like a fully finished product which is hard to find these days
-Has a surpsingly decent campaign
-Good optimization (i was averaging 40fps on ultra but i could have sworn i was at 60 the entire time. 40fps somehow feels like 60 and there is no stuttering or microstuttering AT ALL which really surprised me for a unity engine game)
-Crazy attention to detail, every little chain on every chain link gate swings when you rub up against it, every single light can get blown out, every single board making up entire houses gets torn to shreds with thousands of bits flying everywhere and zero performance slowdown, incredible looking grass and trees blowing in the wind, not to mention the few gorgeous areas where explosions/fires show their surrounds in color.
-Awesome ballistics, bullets fly through/destroy various wood walls based on caliber used and its extremely satisfying chopping houses with people inside to shreds
-Most diverse execution animations i have ever seen. I have seen what feels like hundreds of them while still seeing new ones every kill. I am shocked by what this guy does to people. The executions are so realistic and match up perfectly to the villains care-less attitude. He wastes no time trying to impress the audience with his murders he just psychotically grabs them instantly and stabs them 3 times in the side of the waist without skipping a beat
-Gorgeous maps, every one is more breathtaking than the last. And they are all different changes of scenery. The maps are actually quite huge and boundaries have never been an issue.
-Maps are interactive, i was impressed to see the floating boats on the docks filling up with water and sinking after shooting them, i was surprised i was able to change a trains railway path and make it crash into/explode an entire building, i wasn't expecting a small lot with people smoking meth on cardboard boxes with an achievment attatched (will not spoil it) But other than that there are many sidemissions that begin as a result of your actions in different areas of the map.
-Vehicles. I think the vehicles driving/controls are as perfect as they possibly could for a game like this. I read another reviewer saying the cars were like ice bricks but i find that completely untrue, they ride smooth, turn nicely, and are seemingly bug-free
-You can do a sprinting spin kick
CONS
-Unrealistic and stupid AI. They just run stupidly right into gunfire, sometimes they even run directly at you. It would be cool to see a couple wanna-be hero civlians who try and tackle you or something. Otherwise this game is amazing

I was expecting to like this game 'cause I always like word games, but I certainly wasn't expecting to spend this much time with it.  For the purposes of this review, I've got 51.7 hours in this specific game so I'll use that as the basis for the official price-per-hour calculation; that said, however, it's worth nothing that I also have 68.9 hours in the original (non-remastered) version.  So if you want to think about it that way, that's 120.6 hours with a per-hour cost of just under seven cents.  Soo, I think that part pretty much speaks for itself.  Now, bear in mind that in that 120 hours I played through the campaign four and a half times (twice on normal, twice on expert, and a fifth time on expert going for an epic almost-no-upgrades run before I got stymied halfway through by what I consider to be questionable boss battles, but more on that in a bit); most people won't be interested in playing that much but I'd still say it's well worth the money if you're into the genre.
As far as the core gameplay itself, there's not much I can tell you that the videos on the store page don't cover.  The visuals are fun, the game is controllable neeeeearly entirely from the keyboard (there are a couple of menu situations that require the mouse) and the game is able to keep up with my (very fast) typing speed.  I'm not really a fan of complex RPG-style upgrade systems, but Letter Quest has just enough options to keep things interesting without making it feel like work to manage it all.
The enemies' abilities are interesting and varied; they do different things to the tiles, which make some of them penalize you for using them (think "poisoned tiles", and you get the idea).  This forces (well, incentivizes) you to be more creative with the words you make, since you kinda have to really make it worthwhile if you use one of those other tiles.
All in all I think it's a great game (obviously...did I mention 120.6 hours?) but I do have a couple of negatives I gotta get off my chest.  The first is the occasional -- hmm, what's the right word here -- "counter-productive" battle restriction.  Each level has a "special conditions" mode, and usually they're fun, but sometimes they directly contradict the core skill of the game, to the point where you just have to rely on grinding for stats to pass them.  For instance, when a monster says "takes such-and-such more damage with words that have such-and-such characteristics", what that basically means is "takes normal damage from those words, and the tiniest worthless sliver of damage from anything else".  Which is fine, except when the restriction is something like "you have to use three-letter words".  It's literally irrelevant at that point how good you are, you are not getting through that level without tons of health/armor/damage upgrades.  Not a huge deal unless you're going for an Iron Man playthrough like I was, 'cause you'll eventually get those upgrades, but there you go.  The other thing, though, is the ridiculous replacement letter selection algorithm.  If you're curious, look through
and you can see some of the more egregious examples (fair warning, a couple of them have words that are a little bit racy, but nothing I'd consider clearly NSFW); trust me, though, you
be getting hung out to dry by the letter picker.  Maybe it's just to make the "shuffle letters" function relevant?
Having said all that, none of that should get in the way of your enjoying the game; if you're not specifically going for extra challenge by not using potions or upgrading your stats, then when you can't make a word because 14 of your 15 letters are vowels, just hit the shuffle key.  If you're low on health and you might die because you can't attack (since you're shuffling), drink a potion.  Problem solved.  :) All in all, LQ is a great game and you should definitely pick it up if you like what's in the store page videos.
I'll admit some of these "if you like this..." recommendations are a bit of a stretch, but it depends on which part of the Letter Quest gameplay you like.  If you like the puzzle-meets-RPG part regardless of whether it's words or not, 10,000,000 and Tomb Of Tyrants will fit right in.  If you're not looking to type for the entire gameplay, Epistory might be your thing.  Action gamers will probably like The Typing of the Dead.  For a pure word game experience, Lexica is a good bet.  Of all the recommendations, the closest to Letter Quest is definitely Words For Evil.  Including Steno Arcade is definitely a cheese move, since it's not typing per se, but when else am I ever going to be able to crowbar that in...a segueway from Rocksmith?  :)

Dead Rising 2 is a pretty fun game, I had a lot of fun times with it on Xbox 360 back in 2011-2012 so it's quite nostalgic. The story is your average run of the mill "being the hero and stopping the bad guy" story with a few plot twists here and there later on in the story.
The time limit plays a huge role in Dead Rising 2 like the original Dead Rising. If you don't make it from point A to point B in a certain amount of time then you'll lose the chance to save certain survivors or if you're busy saving certain survivors you may miss the deadline for one of the main story missions thus giving you a game over.
(Though you are still able to free roam saving survivors and fighting psychopath bosses until the ingame three days are up which results in one of the many bad endings.)
So if you want the true ending you have to reach certain deadlines and save the majority of survivors all scattered throughout Fortune City.
Two of the main quarrells I've always had with Dead Rising 2 is:
1. The speed of the protagonist - Unless you save dozens of survivors and level up you'll be walking extremely slow which makes the pacing of the game incredibly slow too.
2. TIR Online - It's seriously impossible or extremely rare to find anyone play TIR Online these days on Dead Rising 2. So trying to gather money or trying to unlock some of the TIR unlockable clothing is pretty much impossible nowadays unless you have three other pals you can bring along.
So I'd recommend Dead Rising 2 but if you're not a patient person you'll find it difficult playing for the first couple of hours until you level up a ton. Other than that the psychopaths are memorable for the most part, combo weapons are pretty sweet and you'll have a laugh or two with certain features within the game especially with friends in co-op story mode.

What more is there to say about Bioshock at this point? It's truly magnificent, and I'm glad I followed the advice of other gamers to play it. I've played both the original and remastered versions of the first game; and though I don't see a drastic visual difference, I appreciate the fact that they gave the remastered version to those who had the originals in their library. Bioshock's story surprised me, as I've never been so mesmerized by a video game before. It's quite obvious it's a masterpiece, as it was released in 2007 and still manages to be rerenowned today.
If I had to give any critique, it would be for 2K to continue working on the Remastered version by starting with the audio, which can be rather infuriating at times since it has balancing issues. Very small aspects of the gameplay can sometimes become frustrating as well, such as weapons not reloading properly, AI not responding, etc. Though small, it impacts the gameplay and can leave a player in frustration, which takes away from the overall experience. I did my best to ignore such disappointing aspects of the game since I realize it was originally produced in 2007 and it was a free rework.
In the end, the story is so overwhelmingly good that I was able to look past the difficulties of playing on PC and enjoy the game. And I'm willing to say that the remastered version felt better even though I'm unable to give specific reasons why, it simply felt more fluid in some aspects. I'm extremely greatful to have been able to finally experience Bioshock, and can't wait to complete the next two!

Worth every penny and then some for any fan of letter games or achievement junkies. With so many word games out there, it's hard to find one that shines brighter than the rest, but Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey Remasted does so brilliantly.  The visuals are appealing, the music is nostalgic, and the drive to complete your goals is always there.  An "Endless" mode is there to satiate your letter crunching once you've completed the meat of the game and does invite additional challenges or competition between friends, if you're old enough to remember when high scores mattered.
It's certainly not without flaw and admittedly, the last several hours I logged were simply achievement grinding with little emotional investment. Disclaimer: I love this game, so while I am going to try and keep this review impartial, there's a very good chance that the application of rose-tinted glasses will still be involved.
To start off: If you're expecting a full-fledged space sim, this is not it.  I would liken it more to a naval battle game.  In space. With lasers.  FRICKIN' LASERS, man.
And it.  Is.  Fun.  Though it's not a super long game, it will still keep you entertained for quite some time.  I have about 56 hours on the books at the time of this review and I only just completed the game.  Keep in mind, though, that I took my time, did plenty of side missions, and have hunted down more pirate kings than you can shake a stick at.
The graphics are pretty good in my opinion.  Good textures, pretty explosions, fairly well-designed UI.  Nothing much more to say about them.
The sound though, or more specifically the soundtrack, is FREAKING AMAZING.  Honestly some of the best soundtrack music I have had the pleasure of listening to.  And even better?  They're all *.ogg files in the game directory so you can easily add them to your favorite flavor of music management software.  The music significantly enhances the game's atmosphere and gives it a nice Firefly-like vibe.
The controls do take a little while to get used to, and can still be a bit testy at times.  However, once you do get used to them, you'll realize that things are actually relatively easy to control.
I would say it's already worth the standard asking price, but if you can get it on sale you'd be silly not to pick it up.

Decided to try it out since it was on winter sale and because the reviews seem better in the 4.0 patch as well as the Home of Light DLC.  I played quite a bit of X2, X3, X3:TC, X3:AP and found that the prior games are pretty fun.  After almost 10 hours in this game -- I enjoyed really only the first hour (as just initialy learning how to fly and checking out the world was fun).   I kept playing after that first hour hoping that as I got further into the campaign that the game would get better.  But unfortunately the opposite was true, and it just kept getting worse.
The campaign missions started getting glitchy and didn't make much sense.  For example, you need to use AI ships to trade by giving them orders, but sometimes they will sit with an order in their queue but just not do anything.   After cancelling the orders and setting them again they might do what you asked them to do.  Campaign missions targets became silly, like deliver "X" of some item to a station.  Except, you can buy that item from that station, and then turn around and sell it right back to complete the mission.   Mission targets aren't explained "how" to accomplish something.  So if you don't already know how to play the game you will need to check online forums and what not to figure out how to do whatever the game asks you to do.
Overall the gamplay is really clunky, full of needless time-wasting, and very difficult to figure out how to do anything.   It seems like they wanted to streamline the gameplay to make it more accessible, but really they just made it more frustrating to play.  The previous games were pretty good, but this one just isn't worth it except for maybe the die-hard fans.  So even with the 4.0 patch, and the home of light DLC, I would not recommend a purchase if you are on the fence -- even if it's on sale.   It's too bad because the engine itself, the graphics, etc seem pretty good.

Rebel Galaxy is a great game that will entertain you for hours
Arcade-feel shooter with RPG elements. Locked on the XY plane, no Z axis for the main ships, though the fighters will fly over/under larger vessels.
> Linear main story arc works well enough to progress you along from one system to the next.
> Side missions offer various mission types: bounty hunter, escort, delivery/trading, mining, mercenary work, etc. These serve to break the main story line up.
> Free to explore the sandbox at any time. This will be hemmed in by the difficulty of the ships you'll encounter and flying around with no purpose will tire after awhile.
Ship controls feel very polished which leads to satisfying combat.
> Fighting, trading, mining. All elments are present and each could use additional varying levels of development to flesh out the components further.
> Weapon systems vary and all have a unique feel, very well done. The sound fx are visceral and add to the combat a great deal.
What I would like to see in future:
Flesh out the faction system.
Increase interactions possible. A few hours in and all interactions become very predictable and few in number.
Something needs to be added to make me feel like I care/belong to a particular system/faction.
If its possible, a persistent world would go a long way to adding longevity. Base control switching hands with visual indicators, along with economic and military impact.
Unique-named npcs that remain in game until destroyed that remember player interactions.
Increase interactions with a wingman. Allow upgrades to their ship. Create wingman storylines with more missions unlocking as you increase your standing with them.
Introduce a galaxy threatening faction (randomly generated?) that will attempt to control one system after another, but can actually be defeated, allowing old wounds/squabbles to open back up between previously warring factions.
More wishful ideas:
Build your own station, recruit people to work/live there.

Homefront has really nice graphics, and an entertaining storyline, following the tradition of the Red Dawn movies, and, I'm assuming, based on the Homefront movie. When reading about the game I thought this story line should have a lot of possibilites for great FPS action.
This game frequently uses the can't-retreat-tons-of-enemies scenario.  This forces a panicked death-match type of play at some point in most of the levels.  Additionally the game forces even more death-match style of kamakaze engagement by sometimes having a timed element.
For example, at one point you are trapped in a fairly small area with limited cover and have to protect a wheeled-drone type of tank from RPGs, while being shot at by the entire Korean army.  Unless you kill enough of  the RPG-shooters the tank is destroyed, forcing a restart of the level.  There is no option but to run-and-gun, suffering a lot of damage from  the Korean army, while trying to get enough of the RPGs to pass the level.
If you like the deathmatch style of playing against tons of bots, then you may like Homefront.  For me, frequently being forced into this style of play is one of the elements that end up being frustrating, rather than fun.  To make it worse, during these frantic engagements, one of your team-mates continues to repeat some instruction, maybe as a "hint"?  For example in the RPG scenario, he will repeat, over and over, "get the RPG in the third floor window", or "...on the rooftop".  This extremely loud repetition becomes so irritating, that I played the last couple of tries with the sound muted.
Following are some other game-play related issues:
The character control seems very sluggish, compared to other shooters-- almost like playing in slightly slow motion, while the rest of the game is normal speed.
Jumping up from a crouch is about half the speed of the enemies who jump from  behind cover to shoot.  This is especially frustrating, as there is no leaning implemented in the game.  So you have to jump up from behind cover in slow motion, getting shot a couple of times before you are even up.
You can only jump the equivalent of about a foot off the ground. Even low obstacles force going around.
Sprinting is a lot slower than the AI team-mates-- they always pull ahead, even though you are supposed to follow them.
This character motion problem is a little subtle, but very noticible after just playing other shooters with much better character control.  At first I thought maybe something was wrong on my machine, until I watched a playthrough of a level I just completed on YouTube.  Same thing-- slightly slow-motion, compared with the rest of the game, ememies, team-mates, and etc.
Not enough ammo, forcing switching guns frequentore ly with fallen enemies.  This is also very "death-match'ish" and lessens the realism, as the last thing a real soldier wants on the battlefield is to pick up and use an unfamiliar weapon.  To make it worse, the guns of fallen enemies dissappear pretty quickly.
I finally gave up on the game during a follow-me type of sequence.  You are supposed to "sneak" through this survivalist camp in broad daylight while "insane survivalists" are walking all around.  The game hint says to follow this team-mate and stay low.  After about four times of literally following so close we were touching, I gave up.
The scenario is so-- well, dumb.  Broad daylight? no cover? enemies all around? Even touching the "leader" still resulted in being seen in a couple of minutes.  This was just too arbitrary, and anti-immersive. It pulled me right out of the game.
Over all the experience for me was more frustration than fun.  With so many other games to try, I'm done with this one for now .
I'm just really glad I got Homefront on a weekend sale.

This is a pretty good space RPG. In addition to the main campaign quest, you pretty much go around the galaxy accepting different bounties so that you can upgrade your ship and complete the harder quests in the campaign. Almost all the bounties are combat-type bounties.
You can also acquire money through trade on the commodities market, but it can be very time-consuming. The key to commodities trading is finding out what outposts will pay the highest for various products. For instance, a scientific oytposts will pay higher for intellectual property and tech stuff, but a rogue or outlaw outposts will pay more for illicit drugs and whatnot. You can also gain trading info by reading news boards and speaking to bartenders. Traveling between space stations and various parts of the galaxy can be boring. It can take several minutes to travel between points on opposite sides of the galaxy.
The graphics are nice and the music is awesome, but it gets a little monotonous after awhile since it plays constantly on a loop throughout the entire game.
The combat is interesting. It is "naval-style" combat, which means your primary guns fire from the side. This imposes a significant learning curve to combat since you have to fight sideways, which makes it harder to see incoming missiles. There are secondary weapons that you can switch to that don't require sideways combat, but then you have to constantly adjust your ship angle if you switch weapons a lot. It is challenging but rewarding when you finally get it all down.

Not all games have nor even need a storyline, and this shouldn't have to be the exception just because all you do is kill people and blow crap up around town. I actually can see where even the developers come from with their say that they don't want to justify The Antagonist or player's actions by including a storyline, or even a background. In my case, I appreciate having only one sentence of a storyline. From my perspective, if I am playing as a character who doesn't mean to commit wrongdoing, then I won't or will only do so if required on missions. In this, however, I feel I don't have to worry about being 'the good guy'.
As for the latter greatnesses, I shall begin with the sound, being what really adds to the tone of the game. The deep insane voice of The Antagonist, the screams and cries of those running away, the 'Human Shields' shouting at you, with the plus of the eerie, atmospheric background music ... are all great additions to what makes the crusade feel realistic, though kind of funny at times, thanks to the one-liners of dialogue. In Survival Mode, everything but The Antagonist's voice, and in my experience, just the Metal music as the background, pumps up my energy with spraying through the waves of people.
(Then, there's the heftiness upon my system. Originally, I did have troubles just starting this up, but usually these crashes happened with my screen recording software (
). Eventually, I'd be able to start up the game without those crashes, whether Dxtory was on or not (although I ended up using D3DGear due to some incompatibility). Before the easier-on-my-rig Survival Mode was released, there was but the Tutorial Level, which ran surprisingly (I expected
part to be the start of the hog) well, but there was the main campaign which is where I was less surprised (in terms of performance). Lastly, I want to applaud Destructive Creations, and thank you for being fearless of anybody—be it the mainstream or other media, or others who may hold some slight politically correct values—and developing what you planned on ... and of course, for this game! I do apologize, however, for being too late to pre-order your game, but regardless of that I know I will be supporting your future projects as well as buying myself some
merchandise!

I generally tend not to review games, since I'm rather poor at expressing how much I enjoy them unless I go on for too long with many tangents. I'll try to keep this brief while still getting my point across.
The Dream Machine, with all its current chapters is simply one of the most creative, underrated gaming experiences I've had well... ever (at risk of sounding like a suck up to the game's developers or something). It's got a pretty original plot considering the heavily-explored topic of dreams and entering dreams. You play as Victor, who just moved into a new apartment with his pregnant wife, only to find out a series of dark secrets leading up to Victor essentially having the fate of humanity in his hands.
The game's possibly most wonderful part is its aesthetic, with painstakingly-made sets made of clay, cardboard, and other such materials and a nice, dark soundtrack to enhance the atmosphere of the world further. While again avoiding spoilers, I'll say that the settings, especially in the various dreams, present varying, beautiful environments that all take full advantage of the ability to highlight the psychological state of the person having said dream. I feel like I'll spoil something if I say too much, but I'll probably have to get back to fixing this review a bit more with more reasons to buy it. It's a delightful game overall and I reccomend it wholeheartedly! Definitely my pick for the Steam awards "I played it before it won an award" award, due to its shockingly-underrated nature.
As an edit, playing the final chapter was riveting. One of my only problems with it was that Vincent seemed to grow to accepting of all the weirdness happening around him, but then I realized that it was more or less exasperation at the fact that he's been dealing with reality-bending and harrowing stuff for days (no spoilers, but he experiences and witnesses some violent or deadly things), and it would only make sense for him to essentially say "Okay, this is happening now." I refuse to spoil anything that happens, but it takes FULL advantage of how weird dreams can get and takes every last opportunity to show how the Dream Machine is trying to impede Vincent on his journey. And the ending... that ending was amazing. I, again, refuse to spoil anything, but I still strongly reccomend this game to anyone who likes the art, point and click gameplay, or even just story driven stuff. People who appreciate any artistic aspect of gaming as a creative medium are going to find at least something to love about this, and I still definitely reccomend this underrated goodness very highly!

Just add this to the list of things that prove that video games are art.
This game has some of the most intriguing, gorgeous, adorable (and in many instances disgusting) designs ever contructed.  The art style is like if the film "Mirror Mask" were made into a game.  And the plot is just as gorgeous and surreal.  "The Dream Machine" is like the ultimate indie game.
You play as Victor Neff, a self-proclaimed "handsome" man, who has just moved into a strange new flat with his pregnant wife, but things get strange very quickly when your wife notices the landlord acting really weird.  I will not spoil any of the plot.  It is a game you must see to believe, but if you can believe it, there is in fact a Dream Machine in the game.
Many players who have received this game negatively because of the short nature of the first two chapters (which can potentially both be completed in under two hours combined) are wrong in assuming because of this, the whole game is very short.  It is not, in fact.  By chapter 3, the length of each chapter exceeds 2 hours (the fifth chapter took over 3 (almost 4) hours to complete as was by-far the longest and most complex).  And yes, each chapter's puzzles are more intricate and complex, making the difficulty just right for players who need to adjust to the weirdness levels this game pushes out. And also remember, a short game is not a bad game.  There are point-and-click adventure games that can be beaten entirely within a half-hour, but they are brilliant.  So if you find yourself getting through "The Dream Machine" very quickly, do not equate that with it being a bad game.
The first two chapters are there to get the player's feet wet with how this game is going to present itself.  It's really surrealistic, thus it needs to demonstrate how the puzzles are going to work and the imaginitive ways to solve them.  (Hopefully, without spoiling much, I will give you an example.  In Chapter 2, there is a character that you have to talk to but he doesn't speak clearly at all.  The problem is one of his vocal cords is bent. The solution is to remove the cord and bang it with a hammer until it is straightened. Then the character will speak clearly).  Hopefully that was a good example of how unconventional the puzzles are in the game.
And the puzzles are very well implimented.  There were times, however, when it is so unclear what to do, clicking everything on everything becomes a method to get through the game.  I only found this problem on Chapter 5 (which was a huge chapter with a lot of map screens).  The level was much darker than the others making it a bit difficult to see items that needed to be picked up and characters were not clear in what they needed from Victor making it difficult to understand what to do, though I do know the developers are still updating the game very regularly fixing this and that, so the problems with Chapter 5 may very well be fixed in a couple of months.
The atmosphere in the game is brilliant, with a slow build to the weirder things (the ending of Chapter 5 was by far the strangest thing) with subtle music and an even mixture of a serious tone from the characters mixed with a humourous tone.  There were two parts that had me laughing out loud: a part with these pumpkins, and a part with a knight in armour.
The artwork of the game is something to behold.  Looking at each screen on the game and noticing the tiny details the developers put in give the game an extra dose of appreciation.  They clearly care about this game (especially since it's been in development for almost a decade).  Regardless of people disliking the game because they think it's grotesque, I think it's beautiful and I truly wish there were more games (let alone stop-motion films) in this style.

Hitman: Absolution is a great game where you play the role of notorious assassin "Agent 47". Each mission tasks you with the elimination of a number of people, varying from local drugs dealers to corrupt politicians. The game offers you a wide variety of maps in combination with an intersting storyline. Furthermore, you have a huge arsenal of weapons, tools and other stuff (smart use of your environment is a thing in this game) at you disposal to bring each mission to an end.
Each mission earns you cash rewards, which can be used to upgrade your weapons to make your character even more deadlier.
Played through the entire campaign? No problem, as the game also has a "Contracts" mode! Other players over the world can create custom missions on existing maps with new targets to kill and new goals to achieve (e.g. use gun X to kill your target, wear suit Y, prevent collateral damage,...). By completing a contract you gain a personal score so you can find out how well you played in comparisson with other players. Needless to say, this gives you an extra incentive to keep playing.
As someone who has also played the previous game Hitman: Blood Money, I would definately recommend this game if you're looking for a action/stealth based game.

This is one of my favorite games. It keeps the micro management from becoming overwhelming no matter how many worlds you have.
Combat:
Fleet composition can radically alter engagments. Capital ships are key, it feels like the death or escape of an enemy (or your) captial ship can at times be major turning points. Every ship has value, even the first ship you start with can be useful late gam when used correctly. Each world can be a campaign itself with proacted sieges or lightning strikes that bypass enemy fleets and defenses. Capital ships and titans level up through combat to increase their stats and unlock or upgrade powerful abilities. a handful of fully leveled captial ships can be increadibly powerful, they also are an irreplaceable loss if you are not careful. the control within combat is relateivly straight forward but be warrned in larger engagments ships may be unable to act in timely manners. If you tell a damaged ship to retreat it may have to push other ships out of the way, slowing it down. there are other small things like focusing fire to take on enemy captial ships but nothing unsual or complex.
research:
four trees that require you to expand to fully move down (each level requires another research station which take critial slots on your worlds) that each move  seperately. It is somewhat boring but there are later powerful and unqiue technologies that can radically alter a game. it is well laid out and easy to understand in a single play through.
Diplomacy:
This is both simplier and a little more involced than most games of this type I have played when dealing with both AI and human players. The reason being that you cannot overrule the will of your empire. Actions on both sides as well as racial relations can effect how different empires feel about each other. Completeting (and assigning) missions can help but failing missions can have severe concequences. Bribing races with resources can also be used but is limited by the other factors and can serve to push relationships over the edge but will rarely turn foe to friend.
Races:
Each race has roughly anologous ship types and some of the most basic research is the same but by the mid game the differences become abundently clear. The TEC, Advent, and Vasari have different strengths and weaknesses that are reflected in their ship specializations, unique abilities and most promanietly on the nature of their captials ships and titans. The Rebellion speciifc split of each faction results in truely have six interconnected races and their natures even effect attempts at diplomacy. The Rebal TEC can align with Pirates and Militas but its hard to gain the trust of other factions and also hard to get your people to accept them in turn.
Culture:
Culture is a mostly passive system that your choices affects. Both race and research as well as building affect when and how it spreads. Culture allows you to get more resources from remote colonies, it can give you abilities such as visiabiliy of enemy worlds, and it can take planets away or keep them safe. A world overwhelmed with hostile culture will rebel and abandon your empire, conversely an abandoned world covered with your culture will not be colonizable by hostile empires even without your control. its another layer that can drastically change the tide or be nothing  depending on how each party uses it.
Colonizing:
Hard but streamlined. if you can clear it you can take it and there are only a handful of upgrades each world needs with the option of a few specializations. additionally you can explore to find benefits, powerful artifacts, or debuffs for your worlds. The most important part is always space, what with you use the tactical and logistical slots on each world for can determine if you are rich, smart, capable of producing a fleet in minutes, or culturally dominate.
Overall its one the best games I have ever played. It has been described as 4X lite and I think its somewhat accurate but not a negative at all. Its a streamlined 4X that tries to keep you from being bogged down with minuta while still having a slower more deliberate pace.

This is hands down my favorite RTS.  It features beautiful space battles, excellent music, and scant but intriguing lore.
Play as the mighty but desperate Vasari, the vengeance-obsessed Advent, or the commercial and industrial powerhouse of the TEC.  Each faction has distinct strengths and weaknesses.
Much of the appeal of the game lies in its emphasis of macromanagement (research choice and fleet deployments) over micromanagements (managing individual units).  Instead of babysitting worker units, your attention is focused on hunting down enemy fleets, capturing new territory, or destroying the recently-constructed enemy superweapon before it rains doom on your planets.
This game also has an excellent modding community with many great mods that add tons of new content and keep you busy.
The game's main weakness is its utter lack of any sort of campaign; you can only play skirmish mode.  Fortunately, every match feels different because of the varied maps, random events, and differing outcomes.  Also, the enemy AI has an annoying tendency to sometimes give up when defeat is assured, bowing out of the game early instead of putting up a valiant last stand, which can make for an unsatisfying conclusion to hours of conflict.
All in all, this is an excellent space RTS well worth its asking price.

Not gonna lie, not recommending this game proved to be a hard decision.  I really wanted to like it, and even fooled myself to for a time, a somewhat refreshing look at a stealth-horror-investigation-shooter?  Here are the reasons that made this game was hard to downvote.
-Amazing environment
-Unique Story
-Solid Gameplay
-Very Fair Price
Now with a list like that, how could I damn such a game?  Well the combat did prove enjoyable though the enemy variety proved to be fairly bland, not the types or number, just how they had the same behavior and mode of attack.  That along with the give and take story that really demanded finishing.  Once you spend an hour or two in the game, you realize it is rather shallow and becomes a grinding Easter egg hunt, wrought with cheap scares to keep you on your toes until you are upgraded enough that you no longer care to be tactical or stealthy.  Then it’s fast traveling back and forth, as well as revisiting areas you’ve scoured already.  The dialogue proved dreadful as well as many systems that appear mostly hollow, like gifting your red friend things you’ve dug up like an obedient puppy and not much to show for regardless of if she accepts it or not.  The game isn’t spotless either as I have also found myself on more than one occasion being lodged into rocks and walls maneuvering with a borderline useless jump key.  Speaking of environments, I hope you like forests, because that is all you are going to get in this game.  So if you are into a cheap romp through the woods with a passible story where you collect junk kill skeletons and talk to ghosts for 5 hours, feel free go on ahead.  I just can’t, although I can safely say I gave the game the benefit of finishing it at least.
