If you like word puzzles, then you will probably enjoy this one.  It plays similar to Bookworm Adventures except that you have a 5 by 3 grid (15 letters) versus Bookworm's 4 by 4 (16 letters).  Certain letters do more damage, but I found that the word length has the dominant effect.  The game throws challenges at you, making you play certain letters, play letters from specified rows, and including tiles with good and bad effects.  Various challenges like playing words that begin with a vowel either as a requirement or for increased damage really changed the way I pieced words together.  What I really like is that this game will give you the definition of the word you wish to play.  Several time, I would stumble onto words I didn't know while trying to form my own and actually learn something.
The main complaint I have with this game concerns the achievements and quests.  Quite a few of these will be attained the longer you play regardless of your skill level.  This kind of makes it pointless.  There are achievements that require
certain types of words like palindromes that are actually interesting.  It is also odd that there is an achievement and quest to play words with no vowels.  Y, and W are considered vowels at times, so I do not think words like SHY, and CWM actually contain no vowels, but that is what the achievement wants.  Mostly I find myself ignoring the achievements and I acquire them as I play the game regardless.
I do enjoy playing this game though.  It is a good, challenging casual word game.

Bioshock 2 is Bioshock with a 2 slapped on the title.
Not really.
Bioshock 2, like the first one, is a really good game in my opinion. The story wasn't as good as the first game's, as many people just love to point out, but it's not 'bad' as a standalone story. It is better than the story in many other shooters, you know which ones I'm talking about I'm sure. The art design once again is spectacular, with environments that allow for strategic combat and cool screenshots to show my friends if I had any. My one complaint is that Rapture, albeit cool, is much less creepy the second time through. I did not, however, get pulled from the experience by this.
Bioshock 2's combat is an improvement on the first, I think. Sure, whacking people with the wrench is fun and all, but 2's weapons felt useful, and I found myself obligated not to melee through the whole game.
I feel I should also mention a crashing issue the game has, but there is a guide on Steam somewhere explaining how you can fix it.
I said it once and I'll say it again, Bioshock 2 is a cool game. I think think the main reason people like to hate on it is because while 2 is good, 1 and Infinite are fantastic, making 2 seem a lot less worth it. I also heard Minerva's Den was really good, so I'll have to play that sometime.

I play and review games a bit different. I review games as what they are and not as what they should be. So, I'll take this game as it is today and ask: Is it a good game?
Note that I didn't play the campaign, so I can't say anything about that. Not because I didn't like it, but because I never played any campaign in the X series. I like the sandbox playstyle.
Also note I got all the DLC's so I am talking about the game with all DLCs. This is not a review of the base game.
What you get when you enter this game is your ship and a huge universe.
With the DLCs you get new sectors in that universe where you have no highways at all -- while in the original universe you got highways that make travelling faster. Having highways or not... for me a universe in a space sim game has to be believably big. The keyword here is believably. And from my point of view X Rebirth has that. The universe is huge. In X Rebirth the universe is divided into galaxies, each galaxy ( there are 8 ) has sectors and within those sectors you've got zones. Galaxies are connected through huge jumpgates, like the gates that connected setors in X3. The sectors in X Rebirth are connected through superhighways, where you fly through, but faster. And the zones are connected... Well in some sectors, some zones are connected by highways. You can enter and leave those highways at any point of the way, but you can also fly all the way with your ship and explore. There are entire sectors without a single highway. Your ship has a boost, but the energy for your boost is taken from your shield energy. So it will not last forever.
Another way to travel faster than boosting through the universe (besides highways if they exist) is the new jumpdrive for your playership. There were some mods in the past that provided a jumpdrive, but now it was implemented by the developer.
This game started with a pretty small variaty of missions. That definetly changed. You got a huge variaty of missions, from assassination over smuggling, patrol, building (stations) requests, trading requests (deliver wares to a station), escort missions ( escort VIP ships to their target location and defend them), crafting and some more I don't remember right now. All are available at different difficulty levels. And then you got complex missions which I like most. Those are missions that combine a lot of different types of missions to a small storyline. It's not like a campaign, but it is a mission where you have to fulfill a varitaly of quests that are connected through a small story, which adds to immersion a lot. I didn't find many of those missions, but I really enjoyed the ones I played.
In X Rebirth you can fight with your player ship and in a fleet with other ships you bought. Many people complain that the fleet control is not good. Well, that is true. It's pretty cumbersome to give other ships in your fleet commands. All ships in your fleet will attac what ever attacs you, but other than that, there is no simple way to command ships.
But my problem about fleets is not the controls. My problem is how the game calculates the simulation when you are in the same area as the fight. In short: If you are in the same zone, your ships fight pretty bad while when you are not there watching it, they fight much better. There are some mods to optimize that, but it will probably never be perfect. I found something that works for me... though, I like to fight alone much more in this game.
Your playership can only load one weapon at the time. That means, you have a variaty of weapons that you can load, but you have to choose one. So you can fire your plasma cannon, and then switch over to the heavy mining laser ( which can be a deadly weapon too) but you can't fire both at the same time.
I didn't really like that when I started the game. But I realized that it adds a small layer of strategy into the fight. Your weapons are all usefull for different purposes: Some are strong against shields... others do better hull damage. They also have different ranges. Because you can not fire all your weapons at once, you got to know which weapon is strong in which situation. When I found out that I can optimize my damage by a rotation through my weapons during a fight, I really started to enjoy this kind of fight.
You have missles available, but you also have to load one kind of missle and use it and then switch over to another one to use another type of missle.
Boarding ships is a huge part of X Rebirth. It is probably the best way to earn money, but it's also a more complicated way. I'll try to explain the most important parts:
The first thing you want to do, is hire a marine officer. That officer will command your marines when you board a ship. Now you need troopers which you can hire from a Recruiting Officer. As soon as you have both, you can try to board another ship. To get your troopers on a ship they will fly in tiny kind of shuttles, so you got to make sure they are not shot on thher way. All ships in the X universe have their own staff on board, which will fight your troopers when you try to board a ship. To weaken the enemy you have to destroy surface elements on that ship and bring the hull down to a low percentage. You should do that before you send your troopers, otherwhise you will fail. It's very important to destroy the ship's jumpdrive first, when you attac. Ships can be repaired by their engineer during a fight. It is slow, of cause, but you should be aware of it, as the jumpdive or the engines could start working again after you destroyed them.
There is not much to say about trading. You can buy ships that can transport huge amounts of wares. You can add those ships to your fleet, but you don't have to. You got two menus to manage your trading actions. The standard trading menu will show you all the offers and demands and you can figure out what would be a good deal. That can be profitable, but it takes time to find good deals. But you got a second menu where you get the best deals in a list and you can see what the profit will be. So you simply click on one of the deals and it will add the buy and sell operation to the ship's trading queue. Ships can only queue up 3 operations ( buy or sell ) at once when you start the game. But you can buy software upgrades for your computer to make more operations available.
Another layer of trading is the item trade system. Items are things you have in your player's inventory. Those can be looted when you enter a station, or you can find boxes of loot with you scanners all over the universe. You can sell them or craft with them.
There are a variaty of items you can craft in your inventory from items you looted. Some of them are items that can be gifted to NPC's during a smalltalk to get special offers from them. But you can also craft a unique engine and spectial items that are needed to hack into stations.
You can hack into the computers of any station in X Rebirth in order to sabotage the station. I will not describe all the things you can achieve by hacking, but let me tell you that it can be very profitable. You will need to practice it a bit though, it's not simple.
I tried to cover as much as I could, probably in too much detail. I reached max characters in this review and I didn't even cover station building, which should be in this list.
Is it a good game after all? Yes it is. It is a universe full of enemies, missions, and opportunities. It has flaws, of cause. Every game has flaws. But none of them break the game for me.

Homefront is an alright game, but I do not recommend it due to the fact that it has more cons than pros. The story is alright. But has quite a few plotholes in it. The first couple minutes though, really shows you some of the depressing things in the world of Homefront and they are actually pretty well done.
The enemy AI is alright but your teammate AI is honestly pretty bad at least from my experience. Graphics are gritty looking and ugly, but the gun models, people other than important characters and dead bodies are weirdly good looking compared to the rest of the game. Especially the guns, seriously, they look REALLY good. Non of the characters are really all that likable and you play as a silent character (Which is a gripe that some people have with certain games. I for one don't mind silent characters if they are properly done, however, in Homefront it adds plotholes. Looking through iron sights is a toggle rather than a hold (You can't change it in settings). There are A LOT of invisible walls. This game is extremely linear. There are invisible walls in places where you would think it makes sense to go. When you're in calm areas where you can interact with people you move at a snails pace. Like, REALLY slow. For the most part the game is boring but it kinda ramps up when you're halfway through the campaign, especially with the last level which in my opinion is the best part of the campaign. When you're in areas with team AI, you have to wait for them to reach the end of the level for you to proceed to another area (It's probably a way that the devs made to load the next level). Also it's really easy for you to die, at least for me (Difficulty is a preference but even on easy the enemy AI were pretty unforgiving).
Oh and the campaign is 4 hours long. Shorter, depending on how you play (I died a lot).
Overall, I don't recommend this game. There are too many cons with this game and not enough pros. I thought almost the entire game was really boring other than the last hour or so. If you want to dive into the world of Homefront you might as well wait for the sequel, Homefront: The Revolution which is an open world game that fixes all the problems I have it this game. But if you want to, get this game when it's on sale.

After over 100 hours on record i feel like I'm pretty well qualified for reviewing this game. This is Civilization V in space, and there is no going around it unfortuantely. If you, like me, burnt yourself out a little playing Civ V, then you're likely to feel the same here, only faster. They (the devs) said you can't research all the techs in one game, but I have, multiple playthroughs on the Fastest time setting on Very Hard. It wasn't difficult, and I did it far before the turn time ended. There is virtually no distinction between any of the Sponsors either, just different bonuses and colors, which, ultimately, mean nothing in the long run. Still don't know what I mean? The ARC and Polyasia buildings all look identical for example, with no hint of European/American or Asian influence on eithers architecture despite these Sponsors supposedly representing entire subdivisions of the planet. The only diversity comes from the Tech Tree which you will inenvitably be forced to research  Supremecy or Purity tech even if you want to go Harmony because there are techs you must have in order to be successful at all.
Finally, what's the point of being in space? There are no real aliens, in terms of sentient factions that is, the native species are passive and by mid game serve as nothing more than cannon fodder in between wars. You can't travel to space, heck, you dont even have AIR UNITS. Yes, that's right, the thing we had in Civ 5 isn't even in this game. There are also other missing features like espionage, diplomacy, and any real interactivity with the AI. Been best friends with the AI for 150 turns? He's going to turn on you, no matter what. The AI is terrible.
Honestly the only redeeming thing about this game would be the new spaceships expansion / standalone game that works in tandum with this game. Even then, I'm not willing to spend 60 for the other half of the game that this should of shipped with. It's really hard to not recommend this game, but if you have Civ 5, you already own Beyond Earth, just, on Earth. Modders are the only saving grace for this game.

I've had this game for some time now and on my first play-through I couldn't understand what the developers were thinking. However, after letting the game sit for a while and going back to play it once more I have decided that this game is an underappreciated, if somewhat rough gem.
There are many aspects of the game that I simply adore, the attention to the detail in the collectable news reports is one of them; the absolute immersion into the politics of the time is simply brilliant, not to mention accurate. Along with this, I think that the story, which is the background story of the US being occupied, is fascinating. Usually in games the US is at the zenith of power and you have to save it from complete disaster, however here, in Homefront, the US has indeed fallen and it is the role of the resistance to attempt to rebuild. The preface for this game is wonderful and I simply love it, however there are many problems with the game mechanics, graphics and AI which let the game down. Unfortunately no matter how good the story is, playability is just as important.
One of the biggest issues with the game is the AI's seemingly scripted movements, lack of intelligence and spawning locations, making a few play-throughs rather predictable. It is a real pain to re-start at a check point, kill the very same enemies in the very same way, get killed, then do it all over again a few more times. The AI, for a realistic and enjoyable shooter needs to be a little unpredictable.
Continuing on from this theme of realism within the game brings me to another issue, the ballistics. I found a few times that I was being pinned down by an enemy but when returning fire it appears that I am out of range, which is strange because the longest distance you fire in the game is no more than 200 meters. For a good shooter the ballistics must be accurate; both the trajectory of the bullets and recoil need to be taken into account. The lack of recoil was not only unrealistic but frustrating
Another, and in a way a very disappointing problem is that I didn’t feel as though I was part of the resistance. The story, the concept and all the potential for a game to truly give you a resistance, grungy, underworld experience felt very much like every other shooter there is. As I said prior, I love the concept and the preface to the game, I think it is fantastic. The execution however was somewhat poorly done. You are dropped in the middle of the action without enough time to become attached to the correctors or the community. In a resistance situation, every single loss would be heartbreaking; I didn’t find that to be the case at all.
There are other issues along the same lines, such as a lack of interaction with the Oasis community; it would have been great if you spent some time gathering for supplies, cutting your teeth on a few raids and what not before embarking on the main story. The game was also far too short; I think that there could have been a few more missions that would have made the game more enjoyable.
I’ve probably given more criticism than praise, but that is because I wanted so desperately for this game to be good, but what stands out are the failings. This game has the potential to be great. After the release of the sequel I recommend the developers go back and re-do the original, fix it up and re-release it. I really do recommend the game if you’re able to look past the flaws, the concept is great and you’ll see just how good this game could have been.
All in all, 5.5/10

I just got back into pc gaming.  4X games are not my favorite genre, but I still like them.  In fact, I haven't played a 4X game since Deadlock back in the late 90s.  So I am comparing this game to Deadlock, not Civilization V or even Alpha Centauri like many people who review this game are.
First off, I liked the game and I enjoyed it.  I will play it again.  I would give it an 8/10.  There were a few bugs, but I wouldn't complain about them unless they aren't fixed in time.
There are several significant embarrasing limitations to the game.  These aren't gameplay issues; these are cosmetic enhancements that I am shocked were not included.
First off, when you build a city, it is generic.  You cannot see the buildings that you created.  Now I haven't played other Civilization games, but if you are building a city of buildings, each of those individual buildings should be shown on the close up view of the city.  How could Deadlock have this feature and Civilization does not???
Next, when you create a wonder or a great wonder, there is a single picture of a blueprint of the wonder with some text and voiceover.  For 2014, this is unacceptable.  There should be a 10-15 second  3D video introducing the wonder you created.  XCom Enemy Unknown does this when you build a new facility, and Xcom is a Firaxis game.  How could this have been omitted?
On the topic of videos, the ending is rather anti-climatic (sorry for the spoiler).   There is a beautiful introductory movie for this game.  There are only five ways to win.  How hard could it be to create 5 victory videos that last about 30-60 seconds each?  Are you serious?   I think the ending to Deadlock was better, and I can't even remember it.  Starcraft from 1999 had multiple videos per campaign.  Funny, I can't remember the ending to Beyond Earth, and I beat it yesterday.  So the ending of a game from 1996 is as good as the ending of one from 2014.  Seriously?
And while we are on the topic of videos, some of the quests should probably have them, too.
Now I am not a 4X game connoisseur, but these are some very simple additions which do not affect gameplay but would significantly add to its presentation.

I've been reading some of the reviews and can conclude that the negative ones were mostly from the franchise fans, clearly upset with the new direction this game takes. Understandable, but it doesn't make this a bad game.
Gameplay: Forget sandboxes. If you're not too picky about body count, there are myriad ways to off the bad guys in any preferred path you take, but for those aspiring for zero non-target kills there's really just one road made out for yer that lets you through unnoticed.
Imagine a particularly difficult piece of music, where a bar of notes may take about an hour or so to moderately master. Once you do get it, you start with the next bar, equally difficult, but still practicing the first bar before you move on. THAT'S what getting through this game feels like. You'll practice again and again, often getting frustrated after awhile but once you mastered the parts it feels like a real expert sneaking in and out inches from peril. I counted 1265 enemy alerts by the end on the game statistics, but on record it's zero. Practice makes perfect.
What I found to be a con was the checkpoints system, but for different reasons than most of the negative reviews: Once you restart the checkpoint, your weapons cache is reset, and the non-targets that you've subdued(or killed) will be back. It's mostly a position checkpoint, not much more.
If you don't find learning and memorizing levels in the way of items placement and guard movement a fun challenge, skip this. Otherwise it's a very engaging title. I know coz my wife will start nagging on how much time I spend gaming.

At the time I write this review I am partway through Chapter 5 (edit for finished game at end).
This game will frustrate the hell out of you, but it's so worth it.
Like many of these kinds of games it has puzzles that don't seem to make sense, and "clues" that don't really tell you anything. You will get stuck when you think you've tried everything, and even turning "hint mode" on won't be enough (as the "hints" it gives you are practically useless).
There are still a few things that need to be fixed, for example full-screen mode oftens crashes or runs slowly so I haven't been playing full-screen. Because of this I've sometimes missed clues as I just can't see them very well on the small screen! And for a game that's so visually impressive it's a shame I can't appreciate it fully by having my screen covered with it.
I still recommend, as the visuals are SO interesting and beautiful (and creepy!!). Without being a full-on horror game you will still feel weird and eerie playing this, you don't need jump scares because the atmosphere is enough. It really is full of dream-like imagination.
I can't wait to see how this all wraps up!
Update: I've now finished the game, and I still agree with everything said earlier and thoroughly recommend it. I was a bit disappointed with the gameplay and art of the last chapter as it felt a bit repetitive, but it didn't make me not want to play! I could tell there must be multiple endings because leading up to the end I kept thinking "this feels wrong, there must be an alternative but I can't figure out what it is..." and I got a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending. Normally this would make me feel annoyed after wasting time on the game, but I'm actually pretty excited to re-visit the whole game and see if I can get a different ending next time.

Not gonna lie, not recommending this game proved to be a hard decision.  I really wanted to like it, and even fooled myself to for a time, a somewhat refreshing look at a stealth-horror-investigation-shooter?  Here are the reasons that made this game was hard to downvote.
-Amazing environment
-Unique Story
-Solid Gameplay
-Very Fair Price
Now with a list like that, how could I damn such a game?  Well the combat did prove enjoyable though the enemy variety proved to be fairly bland, not the types or number, just how they had the same behavior and mode of attack.  That along with the give and take story that really demanded finishing.  Once you spend an hour or two in the game, you realize it is rather shallow and becomes a grinding Easter egg hunt, wrought with cheap scares to keep you on your toes until you are upgraded enough that you no longer care to be tactical or stealthy.  Then it’s fast traveling back and forth, as well as revisiting areas you’ve scoured already.  The dialogue proved dreadful as well as many systems that appear mostly hollow, like gifting your red friend things you’ve dug up like an obedient puppy and not much to show for regardless of if she accepts it or not.  The game isn’t spotless either as I have also found myself on more than one occasion being lodged into rocks and walls maneuvering with a borderline useless jump key.  Speaking of environments, I hope you like forests, because that is all you are going to get in this game.  So if you are into a cheap romp through the woods with a passible story where you collect junk kill skeletons and talk to ghosts for 5 hours, feel free go on ahead.  I just can’t, although I can safely say I gave the game the benefit of finishing it at least.

As a co-op game, this is worth while if you get it on sale.  Full price would be a bit much, but it is a fun game to run around and kill zombies in.  It's reasonably fun and has a lot of gore and humor in it.  But there are a few problems that drag it down and make it somewhat tedius, and which keep you from really getting pulled in.
The biggest issue is how extremely repetetive the gameplay is.  It relies on you never getting tired of killing hordes of non-threatening zombies, and while there is a lot of novelty with weird outfits and strange found-item weapons, it wears off after a couple hours because of how monotonous the game is.  Every side mission is exactly the same: kill a hundred zombies, find an NPC, escort them back killing another hundred zombies.  Most of the game becomes an escort quest with poor AI, which is tiring.  The main story missions are more entertaining, but not because of any interesting characters or story, just because of how insanely over the top the voice acting and cut scenes are.  These are some of the best parts of the game, and all feel like they are out of some horrible B movie that doesn't realize how terrible it is, and where the actors are all either really bad, or are too talented for the material and are hamming it up for a laugh.  The actual game play in those missions is still pretty dull.
Another major issue is the controls.  Movement is choppy and sluggish.  Whether zombies can grab you or not appears to be entirely random.  Most of the ones that look like they will get you miss entirely, most that grab you seem to come from nowhere.  In the stages where you are driving it's even more skittish, and the gun controls are surprisingly bad.  Guns are almost worthless except for the shotgun, but even that is frustrating because of how hard it is to actually hit things.  You more or less move on a 45 degree turret, so any kind of precision turning is all but impossible, and aiming, unless you go down ironsights, basically consists of pointing at the enemy, not moving, shooting, and hopping the auto-target works.  Aiming manually is slow and not particuarly accurate either.  This barely matters against the zombies, who are easy to kill and avoid, but against the bossess, who have a sharp spike in difficulty from the regular game, it can get you killed a lot as you try to wrestle with the controls.
Another problem is that everything is done with time constraints.  For a game that derives most of its entertainment value from sandbox exploration, it's strange to constantly have timers counting down on all your quests, and to have an overall timer on the game at large.  This doesn't hugely impact the game unless you're a completionist and actually care about rescuring every survivor, in which case I imagine it would be a pain.  The worst part of this, though, is your stupid kid with her stupid Zombrex medicine.  You have to bring her the medicine every 24 hours, but you can't give it to her, you can't show up late, and you can't show up early, so you spend a lot of time running back to base, then waiting for her to accept her medicine, because I guess if she takes it ten minutes early she will explode or something.
I played the original Dead Rising when it launched and lost interest after 10 hours or so because it was repetetive and pedantic.  This one feels like it has most of the same problems, but is saved by co-op.  I would reccomend it at half price or less if you have a friend to play with who enjoys zombies and mayhem and whatnot.  But as a single player experience, I can't imagine caring enough to keep playing.

Pro-tip: Turn up the colour saturation a bit for a harder experience, as the enemies and treasure pickups won't be as obviously visible anymore, and you'll have to rely on your keen sense of hearing.

I've had this game for some time now and on my first play-through I couldn't understand what the developers were thinking. However, after letting the game sit for a while and going back to play it once more I have decided that this game is an underappreciated, if somewhat rough gem.
There are many aspects of the game that I simply adore, the attention to the detail in the collectable news reports is one of them; the absolute immersion into the politics of the time is simply brilliant, not to mention accurate. Along with this, I think that the story, which is the background story of the US being occupied, is fascinating. Usually in games the US is at the zenith of power and you have to save it from complete disaster, however here, in Homefront, the US has indeed fallen and it is the role of the resistance to attempt to rebuild. The preface for this game is wonderful and I simply love it, however there are many problems with the game mechanics, graphics and AI which let the game down. Unfortunately no matter how good the story is, playability is just as important.
One of the biggest issues with the game is the AI's seemingly scripted movements, lack of intelligence and spawning locations, making a few play-throughs rather predictable. It is a real pain to re-start at a check point, kill the very same enemies in the very same way, get killed, then do it all over again a few more times. The AI, for a realistic and enjoyable shooter needs to be a little unpredictable.
Continuing on from this theme of realism within the game brings me to another issue, the ballistics. I found a few times that I was being pinned down by an enemy but when returning fire it appears that I am out of range, which is strange because the longest distance you fire in the game is no more than 200 meters. For a good shooter the ballistics must be accurate; both the trajectory of the bullets and recoil need to be taken into account. The lack of recoil was not only unrealistic but frustrating
Another, and in a way a very disappointing problem is that I didn’t feel as though I was part of the resistance. The story, the concept and all the potential for a game to truly give you a resistance, grungy, underworld experience felt very much like every other shooter there is. As I said prior, I love the concept and the preface to the game, I think it is fantastic. The execution however was somewhat poorly done. You are dropped in the middle of the action without enough time to become attached to the correctors or the community. In a resistance situation, every single loss would be heartbreaking; I didn’t find that to be the case at all.
There are other issues along the same lines, such as a lack of interaction with the Oasis community; it would have been great if you spent some time gathering for supplies, cutting your teeth on a few raids and what not before embarking on the main story. The game was also far too short; I think that there could have been a few more missions that would have made the game more enjoyable.
I’ve probably given more criticism than praise, but that is because I wanted so desperately for this game to be good, but what stands out are the failings. This game has the potential to be great. After the release of the sequel I recommend the developers go back and re-do the original, fix it up and re-release it. I really do recommend the game if you’re able to look past the flaws, the concept is great and you’ll see just how good this game could have been.
All in all, 5.5/10

Hatred is a Twin stick shooter in which we take on the role of a mass murder, in his mission to “cleanse the world” from humanity. To accomplish this he, well actually he has no plan whatsoever and just goes from area to area, killing random people by the droves. As you may imagine this doesn't sit too well with the local police force and they will soon set out confront him in a shoot out. Unfortunately for them, our nameless antagonist has the power to regenerate his wounds by brutality finishing off any wounded people. How much he regenerates is based on what difficulty level you chose. Regardless of that strange power, our player character is not an all mighty death dealer and is actually pretty fragile. A couple of shots is all it takes to kill you, so it is best to fight crouched and with suitable cover, especially when some of the tougher enemies show up. Don't rely on it too long though, cover is destructible and will soon be a pile of rubble from all the bullet holes.
To fight back you will be able to carry up to three weapons and some grenades, however the flash-bang grenades are near useless. Your ammo supply will be very limited and the only way to get more is to resupply from the weapons of the recently deceased. Whole levels may be lacking a certain type of ammo for one of your weapons, in which case it is best to swap it out for one that is easily found throughout the level. Unfortunately, you will see most of the weapons this game has to offer in no time and they are all pretty generic. There is one shotgun, one handgun, one assault rifle, along with a few other weapons. Since this game is purely about killing, it does get old very quickly. There is no melee whatsoever minus an epic flying kick, to down people for an easy execution. The knife our character is carrying is pure show and only appears during the cut-scene animations of a execution. Bullet proof armor is also in this game and will double the amount of damage you take if you are lucky enough to find one.
The previously mentioned executions are the main source of controversy in this title, as they show a close up, brutal execution of a pleading victim. Funnily enough they are not even that violent compared to other games and due to the few execution animations there are, will quickly lose their shock value.  Remember how I mentioned that this is the only way to regain health? Yeah, I have no idea how the devs thought this would be a good idea since you will be seeing these over and over again, causing a ton of breaks in the action just to see the same execution pulled off time and time again. To make matters worse, time doesn't freeze when you enter an execution cut-scene, so as soon as you finish killing the victim to regain health, you will find yourself surrounded by heavily armed enemies then will be quickly gunned down. You do have an option to turn off execution cutscenes, which you will want to do as quickly as possible, but that kind of destroys the main gimmick of Hatred.
About 2 of the 7 levels are throw away romps, through linear uninspired environments like a  sewer or a train. The rest feature a small, open world environment to cause havoc in, as well as multiple side quests. These side quests always need you to kill someone or destroy something, which we probably would have done anyways, but you will definitely want to head straight for them as completing one will net you a token that allows you to respawn if you were to die. You will also be able to drive around these environments with a very specific vehicle, which is usually a police car. Unless that vehicle has a mounted machine gun it is completely pointless to get into one of these, since the controls for driving are abysmal and they take very little damage before exploding. Your character takes his sweet time to get out of a burning vehicle as well, so walking is nearly always the safer option. In case you are wondering, no you can not shoot out of your car window, you will be completely defenseless. There are no maps of the areas and some are strangely laid out, so cars are purely a gimmick. One thing I would like to mention is that our character has no qualms with killing random people, but he will not steal a parked car for whatever reason.
Environments look great. Hatred is powered by Unreal Engine 4 and it is the best looking twin stick shooter on the market. From the amount of detail in areas to the limited destructibility of everything via gunfire or explosives, it is a truly impressive. It's a very demanding game however, my frame-rate dipped to the 30's on a fairly high end PC. Ironically enough the very same attention to detail placed in the environments severely harm the game. There are just too many objects that impede your movement and will stop you dead in your tracks in vital moments. Your character can vault over some objects while sprinting, but it is a clunky, unreliable system that feels barely functional. A lot of buildings are designed in a way that makes it have plenty of dead ends , causing you to backtrack, which will be your doom if your objective was to flee from your pursuers. You can jump out of windows with the sprint key, but good luck getting that to work correctly. Some areas have multiple vertical layers which absolutely breaks the AI until they are on the same plane as you. They can not shoot up and you can not shoot down, so it comes down to waiting for them to figure out their way to you so you can kill them.
Plenty of missions require you to kill a certain amount of innocents and that gets old fast. The number required just gets too high and becomes extremely repetitive, not to mention counter productive, as slaying all the civilians will get rid of all your easy targets for a health refill. It's not fun either, they are all bullet spongy and it's total waste of ammo. They can take several assault rifle rounds before they go down and with actual trained combatants it feels like we are fighting cyborgs or something. Civilians are not defenseless however, they will frequently pick up weapons and fire at you. Problem with that is they are equally as skilled with that weapon as a trained soldier, only difference being the amount of damage they can take. It really breaks the illusion of them being victims when they all know how to operate a machine gun and are fearlessly fighting along side soldiers, to the death. That could have been cool, seeing a few people go all John Rambo on you, though seeing them endlessly pull more ammo out of there pocket and refusing to flee no matter what, time and time again is just plain weird. Enemy AI also have the ability to see you through solid walls and will no your position at all times. Cops just appear out of thin air instead of closing in on you and everything just feels badly designed.
Survival mode is what saves this game. It throws away Hatred's inconsistent sense of realism and places you in unique small maps specifically designed to fight in.  The environments in these allow for much more fluid movement than the cluttered messy environments in story mode.  You will be able to pick from three different characters that appear after the aftermath of the end of story mode and all have different stats. Instead of the boring ambient music of story mode, you will have the option of playing an awesome heavy metal track in these maps. After each wave you will be able to buy explosives, ammo or body armor with the points you gain from killing as well as gaining experience to increase in rank. The higher your rank, the more perks, weapons and weapon slots you can access. This mode is a decent amount of fun and shows you the difference of designing a game around the gameplay, over how much edge you can cram into a series of dull, pointless objectives like in story mode. This is a weird one to recommend. If the subject matter does not bother you, this is a mediocre twin stick shooter that will kill a few hours.

Magic is one of the best games ever made, and this is a great intro product to that game. The new commitment to doing videos explaining decisions and curating the cards available to provide the best possible experience is a really important step, and encourages me to think that they're really going to support and improve this experience over the long term.
I would recommend it as an intro product to anyone who wants to learn Magic, and if you like it, it's definitely worth paying for packs.
With that said, the game has had a rough start, with a lot of bugs that should have been caught in Beta. Being tied to the paper Magic set release allows you to get in on the hype (Innistrad looks amazing!), but it also means that the quality sometimes suffers due to a fairly punishing schedule by digital standards. They've fixed a lot of issues, but it would certainly benefit them to fix the rest.
Long story short, give it a try!

This is a very well made game. An almost Freelancer style game with simple mechanics that make learning quick and fun. The missions you take can be legal or illegal - bounty hunter, merchant, smuggler, miner, thief, and so forth. Combat is satisfying and engaging, though a bit over the top at times and occasionally downright impossible until you have had further equipment upgrades. Once purchased though, the difficulty lowers.
The commodity system was great! This was one of the most satisfying games for being a merchant I've ever played. Watch for starvation and run them food from an agrarian planet. Take water from one system that is rich in it to a more barren system and earn 200% or more than what you bought it for. Took a little getting use to, and I still don't understand it all, but the overall mechanic is satisfying once you get an idea of it.
My only gripe is it needs more content. After the main story is over, you have the biggest Dreadnaugh, and you are fully upgraded, doing missions is a little pointless. The devs should open it up for modding. More ships, weapons, equipment, systems, etc., etc., and this game would be more than a hoot.
Definitely worth the $20. The game is great and a definite recommend, even if it's for a few story runs only.

This is the best point & click game in my life. After finishing the game, I was still so obsessed with it that I made every of my friends play it, while I sit behind and watch them playing, and now I'm still obsessed with it.
The story is interesting and has some plot twist, keeping us curious about what will happen next. And if chapter 1 & 2 aren't good enough, the next chapters will probably keep you playing this game. Back then, when I finished chapter 3 and need to wait for other chapters, I was afraid that chapter 3 is too good, and that I would be disappointed when chapter 4 released, but in the end, I wasn't: Chapter 3 is already really good, but chapter 4 is better, and chapter 5 is even better than chapter 4.
The puzzle isn't too hard and is logical, well sometimes it becomes really difficult, but totally makes sense.
Some people complaining that sometimes you can't examine an object until a NPC told you to do it, but to me, that's what make the puzzle better: You need to actually read and understand what's going on in order to process, blindly clicking around won't get you anywhere.
It isn't a horror game, but somehow it gives you the chills, I always like that part of any story.
Due to the fact that there isn't any voice actor, the dialogues won't fade away unless you click on game screen. It's great for someone who isn't good at English like me since I can't read English really fast, on this game I can slowly read and understand every bit of what the characters are saying.
Chapter 6. If you think chapter 3, 4, 5 are good and feeling so hyped about the next chapter, prepare to be disappointed. Unlike chapter 5, chapter 6 is very short and leave many unanswered questions. The ending isn't satisfied as well, but maybe it's just my opinion.
Chapter 6 ruined my wonderful experience on this game, but beside that, everything of this game is perfect, so I would still recommend this game, and yes, it's still my best point & click game ever.

Several years into the future, a biotics company engineers a mutant species with the intent of selling them as pets. However, in the company's greed and arrogance, they neglected the needs of these modified organisms. As a result, they live a life of unending agony and suffering. The government attempted to halt the lab's twisted experiment, but the CEO refused, even going as far as hiring an elite private forces to guard the company's assets.
Pushed to its limit, the national guard sieged the biotics company's headquarters as well as the lab in which the organisms were being grown. In it's rage, the government slaughtered everyone involved; scientists, businessmen, secretaries.
With the company no more, the government found itself in a rough spot; who would be left to take care of the tortured mutants? In an act of mercy, many volunteers have stepped forward to help mercifully put the tormented creatures to sleep.
Chuzzle's main story liberally shares similar themes from classics such as Frankenstein and Jurassic Park, in regards to the costs and risks of unfettered scientiffic progress. There's also a minor sub-plot involving one of the protagonist's struggles with accepting their newfound gender identity, but I am no expert on LGBTQ+ stuff so I'll leave analysis of that specific part of the story. What I can say is that the side-plot does help in tastefully preventing the game from coming across as some kind of unnuanced "Anti-Science" propaganda film.
Another major theme that comes up in the story is the moral dilemma that the general popuace faces when confronted with an irredeemable evil. The two logical extremes of this dilemma are embodied by two central characters; the senate at the beginning of the story, who turn a blind eye to the dilemma for fear of getting their hands dirty and losing the much-coveted "moral high-ground," and the National Guard who remorselessly murder the hundreds of people involved with the experiments.
Overall, Chuzzle's story is a beautifully-written tragedy that asks the audience to truely critically think about the themes presented, which is a daring feat considering how most modern videogames aren't willing to take that kind of risk on an actually meaningful level (Except maybe Mafia III or Deus Ex, but I haven't played those games yet give me time damnit). I easily give Chuzzle a
10/10. Would misinterperet a relaxing cartoony match 3 game about fluffy spheres with eyeballs again.

I bought this game three months ago. I still play this game sometimes now. I wanna show my impression to the community, and let more players know this game.
As a war game, this game is quite novel, you don't behave as a leader of a nation or a soider of killing enimies.  You just play as common civilians here, and everyone else can be your friend or enimy. Killing is an important factor or maybe the best part in a war game. However, in this game, when I find I have to kill other civlians in order to get food or medicines for my own guys, I realize that killing is not that funny. I like the educational experience of the common ppl's life in war.
As a strategy game, new players may find it hard to survive in such severe condition, you have to face starvation, disease, robbing from other looters and death during scavenging. But once you succeed in surviving until the war is over, you will feel much easier to play it again. The strategy is to use stealth killing in the night adventures. Killing bandits or military in supermarket or military base, for example, can make you very rich, and I find it easy as a veteran player of the game.
For the price of the game, $20 is a bit expensive. I spent about 2 weeks to go through all the elements of the game. But if the game is on sale, it is worthy. I hope this game could introduce more DLCs to be dynamic game, so that veteran players can still feel interested in playing the game again.

Blackpowder Games deserve praise for attempting something a little different with BETRAYER, and although it remains, at heart, an action RPG, they have succeeded in taking the genre in an unusual and interesting direction. This is a game that’s big on atmosphere, even if it is a tad light on content. Visually the game is quite unique, and the small indie studio have managed to create a world that’s far more eery and mysterious than can be found in most AAA horror titles. And this creepy atmosphere is further enhanced by excellent audio design. The combat is fun and reasonably challenging, and it does stealth pretty well too. It would, perhaps, gain something from a wider variety of environments and maybe from some voice acting, but on the whole this is an excellent little game. And it’s also great value for money. Some have criticised BETRAYER for being repetitive but personally I found my 26 hours within the game thoroughly enjoyable, and it never felt like a grind. And I managed to get all the achievements – huzzah! Sequel please.

The combat in Betrayer is pretty fun, and when you first start the game the world feels mysterious and full of discoveries.
However, you'll quickly get used to the environment (each new area is just more of the same) and how practically all the objectives are just scavenger hunts. The context can be interesting for some of the stuff you find, but after I'd picked up 20 notes and looked at 15 tombstones I felt like the game was just desperate to try and keep the world from feeling empty. The environment lost it's mystery and became very predictable.
You can enter an alternate dimension type thing throughout the game, and while that does give the story more potential, I was hoping it would affect the gameplay and environment a lot more than it did.
Maybe I'm just impatient and the game's setting and story really come together and hook you after the first couple hours, there is certainly potential, but the repetitive scavenger hunts and somewhat copy-pasted locations might keep me from ever getting that far.
If you catch Betrayer on a good sale than I suppose it could be worth it, the first couple hours are fun. (Don't let my criticism ruin it for you)
Just be aware that the game has weaknesses, and that causes some players to lose interest before long.

Update: It looks like the parts that are specifically fischertechnik cannot be mixed with the ordinary parts in this game, which, if it's true, won't allow any significant designs with the fischertechnik parts.  They would then just more little more than an advertisement.  For example, there's no way to build a marble track with fischertechnik parts and add a lift even though there are lifting parts available in the common objects.  I'm a little disappointed at this.
I also get the feeling the forums might be dead.
=========================================================
If you watch the videos, or look at the example pictures, you might be misled into thinking this is a 3D spin-off of "Amazing Machines" or other games of the genre - and that would be plenty of good reason to buy the game right there.
----- But this game has so much more. -----
This has some (if not all - I'm not sure) fischertechnik parts in a virtual game.  fischertechnik does not have nearly the popularity in the U.S. as LEGO does (at least not that I'm aware), and it's a shame, as I think fischertechnik provides a more flexible system.  For a LEGO cube piece, 1 top male component can mate with 1 bottom female component, and the sides provide no attachments.  But for a fischertechnik cube, it provides 5 female components (1 bottom + 4 sides) and  1 male component (top) on a cube, or elongated cube piece.  There are other pieces (for both LEGO and fischertechnik), but my impression is that fischertechnik has a better design.
For examples, watch the youtube video "fischertechnik Convention Dreieich 2017"
When I was a kid, I had a very basic set of fischertechnik pieces - just enough to understand they were really cool, and they were really expensive.  The models you see in the video above are approaching several thousands of dollars easily.  So this is like a dream come true for me -- a long forgotten dream.  :)
The same basic blocks are in this game, along with a huge number of non-standard pieces of common real-world objects.
Custom parts can be created in a parts editor too.
Everything can be shared in Steam Workshop including puzzles.

Fantastic little word game, which can be described as a scrabble-meets-RPG (or to be more precise: monster mashing in a fantasy setting with basic cRPG elements, if you like).
As in original scrabble, you are building words from letter tiles, but instead of accumulating points, you are using them to defeat your opponents. There is loot, potions, various unlockables, character development and... yes, there are quests! (scrabble-like, mainly about building specific number of words meeting specific criteria).
The game has a high replay value (it's a word game, after all), and after beating Story Mode (there is little story about it, actually - rather a sequence of challenges), there is so-called "Endless Mode", where it's just you, monsters, and the question - how long can you survive?
Production value is high as well - it's a casual game, but a very polished one. Cartoonish presentation adds a lot of charm - it's cute, colorful and clean. Ingame music is diverse and works really well; it didn't force me to turn it off, and I was playing for hours.
I would recommend this, if you find tradidional word games boring, but like the idea of word-building game with defined goals and/or light cRPG flavor. Well, even if you don't, it's still worth trying.
Pros:
+ high replay value with Story Mode and Endless Mode
+ graphics and decent music (and high production value overall)
+ achievements very well balanced - manageable, but giving you a nice feeling of progession.
Cons:
None. This is pretty much perfect for what it is.

Rebel Galaxy is a fun expansive space game that sacrifices complete freedom and dogfighting to bring something completely new to the table, which is fun and unique
Pros:
-Areas feel big and look wonderful
-Awesome music which adds a bit of a Mad Max feel (my opinion)
-Ship combat which reminds strongly combat in pirate games (hence swashbuckling adventure) which requires maneuvering to let shields recover or attack another angle of the enemy that's more vulnerable and using "deflectors" to absorb damage in an emergency
-Fully voice acted with only a few quircky lines and many alien dialects
-huge variety of weapons and defence mechanisms to choose from which can change gameplay, especially the "broadside" weapons
-Possibility to either be lawful or piraty which will make some outposts hate you and others accept you
-Trade or fight and/or join certain factions which have unique ships or items
-You can engage Warp at almost any point and do not have to travel to some gate unless you go to a different starsystem
-An interesting story around your Aunt and a certain object she uncovered...
Cons:
-You are limited to a 2D Plane, same as for the big enemy ships but not the fighters. Can feel limiting, ESPECIALLY when you have something thats below you, like an asteroid you want to laser to get to the goodies inside but your turret is on top so you have to maneuver in a way so that it reaches
-Combat most of the time is just firing broadside weapons, managing your other turrets in combat is not viable
-The camera is almost impossible to control unless you switch to broadsides. Game knows this and hints at it but it can take some getting used to especially during mining
-Nearly EVERYTHING is automated. Meaning, for example, that if you want to engage "Warp" you have to wait for the game to give you the go ahead after you travelled for x distance. And retrieving a specific piece of cargo between many is really hard to do.
-Controller is, as far as I can see, required.
-The "Warp" will not get you to your destination immediately so you can sit back and wait until you arrive. Many time you have to almost drift out of the way of nebulas and asteroid fields. Its  easy to dodge but it can get annoying. If this makes the warping more interesting or annoying is up for debate. (I personally do not mind TOO much but I would want to sit back and let the game take me there without me doing anything sometimes)
Overall: I like this game a lot. I played Freelancer and loved the heck out of that game too. And I noticed that even though you were not restricted to a 2d plane and it was dogfighting and not ship to ship combat in that game, I get a similar vibe from this game too.
You DEFINITELY get your moneys worth.

As generic as they come, Homefront is a game for lovers of the point-and-shoot variety. The story wants to be as poignant as Spec Ops: The Line. The gameplay wants to be as solid as the Call of Duty series. The visuals want to be like Battlefield 3. Unfortunately, all of those aspects fall incredible short of their ideals.
The voice acting is surprisingly strong, but it completely undermined by the utterly dumb AI. Friendly NPCs block you from cover, exposing you to enemy fire. Enemies are very predictable. Difficulty is only ramped up by adding more enemies to the screen. There are a few shining moments of cinematic brilliance, like when you are first escorted as a prisoner through a typical American suburb taken over by the brutal Korean forces, but all of that great storytelling is destroyed by blocky NPC models and outdated textures.
I can't speak for the multiplayer as I only played the single-player.
I give this game a 4/10. It's not worth the $20 price tag, but if you pick it up from a Humble Bundle or on sale, it might be worth the measly ~4 hours it takes to complete the single-player campaign.

This is a great traditional-style point-and-click game with lovely (although a little odd) characters and background rendered in paper and clay. I found the story enthralling and the gameplay challenging, but not impossible - most of it is based in logic (as well as a little old-school point-and-click logic!).
The atmosphere and storytelling was atmosphetic, the characters stood out, and the fact it looks great and the interface is easy to use (and mistakes cannot be easily made, unlike with some games) made is so easy and fluid to play. The story is based around an interesting combination of ideas on dreams, philosophy and a little danger from basic-level AI thrown in for good measure. The puzzles are excellent and logical, and I found that with enough thought, pretty much all of them can be solved without too much stress.
I certainly found it quite addictive, and although stuck on a couple of puzzles, I got through it relatively unscathed - and it was a lot of fun to work the puzzles out; they gave quite the sense of achievement!
This is highly recommended (in fact, it was actually a very enthusiastic recommendation to me) to point-and-click enthusiasts, puzzlers, and anyone who wants to try something with deep atmostphere, great characters, and an intresting, entertaining story. It also helps that it looks pretty great too!

I was going to write a list of "Pros and Cons," but then I realized that although the pros were things done well, the cons were things the game didn't even try to do, because it wasn't about those things.  So, I re-wrote the list as "Things This Game Is and Is Not About."  "Bottom Line" at the top, for TL;DR purposes.
Bottom Line:
This is not a triple-A title, and it isn't trying to be.  It's trying to go in a different direction and do things that triple-A titles *don't* do, and specifically avoid doing the things they already do better.  If you like the "Things This Game Is About," and are not bothered by a total lack of "Things This Game Is Not About," then you will like this game, because it is VERY good at what it *is* about.  However, if you find the game "too slow," "boring," "lacking weapon diversity," or "not challenging enough," then this game is a poor match for you, because it is not about scratching those types of itches.
Things This Game Is About:
~ Spooky atmosphere.  Not frightening, shocking, or horrifying - just slightly spooky.  Something is... *off*.
~ Exploration.  There are numerous ways to pick your way through the game, but turning on all the map markers and following the optimal path will be tremendously boring.  Instead, exercise a bit of self-control and wait to turn on those markers until you've found most of the stuff but aren't sure where those last two or three things are.
~ Isolation.  This is a doomed colony, and you're there to sort out the wreckage, not interact with a cast of dozens of vibrant and interesting NPCs.
~ Paying attention to what you hear (and how audible you are) more than what you see.  The devs wanted to create a game where aural cues are more important than visual ones, and while there are still visual cues for the hearing-impaired, the aural cues are far more important and reliable.
~ Helping ghosts make peace with their deaths, which they can't remember, by figuring it out for them.  You may well piece together a story before the ghost does, but they might need some object or other trigger to be able to move on.  Just accept that this is how ghosts work - it's about their peace, not your understanding.
~ Patiently planning your attacks.  More like Tenchu (the first one), where you can get in over your head if you fail to spot something, than like Shadow of Mordor, where you're *supposed* to overcome superior odds and adapt your plans on the fly.  Actually, it's even farther in the Tenchu direction than Tenchu is.
Things This Game Is Not About:
~ Broad weapon choices (would be period-inappropriate).
~ Slaughtering your enemies in droves (would detract from the atmosphere).
~ Fast-paced gameplay (would detract from the atmosphere).
~ Being super-exciting, epic, or over-the-top in any way (would detract from... look, this is a very understated game).
~ Magic spells, talent trees, mega bosses, epic weapons, phat lewtz, or pretty much anything that most triple-A titles go over-the-top on to try to stand out from their competitors.
~ Puzzles.  The "investigations" you undertake, such as they are, are not intellectually demanding.  There are no puzzles in this game, no intuitive leaps to make; if you can just find the MacGuffins the ghosts are looking for, they'll fill in part of the colony's story for you and be able to move on themselves.  This is not a framework for a puzzle, it's a justification of the fetch-quest mechanic (the ghosts are stuck, therefore they can't go on their own errands).

I have only found/fixed/crafted a gun once in those games I have played.  So they are kind of rare, but luck plays a role here, too.  Food is expensive and meds are very expensive.  Expect to trade nearly half your belongings for a couple bandages or pills.  But that's probably how it would be in war.  Necessities would be expensive.
It is depressing but addicting, Without spoilering it for you, play it.  You wil get depressed and frustrated but that's the reason to play again.  I would love to see Steam Workshop support for mods.  I would definately buy an expansion, too.
Buy it.  You'll be sorry.

I absolutely loved Dead Rising, so when I heard about Dead Rising 2 years ago, I must have written it off because they removed the camera functionality. Which is ignorant, because while I enjoyed the Camera system, the real true draw was the stress of the 72-Hour system.
Recently I picked DR2 up for myself and my GF, and we have been playing it non-stop in co-op. It is freaking excellent. It has all the wacky psychos, hilarious weapons and terribly bad (assumedly purposefully) writing of the first game.
There are some serious negatives for some people, for instance, co-op is barebones, while character progress can be tracked and saved per player, only one players story advances. There are several quirks as well; joining character has no weapons each time you join the game (each play session start basically), and when one player opens the menu it pauses the other players game. I’m sure there’s more, but overall, we have gotten past those issues and still had tons of fun.
Another important note for those looking to play on Win 10 with controllers. I had tremendous difficulty getting controllers to work and I am pretty technically competent. I tried many different controllers and described methods from other people and eventually one worked, but I certainly spent a couple hours on the problem, which is crazy to me considering that the game was made for Xbox 360 and I was trying 360 controllers and couldn’t get it to recognize.
In conclusion, the game is excellent despite its quirks, if you liked the first one and can get past the little problems, then you will probably love this one. Looking forward to playing the DLC as well.

X: Rebirth is definitely a unique entry in the space-sim genre and the game's universe is very sophisticated if you take the time to notice it. For newcomers to the X series the amount of depth may overwhelm you at first, but this game is probably the most user friendly out of all the X games.
At first, I was somewhat of a newcomer to this game since I'd only played X3: Terran Conflict / Albion Prelude for couple of hours. After learning the basics, I came to love that there's so much to do in this game compared to most open world games. You can trade, explore, dogfight, and eventually manage an empire if you invest the time. You may start with just one ship, but a few hours later you could be managing dozens, then a few hours more you could be building stations, and then those stations could start managing even more ships.
One of the most interesting aspects of the game is that almost everything happens in real time. When you order one of your ships to trade with a station, it will actually fly there and line up with the trading port. Then dozens of cargo drones will fly back and forth carrying the wares between the station and that ship. When you buy a capital ship from a shipyard, you can see it being built in real time by the shipyard's team of construction drones.

If you're a veteran of the series you might be a little disappointed since this is not simply a new iteration of X3: Terran Conflict / Albion Prelude. However, if you give the game a chance you may appreciate its new direction for the X series while channeling the roots of X: Beyond the Frontier. There are some limitations such as only piloting one ship, but overall the game offers many new features and maintains the depth of gameplay from previous games without a needlessly complex interface.

The UI in general is a bit too big, the inventory completely obscures the bottom-right side of my screen so exploring to the right is way harder than it should. I'm looking at the screenshot in the store, my inventory is like 25% larger than the one in the store is. The game also lacks screen transitions, so using menus can feel a bit jumpy.
People are complaining about the art and sound design, but i actually kind of liked both. They aren't extraordinary by any means, but they do enough to service the gameplay. The actual game revolves around collecting stuff and crafting it into rope and pickaxes and then going "ok what does this do." The world is crammed with♥♥♥♥♥♥to collect to the point where it can feel claustrophobic, but i like it because it gave me something to do early on. Pick up♥♥♥♥♥♥ tab through the crafting recipes, throw away all the stuff that isn't used in crafting. It does annoy me that a lot of the stuff i collect isn't useful for crafting, but i can eat a lot of it so i guess it's fine. I like how the game straight up gives you all of the crafting recipes from the start. Minecraft made that change in their most recent patch because starting out with literally no directions or tutorial sucks, but in Minecraft at least you had a community or at least a group of friends who would gladly help you learn the game. This game isn't quite so lucky, which is why you're reliant on the in game help which gets you off the ground but not much further.
I ended up doing a lot of exploring and i kept finding interesting♥♥♥♥♥♥i couldn't interact with. There was a bucket with googly eyes, a giant rock with gems sticking out of it locked by a keyhole, and a spooky tree monster that threw branches at me. I really got the feeling a lot of effort went into the world but i didn't know what to do with all this stuff so i had to just keep walking. The combat is workable, but it's not great (like this game). Animals you hit will not react at all, they don't even get knocked back they just stay still and lose health. Also there is a hard limit to the world, literally just a wall where you cannot go any further. The actual area you have to explore is a tiny square.
Overall there's a decent core game here if you're willing to ignore the overhwelming flaws, but you're already on Steam with houndreds of way better games so it's really hard to bother.

TLDR: Whoever made this game deeply and truly loves the point-and-click adventure game genre.
I bought this game with horribly mediocre expectations in mind, and I could not have been more incorrect.
Truly immersive, gripping plot escapes a lot of the newer point-and-click adventure games, which consequently makes them forgettable; the ideas, while solid in concept, lack some of the critical components of cohesion that made the early point-and-clicks so personally endearing.  (e.g.:) Missing sensible characters, correct choices don’t align with player’s intuitive thinking on the problem, game lacks the atmospheric depth and detail that make it immersive, and they often include overreaching or predictable plot elements that fall somewhat flat when played.
This game dodges those pitfalls like a champ.  The storyline is novel-worthy - the immersion, tone, and general charisma of the game are superlative, while managing to strike a delicate balance between elements of adventure, horror and comedy. The (very) innovative and well-executed use of claymation lent profoundly to the overall ambiance and tone of the game.
Well-tailored, organic dialogue coupled with a streamlined and easy-to-use interface make the gameplay seamless.  Normally trading action buttons for a one-click method can trivialize the puzzles or can make the puzzles almost too abstract in an attempt to provide some challenge, but this (pleasantly) was not the case.  The developers tuned and paced the game well by balancing the simpler puzzles with more conceptually challenging ones, to the extent that brute force never feels like the only viable tool in solving the problem at hand.
I don’t like to compare the newer adventure games to the genre-defining point-and-clicks of the 90’s, but in terms of the game’s ability to engage and captivate you as the player, it’s secured a spot in my personal hall of fame next to games like King's Quest, Monkey Island, and Day of the Tentacle.  I can’t wait for Chapter 6.

I haven't played this game for a couple years, but it left enough of an impression that I think I can write up a quick review.
My short review is: Look at (and probably buy) the standalone Dead Rising 2: Off the Record instead.
Chuck Greene is the protagonist for this game, and he's the most bland protagonist I've ever seen. The protagonists in Pokemon games are deeper than him, and that's nearly impossible to accomplish. On the flipside, I've played someone's copy of Off the Record and bringing Frank West back was the best idea ever. In comparison, Frank West is far more self-centered than Chuck Greene, but that just means he's got way more depth.
Next up, DRM. Last I checked, DR2 uses the old Games for Windows Live which is now defunct. Apparently Microsoft decided they couldn't monetize their DRM, so they abandoned it and left it questionably functional on newer Windows operating systems.
There's a new Games for Windows Live that goes under a new name I've forgotten (new name + same thing = cash? who does Microsoft hire to make stupid decisions like this?), but it's completely new and incompatible with older games. Either way, some games with the old GfWL sort of work right, apparently Dead Rising 2 does most of the time, and others don't, which is why you no longer see Fable 3 in the Steam catalogue since that broke with the abandonment of GfWL.
In other words, BUY AT YOUR OWN RISK. The DRM was trash to begin with, and never got replaced when Microsoft finally put it in the trash bin where it belonged.
The Off the Record version of this game would've been a good timeless classic, but the Microsoft DRM takes the 'timeless' out of it. That DRM has been a ticking timebomb since DR2's release.

The game is great, the program is terrible.
It appears as if they found a polished look more important than solid features. It can take up to 10 minutes to find a game, and you have to manually re-queue to find an opponent. Each time the search ends with an error, you get thrown back a few menu steps.
MTG is awesome and it would be really cool to have a useable F2P client, now finally with a growing cardbase like paper magic, but they really did a poor job on the functionality of the client.
The game-mechanics are pretty well done, although there do exist some known bugs. Some parts are bad designed, for example when you search your library for a land, the interface jumps in your way and prevents you from seeing the lands you already own. Sometimes you simply have no chance to tell what exactly is going on (e.g. when someone takes over a Willbreaker with a Willbreaker, you're unable to tell which one is which).
You can create your own decks, though that part really lacks some filters. A simple text search would do wonders here.
It features the popular 2-headed giant format, but since the multiplayer part is so buggy, it takes very long for 4 people to successfully join the same game, and chances are high they will drop within minutes due to disconnect errors.
When you alt-tab, your opponents will be disconnected.
So, to sum it up:
The original game is awesome.
This computer game looks good.
This program is annoyingly bad done.
We all hope they don't leave it like that, MTG deserves better.
[Edit]
The recent Oath / Shadows Update essentially broke the game.
Multiplayer is almost impossible, as loading takes literally minutes, sometimes 10 or 20 or until you shut down the program.
Somebody had the mad idea of skipping the 2nd main phase, they implemented that as a so-called feature, which breaks the game for many decks and abilities.
To be fair, there have been some fixes, some new, good features and, of course, a bunch of cool new cards.
But the technical state of the product is so bad, it lies in ruins. As of now, this game cannot be recommended, which is why I changed my recommendation here. Let's hope they re-establish at least the pre-patch quality which was bad already.
It's still probably the best client for the best trading card game, but boy, they really worked hard to tear it apart this time.
[/edit]

This indie game is a short, quirky platform/puzzle game which took some simple ideas and made it really fun to play. Your evil brother (Big) has stolen your grandpa's magic underpants and it is up to you (Tiny) to get them back! There are 3 main skills available to you:
1. You can slice objects with a lazer beam
2. You can push objects with a rocket
3. You can pull objects with a rope
Straightforward in concept and well executed.
+ The 3D physics engine allows you to slice up anything and it is really fun figuring out how to make use of your skills to reach those hard-to-access locations. Some parts of the game require a bit of creativity.
+ Silly and funny storyline
+ Unusual and interesting music
+ Secrets and collectibles to find in each level, plus steam achievements, add replay value
- Really short - you can finish the game in a few hours.
- Gameplay can occasionally be a bit finicky and imprecise, but you can just restart from the last checkpoint if things get messed up.
I would love to see a sequel that builds on this and expands the gameplay. I'm not a fan of platformers, but I had a lot of fun with this.
