I really like the Idea of this game. Battleship combat in Space witha variety of weapons and enemys. Solving Missions as Mercenary for hire or Merchant or whatever.
The game IS fun, at least in the first 15 to 19 hours. Thus i still would recommed this game, even for it's full price.

However, after 19 hours the gameplay really runs thin on me and is still the same as it was at the beginning, just with a little bit different and statistically better weapons.
If there is more variety further in then that iks bad because after 19 hours the game should have put on it's best gameplay pants.
Overall it doesn't really do variation that well.
These are the reasons why i coulödn't keep going any more.
Equipment/Upgrades are more or less superlinear:
There is no sense in choosing a weaker weapon because you perhabs like the look or how it's mechanic works, if it's of a lower damage and a shorter range then what you actually can get you won't bother because of it's downsides.
This counts for every aspect of the upgrades, everything is rather a linear upgrade because the best things to get will be (numerical as well as trough testing them) only the best Broadsides, Turrets, Shields and so on.
On top of the the lack of variation also comes from the game having not enough actually usefull or rewarding... well rewards. drops of items or weapons. In my 19 hours with the game it dropped maybe 5 Items one of wich i then actually took on till i stopped playing because it was just the best. Or at least i think it were drops because the game sure as hell didn't really tell me.
All the thiongs that the enemys let fall is really boring loot that is also really cumbersome and stupid hard to collect. Because for some reason you can lock on to dropped cargo but if the Tractorbeam just doesn't want to collect the more viable ressource and instead insists on picking up the♥♥♥♥♥♥Nuts and Bolts then there is nothing you can really do about it aside from collectting the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing drive it elsewhere, throw it into space over there and then come back to repeat the same thing until... NO THANKS after a short while i just didn't bother with most of these drops.
Good equipment and weapons you only get in stations. That is not a bad thing per se but it hurts the gameplay fun. Why don't we have a slvage mechanism where we can salvage broken enemy ships?
Samey and thin Mission/Story:
The Story is okay. Nothing really to write home about. It gives you a direction to go for but much more then thin context for the mission it ain't. Not even the Main Ones. Every Mission is more or less the same. No matter what the description or story behind the Mission. You go somewhere, bla bla happens, enemys are there or turn up, you shot stuff, perhabs you have to deliver something and that was it. Go there, pewpew, done.
Well, there WAS one mission that was a escort mission. But that was an instant death of mission target thing. Not that i really could have done something against it. Wich incidentally feeds into the next problem.
The combatsystem is flat:
And i don't only say that because in stead of real space you actually just move on a single layer, an invisible "surfeace" in space. That in itselfe i don't mind at all.
The promisse of the combat system is really interesting at first. You have braoadsides, like a battleship should :-) , and with growing ships you own more and more turrets on top of it. In the Pause menue you can then give the different turrets commands like, only attack fighters , or that rocketturret is only suppossed to shoot at Capital ships. You can also take control over the different turrets youself but that doesn't really make much sense. With increasing Equipment you get the feeling your tactical possibilities grow. But they don't
Aside from limiting missille turrets for the bigger ships the best strategy is to give all turrets the commando only to attack what you actually lock in with the trageting system. THIS is thousand times more effective then let different turrets do different tasls.
You then skirt around the edges of the battlefield picking of the enemys piece by piece because it makes no sense to charge in and do risky stuff. That will just get you killed or addled with immense reparicosts. It doesn't bring you really much to use cover. You can hire ONE additional mercenary but those aren't much more then the turrets you already have. There is nor real strategy to the combat
And that is a problem because it is boring as hell. Okay that's a lie, it is fun in the beginning, i wouldn't had spend 19 hours in the game otherwise, and testing the different weapons did that. But in the end it is always the exact same. And that very same lack of real strategy was also was cost me that one Escort Mission.
With no viable tactics that i could have stopped the different enemys from attacking my charge. There are no weapons that do much beyound damage. There is no REAL variety.
But instead of hammering on that point i will tell you what i WISHED it had:
First off, give me more bigger ships that i can hire with different real gameplay roles (Give me a tank, a repairiship, a ship that can confuse or disrupt(e.g. debuff) enemy systems with AOE Explosions.
Let me give them a strategy and a DIRECT choice of target or missionparameters. Like the repairship´is to reapair (du) us but keep away from capital ships. The tankships is to stay close to me to catch the really heavy incoming fire in my flank. Do the same for the enemys and that would give me an incentive do actually dive into enemy ranks and aim for their specific ships.
Do the same for the weapons. Gve me a variety of functions. How cool would i have been if i could use point defence flak against missilles, streams of bulletts flying away into the sky with a chance that they miss one and some get trough. How about those same guns don't just affect missilles that attack me but an area around me. Or that ramming shield, make that actually DO SOMETHING. Because as far as it stands there is no real gain from ramming your ship into others with it, the name is totally useless in that case.
In a escort mission i would stay close to my charge together with a Tanking ship and my possibilitys would have been much greater.
It also would have given far better tools for the overall mission variety just by playing with the enemycombinations.  It would have had the chance of getting me much deeper into the frau riskl something, drive me to the edge and i imagine how i in a last bit for taking down that pesky Carrier how i ram my ship into his and win day...
or something.
As it stands the game is good for the first ten to fifteen hours or so then it becomes really samey same and uninteresting.
From the fact that i unasked loose my ship when i buy a new one over the mission to the weapons and gagdgets it simply lacks the depth to carry me further.
Wich is sad because i feel this could be more. Perhabs next time. :-P

A unique little Indie gem.  You're dropped on the shores of a Colonial New World, with absolutely no instructions about what you're suppossed to do.  Gradually, you uncover clues about the missing colonists here, and eventually figure out what events took place in this haunted landscape.  If you like mysteries, you should enjoy this release.
As you visit each new location, there's a bit of a  "rinse-and-repeat" aspect that becomes a little repetitive by the end, but it's not really a problem considering the length of the game.  It's relatively short at around 12 hours...more if you're a completionist.  Graphics and game-play are great (particularly for an Indie release), and the story-telling is, imho, exceptional.
Over-all, I thoroughly enjoyed the experience, and given that you can pick up Betrayer for ~$5 during one of the many STEAM Sales Events, I highly recommend it as a great little week-end diversion.

While not as deeply immersive as the previous iteration of the series, Bioshock 2 brings about the evolution of the city down under. The removal of a "one-weapon-only" system may confuse those who have come from the previous Bioshock, or even System Shock 2, but the implementation allows the player to wield their arsenal in a much more fluid manner, unlocking the creativity of the individual when tackling the hostile forces that populate Rapture.
Set in a completely separate area of the city, the storyline ties in somewhat awkwardly with the first's. However, it does open up a completely separate narrative that complements that of Bioshock in a non-invasive manner whilst keeping its own personality for the regions you explore throughout the game.
While Singleplayer contains a storyline that is not as short as its predecessor, nor longer than my attention span would allow; the unfortunate presence of Sofia Lamb as an incessantly nagging and consistently disapproving mother-like antagonist nearly drove me to uninstall the game as she does not shut the ♥♥♥♥ up. At all. Ever. Fortunately if you've developed the ability to drown out anyone that is either bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane or more annoying than sticking your genitalia in a jar filled with starved mosquitoes; you'll be able to enjoy what the rest of the game offers you.
In comparison to the previous Bioshock, they improved a great many things but, unfortunately, broke a few things that were fine previous (Like menacing and horribly-mentally-unstable adversaries, or believable and relatable NPC characters). Replayability is left to personal preference, and the multiplayer experience is pretty much dead and buried at this point.
4 Little Sisters Worth Protecting / 5. Get it if you like Bioshock's art style, single player shooters with slightly-more-than-decent storylines, or feeling like a badass with a giant metallic♥♥♥♥♥♥♥screwdriver for a hand.

Ah, Hatred… the game that was first in the progress of being greenlit, then quickly removed by Valve because it was deemed too controversial and then finally re-added (with some sort of apology). Given the history and success of controversial games like Grand Theft Auto and Carmageddon that can only be a good thing, right? Well…, not always apparently.
While games like Grand Theft Auto and Carmageddon actually introduced some new - or at least improved – ideas to their genres, despite being controversial, this unfortunately doesn’t apply to Hatred. In reality Hatred is just another isometric action game. Here are some of the reasons why:
The story is straightforward, and not very deep: you had it with society and then just decide to murder everyone around you, unleashing Armageddon. You will start at your own home and then work your way through the city of New York. There sometimes are smaller, more linear levels where you have to just escape and move to the next place. But not without killing some people in the progress, of course.
Now, I haven’t yet finished the game but I think I’ve seen enough of it to write a review. Unless there’s something that changes up the gameplay drastically 3/4th into the game, I think the review should be quite accurate.
Since the style is meant to be realistic you won’t find any weird, fantasy weaponry in this game. You will, for example, use pistols, shotguns, machine guns and several types of grenades in your quest to wipe every man and woman off of the face of the earth. As expected, you will be able to find better, more powerful weapons later in the game where you have to face more and tougher enemies.
In order to not get hurt you can always try to hide behind and inside buildings and other solid objects (enemies will sometimes try to do the same) but this is no guarantee to not get hurt because enemies often come from all sides and the bullets can literally fly anywhere you look.
Speaking of enemies: the difficulty seems to randomly spike up at times. What seemed so easy at first somehow instantly becomes hard(er). I encountered this several times during my sessions and I don’t think it’s me (but hey, I might not know myself as well as I thought).
Wounded people can also be executed which will (partially) restore your health bar. Later on in the game they will become harder to pull off, though. This is due to the fact you have to keep a careful eye on your surroundings as more and more enemies will appear and they will also take more damage before they die. Plus, you still can get shot while executing someone.
Still, it’s a cool concept and the fact that the game sometimes switches to a third person view (showing the killing in much more detail) keeps the game from becoming too much of a borefest.
I do think the camera is a little too close to the character. At times it certainly would’ve been nice if we could zoom in or out ourselves to get a better overview of what’s happening and where. The minimap generally does a good job at trying to show you this information, but I’m afraid that it sometimes isn’t enough and you just want to see things for yourself.
There are also vehicles at your disposal, like police cars and SWAT cars. However, they won’t be of much use to you since the controls are just horrible. You have to use the left stick to gas and brake (pushing forward and backward) and the right stick to steer left and right. Sounds easy, right? Nope. I think people will eventually get used to them, but they’re anything but intuitive. I guess the reason for this is because otherwise you would drive just around creating havoc and as a result it might make the game (a little) easier.
Technically the game is more than okay, but the framerate does fluctuate regularly. This might be because of the implemented physics system because otherwise I have no idea what could be causing it. It’s not the most technically advanced game I’ve ever played so maybe with some extra months of polishing we would’ve been able to play it with a rock solid framerate. A missed opportunity.
The songs are generally what you would expect in a game like this: it’s hard - metal-like - music and it fits the mood just perfectly. The sound effects are solid, too, and the voice acting ranges from okay to mediocre, but given everything that might just be a good thing. It certainly keeps things lighter, although it remains a very bleak game nevertheless.
Ah yes, the graphics… This is where the game really shines and I’m not being sarcastic here. As you can see by looking at the screenshots everything is shown in black and white, while other elements (blood, some types of lights and explosions, for example) still show up in their original colors. If you’ve ever seen Sin City then you have a good idea of how it will look. Everything is nicely detailed and animated, except for some of the faces, but this is usually only seen up close when the game switches to the third person view and is therefore not a big deal. Overall it’s a very good looking game.
I never expected to say this, but as you can see I became bored about 3/4th into the game. It’s by no means a terrible or bad game, but it all becomes repetitive way too soon, resulting into boredom. Then again, I guess that’s what one should expect from a game in this genre. I’ve been told the game lasts about 4-5 hours and if you play on Extreme you can expect it to be twice that figure.
So ultimately not very long but long enough. I might finish it up later, but for now I’ve seen enough.
Hatred certainly looked interesting the first time I saw it in motion and I was definitely intrigued by all the controversy. After having played it myself I can hereby tell you that they’ve created a good, but still very repetitive and shallow action game. I think the developer tried too hard to create something controversial that - in combination with the depressing tone and setting - ends up looking unique and pretty, but at the same time is just not very much fun to play.
Grab it to see what it’s all about, but, unless you’re a hardcore action game lover, it’s recommended to wait for a sale.

Beyond Earth, as of right now, is a pretty bare bones Civilization game. If anything it feels like just a super beefy expansion to Civ 5 rather than a stand alone game.
I won't get into the intricacies of the game as other reviewers have done, since they've done it better and far earlier than I.
But I have to say that for me personally, the theme was enough to sell it to me. I've always wanted to get into Civilization because of all of its praise, and I did get Civ 5, and played 1 game. Literally 1 game. And I never touched it again. This is because of the theme. I am simply not partial to starting with sticks and ending with modern military. Or anything in between frankly. All the techs and flavor text is boring to me, and frankly hurts my head to read.

MOBA meets WoW Arena and contains the best of both. The games are reasonably short and very, VERY exciting. I'm just a couple of hours in but the complexity and depth is evident. The characters a very well designed optically and - as far as I can tell right now - gameplaywise. Not too Asian (many games seem to do that lately) and well, the occasional big patch of chest hair. The reward system is motivating, giving you ingame currency or loot crates for daily and weekly quests as well as achievements (simpler ones like "Add a friend" as well as harder ones like "Reach a total champion level of 200"). Of course, there's money to be made for an F2P title, so the ingame shop let's you buy your way to the pretty cosmetics and additional champions. It's far, far away from a money grab though.
Sadly, the game suffered some server problems in the beginning which were due to a power outage on the server provider's side - so nothing the developers could fix. As of 11/10/2017, it seems to be resolved though.

PROS
+ Great art style with cardboard and claymation
+Difficult yet rewarding puzzles with nonsensical "point and click" logic
+A dark, unsettling story that grows on you (might not be great for kids)
CONS
- At the time of this review, the game is not finished (5/6 epsiodess have been completed)
-This game has a very long deveelopment time due to the art style and claymaation
Overall, I would recommend this game to those that enjoy  difficult puzzles and odd and original stories.

This War of Mine sells itself mainly as a game about making emotional choices and following characters through a story, and it definitely is that. However, as a survival fan, I've found an incredible amount of replayability in this game that I would not have expected.
If you are interested in the experience of war and the disturbing choices that you have to make to survive, you'll enjoy playing through this game multiple times with different "parties" of characters,
There's a nice sense of accomplishment in exploring all the locations on the map and making it through the 30-45 days that it takes to survive the war. (It varies by character group, meaning that each group of characters has a slightly different difficulty.)
I figured that after I figured out how to survive in this game I would finish it and put it away. Not at all. I've been coming back to it quite frequently as a casual survival game. It's very well-balanced, and even once you figure out the mechanics of the game, it's still difficult to keep all of your characters healthy physically and mentally. If you don't, they don't get
and will also start to argue with each other or have trouble sleeping. I have tons of fun trying different crafting, scavenging, trading, and combat strategies, and still never kill innocent people in all my hours of playing. I'm slowly working on surviving with each combination of characters just for the satisfaction of getting a nice little "survived" badge on each one in the opening screen.
With all of the different combinations of characters to start with, and randomization of the areas you explore, there's a nice balance of consistency and surprise. For example, in one game a hotel might be occupied by a well-armed gang who tortures people; in another, an eccentric guy lives there and will trade with you, and the rest of the building is abandoned.
One of my pet peeves about the game is that you can only save at the beginning of each day (making it harder to save scum). However, this also makes it a good game to play in short bursts. You only need to use one hand for the mouse, which is nice. I've found it the ideal thing to play while watching Netflix shows I've already seen on my other monitor, etc. etc.
So whether you want to get really emotionally involved in a first playthrough, or want a balanced survival game that will keep you interested for quite a while-♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have 89 hours somehow--definitely check this game out. You can also support an indie studio, and if you want, buy an extra DLC that adds cool graffiti to the game and supports a charity for children affected by war.
tl;dr: do you want to scavenge for parts to make moonshine? shoot a deserting soldier and steal the food in his fridge? slowly die of depression and gunshot wounds after protecting your herb garden from midnight raiders? this is your game

Bioshock is a wonderful game. Rapture as a setting is second to none in my opinion, and it was executed flawlessly. The scares are largely subtle, and that will ensure you're kept on your toes for the duration of your stay under the sea. Please do it justice and turn the lighting down to where the game recommends, it's suggested for a reason.
There is a caveat. In my opinion, Bioshock isn't a full-on horror game. Certainly you're going to be anxious while playing due to the atmosphere and what can seem like neverending waves of enemies, but in terms of horror it pales in comparison to the likes of the Amnesia series.
Combat can only be described as "Ludacrisly fun". Everything has weight to it. The powers in the game (known as Plasmids) all bring something useful to the table. In my mind none of them are useless. For sure you're going to end up defaulting to a couple, but mixing it up and trying something else isn't a handicap like it is in a lot of games. Ammo is scarce in Rapture, and you'll always be fighting to keep a decent supply going. You'll end up using weapons you never would have looked at before just to stay alive. This adds another layer to the survivalist-horror type affair.
Bioshock does have a few downsides to it, however. ADAM (a currency in the game) seems far to common if you're going down the good ending route. By the end of the game in my last playthrough, I was sitting on around 7-800 spare with nothing to spend it on. Don't get me wrong, in the early game you're going to have near nothing, but mid-to-late game you're swimming in it.
The crafting in the game seems unnecessary to say the least. It's critical in a single mission and (iirc) you never have to use it again. You'll pick up various components from around the city and can craft ammo and the two types of health kits used in the game.
Overall, Bioshock is an absolutely wonderful game. If you can afford it I wholeheartedly recommend it. Everyone should play it at least once, if nothing else for the stellar atmosphere and worldbuilding.

I highly recomend Betrayer, for the following reason: You can have a Bow.
All In-jokes I have with my friends aside, I just spent ten hours playing Betraying, enjoying every minute of it. Could I have finished it faster? Probobly. Should I have? No, since I enjoyed exploring, trying new tactics, and just generally goofing around while playing it.
Looking at the reviews of Betrayer on the popular gaming news sites would give someone the impression that Betrayer is an okay game at best, filled with repetative, boring moments at the end. IGN gave it a 5/10 because of that.
I wholeheartedly disagree, for multiple reasons.
+First off, IGN are the corprate ♥♥♥♥♥s who literally give every ♥♥♥♥♥♥ CoD game a '10/10, it was okay', and shill Mt. Dew and Doritos at every chance they can, so they can go ♥♥♥♥ off.
+Secondly, there was not a single moment in the game that I didn't enjoy. I died a few times, sure, but I never got upset at it.
+I've never felt my heart race while playing a video game before, but Betrayer did that for me. Crouching in the shadows, hearing the Loon calls of the savage Burned Men getting louder as they got closer and searched for me, I couldn't help but grow anxious, and when their calls turned to War-Whoops (well, louder, more agressive Bird Calls...) I felt a shivver run down my spine.
+I've never felt such satisfaction with completing Side-Quests and hunting for Treasure, in any video game, but Betrayer made me feel very, very satisfied. Each time I found a chest filled with gold, or dug up a nice weapon (I'm looking at you, Trickster's Pistol!) I very very satisfied, and very happy.
+The game, despite having map markers to show where Treasure/NPCs/Totems or whatever can be found, doesn't hold your hand and give you a big blot on your compas saying 'HERE IT IS, DON'T POKE AROUND AND LOOK, HERE IS THE ITEM!'. The thrill of discovery felt genuine, much like in The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, unlike The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion or The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, or any other first person game out there.
+The sound quality of the game was great, I never once muted it out of annoyance
+Unique stealth mechanics with the wind. Waiting for the wind to blow so I can dash out of cover and get up close to cut the throat of a Spaniard was very, very thrilling and fun. More games need to do this.
+Sensible controls. The G key throws Tomahawks, the B key throws Grenades, the F key is for activating NPCs/Items, C causes you to croutch walk, and Left Shift causes you to sprint. WASD for movement... The people who made this obviously know what they are doing, and designed it well.
+Fun Storyline. No spoilers, but the plot was awesome!
+Realistic weaponry. Arrows have an arc to their flight, Crossbows are powerful enough to oneshot a man in heavy armor, and the blackpowder weaponry has realistic damage - A good pistol shot at close range to the torso would drop any man. Muskets aren't horiffically inacurate at close range as well, so that is nice.
+Your Choices actually mater. Not spoiling anything, but they mater!
Now, the issues I have with the game:
-I wish the Maid in Red had a voice actress.
-Uhh...
All in all, Amazing game. 11/10, would (and will!) play again.

Every ♥♥♥♥♥♥ CoD game gets a "10/10, it was okay I guess" from the borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ivory Tower gaming 'Journalists' at IGN, but this game only gets a 5/10? Now this game is solid FUN! Period! I'm an emotional gamer so for me what makes or breaks a game is the FEELING a game emotes. It does not have to be perfect next gen graphics, or super solid gameplay, or the most original story ever. If it feels right and gives enjoyement then it's a success for me. Now obviously all previously mentioned things add up to the overall feel of a game. However they are like spice and are not the sole source of the 'magic' of a game. The cornerstone needs to be set right with a game or the whole building will start sinking crooked. For me this elusive thing in games is the feeling they magically either have or don't have. Take this game for example. It does not have award winning graphics or plot or even character development. It does not have a particularly interesting story and the game makes no pretentions of it either. This game is not trying to be serious about itself and that my friends is what made a movie called tremors such a great fun flick in it's time. Solid practical effects, avoiding tongue in cheek direction or story for that matter is what made that movie have a great FEEL to it. Same here. By looking on this game's merits on paper by all means this should be a flop, but it's completely and utterly the opposite! This is why people betting on money and calculating companies trying to bank a bazillion of whatever currency they can get a hold of, will never see the light of day how to make a good solid fun entertainment! All I can say is, try this game out if you are a person like me and care for the overall feeling of a gameplay experience. The good thing this game has on paper is it's soundtrack :D Perfect campy fun in a great way!
However no game is perfect and hardly is this title here. This game is EASY to get into, but after awhile it becomes a grindtastic repetitive romp with not so good AI. Beware of these things if you are easily turned off. It did not turn me off so much because the overall easiness and feeling the game churns out kept me at it enjoying getting better ships and weaponry. I am a casual gamer and I appreciate when a game is this accessible. However of course it would be great if this game had more depth and polish into it as it progresses or the main quest line is exhausted. The devs could maybe make DLC for this title? Anyway I'm certainly looking for a sequel that tackles more with this titles shortcomings. I loved freelancer and was immediately at home with this one. Besides freelancer was not so much more complex gameplaywise as this one is. Fond memories tend to get golden in time. I liked this one, so maybe give it a cautious try if you liked freelancer..

It is.
I don't know what pulled me in more: The incredible soundtrack, which while somewhat short, never ever got old and always pumped me up for taking on a whole enemy flotilla single-handedly while being completely out-classed and out-gunned. Or the visuals which are stunning from the very beginning.
This game has hit a perfect spot of being scifi and western: a playable Firefly. It keeps you enthralled even after you finish the story. The developers really hit spot on on the idea of purely enjoyable gameplay. It's not complex and convoluted. It's not necessarily simple either. you have to think about how you approach your enemy. What weapons are best, do you go with massive firepower or shield and hull strength? A middle ground? How can a small cruiser take on a dreadnought 5 times it's size without getting obliterated?
There are a couple pseudo-downsides, other than the (epic) short soundtrack,
The first somewhat downside to this game is that because it's their first one (as far as i can tell), they weren't able to make it bigger, or the story longer. There isn't much character development, however they put a LOT of thought into what was there, such as if you listen to the alien languages, you can actually pick up what words mean what in the translations. I'm a language nerd and that scored MAJOR points for me.
The other downside is that you have to get used to it not being a 'realistic' space game, since you are playing on a flat plane, you cannot do spins or attack from above or below as you would imagine being able to in theoretical 'real' space combat.
But the gameplay is so fun that, at least for myself, i completely discarded that particular misgiving and simply had fun with it.
This is quite honestly one of the best games i've played in YEARS, i can't recommend it more.
This is one of the few games where not only do i WANT more, i NEED more.

Would I recommend it?
YES
Is it as great as the hype suggest?
NO

Hatred is a top down(ish) 3rd person shoot 'em up action, dark-themed psychotic game. I was pleasantly surprised by the variety of options available. The graphics of the game are dark, where the shadows and textures propel a dark atmosphere and tone. The music and voice effects really help set this tone, making the player feel uncomfortable or ill at ease. The voice effects of people
screaming also add to this dark, unsettling feel. The difficulty settings are well done, where harder difficulties will present a challenge.
The story is pretty much nonexistent. Your character feels that society has failed him, and decided to go on a killing rampage to the death. It doesn't hold back; there is no comedy or satire, only pure bloodshed. Because there is no build up or lead in as to why the character became this way, it is hard to immerse yourself in the story,
or relate to his decisions. There is no pulling back for him, just pure anger. The players not  able to stop what is happening, which  may give some a feeling of distaste or horror. Many of the people being killed have no way to defend themselves. As the game progresses,
you start to battle soldiers, and it begins to feel less about doing evil acts, and more about fighting threatening opponents.
The weapons each carry weight, which is nice to see. Adding an option to upgrade weapons would have been a nice addition, as it would have provided a connection from the player to the character, such as having quicker reload times, for example. The enemies will in time shoot you from off screen, and they will start to attack in a horde, which can be overwhelming, as it is supposed to be, but there is no real way to thin them out with ease. Because you get overwhelmed so fast, there is no option to fall back to a fortified location, and no mines or traps you are able to place. This can be good if your looking for something harder in this genre other wise it will be more of a annoyance.
The level design is beautiful. It's expansive enough, with plenty of places to take cover, and the areas feel like what they are supposed to. A neighborhood feels like a neighborhood. I never felt lost, and the directives plus the minimap were fairly straight forward. Walls, cars, buildings, provide variety in escape access, or availability to create your own path, which I appreciate. Its always nice to blow your own door into a wall.

The only way to replenish resources such as health is to perform an execute move, more often successful on civilians than soldiers. If you hold off on killing civilians, you can save them for when you need extra health. They become more valuable as a resource or medkit, rather than just a stain on the wall as they are at the beginning of the game.
What this game nails is the overall tone of painful, almost unbearable discomfort that comes from perhaps feeling of 'this could happen in this society; that could be me'. The last thing you would want to do would be a civilian with this character coming down the road at you. Seeing the evil he depicts, the actions that he takes, causes the player to really think that this sort of thing really exists in the world.
Performance wise, and content wise, this game is great. If you like top down shooters, absolutely this game is for you. The weapons feel heavy and good; there are a few weapons and movement issues- not gamebreaking but sometimes inconvenient which I go  more into during the video. The story and the theme is dark; it's in your face, loud, and extreme, and has been flushed out perfectly to do such. This is one of the best top down shooters I have played. The theme may be hard for some to get past, but I found it very worthwhile in gameplay.

For some reason you were keeping a pair of your grandpa's dirty underpants until your big brother stole them, wore them as a hat, and gained super powers. Now you need to laser, claw, and rocket your way through a desert and accompanying pyramid to get your grandpa's underpants back. There is also a lack of realism that some of the things civilization has discovered on earth somehow does not carry over into the new empire on the new planet and you need to research techs to get things like spies. Speaking of spies the Covert Ops in BE are ridiculously overpowered and I can win the game as ARC easily by just converting everyone else's cities to my empire. Another major problem is that the game goes from very hard to very easy incredibly fast so the first person to get affinity levels basically wins the game. Overall I would not reccomend this game but if you want a strategy empire building game CIv V is INCREDIBLE.

I've finished the game back in version 2.0 (or 2.5). I played vanilla for a long time, and started adding mods slowly. After finishing the plot, I couldn't stand all the issues and quirks of the game and quit. It was, overall, an annoying and hurtful experience.
I played a lot more with version 3.5, and in this playthrough I added more mods as the plot progressed. This made the game become extremely fun, since the game and mods were now much more stable and developed. Slowly adding more mods felt like I was buying/adding/unlocking upgrades.
I had lots of fun and ignored the plot halfway through it, but there were still quirks and rough edges that made a lot of things take days - if not weeks - to achieve or obtain. So I took a long break.
After 4.0 and HoL hit, I added even more mods and finished the game again, and now I'm having a blast and actually finishing constructing stations and growing a trade and a military fleet.
All this thanks to SETA and a mod that makes CapShips jump around faster without refueling. Those two things alone make the game playable on a less insane level.
I mean, if you wait for buses for 60 minutes in real life, you don't really want to wait more than half an hour for your fleet to refuel, traverse Jump Gates, and jump to you..only to wait all that again once you're done doing things on the System you were at.
This game was a crazy attempt by Egosoft at developing something totally new for them, and an amazing display of how modders can completely change, fix and turn quirks and horrible issues completely around.
The living universe is, as always, beautiful. The NPCs messaging you about issues with their budget, or checking with your Architect the state of your new station's construction, or even the silly detail of mass traffic around stations and highways will truly make your mind wander like very few other games can. Even with all the quirks (mostly fixed), you can't help but feel the love and dedication of developers and artists when flying around stations and looking at their tiny details.
It's really insane how such a small team have produced so many inspiring stuff over so many years. I can only hope that Ego hears the community and make even better stuff from now on.

This is a very rough ride. It rattles your perspective and makes you look at yourself (and fellow man) in a different light. The atmosphere is thick with intensity, the gameplay is simple and complicated at the same time, and the sense of loss and danger feels very real.
However, I noticed a big…not a flaw per say, but an issue with your second or third play through. After you figure out how to play the game and after you go through one gut-wrenching story, when you try to play it again it becomes…very, very easy. The first time I played this, my heart broke. The second time, I already knew the game mechanics (which upgrades are worthless, who to not let into my safe house, ETC) and I was able to push through the game with very few losses or real hardships. That is fine because as a game you want to eventually beat it, but it is sad in that the initial intensity of this game can’t really be felt multiple times.
So, yes it is an amazing intense and sympathetic view to the horrors of war, but your first play through will be probably be your most memorable one.

Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey Remastered is an addictive spelling game - this remastered edition came about quite quick, given that the original release was only brought out on Steam a little under a year ago in November 2014. This remastered version hit the store front in August of 2015.
The main gameplay element in Letter Quest is spelling words in order to deal damage to your foes. You play in a side scrolling dungeon crawl type environment, and you have to defeat a number of enemies in order to reach the treasure at the end of the dungeon.  You have fifteen letters each round which are randomly selected for you and you just need to spell out a word, each of the letters have their own special rarity, so if you stick some Ws and Xs in your words, they will end up doing more damage compared to sticking to simple words like "Door" or something, very similar to the likes of the rules in Scrabble or Words with Friends.  Some of the monsters have special abilities, weaknesses and strengths, for instance, one enemy might not take any damage from any words which contain the letter E, whilst others may take double, triple, or sometimes twenty times more damage from words containing other letters. Some enemies may use a special ability and make your letters also have a debuff on, such as rendering them useless and dealing zero damage from then, poisoning them, duplicating them, or stopping you from using them all together. All of these combined with the other strengths and weaknesses of the monsters can really lead to some interesting runs.
Each run through a dungeon you are also collecting gems from defeating the enemies, completing small quests and looting the jewels at the end of the dungeon. You can in turn use these gems to upgrade your character with health points, more damage, and dodge chance increases and many more. This allows you to build your character however you want. Along with a huge selection of weapons to choose from as you unlock more from either progressing in the story mode, completing quests and challenges. There is so much to unlock in Letter Quest that you can be farming gems for hours and still not have it all unlocked.  Each stage has four levels of difficulty; completing each stage grants a star, and rewards you with more gems. You can also replay previously completed dungeons if you want to farm more gems too.
Letter Quest has a really nice looking aesthetic too; the graphics are very simple 2D, but the games own unique style really shines through. The UI is really nicely designed too; obviously you are going to be spending a lot of your time looking at the letters at your disposal, so it's nice that the game also includes a number of different skins for the letter's style, letting you change it up once you get bored of one style.
Even though the game classes the main mode of the game to be "story mode", there isn't really any story at all. There is absolutely no back story, or any dialog in the game, and to be honest, I wasn't all that bothered about the lack of a plot either.
I found Letter Quest to be a fairly difficult game; but as you get playing, you get more and more used to it, practice makes perfect. If you are good at games such as Scrabble, or you know plenty of fancy big words, you'll excel in this game. The RPG element is not exactly difficult to master, you can create any sort of character build that takes your fancy, I focused mainly on health regeneration because my fights tended to last a bit longer due to only being able to get six letter words most of the time - there are builds which focuses on farming gems, doing massive amounts of damage, or just simply not taking any damage at all.
Completing Letter Quest with the majority of the stages being completed on all four difficulties, took me just over twelve hours to finish. I felt that it was a really good length, and given the amount of replay ability, I can see Letter Quest easily hitting the fifteen hour mark if you fancy taking on the endless mode.
Letter Quest can be played entirely with a keyboard, since you are typing out the words. You can also play the entire game without touching the keyboard and purely using the mouse too. I also spent a lot of time using my Steam controller on this game, and that works perfectly with the trackpads, there are a few community made binding sets which all work well too; so if you have a steam controller, give it ago with Letter Quest.
I fully enjoyable myself whilst playing Letter Quest - this is a casual game but will completely suck you in and get your addicted straight away. I and my partner played this game together for the most part, and minutes soon turned into hours and hours soon turned into long sessions ploughing through the levels together. It's a game which you can quite easily keep installed on your machine and jump into every now and again too. There is very little to learn in terms of the gameplay as it purely uses your own spelling knowledge. Letter Quest's regular price is £5,59, which in itself is an absolute bargain for the amount of content on offer, and the quality of it - so if you can get it any less than that, pick it up in a heartbeat as you won't find a better word based game on Steam.

When you are confronted with the choice of doing the right thing or saving your own neck, what do you choose?
I've played a lot of survival based games and I've never felt bad for any of the immoral choices I tend to make to keep myself alive. In fact, I think its safe to say I usually make the immoral choice because 1) Its a video game and 2) In a lot of games, the immoral choice is often highly rewarded. This is not always the case in "This War of Mine". Every decision you make (good or bad) has the potential to bring absolute disaster to you and the rewards are usually no more then a scrap of food, a bandage or maybe some ammunition.
You find yourself confronted with the issue of not only your characters morality, but your own. Setting aside the fact that the game characters can get depressed, this game has a way of making YOU (the player) feel bad for what you've done. The first person I ever killed in this game made me actually stop playing just so I could absorb what happened and how I never wanted it to happen again.
I entered a run down house, it was the first occupied building I had ever looted. I quickly noticed it was inhabited and starting sneaking around, grabbing up all the items not owned by the residents. Realizing the one thing I really needed (food of course) was not among them, I decided it was time to steal. Needless to say, I got caught opening their fridge.
Running into the basement I attempt to leave without a confrontation, only to find I had never unblocked the basement exit and I was now stuck between a locked door, and a guy who wanted to kill me for stealing his food. I did the only thing I could think of and began to smash him with my crowbar. Clicking somewhat madly I didn't notice until it was to late that he was surrendering instead of fighting to the death. To late his cry reachs my ears as my final blow sends him crashing to the floor, followed shortly by his sobbing lady friend. Murderor, she cries, why did you have to kill him? Still in the heat of the moment one thought enters my twisted excuse of a human mind, "No witnesses". A moment later she lies next to her fallen lover as I stand over their bodies in triumph before I come to my senses.
O god, what have I done...
Determined to right the wrongs I have commited I decide to try and play as honourably as I can. Never steal from or kill civilians, avoid conflict at all cost and help out at every chance I get. That lasted until winter came...

Rebel Galaxy is a indie developed game best summarized by calling it a space trucking simulator. Think of Elite Dangerous in the ocean. The games combat takes place on more of or less of a two dimensional plane. In the the way that Assassins Creed IV Black Flag naval combat has become a bit of a standard. However fighter ships can go a bit above or below the playing field. Of course there are contingencies that allow you to deal with these inconveniences such as automated scatter turrets that can have a tactical assignments selected while you are trying to focus aiming your broadside hardpoints.
The game has faction warfare that evokes a feeling of Mercenaries. Some factions are needlessly hostile to you to begin with while others can be swayed through favors or pushed away by other actions.
There is no ship customization other than changing hardpoints, shields and deflectors. Or strait up buying a new ship. The game, despite its open nature, has a very linear progression. I see only 2 ways to go. You either become better at killing other ships or pick a frigate that is better at not dying whilst transporting cargo. Essentially be a bounty hunter bent on protecting the citizenry of the known universe. Be a space trucker and keep your nose clean at least in areas controlled by the militia or become space pirate. This is not necessarily a bad thing but in all honesty it feels very shallow and has a feeling (the entire experience) of being a tutorial to Elite Dangerous. Which again is fine, so long as you expect that going in.
There are commodities at each station. In essence you could just play the market to progress and get ahead. There are often events going on like a tech boom or famine where buying low and selling high should be a strait forward affair.
The game features a custom soundtrack option. And no, I don't mean like putting on a playlist from spotify. You actually set up custom pathing. As in, choose from list A for battles, List B for Exploration etc etc.. However the game features an OST that I consider quite superb. Its consists of some amalgam of slide guitar space cowboy jams and 90's grunge. Which feels not to far to removed from the serious/satire ratio that Borderlands possesses.

An eerie atmosphere of dread and desolation hangs over the deserted colony. The world is painted in stark black and white with splashes of blood red - just like hope, all color fades.
Beneath the grim horror of Betrayer is a nicely challenging FPS with basic stealth elements. Defend yourself with muskets, pistols, bows, crossbows, throwing hatchets, black powder bombs and a basic knife melee attack. The survivor should use a stealthy bow to kill from a distance, aim for the head, use trees as cover, blast armored foes with black powder, and throw hatchets into the ribs for an instant kill on charging enemies.
PROS:
+ Dark atmosphere
+ Great sound design on gun shots, monster sounds, the chilling Night realm, terrifying breathing, and screaming totems
+ Unique art style
+ Color can be turned on if wanted
+ Hefty Muskets and powder Pistols with nice reload animations (powder, ball, ramrod)
+ Ammo is plentiful if you have the money
+ First Person Shooting feels great mid game and late
+ Stealth is powerful and aided by sound hiding wind gusts and damage increases for stealth hits
+ Tragic backstory told through Lost Souls, torn Notes, Clue items, and conversation
+ Colonial setting is creepy AND historical
+ Enemies are threatening and scary, the first time I heard a Loon call I was surprised by what was making it
+ Bells allow the player to transform the world into Night and re-explore the same area with different enemies and loot
+ Different enemy types: Conquistadors (Bow/Rifle/Sword Conquistadors, Armored Giants), Burning Indian Bowmen, Ash People (not in the game much), Spiders (not in the game much), Spectres (Human Skull Mask/Deer Skull Mask), Skeletons.
+ The final act of the game was horrifying, getting closer and closer to the evil heart of the woods and finding out what happened there
CONS:
- You fight basic Conquistadors, Skeletons and Indian Bowmen for 90% of the game.
- On the hardest difficulty the beginning areas can be VERY difficult with the weak starter weapons and weak stealth
- Enemies can rarely detect the player through solid objects such as bushes and fort walls
- Stealth is impossible in some parts of the game (the enemies auto-detect you in certain events)
- Stealth has no detection meter, only a simple sound and you are easily spotted without stealth buffing charms
- Lots of backtracking if you are a completionist
- Hidden best charm in the game is given by the Maiden in Red only if you answer mulitple choice questions a certain way (go for practical uses for gifts you give her) and it is never indicated you could unlock anything
- No voice acting
- No music at all, even slight atmospheric music with colonial instruments would have been neat, or Indian chants
- The story is basic with no huge revelations
- The main game does not have enough enemies to complete the 1000 Kills and 200 Stealth Kills achievements, you must grind respawning enemies
- With no music you'd want more atmospheric sounds, or weather or something
- Never felt much emotional connection, just a sense of curiosity
- Weapons sold at the merchant chest are almost never worth buying, too expensive for the upgrade until the "Common" vaiants
- Variety of areas is a bit basic
- Short-ish game
I played on the Hardest difficulty and did 100% of the achievements for this review.

Slowly you`re sneaking through grass. You´re enemy is near and shows you his back. You can see the conquistador armour gleaming in the sun and covered by the wind you`re only 2 steps away, but then you hear a loud grunt and fastly you recognize you miss another conquistador. Using your crossbow you hope you will get the one in front before they attack as two. You get the one, but it takes time to reload the crossbow. Too much time, the other conquistador reach you, after getting hit, the crossbow is ready again, you fire, you hit, he goes down.  Eased you look up, while the wind surrounds you.
The Year is 1604 .
Welcome to Betrayer.
You were send to the new world to found out what happened to a british Colony. Early you  will be attacked.  Attacked by Conquistadors, who seem to be obsessed. Soon you recognize thatthe Spanish were not the only Danger in this Region. Finding the Fort of the Colony empty without any soul, except 2 Ash Corpses you have to ask yourself one Question: What happened to the Colonists?
Betrayer is a very interesting First Person Shooter Game. Your Weapons are Bows, Pistols, musketry and knives. No Rocket Launcher, no BFG, no Lasersword and no Kitty Bombs. This game got a special Graphicstyle that creats a unique atmosphere. And i mean in a haunting way. Do you remember a walk in a forrest? Remember the the Birds Singing, the Sun between the trees, the wind playing with leafs. How they rustle? Yes? Congratulations, now you are in BETRAYER. I think my Forrest Walks will never be the same. *sigh*
Also you are able to play this game in Black/White Style, which is special, or in colours.
Anyway, on your search for the Colonists you have to fight. You can do it the direct way "HEY GUYS I`M HEEEEEERE!" or the Snake way. Sneaking. So if you`re sneaking you can do it with the help of the wind. No joke! This is a special point of this game. The wind covers your steps and the enemy can`t hear you coming, if you come from behind, hey who would sneak in front, eh? No, you don`t have Jedi Power forget it. This is 1604, not "far far away in a distant galaxy". Well you can decide on your own, how you survive and believe me ... the Conquistadors are not the badest Guys in this game.
Sure, there is very much to read, the Story of the colonists are written words, not moviepictures, but if you ever read an exciting book, you will know what i mean.
So, follow the hints on a map, solve the mysterys and stay alive in a unique looking game. Always have your weapons loaded. It can take too much time to load if you are attacked. And don`t forget your real life. Take a walk in the forrest. Listen to the Birds and the rustling leafs in the sunlight. Enjoy.

Crafted from clay and ingenuity, The Dream Machine is a point-and-click adventure through the mind. The world - or worlds as it quickly becomes - presented here is undeniably stunning, though the misshapen forms of its people and the engrossing plot at hand distract from that beauty. This is a game that demands that the urgency of the plot be forgotten from time to time in favor of stopping to take in the sights. However the novelty of its art style isn\'t the only thing The Dream Machine has to offer. Some of its puzzles are absolutely brilliant and though a few did seem to come out of left field, none felt absurd or out of place. A single mouse button takes care of all player actions making the controls very accessible, but also equally restrictive. Frustration is often born of not having enough tools to come up with a variety of possible solutions or to tell the game what you would like to do, and this is a hole The Dream Machine tends to fall into.
The game is very much a work in progress. It\'s still somewhat buggy and is missing its concluding chapter, but it is very playable even without those finishing touches. The individual chapters are a bit short, but they are priced to their playtime, so it\'s hard to complain about that. Having played five out of the the six intended chapters, the story so far is satisfying, as is each chapter taken on its own, even if it\'s all currently ended with a cliffhanger.

Well, after 85 hours, this is what I have to say.
The game is bland, and is really just an attempt from Firaxis to fill their coffers. The game is very similiar to Civ 5, both in gameplay, and in the fact that the only way it'll get better is with DLC.
Affinities are a new way of showing how mankind will progress in the future, and they are really the core of the game. Units, buildings, and even victory conditions revolve around them. While this seems interesting at first, you'll start to realize that it actually makes the factions very bland. All of the factions must choose which affinity they will go down. They don't have their own ideas or philosophies as in SMAC, instead, they have to choose one of the three templates. While it seems like ideologies made the same impact in Civ 5, they didn't. In Civ 5, you had history to teach you how every leader is going to play. Montezuma would try to take over the world, Brazil would be peaceful and culture loving, etc. With no history behind this story, only a small lore, it makes the leaders all feel like bland politicians. Finally, affinites aren't really things you choose from the start of the game and say "I'll go down Harmony." No, it's your resources that dictate which way you'll go, which is realistic, but you would think a future society wouldn't be dictated by an environment.
Virtues are a nice addition to the mix. They are basically social policies, but will reward you if you want to go and choose every branch to go down, or just going down one. However, as in Civ 5, they are very unbalanced, even after the patch. Any sane person will always go with either prosperity or knowledge and choose a few other virtues in the three other trees to tag along. I really don't understand why Firaxis won't bring back Civics or Social Engineering. This current virtue system is a bit of a step up from Civ 5's, but doesn't make you feel as though you're shaping your nation or government.
Victories are well thought-out and are somewhat different, but all in all, they're really the same. Build wonder. Wait 30 turns. Watch as AI doesn't do anything to stop you. Win game. Boring screen and you're back to the main menu. Really Firaxis? The only victory you'll really only be excited to get is domination, but that one is very hard to achieve when you don't have W.M.D.'s or a powerful army until midgame. Overall, they just feel pointless, and the victory requirements are hidden behind a terrible UI. The first time I played, I didn't even know which techs to research in order to win.
Espionage is a bit of a step forward from Civ 5's system, but once other players get security webs or whatever they're called, you'll only be able to dream of setting a nuke off in Elodie's capital.
Some final points:
-Wonders are bland.
-Trade routes are OP and are hard to manage when you have many cities.
-Leaders are also overpowered, and some are underpowered, such as Elodie after the patch.
-Windows 7 users are going to have a rough time trying to even get on.
-The AI doesn't know how to effectively use the tech web.
-I will admit, orbital units are pretty cool. So are the final units for the affinities.
-Beautiful map. Oooh, aaah.
-Aliens are super annoying at the beginning of the game, and are just an afterthought later on.
-Stations are a stupid approach to city-states. I wonder why nobody has said anything about this yet.
So the verdict is basically a 5 or a 6 out of 10. Pretty bad, especially for Firaxis. Can't wait for them to milk the next poor suckers with DLC.

Cons:

Full written review below.  TL;DR - It’s a fun game.  Try it out - It’s free so why not!
I have a pretty big background playing MOBAs - especially League of Legends and a little bit of Heros of the Storm.  I was a really big fan of those games (especially LoL) but there was a really big aspect of it that I didn’t like: the time investment to play one match.  I work a full time job, a wife and a kid - it’s not easy having to invest almost an entire hour to squeeze just one match in, especially if it turns out to be a pretty bad loss.
When I first played Battlerite, I thought to myself, “It’s like a MOBA where it’s just the teamfights… Teamfight: The Game”.  Matches are quick and fun.  The core game mode is either 2v2 or 3v3, the first team to secure 3 wins will take home the victory for the match.  It has tight controls and feels great outplaying someone and getting a clutch win.
After playing it a little more, I realized this is a lot less than just a MOBA with the “fat” trimmed off of it.  This game is more like if World of Warcraft’s arena mode made sweet sweet love to a MOBA.  It is much more tactical and outplaying the other team is very crucial to secure the win.
The game controls completely different from a standard MOBA - you use the WASD controls move your champion and you use the left and right mouse button for your standard attacks and abilities.  You have your Q, E and Spacebar for additional abilities that are both offensive and defensive and even more abilities that can be used at the cost of energy.
For any attack or move you can land, you will accrue energy that can be spent on more powerful abilities.  If you let it completely charge, you can use your ultimate that really unleashes the pain.
There are three categories for the 22 different champions the game (currently) has: Melee, Ranged, and Support.  It is pretty self explanatory but all of them have their own unique feel and different styles that can be played.
Every champion can have up to 5 battlerites equipped.  Battlerites will slightly alter and enhance your champion’s abilities and there are a variety that you can choose from to really customize the feel for each champion.
I could go into more details about the game and what makes it so enjoyable but if you’ve read my review this far, I recommend checking out my video review that goes more in-depth.  It is a fast paced game that is a lot of fun and you can get a few matches in very quickly which is great for someone like myself that does not have as much free time to invest in long, drawn out matches in other games.

I can remember years ago when I was smaller my Mother loved this game. I recently searched up on Steam as to whether it offers this little bundle of joy. And well, it did.
A classic drag-and-match puzzle game. There are many out there like this. But I would have to say that this one is the grandmother of them all, as far as I'm concerned. I would like to start this review by stating the fact that this was the first game that I FULLY played through. Before I had good games, bad games, but I always restarted them after learning a new tip, or if somebody died, etc. So this was the first playthrough I went with all the way. Now we can begin.
I had just unlocked a new story, with a set of some of my favorite characters, so of course I reset my current game to try out this new set of characters that I was rather excited to play as!
But, as the camera started to pan into the house, I noticed it was snowing.
I got a winter start. I didn't know what to do, I had never survived to winter before! So I went about as usual, not noticing that I already had a furnace down in the bedroom. Night hit and I just did what I normally do, scavenge for materials then come back and build. But when I came back both of the people I had left at the base were ill, so I let them rest and rinse and repeat a few days.
At about Day 6, Marin became terminally ill, he was going to die. I scrounged up my tobbaco, made some cigs, and traded for some meds at the Military Outpost. But, apperantly I stayed to long, and after trading a soldier opened fire on me, hoping to get their supplies back. I ran back with the meds, albiet with Katia wounded, and was going to give them to Marin, but the other survivor, Arica, had also fallen terminally ill, and was dieing. I had to choose between Arica and Marin, and I chose Arica. She still had a chance, she could survive!
They both survived longer than expected, but Marin was constantly ill, and never did anything other than eat.
At around day 8-9, I went on a scavenging run with the now slightly better Arica, to an apartment building inhabited by a small family. I ran into the middle of the house, opened the fridge, stole everything in there, and ran out before the eldest son could shoot me. When I got back, everybody was absolutley torn at what I did, and they all sat on the floor and just stayed there, wasting a day, and a night, as they did nothing.
That night, Marin left the group, leaving a Broken Arica and a depressed Katia in his once home. I didnt have anything to do for the next 2 days-nights, so I waited.
On day 13, Arica died due to diesease, and then there was one, a heartbroken Katia. She sat on the floor all day, and did nothing. And that night, she commited suicide by cutting her wrists, and laying on her bed.
There was nobody left, the base was empty, other than the faint smell of blood.
At the end of the game, you get a runthrough of all the important events that happened, and what happened to the characters after the war, no matter if you win or lose.
As I sat and watched what happened during the game, I realized how much I would be torn if I had to do these things, and then I felt bad. I felt pity for pixels on my computer screen. They felt like real people, they had stories, and it tore at my heart. And as I read what happened to each of the people after the war, I nearly broke out in tears.
Marin took a action figure toy talked about in his bio, and left. He was never found.
In Arica's section it talked about what she might have become if she lived.
And in Katia's section, it said she couldn't take the war anymore, slit her wrists, and layed down in bed clutching her war diary, her parents also never found out what happened to her.
This War of Mine deserves all the praise it gets, as it tears at your hearts with its amazing storytelling and great gameplay. I recommend this game to the end of space and beyond.

Some time ago, I played the living eff out of the original "Letter Quest: Grimm's Journey", and I had a blast. When I saw the "Remastered" version in the Steam Store, I was about ready to buy a copy when I noticed that the developer had kindly given a copy to everyone who had purchased the original. There are two reasons I bring this up: 1., because I got the game for free, so any comment I have about the value of the game may be coloured by that, and 2., because it gives you a pretty good indication of how dedicated, friendly, and all-around great Bacon Bandit Games are.
The game itself is a pretty simple word game with some simple RPG mechanics grafted on top of it. Basically, you play as one of two Grim Reaper sort of characters on a quest to get pizza. For reasons that are neither explained nor relevant, hordes of colourful monsters are hell-bent on keeping you hungry. So, you battle these monsters by spelling out words from a random assortment, with longer and more difficult words doing more damage. These simple mechanics end up being quite a bit of fun.
Fair warning, though: this game encourages quite a bit of book-lernin', so if you're against educational games because of some sort of silly principle, avoid this one. On the other hand, if you'd like to brush up on your spelling and vocabulary, or you're learning English as a second language, or you just like word games in general, I would strongly recommend this game.
Here's a list of a few pros and cons:
PROs:
- it has pizza
- characters and monsters are fairly cute, if that's your thing
- word games can be pretty fun
- simple pick-up-and-play, casual gameplay that you can play in small doses, but is also addictive enough to keep you going
- the game's dictionary is pretty good, and gives you the definition of every word you spell
CONs:
- sometimes the game's dictionary displays a less-obvious definition, which can feel silly. For example, I spelled "bean", and the definition I got was in the sense of hitting something, like a "bean ball", rather than the legume.
Anyway, great game. Give it a chance.

This is a weird one. The game definitely got flaws, a lot of them. It's not very well fleshed out in general, to be honest. But it is very, very compelling where it's at its strongest.
Betrayer is noticeably repetitive and doesn't have many engaging mechanics, and the ending is considered puzzling, cliffhanger or even lackluster by many. All exposition is provided via text, however, and there is little environmental storytelling. It tries to be an semi-open-world RPG, but to be honest it's much closer to a fetch-quest driven FPS with RPG elements.
It's an atmosperic, immersive story of how flawed humans are. Overall, this game is kinda closer to its artsy-fartsy kin, rather than to mechanichally competent products. In my opinion, it's well worth the asking price, and if you're into this kind of janky creepiness - go ahead and try it.

I just finished "Betrayer" a couple of days ago and I really enjoyed it.  It's a FPS set in the early 17th century in the New World, has an interesting story and fun gameplay with contemporary weapons that require some skill to manage.  (You can strafe with the hard-hitting musket and pistol, but both have longer reload times than the shortbow, which fires at a more traditional-to-current-shooters semi auto rate)  There are no different difficulty settings, and the game seemed a little overtuned to me since I usually play games on easy these days and enjoy the story, but I had a lot of fun adapting to the challenge.  If any of you decide to play the game, I'd recommend turning on colors.  (By default it's set in black and white, with important objects and enemies having red outlines to them)  While the black and white might seem artsy at first, (and enemies are slightly easier to see with the contrast) it started to give me a headache a couple of hours in, and the game looks really really nice in color.  I set the shader to 8/10, but your mileage may vary.  The game allows you to customize difficulty to a limited degree, with the option of showing all treasure sites on the map or searching for them, and an option for quasi-permadeath where your items stay on your corpse, and you lose everything on your corpse if you die before retrieving it.  (By default you retain items and gold when you die)
The game also has a cool day/night system that you can activate by ringing a bell in the settlements you come across.  By day, you face soldiers from another nation in the wilderness, as well as giant spider-beasts.  By night, ghosts and skeletons wander the lands outside of the towns.  You have to complete objectives in both day and night to progress from one area to the next, and the nights are particularly spooky.
My only complaints were that the ending was a little meh, and that the game boasted dynamic enemy respawns where when you die, the enemies in the zone respawn in random locations.  The problem was that it didn't work as advertised; there is one outpost where an enemy was outside the gates and charged me literally every time I fast-traveled there.  I made short work of him, but it made me question the game's programming.  Also, the game has limited replayability, although the devs put in Steam achievements to try to encourage players to keep going after the game ended.  (Kill 1000 enemies, etc.)
Overall, I really enjoyed the game; it was original, beautiful, fun, and at times scary.  I had more fun playing it than I've had with many AAA titles, and I'd give it a solid 8.5/10.

A hidden gem of a platformer. Advance through semi-linear 3D environments with extremely open-ended ways of getting to the end; you have three tools available (Laser, Hook, Rocket) that are used to interact with/destroy the environment in order to progress. The levels are designed in such a way that cutting things into pieces, launching them into the air, or pulling massive structures to the ground just feels so good and rewards you with shortcuts or alternative solutions. Creating your own path and finding new ways to advance is very satisfying. Not to mention the kickass soundtrack and charming comic book-like cell shaded art style.
You'll feel like a badass when you master your arsenal, pulling off stunts like cutting an enormous boulder or statue in half midair as it is hurled toward you, or creating bridges by blasting uprooted pillars over pits, or reducing a giant obstacle to mere fragments with a laser beam. Just because you can.

I play quite a bit of Hearthstone and Magic Online. All my friends play Hearthstone but I'm trying my hardest to get them into Magic because I feel it's a much better game, though I just can't recommend Magic Duels.
It's trying so hard to be MTG Hearthstone, and it gets close but there's a few things holding it back.
Firstly, it does that absolutely baffling thing that some earlier games did of only allowing you to have a certain amount of rare cards in your deck. Awesome Mythic Rare card? Only allowed one of those. Cool Rare card? Only allowed 2 max. Meaning that cheap rare cards that are only great if you get them out early are horribly nerfed because you now have a much lower chance of drawing it early game. I have no idea why they'd put this arbitrary restriction on deckbuilding and it really just limits your options. It's not regular MTG but a strange semi-restricted format.
Secondly, and this is possibly one of the worst gameplay decisions I've seen lately. If your opponent concedes, intead of you winning the game there and then, they are replaced by an AI to play out the game for them. Most of the time the AI will be worse than human players, but if they draw the right cards then they can actually turn the game around and beat you. That's right, even in ranked games if your opponent concedes, you have to continue to fight them being controlled by an AI. If the AI beats you then everyone gets a loss! I am genuinely astounded that someone thought this was a good idea? The ranked system itself is a sham also as people just alt-f4 the game when losing and avoid the loss (while you might still get one if you lose to their AI!).
The game itself is a bit broken too. Constantly losing connection, or the game just crashing or freezing. It really makes it hard to enjoy.
That being said, the card variety is nice. I like how they took a leaf out of Hearthstone's book and give you gold for quests so you can get cards at a steady rate but the negatives far outweigh the positives. I wouldn't recommend this for my friends to get into magic as I feel the deckbuilding limitations (one one card of certain rarity) doesn't give them the full Magic experience and limits the fun. And I wouldn't recommend it to die-hard Magic lovers either for the exact same reason.
I honestly doubt WotC are ever going to seriously address the above issues and make a true Magic variation of Hearthstone (though I can dream) due to the presence of their cash cow: Magic Online. Which is a client that will scare Hearthstone users away from Magic faster than a blue player with all untapped lands and a full hand will scare the opponent off playing literally anything.

I admire the risks taken with this game, and I see a lot of things that I like, as well as things that need refining, and things that should have changed, but didn't. Espionage is much better than before, having been completely reworked into a system where agents cannot access missions above the total "action limit" in the city, which increases as successful missions occur, decreasing when your enemy places an agent in the same city. Another positive change is the way higher-tier units are accessed-through the non-essential "leaves" which grant "affinity" points in the tech web. You could achieve some goals without ever leveling your unit types. Annoyingly, however, the good promotions of the past are ditched in favor of a flat 10% bonus every time the unit levels--the good promotions are now embodied by a choice which affects all units of that type on level up. One thing that was greatly improved, however was the continuing significance of ranged units (which no one built past crossbows unless they had the "improved range" perk). This is critical in BE because there are fewer unit types and only three factions--you need all the unit diversification you can get. EDIT: There are also unique affinity units which are unlocked at higher affinities (7+) though they are pretty much all land units.
Other changes include the nice visual style (even the harshest critics acknowledge it looks different) and the ability to totally ignore techs in the web--I think it would be difficult to finish with every tech like one could before.
There are some serious issues, however. The AI still regularly demands trade deals (even when they have poor relations and will reject the deal they suggested) and offers only "favors" (although I guess offering anything in return is a new feature). Furthermore, the "warmonger" feature is broken--I destroyed one outpost (not a city) and for the rest of the game I was a warmonger to every other player, leading to several 100+ turn cold wars. Speaking of annoying enemy factions, Franco-Iberia seems a bit broken, as they tend to interrupt every turn with a hate message. Wonders are accessed through tech, so it isn't clear why this should be, but it is.
Further weaknesses include the further diminished air and navy (if I see these in an expansion I am going to be extremely mad--this better have been an accidental oversight and not a money-maker); and the unbalanced virtues (only might and growth get points when I play, health is poorly addressed by other trees).
Basically, there are good and bad things about the game. I like it overall and I will keep playing it (hence the positive score), but Firaxis needs to patch up some holes (including missing/absurdly long unit animations and unit image superposition in the "specialize unit view" window) if they want more than just fans to like the game (7/10).
