And now for a more balanced approach. My review is based on version 4.0 with both Teladi Outpost and Home of Light expansions.
X: Rebirth is of a space sim genre with strong elements of a strategy game and resource management as well as some elements of a cRPG. The player is responsible for direct control of a single spaceship with numerous sub-systems (ie. remotely controlled drones) and indirect management of a fleet of owned ships as well as stations. The player can also dock, disembark and walk around stations and in the docking bays of friendly or neutral ships.
It is a projected 'step forward' from the previous, well known titles of the 'X' saga and was intended to be a fresh take on the aging idea. While comparison to previous X titles is inevitable this game should (IMHO) be played and assessed as a stand-alone.
The Likes:
- The trading system is diversified and hardly ever boring, there are dozens of wares and a complicated system of supply and demand to tackle.
- The more work you put in, ie. exploring systems and stations, the more benefits you reap. Establishing trading agents on every station pays off handsomely in mid-to-late game.
- All trade details in one screen, easy to execute, feels more 'hands on' and definitely makes the player feel as if they're sitting at the Wall Street Market waiting for this one golden opportunity. Ordering your ships around makes for more immersive experience than just setting everything up and leaving the fleet on auto.
- Capital ship combat. In contrast to many similar titles, the capships are meticulously designed with many parts that can be targeted and destroyed without ripping the hull to pieces and the player can easily take advantage of blind spots.
- Being confined to a small craft brings fun back to flying. Sure, all of us want to stand on the bridge of a mighty battlecruiser and feel invincible... but to be honest, in X3 I have always kept my M1's and M2's on escort duty due to their slow speeds and sluggish response, and used M6's to fly around. Rebirth does exactly that - gives you a perfectly balanced ship to do your day-to-day work whilst retaining the possibility to command a fleet of destroyers.
- Boarding actions. The game expands on the idea first introduced in the previous titles and adds a certain depth to it. Capturing a capship now involves quite a lot of work but it pays off handomely and piracy is much more viable than in other, similar titles, even with the recruitment costs of your
marines.
- Did I mention capital ship combat? Yes, I did. Lemme just add, that witnessing two destroyers slugging it out is a sight to behold.
- The stations are highly detailed and actually 'feel alive'. While some may superficially resemble one another, the final result is actually rather customizable. They are vast installations, spanning several kilometers, with various, highly detailed and targettable components and interiors that may be visited (and looted).
- The station building aspect is very well fleshed out and though out, with plenty of customization options available.
- Missions. I find they are a good source of money throughout the game. They are varied enough not to feel bored after an hour and they are quite rewarding.
The Dislikes:
- Steep, unforgivable learning curve, with not many tutorials to learn from. The actions are also very badly explained and results can be heavy - click a wrong button and you're set to loose thousands of hundreds of credits.
- Ant work. Grindfest. Repetitiveness. These are in-built in some parts of the game and are actually required to lift your new-game off the ground - exploration of the sectors in the beginning coupled with mindless scanning of the stations are a must if you want to earn any credits when trading.
- The profits made are a drop in the ocean of your needs. You may hunt around for good deals and trade massive amounts of wares, but it takes dozens of those to earn enough to return the investments made when buying a new ship or building a station.
- The flight model is simplified and resembles flying through thick pudding. Same with combat - dogfighting, which gets boring quick, against oponents that do the same maneuvers over and over again, is something you will get annoyed by quickly.
- Selection of weapons is silly - only one of each is permitted even though the ship has five hardpoints and the guns themselves are rather generic, ie. a blaster, a shotgun, a machine gun, a laser and a plasma gun. Gone are the days of balanced loadout of exotic weapons.
- Choice of interiors is limited. Sure, there are variations between stations, cultures and even between docking points of the same station, but it's just a 'procedural oatmeal' with rubbish bags generated in different parts of the same half a dozen layouts. You've seen everything after an hour.
- Money! Everything is so horrendously expensive!
- Horribly streamlined. Egosoft made an effort to bring the game to the consoles and in the process has made the UI clunky and hard to control.
- Dumb AI. Duuuumb AI. Whilst better than most, forget any sophisitcated tactics and moves.
To summarize - X: Rebirth is a good game that offers a lot of entertainment, but suffers from many bad development decisions. I know many players feel burned and this is reflected both here and on Metacritic, mainly because they perceive it as a step back. however, I have had plenty of fun playing this game and would recommend it to any spacefaring gamer out there. It is a relaxing experience that gives the player sense of accomplishment whenever a great trade deal is secured or a new transporter is released from the shipyard. There are hundreds of tiny things that make this game enjoyable... but I may well be the only gamer that enjoys 'parking' the Skunk right next to the brigde of my Heavy Sul, giving orders to the captain and listen to the whine of the engines as they hurtle the capship through the sector, dragging me alongside whilst I'm enjoying the view...

Alright. I could go on, and on, and on about how AWESOME this game is. I'd been anticipating it for years after it's announcement but forgot about it. Recently I finally remembered it and I've been having fun ever since. But there's one thing I should mention before you buy the game.
It is dinosaurs vs humans, and this is the version that's no longer being updated. That means no more balancing. That said, dinosaurs are a bit overpowered. It's super fun--that is, if you get a spot on the Dinosaur team. I only know a small few of people that actually enjoy being a human, and it's always an "i'm okay with both" rather than a "i choose human over dinosaur"
Although I've played many-a-time where the humans can win game after game after game. Really, it just depends on how good you are at first-person-shooters.
Dinosaurs are completely melee (with the exception of the dilophosaurus which can occasionally spit at humans to blind them and do a small amount of damage) and function in third-person mode. This gives you a meta advantage because you can look around structures without being seen. It adds to the "horror" feel of the game but it still puts the dinosaurs at a slight unfair advantage.
Despite this, guns in the game are super strong so as long as you have a good aim you should be fine playing as a human.
For those interested but want to know more about the game, here's a short description on each class in Primal Carnage
Scientist: Has a sniper that can 2-shot most dinosaurs (1 hit shot if it's in the head) and a tranquilizer gun which disorients dinosaurs and depletes stamina very quickly. press F to use the Cattle Prod that stuns and disorients dinosaurs.
Commander: equipped with a Machine gun with an alt-fire grenade launcher with grenades that have an AoE and smaller dinosaurs within the range are 1 hit KOd. press F to whip nearby dinosaurs with your gun, which does a fair amount of damage.
Pathfinder: Has a Shotgun that 1-shots most dinosaurs up close. Alt-fire throws a flare that on dinosaur screens looks like a bright, white light that they cannot see past. F to slash at nearby dinosaurs with a machete.
Pyro: Has a standard flamethrower that's hooked up to a chainsaw, which is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing cool. holding alt-fire raises your flamethrower and revs a chainsaw that obliterates nearby dinosaurs whenever they come close to you. Secondary weapon is a hand grenade that works the same as the Commander grenade launcher but is thrown rather than launched.
Trapper: Main weapon is a Net Gun that holds a max of 5 nets at once and takes a little while to reload, but if it hits smaller dinosaurs such as Pteranodons, Raptors, and Dilos it will trap them and make them unable to attack or move for about 7 seconds. If you press F while facing a trapped dinosaur your knife will kill them instantly. Secondary weapon is dual pistols, one is a standard pistol that fires quickly but does little damage and has low range. the other is a Magnum that fires slowly but does a lot of damage and has high range. Both can be shot and reloaded simutaneously.
Novaraptor: Very quick dinosaurs with a standard claw attack that can kill a human in 4 hits. They jump the highest of all the dinosaurs. Alt-fire allows them to pounce in which they launch forward and pin down an enemy. The pounce will use up stamina until you run out, let go, or the human is killed. While pinned a human cannot attack or move, and will stay like that unless you take damage from another human. While they are pinned, you will do damage to them until they die. Roaring empties your stamina but allows you to use your claw attack in rapid succession.
Dilophosaurus: Weak, Mildly fast dinosaur with a standard bite attack that can kill a human in 5 or 6 hits. These bites are poisonous and will make an enemy dizzy and recieve continuous damage for a short time. Roaring allows you to use your Alt-Fire attack twice. This attack shoots a wad of purple spit in the direction you are facing which goes through enemies and blinds whoever it hits. They cannot jump very high but can jump high enough that they can get to some higher places.
Carnotaurus: Bulky, Big-target, slow dinosaur with a standard bite attack that can kill a human in 3-4 hits. Their specialty is that when sprinting, they slowly build up speed until they are running very fast and whoever they run into will recieve a heavy amount of damage and be flung. Alt-fire makes them flail which flings away any nearby enemies which is useful when you're surrounded. Roaring makes you do less damage but any damage you do will refill some of your health.
Pteranodon: Winged, bird-like dinosaur that can fly. Fly mechanics are decent but can be manipulated. Have a normal bite-attack they can swoop down and hit humans with--but their main attack is Alt-fire. If you swoop down and Right-click as you fly just above a human, you can grab them by their shoulders. Repeat right-click and you'll drop them. You can either fly very high up or go over water before dropping them and it will result in their death.
Rex: EXTREMELY op class. That's why only 1 of these is allowed for every 12 players in a game. They are very slow if not sprinting, have a hard time turning, and are a very vulnerable and big target. However, they have heeps of health and are very hard to kill. Walking over an enemy player will immediately kill them, and their main attack is a bite in whatever direction you are facing. The player you bite will promptly be grabbed and swallowed, which refills a large portion of your health. Roaring gives nearby teammates a boost, and they have no alt-fire.
Spinosaurus: Available in GTC games. Same as the rex except they have an alt-fire attack that allows them to swipe at enemies below. This knocks enemies back and sometimes can do more harm than good as it gives them time to shoot.

It's been a long time since I've played Betrayer, and for my first few hours of the game, it was pretty entertaining. One moment I'd be shooting down one guy only then to be fighting three more monsters that caught on to what happened. Another moment I'd be in the Underworld, dodging energy blasts, staving off angry banshees, and doing something similar to a "run and gun" shootoff. Graphics are pretty, and if you're like me and you turned the color way up, the world looks very beautiful and lush. On top of that, the monsters (despite them losing their scare after a while) are fairly good at making you panic, be it a giant armored bear(?) chucking rocks at you or a banshee making cheap blows from behind.
I guess the only thing this game is missing is the desire to come back. Despite some of the fights being pretty entertaining, the combat feels kind of dull. Stealth is also annoying and arbitrary, as most of the time you kill one monster and then everybody else knows exactly where you are.
Another issue is that the story (and how you figure things out) isn't nearly as satisfying as how other games dish out story. There's nothing wrong with the "whodunnit" detective style of figuring what happened to people in the abandoned camps, but when you discover that "this person killed herself over the reckless accidental suicide of her child," you don't get the emotional "pow" you normally get from some other game. This would probably be because of the heavy text-based dialogue or the complete absence of cutscenes, but I don't want to bash the devs for lack of resources.
All in all, this game is enjoyable in some sense, but it can be really hard to keep playing it, especially if there's other games to play. You might want to pick up this game if it's on sale; despite its lack of keeping you fully engaged, the trading cards are cheap and the backgrounds and emoticons are really cool.

Dead Rising 2 is a game developed and published by Capcom and is the sequel to Dead Rising. Think Saints Row, both game series are silly in their own ways. With Dead Rising, you have a number of fun weapons and clothes to try out
With the levelling system present, the game allows you to start a new game using your progress from your previous save, making the game much easier for you, especially to complete the side-missions and defeat psychopaths
The day/night cycle makes the world feel real rather than constantly having the game at night just because it's a zombie game. It also gives challenge to the player, to either stay inside the shelter and wait out night time or to risk going out at night having to deal with stronger zombies but with a potentially more rewarding experience
There is a wide variety of weapons to choose from in the game. The combat is not terrible, just that I felt it wasn't very smooth and fluid. Trying to aim with a weapon can be difficult especially since you're not able to move when you're aiming the gun or to throw a weapon. Fighting against psychopaths, especially when you're still starting the game can be very frustrating
The Survivor AI is just terrible, you encounter survivors who say they want to live but as you try to escort them and look back, they're often standing still or running slowly as if they want to be eaten alive. You can give them a weapon for their self-defense but it's not like they'll be able to use it effectively. It's infuriating but pretty satisfying when you're actually able to escort at least two or more at once to the shelter though
The waypoint system is sort of a triangle, you're at point A, you want to reach to point C without looking at the map so you trust the waypoint system to lead you there, so you keep following the waypoint until you realise it made you take a detour through point B even though the risk of going straight to point C or taking the detour is more or less the same, just that you wasted an amount of time because of the waypoint system. Seriously, you're better off navigating on your own using the map. It's as if it was designed to waste the player's time as much as possible. Once you've played enough of the game you'll probably remember all the locations anyway
Dead Rising 2 has a time limit system for the missions, in which you only have a limited amount of time to complete missions. You're able to ignore the missions but with consequences, you might lose survivors when skipping side missions and you won't be able to continue playing the main mission if you skip them. However, you're still able to continue on playing freeroam after skipping and failing the main mission
Dead Rising 2 can be quite challenging, especially with the lack of difficulty choices, save locations and the stupid survivor AI, however it is a good continuation to a fantastic zombie series!

Letter Quest is a game where you fight monsters by combining letters to form words. Attack damage is based on word length and rarity of the letters.
Positives
+ The game is well explained and easy to understand, so you can start playing straight away.
+ The difficulty is increased in ways that logically fit the theme.
+ You can replay any level (with new letters) which is fun to do and also provides more currency to buy stuff.
+ The developer is active on the forums and is adding missing words.
+ Loads of upgrades and items to buy, to match different play styles and levels.
+ The remastered version was free for owners of the original.
+ Each level has variations, to keep things fresh and increase difficulty.
+ Special enemies have additional word requirements, to increase the challenge.
+ Loads of extra challenges and achievements (i.e. use three words that don't have vowels).
+ Includes definitions of words.
+ A campaign mode with levels and an endless mode, if you want to see how far you can get.
+ Tons of replayability. Every level is procedural and the campaign can be replayed on expert mode.
+ Options: Can change key bindings and resolution. Fullscreen on/off. Different volume scales for effects and music.
+ Makes you feel a bit smarter!
Negatives
- Some of the quests go against the idea of the game. For example: "Take 200 damage". This isn't something to be proud of achieving and it doesn't add any challenge to the game. It just rewards failure.
- A minor design issue occurs when using the keyboard on a level with the same letter on the board twice, but with different attributes (i.e. one is normal and one is poisoned). There doesn't appear to be a way to specify the desired letter, using the keyboard. However, this issue only matters on timed levels and only in that situation, so isn't a big deal.
- Some profanity does not count as valid words. So it's disappointing to come up with a word and then the game doesn't allow it. At this point the player has already typed the word, so I can't see the benefit of not allowing it. This should at least be optional.
Ideas
# It would be nice to get a bonus, if a timed level was completed significantly under the time.
# Bit surprised that there's no quest/achievement for getting really long words (10+).
# Long word definitions get cut-off (e.g. Islam). This could be solved by showing the text in a tooltip.
Overall this is an well-designed and entertaining game. All of the negatives are minor and are far outweighed by the positives. Definitely recommended.

They finally got this game working!
I was one of several that got this for free when it was released and was highly disappointed when I found out it was unplayable. The game would crash within minutes. Sometimes it would even crash during the first cutscene or two so I couldn't even save the game or really give it a fair try.
However, since the December patch I can finally enjoy this darn game. I had already uninstalled it and went back to playing the original version of the game which ran flawlessly on my machine. A lot of people were still complaining the game was still broken etc so I never gave it a fair shot again. Recently though I decided to give it one last try before giving on this game forever. I read somewhere that audio reverb caused a lot of crashes so I made sure I turned that feature off this time and I put a good 20+ hours into it without a single crash or problem at all. They finally got the issues fixed! So happy!
For those noticing the lag or hitches in mouse movement the problem is due to v-sync. There are known visual glitches when v-sync is turned off so the fix is simpler than you might think. Turn v-sync OFF in game and then enable the "Fast" version of v-sync in your NVidia control panel or whatever the heck AMD has and then turn on triple buffering. The game will now run as smooth as glass and your mouse movements will be better than you could have ever imagined.
This remastered version is still a bit dated looking. To clear up some things I will explain what the purpose of this game is; they were mainly looking to update this game to DirectX11 and fix the audio issues, lack of modern resolutions, physics issues and then sell it to a newer audience on newer consoles. Kids that never got to try this game could now try it out for the first time.
The game was poorly ported to PC which was a shame but it was FREE so it is ridiculous to complain as much as people did when it didn't work. Gladly, they have patched it to be working now and it is my recommendation that a new player buy this one instead of the original.
With all of that out of the way, they did a really good job with this remaster. The physics look great now. The audio plays fine. The visuals are amazing and the shadows, lighting and water etc are greatly improved.
This is the definitive edition of this classic game that all fans of FPS titles need to play.

I bought this game because of the trailer set to "Evil Ways: Justice Mix," and I have no regrets. Whether intended or not, the title is a loving tribute to all "Cowboy Movie In Space" stories, from Star Wars to Firefly. As with any other similar offering, the startlingly addictive travel-fight-upgrade loop is crafted to keep you hooked, and hooked I was.
"Rebel Galaxy," at the pick-up-n-play level, offers a nifty sort of subversive, stripped-down take on maneuvering and shooting. This isn't a game about twisting and turning in every possible direction. Instead, you're locked on a 2D plane, with your abilities to both manage your loadout and hop into manual fire-control being of paramount importance. This is not to say that maneuvering and mobility aren't influential. Rather, it's to say that the approach to those aspects is much more focused; The "domain" is restricted to a relatively simple mechanic that's easy for the player to recognize and iterate upon.
What's very interesting to me is how this connects to the overall backdrop of the experience. Especially with the "broadsides" element, the way the ship-combat works makes that part of the game a "Tall Ships In Space" sort of activity, which is usually mutually exclusive from the "Cowboy Movie In Space" genre. An odd sort of outcome, though, is that for all the emphasis on the broadsides, the game ends up subverting them. Matching speed and hammering away at an enemy is fine if you outclass them, but you're far better off getting on their tail and letting your turrets do the work. A smaller ship can really beat up on bigger adversaries that way, because the truly frightening firepower can't hit you.
"Rebel Galaxy" doesn't quite hit a perfect mark. The way the interaction is broken up into three modes is strange and clunky, with two kinds of scanning (the pulse and detail scans) being strangely divorced from each other in both where they are found and how they work. Also, the "loot" value/ mission value/ mission difficulty/ equipment cost curves start off being very nicely tuned, but then seem to diverge as the game gets into the late stages. Particularly frustrating were missions labeled as being relatively safe, where that label apparently pertained only to the very beginning of the mission. A few moments into the actual meat of the encounter, and you might find yourself surrounded by a large number of very dangerous opponents.
The problems are very small, though. "Rebel Galaxy" is a truly worthy effort that is fun to play and manages to have its own identity. I hope there are more like it over the horizon.

Magic Duels is virtual Magic the Gathering on the cheap. If you're hardcore into MtG, you probably already play MTGO, so Duels won't have much to offer you. But if you're a relatively casual MtG player and don't feel like dropping huge amounts of money on virtual cards, Duels is freaking great. It's the only official place where you're going to get to use Jace, Vryn's Prodigy without spending $90+.
My only complaints are that there are some strange rules changes, like how rarity is tied to how many copies of a card are allowed in your deck. So you can only have one of any given mythic, two of any given rare, or three of any given uncommon. You also get one free mulligan, but no mulligan scry if you go down to six or less. And more than that, each set in Duels are missing some pretty big chunks of cards, presumably because they were considered too complicated. That's the biggest bummer to me, because I feel like even casual MtG players appreciate the game for the complexity that it allows, but maybe I'm off base on that.
Either way, it's free, so if you dig MtG, give it a try.

There are so many things about this game I love. The atmosphere, the universe, the ships, the music the controls—this game has so much going for it.
Unfortunately, the campaign is *completely* broken. Plutarch mining Corporation, the entity that runs essentially all but one sector, attacks you everywhere you go, no matter what you do. Warp to a new system? Well too bad for you, 6 ships are immediately waiting to kill you. Thought you would trade some wares, huh? Tough, because there will be 20 ships that are all hostile towards you, and when you fight back in self defence, the station will actually send the police on you as well.
Even in the sector controlled by the ENEMIES OF PLUTARCH, should you dare to defend yourself when they fly into enemy territory and attack you, their enemies, your alleged "allies", will actually get mad at YOU for fighting their enemy when they attacked you in their own sector. It's unbelievably stupid, to say nothing of infuriating.
It has been a long time since I've seen such a terrible and broken campaign.
And it's so painful, because so many other aspects of the game are actually quite amazing. There's notmuch else really like it, it feels like you're a Han Solo out there in space trying to make your way. The atmosphere is top notch, and even the places where the game falters like in the interior stations and characters, just feel like a bonus that simply wasn't done very well. It bothers a lot of people, it didn't me.
But it's all ruined by the busted campaign. Any enjoyyment I've had has been completely trashed by being unable to even play the game, because I can't get futher than 10km without being shot to pieces by 15 ships and a station. I would rather the game crash and just not let me play at all.
Tragic.
Because of this, I just can't recommend it.

So, how can I put this?  X Rebirth in its 4.0 state is like a roughly-cut imperfect diamond; it's got a lot of facets but none of them shine as brightly as they could.  All of the aspects of the game do come together to create a compelling experience, but its not without some slight frustration and disappointment.
The game prides itself upon the facets of TRADE, FIGHT, BUILD, THINK, so let's break it down that way.
TRADE is much more involved versus prior X games, keeping the player engaged with their trade ships, a change I rather like.  You have to find trade offers and send orders to your ships to execute the trades through a manual process.  This is made easier through the acquisition of Trade Agents, who will keep you up to date on current prices on individual stations.  The game provides a handy interface for quickly finding and executing those exceptional deals, once your catalog of stations is large enough.
Despite all the updates, the interface is still your greatest enemy when trading.  The game is asking you to get your hands-dirty with micro-management while providing you an interface that just barely makes it possible.  Wares are given top-billing with stations being sorted by wares, and while this is what you want 90% of the time, there is that 10% where you might want to see wares sorted by station.  This is not a possible way to search, however.
Other small aggrevations, like the routes traders may decide to take, like through unexplored sectors with angry cap-ships blowing up anything that moves, means that you'll encounter frustration from time-to-time as a trader.
FIGHT has also been improved.  Rare is the time I see ships attacking space stations by rubbing their nose cone against its hull!  (It still happens though...  Shameful...)  Dog-fighting is an identical experience no matter what faction or ship you're engaged in.  All AI ships fly out a ways, come screaming in guns a-blazing (almost always out-of-formation), usually collide with you, and then go flying off to repeat it, cork-screwing if you happen to be shooting at them.  Even the tankier ships with terrible maneuverability, like the Xenon P, will do this despite being ill-suited to it.
Almost all capital ships are completely defenseless versus a meticulously-controlled Skunk.  Your little ship, once upgraded, can execute surgical attacks, hanging out in blind spots and picking off systems, breaking the legs of even the largest, most fearsome ships.  Many cap-ships provide perfect little hiding spots for you to even recharge your shields hidden away from enemy fighters (looking at you Xenon I, the most "fearsome" ship in the game).  It just seems kind of weird that capital ships have no defense against this.  At least make it so the Skunk's shields can't recharge while in an enemy cap-ship's area of influence!  Come on!
Finally, fleet-actions are left entirely to the AI, which we've already seen, is pretty dumb.  You can hang out on the deck of one of your cap-ships while it blows things up.  You can tell it what to focus attention on but cannot take direct control or even provide strategic guidance, RTS-style.  Just kick back and hope your ship's AI doesn't do anything completely asinine.
Suffice it to say, combat feels like one of the shallower aspects that X Rebirth offers.  Smarter, ship-class-based combat AI would go a long ways toward bringing this up to par.
BUILD, on the other hand, is one of the game's stronger offerings.  Station construction and management is straight-forward, the offerings of stations are diverse, and a lot of leeway is given to the order that construction will occur.  You can prioritize getting one ware producing before another.  Stations are being handled better than they ever have been in previous X games.
There is very little to complain about when it comes to building stations and your influence on the economy.  The campaign tutorialization left out some important information (that the list of stations that can be built is based on the faction that built the constructor ship; screw you DeVries!) and I wish station traders could leave the system to obtain resources, but these are pretty small complaints.  X Rebirth did pretty allright here!
THINK is a little vague, in concept, but I'll assume it's about integration: pulling all the other facets together to advance in the game.  This is where the compelling experience I talked about comes through.  The games gives so many tools to exploit in so many ways, one play-through can be entirely unlike another.
In building your trade empire, you may want to obtain a small military to protect your ships in contested areas.
Maybe you want to train the toughest marines and sac cap-ships to resell for massive profits.
Be a cut-throat and pirate the cargo of one faction to sell it to another!
Literally, you can do ALL these things as the opportunities merit, and many more things I haven't even mentioned yet, like hacking space stations!  This is where the true meat of the game comes from and why you will spend dozens of hours in this game.  It's just that you will often find yourself wishing for small changes to make the overall experience even better.  You'll wish that last fight was a little more challenging, or that the trading was a little more streamlined, or that the small-talk mini-game would just go off and die already.
The small-talk minigame is honestly the worst part of this game.  Let's just end on that.

This game is just amazing and unique.
The Feel of the game
You are Tiny, and you'll need to get grandpas underpants back from Big. Thats the plot. However the game tells the story of the pants, and about the world the game is set in, just by it's atmosphere, the feel (and ofc there are some murals in levels). And it's awesome. The art style supports this as well, and I think it's very fitting, and certainly not bad looking. The soundtrack of this game is great too, and works well with the game.
The Gameplay
Gameplay consists of platforming, moving objects and most of all, cutting them up. To do this you have a laser beam. The levels are built that way that you can almost always cut most of the level. And you'll be cutting a lot. You need to cut, ramps, doors, bridges and even defend your self against rolling rocks. Also you have rocket and rope so you can push and pull distant objects.
Most of the levels have multiple ways to complete (some of them even can be solved with some outside the box tactics). Sometimes youll need to for example make a bridge, so you cut down a pillar and pull it down (with your rope and rockets). Or you could just insted slice that wall in half and walk to the upper level from there. Overall the gameplay is very unique and fun.
Quality and performance
I found no game breaking clithes, however, this
an physics based game, so sometimes you may loose some collectible as a rock nodged it off a cliff, but these kind of things are probably features ;) Otherwise this game behaves itself very well and as far as performance goes, it runs well (granted I have GTX 760, but still, considering the amount of physics the engine works great).
Summary
This game is really unique platformer, and has amazing feel and gameplay.
Only negative I can think of is the lenght. Only six levels, but on the other hand, they are really good. Also there are collectibles to collect, and one achievement requires you to collect 1000 boring stones.
So there's quite lot to do.
Overall, I recommend this game, and I wish it would get a sequel.

Finally after 2 years in my backlog I've gotten around to playing Bioshock!
Bioshock is an amazing, immersive shooter that is heavily inspired by The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged by Ayn Rand and 1984 by George Orwell.

CONS:
The remaster has some issues with crashing. You should save often so in case it crashes you won't lose 30 minutes of work like I did.
There is a small glitch with flickering lights which when there is supposed to be a static screen on a TV or a small flickering light, your entire monitor will flicker instead.
There is a GIGANTIC difficulty spike in the first three levels of the game in which you have no ammo, no Eve, little to no amount of first aid packs, and of course no money. Be sure to be stealthy in the beggining of the game otherwise you will be in a pinch.
A lot of the game is fetch quests.
PROS:
The city of Rapture is incredibly lifelike and really make it feel like you're there.
The horror atmosphere of Rapture really blends in to its certain style and adds even mor to the realism
Amazing characters
Incredible voice acting Armin Shimerman who voiced Andrew Ryan

The Graphics are amazing
I highly recommend that you buy Bioshock which also comes with the remastered version which is arguably better.

Homefront Review (Spoiler Free)
(Story)
In the near future, global crises force countries to make aggressive decisions about their survival.  North Korea ends up coming out on top and once it solidifies its presence in Europe and Asia, it turns to North America.  The NK's invade from the West and life becomes hell for the average U.S. citizen.  You play a member of the resistance movement and are quickly hurled into the fight to break the NK's hold on the U.S.
(Gameplay)
Homefront is an FPS with rechargeable health, much like COD4.  There is no cover system though you can peak and lean once you aim down sights.  You can carry several weapons plus equipment and pick up weapons on the ground.  Most of the time you will be doing on-foot shooting however there are a few land and air vehicular segments.  You will usually fight with a team of resistance members, though do not expect much in terms AI competency.  Enemies on the other hand show average to below average intelligence.  Other than a few set moments, it's one shooting gallery after another, just at various times of day.  My favorite moment in the game is when you are given the ability to direct an unmanned rover and use it to clear your way through a neighborhood.  Most will complete the game in under three (that's right, 3) hours making this game a hard sell, especially with stronger competitors out there.  Multiplayer tries to mimic Battlefield style gameplay with vehicles, gadgets, and large maps but there are not many people except fans playing anymore.
(Design)
The game looks and sounds decent.  As others have said, the opening sequence sets the stage for an epic game.  There are many good looking set piece moments, but they are marred by short levels and average gameplay.  Dialogue feels okay though nothing is worth quoting.
(Final Comments)
I believe the multiplayer component of this game was the primary focus during its creation.  Unfortunately it could not compete with Battlefield and instead, players are left with an average single player.  With a short campaign experience devoid of replayability and a relatively empty multiplayer, I do not recommend Homefront.  Hopefully the sequel fares better.

I realize there are other space games out there (Star Citizen - Subscribed on and off since 2013) but X was all we had that allowed an open world back then.

I like moving around on the ship and hope they expand on this.  I like running around the station(something many space sim gamers have been wanting for a long time).  Wish there was more variety and inhabitants.  Sometimes I use the highway and sometimes I just let my capital ship carry me around.  I didn't play the campaign (I don't recall the last time I played an X campaign - that's what made it great).  I hope they build on this and improve it as they go.  Yes, like many I miss the variety of ships we had.  I also like the fact that the systems appear alive with all of the ships flying around even if they don't do anything.
To summarize it has its share of problems but overall a great step in the right direction.

I have a pretty big background playing MOBAs - especially League of Legends and a little bit of Heros of the Storm.  I was a really big fan of those games (especially LoL) but there was a really big aspect of it that I didn’t like: the time investment to play one match.  I work a full time job, a wife and a kid - it’s not easy having to invest almost an entire hour to squeeze just one match in, especially if it turns out to be a pretty bad loss.
When I first played Battlerite, I thought to myself, “It’s like a MOBA where it’s just the teamfights… Teamfight: The Game”.  Matches are quick and fun.  The core game mode is either 2v2 or 3v3, the first team to secure 3 wins will take home the victory for the match.  It has tight controls and feels great outplaying someone and getting a clutch win.
After playing it a little more, I realized this is a lot less than just a MOBA with the “fat” trimmed off of it.  This game is more like if World of Warcraft’s arena mode made sweet sweet love to a MOBA.  It is much more tactical and outplaying the other team is very crucial to secure the win.
The game controls completely different from a standard MOBA - you use the WASD controls move your champion and you use the left and right mouse button for your standard attacks and abilities.  You have your Q, E and Spacebar for additional abilities that are both offensive and defensive and even more abilities that can be used at the cost of energy.
For any attack or move you can land, you will accrue energy that can be spent on more powerful abilities.  If you let it completely charge, you can use your ultimate that really unleashes the pain.
There are three categories for the 22 different champions the game (currently) has: Melee, Ranged, and Support.  It is pretty self explanatory but all of them have their own unique feel and different styles that can be played.
Every champion can have up to 5 battlerites equipped.  Battlerites will slightly alter and enhance your champion’s abilities and there are a variety that you can choose from to really customize the feel for each champion.
I could go into more details about the game and what makes it so enjoyable but if you’ve read my review this far, I recommend checking out my video review that goes more in-depth.  It is a fast paced game that is a lot of fun and you can get a few matches in very quickly which is great for someone like myself that does not have as much free time to invest in long, drawn out matches in other games.

With how bleak the game is I got the feeling the game wasn't supposed to be fun but an exploration of the horror of war for civilians, so I ended up feeling kinda guilty when I actually enjoyed it a lot
You take control of a group of 4 civilian survivors in an eastern european city. The city has been taken over by some kind of rebel army and the military is beseiging the city to reclaim it. The objective is to keep the survivors alive for about 6 weeks til the war ends.
During the day it plays like The Sims. You build furniture and tools, cook, eat, sleep, and sometimes conduct trade with wandering traders or make choices as to whether to aid visitors who come for help
At night you pick a survivor to travel to one of a number of locations and loot as much as he/she can carry to aid you during the day or future raids before dawn
You will need to find materials to build furniture and defenses or to use as fuel for heating during the winter, food to not die from not eating, water to cook, medicine in case of illness or inury, weapons and ammo to defend during the night or utilise in raids, and trade goods like tobacco or alcohol to trade with wandering traders
Players can craft items and weapons such as a shiv for combat, a crowbar for forcing locks loudly, lockpick for picking them silently once, spade for clearing rubble, saw for sawing through barricades doors etc. Often an area will have locked doors or collapsed passages and players must plan ahead for future raids to ensure they can clear the obstacles they couldnt pass earlier
When raiding you may encounter hostile people. Some of them are thugs and bandits who are fair game. Others are innocent survivors who may fight to defend themselves or their property, and there are soldiers who are usualyl lethally dangerous and best avoided. Combat is random and depends on the skills the survivor started with and their equipment and the strenght of their foe, and whether or not you or your opponent is injured already and who got the drop on who. As combat is dangerous and injuries take many days to heal and expensive bandages, combat is best avoided. Not all survivors are hostile and some will trade or assist the player. Others must be avoided carefully or killed if the situation is desperate as the player searches for the most valuable items for their inventory space in the time available
Death is permanent so the player must weigh up the risks and benefits of each action. Do you attempt to sneak past the thugs for the food you need not to starve? Do you steal medicine from an old couple to save your sick friend? Do you try to save a woman from a battle hardened well equipped♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥soldier who will almost certainly kill you? Do you pick through the looted carcass of a supermarkt for those last scraps of materials or risk your life sneaking into the rich but bandit infested warehouse district?
Really I loved this game. Highly recommended!

I have never been so scared of loons in my entire life. Crouched down in the tall grass, I listened for the cry of the water bird to come again for what seemed like whole minutes. I heard it suddenly, only a few yards behind me. I turned around slowly, but couldn’t see it against the pitch black shadow of the trees above. Holding my breath, my heart slamming against my ribcage, I took a step forward. Too late I realized I should have waited for the cover of the wind to muffle my footsteps. Four angered loon calls startled me from all directions as arrows flew towards me…
The above passage is an account of what could have happened in
. The initial starting scene of waking up on a beach next to a shipwreck seems a little bland at first, but the game soon after departs from stereotype.
Betrayer starts in greyscale, making the woods and trees around you dark and mysterious. The color red is still visible, though. Enemies dressed in red are immediately visible even from a hundred yards away. Red markers over health, shops, and ammo drops help discern them from the grey background. Some enemies do not have red, making them near impossible to see against shadow and therefore much deadlier.
First and foremost this game forces you to listen. Some enemies cannot be seen easily and can only be detected through  their special call. The most unique feature of this game by far is the fact that the human enemies use animal calls: bears, loons, etc. This serves to makes the player feel isolated – the only sounds one ever hears are the noises of the wild. Audial clues to the next objective in each area force players to use their ears over their eyes. Headphones are a must.

The player wakes up on a beach in 1604, Colonial America. As you travel, you discover deserted settlements, find weapons, and defend yourself from hostiles. You meet one person from the abandoned colony, a mysterious maiden in red who cannot remember her name. As you set out to discover her identity, you notice a bell has been removed from its post. You replace it and ring it out of curiosity. Strangely, you are transported into a shadow world with its own set of enemies and the spirits of deceased colonists. By collecting clues from the area around you and interviewing the spirits, you are able to piece together what happened to the settlements and discover who the maiden really is.
I was immediately hooked when I started this game. I love atmospheric games that throw you into the world with set objectives but no set order to complete them in.
If you are an impatient sort, this might not be the best game for you. Especially at first when you have low quality weapons and low health, stealth and patience are essential to survival. There is nothing more satisfying, though, than stalking one enemy for ten minutes or so and successfully getting a stealth kill on them (not a typical case).
There are a few difficulty settings that you can change. I personally enjoyed the easiest difficulty level, but if you like punishment go ahead and try hard. There’s also a map system that shows you where just about everything is. If you enjoy a challenge, try turning the map waypoints off and using the audial clues to find stuff.
- Enemies’ pathfinding led to some interesting fights with lots of sudden 90° turns
- Some enemies are actually impossible to see against a shaded background. Try flanking them to get a better vantage point.
- Very little explanation of bullet/arrow drop leads to a high learning curve for trying to snipe far-off enemies
- UI graphics aren’t too impressive
- Last area is
with bugs – the devs really should release a patch or something
- Each area feels quite repetitive in terms of tasks – devs should have provided a little more variety of quests

Letter Quest is a casual word game with some RPG elements added to it. It boasts 40 different levels each providing 4 different challenges for the player (giving you a grand total of 160 challenges). If that's not enough for you, the expert mode unlocks once you've completed the game on the regular one. The RPG elements allows you to customize your character and allow for a natural progression since the challenges become tougher as the game progresses.
The remastered edition has improved animations and the new endless mode for a different challenge that improves replayability.
Not being a native English speaker, I consider the game the provide a decent challenge while not pushing me away. It actually has that "just one more" quality that will have you engulf many hours in it without really noticing. A real word aficionado might find the regular mode on the easy side but will certainly enjoy the more challenging expert mode. Just when you thought things couldn't get any more awesome, they do.
If you loved the first Bioshock, you'll love the second (this) one.
For those who want to start the series here, I would suggest going to the beginning of Rapture and then coming back to this one. While the storyline makes sense if you haven't played the first, it will be a complete picture if you play the first.
More dystopia, more splicers, new baddies and a few different game mechanics.
This game carries on from Bioshock and does a nice job of it. Starting from about the time Fontane was rising in power and Ryan in dismay, a new "leader" emerges. Dr. Lamb is quite the accomplished Psychiatrist. Her daughter, Eleanor is to be "the one" uniting force in this "utopia".
You can kind of see where this is going, of course. Ryan had similar visions, albeit without a child as the visionary.
You play a Big Daddy. Yes, those "disgusting and ugly brutes" as Tenenbaum would say.
You are the hero but without spoiling too much more, it gets interesting. 2K did a great job in the latter stages of the story telling process and having Eleanor as a guide worked well.
If you played the first one, you will notice some game mechanic changes.
Keybinds may be wonky to start with but you will explode a rocket at your feet prematurely and accidentally. Well, at least I did.
I found the keybinds didn't translate well from the first to the second game so, a little time mapping your keybinds from the first may fix all of that.
The research is still there and is a little easier to manage. No longer do you have to switch your weapon from the camera, but now its a video. The more interesting it is, the more research points. There are 4 research stages. As soon as you get the camera, roll that video on everything you see. It helps later on.
Hacking is no longer out of the live game environs so, take cover while hacking.
Apart from that, have fun slaying the baddies and stay alive out there.

I want to recommend this game. I really, really do want to say I liked this game a lot and that I would recommend it to anyone. But the tedious and repetitive gameplay, the unclear "path" I am supposed to be following
, the multitude of--what seem to be--red herrings, and many other problems, keep me from being able to positively review this game.
It's classified as an "action-adventure" game, but I think of it as more of a "horror-atmosphere mystery-walking simulator game with a little bit of (pointless) fighting-action." I was initially interested in the game because it seemed like it placed a lot of emphasis on its creepiness--the horror atmosphere. I am not enthralled with it as a "horror" game. It wasn't scary. It kind of pulls off the "creepy"-thing with the black&white color choice, the demonic-eyed conquistadors, the shadowy natives, the periodic blood splatters. But the creepy atmosphere is pretty much lost after the first zone. It's reptitive by the second zone. Nothing changes. It's just a copy-paste of each level, each "monster" or shadow. Horror games don't thrive on monotony. Even if this game is only "atmospherically" horror, it's completely lost in the repetition of the zones.
If it fails at horror, does it at least stand up as a mystery or action game? Ehhh...Not really. The only "action" in the game is killing the demonic conquistadors and natives. And spiders, in later zones. (Woowheee?) At first it was interesting, like I was actually trying to survive because there were creepy murderers (or whatever) on the loose, and maybe these conquistadors are related to that! And whoa, they make this creepy sound when they recognize me! And then I've killed my 20th conquistador and the novelty has officially worn off. Same for the natives and spiders.
This is a short section on weapon options, my issues with them, and how the stealth mechanic works with the weapons. I'm putting it behind a spoiler tag in case anyone feels knowing about the weapons would be spoilery...

It doesn't matter which weapon(s) you choose to use. It doesn't matter if you choose to kill everything you see, or avoid everything you can. The "action" part of this game does not matter at all. There are a few scripted fights, which are fine, but anything outside of the script is pointless. No amount of dead conquistadors has anything to do with anything. I'm not even sure the game clearly explains where the demonic conquistadors/natives come from (and, although I do have a foggy idea, I will spare going into it for the sake of keeping spoilers out of this review as much as I can since it is supposed to be,
, a "Mystery" game).
I also believe it falls flat as a mystery game, though. So many of the stories in the game ultimately did not, I felt, tie-in to the "main" storyline surrounding the Maiden in Red. Actually, I found some of the side stories more interesting than the Maiden's (and, yes, I did play through the entire game, and I still find some of the other side stories more interesting). I wish that all the stories tied together. It seems like some of them tied together loosely, but I wanted more direct connections to the Maiden.
The stories themselves are another complaint I had: there was SO MUCH DAMNED READING. I don't mind reading a sentence here-or-there on page scraps, but when you start getting a dozen or more page scraps per zone, plus clues, plus talking to people, you have completely lost my interest in reading every word on every clue and every scrap by the end of the 3rd zone. I skimmed everything in the end of the game, unless the story was directly related to the Maiden. I do understand this is a story-telling game (much more so than an "action" game), but holy cow it was not interesting enough, or connected enough, for me to give a damn about reading every side quest NPC's sob story about how this-or-that brother or mom or dog or whatever got murdered.
Well,♥♥♥♥♥♥ Lost my interest.
I also think it's a huge problem when there were a couple points at the end of the game where I was totally lost. I didn't feel the game gave me enough pointers about what I was supposed to be doing. I had to do a few web searches to figure out what I was supposed to be doing to progress the story. It is NOT a good thing when a story-driven game isn't able to help prod you along to continue the story. If the developers intentionally left it difficult, saying I am supposed to explore and find these things on my own, that feels very strongly like a lame excuse for poor writing and decision-making about expectations of the players.
Here are the things I DID like about it:
» The Black & White color scheme. Although I see this as a common complaint, I really enjoyed it! I am happy they gave me the option to play in color, but I chose to stick to black&white through the whole thing. It's clear the developers intended for the color scheme (or lack thereof) to be a part of the game's ambiance. I felt it worked very well for creating a creepier environment.
» I did actually like that combat was a little more difficult in this game. If you want me to feel I have to "survive" then making combat brutal is a way to do it. It's sort of a flimsy thing to like, especially with all of my critiques about it, but I suppose I liked the difficulty of it, if nothing else.
» I liked the story-telling concept. I liked the stories, for the most part, when it wasn't starting to bore me to death to read everything and piece it all together (seriously, it requires some willpower to retain and remember all the information you get, especially because it's piecemeal and sporadic). The ending of the main story
I think they had some really neat concepts, though the rest of the game "wrapped around" the story was not as well-executed.
» The totems. I don't know why, but the totems and their screaming was awesome every time I heard it.
» The Thief. I think the idea is interesting, and it was fun to hunt him down. I thought it was silly there was a Thief for every single zone. Maybe make him unique? Or actually worth something unique, and not just gold? I felt like there was a lost opportunity for this "character." Why not make him related to a side quest, or more directly to the Maiden? Why not have him relate to *anything at all*?
» Mild spoiler:
As I said at the start, I REALLY want to recommend this game because it is fairly unique and there were aspects I did like; but, unless they do some major overhaul on the format of the game (which would be nearly a new game at that point), I just can't recommend it.

Cons:

4.0 + DLC Review
TL;DR: This is not X4 and it's not meant to be X4. It's a good space-combat-and-fun-flying-around-in-space-sim which has an ill-designed but workable economic system. Dont expect to play for thousands of hours but you can still get more playtime than most other AAA titles.
I played a fair bit of X3 TC and AP back in the day. I loved those games so much that I pre-ordered the metal collector's edition for XR. However, the game was a mess at launch and I never really played it until now. With patch 4.0 and the two expansions, the game seems pretty solid.
It's not a successor to X3, it's a different game. If you wanted X4, you won't like this. But if you are new to the X series or can approach X:R as a different franchise, free of the trappings of it's predecessors, then you might just like it.
The good:
- The graphics quality and performance is amazing. Though it's not as pretty as Star Citizen (check the Gamescon 2016 demo), or E:D in the Vive, it's still gorgeous and atmospheric. And I am surprised at how smooth the game is even with ultra settings at 1440p and zipping across with amazing speed along the highways. This on my 2 year old 780 Ti. The stations are huge and detailed (from the outside). You can walk around inside the stations if you want to, but that part is ugly.
- Combat is decent- I honestly enjoy it as much as in X3.
- The world seems alive. There are literally hundreds and hundreds of ships chugging along the routes and they actually look like space cars and sapce lorries on a busy space highway. Billboards light up the routes, stations look believable, you can even pimp up the cockpit somewhat.
- No crashes so far, no serious bugs noticed.
The bad:
- You can pilot just one ship- which sucks (though you can hire NPCs to run other ships for you). Also, weapons and equipment types are very very limited. This is my biggest problem with the game so far. It just seems very light on this front.
- The Economy - it's kinda broken. To be fair, I have never played any game where the economic aspect seemed to be perfectly simulated. However, it's salvagable to an extent - at least in some zones.
Also, do check out the Steam workshop for mods. Many of them provide great quality of life improvements. There are even some big ones that fix the shortcomings that I have mentioned here, but then can only go so far.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #50 - The Dream Machine
Before I started my series of reviews, I hadn't really played much in the way of adventure games.  But, it's been nice seeing a resurgence in this genre, and now I've had the opportunity to play through several adventure games.
Going in, I didn't know anything about The Dream Machine.  So playing it felt a little like going to a movie that you didn't see the trailer for, and you don't even know what genre of movie it is.   And I'm glad I did that because I feel like I've just watched the opening act of a mystery, so not knowing anything ahead of time definitely added to that sense of mystery.
I won't spoil anything about the story, other than to say I enjoyed the first chapter, which I just had time to finish in my first hour of play.  The story kept me engaged enough that by the time I noticed the time my playthough was nearly over.  I think this is one of the better compliments you can give a game when it has that ability to suck you in.
The actual gameplay itself seems fairly typical for a point and click adventure game.  It involves a lot of walking around, doing some pixel hunting to find points of interest, and picking up things that you'll need to use later.  Pretty much everything I could pick up I ended up using on something, and often in ways I would not have expected.  Besides the "use this item on this thing" type of puzzle, I also played a different kind of puzzle that involved turning knobs on a machine.
I did occasionally have some trouble lining up my mouse cursor on the right pixel to pick something up, but it didn't happen often enough to be really annoying.  Also, when you move the mouse to the top of the screen, a bar will pop down with your inventory, but sometimes this interferes with you trying to point to something at the top of the screen.  Other than these couple of minor annoyances, I didn't really run into any problems with the game.
Besides the story, I also enjoyed the art style.  Most of the adventure games I've played have an animated, cartoon like art style.  But this game has a claymation inspired art style which really sets it apart.  I can really tell a lot of work went into the art for this game.  The characters look great, and so do the backgrounds.  Everything has this hand crafted look to it.
I'm not sure if the following chapters are any longer to play, but I could see some potential concern about the game being relatively short (for what you pay for it).  There are 6 chapters total (but the 6th is not out yet).   I wouldn't be surprised if the follow on chapters take a little longer than an hour to get through.  For me personally it's not an issue, as I think the game is worth the price, and would happily recommend it.

I enjoyed this game before it was ever on Steam, and that's not something that happens often these days. Now the Remastered version is giving me an excuse to play it all over again.
If you like word games, you probably don't need to know much more than that the letter distribution is good and the mechanics are sound. If you need a little more to be sold on it, there is character progression with power-ups and abilities that you can unlock and buy, and the combat mechanic feels balanced and fun. The enemies have varied attacks, including tainting the tiles with such hurdles as poison or spikes (which deal damage to you when you use them) or even turning them to stone (which you can't use). There is room for strategy (do I use that S to make CASTLE now, or save it for later, when I can use it at the end of the word and get a bonus from my "pluralize" spell?), the achievements are motivating (all doable with a little patience), and there are in-game quests to keep you going and shake things up when it starts to feel repetitive.
All in all, a clean, well-made word game with well-implemented RPG/combat system - and this version even has an endless mode with its own challenges and achievements to shoot for, so after you finish the main storyline there is still more to enjoy. Easily played for a few minutes or a few hours at a time. And as a bonus, the original and remastered versions each have their own set of trading cards to collect! Finally, the developers are friendly and responsive to suggestions! Really, you can't lose with this one.

I bought this game on sale expecting to have a hilarious adventure of building nonsense weapons to kill Zombies.
What I got was the worst controlling game I have ever played in my life. Chuck moves at about the pace of a snail, even with levelups your speed never improves beyond "A brisk walk". When you attack, you are automatically locked into the slowest windup animation for an attack I have ever seen. You want to stop attacking? Nope. You have to commit to every single attack you make, and are usually locked into your three hit combo. Is the boss attacking and you're still attacking? Prepare to get hit, prepare to take damage. Constantly.
Oh you want to dodge cancel? ♥♥♥♥ you. Dead Rising 2 does not want you to be fast or have fun, you want to cancel any sort of movement? Impossible. Want to dodge out of your attack animation? Impossible.
I've been told there's a dodge roll move in this game, and maybe that would allievate the terrible controls, but you only get it by leveling up. Randomly. I hit level 26 and still haven't gotten the privelege of actually unlocking it. Who knows, maybe you could actually cancel out of your movements instead of being locked into a horrifically long animation? I doubt it though.
The plot is pretty barebones and is mostly just an excuse for you to go kill Zombies in a fantastic environment. It's not nearly as fun as advertised. You can combine weapons you find around Fortune City to make new weapons that are by default, just 100x more useful than anything you can pick up. They also give far more PP than standard weapons. There's a wide variety of them too, but you'll only use about three. Most of them are just gimick items used to pad out the system, while only a few are actually consistently useful and reliable. Mostly the Laser Sword.
You can also rescue survivors for bonus PP. That's about all there is to that thing. They have terrible AI, will constantly get grappled, and can't fight worth a potato.
But there are also boss fights you can randomly encounter! Such hilarious and creative boss battles such as &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Mail Man", &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Mall Cop", &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Biker", and my personal favorite &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Chef". They're all relatively frustrating because of the controls, and if they catch you off guard, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. You have to pre-plan every boss fight, save beforehand, come equipped with the best weapons you can make, at least three healing items, and even then you're pretty much screwed due to their invincibility phases, FAR faster than you speed, and the fact their attacks don't take a year to wind up. Most of them do have small phases where they're vulnerable, and you'll get in maybe two hits before they remember that you're not supposed to be having fun and stun you.
Also nearly all the characters are either shallow stereotypes, or annoying. The boss fight against the weird Lesbian Ninja Girls comes to mind. They feel the need to constantly remind you that you are a pathetic man, and that they have boobs, and are not going to sex you. It's not nearly as interesting as it sounds.
All in all, there are far better ways to spend your money. But this review is many years late so you've probably already bought it.

You play as Agent 47, a resourceful, bold-headed badass with a number for a name.
A skilled master in his craft of stealth and assassination.
Agent 47 is the 'Agency's' creation. And as a result, he's disconnected from his emotions.
However, after his former handler sends him on a roguish quest to protect a certain girl and fight against the Agency all by himself, his humanity is revealed through care in very subtle character development.
In the past, Hitman games took the sole ideal that every level in its entirety is the player's playground, and as the player, you are free to act as you wish.
Hitman: Absolution does not intend on hindering that, but some (or most) classic Hitman fans take the full story given to Agent 47 in Absolution as an action of such. And not without reason.
From my personal experience I'd say that the amount of freedom given to me with each level in Absolution is not a laughing matter, however it still pales in comparison to what could have been had this game stayed faithful to its roots.
You are supplied with a variety of sometimes hilarious costumes to disguise yourself and an 'instinct mode' to allow you to see more clearly items (and people)  that are of possible interest to you.
Instinct allows you to go into a mode where time is briefly slowed down for you to be able to mark the heads of whomever or whatever you wish to destroy so when you tell the game you are done marking or time runs out, you go into a killing frenzy.
In order for the game to show you how well you did, they placed a scoring system in which your personal results constantly go down should you wish to enjoy the creativity Hitman is supposedly offering to you.
'Supposedly' not because the game doesn't actually offer it to you, but because it punishes you for it.
Whenever you do anything but the objective itself, a little box pops up, showing your score going down and how much your action cost you in red.
This is a punishing and distracting element that should not be present in the game, or at least while you are still going through the level.
You are basically given a present for you to enjoy and do whatever you desire to do with it, but are punished for doing exactly that. Which is a shame because the game really does offer a fair amount of environmental-murder-activity-creativity.
Although I would not say that the story was gripping or anything of that sort, I will admit to finding it enjoyable and even further than that - interesting.
If that's what's up your alley, or even just blowing sh*t up and slaughtering everyone for pure fun - go for it. While I believe the fun is in the stealth, I am aware that some enjoy this game a lot without implementing this important element in their playthrough.

Bioshock 2 is very similar to Bioshock, which is a steam-punk version of System Shock.
The story is as interesting and with the same gradual build-up to the peak dramatic intensity of the ending, which is great. Although, some things are confusing, e.g., only after watching an explanation on YouTube, did I understand that Bioshock 2 protagonist is not the same as in Bioshock.
They simplified the hacking system, made it more faster. The hacking in the first part was overkill.
The enemies are basically the same, only brute splicers and big sisters are introduced. And it's fine with me. What else to think of, if it's the same environment with the same inhabitants?
In overall, I can say that Bioshock 2 doesn't offer nothing radically new, it feels more like a remake – the way the Bioshock should have been made.
Bioshock 2 offers a smooth RPG-FPS experience with an interesting story. It feels somewhat repetitive, as I approach each level in the same way and all the levels feel the same, too, although the difficulty is gradually increasing. At times I felt almost bored, but the last 2 levels compensate for that, as the story gets really interesting. And the ending is really, really cool. As in the first part, it is determined by your moral choices during the game.
My overall rating is 7/10.
It's a good game, but I wouldn't recommend to play it right after you have finished the first part, as they are very similar and you might get fed up with the Rapture environment.
It's also quite short (less than 14 hours to complete the story), but, I guess, if it was longer, it might have been overkill.
The game also has extra missions (to defend little sisters in different levels), which I personally didn't find interesting to try, and MP, which also offers some co-op challenges, however it is almost dead and it's hard to find at least 4 players to fill the arena.
The Minerva Den DLC: a nice addition to the core game. 7/10. Reveals the true identity of the protagonist.

Crazy Machines 3, rebooted after 5 years. Is that a reboot I was hoping for? Let's find it out.
On Crazy Machines, anything counts as machine. Grab your household items and place the missing parts to complete the machines, no matter how crazy they are.
It offers 80 levels and a recently added free extension, sorted in a wide range of difficulties. Nothing's impossible as long as you think and/or improvise, as it always was. What I most liked is the availabilty of Steam Workshop: Make your own objects and levels, share them and try various works made by the community. All of that is packaged with nice graphics and music bringing you peace of mind.
I remember when I played Crazy Machines: The Inventor's Workshop (2004). Things have changed in both positive and negative ways, often a matter of taste. For example, some parts I loved experimenting with like steam machines don't appear here, as well as spinning and mirroring of parts. The placing of parts is not infinitely variable anymore and instead you get a tile system which might have less possibilities but in the other hand it also means that it makes things easier. Back in the days, every millimeter counted, resulting some nearly impossible levels. I'm kind of glad that it's balanced now. And there's one thing I miss most, the Crazy Inventor. But maybe he sits in front of the computer instead? Who knows..
With everything said, I think Crazy Machines 3 is a successful reboot and can recommend it to anyone who is into puzzles and physics.

First impression 5 hours in is pretty horrible. Knowing myself I'll keep going until I've seen everything the game has to offer even if I regret spending those hours later, so I'll update this review if it gets better. I've played all previous X games from X2 on BTW, but I'll try to have an open-minded approach to this one.
PROS
- Decent graphics in space, some pretty impressive sights
- Basic control with gamepad is good
- Fully modeled cockpit with a copilot is pretty cool, let's see if it gets old
- Shooting feels good
- Capital ships with destructible subsystems
- Some gameplay elements like boarding ships feel a bit less tacked on than in X3
- No sudoku puzzle through text entry (so far)
CONS
- Game flashes brief and vague messages about features and commands at the worst possible moments. There's no way you're gonna learn how to play the game that way. It also sometimes fails to adjust to context, i.e. you can stop autopilot by hitting the "brake/reverse" button on the gamepad, but the game never tells you! It prefers to tell you to press Shift-A.
--> As bad as No Man's Sky is, it does a good job of introducing the game's commands, with repetitive and contextual prompts. Check it out devs.
- With so many commands the gamepad command binding would need support for long presses, dual presses, and so on. X3:AP had commands that worked like that if my memory is good.
- Yawn-inducing story that doesn't mesh well with gameplay at all. It temporarily takes away a ship without warning, puts most opportunities for business in hostile zones... X2 had the common sense of giving you the occasional breathing room in a relatively safe environment to experiment with the game.
- You spend most of your time listening to the highway music, your view obscured by the highway walls. Missions so far involve a lot of boring travelling this way. (Contrast that with earlier X games where you traversed amazing looking sectors with great music.)
- Space stations are all nearly exactly the same inside, there's basically one interior model.
- Travelling involves holding down the left trigger all the time if you want to move forward. Ok in a racing game maybe, not in a space game where you spend most of your time monotonously moving forward. (You can work around that by using keyboard commands.)
- You must hunt tiny icons for docking points, material selling points, station scanning, and so forth. It's really hard to associate those icons with what they're supposed to be floating above (especially the "info" icons) and they get obscured by other objects.
- Everything looks aliased as hell from a distance even with 8x anti-aliasing, with a distinct "crawling" effect on distant objects as you move around.
- What the hell is this map. It's completely unintuitive compared to X3, is useless for exploring, useless to get an overview of services offered in an area, and clicking anything zooms and pans you in unhelpful ways. Highways are not named or numbered and show where they're going unless you've let the game plot a course for you.
- Lack of soul. No news of what's going on around the universe, no description for each sector like in previous X games (occasional video when entering some areas). All you get is descriptions for wares and (apparently) an underlying economic simulation.
Lastly something in a recent interview with the lead designer that really stuck with me: he says he avoids playing games with similar elements to this one to avoid being influenced by them. Well play them you idiot! This way you might learn about best practices instead of (badly) reinventing the wheel.
Oh yeah, he also keeps complaining about how it's hard to keep their core X3 audience happy, as if that's the reason for X Rebirth's failure. I've never been a fan of X2/X3's late gameplay of watching your bank account increase by itself, and I'm still not impressed with this game. Sorry guys, maybe you just made a bad game irrelevant of audience.

tl;dr - An amazing story that suffered from a critically short campaign and a crappy tacked-on multiplayer. Worth it for $20.
Homefront has an amazingly rich backstory and a wonderful premise based on speculation of current world events.  I was incredibly excited to get this game immediately when it came out and dove straight into the campaign.  The story was good, if a bit linear.  There wasn't a lot of room for exploration and invention, though the non-interactive elements of the environment looked fantastic.  I let myself get drawn into the the story and setting.
I noticed a few critical flaws.  First, the controls were not always intuitive.  When new weapons or situations arose later in the game, there was little to no explanation on how to take advantage of this.  (I had to go into the keybinds to figure out how to pilot the helicopter, for example.)  Some weapons were very under-utilized, appearing useful once or twice but otherwise pointless.
The end of the campaign was amazing from a story perspective -- and then simply ended.  That was it.  That's the game, thanks for playing.  I had five hours of gameplay and I'd completed the campaign.  It felt like a solid 'Act One' that had absolutely nothing else to it.
That's not entirely true ... there was a multiplayer component that was bland and wholly uninteresting, feeling like something they slopped into the game to claim 'Hey, we have multiplayer!' that flopped horribly.
At its current price of $20 I would say this is an entertaining single-player game you can enjoy for five or six hours.  Don't bother with the multiplayer aspect and try not to lose your mind over the sometimes awkward controls.
