Unlike about half of the reviewers I didn't really have a problem with crashes; I guess it might depend on the system. Anyway, following the procedure one might already know from series like Fallout (saving often and in different slots), this shouldn't really have such a big impact. With my game there was only a single area where I had (reproducible) crashes; apparently that's a bug from the original game.
Regarding the game itself, BioShock is definitely a work of art. Not only is atmosphere riveting with a rather unique and beautiful art style but the plot is honestly one of the best things ever. I'm not really one for politics but it was absolutely fascinating to see the effects of an idelogy and how a utopa eventually fails and turns into a place of horror and despair.
Really, the plot is frickin' great. The characters are frickin' great.

The minigame is, well, a minigame and thus horribly repetitive after a while. The enemies are not that challenging (though I've only played on medium difficulty). All in all, it's good but nothing especially outstanding.
The plot though. It's just amazing and by far enough reason to play this game.

It's fun, it's cute, it joggs the brain. Whether you're super brain or fuzzy old me, it's playable by everyone who can spell English words.
You play as Grimm, a little reaper who is on a quest to get pizza. You venture through various locations where you have to beat up monsters by spelling words from 15 available random letters.
Along the way, you free shopkeepers who sell you stuff for the gems you earn; upgrades, special abilities, books, potions, weapons. There's even two more characters to unlock that you can play with, with different stats (but all upgrades, special abilities, and stuff transfer)
The monsters vary too, some have special conditions to take damage at all, or to take double, or even quadruple damage. Some throw stuff at your letters that makes them dangerous, unavailable, or adding no points to a word. Sometimes some letters aren't available, sometimes you're limited in the amount of words or letters you may use. and more. Always something new and different!
At every stage (location) you have a plain normal level, one with limited time, one with varied special conditions, and one extra tough one. If I'm not mistaken, there are 40 stages. Plus of course the new endless mode (haven't tried that yet).
And for those like me who don't like timers, just pause the game by clicking help (better than making a screenshot and pausing the game). I like it a lot that the game does not force the timed rounds at all cost.
Also, I got this for free because I own the previous version. That's a very neat move by the developer. He's also very responsive and friendly.
With the new engine opening new developement options, I still hope he'll add a free play mode/level with picked/random monsters, after the final boss has been beaten.
But in any case, as it is it's a fun, charming game. Even losing a level makes me smile with the cute animation of little Grimm lying there with x'ed eyes. Or the Dust bunny whacking me over the head with the duster.

Hitman: Absolution is a game that should be avoided at all costs. Sure, the graphics are decent and the characters and story are interesting, but that’s about where any praise of this pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ends.
Any fans of Blood Money will be disappointed to find that the majority of the levels in Absolution have been simplified, removing more than a slim few viable entry points and execution methods. As if that weren’t enough, the game adds insult to injury with a plethora of “corridor” missions that are even MORE linear and serve absolutely no purpose except as a vehicle for getting 47 to the next assassination area, (something that could have simply been replaced by a cutscene).
Further adding to frustration is the new instinct system which replaces the previously used detection system, which worked perfectly fine by the way, with something completely unnecessary. Guards will now slowly alert on you even if you are facing the opposite direction on the far side of a room and somehow brushing your bald head (spending instinct) is all you need to lower your detection level. Yeah, it doesn’t make any ♥♥♥♥ing sense to me either. Did I mention that instinct is a finite resource if you play in any difficulty mode above easy? (I played in expert)
Another unnecessary change was the removal of sedative/chloroform, previously metered out in finite doses to prevent the player from abusing the knockout mechanic. Not so in Absolution, where as long as you have containers you can continue to knock out and stash bodies with impunity (your score goes back up from whatever you lost after hiding the body). By the way, even IF you knock out and disguise yourself as a NPC, other NPCs of the same type (ex. other police while disguised as police) will STILL BE ABLE TO DETECT YOU at a rate only slightly lower than if you weren’t wearing a disguise in the first place!! ♥♥♥♥ing stupid!
Did you think that was all that was wrong with this game? Let me rattle off a few more reasons not to play it: The map function is gone, you don’t even get to execute your targets yourself (cutscenes handle it), levels have barely any interactivity (controllable lights and other features in previous games are gone), and you can no longer manually save.
I made it to the third to last mission (around 30hrs of gameplay) before I finally decided to throw in the towel. At that point Absolution felt less like a game and more of a chore to be completed and that’s generally where I draw the line at calling it quits.
Do yourself a favor and skip Absolution and maybe go play Hitman: Blood Money instead….and pray they don’t screw up the next game as badly as they did this one.

Hatred is a game that’s popularity is solely based on its edgy concept, brutal violence, and adults only rating. And that may be enough to some people. But Hatred has way too many problems to be considered worth 20 bucks.
(If you don’t want to read my entire rant, there will be a list of the overall problems with this game at the bottom or the review)
Hatred’s gameplay is almost non-existent. It’s a duel stick shooter, where the objective is to kill anyone and everyone because our protagonist, named Not Important, hates everyone and everything for no stated reason. The appeal of a no holds barred killing spree is a fairly large one, the popularity of GTA and other open world sandbox games have proven that. But this game flops due to its repetitive nature. The entire game is shoot everything and occasionally press Y to do a poorly animated finishing move. That’s the game.
Besides being just plain boring, the controls are janky and hard to do anything with, and the game switches between ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥easy” and “Run the ♥♥♥♥ away or die hard”. Not to mention that the framerate is absolute garbage if you don’t lower the graphics to a point where the game looks like♥♥♥♥♥ and the monochromatic styling of the game makes everything just generally harder to see.
Mr. Important is also not winning any acting awards anytime soon. The point of the game’s existence is to be as dark and disturbing as physically possible. Not Important manages to not just kill the people, but to kill the mood as well. The man is hilarious! He’s a walking talking teenage edge machine! Everything he says is either about how much he likes killing people, or swear words (usually both), and it’s all in the darkest, most gravelly voice that I have ever heard. The man has no character, he doesn’t have a personality, he doesn’t have a backstory, and he doesn’t have ANYTHING that could make him a real person. The man isn’t scary because he’s so over the top and unrealistic.
And the game isn’t even good on its “EXTREME VIOLENCE” selling point. When the people you’re killing scream, they rarely sound convincing enough for you to actually think they’re real people you’re taking the lives of. And when they do, Not Important ruins the atmosphere by saying edgy♥♥♥♥♥♥to himself. The blood and damage you inflict on people are hilariously bad. When you shoot someone in the face with one of your pre-animated finishing moves, your victim’s face looks like what happens when you shoot a gmod ragdoll in the face. No splatter, no hole in the head, no blood running from your victim’s skull. Just a gmod blood mark. If you don’t know what that looks like, just google “gmod blood” and go to images, it’s hilarious. And when you stab someone in your finishing move, I don’t think there is any blood at all, I know for a fact you don’t leave stab marks. Your knife literally just clips through them to death. The death effects might be better with the graphics up, I doubt it, but even if it was, it doesn’t matter because the framerate was chugging with the game’s default graphics setting! My computer may not be the best, but it sure as hell should be able to handle a game’s default graphics setting! I don’t even think this should be an adults only game. Besides the concept alone, and Not Important occasionally dropping the C-bomb, this game isn’t THAT bad. It’s even tamer then some M for mature games I’ve seen.
And that’s what really disappoints me, the fact that it’s not that bad! If it had repetitive gameplay, janky controls, horrible characters, but did the one thing that it advertised really well, I would have considered it a decent game that delivers what it promises. If it was more brutal, more gory, more disturbing, it would have done what it wanted to accomplish!
But as the game is now, I’d pay 5 bucks for it. But as a 20 game, it’s just not worth it.

This is where I would like to be able to have a neutral rating.  Bioshock 2 is not a
game by any means.  However, would I, someone who has finished the story, recommend this to my friends as something they should spend their hard earned money on? No.  If it were a standalone game, it might be seen in a more positive light.  However, when related to the first Bioshock and Infinite, this game comes up horribly short.  In it's time, it may have been an adequate snack while waiting for Infinite to release, but buying it now simply isn't worth it.
Pros:
+ Drill dashing enemies is extremely satisfying.
+ Dual-wield plasmids with guns.
+ Nice little insights to the Bioshock franchise, but not really necessary.  Think of it as talking to that one random NPC in the inn that gives just a little extra story.  If you missed him, it doesn't really matter.  Same thing here.
+ Hacking system is a lot better than the first one.
Cons:
- The story overall was very forgettable.  I literally just beat it and I can hardly tell you their names.  I beat the first Bioshock several years ago and can still tell you all of the names from it.
- Lots of ammo and guns to choose from.  Usually this is good, except most of them are completely worthless. You can use upgrades to make the guns somewhat useful.  I never felt like experimenting with all of the combinations because it was such a hassle to be able to do damage.
- The camera gimmick is still not good. It's necessary to make the game significantly easier, but it feels like work to have to keep pulling it out to research before killing something.
- Dying or wasting ammo/money didn't matter.  I played on casual and would simply have an abundance of money.  I could and did play like a braindead idiot and still beat it.  In the first Bioshock I had to make sure I had the resources to kill a big daddy.  If not, they were carefully avoided until I could fight them later.  That was excellent.  In this, just run and gun and win.  Meh.
- There's just a lot of things trying to kill you the entire time.  It was very easy for some stray enemy across the room to just start lighting you up.  More annoying than anything.
- The creepy feel is entirely gone.  Other big daddy's were not scary in the least.  Rapture did not have that same insane charm.
- At some point halfway through, I lost access to all of my guns.  I don't know if this was intentional but I'm pretty sure it was a glitch. ( I continued to find ammo and gun upgrade stations, but.. no guns, restarting the game did not fix it, and it wasn't worth starting the game over)  I still had plasmids and my drill.  Mostly what I used anyway, so not a huge issue for me, but this could obviously be a big problem for someone else who still wants to experiment weapon combinations for whatever reason.
- Harvesting ADAM was a chore.  Nice idea that was poorly executed and rarely worth it.  I stopped bothering with it entirely.
Overall: This game wasn't a waste of time.  But, I will never touch it again, or recommend it to anyone else.  It was $5 when I bought it so I feel like I got what I paid for. Very disappointing in comparison to Bioshock 2's counterparts but if you try to ignore they exist, the game is decent.

First off, this is by no means a bad game.  However, for those who are fans of Civilization, and played Civ 5, this game is hugely dissappointing.  Extremely similar to Civ 5, Civlization Beyond Earth's main variations include a reordered tech tree, a new "aspect" system, and a unique visual style.  I personally liked the new miasma system, allowing players to create vast "dead-zones", in which it would be difficult to survive.  Despite this interesting addition, the core, and a multitude of elements, of Civ 5 are virtually unchanged.  Is it a bad core? Absolutely not.  Is it a dissappointing core for those who wanted to see a revolutionary civilization game?  Yes.
Therefore, for those seeking to hop into the Civ franchise, I recommend buying either Civ 5 or Beyond Earth.  There will only be minor differences between them.  For those seeking a bold step forward for Civilization, despite some interesting units and features, you will not find it here.

If anyone needs any elucidation on what I would consider to be a succinct and sufficient one word review of the game, I'll acquiesce. Meh.
The amount of time I've put into the game is insignificant when compared to absolute time-pits most other Sid Meier's games tend to be, so perhaps I'm not possessed of a more sapient opinion. Enough people have already remarked that the game could easily be mistaken as a well-textured Sid Meier's Civilization V mod. I agree with that opinion with one digression.
Beyond Earth is dry, each turn and strategy more arduous, each accomplishment less fulfilling, each minute passing slower than the last. The biggest criticism I have of this game is that I have never been more accutely aware of how much time this game devours and how empty each task feels. I feel as though I could assign perfunctory names to each of my feet and recreate a live-action simulation of a Beyond Earth match with aggregate sand on a beach, each foot gradually amassing a larger and larger pile at its heel, with each pile inching closer together until they combine together into a larger, indistinct, uniform mound of sand.
Perhaps I'll return to the game sometime in the future, but in the meantime I'm going to return to playing Sid Meier's Civilization V, where I at least feel as though my hands need to manipulate each sand pile to articulate each pile's identity.

Probably my favorite point and click of all time.  It's one thing to have hand drawn art in a point and click, but it's another to have these beautifully crafted real-life hand built scenes.  There is detail in there all the way to 1920x1080 (maybe more?) and truly a pleasure to look at.  Also, the puzzles all make sense and at no point do you "rub every item in your inventory on every interactable object" like you end up doing in some adventure games.  The story is genuinely interesting and isn't just silly, overblown, and played for gags like many other adventure games (not that that's a bad thing, just that since many other games do that it's nice to see something different).  The tutorial segment is extremely cleverly put together and really sets the tone for the whole game.  The puzzles are unique, interesting, and most importantly seamlessly integrate into the world instead of feeling a bit forced and unrelated to the world like other adventure games do (yet another towers of hanoi mini-game anyone?).

Well, I very rarely find that most reviews ever review what I am looking for in a game. First I don't play multiplayer and for flying and racing sims I don't care about long, drawn-out campaigns. I am going for single player solo events that I can jump into and just fly or race in a single event. With that said, I also like arcade style. I don't care about realistic play. I don't have the time or temperament anymore for long drawn out difficult missions and levels where you die a thousand deaths before advancing to the next level. I love arcade style! So, Air Wars: Secret Wars is PERFECT for me! I love the single player solo dogfights that are very customizeable. They are a blast for hours of mindless play to work out all my stress. And AW:SW is one of the better arcade sims to fulfill my love of quick solo dogfight levels. I have tried out numerous other arcade flying sims, but this always comes out on top. It's fun and as easy as you want it to be. And, by now, after all this time, AW:SW is super cheap! So, if you love to dogfight any way you like (arcade style), this just might be your go-to game.
While I am at it, I long for the good old days of gaming where nearly every game had built in cheats. Of course saying this tells you that I am an "old gamer." And yes, in the good old days of gaming I almost always played the game the first time through with no cheats enabled. But cheats added so much to my gaming experience. Now most games have no built in cheats and I find that even on "easy" mode the games quickly become impossible to play. So, older gamers like me are being pushed out of the latest and greatest FPS and racing and flying games. Oh well, I still have the golden oldies on Steam and I still love them. I am not a complete Luddite, because I love ESO and do pretty well with it. But I do almost everything solo. I also have played most all the War/Military FPS titles, but I never do multiplayer. I recently came across "Valley" and found it rather amazing, but it quickly became a complicated platform jumper and I lost heart for it. I looked at a YouTube of the final couple of chapters and realized I would never be able to play it to the end. Even with cheats, it would be impossilble for me to ever again play like a I did years ago. So, my friends, enjoy the days of your youth, but realize that one day you too will be an "old gamer" like me.

Homefront, made by THQ, is a first-person-shooter where you are a resistance fighter in a near-future America, where the North Korean military have occupied your country, and you and the resistance fight for survival.
The Good:
- Atmosphere: The sense of loss and human suffering is really emphasized, children watching their parents being shot, mass graves, attrocities, done well.
- Graphics: while not the most detailed, they are rich and dynamic.
The Bad:
- Cover: Bullets can not even penertrate a cardboard box, enemies are often only killed when they deliberately show themselves. Not very tactical.
- Linear story: Singleplayer is the same, no exploration, and suffers from the "you do as you're told" syndrome, much in the same was as Call of Duty.
- Overscripted A.I: Trying to go through a door or down a ladder to early and the game will block you, forcing your teammates to go first. Very annoying and common.
- Control: 90% of the time you are being told what to do / following someone
- Random deaths: You may kill over 100 enemies in a battle, and then die from instantly from something???
- Enemies: 90% cannon fodder infantry, the occasional tank / heli that is killed by an auto targeting ally.
- Audio: Weapons sound fake, battle music is bland, this is not the game's strong point.
- Sprinting: My grandmother could run faster
- Ammo: Hardly any can be carried, ammo is not shared between similar weapons.

To those who give this a poor review, I have a hint: set the difficulty to "Ace" and set the controls to "Simulation". 90% of the time when watching videos of this game, I see people playing on lower difficulties in Arcade mode. When you do that, the plane turns in a perfect 90 degree turn, and your machine guns lock on to the enemy. No wonder this game got a bad impression.
But if you set it to "Ace" and "Simulation", then this game will truly shine. It's on the same level as Ace Combat, Blazing Angels, Wings of Prey and War Thunder, so if you like those games, you will like this. Of course, Simulation does not mean something like DCS or IL-2, it means you just have to pitch and roll to manuever. Yes, you have unlimited ammo and fuel, no matter what.
And the story is surprisely decent and somewhat original. You play as Dorothy "Dee Dee" Dubrec, a mercenary pilot. Initially she doesn't care about the war but slowly she finds meaning in fighting as opposed to fighting for just money. (Hey, it's called "Secret Wars" for a reason!). She will also learn about her father in the previous war, so you will also have WWI flashback missions too. It's a shame that the voice acting is poor and there are a number of plot-holes, otherwise it would have a great story, on par with the Ace Combat games.
It's $5 now (and it was a budget game in the first place), so if you like flying games, BUY THIS GAME. If you wait for a sale, then that's just theft :D

I've always been a fan of flight sims, although I prefer more realistic ones to these "arcade style" games. That said, I do enjoy these as well. I also prefer modern sims to these WW2 era games, but again, sometimes these are also fun. Just played this for the first time in 2017, even though it was released in 2011. I got it on sale, and it was well worth the money.
While some of these missions are a bit simple and repetitive, there is a progressive storyline that does keep the interest level up. There's a good variety of planes to choose from, and some "flashbacks" in the story that send you back to WW1 for a change of scenery and aircraft while you "re-live" the flashbacks as they narrate the story in real-time.
I had some frustration with certain design elements. There's a "subtitle" bar that comes up when dialog is happening (which I do appreciate, because it helps to "hear" what's being said over the noise of the game), but this subtitle bar comes up over top of where the radar/map is, so you can't navigate while anyone is talking to you. Typically this means that you're going to go off course and get farther from your destination while this is happening. There is a good variety of colorful (if somewhat stereotypical) characters, and overall decent voice acting (save for a few really odd pronunciation choices). If you die and have to repeat a section (sometimes a lot), however, you'll be subjected to hearing the same dialog over and over and over and over...
I also think there could have been some more "multiple choice" aspects to this game to increase the replayability. There really is only one at the end of the game, but even a few more (maybe one choice per chapter) could have made the story more personal instead of just watching things unfold as scripted. Despite this, they did a good job of making the characters and story mostly interesting, with only a few "Well I wouldn't have done THAT!" moments along the way.
The game looks good, handles well, works well with the Steam Controller too, once I got a good layout going. If you're looking for a fun way to kill a weekend (and some Nazis), give it a try... or as they'd say in the game, "Tally Ho! Into the drink again!"

The ignored middle child of the amazing Bioshock trilogy is just as fun, intriguing, and intuitive as its more-successful predecessor and successor. Whereas the first Bioshock was about the city of Rapture, this entry focuses on its people. You take the stage as Subject Delta, who, in a New Vegas-esque opener, gets shot in the head while his possession (in this case, his daughter/little sister Eleanor) is ripped away from him. The rest of the narrative has you searching for her whilst experiencing and surviving many parts of the city years after its fall.
This game has real choices, and each one gives potential for the super good or super evil endings. But as you will see, the good choices are not always right, and the bad choices aren't always wrong. The Good
- MtG is still a great game to play.
- Daily quests help spice up the daily grind.
- The solo A.I. is good for such a complex game.
- Tutorials are pretty good at teaching the game to beginners.
- Game is quite stable, with minimal glitches or crashes.
- Fairly regular additions with new card sets (Return to Zendikar, so far)
The Bad
- Gameplay is very grindy, unless you are willing to pay (no doubt by design).  It will take several months of dedicated play to get a complete card set.
- Booster packs are too small (6 cards).  Feels like a cash grab to me.
- Default card size makes card text hard to read (too small).  This is especially true in the card collection view, where there is no option to magnify the card.
- Card text looks like a scanned image, rather than screen text.  When the card is scaled, the text becomes blurry and hard to read.  A friend of mine, with a smaller computer monitor, cannot play the game at all because he gets too much eye-strain.
- You need to be quick on the draw in order to cast Instant spells in reaction to certain events.  If you don't have fast reflexes, reaction style decks will suck.
- My impression is that the random number generator is not sufficiently chaotic.  In a 60 card deck with 24 lands, I have observed long sequences of zero or one land in the starting hand (start, mulligan, mulligan, mulligan, restart, mulligan, mulligan, mulligan ...).  In my humble opinion, each match should start with a quick trip to
to set the random seed.
My Credentials
- Avid MtG player
- 500+ solo matches on Hard difficulty

I must have come to X: Rebirth at just the right time, because for the life of me I can't understand the issues previous posters had (except the ones who are die-hard X Series fans who were expecting more of the same - this ain't your grandaddy's X!)
PROS:

* Someone airbrushed a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ furry on my ride (bet I can mod it off though)
* Bring the latest CPU AND GPU - you're gonna need both
I've been a fan of Egosoft's space entries since X2. So, I guess I know ahead of time to wait about a year or two after the game is released to actually buy in. I decided to take the same wait-to-buy approach with this game, and I feel it's paid off after reading previous reviews from individuals who either didn't know this or knew this but for some odd reason thought things would be different this time around.
I got a game that's freakin' huge in scope (even with a jump drive installed - and yes, you can have a jump drive on the Skunk despite what lesser-informed individuals might have to say on the subject; if you don't believe me you can look it up for yourself), but is a manageable challenge. Whereas other games like Elite Dangerous and No Man's Sky just throw up an impossible amount of procedurally-generated cookie-cutter content and call it gameplay, X: Rebirth does a much better job of the three of making its universe seem ALIVE. There is still no better economic simulator in the space sim genre.
Another key factor that sets this game apart from its newer challengers is the modding community. Go on. Try modding either one of those two games. See how fast you lose access to the game you purchased. But with X:R? Fuggetaboutit. Mod this thing six ways to Sunday if you like. If it's good enough, your mod may very well make it into the game. It's happened before.
Control scheme is highly customizable, at least for space sim fans. X Series has never been an entry-level game and I'm glad Egosoft didn't dumb it down like so many games (SWTOR, WoW, pretty much any MMO really) are doing to make their product appeal to stupid people. Dummies need not apply.
I was a little bummed that capital ships can't be directly controlled anymore, since my favored ride in X3TC was a Kyoto. But then I installed the Capital Ship Bridge (4.0+) mod, and lemme tell ya - it's hard to keep myself from thinking I'm not on the bridge of a Galaxy-class starship exploring strange new worlds. I would prefer the option to directly control my superboat in the sequel... because I will definitely be purchasing the sequel.
...after waiting for the launch bugs to be smoothed, of course. ;-)

A very fun and well polished action-oriented space sim (no clunky spreadsheet nonsense, but enough trading and customization to provide some options outside of shooting stuff) that unfortunately falls into the same trap that every single space sim inevitably does: Once you've finally got the biggest, baddest ship in the galaxy with all the best upgrades, shields, weapons, etc, there's essentially nothing left to do. Especially since you're likely to finish the (extremely uninspired) main storyline well in advance of that point. Not that this specifically makes Rebel Galaxy any worse than other space sims, as I mentioned this problem is essentially endemic to the whole genre. And I did thoroughly enjoy the progression up to the endgame but, as I said, there just isn't enough endgame content here to continue playing it past about 50-60 hours, and there's essentially no reason to start a new game unless you somehow ridiculously ♥♥♥♥ed yourself over in the first hour or so. I do recommend it because, as someone who is constantly starved for more space sims that arent merely spreadsheet simulators, it satisfied me for a couple of weeks. But it's still not the holy grail (read: a version of x-3 that didnt suck, a freespace 3, other space sim pipe dreams, etc) that we've all been waiting for.

Homefront, made by THQ, is a first-person-shooter where you are a resistance fighter in a near-future America, where the North Korean military have occupied your country, and you and the resistance fight for survival.
The Good:
- Atmosphere: The sense of loss and human suffering is really emphasized, children watching their parents being shot, mass graves, attrocities, done well.
- Graphics: while not the most detailed, they are rich and dynamic.
The Bad:
- Cover: Bullets can not even penertrate a cardboard box, enemies are often only killed when they deliberately show themselves. Not very tactical.
- Linear story: Singleplayer is the same, no exploration, and suffers from the "you do as you're told" syndrome, much in the same was as Call of Duty.
- Overscripted A.I: Trying to go through a door or down a ladder to early and the game will block you, forcing your teammates to go first. Very annoying and common.
- Control: 90% of the time you are being told what to do / following someone
- Random deaths: You may kill over 100 enemies in a battle, and then die from instantly from something???
- Enemies: 90% cannon fodder infantry, the occasional tank / heli that is killed by an auto targeting ally.
- Audio: Weapons sound fake, battle music is bland, this is not the game's strong point.
- Sprinting: My grandmother could run faster
- Ammo: Hardly any can be carried, ammo is not shared between similar weapons.

Bioshock 1 itself is a masterpiece, but this free earned remaster just nailed it!
I'd like to say that contrary to what other reviews reported, there was not even one crash or save bug in my game. It was a smooth experience. The truth is: auto save takes some time to happen. If you don't want to loose any progress, my advice would be to save manually from time to time. I just did as I always do and never bothered to spent some time redoing some map because I just didn't save it.
Now, let's review It.
The story is awesome
Plot twists
Great atmosphere
Great length (~20h to complete) -- specially if you buy it on sale
Traditional, solid and smooth FPS formula with some goodies apart (like spells, but set into game's context)
Good, challenging achievements
Compelling, charismatic characters
Great, atmospheric soundtrack (pay attention to their lyrics!)
Immersive scenarios
Great concept
. Even though I'm an avid Bioshock fan, I don't have the vibe to give another playthrough, even to complete the achievements I missed. Not the game is boring, but there's nothing different to try. If you think you missed something related to the story, just go to Reddit and get your questions cleared. It's a matter of a few minutes and you don't waste your time doing the same.
. I mean, I just loved the game. Breathtaking. But sometimes you'll face a few enemies that you're gonna end up asking yourself what the hell was his purpose. My bet would be they put them there to increase game's length.
. As I mentioned above, Bioshock uses the FPS' traditional formula. Meaning that it's good and smooth, left button to shoot, and it enhances this experience by placing some spells that you can use together to the weapons you're already used to. The issue with that is you always can go without them. I mean, that doesn't break your overall experience, but I think they had a good opportunity to explore new horizons for their franchise to make players ellaborate different strategies to go further.
Bioshock was the introduction of a meaningful world with a unique atmosphere. You'll end up asking yourself questions you never done before. It deeply explores madness, radical beliefs and a dystopian society. And it does it with majesty and fun. The game itself is a smooth experience, with great plot twists and a more-than-satisfying ending. The dialogues aren't boring and placed with minimalism--they'll never bother you, specially because you must trigger the major part of them in order to listen, as well as you don't have to listen even one to go any further.
If you are looking for a game that will you make you chill, give some shots, and tell a great story--have no doubt, it worth every penny!

I played this for hours on the non-Steam version just days before this review but it's only 2 regions completed in a total of 12 missions.
ACSW has 4 difficulty levels with respect to AI - Rookie, Pilot, Veteran and Ace. The differences, well i'm not entirely sure, i played mostly on Ace with occasional dip to Veteran and Pilot. What i can tell though is this, beside the obvious AI flying and shooting skills, the degree of aiming assists for you the player varies greatly between Pilot and Ace not so sure between Pilot and Veteran though. There's definitely no aiming assist whatsoever in Ace mode.
There are basically only 2 modes; Arcade and Simulation and these are tied to control schemes.
I have a new joystick i bought at the same time as the new PC build but i haven't even open it yet. Reserving it for really exacting flight simulators. I tried both keyboard and mouse. While mouse is easy and smooth when it comes to lining up your gunsight, it has a drawback, you can't do barrel rolls nor loopy loops. It felt very restricted. What it does better than keyboard is that the button assignments are easier to use. Switching between bombs and guns is as easy as right and left click. Using rockets is a little trickier. The not so helpful hint states you can use middle mouse wheel roll to switch between bombs and rockets but in reality somehow you can't always do that. Sometimes you have to use the Enter key to fire rockets.
Keyboard gives full flight control. You can make really slick moves but firing bombs and rockets can be a nightmare. Most of the time i missed the Alt key and had to make another pass which oft means getting shot at by Anti-Aircraft guns. At Ace mode those AA guns are worse than enemy planes. Why do i miss the Alt key so much? Yea i miss you Alt, you're there but i just can't seem to touch you when i needed you most. You see the Speed control is on the left - Shift and Ctrl key but the Alt key for secondary weapons is only the right Alt which is so far away from either your left or right thumb. You can't use the left Alt key which would be more natural. Maybe it's just a peculiar thing to my keyboard layout which has 2 keys between right Ctrl and right Alt so it's a bit of a stretch to reach it and i had to look down to find it making it impractical to use.
Another thing about unhelpful hints. On the first mission (sorta tutorial flight) it says press T to change views but actually it's the C key. Well that's not a problem really, just a typo error but key assignments aren't open to debate. Take it or leave it. Neither are mouse buttons but mouse button assignments aren't a problem but maybe for a left-handed player that might be little awkward.
It's a mix between the two. Well they got the arcade part right. Bombs and rockets are restored over time but not plane damage. Neither is there mid air collision; you can fly straight through enemy planes without any scratch but canon fire can bring you down ofcourse. You can crash on landing, not sure if this only applies to simulation mode.
The simulation feel is there but with simplified controls. There is landing gear up and down control but it's down by default and that doesn't pose any structural damage, cause any drag or trigger a warning message when flying at full speed. The different planes do have different weight and durability factors. Differences in turning rate is also very apparent between a bomber and fighter.
Coming back to the T key. Once you begin your first mission that requires taking-off from a landing strip then it works correctly as stated in the hint screen. T is used used for taking-off without using throttle or applying stick movement. Once in the air, if you need to use the speed control, it would make the plane momentarily stall before picking up speed.
I think the graphics quality is very well done, especially for aircraft models. Detail textures, bump effects and metallic skin sheen are rendered very well when seen from external view during a turn maneuvre. Sky, clouds and sunlight look impressive. Clouds even cast shadows on the ground. Dusk is quite a sight to behold but it makes everything looks like yellow monochrome making the red targetting indicators a bit hard to see.
Music is awesome! Epic and orchestral. There's real professional work that goes into it's composition and production. It's on par with Hollywood movie soundtracks in it's design and timing. Gun fire is maybe a little underwhelming but the metallic sounds of bullet hitting metal is quite discernible. Explosion sound effects are dramatic enough, plus the exploding debris is better than the one done in Jane's Advanced Strike Fighters.
Voice acting and narration is awesome IMO. Full of emotion and convincing. One should take into account that the protagonist is a mild mannered privateer and keeping in-line with that disposition, even in a dire emergency when outnumbered and outgunned, she is able to maintain composure albeit with a slightly resigned tone.
Very enjoyable with a good story and character development and interactions. Cut-scenes are a mix of static comic strip and in-game 3D engine scripted scenes all with full voice acting. On completion of each map you are given a choice of upgrading 1 of 4 skills by 1 point: Agility, Luck, Endurance or Leadership. So it's a bit of RPG thrown into the mix of simcade. Aircrafts are unlocked along the way depending on the number of stars you accumulated. You cannot choose what to unlock but you can choose what to fly. Missions are varied and interesting but some are needlessly hard like this one:
The prototype aircraft "Black Wing" won't be loaded until you clear all the waves of fighters so no point in hanging around waiting for it to be loaded if you want to stall the arrival of the next wave.
My score: 8/10

Air Conflicts SW is the first chapter of this serie, but it is still a good game.
Following the sad plot of a young girl, daughter of a decorated aviation man, you will travel all over africa and europe to accomplish the 50 missions of the WW2. The story speak about the memorable missions of the father of the protagonist throwing you inside an old fokker in vintage flashbacks, and then returning to '42 when instead you play as the daughter with modern airplanes.
The plot is good enough to be credible and of course to make you combat against enemy units, shooting in this arcade game without any remorse about simulation. The entire brand of Air conflicts is arcade and I like it. Perhaps the graphic is a bit outdated, but the gameplay is still much funny and bombing and shooting will be a pleasure inside those infinite (but limited in boundaries) valleys.
The only defect that i've found is a boring endurance mission, where a big number of airplanes flying from point A to B must be detroyed, followed by other waves. While this mechanic is deadly stupid to be coded in a game, it results almost impossible to take down heavy vehicles at light speed that can get out of the map to an entire sky region, without reacting to my attacks and proceeding to the destination. I've seen this kind of mission in other games (Ace combat) and I find it stupid to be inserted in 2017 games because they are unlucky and frustating. But a skip mission button can be pushed here for 3 times.
Other less defects are the airplane that fly througth buildings without exploding, but it's just a convention to make credible trajectories in dynamic environment. At last the mission are quick and short, so they will fly one by one until the last.
The good is all the rest: Good skyes, good manouver using mouse and keyboard, good explosion, alternate of missiles and bombs, and a good number of airplanes. Also mission offers a good variety.
I hope you get it for a budget price and that you don't focus just on graphics, here it is just normal. Gameplay must be the rule!

It isn’t perfect, but it’s definitely worth playing especially if you’re curious about the actual card game. Please note that this pro/con list is by no means exhaustive. It is based entirely on my personal experience with the game.
Pros:
-	The game is fairly balanced. Even standard game-ending cards like Ulamog can be easily dealt with assuming you have the appropriate response (i.e. fleshbag).
-	There’s a fair amount of diversity. No longer will you have to go up against an endless line of Abzan midrange or Atarka red decks. That being said, certain color combinations do fall a little short. However, that is to be expected considering how the game only has 2 sets.
-	It is entirely possible to beat players with larger card collections than your own assuming you’re competent at the game.
-	The game has its own “limited” or “ban” list if you will, which helps balance the game. You won’t see decks running four Jaces or four Ulamogs because the game will limit how many copies you put in a deck. This also forces players to play intelligently. I believe a smart player won’t cast Nisa until they know she’ll be able to flip.
-	They’ve finally increased the amount of gold earned from quests and matches. The more casual player base is now able to complete their collection at a decent pace.
-	The game is free technically. You do have the option to buy coins, but I wouldn’t say the game is pay to win considering how skill normally determines the game-state. Even so, unless you have a lot of spare cash and/or have a complete disregard for how you spend your money, buying coins is a fruitless endeavor considering how purchasing real cards will ultimately yield a greater profit in the long-run (If you pull a Jace from a booster pack at your local card shop, that’s instant profit $$$$ whereas pulling Jace in the game is largely meaningless).
-	Although some may consider this a con, I think that the lack of proper fetch lands is nice. Games take a little longer to finish, which I really like. I play the game because I enjoy it and get really frustrated when games consistently finish quickly.
-	RDW can be outpaced even by slower decks.
Cons:
-	The game does have micro transactions, which is a poisonous thing for the gaming world.
-	The game only has 2 sets with the 3rd set coming in April. To be honest, we should already have the Oath expansion. I believe the game needs to keep up with the standard format. In essence, we should be getting new sets a few weeks after they’re released in standard. We should be getting Shadows Over Innistrad next month, not Oath.
-	Even though there is a good deal of deck diversity in terms of card choices, a lot of decks feel too similar when played. Most tri-color decks are either creature beat-down or enchantment based making proper midrange deck somewhat difficult to make. Even some 2 color decks feel similar. I will say that Esper is an arguable exception assuming you have a complete card collection.
-	The ranking system is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and in no way reflects a player’s prowess. It only shows how many games they’ve won consecutively.
-	If a player disconnects or scoops, you’re forced to play against an AI. This should be changed to the following: if a player scoops, then you win the match. If a player DCs, then you play against an AI.
-	The game does have some connectivity issues that by now should’ve been fixed. I and a few people I know have encountered the following problem recently as well: both players will disconnect and the game will not progress past a player’s end-step, which forces you to have to throw the game.
-	Archetype quests need to be changed. I should not have to use the game’s deck building system in order to complete these quests. I should be able to use my own decks so long as they meet the coloration requirement.

A strange game, this is. But I enjoyed it thoroughly.
In betrayer, you first start out as a shipwrecked fellow with nothing but the clothes on his back and the most basic of all weapons. The black and white scenery chills you to your very soul, and every rustle of leaves sets your teeth on edge. As the game progresses, you uncover a series of mini-stories of the Indians and settlers who once roamed the land and gradually discover has happened to them.
Story wise, Betrayer gets a 8/10.
Not because it's boring or bad, but it's because you'll only connect the dots between the clues and notes spread across different areas when you're about 2/3 into game. When you play for the first 3 or 4 hours or so, I can almost gurantee that you won't make head or tails of what it is you're discovering. But overall, I found it rather interesting, but the game loses impatient people and that is just sad, since finding the notes and piecing together an individuals story can actually hit you quite hard. Some of their stories are just downright tragic.
The game is really fabulous.

Visually, I found the black and white aspect very good for creating a tense, creepy atmosphere. The effect drops somewhat when you turn on the colour, but it doesn't decrease the fun you would experience roaming around the country side.
Betrayer is truly a gem. And while it didn't completely satisfy me, it will have a special place in my heart. Because of that damn bell, too.

I loved Betrayer from start to finish. It was a breath of fresh air from the usual mundane FPS games out there.
The atmosphere, gameplay, and narrative, were all spot on. You can tell this was made by a passionate group of developers who wanted to make a game different from the rest.
Mystery and suspense are the key areas of focus when it comes to the story. You're continuously driven to explore and uncover more about the events that unfolded in one of the first New World colonies. It's a very interesting time period/setting, and the feeling of isolation and terror are captured very well.
Gameplay evolves as you progress through the game. Stealth takes a bit of practice to master and becomes more necessary as the enemies become more difficult to fight. Each area has "crime scenes" that let you piece together what happened to figure out what to do next. It's deeply satisfying to find all the clues and work out where to go next. The game doesn't try to do too much too quickly, but rather presents itself gradually and expects you to keep up. Very nice stuff.
I couldn't recommend Betrayer more. It's everything I personally look for in a game, but still managed to surprise me. I can't wait for the next game from Blackpowder Games!

Here is my first review on steam - of X Rebirth.
I review X Rebirth apart from the other games in the X-series and this review reflects my experience with the game as of its state in 2016 with the 4.0 patch and Home of light expansion.
I have hesitated, like many of you, as the game saw quite horrendous reviews at launch. Even though I was deterred, I came back years later to find a game that had been patched up, expanded and closer to expectation. Props to the developers for sticking to it.
After nearly 200 hours in this game I have explored, built a humble trade fleet, a few stations and seen a bit of combat through missions and mishaps. I have earned millions of credits - and I have lost millions too.
Here is what I have found so far:
The good:
- Stations: Great variety in faction stations and modules - and stations the player can build and expand.
- Galaxy: Good variety in atmosphere across systems, many sectors and zones to explore, hundreds.
- Many ways to make a living - trade, missions, combat, boarding, piracy, scavenge, mine.
- The game feels alive with ships around stations and from different factions - living economy and trade.
- Truly build an empire and feel the work you have put into it from your armchair - mourn each ship lost at the hand of your
enemies.
- Organize your fleet as you wish. Assign transporters to station managers, assign carriers to tradeships. assign
100 small fighters to yourself and this part is fairly managable with the broadcast feature.
- Many types of NPCs, wares, ships, stations, drones, missiles, materials for mining etc.
- Play as you wish. Relax and manage your trade fleet in a zen-pace until the alarm sounds - or attack everything and live
dangerously in the outskirts.
- Enhance the game with mods
Things to improve:
- Stations feel similar and repetitive on the inside and small in comparison to their outside dimensions (several km). It would be
nice to see a lot of life and interior.
- NPCs stand in the same place in stations and seem a bit dull to interact with as much of the dialogue repeats itself (Good: You
can do a lot of the interaction from your ship without docking)
- Weapons are good and have modifications, but It would be nice to see a bit more variety in the hardpoints and effects.
- Trading takes a few clicks if you have 20+ ships and upgraded trade software.
- I have experienced some clipping with capital ships where you end up inside them and capital ships flying through station
modules. Drones and smaller fighters often fly into capital ships during fights.
This is a great game with many aspects and it will take a few hours to get to know all of them. Don't buy this game to play it for 2 hours - buy it to play it 50, 100 or 1000 hours for full benefit.
Lastly I suggest watching tutorials by the developers and others to learn more about all aspects of the game.

This is not going to be a long review. I really enjoy the game. It runs well even on my I5 laptop with intel 5500 graphics. It doesnt take long to get the hang of the game. I am troubled by only one thing, that is the lack of movement on the vertical plane. I have Elite:Dangerous on my Xbox One, and coming from that game to this one feels a bit crippling. Many things in this game appear off of the horizontal axis and you have to wait for them to come into plane. I understand fully why the game developer did this. This was done to simplify space flight for those that are not used to the 3 axis of movement available in most space games. It can be disorienting.  I will say that it is a good game. It is fun, and that is the bottom measure of a game. Would I return it if i could? Yes. In real life, I'm a nice guy. I show others respect and consideration. I would never think of hurting someone unless it was to stop them from hurting myself or someone I care about. That being said, within the parameters of a videogame, I can be quite vicious. Vicious enough to thoroughly enjoy Running with Scissors' original game "Postal", which made its debut in 1997. The expansion pack which followed, in addition to the sequels, were crippled with elements of self awareness and parody, turning it into a joke which paled in comparison to the bleak, nihilistic mindset of the original. About a year ago, I wrote Running with Scissors urging consideration of a remake, one that recaptured the initial vision with modern cutting edge graphics. I seriously doubted that such a remake would ever be in the making. Much has changed since 1997, a year in which most people had never even heard of Columbine.
Now, I'm nowhere egocentric enough to think that someone acted on this letter, but it's a good illustration of how others were having similar ideas. The result is Hatred, and it's a spiritual sequel to Postal. Right down to the anonymous maniac, the isometric perspective, and the executions. In many ways, the game surpasses Postal in brutality. For instance, first aid kits are nowhere to be found. The only way to replenish health is to execute victims writhing in pain on the ground. And while Postal kept the three-quarter perspective for an execution burst of gunfire to the head, Hatred switches to a close-up sequence in which your character will randomly act on a wide range of gruesome options. You can commandeer vehicles, kick in doors for a home invasion, and inflict a wide variety of damage to the surrounding environment. Perhaps the most effective decision in game design involved the use of color. Or rather, the lack of it. In a nod to Sin City, the world of Hatred is in black and white. The only color seen is linked to destructive acts: a fire, an explosion, a spray of blood. This has the effect of making the violence all the more striking. Simply put, Hatred is the Postal successor that Running with Scissors either could not or would not make. It surpasses it in almost every way.
Almost every way. And there lies the flaw of this potentially good game, at least if you're planning on playing with a mouse and keyboard. I haven't tried it yet on a twin stick gamepad. Here's the problem. In Postal, I would link my left and right strafing ability to the keyboard. My other hand would be controlling the mouse, where forward and backward motion were linked to the middle and right buttons. Actually moving the mouse from side to side would cause the character to turn in a 360 degree spin. Wherever your character would be facing when you stopped the spin determined the direction of your next action, whether it be forward, backward, or a strafe.
In Hatred, movement of the mouse likewise turns your character. However, the direction your character is facing does not determine the direction you will actually take when you move. Instead, forward is always going to take you to the top of the screen, backwards towards the bottom of the screen, strafing to the left and right. This... is... CONFUSING. I'm still attempting to get used to it. Perhaps I will. And to be fair, it makes some new moves possible, such as the ability to move and spin simultaneously while firing. Ultimately, however, this one factor ruins the game. Game control should be intuitive. Not so here. It's a mess. It took me thirty minutes before I finally managed to maneuver my way through the tutorial. Too bad. And over something so simple. I can only hope that someone mods the control scheme to the original Postal. Then we'll have something.
***UPDATE 3/3/16***
I stand by my original statements regarding the control scheme, and still think that the game would benefit if it were changed. Since the game is essentially a Postal remake, it would have been nice if that game's control layout had been included. However, I did eventually get used to these controls once I was able to wrap my head around the concept. During intense firefights it's still possible to get them mixed up, particularly when simultaneously maneuvering through obstacles, but it is no longer a frustrating experience. To be fair, this game IS described as a twin stick shooter, and use of a controller makes the gameplay more intuitive. However, it does not provide the surgically precise aiming that a mouse offers, and a mouse/keyboard combination will simply require a moderate learning curve. Once mastered, recommendation of the game comes down to one point: If you enjoyed the original Postal, you are likely going to LOVE this twisted little jewel that seemingly arrived straight from the bowels of mass murder.

Let me first try to explain why it was that I wanted to play Homefront.  Firstly it was the first game that I could remember that brought the fight to American soil and wasn't based on factual past battles or wars.  Here was a new idea, a new war as it were, and it was America defending its land.  Rather than America attacking on someone else’s, which is all too often the case.  The second reason was that the story they chose seems almost feasible.  The “Future History” trailer that was released told a great story that felt like it could happen.  It was a great mix of a new idea in uncharted territory with a hint of possibility.
The first thing that I noticed was the graphics, they were gorgeous.  I spend so much time playing older games that I am, for all intents and purposes, a few years behind on the graphics.  This games not that much different since its already a year and a half old.  The game started with my being taken from my home and placed on a bus to an unknown destination.  The drive down the street was eye opening to the world I had entered.  It was some time after the Korean occupation and everything was about what you would expect.  There were some moments that I thought were funny, and others that I knew were there just for my shock value.
It was shortly after that moment that I had fully removed the rose tinted glasses.  I came back to the game the next day, after playing for about a hour the previous night.  This time all bets were off and everything was on the table.
Cut to four hours later as I watched the ending credits scroll up my screen using all of my will not to drop a huge F-bomb in front of my child.
Terrible, simply horrid and a waste of my time.  I have so many other games I could have spent that time with.  And to have the single player of a game that originally was retailing at $49.99 is ridiculous.  Even its current price of $9.99 seems a bit much for the size of its single player.  It took me longer to beat the first Portal that it did Homefront.
Nothing about Homefront stands out above the crowd, hell nothing about it outside its story is unique in any way.  I remember reading once that Homefront was inspired by Half-Life 2, and its guerrilla warfare.  Its clear that it was simply a handful of moments in the later moments of the game and nothing else from Half-Life 2.  Especially nothing about its ground breaking story, graphics, anything.  That’s about the same as saying that Bust-a-Move was inspired by Pong.  In other words, they say they are inspired by an already well known great game and hope more people will buy their game.
There was also mention of using real companies and logos in the locations.  It was stated to give it the real feel of these locations.  I guess this is true, but I saw it more as; “Lets stick some advertising into the game to make more money!”
There was a moment where I realized that I hadn’t seen any health, and in fact had no clue how much I had.  There was no HUD element with health nor had I seen any heath packs or med kits, not even a single bottle of pills.  It was after this realization that I noticed that as I would take damage the HUD would kind of darken, and once I took cover and stopped getting hit the screen would normalize.  Ah regenerative healing.  I don’t know how I feel about this, but on first use I’m not a fan.  Maybe its just Homefront, but it seems like it made the game too easy.  The only weapon I was even remotely concerned with was rocket launchers.
{SPOILERS]
The overall story was acceptable, but left much to be desired.  There were parts however that I found annoying and unexplained.  For example there is a level where you have to sneak into this outpost/base thing controlled by a bunch of crazy survivalist.  When we arrive the other members of  my party make mention that they don’t know these people but one member of the party did, but he’s now dead.  The crazy survivalist turn on us, what a surprise, and we have to sneak into the place and steal their helicopter.  Now once this part happens we head to the church to steal the copter.  But how the hell does this Connor♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥even know here the church is?  When the level starts he states he’s never been here, and now he knows his way around?  I call bull.
Another thing, again with the great Connor, was at the end of the game.  First we ignore the fact that the US Army let use join them on their attack of the Golden Gate Bridge.  Because I refuse to believe that part.  But then, right before the last climactic moments of battle, this Connor idiot gives a little speech and ORDERS THE SOLDIERS AROUND.  Seriously, this guy is telling the army guys what to do.  By this point I had pretty much given up on the game, but when that happened I knew right then and there.  I knew that once I was done, I wouldn't be playing it again.
To make things worse, the whole game you are being yelled at to do this, do that, go here, shoot him.  Just constantly being told what to do, and that gets real old, real quick.  And maybe coming off a game like Far Cry 2 has me a little skewed in my views/opinions.  But I can’t remember any other FPS that was similar to this.  This game is a rail short of being a rail-shooter.  Its really that poorly made, its really that bad.
The story has no real ending.  And to make things worse, the guy that annoyed the crap out of me since the beginning of the game martyrs himself at the end.  Yea, Connor, that idiot.  I was more than happy to hit him with that air strike, but it was a really stupid moment overall.  Because why would they need a guy on the ground to use a laptop to fire an airstrike from a helicopter doing circles over the bridge target?  Why?
And all the cliches where present in Homefront.  The story was pretty predictable on a few occasions, and at times the sheer number of Korean soldiers was just laughable.  Possibly the worst TF2 trade I’ve ever made, and I seriously doubt that I will ever touch that game again.

Simply unfinished. Mechanics, factions, narative, flavour text, graphics... everything. While Civ 5 could be considered unfinished without the DLC, it was still enjoyable to play. You still felt yourself progressing through the eras and interacting with the other civs that provided an unspoken narrative that made you want to build your burgeoning civilization, come to the aid of your allies, rail at their betrayal and annialate your enemies. BE simply does not have that. The factions are completely without personality, which almost excuses the small number of choices (why more when they are all the same?). The technologies seem arbitrarily placed on the web which leaves one feeling overwhelmed and directionless. This is made worse by the fact that none of the techs seem to hold any weight or have any iconic importance like they did in Civ 5, whether it be unlocking a world wonder or an important strategic improvement like railroads. The "futuristic" flavour text quickly seems to blur together. I'm one of those questing RPG nerds that loves reading the NPC quest text to get the story, even if I already know I just need to kill 5 rats. Even I started to feel my eyes glaze over whenever the narration would begin to drone on expounding on vapid attempts at future philosophy. In their attempt to make the world appear alien, like the flavour text, they have made the maps a mess of colours that end up looking like a generic mess with no character.
I could rant/ramble on for pages but I'll just end it with this; so much potential without any heart leaves a bland and dissapointing title which barely counts as a poorly made mod of Civ 5. Hoping it will be improved with future expansions is a fruitless endevour, as it seems they have already moved on to another Civ title that will probably be just as mediocre as this sad offering.

Tiny and Big is an incredibly charming, enjoyable game. The game centres on Tiny, who's trying to recover his grandad's belongings from Big. As Tiny, you must pursue Big through expansive temples with use of your tools. A lazer, a hook, and a rocket. You use these three items to create pathways across gaps and up walls. You do this by cutting blocks and pillars up with the laser and positioning them with the other two tools. It's a platformer where you create your own platforms and solve the level your way.
I got a lot of fun out of this game, 19 hours of it in fact. About 6 of that would've been playing through the story normally. It can be much faster than that, but you'll find yourself messing about with the laser and trying to make the stupidest ways of advancing possible. The rest of my playtime was replaying it for the fun and then collecting all the achievements. So even after completing it I wanted to keep messing around with the fun physics and platforming.
Possibly my favourite thing about this game is creating a platform that just shouldn't scientifically allow me to advance. You'll end up with a platform at an impossible angle and think 'This should not be working,' as you stroll across it, smiling.
The visuals and soundtrack are astounding too. The cartoony art style is really pretty and sound effects are emphasised with comic book-esque splash text that leads to a very charming atmosphere. You unlock the soundtrack through picking up tapes throughout the levels so you're slowly unlocking more music as you progress. Ce jeu est pour moi une expérience inédite : d'habitude j'attends toujours de finir un jeu avant de publier un avis, mais là...et bien malgré de nombreux essais j'ai renoncé à le faire.
Homefront est un FPS uchronique se déroulant dans une Amérique envahie par la Corée du Nord. Vous incarnez un pilote recruté bien malgré lui par la résistance.
...pfff. Hum bref, et c'est là que les ennuis (ou plutôt l'Ennui) commencent.
Le scénario...est couru et inintéressant (-2). Il est servi par des personnages caricaturaux et même pas attachants (-2). Quel énorme gâchis tout de même : le contexte est intéressant, et pourtant, ça manque de spectacle.
C'est drôle, mais ce que j'ai préféré dans le jeu, ce sont la cinématique d'introduction et les écrans de chargement.
La plupart du temps vous enchaînerez des gunfights dans les caisses contre des ennemis à l'IA stupide qui en revanche profitera de la demi seconde où vous changez de couverture pour vous trucider (-2). Heureusement, on a encore le droit à la régénération magique et débile des FPS actuels (-1).
La progression est scriptée au ridicule : le jeu nous interdit même d'ouvrir une simple porte ! Non ! Il faut attendre que ces ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s de PNJ's finissent leur dialogue dont on se fiche éperdument (-3).
Vous êtes sur des rails, comme pour un CoD, mais sans le côté spectaculaire de la chose et la mise en scène burnée : non, on avance, on tue des Coréens dans des labyrinthes de caisse, puis on attend que les PNj's ouvrent la porte. Désespérant (-2).
Ce jeu n'est pas amusant. J'ai testé le multi, et effectivement, il tient la route. Mais à quoi bon ? Lorsqu'on a aujourd'hui des CS, des BF, des CoD en pagaille. Pourquoi aller se perdre sur Homefront ?

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is essentially a glorified expansion pack for SR4. Buy this on sale. There's basically your score. The question is, "but why?" Here's why.
Pros:
+ The game is ultimately one and the same experience as Saints Row 4, but with limitations. Nonetheless, it's an addition to the Saints Row series following the near exact footsteps of, in my opinion, a great game. Also, you play as Johnny Gat. An instant bonus.
+ Flying. In Saints Row 4, vehicles, despite a great deal of customization and work gone into their name, are all but useless. This is because you are armed with super spring and super jump, both of which are obscenely efficient at getting the player from point A to point B. Yet, they were also obscenely boring. Of course, there is still some thrill in jogging along at 60 mph, but it quickly loses its novelty. Here, vehicles are even more useless. Yay! But in this case, rather than just "♥♥♥♥ing run faster you fat♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, you are actually provided a very fun and superbly designed way to travel. Wings! They're great fun and the map has been reworked in many areas to encourage wing play. I can't tell you just how exciting it is to zip through buildings and pipes with these suckers.
+ The map rework, while not exactly earth shattering, is serviceable. It obviously looks like Hell, and it's been reworked for the flying mechanic as mentioned. Wild architecture and all of that whatnot are present for you to fly through.
+ Guns are pretty fun. The seven sins weapons are a clever idea as well. Ultimately however, the lack of weapons overall and lack of customization wind up running the enjoyment into the ground pretty quick, but nonetheless, it's something.
+ The classic Saints Row brand feeling of badassery is still here.
Cons:
+ If you can see my playtime, it's stupendously short. If you can't, it's still stupendously short.
+ The meat of the story is "do random♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. It's not much of a main questline if anything, it's more like "we're going to force you to play minigames" versus "minigames".
+ Lots of the♥♥♥♥♥♥was copy pasted from one place to the next. Not a lot of variation in activities unlike SR4.
Score: 6/10, buy it on sale.

This is a super simple incredibly casual game that's very relaxing to play - as long as you don't mind just wandering about collecting loot. The loot is actually interesting, although it has no stats or bearing on the game and is literally just a collectible item. Why do I want this loot then, you ask? Well, it has an "epic" sounding announcer who declares the name (sometimes with enthusiasm, sometimes disgust) and a tidbit of information when you put it in your display cabinet.
There is an attempt at adding depth. For example, different dogs (3 total) have different abilities (small dog can fit through a small gap, tough dog can scare off wildlife). There are some stats that you have to level up using your loot points, so a dog with a high amount of concentration won't get distracted whilst digging, or a dog with stamina can go longer before the day is over - but ultimately you simply progress from park to park and use WASD to wander around until your dog digs something up. You smirk at the announcer then head back home to read the flavour text, choose a different dog if you couldn't reach something, rinse and repeat.
Yeah, typo included. A ton of the flavour text has typos. There's even a typo in the store description. Indie devs need to invest in a proof reader now and again.
Bit morbid if you ask me. Poor Brent.

This has got to be one of the most beautifully done games I have ever played. In itself you find yourself feeling things you never thought you would feel while playing a game, and balancing those feelings with the sort of life changing actions you have/choose to make.
Playing as a survivor during a war struggling to survive from starvation, illness, wounds, other survivors, and the military, rather then a automatic weapon wielding one man army sent to slaughter hundreds of enemies in the name of your country/organization/religion/whatever. And its that sort of thinking outside the box with how most games are being done now that makes this game a true piece of art.
The combat is unforgiving, just as it should be. If you choose to engage in some kind of combat you had better be prepared to really think about how you are going to take on the obstacles in front of you. Its easy to get wounded, get chased off, or even die if you are not careful.
Scavenging during the night also plays its role, having to balance what is necessary with what isn't. Planning for the future winter by stocking up on canned goods and firewood. Getting the tools and materials needed to truly secure your home, and fix it up with facilities to keep your survivors both happy and alive. Mix in a little trading and you really need to look at all your looting options. Do you take the can of food? Do you really need it? Or is the pile of wood a better choice? Sometimes you will find yourself really balancing it out to because missing some key pieces when your survivors are either hungry, cold, or depressed can really change how the next few days play out.
The music is utterly amazing. Its simple, quiet, and really sets the mood properly with the artistic style the game is designed in. There are times I just left the game on pause while I do some house work, to have that nice ambiance.
My advice, play the game as if you were one of the survivors, don't think of yourself as a player/god controlling these people. When you do that you really start to care about your survivors, what their stories are, and what sort of things they are having to do, let alone what actions you take and how it will effect them.
All in all this game stands out for one main reason. It has a soul. It doesn't need those million dollar CG trailers, seizure inducing lens flares spammed across the screen, sharks with freakin laser beams, Press X to feel aspects that all the recent triple A games have. Its just a well done game with a soul, and as a gamer what more could you ask for?

It is definitely a strange game at first. Red, White, and Black are the only major colors (although you can change that in the settings). Set in the colonial period you utilize muskets, muzzle loaded pistols, crossbows, a knife, and bows to defend yourself from a multitude of enemies. The game throws you in, no explanation outside a shipwreck and tells you to go and find the answers yourself. While easy to get the answers and progress, it is also easy to get lost at times and find yourself wandering through the vast environment and be ambushed by the many enemies that dot the maps including conquistadors of various types, native americans, giant spiders, and spirits.
Everything you learn though, everything you gain is done by your own hand. The biggest hint that one can give without spoiling the game is simply listen. There's no soundtrack, but for good reason as EVERY sound is important. That bear sound might be an conquistador or that robin's quarrel could be a native's ambush site.  Don't take anything for granted and you'll find the game isn't as terrifying as it may have seen mere moments before.

Dead Rising 2 is a great sequel to my all time favorite game. The original game focused on Frank West. A freelance photojournalist who uncovered a plot involving zombies and psychopaths and a military cover-up. This time around, you play as Chuck Greene. A widower trying his best to keep his daughter safe after a zombie outbreak took her mother and left her infected with the zombie virus. To keep her safe, Chuck will have to battle the hordes of zombies, looters, psychopaths, and more to uncover the plot surrounding the outbreak and clear his name after being framed for starting the whole mess.
Credit should be given to the developers of this game. The first Dead Rising had a very charasmatic protagonist in Frank. The easy path would have been to continue his story. Like so many other video games that are afraid to change things up, this would be what most would do. But Capcom Vancouver went with an all original story and an all original cast. Using the events of the original to launch this second tale of the world started by Frank's adventure in Willamette Colorado years earlier. It's a bold move and worthy of praise. It also pays off as Chuck's differences are instantly apparent and lead to the Combo-Weapon mechanic. Where Frank used his photography skills to augment the gameplay, Chuck uses his knowledge of mechanics to mix weapons into more powerful weapons that offer increased killing power when facing off against the games many many enemies.
The game is similar enough to the original in both tone and plot but stands out for offering the new Combo-Weapons, the side missions of keeping your daughter safe while working to find her medicine (Zombrex) to stave off the zombie plague she carries with her. It's a fun dynamic that allows for some drama in amidst the silliness Dead Rising is known for.
If you liked the first Dead Rising, this is a no-brainer. You'll like this one too. The expanded setting of Fortune City is bigger than Willamette, there's a monetary element to the gameplay as well which entices you to play the many casino games to earn cash so you can unlock some of the games better zombie killing tools on subsequent playthroughs. This makes the game stay fresh even as you repeat the story trying for a different ending (5 in total just like the first).
And for those who didn't like the first Dead Rising, this one is different enough that you may want to give it a chance anyway. No camera mini-game, more costume options and Combo-Weapon system all add to the formula in fun inventive ways. Check this one out, it's worth your time. :)
