Let's start with the 4x elements first. There is almost no planetary development. You can grow population, add some slots for buildings, improve your planet's health all with a couple of clicks. It will take a few minutes to fully develope your planet.
The research tree is generic. When you build let's say a frigate factory you will unlock one ship type. There is a research tab for every ship in the game for unlock only purpose.  There are 4 tabs alone for upgrading armor, doing the same thing for every tab. Same thing for laser weapons, 3 tabs where every tab is divided into 2 levels ( need to research 1 tab twice) for every incremental increase in laser damage. There is so much unnecessary stuff in the tree that it is just not tech tree worthy as a whole.
Expansion is pretty straightforward take a planet by force or take it over by influence. Panets are connected by phase lanes (strings) over which are you able to move and spread your influence. I'd say diplomacy is the only 4x worthy element this game has to offer and worked out well. You can accept missions to increase their relation with you or you give them a mission to improve your relation with them. If the relation in both ways is high enough the chance of them accepting heavier stuff is more probable.
You may ask (missions) a faction to destroy ships, capital ships, structures etc and the amount of it. If they kill 5 or 15 enemy ships for you depends on the relationship. You are also able to join pacts. The better the relation, the more pacts you can join like cease fire, peace, vision or trade treaties. Managing your economy is just as thin as in any other RTS, colonize asteroids for metal and crystal income and max out your population for credits.
First of all there is no singleplayer campaign, it is just pure skirmish against bots and multiplayer. Second point I want to make is that the majority of your game time is spend by battling enemy fleets. Gameplay wise you build up a fleet of mixed unit types. Attack the enemy, lose a big chunk of your fleet, rebuild your fleet and go for the next planet. Flanking does not pay off. There isn't any tactics involved other than timing the activation of your ship's special abilities.
There is no stealth, no surgical strikes, no flanking. Every game plays out the same, build a big balanced fleet and overwhelm the enemy. Quick building is your way to succes. This is a casual RTS game with extra bells and whistles (4x elements) which lacks strategic depth. The game has good graphics and the battles are nice to see when you are zoomed in, which rarely happens anyway. I did not expect this game to have such a lack of tactical gameplay, such a shame.
For a casual RTS experience this game is good. Good graphics, flashy space battles, lots of cool units, wonderful sound effects, always things to do, mods and the 4x elements , altough very minor, are a plus. I would not buy the game if you expect a 4x game, total war style of gameplay or the ability to use tactics to decide battles. I would only recommend this game if you want another casual RTS experience (with casual I don't mean quality, but there are more of them on the market in terms of gameplay). I will give this game thumbs down however (has nothing to do with rating but with recommendation), the reason for downvoting is the lack of depth gameplay wise and the bells an whistles don't make up for it.

If you love Blade Runner and you love Space, you must get this. Seriously even if you never engage in the actual gameplay, the aesthetics and vibe of X:Rebirth is so strong with a good space version of Blade Runner. For flying around in space and exploring, checking out the intense detail of the stations and listening to the encyclopedia entries of every module of every station, this game delivers.
Something that separates this from most space games? There is consumer traffic flying around constantly (not just other fighter ships, but civilians driving regular space cars and vans on space roads and highways. This adds a huge amount of atmosphere to the game that is missing from other space games. The ambient AI always moving around while you observe the beauty of this living breathing space environment.
Second thing that separates it? Easy and good feeling mouse control. At night I play this on a freaking laptop trackpad okay? And the fact that I can do that is awesome. Most space games require something more demanding, some don't play well at all without a controller or joystick.
There is some wonkyness to X Rebirth - the first person bits in particular and they could really improve some of the dialogue with NPCs, I don't hate it but it has the potential to be much better. However not many space games manage to have first person control at all, so I am very forgiving here. There is also something very cool about looking off the balcony of a station in first person and seeing how large and cool the stations around you look from ground view. It is a welcome change of pace to have your feet on the ground when you need a rest from constantly flying around.
Egosoft has made an admirable attempt at restoring the general quality of this game to where it should be, and at version 4.0 it's in a very good spot. They have made some very meaningful updates and a lot of them make it easier to get into the game in general. Just be aware that you will only be flying one ship, unlike the X3 series. However the environments are so awesome that I was also able to forgive this.
X Rebirth is a very ambitious game, and with that comes some rough edges. But after these patches it's not so rough anymore, and for what they achieved with the vibe and detail of environments / stations alone, you have gotten what you paid for.
The Teladi Outpost and Home of Light are recommended to expand the universe further! Have fun space fans!

The game was built by a small team, and based on reviews, it seems like it has had it's fair share of bugs. I saw none of them. I am a very long time Civilization player (my first game was Civ I), and so trust me - I know as well as anyone else how Civ:BE compares to other Civ games. I share the view of many reviewers here on Steam that the game feels more like an expansion to Civ 5 than a new game entirely. However, I still think it's worth getting if you're a fan of the series, the genre or of strategy games as a whole. Just don't buy it at full price - and don't buy it expecting a completely new experience compared to Civ 5! Long story short - yes, it was disappointing when compared to Civ 4 and Civ 5 (even though I find it unfair to compare it to Civ 5 + 2 expansions + loads of DLC, as many have done) - but it is still an interesting and innovative game when viewed on its own merits. Civ 5 is a true masterpiece, and Civ:BE does indeed pale somewhat in comparison - but don't let that deter you from what fun experiences are to be had in the game!
Get it if you:
Beyond Earth is a Sid Meier's game and consequently is a beautifully complex and intricate game. A lot of the criticisms against the game so far seem to stem from not recognizing the complexities that exist in the game already. As always, the challenge of balancing food, production, science, energy (akin to gold from Civ 5), health (akin to happiness from Civ 5), culture, resources, military, research, expansion, etc. is what makes these games so brilliant. Beyond Earth is no different. Increasing food output of a city both makes it grow faster but could also allow you to use more workers to focus on production. The relationships between the different resources is never straight forward and there is much room for experimentation with different city set ups, civilization styles, etc. as always. Balancing expansionism with the conflict from neighbours, trade profits with the potential gains from war, etc. is as much a part of Beyond Earth as any Civilization game before it.
Beyond Earth adds a few new interesting features and tweaks some of those from earlier games in the series. The quests from Civ 5 see a resurgence in a new form. They no longer come from City-states but instead form part of the narrative around which your civilization expands and takes shape. Many of the quests are simple decisions to be made between different focuses for certain buildings. +1 here, or -1 there may not seem so much, but as you progress through the game, collectively they offer a wonderful new method of fine-tuning your civilization from the get go.
The research tree has been replaced with a web that allows for much greater freedom of progression. In the beginning of the game, you not only select your sponsor (faction) and map type, but also here there are a few options permitting you to begin the process of customizing your civilization before the game has even started. Taken together, all of these minor changes offering individually subtle, but collectively powerful, customization options create a new experience in the Civilization franchise and attribute to that strength of the Civilization games of making each game feel unique and form its own narrative.
It is true that the game is not as rich as Civ 5, it is likely that we will see DLC content coming soon also for Beyond Earth. Whatever you think of DLC as a marketing method, in terms of gameplay, this will deepen the mechanics of the game. However, I do agree with the general sentiment that
. Civ 5 is a true masterpiece, and Civ:BE does indeed pale somewhat in comparison - but don't let that deter you from what fun experiences are to be had in the game!
In terms of storyline; the story in games such as the Civilization series is never a set a narrative but rather the story that evolves as you play. Beyond Earth offers the same compelling stories as previous games in the series. After playing a game Civilization 5, you always have a story to tell about how your Civilization grew, what challenges it accounted, how they held up to those challenges and a few specific events always stick (like the times Ghandi nukes you!). The same is absolutely true of Beyond Earth. The affinities, quests, interactions with neighbours and aliens all combine to create a rich and interesting story for each game you play.
The interface of the game is mostly up to the very high standard you'd expect from a game in the Civilization series. The map view is nice, the menus are clear and informative, and its never hard to find the information you need. There are a few minor let-downs, however, compared with previous games in the series.
Chiefly, the research web is not colour- or otherwise-coded to give you an overview of what each tech will grant you. There is an option to filter the tree to include only certain categories such as buildings, units, etc., but this is an unnecessarily clunky way of presenting this information. There is already a nice mod that clears up the research web and colours codes things nicely, but for those, like me, who are disinclined to download mods, it is still an annoyance, albeit one that will disappear the more acquainted you become with the research web.
Also, here and there small annoyances pop up, like the tedious trade destination menu (why isn't there a hotkey for "use same trade route as previously"?). These are minor complaints, however, given how clear most information is presented. Yield icons, grid overlay, resource icons, etc. are all still there, though the strategic view from Civ 5 has gone (I never liked it anyway - I always felt so removed from the game using it).
Beyond Earth features an excellent tutorial that, especially coupled with the game's early quests, walks you nicely through the new features and mechanics. It's one of those rare brilliant tutorials that never interfere, can be turned off completely or in parts at any time, and which actually provide useful information. Add to that the civilopedia and there is little you need to know about this game that it can't tell you itself!
I love the graphics of Beyond Earth. They are neat, clear and very atmospheric. Honestly, I'm not sure it's fair to ask a strategy game to look better than Beyond Earth. The sound is of exceptional quality. The aliens sound disgustingly alien, the different affinities have certain subtle sounds associated with them and the ambient noise feels just so alien. And the music! Beyond Earth has a brilliant score of varied themes playing on different sci-fi flavours. All in all, the sound and music in the game will transport you to another world!
The major, and fair, difference between Civ:BE and Civ 5 is the much shorter longevity of the game. Civ:BE will not keep you interested for as long as Civ 5 does. It's just not as sprawlingly complex as Civ 5 with all its DLC at the moment. It is unlikely to become quite as complex as the reception of the game has been lukewarm at best. For this reason, the major turn off when considering getting this game should be its long-term appeal.
Civ:BE will initially capture you like any of Sid Meier's previous games. However, it lacks the long-term appeal of his earlier games; it just can't provide the same depth to explore that Civ 5 does. Armed with this knowledge, make a decision on whether or not to get it! But from someone who has got 40-odd hours from the game - I think it's definitely worth getting on a sale!

I love point and click adventure games.  They are what I grew up with, and at the end of the day, it's the format I'm most comfortable with.  I've spent my time in WoW, and I loved it, and I recently spent two full working weeks worth of time beating the Witcher 3's storyline, and all of these are great experiences.  None of them can take me back to my childhood, the kernel of my gaming self, like a solid point and clicker.  And this is one of them.  This is an excellent point and click adventure game.  That's all it is, mind you, it's nothing more than that.  It's just what it's advertising -- and in its genre, it is absolutely superior.  The story is compelling, even for an old guy like me, the mechanics are fine, and the puzzle strength really isn't that hard if you're willing to stick with it.
Yes, we only have walkthroughs for the first two chapters.  Thats ok.  Play around a bit and you WILL figure it out, and it will be way more rewarding than just reading through a walkthrough and beating the game in a few hours.  I promise, you can do it.  Remember when we had to order a hint book from Sierra back in the 80s, and by the time we got it, eight weeks later give or take, we figured out the puzzle?  There's no need for a hint book here.  Just keep at it.  And you'll feel a lot smarter when you figure it out all by yourself.
This game explores a thing that a lot of people have said a lot about, especially while in an altered state, the Dreamscape.  Ah, the Dreamscape, the Holy Grail of all game creators.  Quite possibly, the next bastion of virtual reality, if we really pick the thing apart.  Go read this review again on an energy drink or two.  If we had some sort of device that would let us fall asleep and log in while dreaming, lets be honest, that's another 6-10 hours a night we'd get to game.  That's all I'll tell you about the plot.  You don't need more.  Play the game.  It's fantastic.

Let's start with the 4x elements first. There is almost no planetary development. You can grow population, add some slots for buildings, improve your planet's health all with a couple of clicks. It will take a few minutes to fully develope your planet.
The research tree is generic. When you build let's say a frigate factory you will unlock one ship type. There is a research tab for every ship in the game for unlock only purpose.  There are 4 tabs alone for upgrading armor, doing the same thing for every tab. Same thing for laser weapons, 3 tabs where every tab is divided into 2 levels ( need to research 1 tab twice) for every incremental increase in laser damage. There is so much unnecessary stuff in the tree that it is just not tech tree worthy as a whole.
Expansion is pretty straightforward take a planet by force or take it over by influence. Panets are connected by phase lanes (strings) over which are you able to move and spread your influence. I'd say diplomacy is the only 4x worthy element this game has to offer and worked out well. You can accept missions to increase their relation with you or you give them a mission to improve your relation with them. If the relation in both ways is high enough the chance of them accepting heavier stuff is more probable.
You may ask (missions) a faction to destroy ships, capital ships, structures etc and the amount of it. If they kill 5 or 15 enemy ships for you depends on the relationship. You are also able to join pacts. The better the relation, the more pacts you can join like cease fire, peace, vision or trade treaties. Managing your economy is just as thin as in any other RTS, colonize asteroids for metal and crystal income and max out your population for credits.
First of all there is no singleplayer campaign, it is just pure skirmish against bots and multiplayer. Second point I want to make is that the majority of your game time is spend by battling enemy fleets. Gameplay wise you build up a fleet of mixed unit types. Attack the enemy, lose a big chunk of your fleet, rebuild your fleet and go for the next planet. Flanking does not pay off. There isn't any tactics involved other than timing the activation of your ship's special abilities.
There is no stealth, no surgical strikes, no flanking. Every game plays out the same, build a big balanced fleet and overwhelm the enemy. Quick building is your way to succes. This is a casual RTS game with extra bells and whistles (4x elements) which lacks strategic depth. The game has good graphics and the battles are nice to see when you are zoomed in, which rarely happens anyway. I did not expect this game to have such a lack of tactical gameplay, such a shame.
For a casual RTS experience this game is good. Good graphics, flashy space battles, lots of cool units, wonderful sound effects, always things to do, mods and the 4x elements , altough very minor, are a plus. I would not buy the game if you expect a 4x game, total war style of gameplay or the ability to use tactics to decide battles. I would only recommend this game if you want another casual RTS experience (with casual I don't mean quality, but there are more of them on the market in terms of gameplay). I will give this game thumbs down however (has nothing to do with rating but with recommendation), the reason for downvoting is the lack of depth gameplay wise and the bells an whistles don't make up for it.

This has got to be one of the most beautifully done games I have ever played. In itself you find yourself feeling things you never thought you would feel while playing a game, and balancing those feelings with the sort of life changing actions you have/choose to make.
Playing as a survivor during a war struggling to survive from starvation, illness, wounds, other survivors, and the military, rather then a automatic weapon wielding one man army sent to slaughter hundreds of enemies in the name of your country/organization/religion/whatever. And its that sort of thinking outside the box with how most games are being done now that makes this game a true piece of art.
The combat is unforgiving, just as it should be. If you choose to engage in some kind of combat you had better be prepared to really think about how you are going to take on the obstacles in front of you. Its easy to get wounded, get chased off, or even die if you are not careful.
Scavenging during the night also plays its role, having to balance what is necessary with what isn't. Planning for the future winter by stocking up on canned goods and firewood. Getting the tools and materials needed to truly secure your home, and fix it up with facilities to keep your survivors both happy and alive. Mix in a little trading and you really need to look at all your looting options. Do you take the can of food? Do you really need it? Or is the pile of wood a better choice? Sometimes you will find yourself really balancing it out to because missing some key pieces when your survivors are either hungry, cold, or depressed can really change how the next few days play out.
The music is utterly amazing. Its simple, quiet, and really sets the mood properly with the artistic style the game is designed in. There are times I just left the game on pause while I do some house work, to have that nice ambiance.
My advice, play the game as if you were one of the survivors, don't think of yourself as a player/god controlling these people. When you do that you really start to care about your survivors, what their stories are, and what sort of things they are having to do, let alone what actions you take and how it will effect them.
All in all this game stands out for one main reason. It has a soul. It doesn't need those million dollar CG trailers, seizure inducing lens flares spammed across the screen, sharks with freakin laser beams, Press X to feel aspects that all the recent triple A games have. Its just a well done game with a soul, and as a gamer what more could you ask for?

DashBored is a game of personality. You play as Nicolas, a young man who finds himself in a surreal world and only wants one simple thing: to get himself home. Along the way the player will explore and compact world and engage in turn-based battles.
The element of this game that most players are going to resonate with is its crass charm. DashBored is a sleazy game where you buy things from a Jason Voorhees impersonator and fight monsters that throw children at you. The characters have diverse personalities but are frequently profane. The dialogue in DB is juvenile but not to an extent where it crosses a line. No, it's pretty perfect.
Graphically DashBored is amateurish but it's cartoony style goes good with its snarky, vulgar cast and with its offbeat absurd plot. The music is a highlight. It reminded me a lot of LISA and Earthbound. Some songs work in sound effects into their melodies which is very evocative. One of my favourite tracks was a town theme that incorporated police sirens with its instrumentation. Very cool.
Although DashBored gets by on its personality, players looking for great turn-based battles are going to be disappointed. The battles in this game at their best are pushovers. You are given about 30 abilities among all your party members and I didn't use more of the half of them on regular. DB suffers that classic RPG problem where you are given buffs and debuffs but since most battles are over in a couple rounds, there's no point wasting MP on status ailments that are very circumstantial when that character could just be attacking to make the battle end quicker. This is averted in boss battles, of course.
I also found myself having trouble getting around. Finding shops, a save point, or even an inn can be frustrating and the last thing you want when you're low on health and items is to be searching for a sanctuary. Maybe that was the intention of the developer but in this game it seems unnecessary. You could give DB the benefit of the doubt though and just assume it was this reviewer's inability to navigate.
Interestingly enough, even though I felt on edge a lot and felt like I was only barely overcoming the game's obstacles, there was never a time where I was out of resources and needed to grind. Even when I was low on items and cash, I always got through without grinding so that might be some expert balancing there.
I'm ultimately going to recommend this game because of it's length. DashBored is no longer than 4 hours and very little of that time is wasted. You're always seeing new and interesting things in this world and the plot moves at a good pace. It's not a great plot but its a plot that allows the developer to tell a lot of jokes and have the personalities of the story's characters bounce off each other. That's what DashBored is. It a game as a vehicle for a lot of weirdness and comedy and if you can tolerate some boring battles then you'd do well to pick it up.
NOTE: Right now DashBored has a few bugs and is a little janky. As far as I know the developer is fixing them slowly so if you encounter any bugs be sure to report them to the dev.

Hitman is a game where your play as an Agent 47. I wont spoil the story for you, but know that it is different then what we are used to seeing from old Hitman games. Instead of killing targets for Agency, in this sequel story is more personal. Agent 47 after killing his friend Diana feels regret and decided to honor her dying wish to protect a little girl.
The storyline is interesting all the way through with a few plots and twists. There are interesting characters that are unique and interesting. However, there are more of them that are simply faceless and not that interesting. It feels like story was rushed a bit. On average it can be completed in 15 hours. Overall the story is one of this game’s good points.
Game controls are easy to learn. They are logically laid out for a third person shooter game. New slow motion mechanic is great as it can help you kill more enemies and also give you more time to think how to properly respond to current situation. Sometimes camera can be a problem, but overall controls are solid.
When it comes to level design all of them are unique in their own way. Levels range from Chinatown to library rooftops. This variety of the levels keeps the game interesting and adds more to the total experience of the story. However, levels disappoint with their size. In previous Hitman games levels where much bigger while in the Hitman Absolution they are divide into smaller chunks. New players to these series are probably going to be okay with this, but for players like me that are used to huge sandbox levels this is not acceptable. Game devs should reconsider this approach and design the new Hitman with big levels like they used to even if that means sacrificing amount of details in each level. Even with levels being smaller they are connected with meaningful cut scenes. Also, levels being smaller encourage players to replay each section without being penalized. There are many things you can do and each level is replayable so you can get your moneys worth if you wanted to. Moreover, because levels are spilt into smaller pieces, you will know that you will find your target at the end of each level. This is a problem because it deviates from sandbox gameplay in the previous games. In older games you don’t necessary know where your target is. This sometimes turned into a can and mouse type of gameplay that is missing in this new game.
Graphics in this game are rally good. There is a lot of detail in each level. My guess is that level size was sacrificed for this. Also, lighting is simply awesome and is one of the best in business. In some games graphics quality is not all that important but in Hitman I think it is really important because it lets you feel like YOU are the Agent 47.
In addition to good graphics, this game does deliver on sound effects and music. Sound effect are properly produced with big attention to realism. Music fits the scene and adds to the overall experience.
Multiplayer experience is not interesting and in my opinion it becomes boring. I think the reason for it is because the multiplayer is not really multiplayer since you are never in the same level with different players. Instead, there is something called contracts. Players create contracts and other players play them for rewards in credits and equipment. You will probably play a few contracts and then just go back to paying the story mode again.
In conclusion, I think that Hitman is a great game and I would recommend it to people who like stealth games with the just right amount of action. If you are a big fan of Hitman franchise you might not like this game the same way you did other Hitman games, but instead you will like it for its own qualities that other games lacked.
Buy this game or you are going on my hit list :P

I have changed my recommendation from recommended to not recommended.  I was unable to finish the campaign of the game without hacking my save file, because there of objectives presented in a campaign mission that were impossible to achieve; specifically, there is a mission that requires you to build a space station; to build that station you must purchase resources, and two resources I needed were made unavailable to me through vendors, side quests, resource farming or in-game piracy.  I cannot recommend a game with a single player campaign that is impossible to beat.
The only way to beat the mission without hacking your save file is to know what resources you need ahead of time and acquire them before you reach the point in the campaign where you build a fleet and go to war with the controlling faction.  That is an unreasonable ask.  In addition, the general learning curve is far too steep, and available tutorials that explain all of the game mechanics are poor in the way they explain mechanics; lacking both detail and clarity, and difficult to find and repeat when needed.
Really, there are a littany of small problems that detract from the overall enjoyment of this game; too many to list, but would include: poor fleet AI, frequent issues with object targeting while in your ship, a poor UI with multiple problems such as illegible fonts, an inability to recolor HUD elements (which is a problem when half of the galaxy is the same color orange as your targeting reticle) and object indicators that are way too small; a poorly implemented dialog wheel, the choice of using a sidecar menu for game interaction instead of superior and more popular radial menus, along with several others I don't care to mention for the sake of brevity.

Beyond Earth. More like Beyond Hope. The game launched with a profound thud by reviewers and raging anger from fans. And why not? After all this time, after Civ5 and the lessons learned... They managed to make CivBE... Worse! In so many ways.
Besides the (few) factions, we now have civ affinities: Harmony, Purity and Supremacy (for the sake of clarity: Hippies, Racists and Weabos). These change few things, from buildings and unit traits to the way the aliens interact with you. Problem is, in the grand scheme of things, they feel more like  skins with a few stat differences. You will eventually get to choose out of 3 different stat sets per upgrade, and more often than not only one is actually useful. In some cases, lady luck will shine upon you and there will be TWO useful sets, but that's about it. Besides this and a few other changes, they all play very similar to one-another. Oh sure, the Hippies can become besties with the aliens, but that's like befriending paint.
Factions will tend to flock to the ones with identical affinities and fight everyone else, which also makes the system seem more like the olden religion system. Gone are specific units. It also doesn't help that some leaders use the same text and audio from the previous title.
The aliens are dumb (big shocker; no really, they seemed smart in the preview videos). They rarely go from the green state (passive), and almost never DARE cross your border (probably think they need visas). You will often witness the "mighty" Siege Worms pile up on the outskirts, shuffling back and forth as if deciding where to eat.
Your "intelligent" counter-parts are none the smarter. I only lost a city once in 50+ hours of gameplay, and that's on Very Hard and because i didn't give a f*ck about a stronger neighbour and his requests. The rest of the time they will usually fall behind on techs, make little to no diplomatic efforts and generally being useless, and short-time, friends. At this point in Civ games, I say scrap diplomacy altogether. It's what they seem to aim for anyways.
The new features are nothing memorable either. The "choose your own path" is just a set of events and choices: one is good, one is bad. Yeah, that's a brainer. A large majority of them are also standard, meaning you will always get them in your playthrough and you will always pick the same option because the other one's useless.
The orbital layer system is also weak. Think you can build or command space-ships to fly by in the orbital layer and bombard cities / drop units in an awesome, futuristic invasion? Well TO BAD. Put this satellite up! They're not all bad, but they have the life-span of soap, meaning you need a new one every 15-20 turns, and some of them take quite a lot to build so just to keep your orbital "units" running you need to be constantly building them. No, don't think about at least adding a "repair" ship in orbit. That might be fun.
Perhaps the worst part of it is that it feels stripped down, to make way for DLC. But even then they somehow managed to f*ck it up. There are dozens of people on the forums complaining about how the new (and only) DLC somehow managed to ruin diplomacy more.
Oh no, wait, the worst part is the game has a breaking bug (crash in late-game) and the devs ain't fixing it.
Everything in CivBE's composition makes you think it's a test by Firaxis/2K, who just want to see exactly how much bullsh*t their clients can take.  Don't buy this. Don't even think about getting it on a discount.
If a friend gives it to you for free, refuse it and never speak to them again as they are clearly trying to psychologically torture you.

Tiny & Big is probably one of the most unique games I've ever played.
To basically describe it, it's a Physics-based 3D Platformer... WITH ROCKETS AND LASERS.
Yes, Rockets and Lasers.
The main idea behind T&B is that your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brother/cousin/etc. (it's never made exactly clear) has stolen your grandpa's magical underpants that have just the right ammount of abilities to rule the freak'n world, so, as a good brother/cousin/etc. would do, you pack a friend (a radio) with you, and begin to go after him. It's an absurd premise, yes, but it's done justice with the ammount of charm on display here. There are multiple witty lines that had me either laughing or at least giving a smirk rather than feeling a slight overdose of cringe. On top of this, the visual style is excellent! It's cartoony and doesn't have over $1000000 worth of budget put into it, but it still manages to be one of the best looking games I've played in a while... and did I mention this game can easily (with no horrifying framedips, going from my experience) run on lower-end PCs'. That's awesome... just thought I'd point that out. Finally, the soundtrack and secrets. The soundtrack fits very well with the game, and has some very catchy tunes. The levels that fill this game also have some pretty cool secrets in them, like hidden mini-games. This game also has some pretty intelligent, but not too hard, puzzles in it... but, I'll get into that in a bit.
I do have some issues with this game.
You can beat T&B in about 2-3 if you're just rushing through it, though this doesn't bother me. Shorter games are awesome if they can provide you with a solid experience despite the length, and this does just that. My main issue with this game relies with the last 2 stages. NO SPOILERS, I PROMISE... but, compared to the other great levels this game provided me with, they came to me as the weaker points of this game. The second to last level was the longest, but it was also the most irritatating and confusing. The final level had one of the shortest bosses, and was one of the shortest levels in the game, which is astounding, considering you can beat the first level in less than 5 minutes! There are little physics puzzles here and there that ARE smart and manage to be easy at the same time, but the second to last level completley ♥♥♥♥♥ over the fun-ness of those puzzles by making you scream in agitation when a block of wood that you NEEDED to progress falls out of sight, and the only way to get it back is to *hopefully* throw yourself off a cliff and die.
1 minor issue I also had with this game: Bugs. They weren't too common, but they were sure apparent... ESPECIALLY in the second to last level. To describe my experience: at one point, I pushed a door down to use as a platform. I cut one of the things holding it back, die, and then magically spawn at the next checkpoint. This also happened to me near the end, making me shocked when a pre-boss-battle boss battle showed up when I respawned for no good reason.
Will get better with DLC and the amazing mod community. But the base game is ok, not perfect but when you have all 3 ultimate units taking down brasilia's capital and winning it's a beautiful sight

Review in Tribute of Charlie Fitzsimons:
From time to time you get to play games that make you think of happy memories. It’s one of the real joys of gaming. In the case of Loot Hounds it made me think of Ainslie’s recently deceased dog, Charlie. Charlie was the first dog that she had after moving out of her parents house and into her own. It was me that put her onto Charlie. I posted an ad on Gumtree looking for a hypoallergenic dog because she was desperately seeking a canine companion and is very much a dog oriented person yet she is allergic to most breed. Someone from a suburb a few over from ours saw our ad and responded to me telling me that she had a dog that she was going to be forced to surrender as she had broken up with her partner and the rental property she was taking would not allow dogs and her ex was not fond of Charlie or dogs for that matter.
Upon first meeting Charlie Ainslie fell immediately in love. He was a excited little ball of fluff who had a heart full of love – and a tongue full of licks and kisses. He was already 7 when she got him so sadly we missed the first half of his life. He was a real little ferret. He’d get into things and get up to all sorts of mischief. He could be a real little♥♥♥♥♥♥but he was Ainslie’s real little♥♥♥♥♥♥and deep down we loved him for it. He had a lot of quirks and would make you frustrated but that was Charlie. He’d pounce on anything and be a real scavenger. He absolutely loved his toys especially his squeaky ho ho (Christmas toy that had ho ho ho! written on it) but most of all he loved his food. Neither of us have ever seen such a food obsessed dog. Given the skill points food gives you in Loot Hounds we’ve finally found our answer as to why. Little dude just wanted to skill up and be better than all of the other dogs! Atta boy! Most of all he just wanted to love. If either Ainslie or I were sitting with him on the couch while watching television or anything you’d have to tell him to stop licking you several times. He’d then look up at you with a real look of mischievousness in his eyes and then he’d lick or kiss you once or twice more before stopping – for a minute.
Charlie had a rough life. We believe that he was a puppy farm dog. He’d react with great fright any time there was a light or a reflection on the ceiling or if somebody had anything with a light in it (for example the light up swords and sabers, torches, etc.). His limbs were already fairly weakened when we got him. He suffered a couple of broken legs when we had him – running around the yard or doing something but he was always a quick healer. We hope that we gave him the best life possible.
The point of this is that Loot Hound reminded me of just how amazing Charlie was and how much I miss him. He passed away on October 15, 6 days after Ainslie’s birthday. He’d been suffering from prolonged heart failure and fought a long and hard fight. But his very last act was after going outside for a nightly toilet stop he saw a cane toad and in typical Charlie fashion he pounced on the poisonous frog and bit it. Of course, the toad as they are notorious for doing in self defence (though sometimes in attack) sprayed its poison into Charlie’s mouth. Ainslie got him inside and we got the poison out of him. We rushed him to the vet who advised us that he hadn’t had enough of the poison to kill him but his heart failure was killing him. If anything the toad’s poison allowed him to reach a state of drunkenness – a happy high if you so choose. He wasn’t in any pain but that due to the heart he wasn’t responding to their efforts to help him. We had the choice of giving him another month at tops of a miserable existence where he wouldn’t be himself or we could end him on that ‘happy high.’  The decision to euthanize Charlie was one of the saddest ones that Ainslie and I have had to make but it was the right one.
If you’re a dog lover and want to enjoy a casual video game in which you can reminisce and remember your favorite memories with your dogs – living or deceased – then Loot Hounds will deliver in spades. It’s a cute game that plays intelligently and is very much worth a few hours of your time.
R.I.P. Charlie. We miss you more and more every day. Gone but never ever forgotten. A void in our lives forever.

Loot Hound is a very casual indie game. It's a calm, relaxing little game. Now, I don't mean it's little because this game seems to have quite a bit too it. I think it'd be best if I started with the general story of this game. You play as a man who has a pet dog. Your first dogs name is Marley, and you can eventually end up with three dogs in total. You and your dog decide to go on an adventure to find the best loot in all of the land. And is it easy? Well, that's where our first point begins...
This game isn't simple at all. It's not a hard game, but that doesn't mean that the game isn't complicated in more than a few ways. Okay, I'm not explaining this in the best way so let me sum this part up on what I like about the difficulty and how it's well balanced.
-Having to upgrade your dogs with the points from the loot you find is an extrememly nice touch, it makes it so that the loot has a reason to be collected and not as if you're just doing it for a goal.
-Having different dogs being good at different things is a REALLY good concept. A smaller dog for small gaps in the hedge, a large dog for scaring away critters with a fierce bark and Marley, the dog that can dig through stone.
I think the next place I should focus on is the actual gameplay itself. How the game controls and how it feels to be played. The controls in this game are very tight and feel very well polished. The game uses some very basic controls. You use WASD to move and Ctrl and Shift to pull in the lead or extend the lead. Overall controlling of the game is very well done and is an obvious sign that the devs have put a lot of time into trying to make the game feel as polished as possible.
The art of this game is very, very neat and really fits the overall charm of the game very well. This game radiates the vibrant, happy feeling that it wants you to feel. When the dog of your choice digs up the ground, the hole animations are very neat and confined to being so neat and tidy. The loot sprites are something that this game does insanely well. With the game containing well over 300 sprites of different and unique little items of loot. The loot which you collect is also accompanied by a very British and enthusiastic narrator. This narrator will also talk to you at the start of the level and never at one time have I ever felt like the voice is being shoved down my throat.
Each level in this game is very different from the other, some may require all dogs to beat the level and some may require a single dog. The levels in this game are so well made that I've never found myself being lost or cursing the game for not being clear enough in how I'm supposed to do something or where I'm supposed to go. Some levels may have a Dog Patrol Officer. He will act as the main enemy in this game, but he's not exactly impossible or unfair. If he catches you, you will be sent back to your home and will be forced to start the level again. BUT, what made me increasingly happy is that the loot you've already found will stay collected, meaning you don't have to redo the whole level. I really enjoyed the first 9.7 hours I had in the game.
Pros:
*The game has a very nice aesthetic to it that can be customized to how you like it.
*There are numerous side stories that you can do. I really liked doing these, and found them to be the better part of the game.
*The game has a decent atmosphere.
Cons:
*There wsn't much music. I get that it might clash with some parts of the game, but the lack of music really holds the rest of the atmosphere back. even a bit more ambiance would help.
*There isn't a huge variety of weapons. There's three types of bows counting the crossbow, and two kind of guns. I only used the bows in regular combat until I could get a gun, then I used the crossbow in any kind of stealth scenario. I feel that bows needed a good reason to be used. Sure around mid game you can get a really fast short bow, but by then the pistol you have will likely out damage it. Heck, by then I was able to oneshot many of the enemies with my weapons.
*Enemies are pretty bland. There's eight enemies that I can think of. For the most part, enemies can fall into one of two or three groups. There is an enemy that made combat interesting on the first encounter, as it requires a specific way to damage it. Once you figure it out, though, they just become a nuisance.
*Combat is pretty basic. aside from the two main types of weapons, you have bombs and tomahawks. I think I accidentally used either of the special items than I did on purpose.
*The ending of the main story leaves a ton to be desired, honestly. The ending left me pretty confused. After watching other people play through the ending, I saw I'm not alone, and it's a case of too little information. This is a serious shame, as by this time I was really enjoying the story. I really wish we could get some sort of followup, because I REALLY want to know more.
*Stuff just isn't explained. there's no lore behind any of the interesting bits.

Bioshock 2 was set up almost from the onset to be a colossal failure. It was to follow one of the most critically acclaimed games of all time, by a different developer, with the inclusion of a seemingly tacked on multiplayer mode to a series that had absolutely no need for one. It had every possibility to be a disaster, which makes it almost shocking that it arrived in a state that was not only comparable to the original game, but improved and expanded on it as well in ways that would be hard to go back from. It’s the sequel I never expected; maybe nobody did.
And important distinction to make before discussing Bioshock 2’s narrative, is that the first game was first and foremost the story of the city of Rapture and its fall into madness through its own attempts to create a lawless utopia. In comparison, 2 is almost entirely focused around a very small cast of key characters; their relationships to each other, conflicting ideals, and eventual goals which clash with each other and create this very personal, self contained narrative, within which Rapture is merely a setting instead of the star.
In some ways this is a good thing. By taking the focus off of Rapture and onto a new, very small collection of characters, developer 2K Marin is able to craft a more personal narrative, spending more time developing the characters that matter and the relationships between them. In other ways, it makes the time not spent directly advancing the plot far less impactful and memorable than they may otherwise have been. Characters outside the very core plot are introduced and then discarded in ways that feel contrived and unmemorable, moving you along but never leaving much of an impact outside of your immediate encounters with them. This also contributes to Rapture being a much less interesting, tangible place to explore, feeling stale and lifeless when at one point it was remarkably well crafted and intriguing.
On the whole, the narrative is rather significantly less mentally stimulating, disregard the deeper themes of ideology, morality, and freedom that gave the original such an astounding sense of scope and inspired so much discussion about the different ideas laced within the game. Bioshock 2 tries to mimic what Irrational Games did so deftly, but it comes out as something superfluously intelligent; tossing about grand ideas in the background of a fairly simple plot that never attempts more than it can feasibly accomplish. Simplicity isn’t a bad thing by nature, as the story is still engaging and arguably easier to follow, but I rather missed the more sophisticated philosophical questions posed by the original that was so substantially more contemplative and inspired.
The change to a strictly linear world design was also rather disappointing to me, as though there are logical narrative reasons you wouldn’t be able to return to locations after you went through them, it’s yet another thing taken away from the original that causes Rapture to feel like a rather hollow environment. It’s still full of the same distinctive artwork, excellent sense of place, and fitting music, but it feels so soulless compared to what it once was that it makes returning to Rapture again almost dull at times. There are things later on which actually add interesting, fundamental aspects to the city’s lore, but by that point it’s almost too late and the moment will likely be lost or overlooked by most.
Whether the changes are improvements or make up for what was lost is debatable, though by and large the plot failed to leave the impression the original did, despite being well written and interesting in its own right. Perhaps its the issue of being in the shadow of such a monumental achievement that was Bioshock, that anything to come after that isn’t as incredibly feels significantly more of a disappointment that it otherwise would. Had 2 been released as in a vacuum I may have been more receptive to what it was attempting to do, but with the weight of its predecessor on its shoulders there was just - something - missing to draw me in quite the same way as I was to the original.
Where 2 far surpasses the original though is through the numerous refinements and additions it makes to the mechanics, turning Bioshock from a brilliantly deep and satisfying shooter, into a smoother, even deeper shooter that streamlines and polishes off the few rough edges of the original. The core of the combat is largely unchanged, utilizing a mixture of firearms and plasmids (essentially superpowers) to take down a variety of different splicers (the enemies of the game), but the introduction of dual wielding, the ability to instantly switch ammo types, a collection of interesting new weapons, a significantly faster and less cumbersome hacking system, and a scaled back but even more customizable tonic (passive upgrades) system do a lot to make Bioshock 2 a much faster and enjoyable experience.
They’re small changes for the most part to be sure, but collectively add up to a much tighter shooting experience that makes it hard for me to imagine returning to the comparatively clunky original. Encounters with the most prominent new enemy, Big Sisters, is another brilliant twist on something the original began (in this instance the Big Daddy fights, which also return), as quicker, more capable and powerful enemies that present a large challenge and require you change your tactics as they are far more versatile and aggressive than their older counterparts.
These improvements make Bioshock 2 one of the most enjoyable and dynamic shooters I’ve ever played. Where it falters in its storytelling and world building, it makes up for with the sheer entertainment to be found in its combat, which only grows as the game goes on. It might not wholly surpass the original, but it surely approaches it in a lot of ways, which is something I scarcely imagined there was any possibility it could. In some ways it feels more akin to an update than an entire new experience, but when that update is so fun and smartly designed I can't complain.
On multiplayer…
Surprising though it may be, 2K has fitted a multiplayer mode within Bioshock 2, and even more unexpectedly it’s not terrible! More than that, it’s actually a rather enjoyable mode that while totally derivative of every other first-person multiplayer shooter in terms of modes, progression, and character customization, it transposes the campaigns fantastic shooting into a multiplayer mode almost entirely intact. Your weapons and abilities might be slightly neutered, but the combat is so strong at its core that I found myself spending a surprising amount of time with the mode and enjoying every moment of it. Bioshock as a shooter is almost completely unreplicated in any other game, so having that in a multiplayer mode that even in every other aspect is fairly uninteresting is rather compelling, and most certainly worth checking out despite its dubious inclusion. 7/10.

First off, Get it, I think you will like it a lot epecially as its not nearly as expensive or load intensive as Eve Online or Star Trek...
If you're new to the modability of the X universe you probably don't know this but, the X3 universe had great components to it.  It still had profound limitations that the raw Vanilla or un-moded program had that confined what a mod script could actually do.  Like you couldn't make the text size bigger very easily...
Why?  To many conflictual errors that bleed into other scripts.  I imagine that XRebirth will still have parts that a mod can not change and will have to come down the pipe later from the dev's.  For this reason, I will add all my comments as I have played with about 80-90 mods installed right now.
Pro's
GRAPHICS:  See system info at bottom of review.
- This is a very immersive space sim, much more so than X3, and most other space sims ever could be.
- It's visually astounding in many ways w/(ULTRA SETTINGS) and I love that you can not only pilot ships but that you can move around them.
- I can't say anthing has seemed "glitchy", produced atrifacts, or caused the texture panels to split when you are close to them at just the right angle like a lot of open world games have issues with.  It's refreshing in that arena for sure.
SHIP/STATION DYNAMICS:
- Stations are vastly more complex, beautiful, and formitable in combat.
- The change from weapon "energy usage p/sec" to "over heating" is and interesting componnent that makes combat more user skill dependent and less "cookie cutter" when piloting fully out-fitted ships.
- In the "skunk", M6 Corvette class, your 5 main assult weapons have their own unique applications and it makes for some more realism.  Sometimes I'd switch to the wrong weapon and well, if I were a space pirate, in the heat of battle, I might just do that so.... again... more immersiveness.
- Sheilds, Engines, and Weapons can also be modified to fit your play style, tanky high sustainability, high damage dealing but overheats quickly, agile and fast shotting or a mix of all.
- Combat, especially with regard to capital ships is much better.  You can target individual weapons turrets, engines, and other ship components like radar to help ensure boarding opperations.
- Boarding opperations are also much more complex allowing you to disable engines and weapons before capturing.
- The addition of diverse and specialized crew holds a lot of promise as well.
- Drone piloting is much more fluid and clear.  In X3 I had very little idea when or what they were doing.
- Scanner functions and Hacking give a modicum of chance regarding profiterring,treasure hunting, and sabotage.
GAME PLAY:
- The story line seems decent and the missions that are available have greater realism.
- I have only logged about 35+ hrs but, have found it to be very fun and awe-inspiring.
- There are many worth while mods now that give the game greater depth, character, ease of interface, diversity, and fluidity.
- Most of the Vanilla music while flying is great at setting more immersive ambiance.
Neutal's
- Having to scan all the parts of a station is tedious for sure.  But, they look so cool!  My favorite is the one with the mono-rail train transporting on top of it!  They have unique sounds and characteristics that make the whole floating in space to investigate much more cool and worth the time invested.
- The addition of so many craftable items is interesting but, how does all that stuff not take up cargo space??
- Saved game and startup load times are substantially longer... maybe its time I got a SSD...lol
Con's
GAME PLAY:
To a large Extent the videos add depth to the main plot missions but they are overall lacking in orginality.  I think more will come through mods... we will see.
SHIP/STATION DYNAMICS:
- The highways and station scanning are interesting components.  Unfotuanatly, they necessitate "no collissions" being instituted.  Infinitely bouncing off stuff with speed and size of objects being completely irrelevent, is gimmicky to say the least.  It does distill the immersive experiance substantially.
- Where are the Boron??  They had some pretty cool ships.  Especially with the "living hulls" mod...
- There do not seem to be very many ships in this version of the X universe yet.  There is some diversity among races still but a lot of bleed over.  As in, multiple factions if not all use the same sets of ships...  maybe more comming??  Its been 2 years or more already...
- - - What happend to having "Wings" with different color codes?
- THE CREW INTERFACE:
- Needs a lot of work.
- I don't see how you can "lockout" the ability to command a MORE experienced but not full 5 stared engineer on your M6 from commensing 100% hull repairs and need to dock somewhere to use another, LESS experienced engineer...do they have access to full schmatics or something??
- The inability to command your docked ships crew at all when on a station is just stupid.  That needs to change.  Com Badge??
- The "Property Menu" was much better organized and complete in X3.  Now, it doesn't show your personel at all, even though you have so many more types of them... why?
- - What would it take to be able to move piolts around??  Now, your pilot gets sold with the ship??  That is annoying...
- - Setting up a squad and quickly initiating commands has always been a problem in the Vanilla versions but this takes it to a whole new level.  I have spent way too much time trying to figure out why I couldn't give commands to a secondary squad or crew memeber and only through the "details" menu under that persons info...  Too many levels deep.  What about a similar interface to drone selection?
- Why are your bargans with particular traders only good for that visit??  Too much to load and remember?  I don't like having to do the more complex conversation stuff through the psudo-dice-rolling-manipulation-interface-thing everytime I wan't a deal.  Especially with the 1-2 minute load times when mistakes are made..
HACKING:
- If you are going to hack something, you should have choices.  I DO think it should be bouned to what a console can do but NOT in such that its just a general "Hack"  that gets the pre-destined result...I'd like something like, I'm in, now what can I do, how much time can I stay in?
Having written this little book, a good number of the cons will probably be changed through mods.  Those that can't be will hopefully grab the attention of the Devs to focus on for updates.  They have already come a long way since its launch and I'm very happy to pay for this version of the game so far.

A nice, small game with a fantastic central mechanic. The art has a lot of charm and, dispite being very short (about 2 hours long) it doesn't overstay its welcome wich is more than I can say about most games nowadays.
4/5

Graphics:
I’m just finishing this game on 12/09/2015. That being said, the graphics are still significantly superior to much of anything you’ll play on a “next gen” console. At the time of purchase I had 2 GTX 680s and they could barely keep up with the game. Areas with heavy tessellation would see framerate dips into the 40s with the game maxxed out. I later upgraded my rig to 2 GTX 970s and the game saw occasional dips into the high 50s.  I have never tested to see how the game was utilizing SLI, nor did I switch the physx setting to prefer CPU; something that can help games heavy on VRAM.
Overall, the lighting is beautiful and the character detail is great.
Sound:
The music, like many other action games, gets suspenseful situationally. The sounds of choking people, the explosions, and the guns all have unique sounds. You couldn’t expect much more from a game.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is mostly solid. There are instances where you should clearly be able to jump over an object but the game will not allow you to do so because it wants to challenge you to find an alternate route. This is all well and good but I found it limiting. I appreciate it for what it is however, and overall I liked the variety in which you can eliminate a target. If you want to go through the game guns blazing, you can do so quite easily but you lose the reward in both satisfaction and score.
Bugs:
I can’t think of anything of the top of my head but there were several circumstances where you’d have to be in the vicinity of the target for the target to consume a poisoned food or fall into your trap. This slowed down the game in my opinion. In one circumstance I poisoned the targets food and immediately egressed to the exit but the target never consumed the poison. Instead of going through the whole thing again, I just used a suppressed weapon as the target walked past my location.
Replayability:
There are tons of fan created missions/challenges as well as other missions.  The game in late 2015 also shows scores of friends on your steam account so you can see their score and try to surpass them. I give it a high replayability for those completionists out there.
Story:
The story was pretty interesting. Not the best in 47’s history but was a fun game and wasn’t dull by any stretch. You sort of know how everything is going to turn out from the beginning but sometimes surprise isn’t necessary in order to have an enjoyable story. Overall a solid story that keeps you interested, though I typically enjoy a broad array of gaming storylines, so long as they don’t jam a political agenda down your throat.
Conclusion:
Game is worth the price of admission, especially for what you can pay for it currently. For being a last generation release, it is much better looking than some contemporary releases. If you can catch it on a steam sale, which you should be able to for single digit American Dollars, I’d say go ahead.

I enjoyed this game quite a bit. Is it Civ V? No, it is not, but it is fun. There are problems with the game, but there are also many things that I enjoy.
Pros:
+ Combat is more fun than in V: maybe it's just the aesthetics, but there is something satisfying about lumbering into an enemy city with a genetically engineered monstrosity. The asymmetry between the ideologies also means that unique units are more than just slightly-tweaked regular units as in Civ V.
+ The soundtrack is stellar (ha, get it?). It's straightforward sci fi stuff, but it's executed very well. A+.
+ City-building is interesting. There are a wide variety of hex upgrades which allow you to focus on particular aspects of the game instead of doing more or less the same thing every time (settle near a river, build farms, mines, and luxuries). Even farms can be exciting if you go for the right upgrades.
Cons:
- Given the lack of interesting diplomacy, it's very good that combat is pretty solid. Diplomacy could scarcely be less interesting. The addition of "favors" as a diplomatic currency is intriguing but vastly underutilized.
- Leader personalities are mostly restricted to quotes in loading screens. Granted, Civ V and other iterations of the primary branch of the Civ franchise have history to supply a lot of the character backgrounds, but regardless of *why* it is the case, the leaders are still mostly just blank slates. This just reinforces how dull diplomacy really is.
- Ideologies could be a lot more robust. As it is, they influence what kinds of units you can unlock, and they are necessary for the respective ideology victories, but that's about it. The enemy AI will dislike you if you choose an opposing ideology, even though those with similar ideologies are just as bad-off if you get an ideological victory as those who chose a different path. Ideology has literally no effect on the world, and that's a big letdown. If it operated more like religion in V, I'd be very glad.
Overall:
Get it on sale. Of course, you should probably get most games on sale, but you know what I mean. After a few more patches and possibly some DLC/xpacks, it will probably be a GREAT game. I can't fail to recommend the game, though, because while it didn't live up to expectations, it truly is a good game worth playing.

Before I get into commenting on the actual game, it should be known that the crash and corrupt save bugs can be fixed (at least for me) by the following method as mentioned by Pyxel Pengu in his/her review. I'll just copy the method below.
THIS CAN BE FIXED by going into your steam directory for the game (Steam\steamapps\common\BioShock Remastered\Build\Final), locate the BioshockHD.exe file, right click it, go to the compatibility tab and make sure to check "Run in 640 x 480" (this doesnt affect actual game resolution), "Override high DPI scaling", and "Run this program as administrator".
When I personally tried this, I've run the game with no problem.
Now, onto the game itself.
If you are looking for a game with pretty good gameplay and a decent story. This is the pick. Since this game is accepted as a cult classic, I won't go into its strength. Instead, I'll talk about some issues I found with this game.
While it has decent gameplay, I found the degree of freedom to be lacking. Sure, you can kill enemies in all kind of manners. Unlike good games that come out nowadays, though, you can only follow the way the designer want you to play to complete the mission, basically explore the entire map and kill all NPCs. A lot of times I found myself searching through already explored terrain for minutes and just not finding the mission objectives. In the end I always resort to searching online forum for a solution. One time, I even discovered that I've encountered a bug that I wouldn't otherwise have known.
The story is told in a fantastic manner. The narratives rely on audio recordings, radio transmissions, reaction of NPCs, and occasionally through brief flashbacks. Bioshock also has a pretty strong theme conveyed in the story. Take the positive compliments with a grain of salt, however. As great as the story could be, it is diminished by a lack of details. A lot of details in-between what we understand from the game relies on reader's own imagination to bridge the gap.
All in all, though, I would recommend this game even for softcore play-for-the-story players like I (and of course that means even more recommended for hardcore players). Performance issues though are a concern, because even with the method I mentioned above there are still problems with steam cloud and you initiate the game.

In my 30 hours (at this point in time) playing this, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, especially for $10.
It has the feeling of a budget game, which I expect it was (the first Air Conflicts has recieved so much Flak [Ha ha ha, get it? Flak? Anti-Air? Anyone?] that they probably were a little scared of how the second would turn out) but they managed to make this game a very, VERY, good budget game, especially for $10.
I'm not sure what people are talking about with the low resolution stuff. These past two weeks I've been able to play it in full 1920 x 1080, no iffy decals or anything. Though, on my laptop (I used to play this on a laptop, ran pretty well actually) I encountered a bug where the text, some of the logos, and most of the decals were very, very, low res. Didn't happen to me when I played it on my desktop, though.
I'll cover a few key parts:
Gameplay - For a budget game (budget game in this context is something that doesn't have EA throwing money at it) the gameplay is excellent, furthurmore with it only being $10. It CAN be repetitive and frustrating at times, but it was still a fun game, for me at least.
Voice acting - Lemme let you in on a little secret I bet a lot of people didn't notice. They had, I believe it was four or five (can't remember) voice actors, for about eight or so characters. Don't believe me? Watch the credits. Despite this, those voice actors deserve some (a lot) of credit. Personally I heard some similarites, never suspected it was because they were all the same voice actor. I just thought it was (no offense) the English accent.
Graphics - In my opinion, 9.5/10. You must remember this is "AIR conflicts" not "GROUND conflicts" they put a lot of work into the planes to make them detailed. Seriously, the machine gun bullets ACTUALLY shoot out of the machine guns! (This is a big deal because this is pretty rare among air sims under $20) The ground graphics were sacrificed, of course. I was able to fly through some of the buildings to a point without exploding, as an example. The building textures seem low res as well. But if you want this game for it's ground graphics, you really should spend your $10 on a FPS shooter.
Camera - VERY well suited for this game. You can change camera locations, such as 3rd person, in-cabin without the cockpit visible, in-cabin with the cockpit visible. There's also a follow bomb/missile ability.
Missiles are NOT lock-on/tracking. You must manually aim them. As said in-game, they did not have tracking missiles during WW2.
My experience was probably made better by the fact that I have a joystick (Logitech Extereme 3D Pro)
All in all, the game is worth the $10, in my opinion.

I kind of enjoyed Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell, but it has some flaws and annoyances.
First off, the game is extremely short, you can beat it in about 3 to 4 hours if you only go through the main story. That said, the story progression is handled in a way similar to some older Saints Row titles did with Respect, you have to♥♥♥♥♥♥off Satan enough to proceed in the campaign.
If you go for a completionist run including achievements, you'll be spending a minimum of 20 hours as one of the required achievements is to roam the streets of hell for that amount of time. Excluding that, you'd probably spend around 10 to 15 hours getting all collectables, finishing all activities and doing all challenges. Basically what I'm saying is the game is short.
The game is very easy, too. If you play on Medium difficulty, it is very easy to just plow through any obstacles without worrying much about failing or dying. I only died twice in the game and the first one was due to a bug that made a health-draining enemy immune to whatever I did to try to shake it off, and the second was intentional for an achievement that requires a death.
Cutscenes, takedowns and almost any scripted animations are locked to 30FPS. The cutscenes are okay since they're pre-rendered and all, but takedowns are generated in-game, making the use of takedowns very unappealing in the long run. Otherwise, the game ran smooth as silk (except saving sometimes caused hiccups, but I don't know if it's my hard drive or the game).
The largest issues with the game are with controls. First, there's no option to disable aim-assist. Second, the key bindings are broken to an extent where you can't bind some of the actions at all, or they only take very specific keys for them.
I'd say the best part in the game is how they redesigned the "flying" from Saints Row IV to actual flying, giving you much more freedom and making it much more entertaining to fly around. They also introduce a bunch of new weapons, most of which are pretty dang fun to use.
Overall, I'd say the price it asks isn't a lot, even though it's pretty light on content.

Loot Hound is a casual scavenger game (emphasize on casual) which revolves around a man who collects seemingly useless trinkets, no 'loot' here.  You start of with Marley, a cute labrador who you take for walks in the park. You guide Marley by tugging on it's leash and let her explore by giving the leash slack. Simple mechanics which only require you to use WASD to move and Shift and Crtl to give slack or tug on the leash. The starting stages are incredibly easy with no obstacles except for a few distractions which don't let Marley focus on digging. You can easily circumvent this by upgrading stats to gain things like better concentration, better digging, better finding, more stamina, and better luck. Each loot hunt only lasts as long as your dog's stamina or until you get caught by the park guards. There is a total of 10 stages, each with their unique challenges and loot to find. By the third stage you will need Wifi, a small chihuahua who has the special ability of fitting into tight spaces to find loot. You will also unlock Mr.Anderson by stage 5 and he will bark at any animal that stands in your way of digging. There are a few secret areas within each level but the overall variety and scenery seems a tad boring with the most interesting moments finding weird trinkets or running from the few guards that roam the perimeter. At this point you maybe wondering why you're going through all the trouble of finding these useless trinkets...well i don't have a good answer for it other than to unlock more stages. When you find a trinket you gain three things: money to upgrade your dogs' stats, gets you closer to unlocking a new stage, and at your apartment you can read a little excerpt that alludes to the main character's background and story while pushing a few silly puns and jokes into the mix. Unfortunately the descriptions don't give you much information and there is no storyline outside of what you read from the trinkets. So what's the point of all this??? I'm not sure yet, i've unlocked 7 out of the 10 stages and all the game has done is made me enamored with the dogs and the cutesy art style. There is not much substance here. It's an interesting concept but it needs to have a bit more depth to keep me interested. The description on steam has a final point that says :"What's landed in the Buxton Wheat Field?" I'm hoping it's something interesting. Overall i think this game is targeted towards young children and feels more of a tablet game than a pc game. The screen resolution is even limited to 1920x1200 which is a shame since 1440p and higher res displays are becoming more common place but that's just a small thing to nitpick at.

The stealth system became so tedious that I found myself putting the game on the easiest difficulty and running from point to point not caring if I had been seen.
Combat becomes more tedious than fun.  The amount of hits required to take even the weakest enemies down (if you don't consistently get headshots) makes each encounter more annoying than fun. You will begin to roll your eyes every time you are forced into a fight due to the poor stealth system. And since there is no teather distance, the enemies will follow you around the entire map!
Those are the main problems with this game.  It is a great story if you can force yourself to put up with the terrible stealth and combat mechanics, but I can't recommend this game if you are looking for good gameplay.

this seemed like a horror survival game, until i played it.  it turns out to be an FPS set in the time era of the discovery of the new world, with good stealth mechanics, a huge investigation focus, and the feeling of a horror game without actually being scary.
+ weapons feel perefect for what they are (muskets feel like muskets, and so on..)
+ using the wind to sneak up on enemies is a unique mechanic
+ the story is interguing, and never stops get more and more interesting with each new revelation
+ the notes u collect r interesting and add atmosphere and intrigue to the world
+ the investigations are interesting to do, and reward you with uncovering more of the story, and do contribute to the ending of the game
+ the atmosphere, this game is ozing with it from everywhere
+ visual style is stiking, and feels fresh (NOTE: if black and white is not ur thing, u can always change that in the options)
+ many areas to explore and cleans
~ weapon variety, while there r plenty of them, the muskets and pistols feel the same with diffrences in states, same goes for long and short bows
~ enemy variety, enemies r varied enough and are fitting of the theme and story
- AI is stupid, it takes away the fear of facing these demonic creatures ( the moment u discover that they will just face u head on, even if u have a musket pointed at them, stealth is completely forgotten and just running around getting spotted and then gunning them down one by one is a much faster option)
- backtracking, there is alot of that to do, even with everything marked on the map
- no voice acting, all dialog is conducted through text, yes u have to read, but thankfully it is not alot, and it only comes in small doses (personaly, i see it as fittign of the atmosphere of the game, and i don't mind some reading in my games cause ur imagination can do better than any other voice acting can do)
- sound effects, while most of them r great, but some of the sounds the enemies make upon death and especially the sound arrows deflecting off of armored spaniards is cartoonish
- diffeculty, the game is abit too easy, i recommend turning on the hardcore mode in the options menu, and turning off the map markers, THEN u will feel the fear
- no boss fights, would have loved to face at least one at the end
all in all, its a solid experience, good story, great atmosphere and setting, and interesting art style.  I highly recommend this game.
