This game is without question, one of the hardest games I have ever played in my life. Not due to difficulty spikes though the game does have its fair share of those but rather its one of the hardest games I've ever played due to the overall soul crushing tone this game has. More than multiple times I had to stop playing as I felt my willpower and strength drain away watching my survivors slowly dying as joy and hope turned to ruin much like their own surroundings.
You play as 3 survivors in a half destroyed building during a fictional war somewhere most likely in Europe for a good 4 to 6 weeks trying to survive. Each survivor has their own unique use to the player such as better cooking, trading skills, to playing the guitar, or in one survior's case being good with children which isnt all that useful. This works well for realism of this game as not everyone you come across is going to be helpful to you much like in real life and really sinks in the fact that at the end of the day these are normal people who are not really prepared for the brutality of war.
After you start your game with your 3 survivors there are no tutorials for what you are to do which would be a negative save for the icons for all your actions are rather easy to figure out. You start breaking down rubble and locks on your doors to get to cabinets and dressers which may have useful materials,parts, food, medicine, or ammo all of which are nessessary to survive.
The real challenge in the game is proper management of resources. Do you burn a book for fuel for a heater? Do you build a patch in the wall now or save your supplies for an useful upgrade? Do you trade your last bandages for some food so you dont starve? Not every choice is gonna have a clear answer and what may pay off in the short term can and will mess you up down the line.
Another challenge is nighttime the second part of the game where one survivor must venture out to the bombed out city and scavenge for supplies. The very beginning areas are generous but eventually you're gonna have to go to hostile areas and attack bandits, soldiers, and rebels. It is best to avoid all combat when you can not because of the combat mechanics they are simple and work fine. It's more so most of your survivors are not soldiers they are civilians fighting more than one person at a time will more than likely end in your death especially if they have guns.
The final challenge is morality as this game will test everything you believe in and push them to its limits. I was astonished at how quickly my willpower faded within the first few weeks of playing. Within one week I had debated robbing an old couples house, killing everyone in the church, killed a vicious psychopath, gave away life saving medicine to a bunch of kids, prevented a soldier from♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman, and nearly died raiding a sniper junction.
This game is going to hurt you if you are the kind of person who gets emotional playing video games. You have to go in knowing full well everyone you are playing as is more than likely going to die and that all of your best efforts are going to be for nothing. There is no quick save either so no restarting if you didn't like how recent events turned out. The game benefits from this though as a quick save would've ruined all immersion with the game. This is one of those 'Live and learn" games where you'll have to learn from previous mistakes as it is unlikely to be able to a complete playthrough on the first try.
However there is a beauty in this game, its art direction looks serene with pencil drawn monochromatic color scheme fitting the tone well and simple music in the background adding to the overall atmosphere. Your survivors have their own backstories and even multiple endings depending on if they survive, overall happiness, or if they died either by the winter, lack of food, or if they take their own life.
Ultimately i only have one issue with the game and that is taking only one survivor to scavenge at night. Everything else is close to perfection. Lets get 1 thing out of the way before i begin, i know a lot of people are disappointed that you cant personally use more than 1 ship. yes it stinks but this game was never designed to be that kinda game, so rating it as such is abit unfair, if you didn't keep up with the press pre-development and didn't know this, then that's your own fault.
So lets get started with my short review.
Egosoft has a Long History of Releasing games that simply don't work on launch, they have MASSIVE potential but they don't work on launch... THAT SAID, they also have a long history of sticking with their products post launch to fix all of the launch bugs, add content, and add community feedback to the game in order to make it amazing.
You will never see me fanboy for or back up any other developers, because they simply haven't earned it. Other devs always disappoint and never do for their games, what will Egosoft does for it's games.
Egosoft is one of the rare devs that shouldn't get rated for their games on launch, to be fair YES it deserved the bad score then, but all of the newer players don't know what us older fans do, and that's that ego doesn't abandon its products. if we wait patiently, a year or 2 later we will have an amazing game to play. Don't believe me? Just look at the new reviews, they are positive!
I highly recommend anyone who gave this game a negative review in the past, reinstall this game and take a 2nd look around at all the new stuff that has been added. Their are also a number of really good mods to try. Personally i have a lot of mods and have a very customized immersive and enjoyable experience each time i login.
TLDR?
Next time you buy a Egosoft game do so in good faith.
Install it, don't play it, wait a year for them to patch the problems its guaranteed to have on launch, then come back and play. It will be everything you hoped for and more! They are a very small studio and it takes time to make a good game.
Also after you have beat the game, dont be afraid to come back from time to time and try it again. Egosoft has a wonderful habit of adding new things to their games after post launch, and all through out its life for years after.

First I would like to talk about launch, as in my view people kind of gave up on this game right out the gate. This game was unfortunately scarred by a bad launch, rightfully so as the game has its few bugs, flaws, and quirks, as ALL brand new games do. Though most people only spent an hour or so before they ran into some minor game stopping bugs and threw in the towel without even a second glance. For those of us who stuck around and could spare 15 min without rage quiting, looked to the incredible fan base who had our backs with bug work arounds and guides to help get through the troubled launch. After launch and a few days of blasting past bugs and finding work arounds we started getting patches, which have fixed a major amount of bugs making that first hour easier to play through and the game itself easier to complete.
Now I want to talk about the game itself. This is a great game, my favorite of the bunch so far.  As expected of the X series this game requires time to progress and unfold into a larger and better game. The depth of this game is immense, and even with 130 hours I still feel as though I have many more hours to go to even begin to master this game. Weither it be trying to run a mining operation or becoming a professional bounty hunter this game always provides a unique challenge. The story line is very well put together and seems almost like a huge extended tutorial, making you learn and rethink constantly. Though tutorial is putting it kindly, as this game will not hold hands with you the whole way, instead this game gives you the push to leave that spaceport and find a path on your own.
All in all, I can reccommend this game to anyone who enjoys space/sim/trader/exploration games. If you give it the time and the effort this game will keep you coming back hour after hour for more fun and more adventures.

I've posted more information than this at various places at around the time this was released, but the long and the short of it is that I regret pre-ordering this. I loved Civ 5, but this game kind of sucks. The "Civilizations" feel bland and uninspired. I'm apparently battling insects all of the time. The insects' AI is random, and insects are overpowered as hell at the beginning.
This feels like a Civ 5 mod. A bad one. It literally went backwards from the original game. I mean people make the argument that Civ 5 started out bad. Well in the first place, I'd disagree with that statement. But moving on, the developers practically took Civ 5 and re-skinned it. So this game starting out bad has absolutely no excuse. They have all of the original resources from where Civ 5 was BEFORE this was released, so why not just focus everything on the variety, tech tree, etc, and then just reuse much of the full code from Civ 5? The direction this took makes no sense to me. Especially variety. This REALLY lacks variety.
Finally, there is the technical aspect. When the game was released it didn't even work on my RoG Swift monitor... whereas Civ 5 worked perfectly fine. So.... basically the graphics look the same, and the engine looks the same, but they managed to screw it up.
This game is so bad my friend uninstalled it after we played it for around 7 hours, and refuses to play it any further. We're going back to Civ 5, and it reminded me of this game and how much of a disappointment it was so I'm going to ahead and leave that review finally. It's been needing it for a long time.

is a mixed bag of things, but mostly an arcade sim with a decent (though hyperbolic) story wrapped around it. You play a female protagonist named DeeDee who, being a pilot smuggler gets caught up into World War II. And she serves with a man who personally flew and fought with her father in World War One. As the missions progress, the story unfolds through static cut scenes that have a pleasant cell shaded hand drawn look. Missions vary from stealthy strike missions to all out balls to the wall multi-plane dogfights. If you’re looking to play an IL-2 Sturmovik imitation, look elsewhere; this is strictly for the arcade fans. Difficulty can be toggled, but some missions are more difficult than they have any right to be. One particular mission toward the end involved destroying fleeing vehicles through the city of Berlin. Tall buildings made it difficult to get decent bombing runs or rocket attacks, and it took me over 50 tries to get it. (But at this point, being so close to the end I had to finish it!)
Graphics are okay, serving the purpose. They look console-ish, and the voice acting is pretty much done by three people. One guy doing four different men’s voices with different accents is cheesy to the point of being hilarious. The music score, on the other hand, is polished and grandiose. It’s on par with a Stephen Spielberg Hollywood feature. I even looked during the end credits to find out who the composer was. Sadly, he was not credited.
The game offers multiplayer, but servers were pretty scant. I did find one each time I logged on, and this is probably a testament to the game’s age. It was fun, but mostly consisted of aerial jousts with rockets being launched at each other. A lot of my kills were dumb luck.
I won’t be in a hurry to play the original
or
, but if you have a few bucks left in your Steam Wallet during a Summer or Winter Steam sale, you could do worse.

My only gripe would be some bugs in the latest chapter such as the game skipping you forward to a later point if you have loaded up an older save. Thankfully the game is constantly updated as the bugs are fixed.
Overall a well made, imaginative and immersive adventure game. Hopefully it won't be too long before the final chapter is out!

Air Conflicts: Secret War is a sequel of the original Air Conflicts from 2006. It is an arcade turn-and-burn WW2 flight game with some interesting story line rarely covered in WW2 games: the Balkan conflict, and how the resistance in Poland, Azerbaijan, and other eastern European countries fought the Nazi invasion. You play the daughter of a WW1 Ace, "Deedee" as you attempt to work your way out of Africa into Eastern Europe, attempting to work your way through the war, as sort of a mercenary / smuggler for hire of the Allied side, along with your mentor Tommy (who flew with your father) and Clive, the best mechanic / drunk. You start working for Flight Captain McIntyre of the RAF, but you'll end up helping a lot fo different factions on the Allied side, not all of whom are that friendly, as you attempt to survive WW2.
The game has quite good graphics, and fully supports high resolution screens, as well as all sort of eye candy, from bump maps to high polygon models to post processing effects, and more. However, your windows need to use the regular DPI instead of any enlargement (125% or 150% under display) or you won't be able to run the config program as you can't see the buttons. Sound is quite good.
The game play has variety of mission types, such as eliminate all enemies. Though it's the timed missions, as well as the "plinking" missions that are the most frustrating. As an example of timed mission, you have to destroy advancing German tanks within 2 minutes (or they'll fire upon the convoy and you'll fail the mission).  Another example is the "plink the parachutes" mission... German transports are bringing in paratroopers. You need to shoot down the paratroopers. Yes, you are here to shoot parachutes (WTF?!)  And you need to shoot dozens and dozens of them... until you killed at least 12% of those darn parachutes. There's another one where "kill 70 soldiers on the ground with bombs or strafing". YIKES.
That parachute missions is the most hideous I've encountered so far, with the "kill 70 soldiers on ground" a close second. And I don't mean the objective, but the sheer frustration attempting to finish such. The parachute mission lasts 12 minutes, and you are barely informed of how you're doing. You simply keep shooting parachutes until you get a 'pass' or 'fail'. And yes, the paratroopers will scream as they fall from the sky. Same with ground soldiers you kill.
On the other hand, there are some missions that are more... subtle, such as the "smuggle" missions where you are trying to stay undetected (with a stealth meter), or a rescue / recon mission about finding a signal (radio finder blips). There's also a mission or two where you simply pilot a captured Luftwaffe plane and fly over enemy territory for recon... and hopefully not get caught by air patrols. That can get tense.
Depending on the aircraft you fly (and you fly a lot, from WW1 fighter to civilian transport, from fighters to fighter bombers, even a B-24... ) you get guns, bombs, and maybe rockets. The bombs and rockets are unlimited but takes time to regen. The guns are unlimited too, but won't fire if overheated.  If you can hit a plane with a rocket, you get insta-kill, but obviously that'll be quite difficult. Hit ground targets with bombs or rockets, but you need to be VERY precise... or you don't get the kill (and fail the objective). The bigger planes have additional turrets and tail guns, and those fire automatically. You can even take control fo the turrets and let AI fly for a while. Bombers may be able to drop salvos of bombs rather than one at a time.
There are missions set in both WW1 and WW2. The story is told from POV of Dorothy "Deedee" Derbec, who fight in the various conflicts (that you play) in WW2, but also relive the missions talked about by friends of Deedee's father in WW1.
As you complete missions, depending in kills and objective completion you gain 'stars', which you accumulate to add a point to your four attributes such as luck, leadership, armor, and damage, giving it a slight RPG flavor. This also controls what planes you can unlock, and there are more than a dozen planes from all sides: German, American, British, Russian, even a few jets and rocket powered planes, not to mention bombers, fighter bombers, and pure fighters.
The locations are interesting, at least to those accustomed to regular WW2 games, as you do a lot of fighting in Eastern Europe (but that's understandable, the developers are from Slovakia), and they mixed in quite a bit of WW2 history (or at least, hypothetical history).
The game has simplified landing... basically fly through a series of "rings" and you're considered "landed". Taking off is easy: full throttle and you'll take off.
Controller is fully supported, and can be set to arcade or sim mode with different control schemes. There's also multiple difficulty levels to customize your game. There's also plenty of quick dogfight missions (random AI opponents) and plenty of multiplayer options.
Enemy AI is not bad, as they do try to get on your tail and stay there.
Overall, my impression of the game is positive, except for those painfully tedious "plinking" missions (i.e. kill paratroopers and kill 70 ground troops). I'm about 60% complete and I sincerely hope I don't run into more missions of that type. Once I got past the female narrator (female French accented English) the game is actually quite enjoyable. Enemy planes smoke and break apart convincingly, and at Rookie difficulty you generally do breeze through the missions (except for those tedious plinking missions).
if you like the genre, arcade WW2 flight game, this game is quite good. Not a must play, but definitely something to try.

I love this game so far. It's like a MOBA without the MOBA portion. You pick a champion, then get placed into an arena and take part in a 2v2 or 3v3 teamfight with a winner being decided after 3 to 5 rematches.
This game is basically what I would call a top-down arena fighter. It's a better version of Bloodline Champions or Smashmuck Champions. You move with WASD, attack by left-clicking, and use abilities via hotkeys surrounding your move buttons, as well as your right-click. This is also one of few games where I'm fine and actually willing to play against other players, because you can turn off chat and it's just a 2v2-3v3 teamfight.
Takes a bit of practice to get used to each champion, but they seem balanced based on the ones I've played. Every champ has a lot of others they work well with, and a lot they work horrible with, which makes it kinda difficult to do random matches. It has a Heroes-style queue system, where if you queue alone, you won't know what character your teammate(s) picked until the match starts. So it kind of incentivises getting friends to play with you, so that you have people you can synergize with while playing champs you can synergize with.
This game is absolutely amazing, and I hope it lasts a long time. I also hope it doesn't go downhill, like most other free game I've played have. I recommend any of my friends who like the team-fighting aspect of MOBAs, or any game with arena brawler combat to try this one, as well as any other people who like those types of games.

More like an interactive novel than a game. There is no voice acting so all of the story is told through text, which is fine since the writing is good. The unforunate part is that things get very difficult to keep track of as each character tells you their story (and there are a LOT).
There are enemies and combat in this game, but both have very little depth/focus. The combat system works, but shows its flaws in battles with multiple enemies. The main thing you will be doing in this game is reading, so if that's not something you're into, then avoid it. Also speaking of the enemies, there isn't a whole lot of variety. There are skeletons, floating head things, spaniards, spiders, and little goblin guys that sound like wolves (also more floating head things that look slightly different). They all kind of do the same thing which is sometimes melee you but mostly just sit back and throw projectiles at you. They're also not that scary unless you find skeletons and spiders scary.
There's a bit of exploration involved but most of the world map ends up looking pretty much the same; Grass and trees and some small settlement. Outside of a few houses in the center of each zone, there isn't much to find or see.
The "game" boils down to three different quest types which you must repeat again and again to beat the game. Find someone's skull and bring it back to them, find a totem and kill enemies to cleanse it, and find clues to figure out a character's story. These get old very quickly of course. Also that being said, there is very little guidance when it comes to these quests and I often found it difficult to tell what to do next.
For a game that is so focused on story, the main plot isn't very good or original. It's hard to describe without going into specifics but the gist is that one girl falls in love with someone and her father doesn't approve.
Personally I enjoyed the stories of all the other characters, outside of the main plot, but ultimately, I would rather have read a novel than play this game.
Also to very briefly and vaguely discuss the ending. It's awful. It goes from "Okay I know what's going on." To "Wait. What?" in literally one second. It's a horrible shoehorned twist that doesn't fit at all.

Betrayer is a first person shooter/mystery/walking simulator in which you piece together the fractured remnants of the history of the island you find yourself on. You take on demonic Conquistadors and spectral horrors as you pass back and forth between diffferent veils of reality, clearing the various areas of enemies and helping lost spirits remember their stories and gain absolution.
It is an exercise in restraint - everything from the soundtrack, to the visuals, to the story is constructed carefully and sparingly with great intention. There is no music but for the wind through the trees and the grass, and the contextual sounds that alert you to the presence of nearby points of interest, and this sound design is excellent. However, the minimalism also extends to the gameplay - you'll do a bit of shooting, a bit of stealth, and a lot of walking from one place to another and back again. The locations exhibit little variation, and you won't see much beyond trees and grass and rocks along the way.
The layers of atmosphere, the oppressive feel of the dark other world, and the genuine tension when you hear the bark of an enemy all expertly manipulate the player's emotions, and the stories themselves are well-written and feel like they reflect believable and uniformly tragic struggles of a once-living colonial population, however the overreliance on mystery can leave you feeling without purpose, and the sheer amount of trudging back and forth is tedious. The last couple of hours of the game are striking in that you begin to get a little variety in locations, the story finally gets momentum, and the difficulty unbalances heavily in your favour, and I found this the most motivated section of gameplay, but to trudge through 4 repetitious hours beforehand was not an altogether enjoyable experience.
This is one of those games that you can really appreciate for its parts, especially from the perspective of artistic risk-taking, but it is not greater than the sum of those parts, and you may have trouble feeling compelled to finish it. I recommend it because it's well-made and unique, but I recommend it tentatively because its design makes getting through it a bit of a slog.

Betrayer is awesome.  It definitely brings something new to the table in a world were every FPS game is the same, Betrayer takes one of my most common complaints of FPS games and smashes it (That being that we always see the same setting WW2, Vietnam, Modern, and most recently the future.)  This takes you to what seems to be the 17th century (more specifically after  the colonization of America.)  where the guns are single shot and the best weapon is a bow and arrow.   This game heavily relies on stealth, most interestingly the wind, you use it in order to hide your foot steps.  Now with all that none sense out of the way let's talk about the most interesting parts of the game.  The mystery and the atmosphere.   When you first get into this game you have no idea what the hell is gonig on, when you first arrive at Fort Henry and start reading scraps of paper that you start to slowly understand what happens.  it gets really interesting when you start talking to the "folks" there.   Trying to piece together what happened at the fort and what is happening in general.  The atmosphere.  When it is day time the landscape is beautiful it's bright, it's lush, it's vibrant.  It makes you feel some what relaxed, that is until you meet your first enemy.  The "ngiht time"  is the definition of forboding hearing things off in the distance like screams when you come near a corrupt totem poll.  To skeletons randomly popping out of the ground to destroy you. So far I have encountered 4 types of enemies.  The game definetly gets frustrating after a while but nothing too bad (as of now.)   How ever the game seems as though it is a little too hardcore at times, which is  never be a bad thing in my book.  However not having a map can be a bit aggrevating, because when you die you end up either at the start of the particular map you are on or at the last place you visited that shows up on the compass.  All that being said I love this game so far, I couldn't be happier.

Open world horror-y FPS with heavy emphasis on exploration. You explore doomed settlements in colonial-era Virginia, fighting demonic Conquistadors and angry indians, and try to find out what happened by talking to the ghosts of the previous inhabitants.
Striking and vibrant art style, glorious sound design, weapons feel good to use, enemies aren't very varied but are quite smart and fun to fight.
The story's VERY interesting (and quite bleak), and told through nice and twisty writing. Genuinely heartbreaking at times.
On the obligatory flipside, the game felt a wee too short, the map's TOO useful (every single item is marked on the map, so exploration quickly gave way to just hopping between markers), the areas felt a little too similar after a while and the "kill x enemies" achievements felt like overblown grinding, as I fought A LOT and still wasn't even halfway to the required kill count by the end of the game. Not enough to dissuage me from recommending it, though.
Strongly recommended.

This game is without question, one of the hardest games I have ever played in my life. Not due to difficulty spikes though the game does have its fair share of those but rather its one of the hardest games I've ever played due to the overall soul crushing tone this game has. More than multiple times I had to stop playing as I felt my willpower and strength drain away watching my survivors slowly dying as joy and hope turned to ruin much like their own surroundings.
You play as 3 survivors in a half destroyed building during a fictional war somewhere most likely in Europe for a good 4 to 6 weeks trying to survive. Each survivor has their own unique use to the player such as better cooking, trading skills, to playing the guitar, or in one survior's case being good with children which isnt all that useful. This works well for realism of this game as not everyone you come across is going to be helpful to you much like in real life and really sinks in the fact that at the end of the day these are normal people who are not really prepared for the brutality of war.
After you start your game with your 3 survivors there are no tutorials for what you are to do which would be a negative save for the icons for all your actions are rather easy to figure out. You start breaking down rubble and locks on your doors to get to cabinets and dressers which may have useful materials,parts, food, medicine, or ammo all of which are nessessary to survive.
The real challenge in the game is proper management of resources. Do you burn a book for fuel for a heater? Do you build a patch in the wall now or save your supplies for an useful upgrade? Do you trade your last bandages for some food so you dont starve? Not every choice is gonna have a clear answer and what may pay off in the short term can and will mess you up down the line.
Another challenge is nighttime the second part of the game where one survivor must venture out to the bombed out city and scavenge for supplies. The very beginning areas are generous but eventually you're gonna have to go to hostile areas and attack bandits, soldiers, and rebels. It is best to avoid all combat when you can not because of the combat mechanics they are simple and work fine. It's more so most of your survivors are not soldiers they are civilians fighting more than one person at a time will more than likely end in your death especially if they have guns.
The final challenge is morality as this game will test everything you believe in and push them to its limits. I was astonished at how quickly my willpower faded within the first few weeks of playing. Within one week I had debated robbing an old couples house, killing everyone in the church, killed a vicious psychopath, gave away life saving medicine to a bunch of kids, prevented a soldier from♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman, and nearly died raiding a sniper junction.
This game is going to hurt you if you are the kind of person who gets emotional playing video games. You have to go in knowing full well everyone you are playing as is more than likely going to die and that all of your best efforts are going to be for nothing. There is no quick save either so no restarting if you didn't like how recent events turned out. The game benefits from this though as a quick save would've ruined all immersion with the game. This is one of those 'Live and learn" games where you'll have to learn from previous mistakes as it is unlikely to be able to a complete playthrough on the first try.
However there is a beauty in this game, its art direction looks serene with pencil drawn monochromatic color scheme fitting the tone well and simple music in the background adding to the overall atmosphere. Your survivors have their own backstories and even multiple endings depending on if they survive, overall happiness, or if they died either by the winter, lack of food, or if they take their own life.
Ultimately i only have one issue with the game and that is taking only one survivor to scavenge at night. Everything else is close to perfection. I give the game 4.5 out of 5 and recommend this to everyone interested in the intial premise. If you can handle the depressing tone and heavy consequences This War Of Mine offers then it deserves a spot in your library.

As a player coming straight from Magic 2014, I love that we can customize our own decks with whatever color/spell combos we want. I didn't feel this way at first, but when I unlocked enough cards, I crossed a threshold where I was able to be creative with my decks.
The free to play model is very fair, and to this day I'll admit I haven't spent a cent on coins. I already have Origins completely unlocked and a chunk of Battle for Zendikar at my disposal.
I think the user interface is a complete joke. It has more bugs than a swamp. Hotkeys often don't even work. Here's an example; last night I tried to navigate the main menu with nothing but a keyboard. I would use the arrow keys to select the option I wanted to choose, but whenever I'd tap enter, it would select another option entirely--assuming I could even arrow or tab over to certain options. That's just nuts to me. I don't see any reason why I shouldn't be able to play the game with a keyboard. If this game can be played with a controller, there's no reason it shouldn't be able to function without a mouse.
I also think the matchmaking system is ill-implemented, assuming there is one at all. My first versus duel was against some rank 13 player. It didn't go well. My third match was against a rank 15 player. I've heard similar stories of my rank 14 friend going up against rank 30. That is an immense rank dissonance.
Another complaint complaint will be about the AI. I'll admit, I was sick of facing the same decks in solo for the Origins set. I would always face black and green, Gaea's Revenge and/or thopters. With Battle for Zendikar, now I exclusively face an Azorious removal deck. I don't see why there was such a dramatic shift in AI decks and personalities. Would it really be that difficult to have Origins, Zendikar, and future expansion AI decks randomized in the same pool? That would yield a much more balanced experience so players aren't forced into a cookiecutter deck that works for a specific expansion's small AI deck selection. They'd have to create much more thoughtful, rounded decks as a result.
Two-headed giant is another issue. The AI was blatantly not designed for it. I've seen them do♥♥♥♥♥♥as stupid as kill each other's creatures or waste instants on them that don't even finish the job or have any apparent advantage to the enemy team at all. This needs some serious ironing out, but at least the AI deck pool includes Origins and Zendikar. It's lead to some very interesting duels.
Including FFA would be a great idea. In 2014, me and three of my friends would have our stay-at-home Friday Magic nights. We'd gather at our computers, get drunk, and have ourselves a good old fashioned free for all. I think it's abhorrent that this experience has been taken from us.
Despite the horrendous negatives, I have over 210 hours on this game. I've enjoyed it a lot, and I'll continue to do so. I think something great was done here. But it's still extremely rough around the edges, and I hope some of this will be softened over time.

X3:TC and X3:AP set a high bar. X:R doesn't reach it, but is still a decent game. On its surface, it seems like a straightforward upgrade to the X3 games. The same core mechanics are there: you fly around in a universe with rich lore, trading, fighting, or exploring, whatever suits your fancy.
Lots of people have gripes about mechanical issues of the game, like the highway system. That doesn't bother me. The universe is less dynamic than X3 (pirates don't really affect the economy, for example, they just constantly send small squadrons to die). In some ways, the mechanics improved: the addition of surface elements to capital ships is a really great addition to combat that makes small ships pack a huge punch if used effectively. But these minor issues aside, the real problem with X:R versus previous X games is lack of content.
By content, I don't mean amount of space to explore: there's plenty of that. But there are relatively few types of ships and stations to buy, and you can only fly one ship, which is bad, although you can mostly get used to it. The amount of lore and numbers of factions is cut down significantly from previous games.
By far the biggest problem is the relative lack of subquests or subplots. Once you've beat the campaign, the game is completely open-ended. Not open-ended like Skyrim, where the only problem is choosing which of the thousands of quests to do. Open-ended as in, there essentially ARE no other quests (except repetitive, randomly generated ones), and sure you can build stations or blow up stuff, but it all feels quite pointless. The pinnacle of X3 was quests like the Hub Plot and Player Station, which gave awesome rewards in return for huge amounts of financial engineering. In X:R, there are a few sub-quests that give you cool rewards, but they are all of the form "find these items randomly hidden throughout the universe". It would be enormously tedious if not impossible without internet guides, and with them it becomes trivial.
So, in future expansions, it would be nice to add ships or factions. But what the game really needs to step things up a notch is things to DO in the X Universe. It's still worth $30 but not yet worthy of the X Series IMO.

Initially very disappointed in this release, but after watching a few video's explaining how to get started, it's quickly growing on me and I'm seeing the depth and inspiration that has gone into it.  Most difficult and annoying aspect is still navigation in terms of maps as well as navigating lists showing what I own.  This greatly hinders the initial ability of a player to easily dive into the game and get a sense of things and probably one of the big reasons it's not more popular.   It's difficult to quickly determine where your assets are or issue orders to them because the navigation is so heirachael and each level is so simple.  I would like to see the addition of the old style lists with perhaps some very good filters allowing you to quickly see what you have and where it's at and what it's status is.  Need that 50 foot view of what I have, and not wanting to have to drill down over and over to see basics.  One would think this is basic smart U.I. design.
Another good example of this would be trying to find a decent captain or engineer for one of your ships.  You are forced to repeatedly drill down and ask them to show you their skills, which is redundant clicking and annoying.  These cases need a nice neat list you can look through so you're not wasting your time.  This is the difference between a well designed menu system and one that was slapped together with a lack of forethought about how real users play the game.  Other than the navigation usability issues, and the cartoonish colors used in some systems, the game does seem to be very cool and I'm getting a lot out of exploring and learning what's out there.  It has a lot of character.

As many other people have already pointed out, X-Rebirth has come a very long way.  I was one of many who purchased the game on launch and felt robbed of my money at the time.  If steam refunds were a thing back then I would have certainly asked for one.  In a way, the lack of steam's refund policy allowed me to hold onto the game until the point where it is today.  Egosoft has not given up or abandoned their project and has taken many of the necessary steps to improve the game.  They encourage ideas and actually seem to listen to what their customers want in the game.  Optimization was terrible at first launch.  The game didn't feel smooth and was quite laggy.  Since then the game is far better and lag is fortunately a thing of the past.  The campaign is ok...at best.  A lot of important points about the game are left out and some things are far easier in the campaign than they actually are in freeplay.  The best way to learn about the game is to use forums and the wiki.  They have been very helpful to me.  Please understand that many of the negative reviews of this game are from a long time ago and do not accurately portray the game as it is now.  With all of that said I would say the game is decent overall.  Personally, I wouldn't pay full price but I would buy it if it were on sale.  As for the DLC, the same can be said.

What to say....
Saints Row 4 was more than just a GTA clone to me.  It was a rip roaring blast that GTA could never provide.  The over the top humor, societal parody of all that is so ripe for poking fun in American society.
So going into Gat of of Hell I expected more of the same.
Did I get it?
Well, yes and no.  For the first hour of so I was a bit confused.  There was no linear progression of what I was suppoed to be doing so I wandered around aimlessly.  It wasn't until I got in sync with the game that things got fun.  It's a glorious frag fest with moronic demons and cookie cutter stereotypes of the typical 80's action supervillan except this time they're on your side.
Visually the game is the same as Saints Row 4, Skill upgrades and progression are much the same but if there's one point where this game goes off the rails is the forced attempt at a narrative.  The core story is about Gat rescuing the Prez from the evils of matrimony with Satain's daughter.
The gameplay itself is fun but your never really connect with why you're there.  Not than any Saint's Row title had anything resembling depth of a narrative but instead of offering a laugh, the obligatory cutscenes get in the way like some unwanted Rock Opera performed a cappella in an otherwise peaceful Sunday at the park.
In short, the narrative could have been toned down because the gameplay itself is adicting and fun.  Not to say it doesn't suffer trhe same weaknesses as Saint's Row 4 with it's somewahat convulted controls and vague combat system but somehow Gat out of Hell manages to pull out an entertaining romp.
Not to the level of full purchase price however.
This sequl/add-on to Saints Row 4 satisfies the need for "just a little more" but as a standalone title I can understand why it almost instantly went on sale for a fraction of it's MSRP the same year it was released.
If you're a Saint's Row fan and want just a little more then this is y our game.
I sincerely hope there's a Saints Row 5 but for now this will do for a few dozen hours.  Buy it.....if it's on sale...

Over the past couple years, I’ve become increasingly interested in the point-and-click genre. As a result, I’ve been buying such games whenever I can get them for a very low price. Of the ones I’ve played, The Dream Machine definitely ranks near the top. Your character, Victor Neff, has just moved into a small apartment building with his pregnant wife. He soon discovers something ominous happening in the building, and must travel through the dreams of his neighbors in order to stop it.
On the surface, the story does seem rather simplistic, and it is, to an extent. However, each dream you visit has its own story, and it is in these mini-stories where the game truly shines. These dreams range from bizarre, to sad, to creepy, and everywhere in between. There seems to be much more of an emphasis on showing, rather than telling. Simply traversing the dreams of your neighbors is enough to give you insight into their personalities.
Another point of note with this game is that it is all crafted by hand, with clay and cardboard being the mediums of choice. The environments are, simply speaking, beautiful, and realizing it was all handmade gave me an even greater appreciation for the game. It also adds to the creepy atmosphere of the game, as many times characters are made to be rather grotesque in appearance.
Gameplay is your standard point-and-click style. You explore the environments, picking up items and using them to solve puzzles. The puzzles vary in difficulty, with some being quite easy and others being obnoxiously difficult and lacking in any sort of intuitiveness. And while the puzzles can be frustrating and take a while to solve, it is never so bad as to be game-breaking in the slightest.
TL;DR: The Dream Machine is one of the most incredible point-and-click games I’ve played. The atmosphere is truly unsettling, the environments are delightfully surreal, and the story is surprisingly engaging and had quite a bit of depth. The puzzles can sometimes be frustratingly difficult and there is no voice acting, but the good far outweighs the bad. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys point-and-click and/or surreal games.

Unfortunately where Homefront had tremendous potential it completely dropped the ball in virtually every other. I really liked the story, especially since I'm from the San Francisco Bay Area where some of the story takes place, but that's where my positive thoughts for Homefront stops. How companies get away with only providing 4 hours of content now is beyond my understanding. The controls are clunky and you have to repeatedly press buttons to crouch and prone instead of holding them like I am used to. The mechanics are extremely unrefined - you can blast enemies in the head repeatedly and they won't die. You can barely peak out from a corner and an enemy far away can pick you off. The game feels too rushed and unpolished, and if they had taken the time to iron out everything and make the campaign longer, Homefront could have been a really good game.
But I do feel like the potential is there especially with it's great concept of a story - perhaps if Homefront 2 ever see's light, it will be refined and polished and provide us with more substance to allow us to really get into the game.

Sort of a "poor man's Ace Combat," this game can be quite fun. The core flight and combat mechanics are simple, but competently executed. This makes for gameplay that remains basically fun, even if it isn't all that varied.
The game does indeed have some flaws. The voice acting is sometimes unconvincing, and every so often you'll catch an error where earlier text dialogue loads into the subtitle area. The stealth mission functionality is not as advertised - there's no "detection zone" displayed on your radar - and so certain stealth missions present a frustrating difficulty spike. There are little hints here and there of features that didn't quite get fully implemented, but still made it in somehow.
But the game is remarkably fun, because even simplified, "arcade-style" air combat can offer lots of opportunities to try a mission in a slightly different way.
No, this isn't a AAA title, but it can be highly enjoyable if you're willing to "suspend your disbelief" a bit and enjoy the ride.

TL;DR: A moderately spooky FPS with no puzzles, a bloated narrative, and tons of backtracking. Buy it on sale if you like chores and nonsensical conclusions to unengaging stories.
A tad harsh, perhaps. The game isn't entirely devoid of fun, after all. The combat and weapons are entirely serviceable, and the environments can be quite pretty.
The game starts off pretty well, too, with a setting somewhat uncommon to games (Early seventeenth-century America,) a sense of dread, and a large area to explore.
Your character (Unnamed) starts the game washed  ashore with no memory of who he is or what he was doing, aside from sailing on a doomed ship. Finding these things out is your earliest motivation as a player. You will not find these things out.
Upon meeting the only other living character in the game, you will find a map detailing the precise location of every item in the game, as well as an item which will allow you to hear spooky sounds which lead you to anything important not on the map. Suddenly, you are no longer exploring a vast and haunted forest, but running errands from point A to point B.
The first enemies you encounter in the game are red-eyed monsters in conquistador armor. They're fast enough to outpace you, should you be spotted, and strong enough to kill you in a few hits. And you will be spotted, more often than not, as their senses are keen. Their armor can occasionally deflect the arrows from your bow, the only weapon you have at the beginning of the game. Obviously, engaging them in combat is a bad idea. You are encouraged to sneak around them, and give them a wide berth. This is the best part of the whole game. The animalistic sound these things make when they spot you is probably one of the more memorable "Oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments in recent memory. Fantastic.
It doesn't last. You will very quickly find a small arsenal for yourself in these woods. Within the first hour of the game I had two primitive firearms and a tomahawk, with which I tore through these poor saps like wet tissue paper.
Stronger enemies did eventually appear, yes, but not before I had the equipment to eviscerate them. The remainder of the game is spent with more of a hope for danger than a sense of it.
Enemy design is nice enough. A zombie conquistador here, a skeleton with red eyes there. Nothing to write home about overall... with one exception. I will admit to a great appreciation for one late-game enemy design. A ghost, made up of a thick black swarm of insects with two long, skeletal hands and a silver skull floating over them. I love that thing.
I mean, you can kill it in one hit, but it certainly looks cool!
So, now that we've established that the enemies won't be much to fear, where else can we get our horror fix here? Well... nowhere, really. Not in the "I'm afraid of this thing" or the "Please get me out of here" ways, anyway. Your character's goal in the game, the chore list I mentioned earlier, is to find the remains of settlers around the forest, find clues as to how they died, and bring their spirits closure. Now that I've typed that out, I realize that it sounds pretty flipping sweet. Sadly, it's not. It's excrutiatingly boring.
Every mystery is solved by following your map to every item and ghost listed on it, and every spirit put to rest in a  brief dialogue tree. It's somewhat interesting at first, but by the end every ghost's story blends together, and their characterization so thin that I could not relate or sympathize with them.
"Yes, yes, you were a terrible murderer♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and/or tragic murder victim♥♥♥♥♥♥victim, I'm sure your passing was very sad. Now, hurry your♥♥♥♥♥up to the great beyond, I've things to do."
And, yes, that's where the game's horror lays, with much♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder, and betrayal. It wears quickly.
Each ghost's story ties to others in their section of the forest, and each section's story ties into the greater plot. Which is great, on paper. Sadly, writing the plot on to paper would result in a page primarily composed of fluff, with maybe a paragraph of interest and a quick nonsensical sentence to wrap it up. So many ghosts end up playing such small roles in the story that you're left only to wonder why so much of the game was dedicated to them. Entire sections of the game could have been cut, and I'd only have been thankful it took less of my time.
The ending has quite the twist, too! The twist is that there is no ending.
And no, not in a Twilight Zone-style "Eternal personal Hell" way, either. The game has no ending.

First, let me tell you that the gameplay of Betrayer feels pretty great. You can use gusts of wind to sneak up to enemies, using this and the environment for stealth works nicely. Also, the idea of using muzzleloaders with only one shot and long reload times is awesome, and makes drawn-out fights tense.
My Problem is with the Narrative of the story. There are 7 maps in the game, and only on the 5.th map, the "real" story starts. Over the course of the game, you will get hints about awesome and mysterious stories, but not a single one of them is picked up again. The "real" story of the game turns out to be the weakest, most clichéd and uninteresting story you find, with all the other mysteries just being red herrings. As for the ending, I would have been content with a sad or tragic ending. But the ending you are given is just ridiculous. It clashes with every detail of the story that you have been told earlier, and explains nothing. The "endgame", which consists of lots of backtracking, completely put me off with its clashing emotional tones.
Don't let me fool you, the mystery of the things you find will make you invested in the game in no time. My problem is that all the mysterious happening lead up to a bland and uninteresting final game.
For example, the mystery of the game lead you to question the origin of the enemies you encounter (and the enemy designs are fantastic, so it first seems likely to suspect a deeper story about where they came from and what turned them into this.) However, only one type of enemy can be connected to the story in any way, while the others are just nice ideas without any backstory.
What I want to say, is: The gameplay first seems to promise you a deep and mysterious story, and if you take the bait, you will be heavily disappointed.
However, if you can play the game just for the gameplay itself, without any interest in the story or narrative, you will have a great time.

Bleeding hearts aside (I spend money on games for entertainment, period) this game is fun if you enjoy making A LOT of decisions and have A LOT of patience.  You struggle to survive in a shelter with other.  Characters have different pros and cons to work with.  You venture out at night to scavenge for items needed to survive.  You have to survive raids (no action), illness, injuries, starvation, cold and depression (yep, no zombies). You have to prioritize A LOT, which create game difficulty.  The graphics were nice and refreshing as a video game but the font used was a challenge when in small print which is crucial in identifying if your character is slightly sick or severely sick.  Game play can get repetitive and slow at some points.   There's no way to fast forward through the dull moments of the day (only skip to night).  There isn't a lot of fighting action any fighing (if necessary) is very basic.  It's really about the decisons.  Should you fight or avoid fighting?  The end game is based on a random number of days to survive (one time 25 another was 42 for me).  The different groups of characters to chose to play with and a couple of different scenarios at the few locations to visit give you a few challenges for replay.  Like most games made in this new era the difficulty of the game comes from not having a manual that tells you some basic things.  Like the game has different seasons (so yes, build that heater), you can't craft bullets until you upgrade to a level 3 workbench (so the box of parts is probably higher on the priority list if you're just level 1 and need parts for a heater).  My advice, read a guide on the characters and crafting to understand the game play mechanics.  I recommend this game if you like making decisions and have a lot of patience for a slow pace game.

Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)
Prep : 30 mins
Cook : 25 mins
Ingredients :
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 cup vegetable shortening
- 1/2 cup hot water
Directions :
1. Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add vegetable shortening and work into flour mixture using a pastry cutter until it resembles coarse crumbs.
2. Form a well in the middle of flour mixture and mix in hot water. Work flour and water mixture together with a fork and transfer to a cutting board.
3. Knead until a smooth, soft dough is formed, about 3 minutes. Add more flour if dough is too sticky.
4. Place more flour on cutting board, cover dough with bowl, and let rest for 15 minutes.
5. Cut ball of dough into eight equal parts and cover until needed.
6. Roll out balls of dough either by hand or with a tortilla press.
7. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Place flattened tortilla in skillet and cook until it begins to bubble, about 1 minute. Flip tortilla over and cook for an additional minute. Flip again and cook for 1 more minute. Repeat with remaining dough.

Get blasted to smithereens in a battle and need to restart....yep, thats right...your autosave restarts you as blasted to smithereens. Ok, I was really, really mad when this game came out because I was so damn excited about it. I had high expectations, because I LOVE the X series. I own every X game that exists (and about 5 or so other space sim games).
Let me just say WOW, now that the game is working and running amazingly smoothly, 1 crash in over 20+ hours of gameplay, that may not even have been atrributed to thier game engine. The frame rate is awsome on my GTX 770 maxed everything.
THE GOOD
--------------------
GRAPHICS:
The grahics are next-gen for a space combat game, they are amazing and fun to watch every, single time.
SPACE COMBAT:space combat is fun and the AI is better than most space sim games out there. It can get repetitive after a while doing nothing
but combat for hours on end but you can just go do something else, build some stations, conquer sectors commanding your capital ships and just watching the battle
from a commanders perspective. You can start a trading empire, or become a pirate and depoy remote detonation bombs on ships... it goes on and on.
ENVIRONMENT:
As a Uninty game engine developer, I'm pretty amazing at what you have achieved with scale in this game. At first I couldnt tell if some of those large scale objects (Planets,Shatterd Moons) in the background were part of the skybox. I am very impressed with how you scaled the game and made it look so good. Though I suspect some kind of trickery at work with your Shaders! You should let me borrow some ;)
GAME PLAY:
You can board ships and take them over. nothing new here BUT, the pods come out of your ship and attract to the target like an action scene in a sci space film. So far it has been fun to watch every single time. Im addicted to capturing enemy space ships at this point just to watch the pods fly out. (they could add some drilling and molten metal types of animations and particle effects to make them appear to drill into the surface).
THE BAD:
-The sound effects can get a little old, if we can add more varition of sound effects and voice overs for the expansion, that would make this game more imersive and truly make it the greatest space sim ever made. Also, they need to write a script to limit how often a voice over is played from a single character controller, since you tend to click on them repeadedly when shopping for better crew members or ammo for your ship. You hear the same person repeating themselves 2-3-4 times... its annoying!
-`They should add the voice over limitor function to the ship as well to keep it from reapting based up what the condition was that produced the previous voice over sound effect.
-I had to look stuff up on google alot to find keys because there are SO MANY controls, there are controls for your controls! The control edit needs a form input search element to search through available controls quickly! This will be extremely usefull and save alot of time for beginners! Most people will be customizing thier controls. I am using keyboard and mouse and hated the default layout. I went from bad to pro once I changed all of the key controls and practiced for a while.
-If you run in between two colliders it will bounce your around until you clip through into the interior of a station or a ship. It has happen to me many times and had to retart because your cant clip out from the interior. You need to control the unrendered side of your verticies and add a program
to remove the physics colliders from the non-rendered side.
-Your "bounce" physics on colliders needs to be toned down, so that clipping is less likely.
- Also sometimes ships in your fleet clip through objects and get stuck, then I believe your fleet will bug out if that ship is within its group. Your fleet wont travel through gates if a group member is stuck. Mabey I'm wrong but,
I had a ship clipped in a station and my fleet would not travel through a jump gate within any time frame. It seems the bugs I have encountered are more or less related to kinks that need to
be worked on in your physics engine. You guys are awsome though for what you have made with such a small team.
I'm sorry that I was so mad, I did not realize the scope and the work that is needed to make a game like this until I actually became a game developer myself and learned c#. You guys should of just
delayed the game another year and avoided that mess and you would have made ALOT more money. Does'nt your CEO get that? Seriosly, that crap launch you pulled hurt your sales!
If you like space sim, BUY this game. It does have a learning curve, but it is well worth it to experince the fleet combat and amazing visuals and to realize that when this is improved slightly, it will
be amoung the top space sim games ever made if not the best single player space sim every made.

Air Conflicts: Secret Wars is an arcade style flight game. This is not a simulator, flight controls are very simple. The resolution settings do not go very high, so you will most likely be playing in a lower resolution than you are used to. The voice acting is not offensive but not great. Hatred is basically a modern version of the original Postal. It's incredibly violent, gory, and contains the worse bad language i've seen, or rather heard, in any game to date. It certainly warrants it's adult rating and isn't something you'd want your kids to play.
You play as a guy who's gone 'Postal' going through each level dealing death and destruction with a variety of weapons. There's a few side missions you can do on the way such as chasing down a politician, derailing a train and wiping out a coffee shop full of 'hipsters'. It plays pretty well, though i recommend keyboard and mouse as i found using a controller just isn't accurate enough. Visually it's very nice, it's well animated with some nicely detailed backdrops and some really great fire and explosion effects. The sound is also good, with a moody soundtrack that's not too distracting and some meaty gunfire and explosions. There's also some nice little touches like clips from Rambo and Matrix played on tv screens throughout and the credits gave me a laugh.
What i did like is the challenge. Early on it's fairly easy with just Cops to deal with but the latter stages, when the Army turn up, are a real challenge. Infact the last two levels took me multiple tries and that was on 'easy' difficulty! It requires a little planning ahead as running in guns blazing will get you killed in no time.
My only real complaint is that because of the isometric viewpoint it's fairly easy to get stuck behind walls, trees, fences and the like, but it's something you get used to after a while.
All in all i enjoyed it. And if you're a fan of Postal or infact any top down shooter i'm sure you'd enjoy Hatred. Especially as it's so challenging.
I recommend it.

Betrayer is a First Person Action game set in colonial Virginia. The gameplay feels very similar to Elder Scrolls, with the ability to fast travel from one location to another via the game map. Unlike other First Person games out there, Betrayer uses a monochrome art style, which is a little disorienting at first. It looks cool, and definitely stands out from other games of the same genre, but I think this particular game could have looked amazing with colored graphics, just my opinion. The tutorial area consists of a beach where you are trying to find out what is going on. You learn how to sprint, melee etc. In this game you also collect clues, loot treasure chests, bust open crates for loot, and of course fight conquistadors. One ofthe first weapons you can get is the bow, so using stealth you learn to take out enemies from a distance. When you die you can try to retrieve your belongings but if you don't get to them in time, you will lose them.
I am curious to see where the story takes me as it seems interesting, a deserted colony, Conquistadores and Natives who seem to have gone insane and a mysterous stranger who has amnesia and can't see the enemies you see. Worth a playthrough, for the story, as well as to check out a game that actually uses monochrome in 2015.

(About 220 hours logged on single player and 0.5 hours multiplayer, as of the writing of this review.)
TLDR: This is a -GREAT- single player game!  Reminiscent of Homeworld, but 2-1/2 D combat (not true 3D) combined with some well executed4X strategy and an excellent user interface.  Great variety of maps and ability to make your own!  Single player experience is 8 stars out of 10 (docked 1 point for not true 3D combat, and 1 point for useless diplomacy tech and dynamics).  Those interested in multiplayer might (or might not) rank the game somewhat lower.
8/10
Details:
SoaSE:R is a 4X space strategy game.  There are three races (Terrans, Varsari, and Advent), each of which has a "loyalist" and "rebel" faction (thus the word 'Rebellion' in the name of the game), for a total of six playable factions.
The game is played on a 2D strategy map (which looks 3D for multiple solar system games).  The object of the game is tailorable, but typically involves crushing your opponent via some means; and military might typically plays a large role in achieving the objective.  Players (including AI players) explore their systems, develop their home world and other discovered worlds.  Eventually (typically quite early in the game) opponents discover each other.  A little later (typically by early mid-game) opponents are trying to strip each other of their acquired worlds.
Economy, military, culture, and diplomacy all play a role in winning the game; and a rich "tech tree" supports all of these.  The tech tree is actually six trees: economy/culture; military; planetary defense; diplomacy; fleet logistics; and artifacts.  Five of the trees (all except artifacts) vary slightly from faction to faction; but are roughly 3/4 the same.  The diplomacy tech tree I found to be rather useless, and is one of the reasons I gave this game an 8 instead of 10 rating.
The single player game can be paused or speeded up at any time.  The games I like playing involve a single large system (over 50 planets around a single sun) or multi-system, with over 60 planets.  these large maps typically take me 4 to 7 hours of unpaused game time; but I play with everything set to slow (slow travel times, slow build times, slow research times, etc.)  So many players would finish such games faster than I.  Smaller maps can be played in much less time.
Combat is very much like Homeworld, but without the rich 3D aspect.  Ships can stack vertically, but I found my thoughts and actions all in a 2D realm.  Two ships of equal strength can take over 3 minutes to do each other in, and a single ship (capable of world bombardment) can take over 10 minutes to capture a small planet; so this is a game of strategy, not fast reflexes.  Ship types and sizes have a large impact on combat; and there is a definite rock-paper-scissors aspect to the game: every ship of every faction is strong versus some ship types and vulnerable to others.  This is true even of Titans (super-ships) and starbases; and I have vaporized many of each without my Titan present.
There is an RPG aspect to Titans and capital ships which gives the game a lot of added interest.  As each ship gains combat experience, new abilities may be chosen/improved from a small menu which is different for each ship in each faction.  Some of the early experience levels can be bought.  Abilities can synergize.  For instance: one capital ship may have the ability to cause all enemy ships in a certain area to take 30% of the damage inflicted on one enemy ship.  Another of your capital ships (or maybe your Titan) may have the ability to inflict large amounts of damage to an enemy ship in a short amount of time.  Using these two abilities at the same time can vaporize a large number of small ships in short order.  Fleets can be formed; and rudimentary tactical formations can be assigned, to keep your ships from peeling off to chase that enemy scout ship that they will never catch.  (Your carriers, transports, and planetary defense hangers have fighters and bombers which CAN catch and make short work of scouts.)
Combat graphics are pretty good (but not extraordinary).  As each ship takes damage, it looks damaged; and the explosions as each ship is destroyed are well done.  Again, very reminiscent of Homeworld, but no noticible improvement on same.
The game interface is intuitive and (in my opinion) very well thought out.  Not perfect, BUT I have not played a 4X game with a better interface!  GREAT user interface!!  The view is true 3D, control of view angle is very easy; and the grapics scale and change as you zoom in and out (which you will do a very lot).  At the solar system level you can see a high level overview of all planets for which you have intel.  If you select a world, overview information appears instantly.  As you zoom in, the picture of the planet gives way to a real time view of all the ships and orbital structures for that planet.  If it is a world for which you have no current intel, the best intel you have, and its age in seconds, are displayed.  Zooming the view in combat works similarly: at a high level you see easily interpreted icons for the situation.  As you zoom in, the icons give way to actual views of the ships, missiles, laser beams, etc.  Very well done!
Music is well done.  No variety, but not irksome after listening for a long time.  As you scroll in and out of different views, the music gracefully changes to fit the scene (i.e., transition to battle music if you zoom into a battle scene, and other music as you zoom out).
The game is very tailorable as to strength of allies, enemies, teaming arrangements, victory conditions, etc.  There are six skill levels of AI players.  I found "hard," which is the third of six levels of difficulty, to be truly hard, and have only tried playing against the next harder opponent ("unfair hard") once (teamed with eight easy allies, to ensure a win; but a win was not easy).  For those up for the challenge, there are (IIRC) "vicious" and "cruel" opponents awaiting.  A typical game for me is to play against multiple hard opponents (and some "normal") while I am allied with one "hard" and one or two "normal."
Excellent variety of maps to play:  scores and scores of maps in every size you might like.  And if you don't see what you want, you can make a tailored map, using easy in game map generator or (for more control) Galaxy Forge, which is supplied with the game!  You can even make your own graphics effects (ships and weapons effects) using an effects editor (forgot name), also supplied with the game!  I have made maps using in game editor and Galaxy Forge.  Galaxy Forge is powerful and relatively easy to use.   You will have to Google up some help (big trick is editing galaxy.manifest in Notepad or some other text editor); but it only took this old dog a few minutes to figure it out.  Any gamer under 30 should be able to do it in half the time.
There is an active modding community.
I went into the multiplayer forums, several times.  Not much happening.  I was not able to get hooked up with a game; but looks like others were.  No big: MP is not my thing.  I see other reviewers are getting hooked up well in MP; so maybe I did not try hard enough...
Bottom line:  BEST space combat game since Homeworld!  Tactical combat on par with Homeworld (lacks rich 3D-oriented combat, but has better ship variety); but 4X strategy gives SoaSE:R a lot more replay value.  GREAT game!!!

Magic is a competitive card game that is free to play.  You can buy coins to unlock extra booster pack for your deck, but it is easy enough to earn coins in the game, that there is no reason to.  The games tarts out with a basic story to guide you on how to play magic, while you  earn coins for your first booster back.  Once the intial story is done, the real fun begins.  You can craft your own deck, or use a pregenerated deck out of the cards you have.  You have enough cards to be vialbe in multiplayer, although you will soon start earning coins from playing the game aginst Human or teh AI to earn coins fro more boosters.  There are additional stroies to learn new techniquest and abilties as well, and the first time you play them you also earn coins.
There are sevral expansions planned, and with each expansion you can can further cusomize your decks and run into unexpected challanges.
The only issue is sometime the card gods are not with you and you may draw several lands in a row, on never draw a land.  Keeping a good land creature ratio will help, but it will happen even it the most tuned decks.

Wow this game is actually pretty great. I picked it up cheap from a Steam sale not realizing how much enjoyment I'd get out of it.
It's pretty much a dumbed down space sim. Everything about it is simplified to the most simple, basic elements, and god damn, it actually works. Everything about this game is simple. There's no vertical plane so you'll be flying your ship around horizontally like a naval ship at sea, but after a while you don't even notice that you can't fly up or down. There are no small ships to fly, all of the available vessels are capital-class - frigates, haulers, dreadnauts, battleships, etc.
The missions, navigation, trading, and controls are all simple and fun. The combat is incredibly easy but still quite enjoyable, it relies on ship upgrades and positioning more than player skill.
If you like games like Elite Dangerous and Freelancer, you'll find this game very easy but you'll still get a lot of bang for your buck. The story is ok and the visuals are pretty enough to keep you interested.
If you like the look of space games but can't get into them, this is the space game for you.
Bonus points: You can actually change the game's entire soundtrack to your own playlist of MP3's. I especially liked this feature.

Tiny and Big is a platformer with a gimmick. You can cut your environment, literally. So for example, if there's a wall in front of you, you can just use your laser tool to cut out a doorway. Obviously this leads to far more exciting and complicated puzzles, but the core concept of the gimmick is easy to understand and fun to perform.
Playing this game, I felt reminded of the kind of games you find on the Nintendo 64 (Super Mario 64, for example). You explore a 3D world, jump on lots of stuff, and collect secret items along the way.
The one true downside is that it's short. It took me only around 4 hours to beat.
Nvertheless, if you like games with creative puzzles, and you miss playing old 3D platformers with a childlike sense of fun, then you'll probably enjoy this game as much as I did (maybe more...maybe less..... It is your money after all....)

Playing video games for the first time long after their release is not always a bad thing. Indeed it enables us to see how they endure the test of time. And only true jewels can stand it. What about Bioshock II ? As I had been blown away after playing the first opus, I expected a lot from this sequel. And so did many Bioshock fans. Here's my review :
(See rating at the end of the review)
____________________________
GAMEPLAY: Quite similar to what we experienced in the first game. The gameplay is really focused on immersive and explosive fighting sequences. The difference with the first opus is that there's no real final boss but very often the player is opposing big waves of ennemies. Hopefully it is possible to prepare your defense by setting traps and mines, hacking security cameras and turrets. But if you want to collect all the Adam, these defensive fights become too repetitive. On a more positive note, some new weapons add more fun to the gameplay. I really enjoyed playing with the drill and the spear gun. Moreover, it's really interesting to combine different weapon's and plasmid's attacks. I liked the fact, that as a Big Daddy you really feel the strength and the weight of your character. There are also different levels of difficulty that you may choose depending on your experience in FPS games. So don't worry if you're not used to this type of game. I'm not, but I still truly enjoyed playing it.
VISUALS, MUSIC & ATMOSPHERE: That's why so many people love the Bioshock saga : a deep immersion into an equally beautiful and horrific world. Of course, I already knew how Rapture looked like but I was still surprised by the beauty of the scenery. And even if the game engine is getting older, the esthetic of this chaotic city is still mind-blowing. The new developers have even got further with more cutscenes and submarine exploration that offers quiet and contemplative moments between the fighting sequences. I also have to praise the soundtrack, the voice-acting and the sound effects that are even better than in the first Bioshock.
STORY: In this sequel, which occurs ten years after the events of the first game, we play in this sequel a reborn Big Daddy who's trying to get back to his little sister. Our quest offers us the possibility to explore many new places and to meet new cheracters. The most interesting ones are the utopist Sofia Lamb and the opportunist Sinclair who take the roles of Ryan and Atlas in the antagonist-protagonist pattern. Because we are more familiar with Rapture and it's doom, we are less surprised by the wickedness of its inhabitants but there are still some strong revelations. Many elements of the story are smartly scattered in the Audio Diaries that the player finds on its way. And as we move towards the end of the game, the story becomes more and more intense.
