As someone who purchased this game at launch and uninstalled after a few hours of frustration, I felt the need to write my very first Steam review years later, after giving X: Rebirth a second chance. I want to encourage those who found this game as maddeningly buggy and unfinished as I did at launch to consider the immense improvements that have come with patches and DLCs, and to give this ground breaking game a second chance. Yes, despite the age of X: Rebirth, I still consider it to be modern and groundbreaking. The level of freedom and immersion achievable in this game is absolutely unparalleled by similar genre titles.
It's strong ambition, however, is also it's greatest failing. The tools provided to the player to build their empire of trade and conquest are exhaustive, but unintuitive. So much so that after 60+ hours I am still learning to navigate the endless menus of information about the economy and struggling to fully comprehend the station supply techniques that allow for self sustaining empire building. I have at my fingertips the ability to see hundreds of trade offers, complete with supply and demand based pricing, but to earn that right I must search out and play a tediously simple mini-game at each and every station I desire to track trade offers from. Likewise, while I have the freedom to issue specific and complex orders to individual crew members of my various combat ships and fleets, the only ship I can directly pilot is my own, which is limited in its combat role. Thus, I find myself in awe of what complexity X: Rebirth permits while I am simultaneously confused about certain design choices that seem to hinder the sense of player freedom that the game strives to instill.
The campaign serves more as a lengthy tutorial to the game's many features than as a draw for those most interested in story and lore. I found myself very engaged from beginning to end, as the player is unintentionally caught up in conflict and forced to take sides while  they explore the X universe for new allies and trade opportunities. The ending is unquestionably rushed, however, and is an unfortunate blemish on an otherwise well told narrative. The voice acting, it should be noted, is far from triple-A quality, but while the lines were not always delivered in the most effective way, it never cripples the narrative beyond recovery.
Many of my issues with game mechanics were easily solved with a quick trip to the Steam Workshop. The modding community for this game is small, but among the highest quality and most dedicated that I have seen. The complexity and scope of many of the available mods really turn this game from a B- into a A-. X: Rebirth does not require mods to make it a tremendous experience, but a minor tweak to the interface here and a slight additional convenience there can really give the player a much more fluid expierence. Add to that a more expansive mod or two, and X: Rebirth can easily surpass even the highest of expectations for a space sim.
In summation:
Pros
-immersive and enormous universe to explore
-very high level of player freedom to achieve almost anything
-engaging story arc
-stellar modding community
-graphically gorgeous
Cons
-unintuitive UI, requiring a lot of time and Google searches to truly grasp
-disappointing design choices that hinder the feeling of freedom (such as inability to fly other ships or take over enemy sectors without mods)
-abrupt plot conclusion leaves player feeling unfulfilled
Despite its flaws, I strongly recommend this title for fans of the genre who are willing to invest the time required to comprehend the vastness and complexity that is X: Rebirth.

Hatred is an isometric top-down twin-stick shooter developed by Destructive Creations, putting the player in the boots of a man whose name is unknown who is a misanthropic mass-killing sociopath who begins a "genocide crusade" to kill as many human beings as possible.
This game can be compared to the 1997 "Postal", which I've played as well, but with a massive graphics overhaul. This game built a lot of hype with the trailers, but with the hype, came controversy. People complained that it was "sickening" and "distasteful." and, "This is why people are violent blah-blah yea sure whatever BS." I don't listen that crap though, it's a game.
Story(?) ---
Sadly, there is no story to why the crusader is killing everyone he can. If there it, I probably haven't been paying much attention then, to hear about it. Hopefully, the DLC will provide a backstory.
Gameplay ---
You have 7 free-roam levels to conduct your killing-spree. The levels aren't really big, they're big enough to see some variation of buildings and scenery and plenty of open space. You can drive vehicles, but only limited to police squad cars, SWAT tactical vans (sometimes with a .30 cal), and Military Humvees (comes with .30 cal machine gun on top). Health system works by executing people. You execute a civilian or an enemy, you get a portion of your health back. If you die, however, you have to restart the level. However, you can earn respawn "tokens" by completing side objectives.
Enemies ---
In the beginning, the first enemy you'll encounter are police officers. They are easy to take out, but in groups, they can take you out if you aren't careful. As you progress, you'll encounter SWAT units. These guys can take some hits before going down and are a bit of a challenge starting off. Here's a warning i'll give; these guys will flashbang you, making you vulnerable to gunfire, so try to keep your distance. Eventually, you'll take on the National Guard. They're like the SWAT units, only sightly tougher. A couple of these guys will sometimes carry a rocket launcher, so keep an eye out. Certain weapons will make easy work of all of these enemies. Civilians will also take up arms and fight back (one of the many aspects of this game that I love) against you. Speaking of weapons...
Weapons ---
Weapons range from handguns, shotguns, and an AK-47 in the beginning part of the game. Later, you'll get M-16s and Mac-11s, a flame-thrower and rockets. You can carry three of any with you at any time. You'll also get grenades, molotovs and flashbangs. So...pick your poison.
Executions ---
Executions are pretty good to be honest. They range from simple point blank headshots to real edgy style such as shoving your pistol into the mouth of an innocent civilian and pulling the trigger. Downside is that they get repetitive over time.
Survival Mode ---
As part of a free DLC, we got survival mode. Survival mode is straight-forward. Survive. You get three different areas that take place after the events of the Crusader's aftermath including a couple of new weapons, rank system, and three new characters for survival. A police officer who was mentally damaged by the Crusader in an attack, a chick who is considered a reject by society, and an ex-criminal. As the waves progress, the enemies become harder to defeat. Some enemies are color-marked with red skulls above them, these guys will take some hits before going down. There is an in-game "store" after each wave to where you can buy explosives and armor/ammo to aid you and give you a tactical advantage.
Conclusion ---
If Steam could allow me to give a so-so rating instead of thumbs up/down, I would give it that. It's not bad, then again, it could've been better. The only thing I wish there was is a story to what made him come to this decision to kill. It's a good game to kill some time on and to be honest, it's something different. We're always playing the good guys and anti-heroes who turns good. We're playing a full on antagonist.
7/10

I love this game so far. It's like a MOBA without the MOBA portion. You pick a champion, then get placed into an arena and take part in a 2v2 or 3v3 teamfight with a winner being decided after 3 to 5 rematches.
This game is basically what I would call a top-down arena fighter. It's a better version of Bloodline Champions or Smashmuck Champions. You move with WASD, attack by left-clicking, and use abilities via hotkeys surrounding your move buttons, as well as your right-click. This is also one of few games where I'm fine and actually willing to play against other players, because you can turn off chat and it's just a 2v2-3v3 teamfight.
Takes a bit of practice to get used to each champion, but they seem balanced based on the ones I've played. Every champ has a lot of others they work well with, and a lot they work horrible with, which makes it kinda difficult to do random matches. It has a Heroes-style queue system, where if you queue alone, you won't know what character your teammate(s) picked until the match starts. So it kind of incentivises getting friends to play with you, so that you have people you can synergize with while playing champs you can synergize with.
This game is absolutely amazing, and I hope it lasts a long time. I also hope it doesn't go downhill, like most other free game I've played have. I recommend any of my friends who like the team-fighting aspect of MOBAs, or any game with arena brawler combat to try this one, as well as any other people who like those types of games.

Like so many people, I wish Steam offered a "neutral" button for this game as I'm sort of 50/50 with it thus far.   As so many other people have already mentioned, base gameplay is roaming around trying to find clues and/or pick things up.  That's fine, not like other games require any less of its players.
My cons:
I guess my biggest gripe with the game (and bear in mind my play time - maybe this gets better) is that I found the combat difficult (I may be in the minority there).  While some enemies can be done in with a single shot to the head, I found this to not really be an easy thing to do.  Where I am having serious  problems is in the "void/dark wold" (or whatever it's called) where the skeletons are roaming around.  You are using period appropriate weapons, so your guns require a significant reload time between shots (since you are using black powder weapons).  Even if I sprinted, I could not outrun the skeletons and the melee attack was near worthless since once they get that close to you, you're more or less dead.
This leads to my next gripe - you die way too easily in my opinion.  Where there is one skeleon, there are usually three or four and they swarm you.  Since you can't outrun them (unless I'm doing something wrong), I can't get away and keep getting killed.  You can go back to your last spot to recover any lost gear, but the game regenerates any baddies you killed before and places them in different parts of the map.  Usually I would be fine with something like that, but it just makes this difficult.
When you are killed, you respawn back at the fort (at least at the part I am currently at which is pretty much the beginning) meaning you have to back track to wherever you were last.  The areas aren't that big, but since the bad guys are also respawned and placed in different locations after you die, it means you are stuck having to deal with the same bad guys over again.  Only this time you don't have the benefit of any ammunition or other items you may have had prior to your death (including money).  So even though you can buy weapons and supplies at the fort, you aren't going to have any money after respawning to actually buy anything with.  If you are out of ammo, you're kind of hosed since all you will have is your melee knife which is useless in my opinion.
With regards to weapons - you can purchase upgraded weapons, but they seem to be priced way too high in my opinion.  As much loot as I've picked up, I still don't have enough money to buy upgraded weapons and from what I've read on other reviews, they probably aren't much of a benefit anyway.
There is supposedly a stealth aspect to this game, but I have yet to be able to sneak up on anyone with success (even when the wind is blowing).  You're better off trying to take enemies out from a distance if you can.
Pros:
Game runs smooth and I think it does offer a bit of a different premise when compared to the average FPS game. I'm usually a fan of this type of game in that it does blend some horror and investigation type elements into the game.  They are limited, but at least they are there.
I got it on sale for a few bucks and that would be my suggestion to everyone else - get it while it's on sale and that should help offset the negatives.
I did not (and will not) get a refund on the game and I'll still keep tinkering with it, but nothing in the game really screams at me to come back and play it like others that I've played.
Love this arcade style flight sim fun to play simple controls a little to easy but enjoyable and good story. If you only have an hour or so to spare you can jump straight in and play.

Dead Rising 2 is a sequel to the original 360 exclusive. It was a higher budget multiplatform release that expanded on the original game albiet not without it's own issues.
Dead Rising 2 features a similar premise to the original game. You play as Chuck Greene, a survivor who has to survive for 3 days in a resort called "Fortune City". Like the original, everything is set in real time and you have a certain amount of time to complete your objectives. And depending on how well you do you can achieve different endings and even a bonus overtime mode. Fortune City is very reminiscient of the original game's Willamette mall but is more goofy and stylized after a Las Vegas casino.
Chuck is perhaps the least interesting part of the game. He's mostly a dull static brick in comparison to Frank West in the original game. His only defining feature beyond his motorcycle jacket is that he has a daughter he needs to bring "Zombrex". A kind of vaccine for the virus that you must bring her every 12 hours. This concept sounds interesting but in reality it makes you feel a little stressed out because you either need to find it in really well hidden parts of the world or buy it for really enormous prices. And ontop of that return back to your safehouse at regular intervals give it to her. In general it just feels very needless and makes you wish the game brought back the original's "Infinity" mode to let you explore the resort.
What Dead Rising 2 does add is the ability to craft your own weapons. Much like the original game you can find weapons out of mostly anything. As you rescue survivors and kill zombies you gain the ability to craft even more fantastical weapons. It is a legitimately interesting part to the game and does encourage actually picking up more useless items for further crafting later. They also added co-op but I generally recommend playing with a friend you can coordinate with due to the time sensitive nature of the game. Along with a time attack multiplayer mode called "Terror is Reality".
In general it's a solid sequel but for all of the wacky inclusions it feels much more tedious. And because Off the Record stars Frank West, features the same content and improved several of its flaws I generally recommend it a bit more. Still it is interesting to play if only because Chuck has a nice jacket and for the differences, how small they might be.

This game executed space combat perfectly. You will read reviews about how the game is played on a 2D plane as a negative, but after just finishing the game I find it completely necessary. A third dimension really would not add much to how the game works but would make the game itself far more complicated and more difficult to use. Regardless, other ships still manuever in a 3D area when flying as well as the environment. The combat is a naval type system with a variety of different combat strategies from ramming enemies, to lazers, cannons, and some very well executed side combat very similar naval games. I like to stick to $1/hr making a good game and this one checks out. I was originally stunned by how great the reviews for this game were and I was glad to see that the game lives up to the hype. The game progression is very satisfying and the story is pretty good. If you are a gamer that likes RPG type games and don't mind a bit of a grind then this is the game for you. When I first began playing I worried that I would be travelling between checkpoints more often than doing anything productive in game but this worry quickly went away as you can upgrade every aspect of your ship. Here are some pros and cons for me:
PROS:
BEAUTIFUL
Best soundtrack of any game I have every played
Space Combat looks and feels fantastic
2D playing field helps the game feel very smooth (far better than a clunky 3D field)
The ships are well thought out, look sick, and different ships fit different play styles
Story works and makes sense
HUD has a learning curve which gives the sense of learning how to pilot well (scan, pulse, manage shields, manuevers)
Characters look great
Trade system is simple yet effective
Very satisfying game progression - ships get massive + more firepower = very awesome combat
The game saves automatically at every station you dock at
One of the best parts of this game for me was how much content I felt like I was getting. I put in many hours to try and upgade my ship, did many missions in and out of the story, and then realized I still had tons of other solar systems that I hadn't even touched. I would have been happy with the one system but the entire web of systems makes the game that much better. It gets involved with trade routs, missions, and you weave through systems throughout the story.
CONS:
Mission diversity isn't the best - (ex: go here blow up stuff, take items here, escort ___ to here...) but it still works well
Some physics didn't feel very smooth, while others felt okay
Menus took me a while to understand fully (esc has multiple menus to cycle as well as tab and ctrl)
Sometimes the game felt like a grind in a bad way when trying to raise money but then I would go back to the story and refresh
Risk levels are inaccurate as some high risk are easy to take down while low risk can sometimes shred you
Late game starts to feel a bit empty and boring (quick traveling point to point) but the story and larger missions make up
I found one bug during one of the first story missions. It was relatively difficult which was okay so I raised money and upgraded then I couldn't find all of the ships to destroy for the mission. Found some others with the same problem and just had to kill myself and respawn so it would reset.
I don't often write extensive reviews for games but I really felt like this one deserved a thumbs up. Hadn't found a game that made me excited for a while and this one did the trick. I got it on sale for $13 and it was worth far more than that to me.

Have you ever been attracted to the IDEA of space sims, but been unable to figure out impossibly dense controls?  Do you love the IDEA of piloting a massive battleship into battle, but can't deal with stupid 3D loop-de-loops?  Do you just like pretty explosions and badass slide guitar music?
Then this game is for you.
It's a pretty standard space game setup-- fly around the galaxy trading, mining, fighting, what have you.  Upgrade your ship, buy progressively bigger and badder ships, rule the world, and so on.  The twist is that it all takes place on a 2D plane.  Objects float around and ships-- especially fighters-- fly every which way, but you only have to worry about one dimension.  The basic play is pretty much like Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag.  You hold down the button to charge a broadside, aim a bit and fire; hit your shields to brace for impact before taking return fire, and so on.  There's a bit more, with turrets and different weapon types and hired mercenaries, but that's the basic idea.  It's easy to get the hang of and fun to play.  And, you know, it looks pretty, the soundtrack is great, and it's nice to have a third person view of your ship instead of trying to make sense of things from a cockpit view.
tl;dr: If you want to fly a battleship in space without wrapping your head around complex controls, this is for you.

Great game. At it's heart, RG is a traditional space trading game in the likes of Elite, Privateer, X etc. What really stands out for RG is its deliberate direction away from the core sim experience of those aforementioned games. RG strips itself of the complex sim-y fluffs essentials of the genre, namely the trading, upgrading, fighting and occasional quest undertaking. Hell it even takes away the y axis, leaving only the ability to manuver in a 2D plane. Some reviews mentioned that the same isn't true with other ships and that's somewhat accurate but their 3D movement is still fairly limited (think the pizza box arenas of Star Trek Legacy) and for the most part your AI opponents ability to move above or beneath you isn't totally unfair. Also like ST Legacy, your ships are large size vessels not the turn on a dime fighters you would expect. Combat are more reminiscent of ship battles in AssCreed where large amount of capital ships firepower are directed to the side not the front. The music is worth mentioning in that it's not your typical scifi affair. It's southern rock, like in Starcraft or the show Firefly. The story is mediocre with some surprisingly decent voice acting. The production value is also unexpectedly high with good visual and sound. RG is also relatively bug free. The few complaints I have is that a lot of the missions are very cookie cutter, which is kind of to be expected considering the budget. The game is also fairly shallow, but the combat is visceral enough to keep it interesting for the 10 hrs I've put in so far. I also don't think the interface is as intuitive as it could be; took me forever to find out that the ship advanced functions are hidden in the system pause screen and not the command screen where I would put it. There are couple of similarly strange design choices in the game, but those are just nickpickings. The game is thoroughly entertaining if you ever fancy yourself as Han Solo or Mal Reynalds, especially for $13~15. You could do worse on steam.

Rebel Galaxy is a fantastic value. Beautiful environments, perfect gamepad controls. The dog fighting is a lot of fun without being painfully hard to learn. Navigation is confined to 2D space, which adds some constraints to simplify gameplay.
If you like trading, shooting and exploring in space, you really can't go wrong here. Progression feels really satisfying--your ship bulks up steadily, while challenges mount. It's very well tuned to keep you in the groove of difficult-but-fun. The save system is strict but raises the stakes of your adventuring and dangerous encounters--without being overly punishing.
My favorite piece, though, is that the game lets you customize its soundtrack. I grew weary of the bluegrass after awhile, charming though it was. On a lark, I stuffed in my own soundtrack, drawn from Mass Effect, Battlestar Galactica, Babylon 5 and Homeworld 2.
The result was so much fun! Shooting up space ships to the tunes I associate most with space battles was such a joy. Especially the Homeworld stuff, which is some of the best space music I have. The game is also smart about its music selections, pulling from different directories for combat versus exploration or idleness.
This is a fun, lovingly crafted game that's very easy to customize to your exact musical vibe. If you like space, you'll have fun.

I have no clue why this game hasn't garnered more media attention. It is one of the most refreshing, accessibly deep, and fun games I've played in quite some time. The developers are sitting on a freaking goldmine of an IP. I fully expect this to be a Triple-A series in the future... and if it doesn't, it should be.
It's like Eve mixed with World of Warships mixed with Pirates!. It's oozing with personality, looks great, has good music (though you can customize your own soundtrack if you prefer... BOB!), a high degree of polish, and the combat had me literally giggling as I perfected the art of assassinating capital ships and darting out of the swarm before the bad guys could react. There's mining, pirating, smuggling, trade, mercenary work, and plenty of upgrades all happening in an open world. It's a game you can jump in and play for 5 minutes... or 5 hours. Oh, and there's a completely competent series of voice-acted story missions in there too. But what really ties it all together is that it somehow the game makes you feel like you're the actual commander of a little (or big) ship zooming through space wacking pirates while trying to eek out a living and getting to the bottom of a family mystery.
And that combat... Balancing speed, shields and armor, deflectors, broad-side weapons, point defense guns all while navigating a crowded battlefield is just way more fun than it should be. Not to mention the different ship types and weapon combos that lets the player customize their favorite way to conduct combat. Big Massive Missile Boat? Ok. Small fast laser frigate? yup. Fast and agile blockade runner? Suuuure. Do it your way.
Im not all that far in but am just totally infatuated with this lil game. I say 'lil' because I got it for only $15 on sale ($20 normally) and yet it plays like AAA game.  The only thing 'lil' is the price because there's enough in there to occupy more time than most big budget titles.
So to wrap it up
Pros:
-Great Combat
-Great Visuals and Effects
-Open "World"
-Upgrades, Ships, and Customization
-Customizable Dynamic Soundtrack
-Accessible
-Runs amazingly well on lower end systems (Which I have)
Cons:
-Movement only in 2 dimensions (Though it adds to the accessibility of the game)
-Umm... it doesn't spit free cookies out of my DVD drive?
Bottom Line. If you like space games, action, or fun buy it.

let me start off by saying i absolutely recommend this game to anyone that enjoys survival games. it is incredibly well done. hats off to 11 bit for this awesome piece of work.
having said that i wouldn't call this game fun. it is pretty bleak, depressing, gritty and stressful at times. all of which makes this game compelling. the choices you make in this game are actually meaningful and are often not presented in a binary way like most games (this happens at the shelter when random events happen, like people asking for your help), however a lot of the choices are just up to you to decide how to deal with your current situation. do you become a bandit, robbing people as much as you can? do you steal from the hospital (which is low on supplies and offers free treatment)? do you hold on to your morals and not steal/harm inoccent people?
how long until you abandon those principles when you are running out of food/medical/crafting supplies and you have sick and or injured people. or when you can't access areas due to snow or fighting leaving you stuck with looted areas and a home of an elderly couple and the hospital left.
if you do steal from people or harm innocents, your group of survivors will be affected by it. they will be saddened and can even commit suicide or leave if things are really bleak. doing such things will most likely become a neccessity, but i for one, still felt bad for breaking into that elderly couple's home and taking half their stuff.
the game attempts to invoke an emotional response. certainly not pleasant ones. the whole game is pretty bleak, once winter rolls around. it quickly becomes stressful. everything seems to get compounded and there doesn't seem to be enough supplies left. the game's mechanics are well designed to create tension.
combat is clunky and intentionally so. you can die incredibly qucikly even fully armored, you're always going to be out numbered. fighting in the open is suicide in this game. it is the biggest drawback in this game, but it does make sense in the context of the game. you're playing civilian survivors in a war zone, it makes sense that fighting isn't something they are good at. so while it isn't enjoyable, i can at least forgive the combat system since the mechanics are playing into the context and setting of the game.
all in all, it is a fantastic game worth every last penny of the 20 dollar asking price, provided you are into survival games and are interested in seeing a game explore some very dark and edgy themes and issues. if you aren't typically into survival games (i myself don't play many) check out total buscuit's excellent video. you might find the subject matter of the game to be interesting as hell, as i did.

A fairly competent though not outstanding shooter, Bioshock 2 revisits Rapture sometime after the events of the first game. While it’s lovely to be back in what is probably my favourite city in gaming, Rapture has lost the atmosphere that it had in the days of Atlas and Ryan. Sure, the splicers look the same and the design hasn’t changed, but the creepy environment of this once great city tearing itself apart is gone and while it looks the same, Rapture feels completely different.
This is the main problem with Bioshock 2. As a stand-alone game it’s pretty good; the design is fine, the shooting mechanics are greatly improved and level design and enemy variety are all fantastic. However when put alongside its predecessor it feels absolutely awful. Bioshock 2 is a game with none of the artistic vision of the first (or third), has a terribly boring and utterly nonsensical story that just cheapens the rest of the Bioshock universe and an antagonist that is absolutely cringe worthy. The whole plot is just badly written and serves no purpose other than to point you in the direction of the next thing to shoot. That may do it for other games, but not for Bioshock.
While Bioshock 2 is the worst visit to Rapture, it’s still a trip there and that counts for something. I wouldn’t recommend it, though it’s worth noting that the Minerva’s Den DLC is pretty great and worth the purchase if the game is going cheap.
That’s not the main reason that I wouldn’t recommend this game though. The game crashes constantly and makes playing an incredibly frustrating experience. I can forgive a game that has a different artistic vision to what I find compelling, but something with game-breaking bugs like this is objectively bad.
The random musical number in the middle is worth the price of admission all by itself.

I start to scan the station thinking this isn't so bad, just then the massive ship blows up in the distance.

I'm very sorry not to be able to recommend this game, because Egosoft clearly put a tremendous amount of effort into improving what was an unmitigated disaster of a game at launch two and a half years ago.  To their credit, they've come a long way and made some good progress on this one.  I can at least say that any product you get from Egosoft, they will absolutely stand by both it and you 100%.
Unfortunately there are still some big problems.  There is currently no good way to control and issue orders to large fleets of player controlled ships.  Even when issuing orders to a single vessel, you actually have to engage in a conversation with the captain of that ship to tell them to do something.  20 seconds to issue a single command?  Not good.  Especially not good in combat situations.
The campaign was an attempt to train the player in all the things they can do in the X Rebirth universe, but it doesn't do a great job.  For example, you are shown how to board a ship.  What it doesn't tell you is that the team of 8 marines you do this with would NEVER be able to take a similar ship during the real game, most especially not one at full health.  Thus when you attempt your first real capital ship capture, you are met with spectacular failure no matter how many times you reload until you finally hit the forums to discover that you've been misled.  Also, now that you've captured your story scripted ship, how does one go about fueling and repairing it?  No explanation given in game.  To the forums, once again!  Not acceptable given the campaign itself is supposed to be answering these sorts of questions.
X-Rebirth has come a long way since launch, and I would definitely do business in the future with a company like Egosoft, who so clearly stand by their products.  But can I recommend this one for a full $30 price tag?  No.  Sadly, I still cannot.  Perhaps some day.

A while ago, I said that Hatred looked like a terrible sort of game. Now, after having played it, I’ve realised that I was bang on the money, just not for the reason I thought.
The game is about a dude who embarks on a self-proclaimed genocide crusade. He despises humanity, wants to be rid of it, and wants to die. But before he dies, he wants to take as many people as he can with him.
If approached correctly, this could have been something. A look into the mind of a serial killer, perhaps. Something that affects you profoundly, not because you relate to the protagonist, but because you’re repulsed by him. A game that resonates in a very particularly wrong way, by being the exact opposite of fun.
You’re shown everything that Hatred has to offer in the first ten minutes and the formula never varies from that point onward. Coupled with an art style that makes it difficult to see anything, let alone play comfortably, Hatred becomes a game that you spent money on only if you really don’t like that money and really just want to rid yourself of it because your pants are too heavy, or something.
But if you want something approaching a modicum of fun, something that you can spend a few hours with and actually enjoy, Hatred isn’t something you should be looking at.

Air Conflicts: Secret Wars is an arcade flight simulation set in a world war I + II scenario. During the 7 campaigns the player has to fly and fight through 49 missions. Before taking off, the player can choose between different aircrafts, each with different strengths and weaknesses.
Within the missions the player gets different objectives like patrolling, sneaking, hit & run, bombing and escorting. Objectives are presented as dialogues between different characters. After some missions the player can upgrade one of his skills in order to maneuver the airplanes easier, have more endurance or have your wingman boosted. Further, the player can choose between two control schemes. Arcade and simulation. The first one makes the game easier to control, while the second one gives more options to control the aircraft.
Beside the campaign the game also features several multiplayer modes, local and via internet for up to four players.

Though the game is rated really badly for it's singleplayer and some restrictions in multiplayer, this game is really really fun and gamers who enjoyed the COD and the BF series should try this game. It is not really worth the price tag but when there's a 75% sale, it's a steal! xD

Around two years ago I was looking for a game about piloting planes and possibly shooting other planes, because I was always somewhat interested in this sort of genre. Since I'm not really into simulations I thought I try out the "Blazing Angels" games, but Ubisoft apparently can't make games work on Windows 7 and so far I wasn’t able to run both “Blazing Angels” games on my pc.
So I was still looking for a game to scratch that itch I was having. I then stumbled onto "Air Conflicts: Secret Wars". Looking primarily for a game that would let me fly something like prototype planes from the Second World War I thought with a title like "Secret Wars" I'd hit the jackpot.
Well, after about 5 hours I'm sure of a few things:
(0. So far I haven't seen a plane I would describe as a prototype, just the standard planes of British and Russian fighter planes and/or bombers. But this is mostly my fault for expecting something that the game probably doesn't provide. That’s the reason I’m not factoring this in my overall opinion of the game, but I thought I let you know.)
1. I had to restart my campaign progression, because I couldn't find my save files after I de-installed the game, so I spent the last hour or so of my whole experience with this game getting back to where I was before.
But after only 5 hours I seriously couldn't drag myself through the campaign again. Story wise it progresses very slowly, since there isn't much happening inside of the mission except for a few radio messages every now and then. "Cutscenes" outside of the missions are made with a comic-like style and subtitles (although they are narrated). Everything else is pure text (mostly diary entries).
Also missions seem to be very repetitive (from what I've seen of the game). So far it's been pretty much about shooting other fighter planes, shooting bombers, destroying stationary ground targets, destroying moving ground targets and sometimes defending other planes by doing the before mentioned things. Although it’s maybe a bit unfair to expect more of this sort of game.
2. Overall control of the planes and how keys are setup works really nice, although some advanced maneuvers, like looping or barrel-rolls don't seem to be possible. I was playing on the arcade mouse + keyboard setting, so it's maybe possible that controlling the game with a joystick or something similar might enable it.
3. Shooting other planes felt like fun, although I couldn't really find a good middle way with the difficulty settings. Either I was shooting everything easily while not really getting shot at (aside from stationary AA) or I was damaged far too fast for me to enjoy the game. So while the original control and feeling for a plane is nice, it just isn’t fun for too long, when barely anything gives you a fight and what you’re doing is pretty much flying circles to get a few hits on target and repeat.
Over all I could say it probably wasn't the game I was looking for (I'm much more sure it was "Blazing Angels" but that didn't work out). I should have also probably checked a few reviews or just some random campaign gameplay before I bought it.
It's just that the game isn't bad, maybe the story gets better after a while or the missions are more varied in the end, but to get there I don't want to go through the first missions again.
Although I don’t have knowledge of the full game, after the 5+ hours I have no desire to play it again, because have tried to get into the game, but it just won’t click, like many other games do.
So no, I cannot recommend this game.

Although I'll admit that you're going to spend a lot of time wandering back and and forth in this game; it's oppressive atmosphere and subtle soundtrack really put you into the game.
The old-school weapons also provide a nice touch. The frustration of dealing with muzzle-loaders, flint-lock pistols, and crossbows also zero in the frustration of these low-tech solutions. I don't mean that this is not a welcome change of pace from games that seem to want an automatic in your hands as soon as possible. Combat in this game rewards both the bold and the stealthy, although once you get to a certain point, you'll hear your enemies, but spotting them before they spot you is REALLLLLLLY hard.
So to break it down:
Combat: Stealth or run-n-gun. Explosives are okay, but I never use them. Use cover to your advantage, and the wind-swells to mask footsteps.
Atmosphere: From the lonely shore you wash up on, to the sad bastions of fortresses where the ghosts of some truly deplorable people dwell all give this game a kind of hopelessness that is engaging and eerie. Moving between day and night worlds is a kind of Silent Hill-esque treat.
Issues: I wish the markers for ghosts that aren't available would disappear until they were available again. After every piece of evidence, I'm back to wandering in the woods to see if a ghost popped up.
This game doesn't give you a ton of info up front, so let me help:
1. The corrupted totems can only be dealt with at night, and you can "listen" to them (starting a battle) with "X"
2. You can switch back to the world map and you don't have to go back through each area, you can warp to any point you've created, across any map.
3. Make sure you check the map that you want everything to show up! I made it to the fourth area before I realized it wasn't showing me ghosts.
4. You won't get the shovel to dig up the rock-piles until quite a ways into the game, so don't keep looking for the damn thing until you get like four or five maps in.
Anyway, great game for the price, and I bought it and forgot I had it in my library for a few months. I then went back and actually played it, and I've been playing it every night for the last couple weeks!

I love first person shooters that have ranged weapons but break from standard FPS conventions. In the case of Betrayer, the convention break to get used to is painfully long reload time with muzzle loaded muskets and ball and powder pistols. It's one of the few games I've played where the reload time really does force you into cycling through your weapons because you just won't have time to reload them when being chased by multiple enemies. I think it could have gone further in this area, since there's 5 primary weapon types but you can only equip 3. I would have loved to cycle through them and fire them off, then swap to another, fire its one shot, etc.
The story is interesting. It's something that only works in text, which is always interesting to observe. This is because the words being said by characters are true, but the picture they paint quite often is not, which was a really unique experience in a world full of unreliable narrators.
The core mechanics for the story progression start off intriguing and fresh, but by the first couple of areas, you'll have pretty much seen what you'll be doing the rest of the game. That doesn't mean it isn't intriguing, however.
If you like slower paced, atmospheric first person games, you should check out Betrayer.

The Good:
- This game really shows what an indie game -should- look like. In my mind, it ups the bar. No more excuses for garbage pixel art assets with the "retro" cop out because the devs wanted an art budget of $1.50. Step your game up, indies. Blackpowder just served you.

- The setting and story are cool, and I thoroughly enjoyed the investigation aspect of it.
The bad:
- Lack of polish, particularly with audio. There are almost no sounds in this game. No music at all.
- The investigation aspect falls into the same trap as a lot of games with investigation: too much walking. Walking is not gameplay, but you're going to be doing a lot of it, even with quick travel.
- The ending is utter crapola. I won't spoil it here, but it's pretty contrived and pointless.
- Speaking of pointless, you can run around the handful of maps after beating the game, for some reason.
- It's very short. I beat it with 100% completion in less than 10 hours.
Though I could come up with more bad than good bullet points, I think the good points are worth more. Definitely worth a play.

Original Review:
This title is a massive, massive improvement over the disasterous and frankly embarrassing Magic 2015, and a fantastic return to form for a series that has had some very worthwhile entries in past years.  But it's a whole new game in many ways...
Duels 2015 shakes up the formula, dispensing with an up-front purchase to embrace the free-to-play and microtransaction model it flirted with in earlier years, and then abused in Magic 2015 to the amusement of no one.
Moreover, instead of annual entries which get retired, Duels promises a series of on-going expansions, in time with the physical card expansions of the collectible card game, and so an ever-expanding pool of cards to draw from – promises they have so far delivered on.
But Magic Duels is free-to-play done RIGHT.
You get a fully functional and enjoyable experience right away with a tutorial and full single player campaign mode, which will not only give a decent challenge to even fairly experienced Magic: The Gathering players but also serve to introduce and teach the game to complete newbies.
The game then provides you with a decent starting collection of cards from which to start making your own decks, and this is where the game really shines.
While you can pay money for ‘gold’, with which you can buy boosters and more quickly unlock the cards you need to make the perfect deck (and more competitive and experienced players will probably put in a few bucks), but there’s no requirement to do so.   The game lets you buy everything with the same gold currency, and that currency can be earned at a fair and decent rate just by playing through the content, doing daily quests, testing out decks and so on.
As an experienced Magic player and deck designer, the selection of cards presented is varied and powerful without being overwhelming and abusable.  I keep finding new competitive decks hiding amongst the card interactions many weeks after each new expansion.  The competitive metagame is challenging and varied, with a skill ranking system keeping newbies from getting crushed.
The game is far from perfect, with many bugs, and many desirable features missing.  But the ability to play fun, interactive Magic easily online is there, which is what counts, and the game is constantly being improved upon.
A title well worth the download.

At first the game was pretty frustrating. It starts players off with a ton of commons. Making a good deck was challenging at first. Then after I unlocked all the cards it was really fun for a while. I quickly hit the 30 deck limit, and I wish that there wasn't a limit on decks. The game plays pretty smoothly compared to older magic iterations. That being said, the game still keeps incomplete without an upkeep step, and without full sets. The sets arent released on the game the same day they are in real life, so I don't see why full sets arent added. This game ultimately feels like a tease that wizards hopes will get players into the real life MTG game or their "Magic Online" game. Which is kind of lame because this game has the easiest platform to play the game on of any of the aforementioned. Even if magic  duels will never be as complete as magic online is, here are a few suggestions id like to put out there:
- Add prestige or paragon of some sort. Once you hit level 40 theres nothing to show if your a cut above the rest or at least a more experienced player. Perhaps adding some kind of experience or level gain that can only be accumulated by winning a match after hitting level 40. Then when a player loses a match, they go down to level 39, and you cant see their "prestige" until they regain max rank.
- This game is called magic DUELS. And yet the ranked play doesn't really feel like a real magic duel. Its one game, you win you rank up, you lose you rank down. Regardless of the opponents rank, and regardless of your own rank. I think that matches should be best 2 out of 3 and players should be given the ability to build a sideboard for ranked matches. This way a player can earn a rank based on a more fair assessment of their deck. There is a degree of luck in magic that makes best 2 out of 3 neccesary and I feel that people would play more diverse decks if their win/loss wasn't determined by one game. Also it would be nice to have something to do with sideboard cards.
Overall, fun game. Would love to see it improve to the point of replacing Magic Online.

Rebel Galaxy is a very nice space sandbox with a distinct wild west feel.
While the story in this game does little more than serve as a progression vehichle, the game does much to let you write your own stories. Be a pirate or a law enforcer, or go mercenary. Trading and mining are also there for people who enjoy these things. Faction-specific ships and upgrades help replayability without being gamechangers.
On the gameplay side, I've found it's easy capital ship flight and combat mechanic very satisfying. Having an essentially flat space never hampers the explosive carnage as you launch volleys of missiles, fire broadsides and maul enemies with your turret batteries - all in the same time. To keep things going, a splendid variety of random missions is available via mission boards - assasinations, assaults, patrols, escorts, contraband and trade runs to name a few.
The technology of this game is not really impressive - no groundbreaking vendor-specific graphics here. On the bright side, overall production quality is high. Ships and stations are done with care, as is the bright and colorful galaxy, which is littered by nebulas, asteroids and junk fields.
All in all, if you've got a privateering itch, but no desire to plunge into the depths of Elite or EVE, you should definitely give Rebel Galaxy a try.

After the insane fun of Third and IV I was eager for more, and Gat Out of Hell delivered. Granted it's a much shorter game where a lot of the lifespan comes from the open world activities, but I still found all of it addictive gameplay. The big new thing - that being able to fly instead of merely gliding - is difficult to get to grips with at first but extremely rewarding once you do. Upgrading the ability and then using it to fly around the city is tremendous fun and it's great to see a number of activities focused around it. There are other fun special powers to play around with too like petrifying enemies with stone blasts or summoning a fleshy tower that impales foes. I don't think much of the aura abilities but the rest are awesome to unlock and use.
Screwing around in the open world is also more fun to me than in IV, although still not quite to the extent of Third. Thankfully there's no enemy as annoying as the sphere tank thing from IV, and causing enough trouble causes an elite enemy to appear that's fun to take on without any weird button mashing minigame to deliver the final blow. Resetting notoriety is also more straightforward once you've had enough of causing chaos.
The humour you expect from a Saints Row is indeed here. After all, one of the main overall goals is to go shoot Satan in the face. There isn't quite as much focus on the story as in other Saints Row games but you're still given some amusing scenes and solid backstory behind the happenings in Hell back and during your own visit.

The major issue though with the remastered edition of both bioshock 1 and 2 however, is that the game does constantly crash. THIS CAN BE FIXED by going into your steam directory for the game (Steam\steamapps\common\BioShock Remastered\Build\Final), locate the BioshockHD.exe file, right click it, go  to the compatibility tab and make sure to check "Run in 640 x 480" (this doesnt affect actual game resolution), "Override high DPI scaling", and "Run this program as administrator". The game will look alittle strange when launching the game but it does seem to fix the issue with the game crashing as i have not had any crashes with 1 or 2 after doing this. It does not however fix the issue with steam cloud saves so all game saves will be on your local machine.
I definatly would recommend this game to anyone but because of the inconvenience of having to manually fix the game for it to run properly, I would recommend only picking up if the game goes on sale.

Tiny and Big: Grandpa’s Leftovers is a fairly short game like the original Portal. The core of the game lies within its unique and satisfying puzzle platformer gameplay, along with an eclectic soundtrack and a hand drawn art style to bring it together for a fun game about cutting rocks and finding your grandpa’s pants. The premise of the game might be strange, but it’s the style that this game oozes that adds to the destruction gameplay in many good ways.
The story does need some short explanation since looking at it, it does sound very strange. Grandpa’s pants were stolen by a man named Big, and it’s up to Tiny to get the pants back. In addition there is The Radio which acts as Tiny’s sidekick in his adventure to retrieve the pants. It’s a simple story, and the game tells the story using cutscenes and dialog boxes. There is quite a lot of small dialogue in the game which tends to add to the humorous nature of the story, ranging from the main dialogue of the story to shorter lines for finding some of the secrets in the world. Tiny and Big does the humor in a good way with some funny situations and lines between the characters, and of course has the strange story as the vehicle for the comedy.
Tiny and Big is a third person physics puzzle platformer, but with a focus on destructing the environment to navigate to the end of each level. Tiny has at his disposal a laser, a grappling rope, and attachable rockets in his set of tools. The grappling rope allows for pulling objects and the rockets allow pushing debris out of the way. Tiny can also push any object by walking into them with more control than the other methods. The laser is the most interesting and exciting part of the game, since it allows cutting of objects with any angle. Cutting things is seamless, all it takes is the length and angle and the game presents the cut object complete with physics. It’s a marvel at how seamless the cutting process is and the robust physics engine is with the cut objects. After a while, cutting becomes intuitive with choosing how to slice things to get across a gap along with using the other tools to position objects into place. The levels in Tiny and Big are quite linear, using the physics puzzles as ways to navigate over gaps and obstacles. The general platforming is not the most robust however. It can be tricky to judge how far a jump can go, and there are times when walking up a slope and moving forward, you actually move to the side and might fall off. Still, these are minor with the amount of checkpoints and the relatively short and linear levels. Of note, the game does have many achievements and secrets, so it does encourage exploration and might make the game longer than 3-4 hours if you do some exploration. Overall, the rock cutting gameplay is fantastic, with the simple levels and straightforward platforming encouraging a good use of the physics puzzles.
While the game does excel at the unique physics gameplay, it also has some great style too. The game is presented in 3D for the physics engine to do its work, but the art style is something different. The textures look hand drawn and cartoony, which matches the somewhat strange story perfectly. Some sound effects are accompanied by visual text, much like a comic book. It’s quite a different style from most games, but the hand drawn cartoony textures works great for the story and adds to it in good ways.
The soundtrack for this game is excellent, as it also acts a great fit for this game. The music is comprised of songs by several indie bands and wasn’t made for Tiny and Big, but boy do the songs sound great. Most of the songs are some funky beats, so trying to cut apart the landscape is more interesting with it. Again, the overall music style does fit nicely with the story, so it’s a nice touch and makes for a good listen.
Tiny and Big places some fun physics puzzle platforming with the ability to cut rocks in any shape and angle you want, and it also has some great style and story for a fun experience. Most of the game is cutting rocks and using physics to get to the end of the level which is immensely fun, but the art, music, and story also plays a role in making a unique experience. With some pretty simple and straightforward levels and mechanics, Tiny and Big puts fun physics gameplay along with strange story and style for a solid game about rocks and pants.

Romance with Chocolate is the second game from Russian developer, Crisp App Studio, and follows in the steps of their previous Steam release with another "adventureless" hidden object title for those who prefer a little less point 'n' click in their HOGs.  While I'm not quite as taken with this game as compared to Time Trap, it still has a certain amount of charm despite an unpolished translation...and the soundtrack is lovely.
Gameplay is simply picking out items from a list of words or silhouttes.  If you're looking to 100% achievements, you'll need to play each level over and over again to decrease the time it takes to finish them and earn 3 stars, but I found this to be enjoyable enough.  Leaderboards are also available for those who like to challenge themselves competitively, which is something not often done in the genre.
My biggest gripe is with the lack of graphical fidelity.  It is clear that the images were upscaled from a lower resolution, and thus many items are blurry and hard to distinguish.  The ability to play in windowed mode would have helped with this issue some, but sadly it's not an option.
That said, the enjoyment I received from this little title outweighed the issues I had with it's presentation, and it's a fairly easy 100% to boot.  Your mileage may vary, but it's worth checking out if you enjoyed Time Trap or are looking for more straight HOGs here on Steam.

Romance with Chocolate – Hidden Object in Paris:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Melody Doux was born in Paris, where she lived for the first six year of her existence until her mother passed away. After this terrible event, her father decided to move to Montreal and both left the Veinard residence. Her grandmother, Mado, never forgave Melody’s father for taking her away from the family home and heritage. Many moons past until Melody received a letter from her grandmother, Mado, who was on her death bed when she wrote the letter. She wanted to pass on the secret that has run through the family since the 1800’s about a magic potion for lovers. It’s all about Romance and Chocolate!
Romance with Chocolate is a casual hidden object game where you follow the story of Melody Doux in a quest to find her grandmother’s recipe for lovers throughout wonderfully represented Parisian locations.
The game consists of three types of puzzles: hidden object stages, picture repositioning, and sequence puzzles. Your goal is to find all hidden objects, or to reposition pictures, as fast as you can in order to score as many points as possible and earn three hearts for that specific level.  The hidden object stages are very well done in terms of blending the object within the picture. You also have the option of replaying a level, in which you will need to find other objects that were not available to be collected during your first walkthrough. The picture levels are fairly simple and easy to complete. There are a couple of sequence stages, and they’re easy, too.
Personally, I really like the feel of the artwork and the places to visit within Paris. However, the game is very short and you’ll finish it within an hour on your first play. Yes, you do have different items to find on your second play-through in the hidden objects levels, and you can also attempt to record the best possible score per stage.  And that’s about it! The story is well done with a twist of Romance and a recipe for chocolate. I would have liked to have had a longer story and more stages.
The artwork is very nice and the game is easy to play and runs well. The soundtrack suits the game very well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good artwork
-	Hidden objects, picture repositioning and sequence levels
-	Different objects to find on your second play-through
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Short game
-	No trading cards
Romance with Chocolate – hidden object is a nice casual game for lovers of this genre.

The following describes my experience every time I play this game.
The first scenario.
I take my sweet time, playing turtly and expanding slowly, mainly because I'm still fresh from Endless Space and rapid expansion is dangerous, in my mind. I fully upgrade every single world until I can make my empire like a house, except I paint each indavidual brick before I lay it, polish it, and make it amazing. A slow process.
Then the enemy fleet arrives, bristling with LRM frigates and siege engines, capitol ships all over the damn place, shredding my meager defenses while I scramble to make some kind of response fleet. I lose in minutes when this happens. Hours of work, gone in seconds.
The second scenario.
I make one capitol ship right off, usually the one with colonization capability, and build a fleet to defend it before I even start growing. From there, I expand. The colonization fleet dives into the universe and takes everything not bolted down, planting my flag in every piece of dirt they can find. While this is happening, I'm researching like a madman. Everything from the civilian tree goes first, mainly mining and expansion assistance. I'm able to colonize any world by about minute fifteen, and do so with abandon.
While the colonization fleet is away, I build up the battle fleet. More capitol ships, hundreds of frigates and cruisers, and a Titan being build in the corner of my home gravity well. My scouts find pirates, enemy players/AI, and all number of worlds. I take everything I can get my hands on and build up more gauss cannons than I can count. If anyone pokes around my systems, they don't leave alive.
Finally, I run into worlds that I can't take with my small colonization fleet. So I pull them back. The enemy mounts an assault, thinking me weak. I let them come, break their backs on my frontier worlds, cracking their armor on my defenses.
Then the battle fleet arrives.
I destroy their assault force in moments, my capitol ships shredding anything in their path, Titan mysteriously AWOL, and drive them back four systems or more before they manage to scramble up a defense. When they do, my Titan and its auxilery fleet arrive...behind them. On a world where they have few defenders, she enters the fray, and ignores the first three worlds completely. Her goal is the capitol. In a desperate attempt to keep their forces strong enough to fight me, the enemy pulls everyone back to the capitol system, and mounts their last stand.
I leave no survivors.
This game is amazing. A little slow, as it usually takes me an hour just to get comfortable with my standing, but oh so very addicting. The above situations happen often, rather than once or twice in a while, and though it does take a long time to build up your fleet, seeing it warp in out of nowhere is a warming experience I've yet to feel elsewhere. Endless space scratched the itch to rule an empire. This scratched my itch to conquer the galaxy.

Rebel Galaxy looks like an odd game to start with. How many games are there that have you flying around space, buying, selling, mining or stealing? I have played quite a few over the years. Most of them have you moving around in 3 dimensions; after all, space is not flat plane is it? So, why does Rebel Galaxy use two dimensions for you as the player but 3 for many of your opponents? Surely this is silly?
Surprisingly I have to say no, it actually works really well. I am around 4 hours into the game now and I must say that I like the battle mechanics and the flight from one part of the system to another is pretty smooth. (Could be a bit quicker possibly but that is just me.
So, what is it that I enjoy? Raking your opponent from stem to stern using broadsides in space is cool. This is why the game is on a flat plane. By using your main weapons as broadsides it would not work if you had to roll to bring your guns to bear.
The ecomomic system seems to work well, I like the way that when buying or selling you can see the average price in the sector. This will reduce the need for notes or trying to remember how much you paid for nuts and bolts, yes this is a real cargo. I like the idea of cola being illegal btw :-)
I think that this is one that I will be playing for some time. It has been on my wish list since its release and in the sale I thought I would go for it. Now, the big question is would I have still enjoyed it at full price? So far I have to say yes I would have. There are loads of missions to do, a storyline to follow or if you just want to blow up asteroids for ore you can. There are loads floating round.
You can configure your weaponry easily, with plenty of ships to fly , I haven't seen any dodgy models yet, all looking rather swish.
So, go and buy the game if you like flying in space, blowing things up, mining or finding lost relatives. You won't regret it.

The underrated/ black sheep of the Bioshock franchise....... or what critcs say. I personally find Bioshock 2 to be a worthy predecessor of the original game. Sure the WYK element, story, and philosophical elements that revolve around the first game could be considered more noteworthy; however, this is not to say the elements in Bioshock 2 are bad either, just different. The elements of love, tyranny, conditioning/brainwashing, condratictory philosophy, communism, and envy are plainly seen and well accomodated throughout the single player campaign.  The length -- even though shorter -- I say was more satisfactory then the original game. The first game suffered from the falling action after the first climax (no spoilers), but the falling action (Olypian Heights/Apollo Square) I thought was the low point of the game, which made it feel a little lengthy. Overall, I prefer this equally to Bioshock Infinite (Infinite, even though having equally amazing mechanics, suffered from the time line plot point {Linear timeline, yet multidimensional} which did not sit well until the dlcs made up for that shortcoming).
Multiplayer: It is fun, if you can round up a group to play with.  Many people find the whole idea of Bioshock multiplayer to an "unecessary" component, but I find the multiplayer gives a more personal touch to the civil war of 1959.  So if you can gather the people, it is an interesting experience of its own.
Minerva's Den:  This is a worthwhile DLC. Putting more backstory into a different area of rapture, while adding a few new weapons, plasmids, and a new Big Daddy (Lancer).  If you were not satisfied with the length of Bioshock 2, this will be the icing on the cake to fulfill satisfaction.

The Dream Machine is an episodic point-and-click adventure game about a guy who has to kill a machine which subsists by sticking its tentacles into peoples' dreams and feeding off of them. This is actually what happens.
Chapter 1 of the game serves as an introduction to the main character, Victor Neff, his wife Alicia, and the new apartment building they have moved into. The Neffs are pretty endearing characters — they can be snarky, but they also show genuine affection for each other, and I like Victor's haircut a lot, if it could even be called that. There's also a lot of flavor text in this opening chapter; I'd go as far as to say there's a unique line of dialogue for every incorrect item use and attempted combination, and the majority of them are quite funny. The chapter ends at a rather odd point (I'd describe it as a cliffhanger with no dramatic tension) but since the first two chapters come bundled together it's not too bad.
Chapter 2 introduces the Dream Machine itself, its background, and the dream diving mechanic I presume will be used throughout the rest of the game. To be honest, the dream explored in this chapter is kind of dull — it's a few screens of cloudy rockland that, while soothing, isn't as fantastical as I'd like to see in a game that focuses on dreams.
Chapter 3's dream takes place on a flying cruise filled with tons of Victor clones. While the concept sounds interesting, it isn't really utilized to any extent outside of one puzzle, making it seem more like a cost-cutting measure than anything else. This is also the chapter where I started to feel that the unique flavor text was forgotten or cut for time, because most of the lines for incorrect actions were along the lines of "that won't work." It was rather disappointing to try out quirky combinations only for the game to not care as much as it used to. At the very least the ending was fairly touching. This is the last chapter I finished thus far.
The clay-cardboard aesthetic the game uses is quite pleasing to the eyes. The environments are modeled with intricate detail and the character models are what I'd call creepy but cute. The sound design is great too; for the most part the music in the game is atmospheric background noise I'd certainly call "dreamlike," but there are also musical stings at times which really add emotion to events like turning a book page to discover something terrifying. While there isn't any voice acting, there is a text-to-speech option that can be turned on which uses the exact same voice as the one for Mumble and I personally find that hilarious.
Unfortunately, it must be said that the engine this game uses is terrible. The Dream Machine runs on Adobe Flash, which has been used for other games like The Binding of Isaac and Machinarium, but it simply does not work as well here. Character animations, instead of being made of sprites like in those games, appear to be made from video clips that, at least on my end, take like a half-second to load each time they happen. This includes basic actions like walking, so every time I clicked to make Victor move the game would hang for a moment before he trots off. It just doesn't seem as smooth as it could be, and it doesn't help that on several occasions the game bugged out and failed to load the next scene, causing me to have to quit out and reload to around five minutes earlier.
Overall, I lean slightly in favor of recommending this game, at least for now. It can be plodding at times, and the puzzles can be both too simple and too obtuse, but I like the environments and the plot has kept me interested enough to see how it will end.

The first one already was a strong experience; but I think I can say this second opus really deserves more love. Ok, so I really enjoyed the previous BioShock. It was an immersive, tense experience with the only things holding it back being some lackluster weapons and some weird physics animations that were framelocked. Going into BioShock 2 I had high hopes, considering I had heard that it was pretty mutch as good as the original. And starting off, it was just as good. The atmosphere was there, rapture was back, and I was ready to sink my weekend into playing this game non-stop. But halfway in, something truly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ happened.
The game hard crashed on me, sending me back to the desktop without any warning or errors. I quickly relaunched the game, just to find that the game had not autosaved once, and that I had to start the entire campaign over again. I looked the issiue up online, but even after turning off DX10 the game was still extremely unstable, and every time i would fprget to quicksave, the game would hardcrash and force me to play through 30 to 1 hour long sections I had already completed.
Yes, the game does have an autosave feature, but as far as I know, this only kicks in when you're switching chapters (wich means it will save about every hour). After this had happened 3 times, I gave up. I lost the motivation to keep on playing. Now, I know that you can blame me for not quicksaving that often, but honestly, any game should have a robust autosave system in place (plus the ability to quicksave), in case of hard crashes and players not used to constantly quicksaving. I'm sure there's a good game somewhere here, but it denies me from truly finding out.
For me, the experience was just totally ruined by the lackluster autosaves and the awful stability. When I had my first experience with BS2, I was running WIN 8. I'm going to give the game another shot with WIN 10, but until then I'll leave BS2 with a negative rating.

This is Mount and Blade in space.  If you're sick of empty "sand box" games like Far Cry, Fallout 4 or Elite Dangerous (so glad I bought this and not Elite Dangerous,) this is your game.  You are one tiny ship in a giant galaxy of space stations, capital ships, freighters and stellar phenomenon.  You can be a pirate, smuggler, trader, police officer, bounty hunter or eventually, shipping magnate and fleet commander.  As is the case in a real sand box game, you're thrown into a well-thought out, functional world and you do whatever you feel like.  Apparently the game sucked when it came out (all that's fixed) and franchise loyalists don't like some of the decisions the developers made.  I didn't play it three years ago and I've never even heard of the franchise before; as someone with no previous bias towards this game I HIGHLY suggest it.  Oh and the dogfighting is a blast.  The world they've created is so awesome, I almost forgot to mention how great the combat is.
Conclusion: Forget Elite Dangerous; this is the sand box space sim where stuff actually happens.

This war of mine is a fantastic game that I adore, a lot, I could say positive things about it almost all day long. The only thing that bugs me is just that.. Bugs, there's a few that drive me insane, such as some sections of ceiling that you can shoot through and be shot through when it's obvious that you shouldn't be able to do that. Sometimes when you play this game you require to move quickly because you've been spotted, or something along those lines, but you can't react as quickly as you want because interacting with objects and spots are rather finicky.. Time and time again I am killed because I click the shadows and realize that I can't duck in there, I don't care if Batman's bulky self is hiding in there, he better fit for two because I'm not gettin' shot for it.
That bit of sillyness aside, this game has its ups and downs, but another 'review' about this game mentioned how there was no way for the survivors to be the bad guy without being severely punished by this... I agree, there are times when I want to play the bad guy just for the sake of being the bad guy, but when all of my survivors kill theirselves or go into a state of depression to where they won't do a damn thing just because some crazy punk ran outside and punched me in the face, I returned the favor with a shotgun shell to cure his headache. However, I don't believe anything that's in the game should be changed, no no, everything right now I believe is fantastic! Don't change what you have, add to what you have.
I love this game but I'm teetering on giving it a good or a bad review just because there is not too much to it. This game doesn't have too much replayability aside from having other survivors in different situations, which is a good tactic to convince players to try each of them. All of my thoughts came down to the newest 'DLC'.. I was disappointed, now, don't get me wrong about this and think I'm being selfish.. But bear with me here, I understand it was for charity, but surely anyone of the people reading probably got a bit hyper over seeing some DLC being added to the game, but was probably abit disappointed it was only to add collectibles to it.. Yes, people will still buy it for the sake of donating, but if you're just wanting donations for all of this then why not make a proper DLC to hook in more players?
More content being added to a great game will make it bigger, and the bigger it is makes it easier to see.. Attracting more people and bringing in more profit that the company can do whatever with. Adding more locations or different events would be great, maybe seeing some of said events around your safehouse would be fantastic, adding more weaponry and perhaps a more juryrigged look to a lot of items would be nice as well. The experienced player will see a place filled with military/militia members and eyeball it like a candy store, mainly because people like myself can walk in with a knife and then walk out with an entire backpack filled with guns and ammunition, even body armor and helmets if they have it.. This will very easilly make the player win the game so long as they continue to stay careful about their spending of such items.
Why not add some new survivors to the pool? Criminals would be a great addition, if somebody wants to have a group of unruly jerks that go around and take what they want.. Well.. That would add a good bit of excitement, they'd get greedy and be more aggressive as they kill and steal, but at the same time they would be probably taking more damage and using more of their materials, perhaps losing survivors in the process. Just as much, if you have criminals that means they'd lie as well, they wouldn't share how they got their materials unlike your other survivors that will feel guilty... This would mean no depression for the group, however, it could mean more raiders to come and punish them more often, bigger groups with better equipment knocking at your door for each place you've stolen from and people you've killed. Hell, being a criminal and thinking you can take whatever you want it would probably also mean they'd steal from their own group, like Arica.
I've got plenty of things in mind that I'd love to discuss, but if you read it this far you'll know that I've been typing a good amount already.. I give 'This War of Mine' a 9/10, it's almost perfect but it could use just a bit more to it, via more DLC or just overall adding out of the kindness of their heart.. I love this game but I would love to see more people play it and more people enjoy things, have different strategies to deal with seperate situations, have a feel of being able to customize your pre-determined group. Since there's no voicing and it's all text, I would also enjoy perhaps adding a customize your own survivor feature, put yourself into the war zone with flaws and traits of your own, backstory of why you're stuck in the middle of that war and what you were doing beforehand!
This is the end of my review, I'd indeed recommend you try it, but don't get too hooked into it since there probably won't be too much, if anything, added to it.
Do not buy it.
