In the first part of this review I'll try to confront the game's infamy and  determine whether or not the reality of the product fits the hysteria. The second part will analyse the product as a game, whether it's something you can enjoy, if it's easy to jump in and if it's fun (however that sounds). Lastly, I'll give my opinion whether or not the game is worth buying.
<<<hate towards Hatred>>>
The whole sh__tstorm that ensued before the release of this game was based on the assumption that Hatred is unnecessarily violent and sexist and what not. There were also concerns that if you play it, you will become a psycho, and that it's basically a terrorist simulator. Having played it for a while, my impressions are rather neutral in general. Yes, the game is very violent, but that is precisely its premise - just go out there and kill as many as you can in a rather vast variety of ways: stabbing, shooting, smashing, exploding, setting on fire, driving over - it's all there. The thing is the perspective is so distanced and the colours so monochromatic, you don't really see that much of the violence. The details elude you even during the infamous execution scenes - there is just a bit more of blackness added to the character model. Playing Hatred I had the impression that I'm playing one of these browser survival games, in which you see your character from above, run around and shoot various things that come in waves, only difference being that here the perspective is isometric. To be honest, Postal 1 was more violent - there at least you could see what you were killing. Yes, there is violence here, but paradoxically it's not really that violent.
What about sexism? Sigh. The antagonist hates everyone equally, regardless of their sex, race or any other distinguishing factors. Everyone gets a bullet, everyone is insulted equally. The socio-political movements that weaved this narrative should actually champion this game as an example of a perfect equality in the industry. Alas, as we all know, some people always see only what they want to see, and they can see it everywhere if they really squint their eyes. No mysoginy, sexism or woman-hating here - just the general misanthropy. Deal with it.
OK, so what about the game corrupting your brain and turning you into a terrorist? Well, unless you're a complete idiot who is incapable of distinguishing reality from fiction, Hatred maybe would tickle you the wriong way. But then again, if that's the case, then it's not the game's fault - you were a nutjob even before launching the title. Again, the violence in this game is really ineffectual in its display. As long as you don't let your kids play it, it will do no harm. The again... Heck, the games I played as a kid were more graphic than this and they didn't warp my defenseless young mind, so I doubt Hatred would either. Ok, and terrorist simulator? O lol. Ok, let's be frank - action movies will teach you more about terrorism than this game. There is no tutorial how to build a bomb, or hijack a plane, or how to plan an attack on a train station. Heck, it doesn't even show you how to operate a gun - you just click your mouse, that's it. It's unbelievable what accusations can people make based on two short trailers...
To sum up this part, the game's violence is in my opinion completely impotent. You just run around a very dark area and shoot at characters you can barely identify as human beings. There is a certain aesthetic to all the darkness, and it is safe to assume that's what the devs were going for - they wanted a dark game that sets a certain tone and ambience for the gameplay. Seriously, if you have as much as two working brain cells, Hatred will not affect you more than your regular evening news report.
<<<gameplay>>>
If you have played any isometric games, then you probably know what to expect in terms of action. This particular perspective generally works for the game, but can also be a pain in the butt at times, especially when your targets hide behind a back wall of a building, and you have to press alt to highlight them. However, you don't have much problems in determining where your own character is. Although the game was patched a couple of times already, the controls borderline physical pain, especially when trying to jump over fences and/or entering or leaving rooms/ buildings. The crosshair could also have been a little bit more visible. Sometimes in the heat of the firefight it is rather difficult to determine where you're shooting and which direction you're facing. Still, the general control premise is very easy and intuitive: WSAD for movement, point and click for shooting - the problem is that the character tends not to do what you want him to do because of bad system of environmental interaction.
Also, the respawn system of you and the military forces can annoy you to no end at times: Imagine having just spent 2 hours on clearing a level, and then you die 2 metres away from the exit, because a fresh wave of heavily armoured jarheads arrived and you were out of respawns - yep, that's starting all over again. Awesome, right?
What about fun then? Well, in my opinion the game is a no-brainer, which is not necessarily a bad thing. There is no plot to speak of: one day you just leave your house and start shooting everything that moves. It's very impersonal and lacks any emotional drive - that's kind of an irony, minding what the game's title is. To be honest, there is nothing to make you excited and want to keep playing. There is the main quest and there are side quests, but both kinds are simply "go there and kill X number of residents." I played it basically to kill time. Get it? Because the game is about killing, haha. Nevermind.
Ok, I can see myself launching Hatred to let go some steam (although I can think of a good number of other games that are way better for this purpose), but seeing myself doing a weekend marathon? No, not really. The game lacks that extra something that would make you want to continue and finish it throughout consecutive evenings of playing. No plot, no context, no real challenges or competitive incentives, not even the titular hatred to be felt -  just shadow-concealed carnage. Fun is very situational and mood-dependent.
<<<summary>>>
Would I recommend the game? Sure, why not. The main reason the game was made in the first place was not ot push the envelope in the industry, but to give the proverbial finger to the powers that be and the rampant political correctness they bring wherever they reach. To their credit, the devs never made any secret out of it and never tried to convince you they are doing something ground-breaking. Also, the game isn't really that expensive, and in my opinion, the price fits the quality. It is possible that you could have a different experience with Hatred than me, especially if the honest point and shoot gameplay is what you need to unwind. In that case, you will thoroughly enjoy the game. Otherwise, this can be a title you will come back to once a week for 15 mins or so, just to kill time before the next episode of your favourite series finishes downloading. Either way, I don't think the money would be wasted. Plus, if you support freedom of expression in the industry, by buying the game you are supporting people who had the guts to say "no" to the ever increasing attempts at censorship in video games. If anything, that's a good thing to do, right?

So I've played through one round of C:BE and can't say I'm interested in jumping back in for another go. All the way through I didn't feel like I was accomplishing anything, with no indication I was advancing in tech except for occassionally receiving a prompt to select an upgrade for some units that I had never needed to look at.
It lacks the structure that I've been used to in Civ IV and Civ V, being thrown into this wide sprawling tech-web was very confronting and I had no idea what seemed like a logic route to follow, ending up just randomly selecting things that opened up opportunities to grab Harmony experience.
The GUI was something entirely different to experience and quite often I was clicking the wrong tab. As I've said, coming from the previous two Civ games makes this change up awkward to get used to, but its functional so I guess its fine.
Now, the aliens had me confused for a long time. I hadn't seen any information telling me that I could choose to be passive or aggressive towards the aliens, as in the beginning I was being attacked for seeming no reason. This was until I learned from trial and error that the aliens didn't seem to be aggressive so long as you were more than 2 tiles away from a nest. Fair enough, that seems logical but it would have been nice to be told "Keep your units away from nests 'cause the aliens don't like you near them"
Overall, compared to the massive amount of content in Civ V, go and pick up the complete version of that instead. MAYBE in several months time and some expansions come out for C:BE it might be worth it, but right now I could not recommend this to anyone.

The game's not very engaging from what I've played:
The black and white aesthetic with the occasional red object is neat at first, but it quickly gets monotone and tiring.
There's very little in the way of sound design, and what is there sets up the mood well, but it's a case that quality just doesn't supersede quantity.
Some experimentation is needed to figure out what all the buttons do on the pad. Figuring out how to switch weapons was especially polarizing, seeing as how you don't get a radial menu or anything, but instead a single button (LB) cycles through all three weapons at once. Otherwise the controls are fine.
The interface feels very clunky in some spots. Cycling through fast-travel locations is a major pain, and so is navigating your equipment menu. The minimalistic interface design also has the unintended side-effect of making the whole thing seem very budget-y and not very well implemented.
The combat is a bit one-sided. At first it feels quite visceral, with enemies dashing towards you as you try to put one more arrow into them, and the game does have a neat mechanic in masking the noise you make when a gust of wind hits your surroundings. However, the combat just doesn't feel deep enough: you get a handful of ranged weapons which all perform very similarly to one another, a short-range tomahawk which you can throw for massive damage, and a few bombs which help to thin out crowds. Enemy patterns don't differ so much from one another that you need to adopt any different strategies: aggro enemies in front of you, wiggle left and right repeatedly to dogde projectiles, fire projectile of your choice back at them. The odd inclusion of an option to drop your equipment when you die is meant to make combat more tense, but it doesn't add anything meaningful to it in my opinion, it just makes it more annoying.
I couldn't figure out how to attach myself to the story in any point. You're a shipwreck making his way inland where Englishmen and Spaniards have set up camp and constantly have skirmishes with indians and each other. Death permeates all of the camps however, and after digging around a bit, you gain the ability to talk to the wraiths of the people that lived in the region, and piece together how they died. Reading by this narrative ultimately isn't really interesting: while the backstory of these people is well-written and often pretty gruesome, the medium by which they are delivered falls short: there are no cutscenes and no voice acting, leaving you with a pretty paltry dialogue box and your imagination (nothing wrong with that, it's just not for me).
There's also a lady that follows you around in the camps, the only other apparent living human you can talk to. You can give her things and talk about the apparitions you're seeing, but she doesn't share in your ability to see the dead or the strange ashen figures scattered throughout the camp. Making you question the main character's sanity like that is a legitimately cool plot point, but the lady herself is hardly engaging: like the other characters, she lacks a voice actor, and any other kind of different idle animations or behavior. Her dialogue isn't even that engaging to make you care for her all that much, and giving her gifts, if it did anything at all after, passed right by my head.
There's just not that much great to say about the game. I gave it a few hours, and made it to the third map you can get to. Maybe that's not enough time, but the lack of sound assets, strange choice of visual style, clunky interface and simplistic (unnecessary even?) combat meant that I didn't want to give it any more of a chance for it to grab me. It asks for a fair price though, so maybe someone with a bit more patience can find enjoyment in it.

I have to question Word Rescue both as an educational tool and as entertainment. It is way too easy to get into an unwinnable scenario since the goo used to incapacitate monsters does not reset on death, becomeing an exercise in frustration as the player can collect a bucket of goo and either intentionally die to respawn with a full meter and an extra bucket to pick up, or, more often than not, use up all of the goo and die to respawn with nothing. It is especially frustrating in episodes two and three as they usually spawn the player surrounded by monsters and mostly consist of very narrow hallways where it is impossible to dodge them to get to a bucket powerup. The game also likes to drop monsters from the sky for some unfair, unavoidable deaths, further exacerbating the problem.
When the amount of goo is not a problem, the game devolves into a repetitive exercise in running from one end of the level to the other and back, as players are tasked with matching very basic, one or two syllable, words to their corresponding pictures, which in many cases are either blatantly wrong (like matching a picture of a snowman to the word 'snow') or hard to identify due to graphical limitations of the time. As a result, anyone young enough to not be familiar with words like 'pen' and 'cup', will likely find the game far too difficult and unforgiving, and anyone old enough to survive the monsters will likely be bored out of their mind.
So uh... ♥♥♥♥ing skeletons, eh?

Betrayer is a game made by Blackpowder Games, a new development studio made up of members split off from Monolith Games, the creator of many of my favorite games. I don't know who went where in the split between what now remains of Monolith and what is now Blackpowder Games, but considering one group went on to make a creative and unique game called Betrayer and the other went on to mash together Ubisoft's franchise catalogue into one big homogenized Lord of the Rings game, I think it's somewhat clear to me which group to look forward to in the future.
Betrayer is largely a game about exploration, and the game's design works fairly well towards it. The game's art style is mostly monochrome (though you can change the color settings in the options if you're a big loser baby), which both gives it a really great look and also serves a gameplay purpose by using color to define things like enemies and items. Sound is also used pretty extensively, serving as your compass as well as providing positional audio cues to help you find enemies before they find you, so headphones are recommended. The combat and story are also well-executed, and finding the stories of each of the members of the settlement is a lot of fun.
However, one thing I will note is that the game has changed since I played it in Early Access. In the original releases, you were left to navigate on your own, using the map like you would a real one and navigating using landmarks and sounds. This worked really well in my opinion, and added a lot immersion to the exploration that made it feel like you were navigating a world on your own and not just following a dot on the map. But at some point along the line they updated the game, adding markers to the map that display both your position and the position of almost everything there is to find in the game. This isn't a deal-breaker, as these can all be disabled in the options, but I want to mention them because I would very highly recommend doing so as soon as you get the opportunity to. Leaving the map markers on is practically the equivalent of playing the game with a walkthrough, and I really wish they had defaulted them to being off so that they didn't encourage new players to play the game with them on and just follow the dots.

Rebel Galaxy is a lot like a shot of cheap whisky in a pretty glass, served in a grungy southern biker bar.  It looks attractive, and it gets the job done, but it has some glaring faults and limitations and can burn like hell going down.
One of the often mentioned features is the sound track, I thought it was pretty cool at first, but after 2 hours I turned down  the music to 10%.  It certainly sets the mood, and establishes Rebel Galaxy as a "Firefly inspired" space western.  however it gets repetative, and is intrusive.  After you hear the title song five or six times in a row blasting in your ears, it gets old quick.
I am susceptable to ear worms, and it's going to take a few days to get this out of my brain completely.   That isn't a good thing for me.
It's not that the songs are bad, by no means, the artist who wrote them is talented, and I like the sound track.  But too much of a good thing can be frustratingly iritating.
Other reviewers have done a good job talking about the games features and gameplay style.   comparing it to the ship combat from black flag, and I think that is a spot on comparison.   It really feels like someone wrote a naval combat engine, and halfway through decided to make it a space game instead.  This could literally have been a WWII naval simulator or something and it would have been the same game.   Just with water and islands instead of space and planets.
To put it bluntly, this is an Naval combat arcade game with a space skin.  Despite this, the game works, it works stylistically, and the gameplay is satisfying enough to keep you playing.
The game is only 20$ full price (I got it for 13$ on sale), and it's worth even full price, but only if you like the genre.
Buy this game if:
You like the Vibe of Firefly or Serenity.
Like Arcade shooters in space.
Liked the naval combat of Black flag.
Like the standard Trader/Bountyhunter/Pirate/miner kind of space game, and don't mind the emphasis being on combat.
Like the gritty southern/blues/country soundtrack.
Like the graphics.
Don't mind being locked into a 2d playing field, even when smaller ships can still fly 3d.  All around you.
Want to control a whole ship using even just a console controller (works very well).
You Like Single Player games.
Don't buy the game if:
You strongly prefer Simulators/realism to arcade style games.
You prefer complex controls, and tactics (you can pretty much phone in tactics in this game).
You are tired of the Trade/fight/mine paradigm of space sandbox gaming.
You hate any form of country music.
You Hated Firefly.
You expect a long complex story with tons of twists and turns (I like it so far, and the voice acting and dialogue trees are fun... but it's not Mass Effect for example.).
Think a "2d limited" space game is too immersion breaking.
Prefer multiplayer.
Final verdict:  If you like the genre, or can get past the burning in your throat, you will enjoy this offering.  It is a good game to unwind with, the fights satisfying the visuals pleasing.
Like that cheap shot of whisky, it may not have the smooth quality of a higher priced drink, but it will still do the job, and if you drink enough of it, you won't even notice the burning in your throat anymore.
Unlike that shot of whisky, this shouldn't give you a hangover, and won't ruin your marraige.
Anyway, I have no regrets, it's a fun game, worth the full price unless you fall in the "don't buy it" category. ).

Magic Duels is fun in many aspects, but lacking in several others. Especially when compared to previous versions.
The story mode in the current game is lacking when compared to last year's version. The story this time is quite short, and doesn't give as much opportunity to explore decks as the deck you use is quite prescriptive.
Further, I will add that the removal of the chat system is a poor change. I enjoyed chatting with components and learned a lot about the game, decks, and just generally liked the social interaction. I'd recommend putting this element back.
Further, changing to a system where the pack purchasing for the game is very dissimilar from real-life pack purchasing is not a positive change. Getting six cards per booster doesn't feel worth it, and the fact that your collection can be capped when you haven't even managed to gather four of a given card is pretty woeful. It's very different from playing the game with physical cards in that regard.
Anyhow, I do enjoy online play and hope others do too. Just don't expect this to replace the full experience of playing MtG with real people in reality. The removal of chat effectively killed that.

I bought this game when it came out and immediately shelved it.  The game was broken and not ready for public release.  I didn't ask for a refund, I like all of Egosoft's X games and I knew they would support this or die trying.  I decided to wait a few years for patches and DLC releases for the game to get more "complete".  I am writing this review as the game stands now in April 2016, with Home of Light and Teladi DLC installed.
I am still super angry that I cannot fly other ships.  X games always allowed you to pick your poison and fly whatever you wanted, or fly around in your space suit if you dared.  This game forces you to drive the Albion Skunk, an M3 with M4 weaponry and M7 missile compatibility.  I would prefer to drive a powerful M6 or hard hitting M3.  I believe the reason for not allowing you to change ships is because they added walk around mode while docked in large ships or stations.
Walk around mode is stupid.  Even on release, the voices were repetative, and everything about walking around the station was like some stupid mini game that wasted my time.  The scenes become repetative as well.  To make matters worse, your ship, the Skunk, can still be blown up in space wherever you entered the station from while you are walking around and chit chatting.  You can get a game over if you are attacked while docked in a space station...
Egosoft changed the stations up.  Each station can be upgraded and extended with different components, nice.  However, every station has the same docking location types for your ship, IE bar, administration section, engineer wrench, and bullet thingy.  They all pretty much look the same on the inside, and specialists can be found in their corresponding section, or anywhere really.  It is random.
The sheer size of the stations makes it a huge problem if you want to talk to the station in general and get the low down on trade.  Trading is also handled by scripted AI and command execution.  No longer can you drive a freighter yourself and play the lowly merchant.  You have to rely completely on your AI pilots.  You are stuck with the Albion Skunk and that stupid co-pilot.
AI is horrible.  Auto pilot is bad, so bad that they added the "Auto Pilot Epic Failure" voice error in the game.  Path finding is bad.  Ships get stuck on stations during combat.  You can actually fly into a station and clip inside and get stuck.  Combat is slow and pointless.  You might as well sit still and snipe.
UI is clunky and it takes forever to assign ships or give orders.  I found out how to group assign and broadcast orders to multiple ships, but it is still clunky and takes time to execute the proper orders.  Fighters are useless.  AI fighters will just die.  Your transport ships will also randomly break down and not repair themselves.
The story is OK.  X games always had terrible voice acting and the story was long winded and boring.  I always just played sand box mode and eventually killed everything in my way.  The story in X Rebirth, however, isn't all that bad, but it is highly unbelievable at times.  I would have spaced my co-pilot the first chance I got.  Though, I like the story in general, even though I can't believe how the main character just stumbles in to being main hero all the time.  The writers portray human greed a lot, but seem to have a disconnect when it comes to Ren Otani's reactions to everything that Yisha gets him in to.  Hell, I don't know why Ren wants to keep the girl in his ship, she literally ruins his life.
The story missions also take forever.  Trading isn't fast, it was slow in X3, and even slower now that the ships have to travel farther and line up on even larger stations.  It is a slow process building up your station to meet campaign objective goals.  The stations that make your components are usually sold out or in the hands of your enemy.  In fact, building the stations for campaign missions nearly ruined the game for me.  You have to raid PMC ships to get what you need, and that takes time.  The rest of the missions are simple, go here, escort this, kill that.  I lost my entire fleet on a PMC boss fight only to find out that the mission was supposed to lose...total burn.
Level design is♥♥♥♥♥♥ and story is meh.  The space highways are stupid, and the music that plays while you are in them is garbage loops.
Fleet combat is also stupid.  It is nearly impossible to tell your ships how to target.  They also don't care about formations or tactics.  Though, X games always had this problem and were usually fixed with mods.  X Reunion, on the other hand, is so bad of a game, that nobody even cared to make the mods to fix this aspect of the game.  You essentially have to zerg your opponent with destroyers to win a major conflict.
Pros: graphics are better than X3.  Sound is similar if not slightly better.
Cons: Only flying the skunk is a low blow.  If I ever meet the Egosoft decision maker that decided this was a good idea, I have choice words for that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  That literally ruins replayability for me.  I hate the Albion Skunk, it is a terrible ship.  Just about everything else in this game is worse than X3.
You cannot build station production loops anymore.
Other: If you are a diehard X fan, sandbox mode isn't too bad.  However, it will probably get boring quickly because all of the cool management features from mods in X3 are not available in Xrebirth.

Short Summary: Gat Out of Hell is basically a short re-skin of Saints Row 4. Instead of exploiting glitches in a “Matrix” style computer world, you are now using magical powers in Hell. Gameplay-wise, almost everything is the same, but with a different look. For example you still super jump and fly around, but now you have wings. You still blast enemies with (almost) the same powers, but now they’re “magic” powers. If you liked Saints Row 4, you should enjoy Gat Out of Hell.
The story picks up shortly after the end of Saints Row 4, so Spoiler Alert. You play Johnny Gat or Kinzie (you can change between the 2 characters easily) as you explore Hell looking for the Boss (your character in the other Saints Row games). In order to rescue the Boss, you’ll need to cause as much trouble as you can, kind of like the “chaos” meter in Just Cause 2, and eventually confront and defeat Satan. Throughout your adventures you’ll run into some of your old friends from the previous games, after all the Earth was destroyed during Saints Row 4, so everyone’s in Hell.
As mentioned earlier, the gameplay is practically identical to Saints Row 4. If you’ve just finished that game, you can move right into Gat Out of Hell recognizing most of the controls. You play Johnny or Kinzie in Third Person Perspective, running or flying around an open world “city” causing mayhem. Since you can super speed and fly, there’s really no need to highjack cars anymore, and in fact there are only a few types of vehicles for you to steal (no more airplanes, helicopters, etc.). The story campaign for Gat Out of Hell is also much shorter than the previous games (maybe it was meant to be a Saints Row 4 DLC?) so most of your time will be spent on “diversions” like mini-games, stealing armored cars, or searching for the 7 Deadly Weapons (powerful weapons based on the 7 Deadly Sins).
You should play Gat Out of Hell if:
+You liked Saints Row 4 and want more of the same.
+You like super speed running/flying around looking for collectibles. There are a ton scattered around Hell.
+You’re looking for an easy game. If you’re getting overwhelmed in combat, just run away and hide to heal up. None of the enemies can run/fly as fast as you.
You should NOT play Gat Out of Hell if:
-You’re looking for something different from the previous Saints Row game. Like I said, gameplay is practically identical.
-You’re looking for a long game. The only reason I played this game so long is for the “spend 20 hours in Hell” Steam achievement. You can probably beat the campaign in 6-7 hours.
-You don’t like “grinding” in games. Compared to previous Saints Row games, it feels like in Gat Out of Hell you earn money at a much slower rate (used to upgrade your guns). This means you’ll be running around with weak weapons for a long time. You no longer have automatic income like in Saints Row 3 and 4, you actually need to go out and smash up some goons for meager wages.
Overall, I liked all the Saints Row games I’ve played (3, 4, and GOoH). There’s a lot of adult humor, cursing, and badassery throughout the games so it’s not for kids, but that shouldn’t surprise you. Bonus, this game is often under $5 on sale nowadays.

This war of mine is a fantastic game that I adore, a lot, I could say positive things about it almost all day long. The only thing that bugs me is just that.. Bugs, there's a few that drive me insane, such as some sections of ceiling that you can shoot through and be shot through when it's obvious that you shouldn't be able to do that. Sometimes when you play this game you require to move quickly because you've been spotted, or something along those lines, but you can't react as quickly as you want because interacting with objects and spots are rather finicky.. Time and time again I am killed because I click the shadows and realize that I can't duck in there, I don't care if Batman's bulky self is hiding in there, he better fit for two because I'm not gettin' shot for it.
That bit of sillyness aside, this game has its ups and downs, but another 'review' about this game mentioned how there was no way for the survivors to be the bad guy without being severely punished by this... I agree, there are times when I want to play the bad guy just for the sake of being the bad guy, but when all of my survivors kill theirselves or go into a state of depression to where they won't do a damn thing just because some crazy punk ran outside and punched me in the face, I returned the favor with a shotgun shell to cure his headache. However, I don't believe anything that's in the game should be changed, no no, everything right now I believe is fantastic! Don't change what you have, add to what you have.
I love this game but I'm teetering on giving it a good or a bad review just because there is not too much to it. This game doesn't have too much replayability aside from having other survivors in different situations, which is a good tactic to convince players to try each of them. All of my thoughts came down to the newest 'DLC'.. I was disappointed, now, don't get me wrong about this and think I'm being selfish.. But bear with me here, I understand it was for charity, but surely anyone of the people reading probably got a bit hyper over seeing some DLC being added to the game, but was probably abit disappointed it was only to add collectibles to it.. Yes, people will still buy it for the sake of donating, but if you're just wanting donations for all of this then why not make a proper DLC to hook in more players?
More content being added to a great game will make it bigger, and the bigger it is makes it easier to see.. Attracting more people and bringing in more profit that the company can do whatever with. Adding more locations or different events would be great, maybe seeing some of said events around your safehouse would be fantastic, adding more weaponry and perhaps a more juryrigged look to a lot of items would be nice as well. The experienced player will see a place filled with military/militia members and eyeball it like a candy store, mainly because people like myself can walk in with a knife and then walk out with an entire backpack filled with guns and ammunition, even body armor and helmets if they have it.. This will very easilly make the player win the game so long as they continue to stay careful about their spending of such items.
Why not add some new survivors to the pool? Criminals would be a great addition, if somebody wants to have a group of unruly jerks that go around and take what they want.. Well.. That would add a good bit of excitement, they'd get greedy and be more aggressive as they kill and steal, but at the same time they would be probably taking more damage and using more of their materials, perhaps losing survivors in the process. Just as much, if you have criminals that means they'd lie as well, they wouldn't share how they got their materials unlike your other survivors that will feel guilty... This would mean no depression for the group, however, it could mean more raiders to come and punish them more often, bigger groups with better equipment knocking at your door for each place you've stolen from and people you've killed. Hell, being a criminal and thinking you can take whatever you want it would probably also mean they'd steal from their own group, like Arica.
I've got plenty of things in mind that I'd love to discuss, but if you read it this far you'll know that I've been typing a good amount already.. I give 'This War of Mine' a 9/10, it's almost perfect but it could use just a bit more to it, via more DLC or just overall adding out of the kindness of their heart.. I love this game but I would love to see more people play it and more people enjoy things, have different strategies to deal with seperate situations, have a feel of being able to customize your pre-determined group. Since there's no voicing and it's all text, I would also enjoy perhaps adding a customize your own survivor feature, put yourself into the war zone with flaws and traits of your own, backstory of why you're stuck in the middle of that war and what you were doing beforehand!
This is the end of my review, I'd indeed recommend you try it, but don't get too hooked into it since there probably won't be too much, if anything, added to it.

Now Lamb isn't as a powerful character as Ryan was but she still is very instresting none the less. She has always fought Ryan even before the 1959 New Year's Eve riots but since Ryan is dead she has taken supreme control of the city with the family or the still very insane Splicers that follower her. Story wise is is pretty straght forward with the same well down vocie acting and diolog, but the story's giant plot twist that the Shock seires has become known for isnt that great. Plus the story was a little contrived, but does this make it a bad game.....no of course not. 2K Marin did a fine job and with the help of Ken Levine they made the game feel like a Shock rather then just run like a Shock game, yet the best thing of Bioshock 2 has to be the combat. Probably the best in any of the three Bioshocks massive improvements made fighting feel very smooth and more importently, fun. Just like Bioshock 1 improved the combat and gameplay machanics of System Shock 2 Marin has done the same to Bioshock 1. From the new trap ammo that allows you to lay traps for the fun ADAM gathering sequences in which you protect your little sister to get some sweet ADAM to the new weapons which look very cool 2k Marin has down a great job at making Bioshock 2 very VERY fun. None the less there are still some issues like the weaker story and some other things like the segments were yourun around with a flash light so it makes the game very spoopy, this really cheeses out the horror bit of Bioshcok 2 and seems to take the easy way out. Sure the game has its low bits but it has its high, Bioshock 2 may not be a bigger and better game os Bioshock 1 but it see,s to fall right next to it. Bioshock 2 isnt a bad game it's just different and different is good like this game is.

Overall this game has been more fun than Civilizaiton V and i hope more will be added in the future.
The first improvment is a less linear technological progression. Rather than having a series of events to replicalte historical progression of technology we instead have a system that allows a player to better specialize their nation in a manner they see fit. This also helps remove the scenarios of nuclear submarines trolling the nations who only bothered to get basic sailboats, or my stealth jets destroying spearmen.
A feature that has been somewhat merged instead was civilization progression, ideology, and unit upgrades. The Harmony/Purity/Supremecy is to somewhat exist in place of the old ideology system of civilizaiton V, but rather than reaching it and replacing your social policy(virtues in this game) it instead progresses besides it determing how your civilization grows. Through technological upgrades and choices you make during your playthrough your civilization will proggress changing physically as well as allowing you a choice in how your units progress. This gives a less linear experience for your unit upgrade. It does remove individual unit upgrade which makes keeping your army up to date much easier but also makes it easier for your broke neighbor to have the same.
One of the upsides of the new ideology is the passive bonuses that occur as you level up this system, but it also allows a hybrid system. A player can earn points in all 3 ideologies (though secondary get penalties to their rate of progression) allowing a player to dip a little into everything they need in the long term as well as creating odd hybrids of units (Ultimate Supremecy who upgrades into a Harmony hybrid).
The final piece on ideologies is the unique resources. Each ideology favors a resource over another, while you can unlock the ability to harvest all of them if you want to progress correctly and get your ideology specific units you will need to spend on Fixarite/Floatstone/Xenomass. This results in your surroundings influencing your progression a bit more. Rather than a random civ V map leaving you without nescessary resources to allow you to give your units upgrades and search until you can get past this resrouce deficit, you instead need to study your surroundings and decide what resource you will need to focus on. This isn't always true but many maps i've seen like to have these resources in clumps with xenomass being the most common it seems, which is understandable as the idea of harmony is being capable of existing more easily with your surrdouning environment (with the harmony tree and technological upgrades eventually turning the annoying miasma that dots the landscape into a invaluable combat resource.)
Final welcome change is the spy system. In civilization V you simply threw a spy at a city to be a diplomat, steal resources, or simply sit in a city you own and hope he can catch enemy spies. It was slow and outside of the rare success of stealing a technology it was a passive system. Beyond earth introduces a still somewhat passive system but now you can more actively gain spies to send out to various areas as well as tell them exactly what you want them to do there. A new intrigue system is added which represents unrest and overall disorganization of a city, the higher this value the more complicated of operations a spy may perform. These actions range from steal science (not a direct techology but the actual resource to boost your own speed), energy (the wealth currency of this game), technology, to recruiting defectors. At intrigue levels of 4 and higher the danger do your spy being caught goes up but lets you do things such as annexing a city from the opponent, of course due to the power of this you need to have a mixture of luck, timing, and skill to get a city's intrigue this high, and eventually countermesaures can be implemented to ensure they can't go past 3 (making fresh outposts a very likely target). This system is nicer as my average game involves me directing 6 spies to steal science from every city just so I can eclipse my foes in general techological prowess.
As for less major changes a new one is a quest system. The quest system is a new way for you to make choices during your playthrough which can influence what ideology you follow as well as how your buildings will function, this can range from chosing culture or energy from a newly constructed building to determing how you want to affect the environment around you leading to later quests letting you aquire new an better bonuses.
The social policy system is changed to a virtue system which is a bit of a sideways change. You lose the 8 social policies in favor of 4 with 3 tiers. The individual tiers and trees grant synergy bonuses for taking a certain number in each tree. Overall this isn't super different and is just a different take.
Now I've listed all of the pros and mehs of this game so to make this fair I will need to list the cons.
First loss is the great person system. No longer will you get great people who can give you random boosts during the game or build unique improvments, this feature is outright gone, as well as the tourism/great work system.
The tourism system isn't a huge loss for me but i know it was a big/difficult win condition to have in Civ V but at the same time it kinda makes sense how quickly these colonies are ready to go to war because their neighbor is hugging too many alien trees or turning themselves into cybermen. Regardless it was a bit of depth to the game lost.
Another loss is the religion system. While it seems the game seems to just have the generic "planet worship" as a theme in the game it is somewhat sad not being able to influence other nations via the spread of your relgion, though I may see the odd nature of missionaries dodging the angry indigenous lifeforms to share the glory of Pelor.
Finally the golden age system is lost in favor of a hybrid. Instead of happiness we have health, and instead of excess giving you golden ages everything after 5 becomes a slowly increasing bonus to production and then other resources for each of your cities. Health is probably the most daunting thing in this game to obtain as there are no longer luxury resources (no longer forcing nations to be buddies because the happiness of their people is balancing barely on their neighbor's supply of truffles). But soon you find its one of the most easy resources to have excess of and cap out on. So of course in civ V fashon this system limits your rate of expansion. This can be fixed with wonders, or more reliably social policies. Buildings exist to boost this but like Civ V there is an invisible cap on how much a city can produce for happiness so don't think buying all the buildings will fix this.
Another downside is the lack of nations. Nations are replaced by sponsors who give the specialized bonuses like in Civ V but rather than having various sponsors you instead then pick 4 bonuses set ahead of time. All together giving a potentially deeper experience with all these options instead robbing the game of variation as there are no unique units and the game has to start recycling sponsors on larger, so have fun facing off against 6 Pan-Asian cooperative clones who all chose different ideologies and are varying levels of bipolar in negotiations with you. Honestly expansions, custom content, and some simple DLC nations will aleviate this a bit but I hope a Gods and kings style expansion will adress the lack of uniquness between the nations as even the bonuses are pretty underwhelming (Maybe i'm just bitter at the loss of my ritual sacrificies from montezuma, or my endless population boon from Ghandi).
Overall An enjoyable experience with some flaws that I beleive can be hammered out with some later content.

Do you like Fighting Games?
Do you like Diablo?
Do you like Team Games?
Meet their child, Battlerite. There's nothing quite like it on the market right now. This is NOT a traditional "MOBA", it shares almost nothing with the likes of DOTA or LoL except for the top-down view.
Inspired by WoW Arenas, Stunlock Studios have worked hard over many years to perfect the "pvp arena" formula, first with Bloodline Champions, which is an amazing game but sadly died due to very bad business decisions probably forced upon them by Funcom at the time, and now Battlerite, which is their first independent game, and it's not far from formulaic perfection.
It's hectic, it's difficult, it has an amazingly high skill ceiling which you'll get to appreciate as soon as you get into a match against other players. This game is not for the faint of heart or those who look for chance elements which can make them triumph over more skilled players ocasionally. And that is why I love it and have been playing since Bloodline Champions.

Bottome line up front: 8.5/10 game, tons of fun. However I do not recommend purchasing Sins on Steam. The Steam verison is buggy and crashes randomly. Purchase Sins from another third-party vendor, or directly from the developer / publisher.
I came across Sins while I was deployed to the middle east, a buddy of mine gave me a pirated copy. I immensely enjoy this game, and I put countless hours into it when I was off-duty. If I had to guess I'd say I played around 8-900 hours over 9 months.
I never had any problems with the game, except for the mulitplayer not working due to it being a pirated copy. It crashed around 7-8 times over 9 months, and most of those were when I was intentionally pushing the game and my computer to their limits. Whether it was single player, LAN, small pre-made maps or huge custom ones, the game worked as it should. I would notice some issues with frame rate late-game, when there would be hundreds of ships on the screen during battles, but that's likely my computer reaching it's upper limits and not any issue with the game engine.
I recently decided to buy Sins in order to support the developers for making a game I have so thoroughly enjoyed. I Downloaded and installed the game, launched it, and the steam bootstrapper kept crashing and rebooting. I didn't restart my computer before attempting to launch the game, and yes I know you should, but I've never had a problem with running a steam game after installing it without restarting. That was the first sign of something being wrong.
I restarted, and that fixed the issue. I get into my first match, a 1v1 on the Gemini medium map, and the game randomly crashes around 20 minutes in. I relaunched and got into another game, this time a 2v2v2 on a huge multi star comp map, and it crashed again at around 90 minutes.
I can count on my hands how many times the pirated copy crashed, over the hundreds of matches I played. The official copy of the game from steam crashed twice in a row in the first two matches. And I bet you my next paycheck it will crash again the next match I play.
A pirated copy of the game is more stable than the steam release. Absolutely pathetic, Valve.
Edit: I have since played 6 more matches, two of which crashed. So Steam Sins is 4 for 8, or 50% failure rate. Going to try reinstalling to see if that fixes the issue for me. Revised some portions of this review, as I wrote this while slightly intoxicated.

This is a niche game. You have to love RTS titles to begin with in order to get all you can out of this game. That being said, this may be the greatest RTS game ever created.
Pro:
- Intricate, detailed gameplay that allows for nearly infinite strategies, compounded by six readily distinguishable classes, each with easily understood strengths and weaknesses.
- Gorgeous gameplay, small battles feel like a desperate struggle, large battles feel like an epic contest of ultimate power, and all planet/star models are meticulously rendered into sprawling heaps of sublimity.
- Early/Mid/Late game all allow for new strategy to be applied, letting the player modify their tactics to better meet the assuredly unexpected challenges they face.
- In-Game map creator allows for pretty much any map style the player could ever want.
- Solid multiplayer mode, far less lag than would be expected for a game of this sheer magnitude.
- Player interface is smooth and allows at-hand modification for hotkeys, etc.
- Extremely advanced AI, on harder difficulties your robot opponents will be very difficult to defeat.
Con:
- The learning curve is a goddamn brick wall. At least two or three hours of tutorial + practice are required before you stand a chance of beating even the Easy AI.
- Micromanaging is a must, although I love it, assigning keybindings for every possible ability and advancement can be tedious, and is unfortunately a must for high-end competitive play. Not much is required for basic play, but for some, dealing with planetary income/resource/optimization issues will be a chore.
- This game is an enourmous time investment, I've played matches that lasted over twelve hours. The shortest match I've ever played was probably about two hours.
- No campaign mode. I hate to even say it, but if this game had one, it would shine brighter than a pulsar.
Essentially, if you like RTS games, strategy games in general, or mentally challenging games in more general still, you will love this. I've spent hundreds of hours (I bought and played independently before buying on steam for multiplayer reasons) and none of them I feel have been wasted. I love this game, and I truly believe it is the best RTS game ever made, despite what minor (to me) flaws it may have.

Some games click with you immediately. Others you have to warm up to. Honestly, Betrayer was a cold fish the first time I played it. It was slow, it was repetitive, and it just wasn't something I felt like spending time on. But I put in the time, and it didn't take long before I started getting to the meat beneath the tough exterior.
You awaken on a beach near a fort in the New World to find the place deserted and bestial conquistadors roaming the countryside. Your only friends are a mysterious lady in red, an equally mysterious merchant, and the sundry spirits haunting the fort and the wilderness. The game is assembled as an open-world mystery, where you are free to explore the VERY expansive map in search of answers, clues, trinkets, and gear scattered about. There's a great deal of walking to be done across the gorgeous environments, but there's a very handy and well-implemented fast travel system that cuts out some of the tedium.
There are a few kinds of foes to face as you explore, and care must be taken in handling them. It's an FPS with a major, MAJOR emphasis on stealth and intelligent approaches to fights. Enemies have basically the same field of vision as you do and will spot you from across fields and valleys. They're just as fast and just as wily about getting hit, and your weapons are limited in their utility. However, shadows and underbrush can hide your approach, gusts of wind can muffle your footsteps, and headshots kill far more effectively. Your bow will be your best friend for much of the game, but the flintlock pistols and muskets have their uses in dispatching single enemies efficiently. You also get a one-hit kill tomahawk with limited range and explosives for when you're feeling overwhelmed. Combat is an involved experience and can get a little repetitive when you really want to get somewhere, but mastering it is a rewarding experience.
The story is intriguing and should keep you moving forward to uncover more and more secrets about the mysterious world you find yourself in. Characters are well-written and there's a very useful journal which holds all your clues and profiles and investigations. There are plenty of items to find, including plot items, interesting trinkets, and equippable gear that improves your abilities. You'll also be helped along by some clever systems like listening for ghostly echoes to point you to places of interest. The sound design is excellent and important, so make sure you have good directional speakers or headphones for this one.
Above all, the atmosphere is top-notch. It's desolate and confounding despite the simple setting, and the graphics push it even further (and can be completely reconfigured, including playing in color, if you don't like them). Betrayer is not a hard game to play but it can be hard to get into, the way it marries open-world exploration and low-tech combat. It risks becoming repetitive at times, but it is most definitely worth experiencing.

Recursion Deluxe is an incredible, yet very challenging, game.
I was drawn to this game immediately from a livestream I was watching on Twitch that had the gamedev as a guest, highlighting the game in a Groupees bundle. So, immediately I pre-purchased the bundle so I could have this game once it released ^_^
I've been following the game ever since, and was happy to watch the game progress. When the key was finally released through Groupees, just as I expected, I loved the game and the challenges it gives. The levels are so adorable, I absolutely love the artstyle and characters. There's quite a bit of trial and error to be had here. You will find yourself raging on some levels, and using the insta-kill control will become handy when you find yourself unable to finish a puzzle because you took the wrong path when doing the puzzles out of order, etc. (I actually didn't know about that control until I noticed the gamedev using it from his live streams).
This game is completely puzzle-driven, and there is not much story elements to it (given I have finished all but 3-4 levels on the last world so I have not completely finished the game), but that does not reflect any negative feelings towards how incredibly well this game is designed and the great variety of puzzles it offers. If you like a challenge that doesn't hand-hold you throughout the game, this is definitely worth picking up.
There is also more to RDX than meets the eye. There are the standard levels to play, but you can also create your own levels with a level creator. Once you launch the game, if you're on the latest version, you will be prompted with the option to create levels. Unfortunately, I have yet to mess around with it but once the community begins creating their own levels, this game will have an incredible amount of replayability.
I've heard about plans the gamedev has to expand the game as well in the future, so I will continue to follow the game and can't wait to see what's in store for this game in the future, as I would be thrilled with more content!
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
On a completely different note, I am fairly new to PC gaming, so I wanted to use a controller to play this game. I only have an Xbox ONE controller however, so I did face some issues using it with this game. After reporting it to the gamedev, and having them look into the issue, it is definitely not an issue with this game.
If you have an issue using your Xbox One controller with RDX, I will leave the guide here that fixed the issues for me (that the gamedev kindly forwarded to me to help resolve the issues). I hope it can help others who face similar issues.

There is something incredibly satisfying in aligning your ship alongside another and unleashing every single broadside cannon you have. In combination with the incredible music giving every fight you take a Wild West spin; you truly are on the lawless outskirts of space.
You start with nothing and climb all the way to the top in any way you want. Trader, Miner, Mercenary, Pirate. Just be careful who you make enemies with, anything goes in this game.
On the subject of trading, Rebel Galaxy contains a simple yet effective trading system with market values that will change in response to local events. Discover trade routes from station to station, capitalise on resource shortages, a station currently being blockaded will be in desperate need of supplies.
When you feel strong enough, use a jump gate to travel to one of the many other systems. Make sure you are prepared though; higher risk brings higher reward but you won’t be smiling facing a Dreadnought class ship armed to the teeth.
This game stands out as one of its quirks is that it is locked on a 2D plane, honestly I think this brings its benefits. You're at the helm of a capital ship, you wouldn't be doing amazing tricks. It also simplifies the controls, meaning you can focus less on keeping the ship level and more on the actual fight.
Just listen to the soundtrack, it completes this game.

Charming and addictive  game. Yes its 2D space. There is no up and down flying. And the sytems are full (sun, planetes) but compressed in space. So there are traveling times, but they're not too long and nicely balanced, focussing more on fun and flowthen on realism.
Generally the flow and speed  of the game is very very good.
Battles feel very much like the ship battles in Assassins Creed Black Flag. The "Space" like a big, flat ocean.
Additionally a freelancer like universe with many systems, multiple ships, in many sizes with different focus. Some only avalable from factions like mercenaries or trading guild.
A large variation of weapons and equipment, boots, boosters, shields for different play and fight stlyes. Shields and boosters for example are not only different in hitpoints or speed but there are versions with completely different focus.
It's therefore nicely complex and flexible. And a smart buy/sell systems mean you can try without really goin "wrong" or being punished for experiments.
With possible problems, concerning difficulty, mentioned below.
Having finshed the Main Story: It's not a storytelling masterpiece.
But it's good enough, nicely presented, fully and professionally voiced, and leads through the first systems of the "universe" and the factions in it.
Before i go to some details and little complaints, please keep in mind:
Its a fun little (its actually pretty big) game for a RIDICULOUS low price. Just dont expect a full 6 axis Space sim! It's a space based action game with strong freelancer elements in it.
I FULLY recommend it. Even for a higher price it would be a very good game!
_____________________________
That being said :a few general remarks, only some bordering on complaints:
Like Assassins creed Black flag, which the fighting is CLEARLY inspired from, i find it a lot easier and more intuitively and precisely to control with MOUSE then with a gamepad. Both is available though, both works good.
My joystick (tm hotas) doesnt appear as option though.
After the Story there are still missions from boards to perform. Leveling up in factions to gain access to better ships. And trading.
However for the trading the small selections of goods and the ship designs don't seem perfect. It doesn't really lend itself well to that. However i didn't really play like that so i might be wrong. There is a merchants guild in which you can level up, getting unique, trading focussed ships.
But i think i can say, the focus of the game clearly is on the fights. And it excels in that!
The 100% system behind the upgrades makes it maybe a bit easy, as there are no hard choices to make. But it makes it also more fun to play. If you buy the wrong upgrade or a weapon you dont like, just sell it for the full price. No wrong ways, no saving money while flying with a weak ship, just to be able to afford something better later.
I like that a lot, some might find it not challenging or complex enough though.
The same for the energy system. Basically nothing limits the size of shields and weapons in a ship. The only reason preventing you from upgrading hull and shields even in the smalles ships is the price. And the value of Damage absorption of shields, hulls, deflectors ( short period shields for emergencies) is the SAME, even in the smallest ship.
If you put (you cant afford without cheat) a mk3 or 4 shield in your starter ship, you'd be immortal in the first systems.
Heavy hull and Shields should be limited to big ships, given that they would consume more energy then a small ship can provide. Or provide less hitpoints in smaller ships.
But they don't. I think that system would benefit from more complexity.
The mission log is too small. Should have room for a few more missions (quests).

Little tips from my experience, they're of course only MY opinion:
1.Mining lasers are op. They imho the best weapon ingame AND can mine asteroids (which isn't profitable enough as a main profession). They make good damage to shields AND hull. The other laser makes  somewhat more damage to hulls but very little to shields. They simply make NO sense. Having a ship with all turrets mining lasers is (in range) the best. And you dont run out of ammo like with rocket launchers. small capacities of ammo make them near pointless.
Disadvantage is the range, but i found my self that close to enemies all the time anyway.
2. In the first systems, in the beginning, as soon as you can, fly to the next system, even if it's too high-level for you to fly missions in, rush to a station, avoiding all fights, and buy the BETTER shield available there.
Even if you have to stick to cheaper wepons for a while to be able to afford it. Remember, selling those weapons later you get 100%of your money back to invest in bigger ones..
Then go back to the previous system where fights are MASSIVELY easier if you have that better shield. Every higher shield MK doubles the shields hitpoints. No matter how small the ship is.
The same works technically with weapons. Mining laser (and other weapons) MK1>MK2  is a MASSIVE jump in damage (and a small one in range). But very expensive. Shield should be #1 priority.
Generally: the jump in difficulty from the first to the second system is the highest. The first basically is an easy going tutorial system.  2-3 is also quite big. After that it's much less steep.
3. Fighting big ships: dont fly into their broadsides of course. Search dead angels and stick there, firing at it. Flying in its engine (does no damage to you) it can't hit you and you can fire. Discovering that made those fights vs capital ships A LOT EASIER for me.
4.Entering and leaving stations saves your game. Having a little detour between missions to do that is worth the time. Dying in the 4th consecutive mission, losing all you got from the last 3 can be VERY annoying.

In many of the reviews on Steam for this game people tell you what happened to their characters during a sequence of days in the game - and I think that shows a lot about how engaging it is. It really draws you in and you care about the decisions you make.
You end up building a real attachment to the characters in it because you invest so much into keeping them alive. In no other game have I been afraid to engage in combat for fear of injury.
Hard to describe it in terms of putting it in a genre. You have to make moral choices, manage your items well and scavange for parts, food and other items. I found it to be part resource management, part exploration game and part story telling. It's all fun mind you - even though tending to two sick people when you have no food and your supplies are low and you are being raided at night doesn't seem fun on paper -  I can't stop playing.
The art work is great and the sound and music set the mood perfectly.
Not sure why people think it's 'expensive for an indie game' - this is hands down the best game I have played in a long while and well worth the money.

I bought this game a while ago so I could rate it negatively for featuring only one ship you can fly, but ended up playing a bit.
The greatest flaw with this game, as of the time I've been playing, are the limitations in content. There are never enough options in regards to everything you can imagine, except maybe station variety. On the other hand, much of the game's main features are now easier to handle, without losing much complexity, which is quite a feat in the gaming industry.
Cons
- Very few weapon and equipment options. 3 types of shield, 4 types of engines, 10 different missile models, about 6-7 different weapons, 3 scan upgrades, a few licenses, 3 or 4 different software, some cockpit configurations, and thats all you can buy to upgrade THE ONLY SHIP YOU GET TO FLY THE ENTIRE GAME.
- You can get money quickly by farming lockboxes in Nirins treaty. There are plenty of other opportunities to break the game by farming resources real quickly.
- Little ship variety. At the capital shipyard in Home of Light there are only 4 XL models available to buy LOLOLOLOLOLOLOLOLLLLLLLLLL
- YOU CAN ONLY FLY ONE SHIP
- Combat is less fun and rewarding than in previous games
- Pointless and repetitive station interiors. Has first person exploration but no combat.
- Long loading times (although no loading time between sectors)
- Crafting is limited. Got little use for most items.
- Trading ships have a deplorable small cargo capacity
- No SETA, but as you upgrade your shields, your turbo capacity will increase, making traveling over long distances faster.
- Your co-pilot is there, but useless
- Cannot fly in a fleet, no SETA means you have to keep the pace of your slowest ship, which makes traveling in a group *VERY* tedious
- Number of sectors is very small
- No stock market
- Bad voice acting, as always
- Missions are still very repetitive and do not feel like they are part of the rest of the game, and are there just because of the player, which breaks immersion. They do not feel like contracts or mercenary work. The "bandit leaders" and "raiders" only exist within the context of a mission, they are never really there, harassing traders and stuff. It also has the mission variety one would expect from a sandbox game: very poor.
- Aim assist won't work against some ships. I dont know whether this is a bug or intended behavior.
- An MK4 shield costs almost 4kk on your ship, but a capital ship shield is only 300k. This is clearly an example of how certain parts of the market were not integrated to the economy at all.
- You cannot combine weapons anymore. You can only use them one at a time.
- You cannot build stations wherever you want anymore. There are predetermined places to build them now.
- Soundtrack is nice but repetitive
- You can hire engineers, but they won't repair your ships. They do nothing at all. You have to keep sending your ships back to the shipyard to be repaired. You dont even have the repair laser anymore.
- Exploration consists of finding lockboxes. The thrill of finding hidden stations and rare ships has diminished.
Pros
- Graphics are reasonable
- The cockpit view adds to immersion
- Trade is said to be oversimplified, but I dont think so. Some parts of it are actually better than in previous games. Less micromanagement without eliminating a lot of the complexity. Trade menu also helps a lot.
- Ships are dedicated to carrying certain types of goods, adding to complexity.
- Mining is more complex, interesting, and can be fully automated.
- Supply chains are bigger, more logical, and more complex
- Interface is ridiculously better than the ones from previous titles
- Drones are a good addition
- Commanding other ships and fleets is easier now
- Bulletin board gathers information on all missions available in a region.
- It is much easier to grab floating cargo
- Mission rewards are more balanced than in X3, but, as I've mentioned before, there are other ways of farming money.
- Hull damage no longer directly affects ship speed.
- Boarding is easier, more functional
- Docking in a station or capital ship is easier
- Station composition is improved by modularization. No more complex hubs!
- There are now weapon mods, a minor feature that lets you customize what little number of different models are available to you.

The only difference between this platformer and others is there's no hub world. The game is in constant adventure, through 6 different stages of varying atmosphere, difficulty and length.
The plot is that at the beginning of the game, Tiny gets in a car crash with his radio robot that's trying to guide him, presumably to these pyramids that are seen throughout the game. Well, this other fellow, Big, steals the underwear from the car crash and gains the powers, throwing big rocks and levitaion and what not. Anyway, radio robot helps you along the way while using your tools to fight Big throughout 5 of the 6 stages.
Pretty great game overall though, might have benefited from a full soundtrack of orchestra, platformer music, instead of jams and beats.

It might feel repetitive at times, so the best way to enjoy the game is probably to do half a level here and there, and not to rush head on to finish the game.
Talking about shortness, I would say that the game is long just right: not short enough to feel rushed, but not so long that it overstates it's welcome, with the only minor complaint that, until the last level, the graphic is pretty even and kind of meh (desert, desert, desert... you get used to it quite fast).

1.- This is game is super complicated, which is something I very much like, hence the 230 hours!
2.- Because the game was buggy at the beginning people think that some things are bugs, but you just need to figure them out e.g. you order a capital ship to buy something from somewhere, but it just sits there. Most likely it's either a) you're sending it to a sector or station you haven't discovered yet or b) very commonly, you're sending it to a station that, even though it advertises its products on the market, it doesn't actually have a trading port! I know that's complicated but I love it!
3.- People don't like it because they compare it to previous iterations. Nothing to add here except I find this game much richer, prettier and deeper. You can literally do anything you want: become a bounty hunter, a taxi driver, a warlord, an imperialist, a business man, etc. You can eve get off the ship and walk-around the stations or even the back of your ship. It's not very useful, but it certainly adds immersion.
If you do get this game I strongly recommend getting the Cheat Mod from the Workshop area, as this allows you to take over, not only over stations, but also claim whole sectors!

Fun little isometric arcade game. At times it can be a bit repetitive, but that's a problem most isometric shooters have. This is the type of game you play for about 20-30 mins to blow off some steam and fill up your time with. Lots of people have reported having graphical problems, but I've had no such issues, the game runs solid for me. Pretty much everyone that has said issues has AMD hardware, so that kind of explains it ;P
The only big thing that's really affecting my enjoyment of the game is the health and respawn system. I get the idea behind executions healing the player, it's honestly a pretty good idea that fits with the game's theme, but come on, have some medpacks lying around too, or have the player's health regenerate halfway. It's hard as hell getting people to become wounded.
Also, PPPLLLLEEEAAAASSSSEEEE get rid of the current respawn system. I get that the game doesn't want people to save scum, but having to earn respawn tokens lest start the huge♥♥♥♥♥level from the beginning is annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥ Have the player's progress after getting to a respawn point undone, but have the amount of respawns at said point unlimited, that would be much better. Or at the very least, give the player some respawn tokens on the fly.
Still, it's a fun game. If you like the Alien Shooter series and have a taste for dark exploitation films, you might like this. It's really not the threat to gaming and society as a whole that it was made out to be, it's just good ol' arcade action delivered from a different perspective. Really didn't deserve the AO rating.

Not as good as the first or the last, the story of Bioshock 2 was interesting but ultimately opened up numerous plot holes compared to the neat and clean story of Bioshock. It takes places years after the events of the original game, and suggests that Rapture has somehow managed to cling to life despite looking as if it would collapse upon itself at any moment. Furthermore, the game presents your character as one of the prototype Big Daddies, but you are stronger, faster, more agile than the Big Daddies of Bioshoch, and can use plasmids at will. Why is a prototype so much more powerful than anything else in the game? Bioshock Infitine Burial at Sea Episode 2 pretty much undoes all of the backstory for this game, and thus renders Bioshock 2 noncanonical.
But this is nitpicking the story, the gameplay, however, is great. Despite the flaws of the story as it relates to the other games in the franichise, as a stand alone game Bioshock 2 is still compelling. The gameplay took the very good, but slightly clunky weapons/plasmid swapping engine and updated it into a smoother and more refined state. The engine was good enough to be directly adapted into Bioshock Infinite, and copied verbatum into the Burial at Sea epilouge DLC missions.

Sins of a Solar Empire was one of the first games that made me want a gaming computer when it first came out in 2008. Lacking the funds, I was stuck with low-end graphics and abysmal load times. Its been 8 years since I've played the game, and seeing it on sale, I grabbed it for some quick nostalgia.
The game runs fine. Any computer from the last 3 years should handle it with zero problems. Technically, its almost flawless, completely delivering on the promise of full scale immersion in a 4x game, zooming effortlessly between multiple star systems down to the individual starfighter. The graphics are decently done, and large-scale battles have the potential to be impressive and pretty, if not awe-inspiring. Thats about where the positives end.
My major complaints with this game is that the amount of effort that was put into certain areas of the game is severly lopsided. The tech tree is the biggest transgressor, with tiny, incrimental techs that require constant micromanaging to ensure that you don't get caught woefully behind. When trying to construct a unit or building that you don't have the tech for, it takes many frustrating minutes (ESPECIALLY with a new civilzation) to figure out which tree it is under, and then locate the correct icon. The tech interface is tiny and wastes a lot of space.
In fact, nearly every interface is a mess. From simply having to click through each and civilzation to see which are defeated and which are active (maybe a red <DEFEATED> next to their title would help..?", to confusing and unexplained treaty organization, it seems that information is deliberately hidden. Massive amounts of work apparently went into the detailed sidebar which I have never looked at even once while playing. With each of the available civs having completely different icons, names, and abilities for buildings, and totally different sets of units, there is a steep learning curve to just understanding what each of them DO.
Upgrading planets is boring and repetitive. The game punished you for expanding, and it takes a lot of time to make new planets worth the investment. So all of this takes MASSIVE amounts of time to learn, and to balance effectively. Which would be fine, except that none of it is fun or rewarding. Its the most frustrating part of the game, but it requires huge amounts of time.
I know what you're thinking, 'dude, thisi s a 4x game, micromanaging is kind of a given' Which is true on its face, and for any other game, I'd agree. But its sooo boring. And unrewarding. And this is where Sins breaks down, because all of this should have some kind of payoff, namely in space battles. Battles are basically just jump your ships in, have them attack the largest ships in order... they just sit there. It would be amazing to divide your fleet into squadrons, have flanking options, order all of my bombers to prioritize carriers or support ships first... but no. You have to do each thing manually, and again, if you haven't played the other civs, its IMPOSSIBLE to tell what ships do what.
I can't recommend this game. Its just not fun.
