I feel almost compelled to write a review after seeing some of the negative posts and reviews of this game.
Let's get one thing straight- this is far from a "perfect" rugby league game.
I've poured countless hours into pretty much every rugby league game from ARL 96' on Mega Drive through to Rugby League live 3 on PC, i'm also a huge rugby league fan and sports fan in general.
If you were a master at Rugby league live 3 and able to beat teams on the hardest difficulty setting with your eyes closed, chances are you will struggle to beat teams even on the pro diffiuclty level, the AI is that much harder to get through now.
GRAPHICS- The graphics are a huge improvement on RLL3, players look spectacular, face mapping is absolutely spot on, the stadiums look good, the tackle and running animations are hugely improved, the crowds look poor but I don't really take that much notice of them.
The lighting and shadow effects are pretty good although I have noticed some odd shadows when playing at night in some stadiums, it looks very dark.
GAMEPLAY- Probably where this loses a lot of people. It is fundamentaly very different to RLL3 even though it may look very similar.
One of the things I found very hard to get used to was using the left trigger and right analog to "wrestle" the ball runner to the ground in the tackle. If you don't implement this in pretty much every front on tackle you are going to get smoked and the other team will make easy metres. After 15-20 games though i felt pretty comfortable doing this and like the extra element it brings.
Gang tackling is heaps better, the AI will often come and join in to help get a difficult player to the ground which is pretty cool.
One other problem I had initially was I was head highing people all over the show, in RLL3 you could tackle the opposition while holding the turbo button without much of a worry of giving away a headhigh penalty, this isn't the case anymore and personally I think it adds another good element to the game once you get used to it.
Same goes for the "big hit" button (in defence), spamming this isn't happening anymore and you have to be more selective with who you try to use it with.
In game kicking is fairly similar, although I find standard kicking to be a lot hader to aim accurately but I am slowly getting the hang of it and it's pretty satisfying having to think before you kick and making good metres.
Field goals are essentially the same and still easy to pull off, I find Grubbers, chips and bombs are better utilised now and add more of an attack to the kicking arsenal.
In terms of attacking running, I like the fact that if you spot a gap and hit it hard you can run through it without the AI defence seemingly able to "morph" into your path.
The line and support running of AI players is another improvement i've noticed, delivering inside balls and cut out balls to players running the right line can truly look spectacular.
Linebreaks are a bit too easy to make due to being able to spam the big hit button on attack although actually finishing into a try is a lot harder. I'd like to see the big hit/hitup button tweaked in upcoming patches.
I've seen lots of people complaining about "floaty" passing, unresponsive passing especially out of dummy half etc. Can't say i've noticed this issue although I got the game after the latest patch so it may have been rectified somewhat.
One little thing that is annoying is there is an unusual amount of intercepts, I thought this was an absolutely horrible thing at first but in retrospect the more I play the more I think about where i'm actually passing instead of spreading it out to the flanks quickly to get it to the wingers like RLL3 to score. I do think that it could do with a tweak in the next patch though.
Knock ons and forward passes are pretty much in the same boat, I swear some of the forward passes I've been pinged for are backwards or lineballs at best.
I find the offloading to be almost non-existent and when I do get one away it feels random and clumsy, maybe i'm too used to RLL3 where I could offload at will but it seems like it could use some tuning in future patches.
Goal kicking, kicking off etc is different in this, not worse, just different but doesn't detract from the game at all and if anything adds an extra bit of realism to it.
I find fending and sidestepping a bit harder to pull off (in fact I don't think i've actually managed 1xfend in the 12 hours I've played lol).
CONTENT- All the usual you would expect, career mode is very similar to RLL3 which is a bit of a shame as I feel it could have been expanded on. Fanhub is cool, being able to create and download old school players and as a rugby fan it is pretty cool to be able to download the Hurricanes and All blacks and use them.
I love stats and what we get with this is pretty standard fare. Nothing to write home about.
Haven't actually had a game online yet, had a lot of bad experiences on RLL3 of people rage qutting and It used to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off big time, not sure if they have found a way to punish rage quitters yet, i they haven't i'm not really interested in playing online unless it's against someone I know
SOUND- Thank god there is no more Phil Gould is all I have to say. Hah, not really all I have to say though.
Crowds sounds OK, can hear players shouting and calling for the ball, can hear them grunting etc in tackles.
Commentary is probably better than RLL3 although some of the phrases have obviously been lifted from that, Vossy and the engish guy tend to repeat themselves a fair bit but I'd say it's of a better standard than RLL3.
The soundtrack is better than RLL3, at least to me, has a bit of a metal theme to it.
OVERALL
All in all I will say the first 15-20 games I played I absolutely hated this game with a passion.
I was on the verge of getting a refund for it but thought "i'll have one more game of 20min halves and see if I can get used to it" (had been playing 10min career games before then with 5min halves).
About 50-60 mins into the game I started getting used to all the little new nuances in the gameplay and started finding it extremely enjoyable and rewarding.
So what I'm basically saying is this- it's not RLL3 or RLL2, this feels like it's got a whole new element of tactics and fundemental gameplay, I think you need to go into this game not expecting to have an extremely polished version of RLL3, because like me, you will be dissapointed.
If like me however you persevere and try to understand the new elements Big ant have introduced I am fairly certain rugby league video game fans will find it as rewarding as I do.
Hopefully in the next patch Big Ant can sort out some of the little annoying bugs that still exist and deliver a more polished experience.

In the beginning, Betrayer was really interesting. It has a pretty unique art style, a fun combat system, realistic locations and dark stories to discover.
But the game tries to be something it isn't. It's not about shooting enemies, it's about investigating. You find ghosts who don't remember their names and their cause of death, so you have to find out what happened by finding other ghosts, clues and objects.
So, for example you find a flute and a shoe. Each one belongs to a different person. You talk to a ghost and you are able to ask him if he knows the flute - he'll say yes and voilà, you know his name. But you can't even ask him if he knows the show because the game only allows you to ask the right questions. Investigation at its best!
Objects, clues and ghosts are scattered all around the map, so you have two options: You either investigate the whole map on your own (everything is marked on the map) or you just let the game show you where to go next. Which is basically unavoidable unless you want a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because the ghosts and dialogues are triggered and you never really know whom to speak to next. Also, the ghosts are the only thing not marked on the map.
The stories itself are really dark and fit into the historic background, but once you clear one of the maps you just move forward to the next one and forget everything that's been told before.
It's always the same: You enter a map, explore it until you find the bell to enter the "dark world", let the game lead you through an extremely linear detective story and then enter the next map. It's a shame because the combat system is really good and challenging, but that just isn't enough to keep you excited for about 7 hours. Open world is pointless - the only freedom the game gives you is grinding. Lots of grinding.

Rebel Galaxy is a thoroughly enjoyable space RPG-style game.  The game page and other reviews do a good job of providing more detail on the gameplay, so I won't waste too much time covering that.  Basically, it's a naval combat game in space (movement is in 2D only).  That being said, this style in no way detracts from the game's value.  You spend your time doing missions, mining, trading, and/or hunting bounties to make money which goes toward upgrading your ship.  There is also a "main campaign" that takes you through a simple yet adequately interesting story.  On the downside, the factions are a bit bland (as is mentioned in several other reviews) and there really doesn't seem to be much replayability (at least I personally have no desire to replay now that I've beaten the game).
If you want to pew-pew other spaceships in a beautifully rendered, decent sized "universe" while listening to an admittedly catchy soundtrack (seemingly ranging in influence from CCR to Pearl Jam at times) then this game is worth looking into.  It runs smoothly with no bugs or glitches (for me, anyway).  Ultimately, I found the game experience to be well worth the cost.
8.5/10

A lot of people already said what this game is: a mix between Freelancer and Assassin's Creed Black flag.
But this game misses the passion of both games.
First of all the main quest is short and you will not get emotionally involved into it; that's why we hope for a DLC
Second of all after some hours you will find yourself doing the same things over and over
Last thing you will reach a point when your ship is so updated that you will technically became IMMORTAL.
So why a positive review?
Simple, if you love space simulators, this game will become a drug.
Yes it doesn't have the story that Wing Commader gave us
Yes it doesn't seems various as Freelancer
Yes it doesn't looks badass like Freespace
Yes it doesn't need a manual of 75080 pages to control your ship like X or Elite Dangerous
Yes it doesn't have half naked girls inside your cabin
Yes indeed it missed all this but its semplicity is even its stronger point.
You buy a ship, upgrade it as you want (offence side, defence side, optionals, cargo) you go there and play as an hero or villain you get the money you buy a new ship and you get out there again to kick someone!
You will only be able to move yourself into a bidimensional way (so only right and left and not even up and down) but even this it is a fun part of the game that introduces broadsides....BROADSIDES...into a space game!
Have you ever been able to do this stuff into Wing Commander? X-Wing? Freelancer? Freespace?
That's why you played Black Flag!
The scenario is a huge sand "space" box with indeed a lot of activity (you will get involved into huge space battles more than one time) and even some events in several space stations (war, crime waves, embargoes, famine, invasions etc...) where you can decide to get involved or not.
Is just up to you.
Some said that they came to this game for the music. Let's be honest; after few hours you will get tired of listening them!
So that's why you can customize it from the start menù!
And here is where I ask myself: why adding music customization but there is NO POSSIBILITY to customize your ship with stickers or skins and so on?
TL-DR:
This game has got a lot of potential and that's why we hope for some DLC to get a better and more deep experience from it.
If you are a Sci-Fi fan that likes space battles, simple games with easy controls, a lot of BOOM BAZAAK SWOOP BAAAAA and freedom: GET THIS GAME
If you are looking for a deep story, simulation, lot of loot and lore...no this is definitely not the game for you.
Overall:
Graphic 8/10
Sounds 9/10
Gameplay 8/10
Longevity 6/10
Fun 9/10

I have never written a review about a game before but being a long time X fan since X3 Reunion and loving Egosoft for always supporting thier games forever ... not for money but to do the right thing for thier product and customers, I feel that the overall review score on Steam is now an unfair one. Seriously everyone completely forget the reviews from 6+ months ago or so.  This is a different game.  This is a playable game. This is a very emersive fun to play game that has the unique X universe feel.  You can really do what you want in the universe Egosoft created.  Be a pirate, mercenary, trader on a micro scale doing everything yourself or simply sit back and coordinate your fleets, fighting or trading, and let the game be more of a macro sim.  Even better ... mix the two!!
The character models are not the best and walking on stations and interacting with NPC's isn't as emersive as something like Mass Effect, but the space sim feel is deep and emersive.  If you like open world type games like GTA and you like space, then give this a try.  If you are an old X fan who was burnt when this was released or if you never have picked up an X game, after this 4.0 update now is the time to do it. I have the Teladi DLC and I will be buying the Home of Light DLC too.
This game will give you many hours of fun and has high replayability as well.  There are some high learning curves if you have never played an X game before, but it is very much worth it.

Egosoft the best developer who doesn't chase profitttsss but supports thier product and customers for years after release. Seriously, just wait for No Man's Sky. On its worst day, it has to be better than this. ASTEROIDS is better than this.

Hitman: Absolution is a stealth game, developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix. This instalment is the 5th game in the Hitman series. The game was released on November 20th 2012; ironically this is the 47th week of the year, referencing the main character Agent 47.
As with the rest of the Hitman series, you play from a third person perspective. You play as Agent 47 who is the best hitman around. Gameplay is very similar to the previous games, with a strong focus on stealthy progression on every level. At points there will be times where a gun fight will break out, but that usually means you are either very close to the end of the mission or have chosen the path of a deadly mercenary and just going all guns blazing anyway.  Each mission has multiple ways of completing it; you can actually finish the whole game by not shooting anyone, you can set up scenarios so that your “targets” die in an “unfortunate” accident or poisoning.  One of the major changes to Absolution is that Agent 47 now has an “Instinct” ability – this allows you to  track enemies more, and shows up interactable objects more easily. This of course has a limited supply but will slowly regenerate over the course of the mission. The stealth side of the game is done very well, and has the right amount of challenge for you to not get stumped with not being able to progress, but not so easy that you can do it blind folded.  The ability to pick up objects around the world and throw them into enemies path’s to distract them is always a good addition to a stealth game; but also sabotaging items such as electrics to also cause a distraction. The main aim of most of the missions is to take out a target, whilst causing as little disruption as possible, you are scored at the end of each mission taking into consideration how many “non-targets” were killed and other variables.
Graphically, Absolution is stunning.  So much so that the actual gameplay looks better than the cut-scenes. The animations are perfect both in game and in the cut scenes too; it looks like you are playing a film at times. On top of the gorgeous graphics, the sound effects and voice acting are all perfectly spot on.
Sadly this game is not as challenging as previous games; this was done to bring in a broader audience to the franchise. You can play the game on a fair few levels of difficulty; hard-core fans of the series will need to be playing this on the harder difficulties. You can always make the game even harder by playing through the game in a complete stealth style.
All of the Absolution’s missions are huge and extremely well designed. Each of them has more than two ways of completing the objective, on each level there will also be evidence that you can destroy, this will grant you more points at the end of the stage by doing so.  The levels have plenty of buildings, and rooms to explore and you’ll spend most of the time hiding in them to be fair!
The game is very an extremely good length; it took me just under 28 hours to complete, this was mainly because I tried to complete each level as stealthy as possible, but even then, twenty eight hours for any game is long! There is also a huge amount of replay ability in the game too; not only can you replay the story mode on different difficulties and trying out different methods of taking out your targets, but there is also the “Challenge Mode”, which is player made missions giving an almost infinite amount of gameplay for you to play through.
I had no technical problems with Absolution, I wasn’t able to push the game out on 4k resolutions, simply because it dropped my frame rate below 60, but that is because the graphics would have been mind-boggling. The game can be played with a controller, but I would suggest playing it on keyboard and mouse as you may need quite a bit of precision when it comes to planning your attacks. The game also has plenty of graphical options which are always nice to see; a field of view option would have been nice though.
To sum up, Hitman Absolution is in my opinion one of the best Hitman games; nothing will ever come close to being better than Contracts, but this one is easily second to that. The game’s gorgeous graphics, stellar gameplay and Hollywood like plot easily makes this one of the best games of from recent years. Before I get into the specifics, one has to make a comparison. Does Beyond Earth measure up to the standards of the previous game, Civilization V? The answer is complex: the launch for Beyond Earth, other than accounting for a few occasional glitches and gameplay balances (arguably fixed in the following days' patch) was better than Civilization V's launch, at least from accounts of repeated issues and monitoring of the 2K forums. It is the full game, as promised, with most of what the gaming news publishers heard about from Firaxis's team. However, where the game experiences a certain overexpectation is in the belief that Beyond Earth would take in the features and improvements made by the expansions up to Brave New World.
There are some that made it in: the system of trade is similar if not identical to Civilization V's, but the religion and ideology systems experience a convergence in the form of affinities. Combine technology with the beliefs in human evolution, and (in the Beyond Earth's sense) culture, research, and quasi-spiritual and/or transcendental beliefs and then there is affinity. The game hardly expects you to deal with the exact same graphical palette as well, providing new and unique terrain skinning, of course, many different styles (generally affinity-based) for each unit present. Of course, one cannot neglect the new buildings or wonders shown in the game, though they are somewhat similar in mechanics and function to those of Civilization V. In general, one can say that Beyond Earth is a new product with different takes on the standard formula, especially dealing with the different combinations sponsor, ship, cargo, and colonists and traveling to a certain planet.
Where the criticism comes in is with what I have heard from the players on CivFanatics and 2K Forums. First, many of the critics had problems with the AI; in war, the AI would frequently make blunders and fail to account for proximity/type of units the player controlled (AI puts weak ranged unti next to strong melee unit), or take the most immediate strategy. Likewise, some thought that the AI, even on its hardest difficulty (Apollo) was too easy [there are many variables to factor in]. There were original complaints of AI diplomacy which continue to exist both about Civ V and Beyond Earth, though arguably there are certain precedents for the counter-arguments, namely in historical realism and relevancy, regards to scale of territories, and the nature of war in general. The main criticism, however-and one which most certainly rings true with the majority-was that there was not as much flavor to the personalities of leaders and the units lead. The flavor that people may consider more sophisticated is found in the online civilopedia, which I will provide here.
On a personal note, and hopefully with a more full review included later: I still recommend this game to fans of the Civilization series. Beginners to the series might also find it appealing, though I would recommend changing the advanced settings of the game such that timed victory is off. This can be done by going to "set up game" and clicking advanced settings, and going to the max turns option, setting it to "0". It makes the game far more appealing and have more of the one-more-turn quality and allows for a greater liberty in making decisions not constrained by the scores in the diplomatic menus and the normal turn limit.

Civilization: Beyond Earth is a good game when looked at in isolation. The problem with Civilization: Beyond Earth is that it will be compared in one of two ways by almost anyone who plays it, one of which is a unflattering comparison to a huge degree:
1: Against Alpha Centauri (not really a fair comparison in many ways, but understandable given that this is a sci-fi setting)
2: Against Civilization V (an incredibly fair comparison, since much is reused from Civ V and a majority of players probably owned Civ V before getting Civ:BE).
Now, let's deal with the first comparison: Alpha Centauri came out a long ways ago, pre-dates the game that Civ:BE is based on (Civ V) by a good number of years, and Civ:BE clearly was not going to have the same mechanics as Alpha Centauri. So, what's left to even draw a comparison to? Well, the sci-fi setting. Believe me, there are issues with Civ:BE, as I'll get into, but the comparison with Alpha Centauri is mostly not a fair one. That said, passing mention in interviews with those working on Civ:BE was made that Civ:BE would be a sort of 'spiritual successor' to Alpha Centauri, which may be true in one sense but in another sense was only going to encourage comparisons to AC despite the games being rather unrelated.
But the big, fatal flaw with Civilization: Beyond Earth is that it fails in every conceivable way when compared to Civilization V. First of all, if you own Civ V with all the DLC, then you have the classic 'Civilization Sequel' problem of every Civ sequel having none of the DLC features of the game prior. Even Civ V launched without religion, which, actually now that I think about it, was a standard feature at launch of Civ IV. But what saved sequels in the past was that new mechanics were brought in that couldn't be added in another expansion: in Civ V, we have 1UPT (1 combat unit per turn), among other things, which really changes combat. But then we have Civilization: Beyond Earth, and whether you call it a sequel or a spin-off, it's still the next Civ game to come out. And it does virtually everything Civ V did, with a few minor tweaks, a less-linear tech tree (that still has distinct paths for certain strategies anyways), and way less content.
If you already own Civ V and all its DLC, you have almost everything in Civ V as well as a bunch of things Civ:BE got rid of. Civ:BE eliminated different air-unit types... there's only one air unit now, which has branching upgrades that give you a choice of an ability. That's it. No bombers. No fighters. Just one basic unit. Civ:BE also back-tracked to having no melee naval units. Civ:BE also has no unique music (all music plays for all sponsors). Civ:BE also lacks unique units (no sponsor has any units that the others can't also get). Civ:BE also lacks artistic details for leader screens (very minimalistic  indeed).
Add all that to the already in-grained issue of every new Civ game losing some features from the previous games, and you have a really good game that is virtually identical to the last one that probably a majority of prospective buyers already own.
Even 'new' features are not all that new: aliens are barbarians with a tiered system of aggression... affinities are basically an extension of the tech system since most affinity levels come through teching and not quests...  the tech web itself still plays out in a way where you will bee-line key techs and follow several linear paths. In fact, the tech web most-of-all is a let-down, because it's really just a different-looking tech tree you already saw in Civ V. To be fair, there are fewer pre-requisite techs for bee-lining certain things, but the new lay-out is not as different from Civ V, strategy-wise, as you might first suspect.
In the end, Civ:BE is a really good game... but is one that is likely to irritate its purchasers, as a large chunk will compare it to Alpha Centauri despite the two games being quite different, while an even bigger chunk will look at it and find it to be far less immersive than Civ V and drastically lacking in content *even before factoring in DLCs*. That's right, Civ:BE is one of the first Civ games in a long time that is virtually no better than the vanilla game before it (and Civ V vanilla wasn't even all that good). Which is ironic given that Civ:BE does incorporate some elements from Civ V's expansions (trade-routes, for one).
I can't recommend Civ:BE. It's just too much like Civ V, which with all its DLC is not significantly more expensive than Civ:BE. I can easily recommend getting Civ V, but not Civ:BE. In an alternate universe where Civ V does not exist, maybe then. But the fact is that Civ V exists and does everything better, especially the artisic elements.
Don't get me wrong: I like Civ:BE and will continue to play it. But not nearly like I played Civ V, because Civ V came out first and was a better game right-out-of-the-box in terms of interface and presentation. And even content-wise, Civ V had far more interesting unique elements for the civilizations than we'll probably ever see in Civ:BE.

This game's been sitting in my library for far too long...definitely one of the most fun indie games I've ever played. The gameplay is incredibly unique and kept my interest for the whole game. My one complaint is that the story is reaaally short. I beat it in one sitting in a little under 2 hours. I wish it had gone on for longer, since the mechanics are so interesting and fun to use.
Gameplay: The main mechanic is the ability to cut up the environment, pull it, and push it. Basically, you can create bridges  and pathways by selecting a certain region to cut up. It's utilized in many ways throughout the game and I was always amazed with the intuition required to complete some parts. It never got old, and I wish it had gone on for longer. Definitely one of the most creative ideas for a game I've ever seen.
Story: The writing and story is very cute and funny. You're set out on a quest to stop your evil counterpart, "Big", from getting his hands on your Grandpa's underpants. It's a pretty hilarious concept, but it actually gets somewhat deep towards the end.
Level Design: I LOVE that you can create your own pathways and solve puzzles in different ways every time. There is a great amount of replayability in this game because you can always approach things from a different angle. The levels are very well designed and it's generally pretty easy to find where you're supposed to go.
Graphics: I love the style of this game. It looks like a comic book or something. It's always pleasing to look at, and it runs very well.
I had no idea what I was getting into when I started this game, but it turned out to be one of my favorite indie games. The one problem is the length...definitely get this game if you're into interesting gameplay and cute storylines. 9/10

For a space RTS game, this is definitely where it's at. Although it doesn't hone the capabilities of taking control of a single ship, it does give a good space fun their fill of fun. Be careful as you can get caught and quickly start pouring hours into single player missions or playing against your friends online! If you are looking for me to expand on the personal story of Sins of a Solar Empire I cannot do it. Why? I don't have enough background information to tell you exactly what the story is but I can tell you how the game holds up! Even if you're not a hardcore space fan, you could most likely easily put 10 hours into the game. This may be in part in how the game develops to play style.
Sins of a Solar Empire is described as an 4X type of game (explore, expand, exploit and exterminate). There is quite a bit to do and manage. To begin, there are three races that the player is able to choose from : the (industrial) TEC, the (psychics) Advent and the (alien zergish looking) Vasari. Each race has it's own unique distinctions and units but all sort of share the same build options regarding ships and buildings alike. The TEC (human race) is not as good technologically as the other races but is good at poking away at opponents slowly (attrition warfare). The Advent race has great energy weapons but lack armor and prefer shields. They also can use their cultural influence on other planets in an attempt to shift opinion. The Vasari beat both the humans and the Advent regarding their technological and ship abilities. However, these high quality ships come at a steep price!
The game play itself is actually pretty good. It's easy to keep track of what's going on from planet to planet and they made it extremely easy to upgrade/build. If you are wanting to upgrade an aspect of a planet (say civilian infrastructure, emergency shelters, exploring more of the planet and (not limited to) industry or social focus), it can be done easily. Managing planets was made with ease while managing fleets takes a bit of work. There are lot of commands in games that the keyboard can take care of. It will take a while to figure out what is what but as long as you know what the icons mean, you're gold. Research and diplomacy can be taken care of by clicking the tabs up top. Research is broken into a few categories in which focuses on either military, defense, diplomatic, civilian infrastructure and fleet upgrades. New units, abilities or even additional damage can added to your arsenal. Be wary though! To create capitol ships or titan units (mega ships), you will need "command" staff and will have to upgrade not a unit amount, but the command slot amount.
I'm a bit confused regarding single player as there doesn't seem to be a campaign mode. Rather, it seems they took the approach of single individual missions against the AI. This might irritate a lot of players but may also entice a lot of players into playing single missions. Multiplayer saved games are a bit tricky (see :
). All players must have their own save file but the save file cannot be sent player to player (as one player may be using your race/units). The diplomacy portion of the game is a little weary as well. It's good but nothing too outstanding. Missions can be given to factions and vice versa (as well as trade options and the sort). Completing these missions reflects on your relations with factions. Pirates can also be hired within the game in case you don't want to attack your opponent directly. It can cost you a pretty penny though!
There are a few things you can tweak in-game considering winning conditions. Default mission settings uses domination, which means that you basically have to take over the map. There is a diplomatic victory in which you need to acquire the most diplomatic points to win. Research victory where (obviously) you need to complete the most research or reach a specific tier. There is an occupation victory in which special militia will keep spawning at a certain planet and players must control (occupy) this planet for a certain amount of time. Reaching this time means victory. There are other winning conditions such as capitol planet and capitol ship in which both (or one - your choice) have to stay alive. If your capitol planet becomes occupied, you lose. If your capitol ship gets destroyed, you lose. Within this menu you can also change how many planets are within the map and starting conditions. They give you a decent amount of options to customize your game so you can enjoy how you wish.
The game's currency system is quite simple and has some nice additions. Coins are your basic income and will need it to buy majority of things. (NOTICE : if you are losing coins and do not know why, you do not have enough civilian infrastructure on your planets)! Crystals are the next and finally metal. Metal and crystal are harvested from asteroids and can be traded if you build a trade system (increasing your economy). Metal and crystal can be sold or bought. They attempted an interactive market where the prices will drop and rise. The game will give you a small heads-up but it's always a good idea to keep an eye on the prices.
The
themselves are actually decently good. They is a lot of attention to detail and most phaser/ion cannon shots are noticeable. Ships taking damage is also apparent as well as when ships attack planets (you can see mini explosions on the surface)! In addition, you can see traffic moving about the planet and cities.
are pretty good (explosion sounds could vary a bit) and you can hear ships jump from planet to planet. The dialogue in game is good but as most RTS games, you'll start hearing the same voices in your head.
Overall, a pretty good space RTS game. I would recommend it for die-hard space fans and would recommend the casual gamer to buy on sale so there is no love lost. After playing for 10+ hours and playing different game modes (victory conditions), it is beginning to be redundant. Like I said, I can see a lot of gamers immersing themselves into this game. I would love to see some individual control given to the player as well as maybe adding a campaign? All the space RTS stuff is right, maybe it's now time to take it an extra step?

If you are looking for a stealth game, Betrayer is just barely worth it, and only because there are so few stealth games that it gets into the top 10 by default.
If you are looking for an FPS game, a story game, a game with unique art style, a game with intersting morals, or a game that will be fresh, new and unique; you will find some exquisite morsels drowning in a cauldron of time consumption. What was there wasn't enhanced, built up, or polished to a shining beacon, but instead buried and muddied and lost in overgrowth.
It really is a shame, because this game had amazing moments. I looked forward to every conversation I had with the Lady in Red. Though they ultimately weren't substantive, they were still emotionally interesting to me. The setting was extremely unique, and supported and enhanced by all the types of interactions in the game. The enemies were strange and exciting when they were newly introduced. There was a strong atmosphere of forbidding at key moments. Atmosphere was created naturally, not artificially. The weapons felt nice. The graphics were beautiful and it felt good just exploring the area and engaging in skirmishes with the enemies. The stories were realistic in the sense that they were tangled messes of human tragedy, without simple solutions.
But then Betrayer backpeddled hard over all it had going for it.
The progress is entirely composed of digging up items after circling and crisscrossing the map two or three times. The maps have a nice coat of paint, but underneath they are just empty expanses. There are ferns. There are trees. There are some forts. There are large boulders. There are some broken fences. I might not have noticed the lack of substance, I might not have even minded.... except first I had to clear the locations of enemies so I didn't die constantly or have to circle around them for an even longer traversal. Then I had to clear the map of items and clues scattered across the landscape. (this is just arriving at the location, clicking, reading a sentence description, then moving on to the next 40 items.) Then I had to run around the map for a third time, but now in the dark, to retrieve a few more things. Wash, rinse, and repeat for all 8 maps. Don't expect the gameplay to vary or become more interesting (which the game conveys openly reasonably clearly). There are a few new enemies introduced over time, but the interaction with them is largely the same. Worse, what was once strong and salient in the game, becomes tedium and annoyance.
Almost all of the above problems could have been solved if this game was 1/3rd the length. But of course then it would have only been 1/3rd the length. Not a problem in my book, but it would demonstrate more obviously the lack of new content in the game. It is hard to say the game "lacks content," because the maps have loads of treasure and things to find scattered across them. Clues are unique, notes are unique, stories are unique, but they don't really add more to the experience. If you have read Atlas Shrugged, you might know what I mean about it being good except that the second 2/3rds are just the first 1/3rd over again.
It is worth it in terms of unique experience and good storytelling plus excellently executed atmosphere early on, but not worth it in terms of time spent jogging across maps and slowly dissolving amounts of fun. 10-15 hours total, ~4-8 hours of worthy content.
It is enjoyable, and yet a slog at the same time. (Maybe get it anyway?)

And it's probably best to think of the game as Homefront: Episode 1 due to its length. But armed with that knowledge, I came out of it with an enjoyable experience overall.

In my years I've played many rugby league and union games, and I can say this is poor.  I really wanted to like this game.  Having read other negative reviews I had hoped that they were overly critical, but no, this game is mediocre and you should avoid it right now.
PROS:
- The players faces look realistic and adds to the viewers immersion into the game.  I'm interested to know how much time was spent on face scanning and player models because the game is constantly zooming in on their faces.
- less annoying commentary allows one to enjoy the game
- In general good! Considering rugby league live does not have close to the same budget as EA Sports FIFA or 2k's NBA2k the game looks nice
CONS:
- Aside from creating a stadium, there is not anything new to incentivise people to buy this game.  This game does not do anything better than RLL3, except player faces.
- Frustrating.  Forward passes seem to happen at random.  Running from dummy-half is pointless.  Tackling system is awkward, holding down the player in the tackle to slow the play is worthless.
- Players stand still for no reason.  Attackers make a line break and the defending fullback will run next to the attacker to the tryline when it could easily move closer and tackle.  AI runs on the last tackle far too often.   AI doesn't position itself well for kick returns.  AI runs past tryline.
- Similar to RLL3, if you pass just before the defensive line the player in possession with break the line by a few metres before passing without being touched because the defenders can not tackle during the passing animation, just looks ugly and does not flow well.  I've seen the AI run past the tryline because the putdown animation took too long.  Tackle a forward 8 metres from your tryline? Watch as he slowly walks over the tryline and scores while you do nothing because the tackle animation will not allow another player to enter the tackle.
- Beyond Disappointing for many reasons. Exactly the same as RLL3.  The season statistics does not show how many points a player has scored.  Want your player to win top pointscorer at the Dally M Awards? Good luck because unless you count the tries and conversions yourself you'll have no idea how many points they've scored, or any other player for that matter.  There is no way to look at other teams roster, annoying because those who play career mode want to see players move teams and develop.  I played career mode as the Cowboys and Lachlan Coote improved to a 95 rating, wow I wonder how he compares to other players.  I couldn't compare him to other players unless I was in the recruitment section in which you can only see the ratings of players with expiring contacts, or by managing representative teams and comparing myself.  Player contracts were unrealistic, Shannon Boyd a 94 rating as one of the best (he could have been the best, but there is no simply way to check that) wanted a $350k contact.  In an era of rugby league where top players are earning million dollar contacts the game does not reflect that, allowing you to stockpile top players on small contacts.
- Simple spelling mistakes on loading screens really annoyed me.
I accidently skipped the Dally M Awards screen and there was no way to go back and see who won!  There was a headline on the Dally M Team of the Year but you can't open it to see who made the team.  What is the point of including that in the game?  A major part of a career mode is seeing progression and recorded statistics of seasons one plays is important.
- Not annoying, but noticeable
Hopefully in patches this game will improve and it will be worth the listed price, but in it's current state I can not recommend this

I played this a long♥♥♥♥♥time ago on 360 back in 2010, and heard the initial release of deadrising 2 was botched on pc for many reasons (windows live being a thing unfortunately being one of them). Never completed it, found it difficult to play back in the day, and even now the game can be difficult to play. There are still some issues left even when windows live stopped going on. some of the cutscenes are clearly rendered for 30fps when it is running for 60fps, and the loading times are still long and tedious and in abundance, like the original deadrising and on the xbox 360. unfortunately, it seems regardless of PC specs the load times are long and annoying. The number one complaint I hear about this game is the TIME CONSTRAINTS and how it doesn't allow time to be invested in doing whatever you like completely. For example, getting Katie (your daughter) the drug she needs is something a lot of people really did not want to bother with, but it is obviously a key component to making this zombie game different from the rest. The time constraints for me do not take away from the experience, but rather, make me invest my time well into what things I want to do in the playthrough, like doing certain missions and ones which I can live with missing, saved for another replay.
Anyway, besides those obvious issues, the game itself still holds up fantastically, and it makes me sad the game is almost long forgotten at this point, that being obvious with the global achievements tracker showing people that have played this game lately, only 2 percent have beaten it. To me, the game holds up remarkably well, despite its age, and while I haven't played deadrising 3, mainly because of apparent issues with the port on PC, this game still does the series justice. TONS of replayability, the co-op is weird but still amazing to have with a friend, and the soundtrack to this game holds a special place in my heart. for example go look up Kill the Sound by Celldweller, it is a fantastic song from this game's official soundtrack. It is just so sad seeing the game on Steam being long forgotten because of its horrible PC launch probably botching the popularity the game deserves.
Overall, if you enjoy co-op zombie games with a million and one creative ways to kill them, don't mind using a plug in controller over mouse and keyboard, like your game to not be taken seriously in most cases (the story is incredibly parody-like and quite self-aware) and do not mind the time constraints, this game is definitely worth a purchase for that experience alone.

Gat out of Hell is a standalone expansion to Saints Row 4 and so far, the last game in the seminal gangster and crackdown-like series, Saints Row. Directly continuing from an ending to Saints Row 4. Unlike Saints Row 4, they don't get lazy and re-use the same city design, and instead design a city of floating islands and seas of fire and brimstone. Compared to Steelport, the playable space, despite being smaller and somewhat held back by the ugly graphics that the series has come to bear more and more sequel after sequel, it is far more exciting of a setting because it doesn't look ot feel as dull or generic as Steelport. Some of this is lost through a lack of selectable radio stations though. Even if it doesn't make any sense, open world games can sometimes build themselves on their use of music, and the lack of anything that you'll remember is to say the least, extremely disappointing.
Gameplay changes from 4 by giving the playable characters wings, allowing you to fly around almost uninterrupted instead of having to chain jumps like in Saints Row and Crackdown. However, it doesn't feel new anymore. The powers in Saints Row 4 were new and added new twists to the somewhat choppy formula of Saints Row The Third to make it more enjoyable, while here, it doesn't feel improved and feels more akin to a total conversion mod or a mission pack sometimes, despite the higher production values for the playable space design.
People who were into the over-the-top plots and set-ups of Saints Row 3 and 4, or those long-time faithfuls from Saints Row and Saints Row 2 will be extremely disappointed if they expect plot. The entire game is built around activities and diversions, and some of the activities are really slow and boring, and the story content is completely pointless as is, so your value in this game will be down to your enjoyment of Saints Row 4 in particular. If you enjoyed the jumping around, then New Hades is far better suited to that sort of gameplay.
Character customisation in all forms is gone, disappointing, but if you have a Saints Row 4 save present, similar to Fable, it will read the last saved SR4 save and import your character from that save into the cutscenes that feature the Playa.
There isn't much to say about Gat out of Hell. If you like jumping, flying, collecting and Saints Row activities, then you'll get something out of this. If you wanted an ending to the series that wrapped up all the loose ends of Ultor, the Zin Empire, and the advertised Dex revenge if you care, then you'll be disappointed with what you get here. Recursion Deluxe is a quaint little 8-bit puzzle platformer. Gradually ramping up in difficulty over the course of 60 mind-bending levels (that I'm aware of at the time of this writing), the game utilizes gravity switching, reminiscent of parts of LIMBO, and other physics based game mechanics, to allow you to solve puzzles and reach the level exit. Recursion Deluxe should scratch your retro and masochistic itches in equal measure. RECOMMENDED!

I don't really get all the bad press on X Rebirth. There are definitely some serious flaws in the game but there is still alot to like about it and I wouls still recommend it, although with only about 18 hours in the pilots seat, I still have allot to investigate and try. Here's my opinion about what is good and bad about X Rebirth, not that my opinion matters...
Good:
-Awesome graphics. The game looks amazing and runs perfectly smooth on my system (i7 4970 @ 3.6ghz, GTX770, 16gb DDR3).
-Lots of huge and wildly varied space stations and other vehicles to see.
-Really cool Bladerunner/Fifth Element kind of atmosphere.
-You can actually dock at the stations and get up and walk around the ship and into the station.
-The "highways" and "super highways" IMHO are kind of a cool way to get around systems.
-I have found ship to ship combat to be great fun in XR.
-The "flight" controls, for me, are about as close to perfect as they can be. I use a G940 stick/pedals/throttle in a fighter jet sort of arangement except for the addition of strafing controls assigned to a little mini x/y axis hat. IMHO thia is an ideal setup for the way I like to "fly".
-No fuel issues!!! In other space sims it seems like I am always about to run outta gas. Not an issue in XR.
-The navigator argues with the ships computer.
Bad:
-Extremely limited systems and sectors. The XR universe, although quite varied and beautiful, feels very small compared to other space sims. I have an XR "galaxy" map and there aren't but maybe half a dozen systems on it. News flash! The 'verse is a whole lot bigger than that!
-The system and sector maps just plane suck in XR. That's all I need to say about that.
-I rarely ever have time to play multiplayer anything so it isn't that big of a deal to me, but no multiplayer at all? Really?
-Only one ship with a really stupid name that cannot be changed. Although you can own other ships, you cannot pilot them although I have heard there are "bridge" mods so you can sort of "be there" on the bigger ships.
-My trackIR 5 won't work in XR.
-You can get off your ship and walk around the stations but all the stations and people are very generic and look alike.
-No standard FTL/jumpdrive.
-An FTL/Jumpdrive can be found now, thanks to the version 4.0/HoL update, but it isn't something you can just buy and install. Apparently there is some sort of quest for this experimental drive that has you trekking all over the galaxy, such as it is, looking for parts and pieces.
-Did I mention that the system/sector maps really suck?
-The navigator is always arguing with the ships computer.
There may seem like more bad than good, but other than two or three of those issues, they are mostly just personal preference. There is still allot to like about XR and I definitely enjoy playing it.

Recursion Deluxe is an accessible, yet challenging, game that will test both your twitch platforming skills along with your puzzle solving aptitude.  I've included my full thoughts in video form here:
- Graphically charming
- Catchy soundtrack
- Tight controls
- Excellent level design
- Enticing 'one more try' gameplay
I feel the level design in particular is worth expanding upon a bit more.  Levels and level progression are designed to teach the player the mechanics naturally through gameplay.  There's no tutorials here, just design that promotes learning.  Mechanics are introduced one at a time throughout the levels, allowing you to both feel like you're getting a grasp on things and feel accomplished when you put all the pieces together to complete a particularly difficult level.
Also, at $5 it's hard to pass up!

A charming puzzle platformer with an emphasis on puzzles, timing and precision.
There's nothing particularly new at work here, though most of the levels are well crafted and unique feeling. The main gimmicks are the non-euclidean geometry and gravity reversal, with plenty of switches, keys and obstacles to make for interesting puzzle solving and platform jumping. It definitely feels like a game I've played before, and yet it kept my attention from beginning to end.
The game is quite short, but for the price seems about right. The difficulty curve is slow and steady, with most of the game feeling a bit on the easy side, though I do consider myself well-traveled in this genre. Most of the challenge comes from collecting the game's completely optional stars, and dying has no penalty.
Recommended to puzzle fans, platforming fans, and retro game fans alike.

TL:DR - It was fun and very nice to look at. Just make sure to switch the color saturation to normal if your eyes start to hurt from the base color style.
Game isn't very long but will occupy a good 6-8 hours if you take the time to read the dialogue and do the side investigations. The combat is very basic. Look at enemy and either shoot it with an arrow or musket ball or slash at it with your knife. There are stealth mechanics but it's only helpful some of the time. You find charms which act as modifiers for your weapons and melee but for the most part they seem to have been a feature that felt like it was quickly added versus being well though out as you can get some hefty bonuses from them later in the game.
The story is interesting but strewn about the game world so if you don't take the time to dig up every hole and open every chest and talk to every NPC then you will end up leaving this game lost and confused. There is some back tracking but it's not terrible and for the most part if you can get this game on sale or from a bundle then it is worth taking the day to play it.
The game itself has some "funny" sound effects and it won't win any awards there but the world itself is beautiful. The areas could have been created a little better by possibly adding some wildlife or more interactable objects but the base game is fine the way it is. You are supposed to feel alone in a hostile world where everything wants to kill you, afterall. It does seem a bit odd though to hear birds chirping and crows screeching but to not actually see any flying or wandering around on the forest floor scrapping for food and what not but it isn't exactly going to hurt the game any by not seeing them.
Overall the game was a wonderful experience and maybe with time there will be some DLC or a sequel that will utilize the  base game's features and world to create a successful sequel.

This was a fun game.  I'd like to see a sequel expand it and smooth out some of the flaws, but it was certainly a good time.  It definitely has the mark of Monolith all over it and I always dug their style.  The 17th century, colonial setting was definitely a highlight.  Unlike some reviewers, I found the old school sometimes frustrating weapons to be quite a blast to shoot.  Since the enemies weren't overly difficult, the slow and possibly accurate reload times made for a few tense fights, especially against the floating skull like enemies in the dark world.  The story/backstory that you discovered by interacting with ghosts, journal entries and spirits was appropriately cryptic and swirling with American Gothic touches.  Oddly enough, it reminds me of a more polished version of the underrated Gamecube game Geist sans the possession element.  But it has that similar mix of low key exploration and bursts of combat.
The option to play with different color saturations was pretty awesome and despite the temptation and a few experiments with color, I found the default black and white to create a trippy, foreboding atmosphere.  When you break it down the overall mix of the game was like combining a hack n' slash loot collector with survival horror and typical first person action/adventure/shooter elements.  I ended up mixing up my arsenal quite a bit, even if the longbow is man's best friend and the ultimate equalizer.  All told the environments were alot of fun to explore and I found myself trying to locate the majority of POIs during my time in the game, although I missed a couple of things.  I also actually enjoyed that all of the story and character interactions were with text instead of bad voice acting of some sort.  It lent a relaxing feel to the more town-based segments of the game; a good breather from all of the woods wandering and shoot outs with psychotic conquistadors.
With all of the positives I feel about this game, it did have some drawbacks.  After awhile the gameplay started becoming a tad repetitive.  It wasn't a nailing mistake but towards the end a few objectives borderlined on tedium.  Perhaps after beating Deadlight on nightmare, this game just didn't feel challenging enough.  Once I got the shovel and had all of the strongest gear and most of the upgrades, I was a pretty unstoppable force.  Those friggen spiders put me down a few times though.  Enemy variety is also pretty scant and though they were fun to fight, I got somewhat tired of mopping the floor with the same dopes over and over again.  As a hardcore gamer I of course played with the deadliest enemies setting and while I got taught a few lessons early on whenever I was still figuring out the gameplay/mechanics, once you get the hang of what you're doing and stock up on deadly gear, only a few select sections provided any challenge.  The final boss battle was also a joke and took me only one try to complete.  But overall this is a pretty great game to play through once.  I might leave it installed and someday go back and earn some achievements I left in progress, but once you're done there really aren't any extra features/modes to come back to besides a free roam of the environments with baddies still lurking.  The Steam achievements I did miss are already mostly completed or on their way, so even with the things left undone, I really feel that I got the most out of the game I could get...  The campaign was a blast though with a runtime that should take you over 10 hrs to complete, depending on how much you want to upgrade (I personally maxed out health, ammo capacity and weapon types to their fullest).
Overall this is worth your time if you're looking for a first person blaster with more esoteric ideas and rural Americana vibes.  So, for those who don't want to read all of my b.s., let me break it down a little further from a gamer who has been smashing buttons since '84!
Pros:
-Very cool atmosphere with unique color saturation options and an eerie black n' white world
-Lush colonial setting with fun period weapons
-Not alot of monsters but the ones you do encounter are fun to fight (even if they are a bit thin in the IQ department)
-Interesting use of two distinct worlds (light/dark) with a gameplay rhythm that develops between the two
-Solid graphics and excellent landscapes with intricate special effects (wind gusts, dynamic lighting, etc.)
-Mostly satisfying campaign with enough to do and see to keep you progressing
-Adventure elements well-employed with almost a light Zelda style exploration/backtracking for loot/treasure/equipment
-Intuitive inventory/map/journal system that was fun to use/manage
Cons
-Easy enemies even on the hardest setting once you have the mechanics down/enough upgrades
-Safe zones/forts were a nice touch, but could have used more fleshing out (like being able to enter buildings)
-Some design choices seem half-baked (giving items to Alison/lady in red with seemingly no game effect, etc.)
-Tasks/objectives become rather samey 2/3s through the game.
-Only a few enemy types and weak final boss encounter
-As much fun as I had it's really a one playthrough affair.
-Could have used a few actual boss fights for some variation...it would have been fun to see how they would have played out with the primitive weapons.
-Sound design was average which took away some of the potential horror chills.  The creepy ambience of the nether world, wind and atmospheric cues were all good.  Guns, weapons, enemies were all rather laughable.
Rating:  7.8/10
For me this is so close to an 8, but just not quite that good.  Still, I think it's well worth a go and I'd sign up for a sequel or any DLC content in the future.  Happy gaming gang!

This is a good game. But more detail will be of use to you here so I shall break it down in stages for you.
Graphics/Aesthetics = Excellent
The game is both visually pretty with nice graphical capability, but more importantly the aesthetics, the look and design choices made in this game, portray a frontier style space sim. All the ships are scuffed and looks like they get used, the weapons aren't overly flashy and suit the rest of the game well, satisfying to connect with broadsides and powerful looking beams. The only slight complaint I can draw is that the CGI for the rare interpersonal scenes is shown to be pretty basic when you see it try to draw a human, in a way that the aliens don't make so obvious.
Sound = Excellent
The music in the game is great, kicking in different tempos for the action or the cruising and really helping to complete the frontier aesthetic the graphics present. The game makes it easy to put your own playlist in so you can dictate the range of music during fights or time on stations or cruising. I don't think this is needed at all, but the feature is nice. There is sound in space which is of course a break from reality but definitely neded, as a quiet game with no audio feedback on your actions would not be as absorbing.
Gameplay = great
The campaign is there to give you something to do, but you can ignore it as long as you like and just enjoy an open sandbox if you want. There are various missions you can take on for cash or you can try and mule cargo around for fun and profit, or look for juicy asteroids to mine. The game decides to stick us on a flat 2D plane, which is unusual for a space sim but I think a very good decision. The controls are fairly simplified, and as you are not in a fighter but rather a capital ship you don't really notice this as a problem. In fact it feels just about right, and by removing the up/down axis it makes a space environment a lot more accessible to the player.
Travel times while you warp about are small enough, as the speed increases when you are further from other objects. The warping can and will be broken up by things like debris fields or enemy encounters, or you may be notified that you are passing by a distress signal or something to investigate, so there is none of the waiting around that often leads to boredom by a space game trying to show you how vast their world is by dragging you through long travel times.
Encounters are either challenging, easy or out of your league. Mostly the area you are in will dictate how hard encounters are. This means that the difficulty will be roughly right for the section of the story mission you are up to, though when you move to a new system you will not realise how outclassed you are until you are being blown away. Fortunately leveling up your gear and ship is not actually very time consuming as rewards for missions scale up with you. Grinding is not something that doesn't exist in this, but it is minimal.
The biggest annoyance in this game is one that feels like it was meant to be a better, more robust feature but was left in a basic state. When you are hailed by an enemy or even the system police force, you get a very basic dialogue system. All the enemies give you is four options, two of which are utterly pointless, one is possibly useful if you are in good with them, and one allows a surrender. It feels like this was meant to be a more in depth feature to allow you to talk your way out of it if you are way out of their league. Eventually I ignored incoming hails entirely because they were pointless.
There story completion also doesn't end the game allowing you to go to greater lengths with your ships and tech, but by the time you reach that point there aren't many more mountains to climb so while there are plenty of game hours to be had, and replaying can likely give you a different experience, unless you are all about completing your achievements you will run out of things to do.
Story = Good
The story is fine and there are no real complaints. It is a little basic, and despite a few dialogue options you are pretty much railroaded to the next story chapters. You can differ your means but the outcome isn't going to change. That's fine, this isn't a grand space opera. The game is simply aware of its own scope and doesn't try to be more than that.
If you like Freelancer, this is a game you can probably sink your teeth into, and I do reccomend it for anyone who likes non-fighter based space simulation single player games.

Oh, Hitman Absolution..where do I start? After 43 hours of trying to get the "perfect" score, according to the scoring system of course, I finally beat this.. (terribly) flawed 'masterpiece'. Hitman Absolution, could've been the best Hitman, as of previous Hitman game, IO fix some "annoyance" in previous title, refining existing feature, and adding new one to keep it fresh and open up new feature. That's exactly what Absolution did, but along the way, they implementing some 'questionable' (and sometimes rather terrible) changes to the games, preventing it from becoming the best Hitman ever created, hell.. at some moment I feel like rating Absolution my 4th favorite Hitman game (my least favorite was the first one),
Well, just let's just go on with the actual review:


+ Gorgeous! I love the attention in detail this game shows, I really like the atmosphere and tone. It looks really cinematic. And talking about cinematic, IO's presentation has gone up by 300% in Absolution. From the map detail and cinematic, it has a top notch presentation. Hitman Absolution is a downright nice game to look at. Oh, and the animation is pretty smooth.
+/- I might like the overall feel of  Absolution, but sometimes I think this kind of tone is a bit off for Hitman. Way too cinematic for me, everything's is just so shiny (especially 47's head), in oppose of the dark/gritty atmosphere of the first 4 (especially Contracts). The effects is a bit overdone at times.

+The ability to take cover, and subduing enemy from cover, auto dragging after garroting someone, hiding a body in closet are some really welcomed addition. The UI is greatly improved, less obtrusive and more intuitive , though I never had a problem with the previous one, Absolution just modernized it in the right way.
+/-: The disguise system. In a way, it's nice to see that 47 isn't completely safe when he's in disguise, when people question "Is this a new guy? Have I seen him before?", it adds up the realism, but in quite many cases, it becomes an annoyance where you just can't concentric on observing the various possibility a map can offer, and it brings up the flaws on Hitman Absolution..
+/- Oh wait, the scoring system. It's an overhaul that no one asked for, OK, the leaderboard thing is cool,  and brings up a nice competitive heat. And the obtrusive-ness depend on how "perfectionist" the player is. As for me, it's a double edged sword, at one side, It pumps my inner "Perfect Assassin" soul, but in the other side, I don't like my definition of a Perfect Assassin is dictated by a score. Like: "OK, I'll shoot this guy with a Sniper Rifle, perfect spot, no one's looking" *shoot poor guy* *Gets 20,000 points*  "OH GOD I SHOULD USE THE GARROTE WIRE FOR THE EXTRA 7500!" *Spent extra 45 minutes to get past guards*.
- Linear map design. Absolution might have an amazing attention in detail on the map's texture, props, and all. But detail in term of gameplay and layout, it's rarely to be found here. Gone the blueprint, majestic, open-world playground, replaced by a map that is designed for the sake of the progression of the story. The less obvious pathway is actually obvious in comparison of previous title. There's an entrance, you can go by 2 way, front or side, there's a property, we make it stand out, it means it can be used to kill the victim, and there's an exit, guarded by annoyingly lots of some patrolling and stand-still guards. Of course, it's not true for all levels, Chinatown, Blackwater, and Street of Hope are the stand out there.
- - The checkpoint system, the biggest sin of Absolution. THAT AT TIMES-OBSCURELY-PLACED-DAMNED-CHECKPOINT. I hate it, with a passion. They replace the perfect traditional saving system, where I can save anytime-anywhere, when I want to experiment things, that I know it could go wrong, they replace it with this..thing... And everytime I reload a checkpoint the enemies that I previously subdued magically re-appear, is this secretly a resurrection tool or something? This thing..is just.. I'm speechless, for no good reason..at all..
+ The voice acting is a huge step up from previous title. The characters feels more alive, and adds up a bit of emotion, and overall the sounds / sound effects is fine for me.
+/- Great, but didn't quite match up the previous title. Jesper Kyd departure does make a noticeable impact to the musical tone, though I'm not attentive enough when it comes to soundtrack, but I know the OST is pretty great when I come to YouTube just to listen to it. Absolution, doesn't give that feeling to me, or at least, not much.
+ I like how the story is presented, in cinematic perspective. The progression, some twist, and clearer sense of plot and decent character development. A smoothly flowing and intriguing story.
- I like the story, I like the presentation, but I don't like the type of narrative, the way it's told. It's trying to be dramatic, and it becomes out of place most of the times. I like the "Get in, assassinate, get out" kind of narrative, while the story is told through the briefing and short opening/middle/ending scene. It just feels like a more proper assassin story.

Hitman Absolution is an ambitious entry of the game, over-ambitious perhaps, and it's quite obvious. And ambition can result something like Absolution. A game with really high production value and very polished, yet tends to overdo everything, to the point that it forgot what it is in the first place, but it's awfully familiar in many elements. My review might seems harsh, especially in the gameplay section, but trust me.. it's still a fun game. A sneak-em-up action/adventure with a lot of decent, yet limited assassination, a, at times, way too strict sandbox game. A more 'methodical' Hitman, rather than the 'imaginative' one. But, it's still an awesome game, but  it's a "just good" Hitman game. It's still a fun and solid game, with a deep and rewarding stealth system, though IO's attempt to keep every Hitman entry fresh is riddled with few bad design choices this time.

I am very sad and a bit conflicted about giving this game a negative review.  In truth I consider it "meh".  Its only real contribution to gaming as a whole is the broadside, Assassin's Creed 4 style ship to ship combat, which is a lot of fun.  The rest of the game is a pretty stripped down and bare bones space sim.  Almost all missions involve combat, even the trade runs.  Being knocked out of warp is commonplace and makes just getting from point A to point B needlessly tedious.  The universe has no depth, there are several factions with friend/neutral/foe ratings you can adjust, but none of them have any substance or even an explanation as to who or what they are.  Trading and mining profits scale poorly as such that they're not a real way to make money as the game progresses.
All of these things being said I did put 50+ hours into the game and earned all the achievements.  I enjoyed myself through at least some of that or I wouldn't have done it.  The real problem comes down to the fact that its just a bare bones game that does one thing well: combat.  This is a space game to get if you want to get in quick shoot stuff and get out.  Its also good for fans of the show Firefly who like that type of universe and that type of "space-western" soundtrack.  Personally its not my cup of tea but that's just a subjective opinion.  While I don't necessarily regret buyint ir or playing it, I don't think I would have missed out anything had I never bought it.

Let's play a game. When you read something that makes your heart sink, you can stop reading this review and take it as assurance that this game/DLC/toothbrush on Halloween of an experience isn't for you. Ready?
1) This game is short. Don't take my "time played" as gospel - I played most of it in offline mode. But I'd estimate I beat this in around 4 hours. Maybe a little bit longer. Not horrible for a DLC, but I'm not 100% sure it was meant to be one. Jury's still out.
2) The already slimmed down gameplay feature set of SR4 has been stripped even closer to the bone leaving gristle and stringy bits. Cars and characters can no longer be customized (not even clothing), radio stations went the way of the dodo, a bunch of diversions/activites from previous games weren't included here, and the open world has the smallest map of any of the games to date. But all of that pales in comparison to the heaviest loss of all - story. This game has a premise at best. There's no main quest vs. side quest distinction here. You jump into an open world right away and do endless side content until the final boss waypoint populates itself on the map. The loyalty missions for your "allies" don't even have the story mission payoff that 4 had. And the callbacks to previous games and character cameos felt very half baked.
3) The flight mechanic... easily the feature with the highest potential... is a dud. It's inverted by default for some weird reason, and even after you change that it doesn't feel natural like some of the flyable vehicles in SR2 through 4. Luckily, upgrades are all cheap and come quicker than they did in 4, but none of them seem to fix the problem, just make it slightly more easily tolerable. Oddly enough, the flying races ended up being the most entertaining of the side quests available somehow.
Still with me? I'm surprised. Well maybe the last point will be enough to bump you out of the back of the wagon.
4) This costs more than SR 2 and 3. Almost as much as both put together. That's a crime seeing how it has maybe a third of the content 3 did which only had about half of the content of 2. This game is a rip off. I liked 4. I enjoyed 3 enough to finish it and then play a good chunk of the open world content afterwards. Even I can't justify GooH. I feel so lucky I got it as part of a bundle rather than being flattened with regret for wasting 15 bucks.
I can't even recommend this on sale. I can barely recommend playing it if you got it free. You're better replaying the previous games seeing how you'll get the same experience that you get here, only done better with more thought put into it and a g**d*** radio station to listen to.

It seems like most people are either gamers who enjoy experiences like this, or you deplore the idea of supporting something that’s so heinous. There’s so much controversy to this game, it’s unbelievable considering how tame it actually is. No matter how my, or anyone else’s review turns out, the game will likely be remembered over its controversy alone. This for me is really unfortunate, considering that Postal and other games that stirred up massive amounts of much-ado before their release; this game simply isn’t very engaging.
While everyone was debating the morals of this ‘mass-murder simulator’, accusing supporters of being psychopaths while the others defended their rights to enjoy whatever content they wish to support, we all forgot to ask ourselves the bigger questions; will this game even be enjoyable? Obviously, that’s a hard question to answer when you’re debating the ethics of it, but like all these outings- the quality took a backseat to the controversy. The outrage drove a spike between party lines, and once it did, it was guaranteed to make the developers money.
I’m here to tell you the truth as I see it, to look at the game as objectively as possible. Yes, there’s some fun destructive bits to this game- but overall the game becomes a bore rather quickly.
The gore, if that’s what you’re into, is kind of dull. Pulling people up to your waist, slitting their throat and then rinsing and repeating lacks any emotional weight. You’ll be forced to do them regardless though, because you need the health you only get by executing people. After a few of these killings, they lose any ‘charm’ you might get out of them- somehow making the task of merciless homicide an indifferent experience. If this is the selling point for the game, I just feel Mortal Kombat X’s fatalities are far gorier and have actual personality to them.
On the whole, this is an average game, with some impressive physics. I actually hope the studio gets some money from the hype machine they helped stoke, because I honestly believe this young studio will be able to develop more complex and interesting games. This game however was created for one reason- to upset the news shows, and raise up the whole ‘violence in games’ issue yet again. They’re not trying to make a statement- just like how they’re not condoning murder- they made this game in order to sell copies and pre-order shirts. Congratulations Destructive Creations, you’ve proven that people are easily offended- why don’t you prove in your next game you can actually impress.

The game really needed an additional year in the oven before releasing. What Egosoft was thinking when they released it in 2013 is beyond me. At its launch, the game was terrible. Barely anything worked, game breaking bugs were everywhere, it felt more like an alpha test for the game than anything else and because of that it suffered.
I decided back then that I wouldn't give it a review due to the sour taste it left in my mouth and just put it on the backburner for 3 years. Yea ... 3 years.
When I saw the 4.0 update I decided that it was time I gave the game another chance, a lot of people were praising it since the Teladi Outpost DLC for beginning to show its colors as an X game.
All the bugs that existed since launch have been fixed, I've managed to complete the campaign without hitting any kind of issue. The story has its ups and down, but in my opinion its final act and ending are not what I expected and somewhat unimpressive. The good part about it is that it leaves you wanting more.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from an X game. You start with a ship, some credits and your personal skills. What you do from there (if you don't start with the campaign) its up to you. Either go the route of a pirate and harrass the NPCs till the dawn of time, take on missions that are either combat, trading or exploring, go out on an exploration trip to find rare materials that can sell for a high price or maybe even some derelict ships you can capture or just build up an empire and slowly conquer the galaxy. Yep, just like an X game.
Now there is one thing I need to mention. What is a very big different between this X game and previous titles is that you cannot fly more than 1 ship. You better get used to the Albion (Pride) Skunk because that's the ship you'll fly till the dawn of time. And yes, you can reconfigure your cockpit so you can have a difference look about your ship, but honestly, its still just one ship.
Right now, the game is worth buying. If you can overlook some minor gripes like the 1 ship only thing, then the game is very enjoyable. Especially the empire building aspect of it.
