Will you rob the hospital for meds?
Will you take the fight to the bandits for parts?
It's about you
It's about how far YOU will go
It's about whether you can make your actions worthwile...
I can tell you that I would kill, rob and do anything for food when winter came, but in the end after all the deaths and blood on my hands, I too died and everything I did became a waste.
It's unlikely you will play this game for 1000+ hours, but I can tell you from experience that your actions in this game will remain with you for much longer.
In my eyes, this is a 9/10
The combat system could be improved but apart from that it's almost perfection + on the main screen you can choose to donate to the 'War Child' charity which I found to be a very heartwarming gesture from the devs.

Do not be drawn away by then 'mostly negitive'. This game had a bad release...very bad in fact. But guess what, Egosoft dosen't abandon it's children. No, they stay and rebuild, and what they have made out of it is worthy of the price tag.
Honestly there are a few things to note.
1: It's X:Rebirth, and removes a lot of ship controling and other features since X-3. It's more liken to the older X-Beyond the Frontier, in which you only owned one ship to fly, and upgraded it to suit your needs. X:Rebirth has attempted to bring back that feeling.
2: They tried something new and it didn't turn out right. Honestly I hate when these games come out and everyone bashes them for being 'off target' from it's origenal. Do you seriously expect a game to sell if it's just a copy each time and no risks are taken? It dosen't work that way. Even Nintendo, the big daddy of video games, has experimented and gotten smashed. Paper Mario Sticker Star for example... The fact is, you can't judge a game completely on it's predisesor, as everyone is diffrent, the new game that comes will also change.
So the game it's self visualy is breath taking. Giant super structure stations, wonderful space backgrounds, massive fire fights. The AI is also nice (But it's definatly not AGI) they can do some weird things, but are there to bring the automatic ecodemy and atmosphere of thousands to life. Gameplay can be rather dull at times, scaning stations, trading long distence with radios, running around on stations for offers and hidden godies. However, once you get an empire going you have meny things to do. The X series is a trading simulator in space with combat. Not a go shootem all up (that is until rather angry AGI and aliens attack.) My personal experience with the game is good. I've experienced very little problems other then a few scan points being inside the super structures (which you can glitch in and out of if you bounce around enough on it.) I recomend it for X series fans or someone who likes this type of game, but don't take this as the X series greatest impression. Play X-3 and it's expantions to get the full idea of how it works in good practice.

This game isnt my favourite. The game is a port from the Xbox and it never saves your controls. There are only a few positives on my side. This game is mainly focused on Ferrari as the title says.
Firstly I don't like how the game is just a failed port from the Xbox 360. The mouse doesn't work with any of the UI unfortunatley but you just have to figure out how to configure the keyboard with the buttons at the bottom that say "X, Y, A, B". I found navigating it quite easy because I used to play on a 360 but now im not sure why the kept that all in the PC version. The game only starts you off with a few cars and tracks which all seem impossible to play.
Now the reason why im writing this negativley is because the whole game feels extremely hard on easy difficulty and to drive you have all of these buttons that don't have any tutorials. I used a save file with the game because unlike games where all of the tracks and cars are unlocked and you just have to get money to buy new cars (Forza motorsport 4). The game has a nice graphics engine which is easially run on any computer. My older computer (Dell 9200) could run it at around 60fps. The reason I didnt list the settings is because there is none, no resolution change or motion blur disable. The game is designed to be on the Xbox with its simple graphics and forward facing sprite crowds. The sounds in the game are ok, they sound like a car would but the fact that the crowd is so loud you can hear them over the car sometimes. I would reccommend disabling all of the hud so that you can see the entire track ahead of you. The game is rather old now and it still has a community of around 200 people.
If you wan't a realistic driving game that has nice graphics I would reccomend a game like "The Crew" or "Forza motorsport" (it can easially be emmulated onto the PC). So overall; if you like Ferraris and one type of car only then this is most certainly the way to go, if you wan't a nicer more modern game that isnt ported from the 360 in such an awful way go for the games that I listed. This game isnt the greatest and I can understand that porting from the 360 wasnt to great back then, niether was the graphics. The game is not worth buying, unless you're a massive Ferrari fan who has an extra £15 or £3.75 to spend on the game then go for it.

This game is not what you'd classically call "fun." But that doesn't mean it's not good, because it's exceptional. What it excels at is putting you into the shoes for a group of survivors in a war torn nation struggling to survive hand to mouth for days on end. During the day you need to feed your survivors, keep their mental health sound, and occassionally deal with visitors there to trade or ask for help. At night you send a lone survivor out into the wild, picking a location to scavenge and hope that they don't get caught intruding or stealing. What makes these scavenging missions more interesting is the semi-random nature of what they contain and the encounters that can occur at them, such as witnessing the attempted♥♥♥♥♥♥of a young girl by a very well armed soldier? Do you let the soldier defile the women in exchange for a free run of the area, or do you risk your survivor by engaging him in combat?

First off, I have to say that my ultimate feelings on the game are... It's boring.
A lot of people have likened this game to a modern remake of the original problem. Here's the big problem with that notion. Postal offered a legitamite challenge to the player. There were varied forms of opposition, and a genuine challenge from level to level, and if you kept track of the journal entries of the character that were in the manual, there was a story about a man who was truly snapped in half. The reality of your actions in the game do not match the journal entries in the manual. You truly got more out of the experience than something like Hatred gives you.
Hatred has you playing a parody of a mass murderer. You go around shooting people. Then you do it again, and again, and again. Now, many will ask how that's any different from a game like Doom? Well, again, there's variety there. Different enemy types, and you're not *just* shooting things in a game like Doom. You're exploring a maze, you're tracking down key cards, or solving the hostility found within environments. Hatred doesn't have that. The only progression to be found in the game is that you go from completely unarmed civilians, to regular cops, to SWAT team guys, to soldiers. They're a little tougher. Ultimatel you're just slaughtering unarmed people with devastating firepower. It get's old fast.
My personal reccomendation? Buy Postal, Postal 2, and it's new DLC "Paradise Lost" you'll have far more fun that way.

Not sure why this has mixed reviews. It honestly doesn't deserve such negativity.
I've played Bioshock three times now and finished it once. The previous two times were both on the Xbox 360. The game had its fair share of crashes and glitches on the console. I never ended up finishing it on my console play throughs.
I picked the Bioshock collection up during a sale since I really wanted to play all the way through all three games and get the full experience. I've just completed the first game and I've got to say that I absolutely enjoyed it. The game was smooth, ran well, and had compelling story and gameplay that kept me hooked. Much, much easier to play on the PC than the console as well.
The majority of people are complaining about crashes and errors. I don't really understand all of these complaints.
The game crashed twice while I was playing. Once during a save and once when loading a new area. Two crashes. In nearly 18 hours of gameplay. For a game that was originally released roughly a decade ago, I feel like that's a pretty solid chunk of play time. After the first crash, while saving, I started saving more frequently. When the second crash occured, I actually only lost a minute or two of progress.
Other than that, there were one or two audio glitches that acted almost like a scratched disc (obviously not the case), but they corrected themselves and didn't impact gameplay at all.
The remastered quality is absolutely gorgeous. Like I said, I previously played on the console version of the game and the difference in quality was like night and day. The opening sequence when you first get a glimpse of Rapture is absolutely breathtaking. Everything after that is icing on the cake.
I highly recommend that you ignore all of the haters and complainers and try the game for yourself. If it's truly unplayable for you then return it, but don't let these whiners put you off getting what is an amazing game that has truly benefited from being Remastered.

Well.. BioShock 2... The premise is the same as in the original-Rapture, the underwater 'utopia' turned into hell when things go south. This time, I realised the character plays a big daddy (which is a pain and difficult to handle in the original) which goes by the name 'Subject Delta'. The gameplay in this one was almost the same with the original, with some extra new features like 'rescuing' little sisters from other daddies and to choose whether to gather adam, save or harvest them. In a way, the choices that you made (as well as killing other characters) will affect the decision at the end.
The graphics is awesome as always along with great music. With some scenes where you get to go outside and stroll around underwater, the details (and items hiding there) are great.
As the game progresses, you are helped with a few characters along the way (e,g, Sinclair and Eleanor). You are also helped with the usual upgrades throughout the game and what surprises me is that the number of secondary plasmids are heaps more than the original! Combined with some new weapons, different hack systems, defensive games (while little sisters gathering adam-be quick little one! I'm already using plasmids to make you gather more and work faster!), great audio logs, and nonetheless great story.
Well.. for the verdict...
Score: 9.2/10
While the fighting system had improved by leaps, it felt slightly... off. I couldn't explain exactly what, but I guess it was because of the high expectations of the original. I was expecting a bigger twist, and something that the original lack, satisfying finale.
All in all, this is a great game to play and a very good sequel try, knowing that numerous games failed to deliver on their sequel.

I’m still not completely sure how I felt about this one. Betrayer is a FPS exploration horror game from Blackpowder Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
I just want to lead with this: when it comes to reloading, Betrayer has it’s♥♥♥♥♥♥together. You can reload your gun while you sprint, consult the map (which I didn’t know I had until about three hours into playing the game), open chests, interact with various objects, jump, etc. Every shooter game out there should be taking notes when it comes to this. Every. Last. One.
Using flintlock weapons throughout the game was very fun and, for me, a first outside of the Assassin’s Creed franchise. (Well, excluding the Gekokujo mod for Mount & Blade: Warband, but that is a story for another time). The guns were incredibly accurate (something which is, by no means, historically accurate, but what is?) which made sniping enemies at a distance not only feasible, but a regular occurrence.
I loved the quasi-day and night cycle. Ringing the bell in the game turns the area from day to night and unleashes different enemies upon you as well as revealing wraiths and lost souls scattered across the maps for you to track down.
Betrayer had a consistently unsettling atmosphere. The lack of music was a big addition here, but also the feeling of loneliness. Apart from the wraiths, monsters, and the mysterious hooded lady, you’re completely alone in a fairly large wilderness. It was great and it really worked for the game.
The Bad
Compared to everything else you encountered, I felt like the skeletal enemies were poorly animated; as were the spider creatures. This was my only real complaint though.
The Meh
The game being set in (predominantly) monochrome was kind of cool to begin with, but it gets old after an hour or two. Splashes of red break up the monotony, but it’s just not enough. That’s right kids, don’t be fooled by the trailer, this game is colored in black, white, and red.
While the weapons are fun to use, there are not many of them. You’ve got your trusty knife and you have access to longbows, shortbows, crossbows, flintlock pistols, and muskets (all of varying quality). There are unique weapons to find, but they don’t look any different from any other weapons.
There are not many types of enemies you’ll end up fighting either. You’ve got your conquistadors, big conquistadors, natives, ash people, spider creatures, skeletons, and demons. That’s all there is.
Verdict: Yea
For a $9.99 price tag, Betrayer is worth a playthrough or two. It’s a fun game with an interesting story, but it doesn’t have a whole lot of replay value. If it goes on sale, definitely pick it up.

Fun, light, 3rd person 3D puzzler. I picked it up a while back on a sale for $0.99, was not dissappointed. The gameplay was good, it wasn't really challenging but required a bit of thinking, the concepts were pretty unique, and the soundtrack was very good. Good for a bit of a change of pace after a heavier game. Like a pallette cleanser of sorts.

The storyline is decent as far as storytelling (Mary-sue be warned) goes and good on the aspect of playability. And despite the many other commenters claiming the contrary I rather enjoyed the black deck. And the cards themselves do a very good job on a storytelling level. They explain the setting and events very well especially combined with the art, something I value, even if this is by and large a strategy game.
Magic itself has always been a very good principle for an online game, (even if I dislike the eldrazi additions, a card like Ulamog is just plain silly even if games can still be on despite it) but the matching system is more than a bit skewed. I've been matched several times with people that had 10 to 20 ranks above my own. The game's deck-rating system also feels inaccurate. Even if it only calculates the relative power (to itself) of a deck rather than the absolute, I've noted several decks that were faster despite slower ratings, among others.
What will also never happen, but would actually fix the biggest problem this game has, is if the matching system were to be balanced according to the amount of booster-packs a player has opened in combination with won-matches. Since there is a fair amount of players that buy in large, which effectively breaks the game.

1st off, this game uses the Unreal engine...poorly. The game looks like something about 5-7 years old, but runs very poorly. Just not optimized I suppose. Skyrim came out in 2011, has vast terrain, mountains, hills, forests, you can see faraway, runs great. This game, is like taking some outdoor map in Unreal Tournament 3, and making it bland and unable to rival Skyrim graphics. Not to mention, it runs like POOP! OMG, it's a "confined area" level design, just small bumps for hills, trees, and rocks. This is inexcusable.
2nd. The game plays out in Black and White. I really tried to play as intended. I had no problem with the "somethings are red, somethings are not" gimmick, but here is what killed it for me, forcing me to turn on the color: you can see better in color, it looks better, and the red became annoying. Like seriously, arrows and other weapon related items are in red. Clues, chests, things you need to find or will help you progress are red. I think the B/W was to hide the "Captain Obvious" that people couldn't find crap, so they make those things glow red, then people feel they are being hand-held, so they say "Let's make everything else black and white, this way, the things we painted red...MEAN SOMETHING. Like it HAS MEANING NOW. WHAT MEANING? I DON'T KNOW! ITS A.....MYSTERY! YES! THAT'S IT! OOOH!"
Naaah, no thanks. It would have been cooler to play in B/W if there was tons of blood, you know, like in other FPS games using the Unreal engine (or any). Seriously. A horror-FPS-type game and there are no blood splats on the ground or everywhere? I mean, when your whole game makes "A THING" out of the color red being the only color, and it's a horror game, why make it so bloody BLOODLESS (except for a few red puffs from hits?)
Makes no sense, and people will find it annoying. They'll think "OOOh Red is only color? It's a horror game? It's also FPS? I'm ready for some horror splatterfest!" Instead it's like "The Red, you see, it means something. It represents a reflection on humanity's fascination with violence and looking for truth, and answers in those truths. Take for example the history of colonialism and the native americans, which the story of the game....." BLAH BLAH BLAH BLAH - that's basically the impression the game gives you throughout as far as Red relating to the story goes. Or rather, in color, as probably game was intended, Red was simply to show the clues which leads me to 3rd.
(Quite note, I went to a pile of glowing rocks, "a clue", that gave a pop-up describing there is blood on the ground around the clue" instead of just showing it. HAHAHAH.)
3rd. The game holds your hand ridiculously. You are dropped on the the coast of what I will call "Level 1". As you go through, you immediately have the "4th Wall" (those who don't know what this means should look it up) to hold your hand from the start. Wow, really? I thought. So basically, you have to figure out "what happened to the colony" or colonies since there are "Levels 1, 2, 3, etc." which each have a settlement/fort of some type. There are literally FRICKEN NOTES or clues laying in a fricken field in the middle of nowhere, or in piles of rocks. When you go to use it, you get a pop-up telling you what you find (RATHER THAN JUST SHOWING YOU lol). How to find these? Look for glowing red spots, but some are very deep so you must explore. THAT CAN TAKE FOREVER.
So why do that when you can simply pull-up your IN-GAME MAP of the ENTIRE "Level" that comes with a legend already marking where everything is? You can even filter it out to only show chests, only show clues, or spirits that are not actually there, in fact, some things are not even there. Instead, you have to somehow progress and unlock stages of progression to where that thing marked on your map will not spawn. This means you have to run all the way the hell back there to then continue progression so you can what? Get the hell out of that level.
Rather than have some kind of plot device or something like that in the game to give you a clue where to go, you get a map showing you. The kicker is not all things are there. So THIS, THAT, THIS clue will progress the "quest?" so THAT, THAT, and THIS clue, will be there, basically. So you will still spend the whole fracking game running around from one side of the map, to completely the other side. It feels they designed it this way to extend the play time, to make what would really be a short game, much, much, slower.
4th. You die alot. The game's combat mechanics are brutally frustrating. If they are going for realism, I GET IT, musket weapons take forever to load. But if going for realism....why are weapon racks "Stores" where you can buy/sell stuff? Why can't I buy health potions? Instead, you have to drink from a glowing red barrel of water, that doesn't heal you right away. Instead, you store up "invisible" health potions and usually third time you heal fully. That's great.
So, you leave a place that is at, and then get attacked. You get shot, arrowed, fisted, and almost dead, using up your "healing water invisible things" only to have to go back and get another drink of water from the barrel. SO, can you imagine? You leave the center of the "hub", immediately get attacked by 3 dudes who move very fast (and some spawn from nowhere), if you survive, you have to run back to refill. Then, you go out again, maybe that spawn-point has refreshed, or maybe you run into another mob, and then get beat up. Then you have to run all the way back again. In one level, they put a barrel on the road. HOW NICE OF THE DEVELOPERS TO DO THAT!
So, the whole "realism" thing is a completely mental argument. If it was done for the sake of horror, that makes more sense but still sucks compared to the combat mechanics, and people complain. You can take the stealth approach, which works best, but as some others have mentioned, as soon as you tag an enemy, the "magically" know where you are no matter what. Eventually, the game turns into a death-fest and "avoid the spawn point" fest.
OH, AND GET THIS, THIS IS THE BEST: If you die: you simply respawn! Of course, you respawn back to wherever the game decides was your last "checkpoint" (it was never clear on this). But so do all of the enemies, and all the respawn points reset too. That means, you get to run the FRAGGIN gauntlet ALL over again.
It becomes like playing an old-school game where you have to "beat a level" and it's a tough level, and you always die, but you have unlimited lives to keep trying and trying. "Like someone unraveling a cable-net sweater you keep on knitting, and knitting, and knitting, and knitting, and knitting....hegh-hegh!"
5th. It feels like what we are playing is not the original intended design of the game. Almost as if people complained about so many things, that they did all those things I mentioned above.
Last. Why recommend? The game succeeds with the, albiet illusionary, non-linear design. Here is the next "map". Figure it out. Collect the pages. Whatever. The sound design is excellent as is some of the art style, the dark-world mode is incredibly creepy and works well. They hit the right marks in all other areas than what I mentioned (REMEMBER, I spoke of the bad only).  If you want a game with great atmosphere, a bit of freedom to explore (try it without using the map!), some interesting surprises, then buy it. Prepare to spend 90% of your game time, running around. This game requires A LOT of patience. GO INTO THE GAME WITH THAT IN MIND, and you'll be fine. Maybe, play at a party where everyone is wild. HAHAHAH!

Betrayer is a game best played without prior research or information, but it's also a very polarizing game that you will probably either love or hate, and I'll try to talk about the things that would hold you back from purchasing this title and the things that you might come to love about it while trying not to leave you feeling like you've already played the game.
In simple terms Betrayer is a fantastic FPS with a huge focus on immersion with discovery, exploration and detective elements. Set in the first decade of the 17th Century as a colonist arriving on the shores of Virginia, there are a number of interesting and fairly unique mechanics that all help to compliment the world and the players exploration and while it requires a level of attention and self learning, it delivers more the more you put into it. For me, this is a game that exemplifies underrated or hidden gems.
The last game I can remember grabbing a hold of me and making me feel so immersed and part of its environment was Metro 2033, and with a much smaller budget and development team, it's commendable how incredibly well designed this is. There's a depth of elegant graphical and audio options for players who want to get rid of the HUD, turn up the difficulty and increase the realism even more, but even out of the box it's very reactive and real. Everything from the get go is designed with this in mind, the HUD elements can be mostly forgotten about and blend into the background, the weapons are all accurate to the period, and reload animations look and feel natural and even small things like reloading while running support the level of realism.
The audio and animation and art style all stands out as exceptionally well made. Using the games listening mechanic feels like stopping to♥♥♥♥♥♥your ear and is a genuinely useful part of play. The rustling of leaves in the wind can give you a scare if you mistake them for something else and paranoia takes hold often. Similarly, visual elements like light shaded ferns and foliage or bent tree branches blowing in the wind can easily be mistaken for assailants or hazards and catch you off guard.
A common complaint about Betrayer is the lack of depth in terms of gameplay, and that it quickly gets boring. While it's true that the combat and actual progressive gameplay are straight forward and arguably limited, they're not the whole focus of the game, and shouldn't be viewed as the reason for playing. Instead, the game is about discovering clues, finding out who and where you are, what's going on and what happened in and to the environment and characters around you. Still, players expecting a different take on an FPS are justified in feeling out of place here, I just feel it's a complaint that doesn't take into account the rest of the game.
Finally, the ending receives a lot of criticism for being abrupt, not making sense, and explaining very little. Like the rest of Betrayer, it requires a level of thought and comitment from the player, and a developer explanation helps confirm what most people will take away from the ending, but it still feels poorly conveyed and ends like a movie that left you feel wanting for an explanation after viewing.
All in all the biggest issue I had with Betrayer is that it's one of those games that leaves you feeling like it could've been much more. I can't criticize a game that's taken interesting new approaches to common gameplay mechanics, and I feel they've simply been used as the best solution to the game design in mind and they serve it well, but players should know that it will probably make them want for more, or for one of the mechanics to be explored more in depth. Whether that's a good or a bad thing is more down to individual taste.
* Due to the ambiguous nature of gameplay and the focus on realism, almost everything is left unexplained, be it the mechanics, the enemies and even the controls. It compliments the playstyle very well, but also creates for some frustrations. I remained ignorant of the fact that I could use melee weapons far into the game purely because an enemy spawned too close during the brief explanation of the controls, and made me feel like a fool later on.
* Spoilers
With an average playtime of around 8 hours, and a price tag at £6.99/9.99€/$9.99, Betrayer feels fairly priced and fair value for money. The caveat is that, being a love it or hate it kind of game, it may be worth waiting for a sale of -50% or more for anyone who's unsure. Though a demo is available on the Store page and will help anyone on the fence.
The already visually impressive graphics can be heightened further via use of SweetFX settings, and FPS can be unlocked to allow greater than 60fps.

REVIEW – REBEL GALAXY
If you’ve ever prayed that Firefly would be turned into an action-packed space sim, just pour yourself a tall glass of bourbon and strap in, pardner. With the crunchiest roadhouse-cowboy soundtrack this side of the ‘verse and a visual feast that can only be described as f---ing majestic, Rebel Galaxy has been lovingly hand-crafted to appease the most deeply rooted spacelust in us all.
Gods. Be. Praised.
Here’s the story: Your aunt Juno, a semi notorious ne’er-do-well, has vanished under mysterious and potentially dangerous circumstances, leaving you with a junkheap of a ship and a cryptic message. You’re then set loose in the Xanthe star system (the beginner zone) to carve your own path, choose your side(s), and blast through the near and far reaches of space trying to save the old gal from her fate. And that's just the start of it.
The solar systems are randomly generated but feel fully realized, with fluctuating economies, random events, and an endless torrent of side quests. The factions are pretty clear – there are “good” guys and “bad” guys, and it’s rare to help someone without♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone else, and you’re definitely going to be doing that. You’ll make heaps of money, buy bigger ships and WAY bigger guns, and doing lots and lots of killin’ folk, often in self defense.
A majority of your time will be spent fighting nasty people and blasting around the systems for your quests, and it can feel grindy sometimes. That said, I managed to spend WAY more time than I expected doing just that without it feeling tiresome. Hell, it took me 13 hours of gameplay before I felt like finishing the story quests in the very first system, and there are 14 systems.
The physics are just delicious, the visuals are head-shakingly grand, and the sound design is so good it hurts. It’s all more than enough to make you forget you had a life outside which, frankly, is kinda the point. Rebel Galaxy is heroin wrapped in crack and drowning in whiskey. So, giddyup.

Score: 4 out of 5
Why: Gameplay is unbelievably good. Character interactions feel a bit railroaded, but let’s be honest – that’s not why you’re playing.

I played the original Dr on the 360, and in the usual capcom style- the game was punishing, frustrating, and highly addictive.
Dead Rising 2, like it's predecessor, focuses on placing you in a zombie  infested town with lots to do and only so much time to do it. The game is very effective in creating tension, and you will often feel conflicted by the decisions you make as you will not be able to do everything DR 2 has to offer on the first playthrough.
The game play is straightforward enough, you guide chuck Greene (motorcyclist extraordinaire) through a collection of zombie infested zones- each broken up by a 15 second load time, and along the way you will encounter bosses, looters, and survivors. Much of this content is optional, but you'll want to complete some of the side quests as they help Chuck level up, learn new moves, and become faster and stronger.
The story of Dead Rising 2 is good, if a little uninspired. You begin  at the end of a "Terror is Reality" motorcycle show to find that fortune city is overrun by hordes of the undead. It's up to you to get chuck and his zombie infected daughter to a safe house that becomes home to you and your fellow survivors. The rest of the game's story feels more like a patchwork of cutscenes that feel like they sort of blend together, but do not feel directly linked to your actions or playstyle. Because you will only play about a third of the game'a content on a single playthrough, and because so much of that content is optional the story in Dead Rising 2 feels very loose and definitely takes a backseat to the game's truly excellent action.
On my first play Dead Rising 2 took me about 15 hours to complete. And with multiple playthroughs available there is easily plenty of zombie killing value here for your dollar. This is also a well optimized port that works well on lower end graphics cards. I had no trouble playing the game on a radeon R7 240. So if you are looking for a violent, zombie-infested romp look no further- Dead Rising 2 is here on pc and it's great!

Genre - Modern War-torn Survival
I got this game a while ago but only just decided to play it tonight, due to the new DLC for the charity War Child.
At first I thought it would get boring very fast as I was just rooting around the starting house for resources. Then after my first night's scavenge mission I started to see the true complexity of the game. You have numerous places to visit, with new ones added overtime, each having finite resources to gather. Sometimes obtaining these resources can put you in a morale quandary, and other times they put your people at unnecessary risk. The game will save at the start of each new day so you can come back to a game at a later date. However, you can't undo decisions done before, a bit roguelike. Like taking on a heavily armed group with a shovel, RIP Pavle. It is a bit like the SIms as you need food and rest, but this time as oppose to just partying you actually have to survive in a harsh reality that isn't too far rremoved from some war-torn places in the world today.
I think the game does convey a serious message, but does it subtly whilst also offering an enjoyable game to play and come back to.

Typically, with episodic games, each chapter is produced within a reasonable time frame.  When I purchased this game in December of 2012, I paid for a complete game and wholly believed that delivery of a final product would be imminent.
Four years have elapsed since my purchase and the final chapter has yet to be released.*  It's been two years since the release of any new content and six years since the introduction of the first chapter.  Not only hasn't the game been finalized, but the developer can't even provide an estimated release date for the final chapter.  They have, however, posted some news recently--I've been happily informed that they are enjoying themselves in Switzerland and getting drunk off absinthe.  Seriously, that's what they said.
Now I may not know a lot of things, but there's one thing I am sure of--I'm not a bank, I don't give loans to people so they can develop products at their leisure, I don't take part in crowdsourcing, I never buy Early Access, and I definitely would not have purchased this game, or any other game, knowing that it would be at least four years until I experienced its conclusion.  I would not buy a game that I would play for 3 hours, then put down for several years, only to pick it back up again, smack dab in the middle of the story, just to play for another 3 hours.  Who the ♥♥♥♥, in their right mind, would knowingly hand their money over to someone so they could do that?  No one, that's who.  No one would--it's absurd.  Now, knowing that I would never consciously do such a thing, I can only conclude that there has been some amount of deception involved concerning the sale of this game.
I may not have asked when the final chapter would be released, but I did not have any reason to believe it would be at least 4 years until that occurred.  Being a linear point-and-click adventure game, with each chapter only a few hours long and having no replay value, it really doesn't make any sense for someone to sell this type of game piecemeal if there was going to be several years between each chapter's release.  I think it's quite reasonable to assume that this game would have been fully developed within a short span of time--several months, perhaps a year at the most.  Early Access did not exist at that time and I had no reason to believe that Steam was in the business of selling games that were at the beginning of a 6+ year development cycle.
Based on my experience with this title, I will never make the mistake of purchasing another incomplete,
game again and I will definitely not be supporting this developer, by any means, in any of their future endeavors.
*The final chapter was released yesterday, May 12, 2017--five years, five months since my purchase.
For reference, here are the chapter release dates and the time that had elapsed between them:
Chapters 1 and 2 - December 2010
Chapter 3 - October 2011 (10 months)
Chapter 4 - August 2013 (1 year, 10 months)
Chapter 5 - November 2014 (1 year, 3 months)
Chapter 6 - May 2017 (2 years, 6 months)
Total time since the first chapter's release: 6 years, 5 months
Average time between chapters: 1 year, 7 months
This review was edited on May 13, 2017.

Best Bioshock in the series in terms of gameplay. The original Bioshock is already pretty great but Bioshock 2 improves the gameplay mechanics in almost every way. With it's vast selection of weapons, ammo types, plasmids - the combos are already endless. Throw in the turrets, security camera / bots and the different cyclone traps - you're going to have a lot of fun experimenting and creating awesome offensive strategies.
The story itself is a little weak; however, the game is masterful in its portrayal of Rapture after the collapse. The horror / shock element is definitely still there and the visuals still holds up against the test of time.
The Minerva's Den DLC is pretty great and a nice extension to the game. It's not a must-have but a good sub-story if you are a fan of the main campaign.
Overall, with its high replayability and excellent execution, it's definitely worth every penny - an fantastic, underrated but worthy entry to the Bioshock series.

“Bioshock, buddy! Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ sorry bro—Bioshock 2. I'll remember that. Here, try this. No, no, you hold this end. Yeah, that's it. Don't exhale yet, let it settle. Anyway, Andrew Ryan...pretty legendary antagonist, right? Everybody still talks about that. Must have been crazy being around that and trying to come up with something comparable, huh? Looking forward to seeing what you've got! Enjoy the punch!”
The funny thing is that in some very important ways, Bioshock 2 is better than it's happily-married-highly-paid-architect-that-also-kills-at-guitar older sibling. Playing as a 'Big Daddy' is a blast, and the 'walking-tank' that most end-game protagonists begin to feel like makes complete sense here as, well, you're a walking, copper-and-barnicle tank. Ferrying Little Sisters about is great fun, and ends up making the whole game feel like some quasi-parenting simulator, if parenting sims focused on violently dismembering drug-addicts who try and touch your kids. Either way, it makes 'protect the transport' missions fun, which is no small feat. Big Sisters, Brute Splicers, Rumblers, and...different Big Daddies go a long ways to make Bioshock's enemies unpredictable and exciting to introduce to your drill. Plasmids and Gene-Tonics are expanded, and allow for some wildly different (and a few extremely over-powered) combinations that help you introduce enemies to your drill. Even the (silly) boss fights that Bioshock 1 fell back on towards the end have been mostly exorcised, and replaced with climaxes in gameplay that makes a bit more sense, usually involving you, lots of assorted splicers, and the challenge of introducing all of them to your drill in an adequate amount of time.
However, most people will focus comparisons on what was the absolute star of the original Bioshock—the story, the characters, and the setting itself. Sadly, like the second sibling, who can only chug-a-lug five pints (still impressive) in succession as opposed to their older sibling's eight, these comparisons are not terribly kind to Bioshock 2; who's story simply doesn't have the drive, who's characters are noticeably flatter, and who's setting remains largely unchanged from that of the first game.
Don't get me wrong—the idea of Bioshock 2's collaborate-for-the-collective-good yin is a great companion to Bioshock 1's capitalism-trumps-all yang. Throwing in some mid-century ideas of self/ego and conscious/subconcious wants/needs is intriguing as well, but the fact of the matter is that Sophia Lamb isn't as fascinating as an antagonist as Andrew Ryan, socialism is a poor stand-in for Ayn Rand's erotic sub-oceanic fiction, and none of the locations of Bioshock 2 have the morbid facination of Bioshock 1's Medical Pavillion, Arcadia, or Fort Frolic. Flooded rooms are great, and Paulper's Drop is good fun, but lots of Bioshock 2's story and reveals feel...rote. I love the lore, and playing Bioshock 2 served as a shameful catalyst to read the Bioshock wiki for an entire Saturday afternoon, but at the end of the day, five pints chug-a-lugged is simply less impressive that eight. That's the way it is.
Speaking of drinking, the multiplayer component of Bioshock 2 is *empty.* Through multiple evenings, I managed to find one laggy match. The other sessions came up completely barren, and ended with my character trudging back to their lobby...hotel room(?) and staring at the fire.
Also, can we give it up for burgeoning crop of fully-featured-progressive-unlocks-hamster-wheel-grindy-oatmeal-blah-multiplayer-components that DON'T HAVE LAN. Here's the deal. Any online multiplayer you bake into a game is going to die. Players *will* leave. Servers *will* be turned off to make way for the next year's game. GameSpy WILL shut down. (Rest In (High) Ping). Throwing LAN into your game is the least you can do to help give your game the legs that will carry it through years of playability by people who genuinely enjoy your game. Those people are the ones that'll keep circulating the tapes, release compatibility patches, or mod Randy Savage into your game. It's the little things.
The one good thing I can confidently say about the multiplayer is that being able to freely walk around a golden-age-era apartment in Rapture completely sold me on the reasoning behind becoming a raving, ADAM-obsessed, bulberous addict dandy; not having the sun/sky visible is...unsettling. I continue to wish for a Rapture (circa golden-age) tour simulator. I'm told I'll be disappointed by the Bioshock Infinate DLC that's currently being downloaded by my Steam client. Prove me wrong, Ken Levine.
One additional positive note is that the now-flatlined Games for Windows Live infrastructure has been completely removed from Bioshock 2, and replaced with yet-to-flatline SteamWorks. Also, all the DLC available for Bioshock 2 has been lumped into the game for free. Thanks, large corporation!
Steam seems to want me to boil down all my thoughts, qualms, and/or musings on this game to a 'thumbs up' or 'thumbs down,' and I've always been one for over-generalizations, so I'll dance when my omnipotent DRM overlords wish to see me get down with my bad self.
Sure, Steam. I recommend this game. Thanks for asking.

Betrayer is a game best played without prior research or information, but it's also a very polarizing game that you will probably either love or hate, and I'll try to talk about the things that would hold you back from purchasing this title and the things that you might come to love about it while trying not to leave you feeling like you've already played the game.
In simple terms Betrayer is a fantastic FPS with a huge focus on immersion with discovery, exploration and detective elements. Set in the first decade of the 17th Century as a colonist arriving on the shores of Virginia, there are a number of interesting and fairly unique mechanics that all help to compliment the world and the players exploration and while it requires a level of attention and self learning, it delivers more the more you put into it. For me, this is a game that exemplifies underrated or hidden gems.
The last game I can remember grabbing a hold of me and making me feel so immersed and part of its environment was Metro 2033, and with a much smaller budget and development team, it's commendable how incredibly well designed this is. There's a depth of elegant graphical and audio options for players who want to get rid of the HUD, turn up the difficulty and increase the realism even more, but even out of the box it's very reactive and real. Everything from the get go is designed with this in mind, the HUD elements can be mostly forgotten about and blend into the background, the weapons are all accurate to the period, and reload animations look and feel natural and even small things like reloading while running support the level of realism.
The audio and animation and art style all stands out as exceptionally well made. Using the games listening mechanic feels like stopping to♥♥♥♥♥♥your ear and is a genuinely useful part of play. The rustling of leaves in the wind can give you a scare if you mistake them for something else and paranoia takes hold often. Similarly, visual elements like light shaded ferns and foliage or bent tree branches blowing in the wind can easily be mistaken for assailants or hazards and catch you off guard.
A common complaint about Betrayer is the lack of depth in terms of gameplay, and that it quickly gets boring. While it's true that the combat and actual progressive gameplay are straight forward and arguably limited, they're not the whole focus of the game, and shouldn't be viewed as the reason for playing. Instead, the game is about discovering clues, finding out who and where you are, what's going on and what happened in and to the environment and characters around you. Still, players expecting a different take on an FPS are justified in feeling out of place here, I just feel it's a complaint that doesn't take into account the rest of the game.
Finally, the ending receives a lot of criticism for being abrupt, not making sense, and explaining very little. Like the rest of Betrayer, it requires a level of thought and comitment from the player, and a developer explanation helps confirm what most people will take away from the ending, but it still feels poorly conveyed and ends like a movie that left you feel wanting for an explanation after viewing.
All in all the biggest issue I had with Betrayer is that it's one of those games that leaves you feeling like it could've been much more. I can't criticize a game that's taken interesting new approaches to common gameplay mechanics, and I feel they've simply been used as the best solution to the game design in mind and they serve it well, but players should know that it will probably make them want for more, or for one of the mechanics to be explored more in depth. Whether that's a good or a bad thing is more down to individual taste.
* Due to the ambiguous nature of gameplay and the focus on realism, almost everything is left unexplained, be it the mechanics, the enemies and even the controls. It compliments the playstyle very well, but also creates for some frustrations. I remained ignorant of the fact that I could use melee weapons far into the game purely because an enemy spawned too close during the brief explanation of the controls, and made me feel like a fool later on.
* Spoilers
With an average playtime of around 8 hours, and a price tag at £6.99/9.99€/$9.99, Betrayer feels fairly priced and fair value for money. The caveat is that, being a love it or hate it kind of game, it may be worth waiting for a sale of -50% or more for anyone who's unsure. Though a demo is available on the Store page and will help anyone on the fence.
The already visually impressive graphics can be heightened further via use of SweetFX settings, and FPS can be unlocked to allow greater than 60fps.

The game consists of a platformer with some twists. Graphics are definitely great, cartoonish but also detailed.
If you're an old player, the mechanics and the environments will probably remind you of many platformers in the '90s.. :)
You play as a jelly (controls are awesome, they respond always quickly and without lag at all, so that you can do your timing right) and you have to jump and go through every level like a classic platformer, but you also can possess other characters who all have different characteristics (they can move boxes, they can jump higher, they can shoot with a gun and so on) and you can get out of them when you need to pass through small blobbish tubes or such :P
There's plenty of skills needed since you'll have to time your jumps, you'll have to decide which NPCs possess and when and if leave them and return as a slime and so on. It's not a casual platformer at all, and it has also different difficulty modes.
There's also plenty of levels, almost 60 different areas, and you can also use a controller although the WASD configuration is keyboard-friendly and responsive.
If you're looking for a good platformer this one is definitely worth it, maybe not for 3€/$ but has to be played :)

If we put aside the grindfest and micro-transactions for a moment there's a good game here. Magic: the Gathering has been a solid card game for decades, and this latest addition to the duels series really highlights that - there's plenty of collecting cards, deck construction, and fun to be had (and yes we have 2-headed giant, as was requested by the players).
There were quite a few hiccups and bugs on release, but the swift bug-squashing that ensued has at least left me with some faith in Wizards of the Coast. There are still quite a few bugs, but they seem to be more infrequent with each passing day.
I can't recommend spending money on the micro-transactions. If you enjoy the game, you'll eventually unlock everything anyways, and it feels nice to actually have something to spend your coins on (besides "foiling" cards). Besides that, my only complaint is that there is no Android version - I won't pretend that developing for Android is easier than developing for iPhone, but I'd still like to see an Android version some day.
Ultimately I still enjoy the game too much to not recommend it. It runs better than its predecessors, is "free", has ranked online play, and it seems we'll keep seeing updates to the game as new sets are released - a pretty good experience overall.

Sins of a Solar Empire – Rebellion: This title is too long already
I was originally going to name this review, “Hold on, I just need to nuke their entire population” But then the title would have been like an entire paragraph and… Honestly, I couldn’t be bothered.
But that would have been a great title because that’s basically been my experience with this game so far. Casually asking my friend to kill entire planet’s worth of people in exchange for military support, resources, or just because they’re annoying.
Just because I am bad guy, doesn’t make me a bad… guy.
I bought this game during the Christmas sale on Steam last year, but hadn’t played it until like Tuesday of last week, that is to say on or around the 15th of March. Remember when I played Helldivers for like fifteen hours over a weekend with my buddy? Yeah… Same thing here. Sins of a Solar Empire is pretty dope. I played about five or six games over spring break, and enjoyed every minute of it.
Sins has been on my radar since the original came out back in like… 2008, wait let me check… Yeah it was 2008. I’ve always thought it looked dope, but never took the plunge. Well, I can say that it was definitely worth the wait. It’s a lot like a real time Endless Space, crossed with Supreme Commander. Except it’s approachable and is just deep enough to be rewarding, and ‘lite’ enough to be easily grasped without being daunting.
The game centers around … well I actually don’t know the story, but what I do know is the game sports three factions, each with a Loyalist and Rebel side. Which means in gameplay terms, that there are six factions. Although the Loyalist and Rebel sides are similar, they have different research that allows differentiated gameplay. Like for example, there are giant fleets of space Pirates present on the star map. They will put bounties on players and eventually attack them. And although you can manipulate it by placing bounties yourself, if you’re on the receiving end of the attack, it can drastically hamper your success in the game.
The TEC Rebel faction can become allies with the Pirates, completely negating the disadvantage. Not only will they not attack you, but the Brigands surrounding un-colonized planets basically become free body guards. It’s incredibly powerful, if not a bit overpowered.
And although each faction has ships that fill the same archetypes, their style of play definitely makes them all feel distinct. After playing each, one you will quickly get a feel for their strengths and weaknesses. They all feel unique but familiar– which is nice. It’s not hard to jump from the TEC to the Vasari, or the Vasari to the Advent.
And while the game does have many different win conditions, I found that it’s best suited for ANNIHILATION! Or rather, that’s how we played, because we’re noobs and blowing things up is easier than talking to them.
And while the game is definitely more approachable than other 4X games I have played, it does still have many of the quarks that that are always present in the genre. Such as the ‘culture’ system, which is interesting to say the least. You build massive orbital Media Hubs around your planets and they blast your Media through the star systems, spreading your culture into the surrounding planets. This will lower the enemy planet’s allegiance and presumably convert them to your empire at some point.
Hearts and minds.
But all that aside, my twenty hours were spent committing horrible genocide across the galaxy. Paul Atreides, Muad’dib–  lamented that his forces spread across the galaxy and killed sixty billion in a needless Jihad.
Child’s play.
Why go to an enemy planet when you can bombard it with interstellar nuclear missiles? “Hey, I’ll bombard their capital if you send reinforcements to my planet.” And then billions died.
The scope of Sins of a Solar Empire is certainly one of the stronger points of the game. The maps range from a handful of planets around one star. To Hundreds of planets around dozens of stars. In some cases the game feels intergalactic rather than merely interstellar. And it’s definitely compelling to think about launching a massive three fleet invasion into another galaxy. Taking it one hard fought planet at a time, systematically dismantling what could only be centuries of hard work. But I have an overactive imagination… Also they started it.
Sins focuses heavily on the Macro aspect of things, which lends itself well to the Supreme Commander comparison. There isn’t really much that you can do on a micro level; other than the positioning of planetary defenses, such as mines and missile platforms. But other than a few abilities the Capital Ships have, most ships are capable of taking care of themselves. They don’t require commands other than to retreat or to focus fire. If you’re more into the micro aspect of RTS games, then sins might not be for you. It’s definitely more of an abstracted “Big Picture” type of game.
But despite there not being a lot to do in moment to moment combat, there is a surprising amount of plates to spin. Especially when you’re Empire stretches across more than a handful of worlds. You need to make sure your trade routes are properly constructed, that your outer planets are properly defended, while also defending your inner planets. You need to be sure to actually develop your worlds to increase the population and rake in more tax income. You need your centers of production to be near the active areas of your empire; otherwise your fleets won’t be able to respond in time if there is an attack.
One of the things that really adds to the scope, but could definitely turn people off… Is that it takes forever to get anywhere in Sins. And while it doesn’t necessarily bother me… It could take upwards of ten minutes for your fleets to arrive at their destination. Maybe even longer depending on the size of your Empire. And as far as I can tell there isn’t a way to make them travel between planets faster, other than being the Vasari– but that’s a different story.
There have been many occasions where my friend needed support to defend a planet from an invading fleet. And I would try to send reinforcements, only to have the battle be over by the time I reached the next system over…. Space is big, yo.
But I really don’t have a lot of negative things to say about this game. It’s just a big fun space war simulator; and I really enjoy that. It’s not trying to be something it isn’t. There’s enough there to be entertaining, and it’s just deep enough to hold your interest. It’s like a lean beef Po’Boy sandwich, it might not be the best sandwich ever… But it sure does hit the spot…
You should check it out, at the time of this writing it’s currently on sale too!

Rebel Galaxy takes the classic free-form, open-world space sim a la Darkstar One, gives it amazing, brutal, fast, exciting combat, adds a strategic economy with stock market-esque line graphs, a bunch of well designed, fun-to-fly ships, pumps in some grungy western blues rock, and then throws you into the middle of your favorite outlaw studded sci-fi show. We're talking Outlaw Star, Firefly, Dark Matter, Battlestar Galactica, etc.
I was initially sold on the soundtrack alone (seriously, just watch the first trailer and you'll know what I mean). I thought I would lament the loss of a Z axis in flight/combat, but because of playing on a flat plane, it plays very similar to Assassin's Creed Black Flag's ship-to-ship combat, and as such it's very smooth, easy to grasp, and fun.
Pros:
+ Excellent Soundtrack
+ If you don't like the soundtrack, or want to add your own flair, the soundtrack can easily be replaced with your own music, separated by category (idle spacefaring, combat, space station), and your own music can be played along with the included soundtrack
+ Smooth combat
+ Lots of spacecraft
+ Well made stock market style economy
+ Planetary events add strategic value to trading
+ Feels like you're right inside the Outlaw Star or Firefly universe
+ Later fights are challenging, but fun
+ Warping between planets is very relaxing
+ Space is big. Each solar system is pretty massive, so expect to warp a lot
+ Inside jokes and references to other sci-fi media is plentiful
Cons:
- A bit grindy, especially early on
- Missions are fairly repetetive
- Some later fights can be brutal
- Losing a big battle means going back to the last station you docked at. Dock often
- No piloting small fighter craft

As a veteran of the X series I learned to build armadas in X2, rinsed the XTM mod for x3 and after blitzing Terran conflict amassed the best part of 2800 hours in Albion Prelude. Safe to say I love the series and all the freedom it brings. As you could probably have guessed I pre-ordered X rebirth and as a result was one of the many that were shocked at how Egosoft could even dream that the game was a finished product. I persevered but after about 10 hours of pain I resumed Albion prelude and tried to pretend Rebirth never happened.
That was 2 years ago...
I recently returned to X rebirth to see what 2 years of bug fixing looked like. Credit were its due as the game is much improved. Yes there are still bugs and no it's not the same as the games that preceded it but I have to say it works. /!\ THIS REVIEW IS ABOUT THIS BEING A REMASTER, NOT HOW GOOD THE GAME ITSELF IS /!\
Oh dear......dear oh sodding dear...
I was hoping this game had improved after its initial release in September 2016. Unfortunately, however, I was mistaken.
I recently did a Let's Play of the original BioShock, and had initially considered using the Remaster for the Let's Play. However, that hope was dashed when I played for an hour, got about halfway through the Medical Pavilion, and crashed upon attempting to save.
And by that, I mean...what happens is:
> Start the level.
> Play through a fair chunk of the level (got to where you get the shotgun).
> Decided to save the game.
> The game crashes back to desktop and fails to save the game.
The annoying thing is, I'm very much used to playing thought the game without having to save the game normally unless I want to stop for a bit. Playing through for the first time upon the release of the remaster, I felt an overwhelming sense of disappointment and anger towards this game after completing the Farmer's Market (an admittedly not too long area, but still has quite a lot in it if you venture off the beaten path, much like everywhere else in Rapture), only for the game to crash and vomit me back to desktop, only for it to demand I replay the Farmer's Market again.
And aside from the saving issues, it doesn't really look a whole lot different short of the addition of tons of starfish for some reason, there are occasional, and I experienced a few shader glitches here and there.
A note to the developers of this remaster:
As developers of a remaster, you failed in your quest to improve the game after its initial release nearly ten years ago. The only remaster collection I can consider to be worse than this is the Silent Hill HD Collection, simply because at least in those games,
is made worse, whilst the developers of this collection at least made the attempt to include new features like an FOV slider.
But if your game somehow runs worse than the original version......you messed up somewhere something fierce.
As a game in its own right, I recommend BioShock.
As a remaster of a great game, I
recommend BioShock Remastered. At least, on PC.
If you want to play the BioShock games, you
find the originals somewhere on key reseller sites, but the only versions on Steam now are the Remasters.
You are essentially left with three options:
Whilst I cannot personally vouch for how the remasters play on console, a friend of mine is quite pleased with the performance of the games on console. Fair enough I suppose.
However, since I have not played them on console, I cannot guarantee they are as good as he said, and since his judgement refers specifically to the console release, it does not sway my own judgement of the PC release of the remasters.
As I said earlier, as a remaster, on PC at least, this is nothing short of a failure. Don't consider buying the PC release of the remaster collection for £40. It's a botch job of a remaster that only serves to make the source material worse.

I've wanted to love this game since before it was released. Following the horrible reviews, I put it away and played other games. I knew Egosoft was going to get around to making it better and all I had to do was wait.  Well last month, I decided the wait was over. I loaded the game up, created a new campaign start and off I went.
There are a couple of good things about the game. The ship, station and general space travel graphics are pretty nice. And that's about it.
The Bad:
Graphics for people are repetitive and worthy of something released circa 2005. Maybe earlier.
The Skunk should have been more welcoming. As is, you have a cockpit that amounts to a cutscene to sit down, a ramp, and a crew quarters that really doesn't do any justice to the game.
You can only really fly the Skunk. I know this was planned from the early days, but there are not enough modifications or modification types to keep the Skunk fresh. It gets really boring, really fast. Just a few small tweaks and that would've not been a problem.
Trading is confusing. Only really big ships can trade but there is no real tutorial on how the whole system is supposed to work. Honestly, I have better things to do with my gaming time than doing extensive research on how to perform a basic task. A task that should be obvious.
The dialog and story are pretty horrid.
Some of the quests are still buggy as of the 4.0 release. I remember reading about the Energy Cell transfer being bugged in one of the missions. I ran across one where my carge ship would only sell a handful of Energy Cells at a time. It took me about two hours for the ship to dock, sell 6-10 energy cells, undock, fly around the sector, dock, sell 6-10 energy cells...
Combat is boring. I've come across enemy ships that just sit there while I pound on them and still others that die quickly while reciting the same old threats. When the enemy ships do present a challenge, it is usually because you have so many of them pounding on you that your shields get depleted fast.
Conclusion:
This could have been a great game. This SHOULD have been a great game. As is, the earlier X3 games run circles around this one. I hate to be that guy that looks backwards, but I just cannot look past all of the shortcomings that X: Rebirth has. Stick with X3: Terran Conflict or Albion Prelude. That or wait to see if Star Citizen lives up to all of its hype.

Bioshock Remastered gave me a few headaches, but was ultimately well worth the playthrough. Firstly, I must say this was my first time playing any Bioshock game, so unlike some others here, I had no experience with the original. I bought the games a while ago on steam, but never played them. I decided to play through the first game last weekend and realized I had the remastered version in my library. I installed it, started it up, and everything worked flawlessly...at first. About 30 minutes in and the game freezes, crashing to desktop. I restart the game and play through until another crash when finishing the first level and moving on to the second. I reinstalled the game to a different drive and tried to start it up again. This time, everything worked fine until I got to the Arcadia Gardens area, where I attempted to save and the game froze up once again. When I reloaded, all of my quicksave progress had been lost, the files simply deleted. I was extremely frustrated, as the crash had cost me over an hour of gameplay.
I researched the problem and realized many other players were experiencing the same problems, all with different solutions. From my own experience, I reinstalled it one last time, but with a few changes. This time, I changed absolutely nothing in the options menu; no controls, graphics, etc. Secondly, I created a new, manual save slot every 10-15 minutes (yes, this is annoying, but it is the only tactic that saved my games correctly). When I started my new playthrough, there were no freezes, no glitches, no crashes. However, when attempting to save two or three various times throughout the game, it did crash to desktop and I had to revert to the most recent save when loading up the game again (which was fine, as I had saved periodically while playing).
To conclude, my frequent crashes and freezing seem to have stemmed from some unknown changes in the options menu, either antialiasing, anisotropic filtering, or some other graphical setting. Once these changes were reset to default, I had no crashes or freezes during gameplay, only when manually saving, which happened two or three times. So, I will say my first experience with a Bioshock (Remastered) game was somewhat frustrating, but the storyline, gameplay and graphics were all amazing. I can't recommend the game itself enough. Just take this advice: leave all settings as default, if the game crashes during saving always revert to default settings when it asks you to do so upon booting up the game again, and manually save in a NEW slot EVERY single time and very consistently throughout your gameplay or you will have to replay through large parts of the game. I am about to start Bioshock 2 Remastered, so I will post my experiences there as well once I complete that game. Good luck.

I got this game a while ago but only just decided to play it tonight, due to the new DLC for the charity War Child.
At first I thought it would get boring very fast as I was just rooting around the starting house for resources. Then after my first night's scavenge mission I started to see the true complexity of the game. You have numerous places to visit, with new ones added overtime, each having finite resources to gather. Sometimes obtaining these resources can put you in a morale quandary, and other times they put your people at unnecessary risk. The game will save at the start of each new day so you can come back to a game at a later date. However, you can't undo decisions done before, a bit roguelike. Like taking on a heavily armed group with a shovel, RIP Pavle. It is a bit like the SIms as you need food and rest, but this time as oppose to just partying you actually have to survive in a harsh reality that isn't too far rremoved from some war-torn places in the world today.
I think the game does convey a serious message, but does it subtly whilst also offering an enjoyable game to play and come back to.

Have you ever seen the Disney movie, Pocahontas?  Be prepared to be led on a magical journey through the wilderness surrounding early English settlement in Virginia.  You will learn to appreciate the things you take for granted and about the life altering passions of human nature.
"Quit jerkin' me around, reviewer," I hear you saying.  "This is a horror game about exploring a black and white world filled with scary monsters.  There is no way Betrayer is at all like Pocahontas!"
Betrayer
like Pocahontas; not because they share a setting but because they are both stories of outsiders coming to understand and appreciate the world around them by introduction to a foreign culture.  You, the player, are the outsider.  You are learning to appreciate the world of sound design.  The culture that will teach it to you is the setting Betrayer presents.
Okay, I'm jerkin' ya around a bit.  I'm sure as a clever reader who enjoys my long-form reviews, you already appreciate what good sound design can mean for horror and stealth games.  But Betrayer has built its sound design into its every aspect to create the perfect study.
The stealth elements of Betrayer are entirely sound focused and are essential to your ability to remain hidden and to detect enemies.  Those enemies have a very small vision range.  However, if you run or use a firearm, they'll spot you in the dead of night, through a blizzard, in a concrete bunker, on another planet.  You'll need to move slowly or run in short bursts while gusts of wind cover the sound of your movement.
You won't hear the wolf cry to the blue corn moon.  But you may learn which animal calls are made by an enemy that's just a silhouette hiding in pure, black shadow. Only by identifying the calls they make will you pinpoint their position and save yourself from a deadly ambush.
It's like Marco Polo for keeps.
Likewise, sound contributes more to the game's tension and atmosphere than the visuals ever could.  Oh yes, the conquistador enemies you encounter early are unsettling for their hunched posture and the segmented movements of their armor.  But it's the bear roaring that makes them frightening.  The use of animal sounds for humanoid enemies lends them that elusive otherness that makes them horrifying.  It also characterizes the savagery of their nature brought to life by the cursed land.
While stealth and combat are important parts of Betrayer, I would say the core gameplay is about exploration and investigation.  And like the others, sound is key.  Objects of interest give off directional sounds to help you locate them and you can press a button to hear a directional sound leading you to your next main objective.
Your goal is to find physical evidence of the events that transpired and a bell to ring to visit a dark world haunted by ghosts.  You'll need to use your evidence and their testimonies to put together the story of the colony.  You won't paint with all the colors of the wind, no.  You will paint yourself a picture of racism, murder,♥♥♥♥♥♥ betrayal, and all the other destructive passions of a people unleashed by a wild land they weren't prepared for.
There is a map and visual cues so that the hearing impaired might enjoy the game.  However, Betrayer has all kinds of new and exciting ways to diddle your ear-hole, so you should lean back, put on headphones, and enjoy the ride.
Combat is fitting for the game's time period and tone.  You'll have access to a variety of bows, pistols, and muskets.  The latter hit - you and your enemies - for deadly amounts of damage, but make noise sure to give you away.  And you might as well go for a coffee while they reload.
Bows are silent, but the early bows you find only do deadly damage if you can fire them with precision while hidden.  And as everyone knows, an arrow bouncing harmlessly off your armor is the universal greeting for people who would like to be unceremoniously shot.
The game flow is similar to Bioshock:  you start poorly equipped and combat is hazardous and resource depleting.  By the end of the game, though, you'll have found powerful weapons that reload stupidly fast and have tons of health restoring items and ammo.  Fortunately, combat never stops being deadly where groups of enemies are concerned and the last segments of the game put your resources to use in large, difficult fights.
Like that adventure under the sea, Betrayer's narrative is similar.  Take it from me.   (What is it with me and Disney films today?)
You play as an outsider washed ashore and left to discover the fate of a fallen society after the fact.  Unlike Bioshock (you didn't think I was talking about The Little Mermaid?), Betrayer takes place in the very real setting of Virginia in the early seventeenth century.
Can you imagine being dropped into a proper wilderness with nothing to help you survive? Try to imagine it without all the cabin building karate ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of recent survival games.  What I'm getting at here is that Blackpowder Games chose a naturally scary setting.  Life as an early American colonist couldn't have been anything other than♥♥♥♥♥♥terrifying.
They nailed that fear of being isolated in a very alive land you don't know anything about and threw in some monsters for good measure.  You'll find this Virginia's abandoned forts swarming with wraiths, Indians made of ash, and growly shambling conquistadors.
The only living thing not trying to kill you seems to be a lady with a pragmatic attitude who nevertheless wears her best sexy Little Red Riding Hood Halloween costume.  Like the ghosts, her past is a mystery to be solved and tied into the omnipresent curse.
Wait, what?  I haven't talked visuals, yet?  Sing with all the voices of the mountain, indeed.  The sound design here is that good.  But Betrayer also looks good.  Everything is in a stylish black and white with touches of bright red that direct your focus.  The wind effects through the dense foliage of your surroundings look great and the enemy animations strike a nice balance between natural and surreal.
The game also gives you the option to play the game in full color in the light world.  And the game looks just as good that way.  The only notable weakness is that the contrast is turned up to eye-gouging degrees.  I think the purpose was to try and give the light world a sense of hyper-real vibrancy, which it kind of does. But its biggest success was giving me a headache and making some things really hard to see.  That might be by design, but it's too much in my opinion.  I turned the contrast down halfway through and felt no shame whatsoever.  Fortunately, the option is there.
There are some other minor criticisms to be made.
The in game map is at-odds with using sound to navigate.  If you only use the map, you'll get confused about  events that only trigger in a sequence that the sound navigation would unveil.  The sound navigation will disappoint your Nazi robot-like need to follow the most efficient course through all the treasures and objects of interest.  And you will have that need because the pattern for each area - explore light world, ring bell, find ghosts - becomes routine.  So neither method is ideal.
And if you want a pure stealth game, this isn't it.  Stealth is a tool that you can and should use, but even early enemies are designed so that they
ambush you.  There are several big fights that are unavoidable.  In the dark world enemies pop out of the ground right in front of you.  And, worst of all for stealth-lovers, there's no way to run away and hide.  Once enemies have found you, they will follow you to the ends of the map (barring the perfect storm of big cover objects, wind gusts, and timing).  It's not terrible that Betrayer isn't a stealth game, but I'd sure love to see a proper stealth game use some of the ideas here.
Worth ten bucks?  Well, I know good sound design and horror has a life, has a spirit, has a name.  It's Betrayer.

This is my own opinion, I'm not trying to be mean here. Whether you're a fan or even the dev team try not to get to mad, or sad over 'lil old me. Just voicing what I think. Feel free to politely disagree.
What is
? A pixelated nightmare of 2D platforming, that's what. I'll admit, it's a good concept, but like many things when put into action it just does not work. The controls are hard to nail down, several areas are way harder than they should be, the puzzle aspect is fairy undermined by the soldiers or whoever they are, and frankly I'm not even sure if this is supposed to be a puzzle game.
It's in some awkward place in between puzzle and combat, and it just doesn't feel right. You can't fight by yourself, you've just gotta dodge and jump around
. And in that case the theme seems to shift far more to combat.
I'm not one to complain about things like graphics and art style often, infact I quite like pixelated things. However, I suppose I'll have to make an exception here, because I do not like the art here one bit. Whilst it gets points for good pixel art(far better than my own I'll add), it just all seems so bland. The color scheme is just off, a bit too brownish. Doesn't add for a good feel at all. On top of that, there's black outlines on
. Don't get me wrong, putting these on your art serves very well in practice, but when put into the final product, just looks unprofessional and choppy. And lastly, the art and environment doesn't make all that much sense considering the backstory. It doesn't really scream "Science Lab" like it should. Looks more like a renovated cave or dungeon. The spikes are also a bit weird, not something you'd find in a science lab. I'd expect something more like tesla coils or lazers.
Whilst normally alright in playability,
still has its problems. Take the controls for example, I may be a special little snowflake here but I've had a very bad time trying to figure them out. But let's not forget the two other errors I've found, loading time and difficulty. The longish loading times may be just something to do with my machine or Wi-Fi, though I doubt it as
would be the only thing to have this effect, so you shouldn't really take this one to hardly. Diffuculty however, is another story. You're lucky there's no real cheats for this game, because I would definitly have used them. The reason why is due to the unbalancedness of it all. Some areas are severely diffucult, where you just have to do the same thing over and over until you finally succeed, and others where you just can't figure out the solution. Then there are areas which run smoothly and easily, no real in between making for a very choppy and annoying experience.

Overall - 2/5
