Quick review so I don't ramble for days.
Game is solid overall. Explorations elements are cool, but turn off the map if you want the real experience. I played the game before the map was added and it's a much better experience.
Combat is a little on the janky side. Hit detection is questionable but each enemy can be defeated without taking damage. Enemies do a lot of damage, you will need to practice before you get good. You can enable Dark Souls mode which will cause you to drop all your money upon death.
The biggest drawback is how repetitive the game gets. Every time you get to a new area you repeat the exact same sequece of steps in order to move to the next area. There are ~12 areas in the game and this gets old fast.
As for the story, I skipped the vast majority of it. It's there if you care about it, but I didn't. If anything, pay attention to the Maiden in Red as she is the only other human character in the game.
Visually the game is very nice, but not extremely well optimized. Expect to get huge frame drops if you are running at high settings. I experienced framerates between 75 and 144 on a 980ti at 1440p.
Worth the price for one playthrough, subsequent playthroughs can drag due to the repetitive nature of the game. Atmosphere is very good and the game gets darker and darker as your progress through.

Alright, Jelly Killer. A game where i don't exactly know if the Translator made a lil hickup or if it's intentional (Spoiler: You actually play the Jelly and kill people, not the other way around)
Either way, i got this game back then for i think only a handfull of cents with a Coupon i got from making badges. I actually had to look up to regular price for the game to make sure what to expect and rate it better. I will disclosure that in the end of my review.
Note: The Game description describes the game extremely well and puts every feature nicely and shortly into detail anyway, so i won't go on to long over key features.
Jelly Killer is a very sweet short Puzzle Plattformer for cheap money. Basically you are a little Jelly Blob Bioweapon trying to escape the Facility. You go through Areas, short little levels. Goal: Get from Point A to Point B, which are recognizeable as tubes.
On your way to get to your goal you must jump yourself through the area but also avoid Traps, such as Turrets or Lasers on the wall throughout the level. Your little Jellys main ability is controlling the bodies  of humans though. There are 5 different Human types all throughout the game, some show up in an area, some don't. These humans all have different abilities, the scientist can jump higher then the rest, the worker can push boxes, etc. . Your goal is to figure out which way to go, when to possess them and how to get to your goal. For example, a box blocks the way to the exit, so you need the worker, but he is on a ledge you cant reach, so you need  the Scientists higher jump to give you a boost. But watch out, once you get hit by one of the Obstacles, the body you possess dies, means if you did a mistake, you have to restart the Area. Thankfully, you can restart anytime you want in the menu, and the Areas are so short it never gets really frustrating.
This concept of possessing the characters isn't really groundbreaking by any means, but it's fairly nicely done here and fun to play through. Some could wish there was more variations and more people to possess, but the game is so short it's not really a problem. Overall, what the game tries to do with it's gameplay is well made.
Also, another cool thing i really liked: Some Areas let you act differently and use shortcuts or give you easier routes to reach your goal. Allthough i must say, i wasn't completely sure if that was an unintentional oversight by the dev or on purpose to make Speedrun strats for example. Either way, i welcome it alot!
The graphics for that price look suprisingly pretty well, considering it's price and simply concept. The animations are cute and look nice aswell. Game runs with constant 30 fps per second and looks perfectly fine.
Now for the things i disliked about the game, those are only small criticisms though.
Allthough soundeffects in the game are alright, i wish a way better music would have been chosen. Not even 4 areas in i decided to put on my own playlist to play through. The song playing is a.... rather weak Midi song that loops throughout the game. It's not really spectacular and rather boring to listen to.
My second problem could only affect me, but i had at times bit of input problems (i used the PS4 Controller to play this game). At times, Jelly didn't jump right way or not at all or didn't self destruct the human body when i needed him to, missing a few jumps or getting the timing wrong. This made some areas a bit frustrating to play through unfortunately.
Some people would also put the short lenght as a legitimate criticism point, but i think this game is alright with it's price and lenght.  The game can be finished in 1-2 hours depending on your skill (the game isn't too difficult to begin with), so take it as you will. I for myself didn't thought i wasted my time or my money, it was a fun experience.
After finishing the game i also tried hard mode for a few Areas. It's basically the same exact thing as Normal mode, but with landmines scattered around the areas to make you watch your little step a bit. Doesn't turn the difficulty to much up though.
Overall, i had fun with it. Would i recommend it for 3 Bucks..? Tough question, but i would go with a Yes. The game is charming for what it is and if you need something quick to play it certainly isn't a bad choice either.

'Unique' is the number one buzzword to describe Betrayer. I'm unable to find a more meaningful description of the game - Betrayer is quite simply, a very idiosyncratic experience.
It's basically one of those 'atmospheric' walking simulators that have been popping up in recent years on digital platforms, but with a dash more substance. It has shades of Far Cry, Skyrim and Dark Souls, so it isn't shy of taking inspiration from the AAA games industry. Gameplay is first person, with an emphasis on stealth, sneak attacks and fighting from a distance.
It can be played in colour, by the way. Trailers on the steam page show much of the game in black and white, with only certain things (like dropped items and enemies) highlighted in a rich blood red tone. It's certainly arty to look at this way, and a good challenge to play, but its just as good to play by applying colour to everything.
The game is set in the New World, in early colonial Virginia. You awake upon a beach, with your only motivation to head inland and explore. You soon meet a mysterious girl in a red hood and the motivation then shifts to you finding out about who she is and what she wants, though this takes a fair bit of time and interaction with the other elements of this world.
Betrayer exudes elements of bizarro, Lovecraftian horror in it's story and the enemies you encounter. I won't spoil the fine details as its certainly a game to go in with very little forward knowledge about, but a large portion of the game is spent in a spirit plane which mirrors the living one. Except its constantly night-time and has this very oppressive and heavy darkness where things immediately ahead of you is enveloped in an enthereal fog, which covers the approaches of many of this world's adversaries, unsurprisingly comprising of skeletons and wraiths.
I mentioned it takes inspiration from Dark Souls before - this being in the fact that, when you die, your inventory remains on the spot you died. You respawn at only one location within each map (usually a fort in the centre). You have one shot at retrieving it, though dying in the attempt or elsewhere on the map makes it vanish from the game entirely. It would give the game an element of strategy, if only ammo and money weren't easily expendable resources. Supplies are all over the space. There's even a trader, though he exists only in some other plane of existence even beyond the capabilites of our unknown protagonist to reach, and offers his wares via a weapons rack at each fort.
The main strength of this game is really its atmosphere alone. Combat is simplistic, what with the weapons on offer being old guns which you slooowly reload after one shot and bows, not always the most accurate quickfire weapon when the AI enemies almost always exhibit the classic tactic of running right at you. The game's story has no real variety to it
beyond solving mysteries of some dead folk. The main story I won't discuss in detail but, overall, I found it rather bemusing and very much open to interpretation, which suits the ethos of this kind of game I guess.
What the game is is part relaxing, with the lush vegetation swaying in the breeze, and part spooky, often edge of your seat scary, though never enough to make you, ahem, pee :D. In terms of stealth, its not great - killing one enemy often leads to another auto-detecting your position and sprinting towards you, to kill you often in two hits on hard difficulty.
For all its charm as a unique game, Betrayer's fundamental gameplay elements fall short of its bigger and better competition. However, it's atmosphere and world are actually strong enough positives to give this game merit and make it worth a recommendation from me. 7/10 overall.
+ excellent, brooding atmosphere
+ its an exploration game to its core and its generally fun to find out the fate of the world's inhabitants/visitors
+ main story and the other little stories/mysteries you solve are generally interesting to unravel and are strictly
tied in with the collectible documents you find
- combat is serviceable but nothing special
- stealth is actually quite bad
- not very replayable

A giant mixed bag.  The game itself is pretty decent: exploring the settlements and investigating the deaths of their former residents is decently entertaining, the combat isn't terribly deep, but still handled well, the visuals are all excellent and effective.  Unfortunately, though, the overall narrative (especially the ending) is flat to lackluster.  While the backstories of the ghosts are quite tragic and thought out well enough, having them told to us flatly by unemotive, similar looking ghosts via text simply isn't that exciting and worse yet, gets repetitive.  Only making matter worse, the end is unsatisfying, raises questions that almost no one is bound to care about, and ultimately leaves us with zero answers regarding our character's identity.  Seriously, who are we playing?  As far as I can tell it's a generic nice guy wandering through the forest armed to the teeth, talking to spirits, and suffering from schizophrenia so severe he thinks all spaniards are beastly monsters and all native americans are on fire.
It's ultimately not a bad game, and if you're really interested, give it a shot.  That said, I really can't recommend this game to the average person.

[TL:DR] - Hitman: Absolution™ is a very well put together game, high quality, and fluent. Sticks to the classic look and feel of past Hitman games. Definitely worth getting whether new to the Hitman games or old.
I was going to post a review a bit earlier, but wanted to gain some more hours of gameplay. From my experiences, the game is well put together and cohesive. The graphics are very good for their time, as this game did come out in 2012.
The presentation of the game is unflawed. The cinematics are very well made and make sense. The entire story makes sense and is executed in a professional manner. In order to feel the full atmosphere of the game, you are required to be patient. If you are not a patient player, and willing to take the time to explore each and every map, as well as explore the multiple ways to carry out an execution, this game is not for you. Each map is elegantly crafted and aesthetically pleasing. The kills are very much like other Hitman games. They allow the player to have freedom. Freedom is a key element to any Hitman game, and Hitman: Absolution™ carries out the tradition. The way that Agent 47 carries himself is 100% organic and realistic. His character model does not walk stiff, and have flow.
Let's talk AI. The AI's interact very well with Agent 47 and his many disguises. While there is not much variation in voice acting (I wish they had more people, and different voices, instead of the same recurring voice saying the same phrase over and over), each NPC reacts a certain way to their environment. There are some flaws, such as; while crouched, you can pretty much be out in the open and not get sighted, this is not anything realistic. Also, regarding disguises, you are able to walk just about anywhere a disguise lets you go. However, the people in your same group (for example, an entire squad of cops), do not seem to realize you are out of place. In actuality, you would think that a small-town police squad would know the faces of everyone on their team, and their names.
Overall cons? Checkpoint system. If you spot a Hitman symbol on the ground with bright lights beaming up, you can lock in a checkpoint. A downside to this is, if you go to restart a checkpoint... it does not save the enemies that you've killed, and re-spawns them. All is not left as it was. When re-starting to a checkpoint, keep this in mind. Instinct is another con, and not in itself. I can see abuse when using instinct. Instinct highlights the entire map for you and what you need to do to escape. It gives a quick point A to point B feel and takes away from the slow paced stealth that is needed to carry out a hit. I feel as though this should have been changed. None-the-less, the pros do outweigh the cons.
The last thing I would like to talk about are mechanics. The mechanics of this game are very interesting! You are able to use different tools such as a fire extinguisher, or a hammer, and throw them to distract guards.  You can climb through windows, throw enemies out of windows! You can sneak up behind targets and garrote or subdue them. There are also 5 different difficulty modes! Each mode uses your critical thinking skills differently, and shows country, world, and friend scores on that level! Contract mode lets you create your own targets to kill, and lets you challenge your friends and other players to execute your contract faster, better, and more efficient.
Wrap it all up! All-in-all, Hitman: Absolution™ carries itself well and IOI should be very pleased with their execution of this product. This has to be my favorite Hitman game among all... It sticks with a classic feel, as well as some add ons! These extras give the game more free-flow and variability.

In short, buy this game if you're looking for:
- Naval-style space combat on a two-dimensional plane against capital ships ranging from frigates to imposing dreadnaughts, ripping them apart with your broadsides while your smaller turrets attempt to deal with the fighters and bombers, while positioning your ship's quadrant-based shield and armor so the strongest side takes the hits while the weakened side recharges.
- If you run from a fight just to upgrade and return to slaughter everyone later.
- An endless supply of side missions to fund those upgrades.
- An economy that highly encourages you to experiment with different weapons. Weapons, defenses, and components transfer to any ship you purchase. Don't like it, just swap it back for a full refund at anytime.
- A game where bigger is not always better. Smaller, faster, more maneuverable corvettes, properly upgraded, will see you through nearly everything but the last set of missions, where your lack of 20 broadside turrets won't allow you to crack the shields of the bigger ships of the final missions.
- If you don't care about a forgettable, anti-climactic story, because the rock 'n' roll and dark country makes you feel like an unstoppable badass anyway.
- A checkpoint-based death penalty. Other than sending you back to the last time you docked, death has no ill effects. You will get a lesson in humility when you're doing your fourth mission in a row without docking, only to watch your hull turn into swiss cheese.
All in all, this is a rather entertaining space-based swashbuckler that places gameplay and action above narrative.

I cannot stand this game. I was a big fan of X3, and I'll admit that might have shaped my expectations. But I bought this thing when it was released fullying knowing it was going to be a different experience. I was fine with that.
But here, in 2016, version 4.0, this game still sucks. It's not fun.
In X3, people talk about a learning curve. When you first enter the game, it's pretty daunting and you really don't know what you're supposed to do. But the pieces are there for you to figure out. I see a station in the distance. I fly over. It has some stuff for sale. They seem to be producing it here (I can tell because of function of the station is in the name), so it's probably cheap. I buy some and continue on my way. I see another station. I fly over. They are buying this good for more than I paid for it! Profit! Other times, a station will have a red cross next to it. That means they will pay me to kill something. The game doesn't specifically tell you what to do, but the world is simple, and you can gradually start piling on the complexity by your own design,
X:Rebirth is a convoluted mess. Stations are no longer stations, but big sprawling space cities with 20 different contact points you have to nose around to see if they offer any function whatsover. Chances are, there may be nothing worthwile to do in the entire city, so you have to move on somewhere else. Travel takes forever. Apparently SETA is back in the game, but its some mission reward (god knows what mission or where to start it), so you are forced to sit through a couple of hours of complete boredom before you can start to shape how your time is spent in this game. Instead of simplicity in design and presentation, X:Rebirth has caked on layer after layer of obstacles between me and what I'm trying to do. That means having to walk on stations and talk to♥♥♥♥♥ugly NPCs just to do basic interactions. That means having to fly around and scan things just to know if there is something being sold. That means having to look at a big, bulky 3D model of a cockpit just to have some basic HUD elements.
I'm aware that mods can fix a lot of these complains. I'm aware that the game will probably seem less grating the more time I spend with it (though I don't think Yisha is going to get any more pleasant). But this is a $40 game and I have a life. I know I spent hundreds of hours in X3, but I could see where it was going pretty early on, even if I still had learning to do. I can't take it on faith that anything interesting is going to happen in X:Rebirth and I don't have to time or energy to find out.

I pre-ordered this game. It wasn't playable when it came out.
Eventually I was able to finish the campaign with a great deal of effort.
Now that 4.0 came out I thought I'd see what playing this was like. I was looking forward to some "empire building".
The native game requires too much micro management, and has completely idiotic design ideas.
- Trade ships only remember stations for certain amount of time. It doesn't seem to matter if they just traded with it 5 minutes ago. All that seems to matter is whether the player ship has seen it recently. Present day is more advanced and efficient than this silly futuristic space game.
- You have to fly near the stations and visually inspect them in order to get trade information. Sure, you can buy trade software to make it so you only have to fly near the station. However, are you kidding me? I can buy things I didn't know existed from towns I have never heard of using this magical thing called the internet. I can have people I've never met ship these wonderous things to me. The designers of this game have failed in so many ways.
- Bugs are still present in this game, and they're silly similar to the bugs I encountered at launch. It is the same now as it was back then. The AI of certain ships die and they no longer do anything, ever. I bought a 10 million credit ship only to have it bug prior to making a single trade. Super cool. I've read online that I can edit the save game to fix it. Awesome. I remember doing that when I bought this game. I'm not doing it again. Not after all this time. Not after all the supposed bug fixes. It is clear that fundamentals in the design of many game systems are flawed and simply prone to error. Apparently if dust falls in the right place, a ship's soul will die.
- Fighting is alright, though imbecilic. Super smart ships will jump to nav beacons in a hostile zones and get immeadiately pummelled. Meanwhile the player sees this and thinks there might be loot nearby. Yes, there is indeed loot nearby. From the half-dozen trade ships that oh so intelligently jumped into hell. Awesome. It's a shame they spent so much effort creating a visually immersive game only to have it be the most non-immersive game in a functional sense. You cannot have one without the other. It doesn't work like that. Ok, it works on the naive. Like, kids... I don't think many kids are buying a game like this...
- Stations! You can go on them! You'll go on these stations a few times before realizing it is a terribly hollow experience. It tries hard visually, again, but fails hard in functionality. There is stuff for you to loot, but again... what? You can take stuff from peoples lockers and it is OK? Of course, because it's just a game... and we don't need immersion or logic here.
Maybe some designer had grand ideas, and some silly person bought into them. Maybe then half way through their timeline they realized they were never going to complete their initial design specification. Maybe this could have been an amazing game if enough money and time was available. I don't know what happened. But, it just isn't good.
Oh and see how many hours I've played? Yeah, that's me leaving the game on overnight hoping SOMETHING WILL HAPPEN.

It's the first time I write a review of a game and I'll keep it short since I hate to waste my precious time...
First and foremost SMBE is a good mix of the old SMAC (Sid Meier's Aplha Centari) from 1999 and the CIV V mold where they introduced the 'City-states' for the first time (if I recall correctly).
Upon purchasing the title I thought I would be treated to a full remake of SMAC, with the very charismatic voice-overs from that time (to this I still play that game just for the immersion value of the various faction leaders agenda AND the FMV's although the latter are starting to show their age by now naturally) and perhaps some updated graphics and an even more compelling storyline.
Unfortunately SMBE isn't a remake of SMAC in that sense and instead relies heavily on CIV V in the way it plays.
We have the city-states which in themselves are a very good partner in the early game trade-wise (which nets you some very nice pace to your various 'city upgrades' per standard CIV) but also some 'new random upgrades' which can be explored by the explorer unit in the form of crashed satelittes and relics, derelict stations and other mysterious junk that keeps you interested for the novelty value they represent to the genre.
We have nicely balanced units (gone is the hilarious Air superiority that was SMAC's most fatal flaw), and a very changing environment as the game progresses (buildings and units change to a more 'advanced' look the further the game progresses and even the faction leaders appearance change during the game which is a nice twist but nothing entirely new).
However what I really miss from SMAC are the FMV's  that would align very well with the various faction leaders credo.
Instead I'm treated with a voiceover and a somewhat rushed graphics of whatever my scientists have been wasting their time on. They've clearly tried to use the same approach to the 'wonders' you made in SMAC, but I for one, feel SMBE has been somewhat rushed and on top of that they've made the decision to not make any FMV's...at...all.
Even after numerous hours and actually winning the game in various ways there's nothing more than that, and that detracts from my overall experience and leave me wanting for more.
If you liked CIV V and can't get enough of it, then this game is for you and now...in...Space YAY!
If you liked SMAC and hoped for more of the same especially with the very different tech-trees and different agendas then sadly SMBE falls short, without being totally bad.

First thing's first: the elephant in the room needs to be addressed. There is no excuse for a ten-year-old game to have problems like crashes and bugs upon re-release. I am glad they released a patch to fix things and it did get rid of the worst of the mess. But I still had problems with muddy textures and annoying glitches with the lighting even with the patch. I even had one point where a scripted event did not happen and I ended up stuck in a room until I loaded a save. I don't understand why a decade old game has these kinds of problems. Unacceptable.
That being said, the game is classic for a reason. I'll be honest, it's difficult for me to be objective because this game holds a special place in my heart. This was the first game I ever played in my life. I have a pair of rose-tinted nostalgia goggles superglued to my face. So I may or may not be able to be totally objective. If you don't want to read to the end, here's the tl;dr... The game is still good. Play it if you haven't already. The bugs are still unacceptable.
It's not a perfect game but it is damn close.
The story is the reason why you are here. It is well told, thought provoking, and interesting. That's all I'm going to say about the story. It's better to uncover the twists for yourself (if it already hasn't been spoiled for you already). The gameplay is good if a bit clunky. You have a real sense of accomplishment when you take down your first Big Daddy. Those fights never get stale. Ever. They remain tense and fast-paced as you adapt your techniques with new plasmids and weapons. Definitely a highlight. However, there is a stiff difficulty curve in the last third of the game. It's a bit frustrating.
The game is beautiful. There is a sense of wonder when you first sail into Rapture and start wandering around. I spent absurd amounts of time absorbing the details of Rapture. And I'll say that while the remaster added a layer of polish, the original game held up quite well over ten years. Even before the remaster, it looked pretty good for its age. If you decide to play the original over this one, I wouldn't blame you at all. It's very good.

The worlds take on very few possibilities and the tech tree, which could have been truly amazing, instead comes of half designed and again without much meat to work with.
Despite these reservations, Beyond Earth is not a bad game. The UI is servisable, the AI is ok, the graphics are the same as Civ 5, and the sound is still top notch.  Its just that this iteration of civ seems so much less like a numbered entry and so much more like an overpriced expansion.

Rebel Galaxy is a stunningly beautiful and smooth to play. The soundtrack really gives the game a "space cowboy" feel to it and I never tired of the music even after hours of gameplay. This game is worth the money.
That being said, there is plenty of room for improvement. The main quest thread, while intruiging, fell a little flat with characters that I never really bonded with and an ending that felt... unfinished. The systems blurred together into a sort of "sameness". It never felt like I was anywhere new and other then slightly more powerful ships to fight, I never really needed to know where I was anyway. With all the ovious beauty, color, and art talent on this team, I was suprised not to see more planets and variety. Where are the habitable worlds? What about gas giants and ring planets? Where are the location descriptions on docking that make me feel like the places I visit have some personality? The ships, on the other hand, were done very well though, each felt artistically distinct and I enjoyed the variety. It would have been nice to have some variety in mechanics though. The weapon selection was somewhat limited and I didn't feel like I had to carefully equip my ship to survive. You either outleveled your opponent or not. I ended with an enormous capital ship, which was cool, but found I had no fighter bays. I found myself limping across half a galaxy while fighters far from my reach fired a stream of engine crippling torpedoes at me.
In closing, this game has great potential. But, it could take a few tips from old, relentlessly addictive space trading and exploring games like Ambrosia's "Escape Velocity". Factions that matter would be nice to see. Factions with territory would be nice to see. Planets and space stations with some location information would be nice. A greater variety of technology, that you actually have to work hard to unlock would be super! How about some alien weapons? Cloaking? Or alien ships? How about the ability to board and capture ships? Have your own fleet? Dominate space stations and make them your own? How about... every once in a while... when your ship VASTLY outclasses some random bandit that warps in to fight you... they hail you and show a little damn respect?

Rebel Galaxy is the first “space sim” I've ever played to completion. I've tried getting into a few others (Elite: Dangerous and Dark Star One come to mind), but after the initially overwhelming but ultimately satisfying learning curve of those games had been conquered I got bored and dropped off once they devolved into tedious job simulators. Rebel Galaxy includes all of the main features of those more complex games, but streamlines them into something more digestible. It takes a hit on it's sense of “realism” and scale, but it's engaging and simplified loop of progress is enough to make up for that.
Did you know space is actually a flat plane? It's a silly concept and not really a complaint, I know, but Rebel Galaxy's one dimensional representation of open space is a good example of what you're in for. You never have to worry about vertical thrust or rolling your ship, just 360 degrees of activity. This feels like literal, ocean-based ship-to-ship combat and navigation with a space backdrop. And it works if you're willing to accept it. What you're losing in freedom you're gaining in ease of use. Most extraneous, technical fiddlings are stripped out: just point your ship where you want to go and hit the warp drive. Hold “A” to dock. There are four speeds to pick from, but just go full throttle and if you want to slow down or stop hold back on the left stick. You know it's a casual sim when the game's launcher recommends you use a gamepad. Again, none of this is inherently bad, it just is what it is. It's an arcade representation of a notoriously complicated genre.
Also unconventional is the personal story that is the driving force of the game. You inherit a ship from your aunt that contains some fragment of something or other that a number of local scumbags seem interested in acquiring. It's pretty clear that there's more to the fragment than meets the eye, and sure enough it soon awakens as an AI. The AI, Trell, directs you to other fragments scattered around increasingly dangerous sectors of the galaxy, which she uses to upgrade your ship to make it feasible to travel to even more dangerous parts of space. She also warns you that there are bad space guys after her, and if they get her it's bad news for everybody. This is all told through really nice looking close up conversations with Cortana's cousin Trell and other characters you meet in seedy space bars. You have some options for responses, but they're pretty limited and don't seem to matter too much. While the story starts off strong and shows promise, it ends up falling apart and fizzling out toward the end. It's the most disappointing aspect of Rebel Galaxy; it had the potential to be a grimy, emotional space opera but doesn't know how to progress or wrap up. It ends so abruptly I actually had to back out of the game and check my achievements to make sure the story was actually over. It was...
While it's a shame the fantastic but rather shallow characters are underutilized, the story is just a jumping off point for the familiar loop of space truckin'. Earn money by any means to upgrade your ship to make it easier to earn even more money in order to buy even better ships to make more money faster. It's a grind at it's core, but the ships look cool and the job simulator repetition is painless enough. You pick missions up from job boards at any space station. These range from delivering cargo to other stations, hunting (space) pirates with bounties on their head, picking up data at dead drops, etc. The higher the difficulty the more money you receive. You could also buy and sell goods for profit, but I didn't find the investment worth it if you're not nuts; you regularly pick up salable cargo from defeated enemies that you can exchange for pure profit so don't bother. You'll also run into distress signals in your travels where you can assist for some easy cash, or take out random bounties. Basically: play the game to earn money.
Almost any path you take will involve combat. Thankfully, like the rest of the game, getting into scraps is simple and enjoyable. You maneuver your ship as you would in naval warfare, with your main means of attack being your broadside cannons. The longer you wait to fire the more focused and accurate your shots become, so you can pinpoint a distant enemy for devastating damage or spam a barrage of wild shots to keep a ship's shields down or harass smaller swarms closer to you. You're also outfitted with a secondary weapon you can use with the “X” button. I went with flak cannons to destroy incoming missiles and smaller vessels, but you have options like homing missiles as well (which you need to buy ordinance for). Depending on how large of a ship you're piloting you can equip a number of turrets like shield destroying missiles, long range lasers, or mining lasers. You can control these manually, but I found the simpler my approach to combat the better the results. After experimenting with using the secondary lasers to take out smaller ships and targeting individual modules on capital ships, it took me an embarrassingly long time to realize I was overplaying the game. Just focus on your broadsides, spam your secondaries, and let the auto turrets do their work and you're playing optimally.
Rebel Galaxy offers a custom soundtrack option, and it's a small feature that goes a long way. The included soundtrack is decent, twangy Space Western tunes that sell the premise, and the ability to add your own songs is invaluable. You have several pathways to store the music, so you can divide your list to play only while at space stations, at the title screen, while traveling, during combat, etc. If you don't have Deep Purple's “Space Truckin'” on there you ♥♥♥♥ed up, but other than that it's great to inject your own mark onto the game and it makes travels through deep space feel like a road trip. This was a standard feature of the Xbox 360 but has sadly dropped off, and having it fully integrated here is fantastic and certainly welcome.
If you're looking for a deep simulation that requires every button on your keyboard for knobs and dials and subsystems Rebel Galaxy might not be the game for you. If you've come to the realization that those games are for crazy people and want to relax to some Johnny Cash as you cause some space wars and marvel at how such visual chaos can be distilled into simple arcade controls, Rebel Galaxy delivers. The promising story ends up being kind of crap and there's a definite grind to endure, but the game has heart and personality and delivers what I value most: fun.

Quick Summary: Rebel Galaxy is an open-universe space combat/exploration/trading/mining/pirating game.
Quick Score: 8/10 - Great gameplay, graphics and sound, can get grindy and repetitive.
Full Review:
I'll talk about, in order of relevance to me personally, Gameplay, Graphics, and Sound.
Gameplay-
If you liked the ship combat in Assassins Creed Black Flag, then you'll find something to love here. The game takes place on a flat plane, which means no z-axis navigation. You're solely on the X-Y Plane. And that's a good thing, once you see the competition you're up against. But don't worry, only the smaller craft go up and down, the larger ones don't. You can individually man a selection of turrets or your broadsides in combat. There's a variety of each type to choose to suit your playstyle. If you like to get up close and personal, or keep your distance, there's a weapon for you. When you are not controlling the turrets directly, they are controlled by the AI, which you can configure. You can set them to lock onto specific targets, fire at will, or be completely manual. It's up to you. Even navigation is largely the same as Black Flag. Accelerate in stages, decelerate in stages with optional braking, and turn from side to side.
Aside from that, there's things like factions you can side with, an economy to exploit, mining activities, and so on. A story is present, but can go largely ignored. Feel free to blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and rack up the credits to the next ship upgrade. Speaking of, aside from aforementioned weaponry, defenses such as shields and armor and subsystems, which run specialised tasks as additions to your ship, can be upgraded. In a refreshing change of norm, you don't lose any credits when buying and selling items for your ship, so you're free to experiment until you find something that works. Even the ships you purchase come in a variety of sizes, from meek little frigates to massive and lumbering dreadnaughts and destroyers. There's plenty of ways to find a loadout more to your playstyle.
One complaint I often see in space games is the sheer lack of things to do between travels. Fortunately, Rebel Galaxy keeps you on your toes. What may seem like a routine flight to another station may result in attending to a distress signal, getting ambushed by the enemy, or crashing into a nebula, with rocks (sorry, unsure what it's actually called) to dodge, mine or destroy. You can't expect to set your target and make some tea.
There's also significant strategy in taking down opponents. Firing at the left side of the ship reduces the shielding for that side only, and not all the way round. Same goes for armor. So do you take an all-sides approach, or focus on one side of the ship? It's not so easy to just fire away, as you need to consider these things when attacking.
Should you wish to make some dough, you can take on side missions or perform things like trading, mining, bounty hunting, and so on. It shouldn't be too hard to get the credits required for your next purchase.
Graphics-
I'm not one to stress on how pretty a game looks. I'm more for graphics. But my oh my is this game pretty. I'm more the person who feels Mirror's Edge looks better than Crysis 3, and the same goes here. Not the Crysis 3 thing. Space is beautiful. Instead of making it a black cosmos, with little white dots, it's colourful. Distant nebulae pepper the view with dashes of red, green, blue, purple, etc. Ships look worn but strong. Damage modelling is pretty impressive. ou can see scorch marks and chunks missing, embers glowing with some of the inner components revealed if you suffer significant damage. Weapons look beautiful when fired. They glow brightly, be it lasers or missiles. Speaking of, there's a flare effect from oncoming missiles fired from afar. Gives it a very cinematic feeling. There's also enough lens flare to make JJ Abrams happy, but it's done tastefully. Rest assured you won't have your view blocked by it. The UI is clean and uncluttered, letting you really soak in the surroundings. Rocket trails, when at warp, leave long blue lines behind you, and they each have a different layout depending on the thrusters of your ship. The Pulse effect looks good, akin to sonar visualised. When braking your ship, the thrusters turn red, as though they were brake lights. I considered it a nice touch.
Sound-
Best soundtrack so far. The game comes with a preloaded country/western soundtrack, that actually fits really well with the game. Should it not be your thing, feel free to add your own music collection, with the ability to set specific folders to different moments in the game, ie Combat, Travel, and so on. I personally set some dubstep for combat. As for sound effects, they're powerful. Flak cannons properly deafen, missiles have their own distinct sound, and everything comes together without sounding deafening. Even the AI which reports on your ship's status is plucked straight outta Sci-Fi stereotype, but hey, it works! Voice acting for the other characters you meet along the way is decent, but some of the quips from your enemies will begin to repeat fairly early.There's variety in language too. Different species may speak different languages, but in a way that sounds realistic. All in all, pretty good.
Conclusion: The game gets repetitive, sure, so its longevity  really depends on how much fun you can have. I personally see this as the kind of game I can invest quite some time it, but your mileage may vary.

A compelling tale of discovery, ghosts, regret and, naturally, betrayal.
You travel around a section of woodland near the coast of the New World with no real understanding of who you are or what you must do, meeting variuos trapped spirits along the way. Each wraith you encounter has its own unique baskstory, which normally ties into the stories of the other wraiths in the area. There is areally chilling overarching plotline which retains a couple of eerily ambiguous elements and it only picks up speed as you go through the game.
This is a superb short game (you could grind it out in a week easily, and I fully suggest you do so) but not without content. True, there could be a bit more variation in the maps/objectives, but that's really not what this game is about; rather it is something to play slowly and contemplatively, exploring every tree stump and rock face and traversing every inch of the woodland on the hunt for clues. It somehow avoids being boring despite being really much of the same for the duration.
The graphics are great and run wonderfully, the sound design is EXCELLENT and is one of the few games I can think of where sound was actually an aspect which jumped out at me, and the gameplay is simplistic and smooth. Loot and weapons are fairly standard, but you do find some interesting variations on the same weapons as you get later in the game. There are multiple incarnations of each weapon type, getting progressively stronger as the game progresses.
At the start of the game you feel so weak, only being able to take on a couple of enemies at once at a push, stealth really is the preference for early game. Towards the end, however, it is possible to find weapons capable of taking down a skeleton in one hit, even the floating skulls are no match for you near the end, but combat is not the focus of the game and you never feel overpowered.
My favourite aspect of Betrayer is the level of customisation the game gives you. you can choose to play the game in black and white or colour, with variable saturation, as well as having control over the enemy difficulty at any point in the game. The best part of customisation, however, is the map, which you can set to display the locations of various goals, or, as I prefer, not. It is useful to be able to turn these settings on after the plot draws to a close for completionists out there, just so you can polish off the few chests you might have missed.
One downside is that it also seems to highlight chests/objectives you have previously attained in the map, although this only happens once you return to an area you have previously visited. I also noticed that, at one point in the game, it decided to invert the stereo; so what should have been in my right ear was suddenly in my left visa vera, which was incredibly disorientating in game which utilises sound to direct you to the wraiths. However the fix was easy, as I just swapped my headphones round.
Apart from these two very minor greivances, Betrayer is a great game from such a small developer and at a great price. I fully recommend it to anyone looking for an atmospheric daytime-horror game. Theres something in this game which is certainly creepier and more harrowing than any xenomorph jumping through the air vents. Its more subtle than that. Buy this game.

Have you ever had your mouth and eyes wide opened while looking at something? That was my constant reaction during the 9 hours it took me to finish Betrayer 100%. During these 9 hours I journeyed through these sinister and ominous places filled with mystery in this colorless and lonely world. Filled with nothing but skeletons and other horrors during the unnatural night and Spaniards that resemble more beast than men during the day. I had never heard about this title before. Seeing it's black and red image with a skeleton walking on a hill quickly seduced me into trying it out. Before I could say 'I love this game' I was already in awe when I started the game on the shore of an unknown land after a shipwreck on a black and white world where at the ring of a bell the sun vanishes from the sky and the unsettling terrors of the night come out to haunt the land.
Betrayer is extremely beautiful in it's black&white choice of art direction. If you want you can access the options menu and get rid of the black&white and add color to the game but I really don't see why anyone would do that if they want to experience the game in all it's dreadful wonder. I have only chose to add color after I finished everything just so I could see how everything looked. But after a couple of minutes of seeing how things looked with color I instantly changed back to the black&white because I think that's how the game should be played in my opinion and that's how I enjoy it. I think it adds to the strangeness and mystery of the whole adventure. Regardless of the visual art choice you prefer, the game is beautiful with or without color. But give it a shot with black&white and after you finish the game you can always replay it all colorful.
You start off at the beach like I mentioned before and as you make your way through the woods you come across Spaniards that growl and moan like animals and charge at you the moment they see you. You then reach a village where you meet a Woman in Red and that is where the game truly begins. You can free roam as you see fit. The game is composed of diferent zones where you can play. You start in one zone and if you want to change places you gotta go to the waypoint that connects that place to the other and go through the loading screen in order to change locations. Kind of like Fable. Where instead of having an open world like the GTA franchise. You have a world that you can free roam as you want but it's sectioned into zones.
On these zones you will perform the necessary quests to advance the story. You will find the locations of your objectives via your compass displayed at the top of the screen and via a haunting sound that guides you towards your destination. At the ring of a bell that exists in each town of each of the diferent sections of the map, you turn day into night and vice versa. Your objectives will consist of talking to ghosts and finding out what happened to them and that place. This will involve walking around the map looking for places to dig, shrines to cleanse and finding journals and letters and other types of items that will help you piece together the story of each individual trapped in that land as well as the story of the haunting place where you find yourself in. So maybe it can get a bit repetitive though I must say that I never got bored because everything was so hauntingly seductive to find out. At least for me because I am a big fan of games that set a nice dreadful and mysterious mood.
The stunning visuals goes hand to hand with the sounds present throughout the game. While the game only has 2 or 3 actual songs that are used basically on the menu and at the credits. It doesn't need an actual soundtrack to add to the imersion of the game.
The menacing stillness of everything around you is amazing. Everything is so frozen in place and quiet it's unerving. From time to time the wind will blow through the fields, masking your footsteps sounds and thus enabling you to sneak up on enemies and it's a sound that you will quickly associate to running as fast as you can while the wind is blowing. The sound you hear when you headshot a Spaniard with your bow at a rather long distance is extremely satisfying. The growls of said Spaniards when they are alerted of your presence will make look around everytime. The sounds of wraiths and skeletons will unerve you. And the sound you have to follow in order to get to your objective and the sound the bell makes when you ring it will stay in your head throughout the whole game. Those two sounds stuck with me for a while as I thought they were really awesome.
The game was very fun for me to play. I can't express this enough but to me the most important thing is the ambience, the mood the game sets and that weird gut feeling you get. By saying this I am not disregarding the aspects that compose a game such as gameplay mechanics. But to me if a game sets a good mood and ambience it won't matter that much if the other aspects of the game aren't as good. This is what I look for and I was extremely surprised to find Betrayer in this day and age. Making something diferent that modern games no longer try to do. Games have become rather generic but once in a while you find a cult classic like this that deserves to have a bigger community.
Like I said, mood and ambience are very very important to me and Betrayer nails it. I was instantly gripped to it the moment I saw everything black&white. It fills me with a will to find out more. To think there are mysteries and secrets on that universe that I must uncover. Wanting to find out what everything means, the 'why' and 'what' of everything. It's a game that leaves me going "Han? What is this? What the hell? I don't understand!". Even after you finish the story you hope there is more!
Betrayer will seduce you from the start with it's gripping ambience. And will keep you hooked with the amazing mood set through out the game. The sound of the bell will get you everytime. That journal you just found and read will tell a story that will stay with you for a while. And it's these things that matter to me. These simple things like reading a journal and at the end of it thinking "what does it mean? does this mean something?" that make a game go a long way and immerse those who play it. You will most certainly feel the palpable dreadful strangeness of this hauntingly captivating world as you immerse yourself in it.

A wide variety of endings that you can attempt to achieve. Or you can be like me and get the 2 most common endings and call it a day until you feel the need to get the other endings. Eventually. Probably one of the deepest video games I have ever played/not played.

X: Rebirth is, for me, the VERY BEST GAME Egosoft have ever released, by a HUGE margin!
To put that in context, I'm a LONG time X-phile, having played every game since the very first release: X: Beyond The Frontier (1999). While I've enjoyed each iteration in the series, there have been many things I found frustrating and, ultimately, after Albion Prelude (2011) I decided I'd had more than enough of being punished for my dreams: I vowed never to buy another Egosoft game.
Earlier games were massive time sinks, Pretty and often fun, but requiring weeks if not months of REAL TIME graft to get to the big ticket rewards like capital ships and fleet battles. There was also an inordinate amount of tedious repetition involved in trading between sectors and stations. Worse, items always cost so damned much. New guns for your ship? That'll be hours of monotonous trading, please. New ship? Come back in a week!
At their worst, earlier X games felt exactly like that real life job we are supposed to be gaming to escape from.  Dull, monotonous and frequently punishing. Some like that: for me, it was torture having the dream of a space game so close but unable to achieve it thanks to some obstinate design decisions. Because I love space games, and because Egosoft were producing the ONLY A-grade space games out there for the longest time, I held out like a battered husband, hoping things would eventually improve.
It had a very rough start. Egosoft should not,
, have released the game in the state they did. By all accounts it was buggy and broken, on top of being a severe departure from earlier games. Not having bought it I sat back and laughed at my bullet-dodging cleverness.
However, a couple of years later, after huge amounts of polish, tweaks and additions by Egosoft, Rebirth is now an absolute gem! A sparkling diamond in place of 1.0's jagged black coal. I've been playing it non-stop since I bought it. I
playing it. This redesigned universe just makes so much more sense than it ever did. Activites make more sense, feel more logical. The graphical improvements are enormous, and a joy to behold (the stations are
!), but it's the gameplay that now really shines. So much opportunity everywhere! Missions that finally pay out decent rewards! Items priced low enough that a mission or two can afford them! I can repair my ships now without spending a week trading to offset the cost!
!
Yes, there are still wonky bits. The narrative is compelling but awkwardly told. NPC modelling and animation rarely looks right. Voice acting is average at best, ear-destroying at worst. The menu-driven UI can still be a bit fiddly. And there's so much to [re]learn. But these are now minor complaints considering the rest of the game design now offers so much fun.
I heartily recommed buying X: Rebirth at the earliest opportunity!

Yeah, I know. This game is published by the company that brought us two unplayable products before. All non-Russian reviews are negative. Even the two positive reviews hardly count as such - one is sarcastic (the reviewer seems to have refunded the game), the other one is from a guy who played for just 40 minutes. The almighty Jim Sterling has publicly called this game "sh*t" and "utter garbage". So it must be complete trash, right? Right?
You know what? I approached this game with an open mind, and I really enjoyed it. Yes, it's pretty rough around the edges. But it also provides several deliciously surreal environments to explore. I liked how the artists used scale, transparency, and reflection to create interesting surroundings. The atmospheric sound-work was outright excellent in my opinion. The story, even though it was told in a very clumsy way, with text in broken English that sometimes wasn't even fully visible, touched interesting subjects. The puzzles gave me a sense of progression and accomplishment, but were also easy enough to not detract from the experience. (At two points I had to look up non-obvious solutions in the forum.)
That said, I fully understand why people might not like this game. If you expect a polished experience, then a game where you can easily wander off the map and fall endlessly into the void will hardly meet that expectation. If you expect a story with the philosophical depth and skillful execution of "The Talos Principle", then this game's broken language and buggy text display will feel jarring. If you expect challenging or diverse puzzles, then this game may feel bland - most puzzles are simply key collection quests, or mazes to navigate.
But if you're the kind of player who likes being taken on strange journeys, give Invisible Mind a chance. If it sounds interesting to you to walk through a valley where transparent human silhouettes desperately slam their hands against non-existent walls, watched over by two massive skulls and a cross above a fire, then have a go at it. I found the journey enjoyable and inspiring, despite the flaws.
(Disclosure: Key was bought with a bundle. No prior contact to the developer.)
(Side note: I'm not sure if an army of fans will downvote this review if I mention this, but I really think that a certain video game critic could treat quirky games with more respect, instead of seeing them just as fodder for sarcastic comments. I'm absolutely fine with critics not liking or even panning games, and I totally agree that Invisible Mind is not a game that lends itself to be showered in praise. But, seriously - if a critic clearly shows no inclination at all to even get in the mood for an atmospheric game, and talks half the time about his unfinished business with the No Man's Sky community before then offhandedly dismissing the game he's (not actually) playing as "garbage", then I think we're overstepping a line. Am I asking for too much when I say that a critic should, perhaps, actually give a game a modicum of attention before panning it?)

My time with Civilization: Beyond Earth wasn't *awful* but the game just felt... Soulless. It might not be fair to compare it to Civ V with all its expansions but it's the one that will inevitably be made and, unfortunately, BE doesn't hold up. All the depth and multiple layers of strategy present in Civ V were greatly diminished here, with the only reall addition in terms of strategic depth being the affinity system, which I personally didn't enjoy since pursuing a certain affinity ties you to a very defined end goal when compared to Civ V's much freer victory types and Ideology system.
A major bugbear for me was the horrifying slog of the early game. The game, even on lower difficulties, throws an obnoxious amount of aliens at you and, although they rarely attack, it's quite discouraging to have your vital early units murdered in one hit by a siege worm. Additonally the mechanic of miasma, a toxic alien goo that initially damages your units, only serves to increase the grindy nature of the early game as you mechanically clear miasma before building an improvement on that tile. It just unnecessarily lengthens the early part of the game and makes for a somewhat dull experience.
I did have some positive thoughts about BE, however. The game runs fantastically on my machine, even better than Civ V (which occasionally dipped just below 60 with large amounts of units onscreen and when loading in the map). It maintains a rock solid framerate at all times and the game has all the options one would expect from a top-notch PC game. I also loved the general aesthetic of the game, the sleek, white human units and settlements only serving to enhance the alien nature of this initially hostile planet with its colourful, vibrant terrain. I also enjoyed the overall theme of human endeavour and scientific progress overcoming vast hardship. Like other Civ games, it's a somewhat celebratory experience that makes you feel good about humanity (until you decide to send in the military units, of course).
Would I recommend this game, based on my admittedly short play time? No. It's a solid foundation for a good game, but not a good game in itself. Just like with previous entries in the series, I suspect this game will be an absolute corker once it receives some expansion content but, until then, I'd leave it alone and spend your money on the vastly superior Civ V with its two main expansions.

You see that house over there? The one with the elderly couple? That's where your food and medicine is. Now you can either ignore it and try and find a small tin of food buried underneath some rubble, or you can kill those innocents and take their stuff.

I bought this game a while ago as an episodic package after seeing it on the front page of Steam. I was taken by the look of it and I am a fan of point-and-click adventure games. I'm still very happy that I stumbled upon this game.
The artwork is amazing and adds a depth to the game that complements the story very well. The few animations that are present feel natural for the artstyle even if they aren't perfectly smooth. I can appreciate the time that goes into creating each scene in this game.
The story has been very captivating thus far. It builds up very well and I feel very anxious to continue the story after each chapter. Although it would be nice to have audio instead of full text, it is very easy reading with short clips of text instead of walls.
The actual gameplay is pretty generic for a point-and-click adventure game with puzzles and a fair amount of walking from room to room using simple clicks for mechanics and a few drags to piece things together. For a real story-driven adventure game, though, I can deal with simple mechanics that allow for greater concentration on the puzzles, story, etc.
The developers are working hard at keeping the game updated and fixing any known bugs or issues. Fortunately, I haven't come across any issues with the game, myself. They've been constantly refining and adding to the game so it's likely better to pick up a copy later in development. It has been released on more and more platforms as the game ages.
The only real qualm that I have with the game is the extremely slow release of the chapters. When I purchased the game, I believe chapter 3 was just being released or had just been released. The release date for chapter 3 was October 31, 2011. To put the delays into context, chapter 4 was just released August 6th, 2013. I'm never one to mind waiting for a delay on a release for a well-refined product but that was a bit extreme. Fortunately, the developers have mentioned a release for chapter 5 in just months instead of years. Here's hoping. A miserable part of waiting so long is you have to revisit places and puzzles you've done in previous chapters; however, the game is quaint enough and easy enough to follow that forgetting shouldn't be a problem for most.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. The price isn't bad and it does go on sale on Steam. There is a demo available on the official website that allows you to play the entirety of chapter 1 through your browser. I'd say that the demo, at least, is a must-play.

If you noticed the game on a sale and you are either struggling to pay the required amount of money or just looking down the comment section to see if it's worth it... BUY IT. Like a great person and an ultimate memelord once said: "JUST DO IT!". This is an RTS video game which main goal is to rule a growing space empire. The game is filled with content, it features real time combat (the unit limit is seriously high, so the battles are not only challenging and exciting but also huge and spectacular) which requires input from the player since you can manage every single ship on the battlefield separately, especially capital ships that will level up after gaining enough XP points and require the player to put some input in the direction of where the upgrade points go. However the game is not only focused on combat unlike the majority of other RTS games with such massive battles. While the battle is going on you can just zoom out and control your empire, send reinforcements or either start an another battle in a different spot. As I mentioned before, not only you have to fight and conquer, but also do research, gather resources, manage the planetary and orbital infrastructure of each planet you own, run a diplomacy between you and other players, give missions to factions or pirates, bribe pirates to strike empires other than yours and do other stuff that a space emperor would do. The point is, there is so much content, such a huge game world (if you feel like a single solar system of 30+ planets isn't enough for you, there is an option to play on a map based on several solar system each one with tens of planets ) with so many planets/sectors to rule and various ways of victory (diplomatic,total annihilation etc.) that it's hard to put everything into a smal steam review. Even though it is an RTS game, the matches can stay up to several hours or days as it is in Civilization V. It makes the game a fun multiplayer production with an option to host a multiplayer lobby and save the game progress so it can get loaded next time you want to play, that's why the game plays the best if you have friends who are willing to play it with you.
In a nutshell - it is a fun RTS game with many gameplay possibilities and a great multiplayer module. If you are a fan of RTS games you should definitely get it !

I played using the bow almost exclusively, because it felt like the other weapons were just slight variations on range, fire rate, and reload speed. You can apparently try to sneak up on enemies from behind, but let me tell you: This is NOT a stealth game. It's all outdoors. You're out in the open. You encounter a woman in red, who has forgotten her name. For some reason, you can give the woman trinkets that you find. She immediately questions your motives for giving her a gift. She will then either begrudgingly accept the gift or refuse it and send a passive-aggressive insult at you. Look, I don't know why I'm giving you anything! Mystery solved! I'm Sherlock-effing-Holmes!

Before I start, I need to second the other review that suggests adjusting the saturation to make the colors appear. The game is absolutely gorgeous.
So where to start... The story telling is pretty amazing. Without spoiling, your goal is to travel through some settlements to find out what happened to everyone. You explore the towns and wilderness to find graves, lost items, and ghosts that each tell a part of an overall story. Some of the stories are sad, some unsettling, and some are horrific. All of them are pretty well written.
One cool mechanic the game has, is the second world you enter through the town bells. Ring the bell and jump into the next world where you get to talk to the ghosts of the people who have died to piece together the stories. There are new enemies in this world, and everything is black and white. You go back to the normal world by silencing the bell.
There isnt any music, but the game sound is pretty well done as well. You can hear enemies approach, and you hear animals (though you never see those) as well as wind. The ambience in the second world is absolutely creepy.
The combat stuck out to me as well. I loved it. The weapons are simple, though varied, and you can "equip" three different ones. There are guns, as well as bows, and your mele weapon. Ammo is limited, and if you choose to rely on bows, you can go find your used arrows, or claim them from fallen enemies. In a prolonged fight, you might end up having to dance around picking up arrows as you use them. I loved how missing a shot felt like it actually mattered, as did landing a shot. The enemies, no matter the difficulty, are all fairly strong, and you will probably die at some point. The game has an option for you to drop your items when you die if you like making things even harder.
The map also has options to show where all the chests, graves, ghosts, etc are on the map, or lets you hide the locations. I left them all revealed.
That also reminds me of an interesting mechanic the game uses. There is an ear you find early on that lets you "listen" to find where ghosts are, items, and things of interest. You go into the dark world and "listen", then follow the whispery sound. Its like quest tracking through audio, which is great if you dont want to keep checking your map every few seconds to see where to go next.
Overall, I would highly recommend it, especially if youre into a more subtle, creepy horror style, or if you just love a great story.

I had been looking for a single player space based game that included missions, mining, exploration and ship to ship combat for a long time before I came across Rebel Galaxy. I picked this game up on sale hoping it would provide me with what I had been looking for and was happily satisfied.
You start Rebel Galaxy off in a tiny ship and are quickly thrown into this massive galaxy head first with no real direction and plentiful choices on what to do first, an amazing first impression. After a few hours I found that some of the missions were kind of repetitive so I moved on to a different sector to try a new guild. While the missions did vary there are a lot of fetch quest style side missions that unfortunately did not change as the game progressed.
Rebel Galaxy shows you straight from the start these giant dreadnaught class ships worth $15m+ while you are making a measly $10k a mission. This while great, also lead to a desire to acquire better ships and gear as quickly as possible. The problem with this choice is due to the games difficulty system, which  is never explained. Rebel Galaxy seems to use four mechanics to set difficulty; system rating, mission difficulty and the last two are based on what hull class and gear type you are using. The game only considers your highest individual type of gear to set the difficulty which can lead to some annoying situations where you are severely outclassed by the enemy ships .
These two points should not dissuade you from this game, however. Almost every other aspect was fantastic. The music, while I found not suited to space exploration, was great and has been well received by the community . The ship types and styles all were unique and looked great while offering a variety of build possibilities and attack styles. The weight and feel of the ships during combat and the combat itself.
The battles at the core of the game can be amazingly chaotic, the large varieties of ships / builds with different amounts of each in a fleet can lead to some of the biggest fights you have ever been in. I went into a great number of battles ridiculously outnumbered and when surviving in the final moments after a tense and carefully executed fight,  let out a profanity or cheer due to the satisfaction of these sometimes epic encounters.
Overall this game scratched an itch that I've had for years that nothing has come close to. For the price and the amount of time you can get out of this game I couldn't recommend it enough.

My overall rating for Betrayer: 71/100
Betrayer is set in New England, year 1604. The mystery, what wiped out the whole colony is to be solved by you, an unknown adventurer in a grim world coloured by white, dark and red. Game promised to be a stealth detective horror experience, what was not always fulfilled. But let's see in detail.
GAMEPLAY
+ Wide locations
+ Various enemies
+ Day/Night possibility
+ Possibility to turn off hints and still find your goals
- Grinding and collecting things
- Tendency to be repetetive and boring
- Stealth not always possible
Gameplay is definitely the weakest part of whole game. Though there are various locations you can explore and feel free to do so, enemies designed as Spanish soldiers, or ghosts and skeletons at night, most of the time you will be running from one end of map to another and collect things needed for the solution.
Progress is linear, clear the map, release all the spirits and move to next region. I got bored several times here, even the horror atmosphere was weaker, because I could expect the same change after moving to the night and back. It seemed later to me, that day is even more scary than the night!
It states here, that it should be a stealth game, but a lot of enemies appear right next to you, when you are passing them by, so there are not a lot of chances to get them undetected. That pays also for groups, longbow or crossbow, stealthy or not, you are hunted by the whole group, does not matter what your tactics are.
But there is one point, that you cen turn off your hints and try your detective skills at their best. Good luck!
VISUALS
+ Perfect atmosphere in a comics' book style
+ Details of armours and colonial stuff
- Possibility to play in regular colours
At this part of the title, I am amazed. The white-dark-red combination set a grim and uneasy atmosphere, it really has somethign from horror, I do not recommend to set natural colours, because after that, it becomes just a colonial-style FPS. What Betrayer is not at all.
CHARACTERS
+ Variety of characters
+ Releasable or banishable
- Most of them are not important for the story
There are plenty ghosts, their stories need to be revealed. You can search and find out, what was their crime, or that they were victims. But most of them are just for keeping players in the game and their only purpose is to unlock next destination. But in the end, you can decide, whether their acts are forgivable or not. Interesting point.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Eerie sounds
- Not existing
Eerie sounds are good for this type of game, but in the end, it is not sufficient to create all the impression from playing. It is just a part of the composition and there needs to be something more, that drives player further into the story. And there was nothing else, sadly. What a waste of potential.
SUMMARY
Betrayer had a great potential to be one interesting and captivating game. But it seems to me, that the developers did not see, or were not able to use it all and their work acts half-finished and tacky. I was very puzzled after finishing, open end did not change anything and it was predictive as hell.
Therefore, I can not recommend this game. Either buy it during a huge sale (-75% at least), or, better, watch a gameplay from YouTubers.

Betrayer is a stealth horror action-adventure played from a first-person perspective. It uses a monochrome art style that Eurogamer‍‍ '​‍s Dan Whitehead described as "undeniably striking". The game has no clear missions or markers for quest objectives, aiming to initially perplex players by not providing a defined sense of direction. Sound plays a central role in exploring the game world, as it is used to lead the player to clues and other points of interest. While progressing, any clues found are meticulously documented in the inventory windows. Similar to The Elder Scrolls series, players can quickly navigate from one location to another by clicking a point-of-interest icon on the game's map. In the game, players stealthily kill enemy conquistadors by creeping through tall grass and hiding their movements by timing them with strong gusts of wind. Enemies are killed using a variety of antiquated weaponry including bows, crossbows, pistols, muskets, and thrown tomahawks. Taking inspiration from Dark Souls, when the player dies in the game all of their items are left on their corpse at the location of death. The player then respawns at the base fort and must journey back to where they died to retrieve their items from their corpse. If the player dies again before retrieving their items, then the items on that first corpse will disappear and can not be recovered. Sometimes Betrayer seems like more horrible  than Outlast or Amnesia. One time my emotions get the better of me and i was screamed .I sincerely recommend this game for all people who likes horrors and stealth in one bottle.

As a big fan on Civilization 5 and many other 4x games, I was looking forward to the strange new world and interesting mechanics that Beyond Earth would bring.  Unfortunately, what I found was a competent, but lifeless, game held back by unambitious design and a completely unremarkable aesthetics.
As a 4X game, you take turns with the AI or in multiplayer expanding accross a world.  Each tile has various resources that must be cultivated, allowing you to access new buildings, technologies, units, and special bonuses.  I'll assume that newcomers to the genre will read other sources (or just try the demo) for a more detailed description.
Beyond Earth broadly copies the same features that worked well in Civilization 5.  That series, however, has had  expansions and many patches to add content and make significant balance changes.  Beyond Earth, by contrast is missing many of the more interesting features, and what's present lacks personality.
You may choose between 8 factions, but the gameplay differences between are very minimal.  There's nothing that would significantly change how you play, nor, indeed, are there many diffferences in the dress or mannerism of each leader.  By contrast, Civ 5 and most other 4x games offer leaders with dramatically different appearances and behavior, with gameplay differences to match.  A game set in the future was the opportunity to go wild with different ideas, but instead everyone seems the same. As the first choice of many that you make in the game, the unappetizing leader selection sets the tone for the whole game.
Worse, buildings and special projects all follow this same limited, conservative design philosophy.  Most buildings only offer an incremental bonus of a few resources like science or energy.  Even the 'wonders' that you build are only modestly more powerful versions of buildings most of the time.  There's little excitement or satisfaction at completing them.  More successful games make unlocking a new building or wonder feel like a real game changer.
All told, there's nothing truly bad about Beyond Earth.  It's a lesser copy of a more vibrant game.  It'll hold your interest for one game, but afterwards I felt no desire to go back.  I'd choose to go back to earth, and play Civ 5 instead.

Whenever a new Civilization game comes out, there’s always the anticipation of a small revolution for all lovers of this micro and macro management turn based strategy title (that sounds more complicated than it is, right?). With Beyond Earth, Firaxis wanted to break new ground by offering their vision of the humanity close future. Besides, it’s a bit like the original game concept: what will our future hold to us and what will we accomplish as a specie?
Let’s move quickly on to the context and history of the game: humanity has become too big for our little blue planet and it’s time to conquer a new world. Humans were picked by their skills and luck to fly across space into unknown planets, building new colonies, making hard choices to survive but also forge their history. A perfect time for this game, after the release of Nolan North’s Interstellar, don’t you think?
Civilization V already became the title to be deemed more accessible than the previous ones, and Beyond Earth continues to improve things with the help of quests. These help as both a tutorial for new players to guide them in their choices, but are also a way to tell the story of your civilization. Moreover, depending on your style of play, you’ll tend to pledge allegiance to one of three affinities, which will affect the quests, and influence its different bonuses throughout the game.
Beyond Earth at first seems chaotic, especially for those used to the Sid Meier’s franchise, with its immensely color scheme and details of the alien planets we are about to settle our first colony on. The interface might have not changed much from Civilization V, but it’s the heavy change of scenery that becomes quite overwhelming. Gone are the lands filled with barbarians and coal to be mined, but hello to Alien nests and Firaxite minerals to exploit.
