It is a game that has potential but somehow manages to ruin it with a bunch of small flaws that soon add up.
Firstly the rocks as a way to lead you through the level is fine if you have a linear path through (which you don't), it is quite possible to follow the 'wrong' rock to a dead end and have to rethink completely where your going. This leads to unneeded fustration and could be solved with either a local minimap, a compass pointing you in the correct direction or even just numbering the rocks in a way to make it clear.
Second the FOV is awful, it rescticts what you can see and actually makes it harder to position yourself for a laser cut as you have to be able to see the whole object to cut it.
Thirdly for some ridiculous reason when you push an object instead of zooming out so you can see where your pushing, it zooms in so you can't see where your going.
The final and perhaps the biggest problem is the way the game is set-up it is quite possible to have dumb luck by a rock falling in the wrong place or a cut not quite going right to be completely  stuck and have to restart from the checkpoint.
The developers got too ambious and tried to make the game too open and this was ultimately for me at least turned out to be its undoing.
All of that being said the music in it is great, and although I initially liked the visual astetic of it the desert setting started to feel like an excuse to make things bland.

It’s funny what grabs your interest at times. Today’s spotlight focuses on Immortal Game Studios’ first game on Steam, Jelly Killer. The game looks like a cute enough little platformer when you view it on the Steam store but it doesn’t look like something that will grip you. I’m a little taken aback at just how much I was attracted to the game while playing it and just how much I wanted to continue on before writing this review.
It’s an action platformer where you have to complete 54 different areas while mind controlling five different and unique characters who have abilities that your normal jellyself is unable to do himself. For example, you have a workman looking dude, a plumber I think they called him, who has the ability of pushing boxes and you have the professor who can jump higher and further than the jelly. The game is very simple and straight forward and really takes more brains than brawn to be able to complete. This increases the game’s accessibility as anyone from a small child should be able to learn to play the game and do well.
What gripped me was the game’s presentation. It’s cute and it is full of charm. I love the way the game animates the jelly releasing the characters that you mind control. Great Game, great experience.
I'm, I think, at the last level of the game and it was so much fun.
The idea of sneaking around just to stay alive (cause if an enemy sees you it would likely call the sorrounding friend, leaving you against other five guys) is amazing.
Weapons in the game are basically three (bow, musket and a gun), the bow is fast but its hard to aim and normally the first arrow will be deflected by enemie's armor, the second will hit.
Musket are the strongest weapon, but it will take to much time reloading leaving you dying.
Gun is weaker than the musket and the bow, but it takes half time to reload (never used it tough).
Enemies are different by switching from living world to the other world: in the living world you will encounter:
- The Spaniards: strange man-like monsters wearing the spanish armor. There's even the Spaniard "Brute" (called brute by myself) that is a giant Spaniard that will throw rocks at you, and if you go to close to him he will kill you in two hits.
- Giant spiders: normally there's the mother with 2-3 little spiders, the little ones aren't that strong, but they're hard to be hit, they normally die in one or two hits. The mother is huge and she will die in four or five hits and will spit at you stuff hurting you and if she comes to close it will take down a lot of HP.
- Burning/Ashes Salvages: These enemies will appear from the third or forth level. They're basically man, made of ashes or in flames, they'll spot you from a long distance and will go around with a group of four. They're strong and you better have lots of healing points to fight them.
In the other world you'll fight:
- Scheletons: normal scheletons, like every medieval horror game.
- Strange Ghost figures: These ghost figures are like made from a dark essence and have a silver skull as a face and boned arms, they fly and they'll try to kill you on sight. They're strong but not that hard to kill, just hit them in the head.
The World is nice, well kinda repetitive, but it's the New World in the '700s it was all basically a forest.
Grapichs: I found them very nice, even the option to take out all the colours (saturation). The world is well built and the monsters are well created.
Exploration: The game is based on exploring the whole land to uncover secrets and what happened in that land.
You'll explore to find different things (clues like bloody knives, notes, shrines, chests, graves, beried items).
All the items will help you resolve what happened to the wraith that you will encounter and discover what happened in that fort.
Throughout all the game you'll find some beried objects that require a shovel, that you will find in one of the last levels, and all the items that you can uncover with the shovel aren't that usefull for uncovering the story, so you'll not be bodered to undig all the objects you left behind.
Awesome to put in the "Listen" button, where you press this button and you'll hear like strong wind and on your compass two white rectangles will appear leading you to the next clue, so that you'll never be stuck looking for them (to feel the real experience I suggest to use it only when you're stuck and you don't know where to find the next clue.).
For my experience the game is awesome, challenging and even difficult sometimes (specially when you tick the box that will make you leave all your loot where you died so to recover all your money you need to go back where you just died, and all the monster will respawn when you die.), the story is great and gets you involved.
The only "con" in the game is made after an update: game developers updated the map.
The map was a crucial thing, because before the update the map was just like a normal map and there was a red circle that meant that you were somewhere in that circle, so it was hard to know where you were going, luckly you could "Listen" and know where to go.
After the update the map changed, and for changed I mean that the red circle was gone and in his place there was a red arrow, so know you'd know where you were pointing and were you were exactly. The only thing that ruined everything is the possibility to turn on the location of all the things in the level (shrines, chests, notes, wraiths, graves, ecc...) so that all the exploration part will be abandoned cause if you know where the things are you'll never wander around, but this option can be set off, but who would do that?
So if the map would get back like a normal map with just the red arrow, this game would be really great cause you'll have to explore it all and I can't see nothing wrong in exploring to find clues.

Betrayer is a supernatural mystery game mixed with stealth action combat played in first person.
The game starts off with your unidentified character washing up on the shore of a faux New World forest circa 1600. Much in the style of an old school adventure-mystery game such as Myst, little explanation is given to who you are, how you got there or what your purpose is.
The visual art style is striking in that it is entirely monochrome & desaturated apart from striking flashes of red to notate items & people of interest, such as hostiles or settlement flags. The colour can be adjusted to be on in the settings, but I feel the game loses some charm in doing so.
The game world looks easily on par with equivalent titles such as Skyrim's forest areas, though the lack of wildlife & fauna can make it seem a little empty at times. What is excellent is the wind mechanic, which as well as making trees & brush sway side to side also acts as the cover for your sneak mechanic when approaching enemies.
As you progress through the area, you'll find deserted settler outposts with Wraiths & Spirits who all have troubled stories that you need to uncover to get to the truth of what happened in the area. This is performed by finding clues littered around the surrounding land which are obstructed by Spaniards, Natives & creatures of more ghostly origins.
Combat is performed with period appropriate weaponry such as flintlocks, muskets and longbows which allow you to stealth kill. The former two weapons having such a long reload time, mean that stealth & arrows are the way to proceed in the early through to late-mid game.
The major problem with Betrayer is that after the initial 1-2 hour discovery of how the world works & how to progress in the story, it becomes a case of travel from circle to circle on your map, clearing an area out, clicking through a few dialogue boxes & then having some forced combat before moving onto the next area.
It's also worth mentioning that if you do make a point of collecting all the chests and digging up all the secret items as you progress map by map, the late game becomes trivial in how OP your characters equipment & skills become. This negates any need to either be stealthy or conserve ammunition for your gunpowder based weapons.
With the 6 areas that you visit, it'll take you between 8-10 hours to get through the entire game.
The stories you uncover are actually quite good & some have some surprising twists. It would have made a better game if you had some choice in deducing what the clues lead you too rather than it be spelt out for you. There is a twist to the ending you may see threads for on the game forum. Some people think it's great, I personally thought it was confusing. So, jury is out on that one.
While rough in edges & definitely a small budget indie title despite the use of the Unreal engine giving it a visual pop. The game has charm & while not quite hitting the scare factor I think it tries to aim towards, there is still a certain level of tension with above average story telling.
It won't be for everyone but at the right price, it might be worth spending a weekend with.

I will just barely recommend this. I like the gameplay (simple, but effective), the ship designs, and the overall graphical feel hits the mark. However, the lack of story and dumb (though often hilarious) AI may turn people off, and I wouldn't blame them.
Controls seem tight enough, once I got used to them, and the lack of a z axis to move in is fine with me. It allows for some tactics, such as hiding behind asteroids to regroup and attack the enemy, that I otherwise feel I couldn't easily pull off if the enemy could easily move above or below me (I'm talking the main ships, small AI fighters don't have this restriction).
I don't have a huge amount of time to play games, so the simplified but tight combat, and decent upgrade system for the ships - who doesn't love upgrades? Nobody important, that's who - make this game enjoyable and relaxing. I've only really gotten blown up once, and that's because I was stupid.
So, tl;dr:
Pros:
+ Combat, simple but nice, more like "boats in space", but not necessarily a bad thing.
+ Upgrades. Everybody loves upgrades. Wait, you don't? The heck with you, you don't count.
Cons:
- Story. Wish there was more to it.
- AI. I both love it and hate it. Hell, it was an enemy ship bashing into his bro and finishing him off that was one of my highlights of my gaming week. At the same time, it keeps the game from feeling as immersive as it could.
In conclusion, the gameplay is nice, but the story will likely make the game boring after just a little while. However, it's a fun enough ride so far that I'll give it a thumbs up.
Take care, everyone, and Pew Pew!

I wnted to like this game, I tried my hardest to like it...  but despite the things it has going for it, good graphics and a great soundtrack, well. Their's just no getting around the many bad things.
The game starts off by just dumping you straight into a ship heading for a space station. The only back story is that your aunt gave you the ship and told you to meet her there. You pick up your first quest from the bar tender who also gives you a broken AI module that when you wake it up later has amnesia...  I've seen weaker plots, but barely.
The speech system is almost entirely irrlevant as it boils down to "accept quest y/n".
The entire game, nay, the entire universe is two dimentional, well for you the player anyway..  Enemies and objects have access to the mythical Z dimension, but you dont. This becomes especially frustrating when trying to line up shots on asteroids or enemy ships that fly above or below you.
When mining or just loot colleting after a battle, you have to keep pressing the scan button in orer to see where the loot has dropped as it doesnt stay populated on your screen or radar for more than a few seconds. To make matters worse, the majority of the commands in the game are bound to the same damn key, forcing you to pay close attention to the context popup at the bottom of the screen so you dont accidentally activate your warp drive instead of using your tractor beam to pull the loot into your cargo hold. For that matter their is no easy way to switch between what you're trying to target and what's closest to you, so if you want those gold bars that dropped from the freighter you blew up, you're also going to have to pick up the box full of kidneys that's floating next to it.
Missions are the typical go kill this or go escort this ship someplace else. The escort missions wouldnt be so bad except that when you slave your warp drive to theirs you lose all control of your ship and the games pathfinder AI honestly believes that it's perfectly ok to ram into asteroids, other ships, the giant freaking space station etc.  Couple that with the fact that space is a LOT more crowded than I've been led to believe and you almost cant make a trip from point A to B without having to stop and fight or run into an asteroid or debris field 3-4 times.
The quest system also seems to be broken, as missions marked low risk seem to often have 3-4 destroyers and a capitol ship or two where as missions the game says i shouldnt be able to complete are complete cake walks.

shoutout in Chapter 1.

Then again, considering the sorts of things I'm able to take in stride in my own dreams that would weird the hell out of me in real life, I suppose they aren't quite so lucid after all. The Dream Machine is a pretty simple point and click adventure game. The puzzles, like most point and click games, range from stupidly easy to esoteric beyond belief but this game manages to have a pretty consistent degree of difficulty. Unlike a lot of point and click games the puzzles reveal themselves through interacting with the environment and being patient, not many puzzles require outside help to finish or understand. The art style in this game is really interesting, I believe they used claymation to model everything in the game which makes for a really unique style. The only complaint I have about that is that the characters are horrifying, especially the wife character but then again maybe that’s the artist’s intent. The story is alright but nothing to write home about. I don’t know how to fix it but they had the ability to make something super interesting and out there, like Twin Peaks, but it just kinda falls short and feels like a semi-surreal romantic drama. Another complaint I have about the game is the length, ~45 minutes a chapter is too much to ask $5 fo. So while I enjoyed this game I don’t think I’ll pick up the last two chapters unless I see them on sale. Overall it was enjoyable, if you own it I suggest giving it a play through if you don’t I suggest wait for a sale to pick it up.

Pre-Update review:
Hitman Absolution is an interesting game, and there is much to talk about. (No big spoilers, but some story discussion)
I'll start with gameplay. First off, I should get it out of the way that it has a campaign that I find that to be decent length, and it has good replayability due to bonus challenges, but some people disagree. Contracts mode is as fun as you make it, where you and your friends compete for the best score in custom assassinations.
The difficulty is toggleable, and goes as you'd expect. Easy is casual, normal is an alright challenge and anything above hard can be brutal at times, specifically Purist. That said, Purist mode (hence the name) feels closest to a Hitman game to me. The Instinct ability can dumb down some of the action, but adds a neat aspect to gameplay. Stealth AI has the usual quirks, but is smarter than I expected.
Now for the story. As much as this game tries to take itself seriously, there are some questionable design choices that take away from the experience. The basic overview is decent; Agent 47 has to assassinate a bunch of people to find out a thing and save a person. That feels sort of like a Hitman game, and making 47 a kind of anti-hero works well for the character. But the humor of this game, which I enjoyed in other parts of the series, just seems off here.
This game is not about being tasteful. That's okay if you know what you're in for ahead of time, but some jokes may catch you off guard. For instance, a running gag is the deaths of mentally handicapped bystanders. Yikes. The Hitman wiki says that this game has a number of 'gay jokes', which I won't get all up in arms about, but they range from poorly written to just confusing. An example is that hiding two bodies in a closet causes one of them to fall forward and form a sexual pose, but also blocks the closet, while if the bodies stayed upright you could easily fit. The game repeats this bad habit of sacrificing gameplay for the sake of immature jokes, which gets frustrating.
That said, the core story of this game is gritty and thrilling, and there are some genuinely funny and badass moments. Pacing is good, 47 gets a lot of development, his dynamic with the other characters is intriguing and changes a lot in the series for me. Gameplay is satisfyingly complex and action-packed, and the rating system gives some morality to your actions, which I really like that they added. It runs okay, and the graphics are pretty good, but nothing too bad or good worth talking about much.
Overall, I give this game a 7/10 rating.

This game disapointed me.
For the first hour the game was very fun. A new map, some cool new ways to travel, absurd plot, another after Saints Row 4 "superheroish" game. I played mostly using Gat, since I couldn't imagine Kinzie being that psychopatic.
The story in Gat Out of Hell is short and it is pushed forward by doing the sidequests. I was really dissapointed with that, since I wanted to have some more connection with the characters. There are only 6 missions which are not sidequests! So there are only 6 missions, which are somehow important to the plot.
For most of the game I fell Gat and Kinzie are random characters. Fly there, kill that, grab some collectibles. I really wanted to havesome more dialog between them and with the new characters they've found on the way, but the conversations are down to "Do more sidequests". I know it is Saints Row, but in the previous games the characters were more powerfull, had more connection to other characters and the plot was more complex.
I don't recall any music in this game, I can't remember if it had any. The graphics look the same, as in Saints Row 4 (I was hoping for some more eyecandy).
I still had some fun with this game. The flying is cool, some upgrades are quite fun, but I ended the game with a lot of souls and money to spend, but after some minor upgrades I haven't found anything useful (but I was almost indestructible anyway with those minor upgrades). Cutscenes are quite funny, I wish there were more with the new characters.
The world in this game is small comparing to the previous games with a lof of hidden collectibles. Finding those is fun, since you are flying between bulding, in some narrow spaces to get them. I found it quite entertaining until I figured out, that I've unlocked everything I wanted to unlock. After that looking for the souls, voice recordings, repetetive sidequests lost their sense.
The car psychics is bad. While driving them the cars almost floats and you feel, like the car is just a cardboard box. The cars are also quite ugly and a very limited number of models is riding through the streets. I feel, that hell should have a lot of fast, bloody cars, not old junks.
In the end, you can finish Gat out of Hell in around 4-5 hours, after that the upgrades are not important, the collectibles are not worth searching and I do not see any replay value for now (unless the multiplayer campaign, which was very fun in SR4). This game is like a DLC for SR4, but with smaller playfield, almost no story and no strong characters. But I was expecting a full game, not a DLC.

I was initially skeptical about playing a game which PANDERED solely to the colour blind, but my initial displeasure was soon overcome upon realising that Betrayer is not about some pseudo-medieval fantasy thing, but actually the worlds best world war I simulator. The aim of the game is to run around the maps and kill untermensch (including inexplicably spanish lions, spooky skeletons, gollum, and ♥♥♥♥ off irritating floaty skull things) in order to put down an iron cross on the map. you can then use the power of the kaiser to teleport to these bastions of teutonic power, which makes the game of 'touch the small circles on the map' a lot less boring. there is also an 'interesting' minquest about finding an elusive spade who has run halfway across the country for no obvious reason. this game really explained to me that it's not really surprising that the germans lost world war I, because all of their weapons are shockingly bad and it would have been so much easier if they just artillery striked all the skeletons, who can shoot lightning while you can only shoot arrows and crossbows and those type of bullet which you have to assemble before firing. the other half of the game involves being a psychotherapist to some ghosts. overall a pretty good training manual worth the two quid i spent on it, and it taught me a lot about world war I and ghost counselling, but i fear i will not be able to put this experience on my cv because of how niche these vocations are.

I might be a little biased since I loved dinosaurs as a kid, but I'll try and break it down as unbiased as possible. Primal Carnage is a team-based PvP game with, you guessed it, Dinos and Humans. The only plot is that there's an island where Dinosaurs have been reborn (Jurassic Park gone wrong?) and humans get trapped on the island. The classes are pretty basic, each one has a main and secondary attack, along with Dinos getting a roar ability which buffs other Dinos. The concept of gigantic Tyranosaurs and Spinosaurs isn't as overpowered as you might think, and they pulled it off pretty well, although obviously if you got someone good playing he'll probably wreck your team.
There isn't a big community left, mind you, but it isn't hard finding a full server if you want to play a couple rounds of Dino smashing or Human stompin'. It's worth the $8, but if you can pick it up on a sale go for it. It's freakin' Primal Carnage.

So, you know that BioShock game, right? How it had a really good story, with neat plottwists, neat underwater world inspired heavily by Art Deco, and lackluster gameplay?
You can't say anything about BioShock 2 without comparing it to the first one. BioShock 2 was an improvement in gameplay, that's for sure. Plasmid in one hand, gun in the other made a fine combination and killing was finally... well, fun. Gene Tonics added another layer of depth, even though at the end you can easily buy all the slots and fill them with the best tonics. Also, you get to be a Big Daddy, finally. After playing the first one, almost every player had this thought, how nice would be to play as one. So you get a drill and a rivet gun. Didn't change much in gameplay, but is neat.
Can't forget about hacking though. First game had this water flowing in pipes minigame, thought it was nice, and a bit of a challenge. In the second game, they possibly decided it was too hard for consoles and replaced it with "click at the right moment" minigame. Pathetic. Boring. Click, click, click. Auto-hack darts help with that a bit, but still it left me with a bad taste in my mouth.
Enemies. The main issue I had with the first game is in here too - splicers are supposed to have some personality, with small talk in some moments of the game, but they are still mindless and not challenging at all, just bullet sponges. Their quantity doesn't help with it - in my opinion, in such a game killing a person should make you feel bad at least a bit. I guess making them smarter and use elaborate tactics was too hard, so they just blamed splicing for messing with their heads.
And the last thing - story. We all know it's weak. Has some problems. Disappearing (Tenenbaum?) and appearing for no reason characters make little sense. Main enemy is a woman that somehow gained followers that holds a teenage girl hostage. Her motivations are unclear, just like her modus operandi. Somehow she knows all and does nothing else, but monitors my movements. Sends me propaganda messages that are sure not to work. There's no plottwist or anything to make it better. Smaller bosses stories were much better. Grace had a solid story, Stanley did some weird stuff (but still better than Lamb), and Alexander had the best level. So, the story was far worse than in the first game. Good thing to note.
But you know what? Story was definitely fixed in Minerva's Den. This DLC makes the entire game worth it, even though you have to play through the entire basic game to undersand it all. I know, it has backtracking, and hacking/enemies issues weren't resolved, but it's good even then.
Even without the free DLC, I would recommend the game. It's not perfect, has some flaws, but you can't say it's bad or mediocre either.

I enjoyed it for the most part. I have just a few criticisms:
- Once you reach a certain part of the game, it switches from killing innocents to trying to infiltrate these impossible fortresses guarded by soldiers. Takes some of the edge away from the game. I didn't sign up to play Command and Conquer.
- Upper-right to lower-left fighting is extremely frustrating. I understand this is inherent to isometric gameplay, but I hoped they would have done something to mitigate getting shot by unseen enemies as you fight into the Southwest of the screen.
- I can defeat an entire army base single-handedly, but walking through doorways or around trees is my Achilles heel.

+ Great selection of tracks avaliable in multiple layouts throughout the history incl. the old Hockenheimring.
+ Users with popular racing wheels need not any tweaking. Also has good force feedback that transmits plenty of road feel to the wheel.
+ Teaches you about Ferrari's history by providing a wide variety of Ferrari's creation throughout the eras. All of them are meticulously detailed and sound nice as well.
+ Robust replay feature that allows players to watch the race from AIs' perspective as well. What's more, replays can be saved too.
+ Better physics than Shift 2: Unleashed so you don't have to turn all the aids on in order to drive clean.
+ Great damage both visual and performance-wise on Formula 1 cars.
+ Good graphics that makes you awe from time to time despite being a tad rough around the edges.
+ Lots of contents for the current discount price of $3.99.
- NFS: Shift physics. There's no getting away with that. Classic cars feel quite good but the experience deteriorates in the faster cars. Make even the slightest contact with other cars and you'll have to brace for a somersault.
- No option to individually tune driver aids. Auto-clutch and ABS can't be turned off at all.
- DUMB AIs. They're very slow and are prone to amateur mistakes. Expect to overtake all of them before even getting into turn 1 and build a 15 second gap by lap 2. I managed to fall to last place twice in a 3 lap race and STILL managed to win at the hardest difficulty setting.
- Lackluster damage in all the cars excluding the F1 cars. Slight scratches, dents, and misalligned steering rack is just about all the damage you get.
- Time trial in hard difficulty setting requires you to set ridiculously fast lap times, but there's NO incentive in playing the missions at higher difficulty or completing bonus objectives. So why even bother?
- Missions are mandatory to unlock the wide roster of tracks and cars. Yet only about 20% of them provide unlocks upon completion. Other 80% have no rewards whatsoever, giving a feel that developers crammed in missions just in order to keep the players continue playing.
- Repetitive. All missions are either 'set a lap time', 'overtake your opponents before the race ends', or 'get a podium finish'.
- You'll most likely give up on pursuing on unlocking the cars and tracks because of its tediousness. It's strongly recommended that you use a mod that unlocks all the cars and tracks.
In conclusion, it's Need for Speed: Shift, but with slightly worse overall gameplay and Ferraris. It's a great buy at $3.99, but there's no reason to bother spending $20 or so.

Pros:
- The factions are unique and immersive. Everything from the voice acting to the UI changes with each faction and the special abilities of each really gives a flavor to playing each faction.
- Truly customizable fleets. Every ship/cruiser has a special ability that is further customized to the faction you are playing. Ever wanted a fleet that could push enemy ships away? A ship that can draw aggro? A ship that takes control of other units? It's a lot of fun.
- Extremely good pacing. I felt like I could actually finish a game with my friends but it isn't so fast that you feel rushed or overwhelmed.
- If you play through the tutorials, you have a good enough grasp of the game to enjoy the game, but the game actually has a lot of depth to explore to make more intricate strategies
- Beautiful graphics for the ships and planets. I wish it was easier to play with your ships actually visible and not icons, but I love the amount of detail when you have time to zoom in and watch a battle up close.
- Pirates are bad♥♥♥♥♥ Whether you are fighting them or using them against people. I love that you can physically hunt down the pirate bases and get some well earned payback.
Cons
- Diplomacy still seems somewhat clunky to me. Instead of starting in a cease fire with everyone, everyone pretty much starts in a cold war. Trying to contact someone means dodging their ships as they try to destroy you and hoping your envoys can survive long enough to make it to a cease fire. The missions are a great idea but are hard to utilize since they usually are "attack this person we don't like" with no consideration of your relationship with them or even if you know where they are!
- The victories could be expanded upon for more unique victories. Most victories revolve around going to war at the moment despite having a highly developed culture, economic, and diplomatic system.
- With so many good strategy games out now, I feel like $40 is not a very competitive price.
This definitely a game to lunge at if you ever catch it on sale but, if you don't mind the price, I think you will get your money's worth in playtime.

I really don't write reviews very often. However, I felt that this one really deserved one.
The Short:
This is an incredibly well-designed game. The developer's were able to capture that very rare "spark." While it may be a little short (I really took my time and it took me an hour per chapter), it is one of immense quality. Overall 9.5/10.
The Longer:
- Gameplay:
It is your standard point-and-click adventure game. You are given a small story or situation and you have to solve puzzles to progress. My only real complaint, which isn't much of a complaint, is the sudden advancement in difficulty. In the first two chapters, I didn't really come across any problems/difficulties. The third chapter was really hard! You'll understand when you have to make a certain drink.
- Music:
I loved the soundtrack. It matches the situations and environment very, very well. It ranges from the caretaker's creepy jazz song to minimalistic ambience to Silent Hill-esque rhythms.
- Story:
This is easily one of my favorite stories that has come from recent gaming. Without giving too much away, it begins as a simple tale about a couple moving into a new apartment. Soon, it evolves into an (without exaggeration) epic adventure involving the dream world, a science project gone wrong, and horror.
- Graphics/Environment:
The clay animation was a really smart artistic choice. It helps to add a fresh perspective on the genre. The environments are all interesting and enchanting. The characters are... scary looking.
To the developers, I sincerely enjoyed your game.

I had already played the game once on PS3 when it came out and I bought it recently on PC to try it again. I have just finished replaying it and I thought I should share my point of view.
The game looks good, you have many weapons available and the missions are more or less linked to one story.
Now time to talk about the problems of the game. To me (and as I have been able to see a few comments here, I am not the only one), it is not really a Hitman game. I remember playing Hitman 2 on PS2 as a teenager and later on playing Contracts and Blood Money on PC. I really liked those games. 47 was really a pain to control because he could not directly attack his enemies for instance but the missions were memorable: killing the mob leader in Italy, exploring an Indian hospital, sneaking into a Japanese castle, sniping villains in Russia, fighting the assassins in the bird costumes. I could name even more and I vividly remember most of the missions because it was so rewarding to finally do it the right way, going in and out unnoticed.
In Absolution I get the feeling that they did not really think of stealth as a priority. I have spent most of my time looking for unguarded routes and usually found myself forced to kill a guard because he was standing in the way.
I don’t mind action but even in Deus Ex Human Revolution you have two paths offered to you (stealth or bloody action) and most of the time you really have a choice. In Absolution you have to kill or subdue guards to do what you want and you simply end up killing every living pixel (the subdue system takes forever and 70% of the time you are spotted and killed). A tranquilizer gun could have been added if you really wanted us to take down most of the guards.
Another problem with the game is that it takes away most of the good stuff from previous games. You just spent fifteen minutes sweeping the area for a gun you find really cool and want to use again? Too bad you are going to start the next mission with the default gear (same with costume). You want to use a syringe to pacify a target? Good luck finding one. You want to use the cool silverballers or the nice sniper case? Not possible (you get the silverballers back in the second half of the game).
The game lacks most of the components that made the previous games so cool. You hide in semi opened corridors and put a bullet in each guard you find nearby (if you want to choose stealth you have to wait a lot and pray you don’t get busted).
The instinct system makes no sense within the universe and is essential if you want to walk five feet or if you want to clean a room. The game is hardly ever a matter of skill or of stealth but just mindless killing. The story has its ups and downs (the bar fight, Chinatown or playing hide and seek in the crop) and is very generic.
I can’t possibly give it a thumbs down because the game is not plagued with bugs, it is very good looking and at a low price, is good value for money but I can’t shake the feeling that I have not played a real Hitman game.

This War of Mine, released by 11-bit Studios in November 2014, is a survival strategy game based on the civilians’ lives during a devastating civil war. The players' goal is to survive to the next day, and ultimately the end of the war, by utilizing the materials found by scavenging to craft the bare necessities for survival. With gameplay somewhat similar to The Sims, players are responsible for their characters’ health and mentality. The game ends with the announcement of a ceasefire around Day 30-40.
During the day, it is too dangerous to go out, you must stay at your shelter and do what needs to be done. The first day is spent scavenging through the rubble left behind by the previous owners to find anything useful. Once you have acquired enough materials, you can go downstairs to your tool bench and craft things you’ll need either now or later on in the game. (TIP: While beds are important, yes, wait on them until you’ve got weapons—from the metal station—and a stove. Those are more important, since you can sleep on the floor.)
When you make crafting stations (metal, herbal, plant) you are given the ability to upgrade them for more options or better efficiency. You should definitely upgrade the original craft bench first, because it gives you better basic crafting options, such as ‘board-up,’ which protect your shelter better from intruders.
At night, your players deem it safe to go outside. You can send one player out into the night to a location to search for anything you may need. If you’re in desperate need of something in particular, certain places have more of certain things. While scavenging, you will find many things you’ll need, such as materials and wood, but you’ll also find many non-necessities. Things that aren’t necessary to survive, like cigarettes or coffee. These can stay in your inventory and be used by your characters to make them happy, or can be traded for something more useful.
During the game, your characters will quite often react to things around them, either negatively or positively, based on the nature of the event. If you save someone’s life, they’ll be content. If you kill someone or steal, they’ll gain a ‘sad’, ‘depressed’, or ‘broken’ moodlet. Once you reach the ‘broken’ status, that character will do nothing but sleep and eat, if given food. They won’t move on command. To fix this, you must have another character ‘talk’ to them in order to bring up their spirits.
There are many different characters in the game, each of which has different abilities. Each character has a backpack that, when out scavenging, can hold a certain amount of items. If you have less than 4 characters, you may get a random special event from a new character asking to join you. The maximum amount of characters you can have is 4.
While this game is an extremely fun strategy game, it is also a reminder to us of the horrors of war – not just for the soldiers, but for the innocent civilians and families.

Behind The Door was a decent, short atmospheric horror experience. Also knocks out yet another of my SG wins. This is essentially a walking sim, where you solve minor item puzzles to unlock new areas as you investigate these murders. Aside from notes periodically warning you to get out or that it's too late, things like that, there really isn't a lot of information provided as to the story outside of the actual product description and the intro. There is a minor surprise towards and at the end.
There were some bugs, most notably with the combination lock, which froze the first time around. I had to exit and restart to get it to function properly. Overall though, the performance was good.
Visually, Behind The Door is a dark and decrepit place, the place where terrible things have obviously occurred. You are armed only with a flashlight, which starts to burn low as your batteries drain. Fortunately, there were no lack for batteries around the house, so you won't ever really find yourself completely in the dark. Which reminds me....I don't recall if I ever found a use for one of the items (the fuse). It's possible, but I don't remember what I used it for if I did. The soundtrack similarly serves to enhance the sense of dread in the house. There are a couple lite-shock moments as well, but nothing that will make you concerned if you have a heart condition or some such. :)
Overall, I thought this was a decent but average title. Definitely interesting enough to keep you invested for the 45 minutes or so it takes to complete. However, the game really nails atmosphere, which ups it's overall rating I think. Not a bad effort. I think a straight 5 out of 10 is warranted. I don't think you will regret a purchase at its more than reasonably price point, and it was a nice time killer.

What struck me at first glance was how much customization this app makes possible for the start menu and the taskbar.  It offers a wealth of options!  The Start Menu can have different styles (Windows 7, Modern Style, and Windows 10), themes, and looks.  It can be solid, transparent, have different icon sizes, different sorting methods, and exhibit different behaviors that make the Start Menu much more useful.  For example, recently used applications are highlighted, submenus open when you pause on them with the mouse, and Cortana can be replaced!
The Taskbar can be customized based on look, transparency, color, blur, texture, and behavior.  I'm hooked on the textures!  Some of the textures include:  Marble, Metallic, Marble, Carbon Fibre and Dark Wood.  Oh, and check this out...you can change the icon used for the Start Menu!  It sounds so simple but is pretty neat.  My Start Menu icon is a biohazard symbol!!
Start10 gives you incredible control over how the Start Menu and Taskbar behave.
Linux users, particularly KDE users, will recognize many of the features since KDE has had them for years.  Thanks to Start 10, Windows users can too.
NOTE: My usage time of 5 minutes is misleading.  I've been using Start10 for over 10hrs now.  It seems that when Start10 is launched, it logs a few seconds of usage in Steam then detaches from Steam and runs on its own.  To make this review, I had to launch Start10 about 60 times to get the 5 minutes of usage.

Betrayer is first person action adventure game set in The New World, 1604. The player is set to a part of Colonial America where the horrific truths remain undiscovered. The game world is open area in each section which allow player to collect clues and search for better gear to survive from relentless world.
The gameplay is about collecting clues and conducting investigations to learn the past of lost souls. Thus, it will reveal the truth behind the colony. Thanks to Blackpowder Games, who had worked on games F.E.A.R. for creating of two different worlds that allow player to switch and play major role to solve the puzzles. The silent New World is full of hostile conquistadores and Native American warriors while The Otherworld presents you an uncomfortable and depressed world as it stripped with black-white and red to indicate the important stuffs. It looks stylish and serves well on game theme, but you can adjust color saturation if it’s not your taste.
The combat is simple FPS game, even on normal difficult. The enemies are deadly and straightforward in AI pattern. You need to take them out quickly which force player to use bow most of the time or rely on inconsistent stealth mechanic.
There’s no voice narrative, all you need is to read from scarp papers to gain information and seeking for right NPC. The map marker and smart fast travel are useful enough to avoid player lost in track.
Overall, Betrayer offers a short but impressive experience with unsetting and strong atmosphere. Although the combat is quite unbalance and puzzles are too simple, the feeling of horror/mysteries game love is back as the credit start to roll.

X: Rebirth, a game at launch that suffered terribly and seemed in many peoples eye the deathknell of the X Series. When it first released, Rebirth copped a lot of deserved flak, it was buggy, it was confusing and many of us were questionable about particular game elements. But that was a different time for Rebirth, and it has improved significantly since that time with its 2.0, 3.0 and soon to be released 4.0 and Home of Light DLC. Kudos to Egosoft to sticking to their guns where most developers would sink the franchise and move on.
What stands out in Rebirth compared to other space sims of the day? It has incredibly deep gameplay in an incredibly beautiful and dynamic universe. There is a satisfying early, mid and late game as you gradually build up an empire of ships and stations and dominate interstellar markets with your own assembly lines and your fleet of trade-ships. You will always be up to something in Rebirth, whether thats scouting out potential bargains for your tradeships to supervising the construction of your first station or commanding your personal battlefleet into a war against one of the major factions. You can even be a pirate and steal wares and ships from any of the factions in the game.
Every Star system in Rebirth is very unique, offering its own visual style, ship and station types (mostly), story and culture. Where other space-sim games like to go the procedural generation route, Rebirth offers a beautifully handcrafted galaxy that on the most part seems authentic.
Rebirth still has its fair share of issues, the command system when dealing with NPCs can be frustrating at times and fleet commands still aren't that great, though it has improved substantially with adding basic commands that are necessary. NPCs are still stiff and bland and don't match the visual style of the outer galaxy, this was an issue with previous X games as well but its more jarring here as you are forced to interact with these NPCs more.
Overall, if you like base-building, economic games, space-sim games, i'd definitely recommend X:Rebirth. With the Home of Light DLC coming out in the next few days which adds 3 new star systems (There are currently 6 systems pre-HoL ) it may be a good time to pick it up and give it a go.

Rebel Galax Review
I want to start out with a rough outline of the game. Rebel Galaxy is an action oriented spaceship game. Its NOT a simulator and its NOT a strategy game. The developers last title was Torchlight II and they managed to pack the ARPGs elements into this game as well. Theres loot theres upgrades, lots of ships and all this in a space setting which looks beautifull.
So....action oriented Space game.
Who are you in this game?
You are a young starship captain and you dont start your carreer in a space fighter either. You start out with a frigatte. Sure its small and doesnt have a whole lot to it but its in the capital ship class and thats what all other flyable ships are as well. Capital ships. From the measly frigatte to the mighty dreadnaught. You will curse the bombers, fighters and gunships all around you but you ll never fly them yourself. And why would you? The weapons you have at your disposal are frightening and extremly destructive.
The game drops you in front of a Space station and your "campaign" is to find your aunt which vanished and is rumored to ve run into some trouble while following her not-so-white activities. Your ship has all the things you need to set off and start playing but pretty much everything is crap...at first.
Lets be clear about something.....when you "fly" your ship you ll do it on a 2D plane only. No fancy going "up" or "down" with such a large ship. You can only turn left or right and increase or reduce thrust.
On the other hand you are given your hull, armor on top and a shield generator to protect yourself from other big ships and small ones alike. In order to defend your newbie hide you have 3 weapon categories with multiple weapon choices in each being your Broadsides, your secondaries and your turrets. And here is where the game "hooks" you (or not) with its addictive elements. Pretty much every station offers a wide variety of modules in different qualities (starting at Mark 1 going to Mark 6) and in order to being able to buy these lil babies you gonna need a lot of credits. Sadly credits dont come around on their own so you got to chose from a list of activities in order to EARN credits until you can afford the next upgrade.
Mining, treasure hunting, bounty hunting, guild missions, cargo missions, combat missions, escort missions. This game offers a wide variety of things you can do. You ll still do it all on your ship of course but with the right pick of modules you can "specialize" your ship to certain mission types.
Missions vary in difficulty based on your total worth and the opposition you ll encounter. Gear apart "how" you fly has a big impact on your survivability as well which is a nice touch IMO.
The flow of the game.
Your playground is a star system with all its gas clouds, asteroid belts, planets and other space farers you can encounter. Each system is several AUs big and once you upgrade your engines (seperate module) you ll be able to visit other star systems which makes the whole picture bigger. Star systems offer different tiers of servces and challenges meaning in order to get the higher Mark modules you ll need to switch to different systems which are populated by harder enemies so this is the circle you face in RG. Upgrade to be able to do harder stuff which in turn leads to better upgrades etc.
System to system travel is done via "jump gates" which are an instant switch. In-system you rely on your trusted warp engines to get you from A to B. The whole system is easy to understand and easier to use and it ensures that you can jump into RG for 15-20 minutes at a time and get things done. Yes missions are short affairs but nevertheless they can be engaging and entertaining.
Rebel Galaxy looks lovely. Its overall colorfull and the default music track I would describe as "cowboys in space" but hell....it fits.
Its easy to use and hard to master. Upgrading to a new ship is always a big moment and find myself "itching" wanting to try it out. I dumped a whole lot of hours into this game simply because its FUN. Its not overall realistic and it could use some more complexity but its a cheap title made by 2 people. What you get for your money is AAA material in my book.
I play several saves at the moment because the game allows you to take speific paths which dont go well with other paths so decisions need to be worked on and are really hard to lift once done. For example I have a save where I aligned myself with the pirate factions so most stations fire on sight, I m a wanted criminal by the militia and traders dont trade with me anymore. On the other hand I can pillage and loot whatever I find, spit on enemy militia destroyers and smuggle with illegal subtsnces to my hearts desire. Also there are some "pirate-only" ships and modules I can aquire this way.
The same is true for a military career. You ll be hunting pirates mostly and will be a respected captain in most corners of the galaxy. Some militia-only ships taunt you in case you are not doing all this out of your heart.
Its kind of a "short" game. You have your storyline which brings you to mid game I d say after that the open game starts which is the whole galaxy with you dumped in the middle. From then on you gonna have to find your own goals sandbox style. Eventually you ll run out of ships to switch and modules to upgrade and will swim in credits. Thats when you ll notice your motivation to drop. Either you drop by from time to time to enjoy a mission or you start over. Apart from the storyline which is always the same you can pick fromseveral different approaches in the game which are all viably.
I certainly dont play as much as I used to anymore but its still fun and to be honest, I consider it a good purchase....never regretted shelling out the cash (and for such a title thats actually cheap)

Do not listen to these horrible reviews. Ferrari Racing Legends is a sheer driving pleasure. Slightly Mad Studios have done a fantastic job with the driving physics and making the game both accessible and exciting, as they did with Shift. The car roster is huge, and has a lot of variety too. There are some great tracks here from classics like Monza and Silverstone to favourites like Nordschleiffe and Mugello GP. The sound of the engines and life-like interior views coupled with refined driving mechanics make this a blast for racing enthusiasts. The controls are great and there is extensive support for wheels, controllers and keyboard. The events are scenarios, so you could start a race on the 3rd lap in last or it could be a more arcade-style overtaking exercise, where you have to pass all the cars within a time or distance limit. The variety in cars, tracks and races is surprising. But make no mistake, this game is pure racing nothing more, nothing less. There are no upgrades or RPG elements it's just you, the car and the track, although you have to unlock most of the cars and tracks through the campaign. There are no distractions, and there are of course time trials, quick races and multiplayer alongside the very long campaign. The only problem I've found with this game is that environment textures are terrible trees keep popping in and frequent graphical glitches with the scenery when using certain anti-aliasing. Other than that, it's exactly what a racing game should be.

Easily the best dino-based multiplayer action game on Steam, bar none!  Though the game is a little buggy at times (personally I suffered many crashes and random server drops) what you'll find therein is more than worth the minor programming headaches you'll encounter.
The graphics, including the animations for the dinos, are for the most part exceptional.  When paired with the sound design, namely the dino-based sounds, this all makes for a believable experience.  There's a good mix of dinos and just like the humans, these each have their own unique strengths and weaknesses but all share 1 thing in common - their roar.  Example: the T Rex has a ton of life (2000 HP) and can stomp on people and eat them, though it is somewhat difficult to control in tight spaces due to its size and its roar gives an adrenaline boost to nearby dinos which won't benefit you too much; the Novaraptor moves really fast, especially when sprinting, has a vertical leap that would make a professional basketball player jealous and slashes fairly quickly and when it roars it goes into a frenzy which will prevent it from jumping or sprinting for a time but will double its attack speed....)
The same goes for the humans - the Trapper has two pistols that don't hold a lot of ammo but which deal massive damage when aimed properly + he has a net gun that can trap lesser dinos, allowing him to go in for a single hit melee kill with his knife (or he can just shoot it); the Scientist has a very powerful/low ammo rifle and a tranquilizer gun that causes disorientation and eventually death with enough shots; the pyro....well, he's a pyro w/ a flamethrower and  some grenades.
Sadly, due to the developers stepping away from their project when they passed on the reains to another developer for the pseudo-sequel (Primal Carnage: Extinction) there were still some bugs left which will not be fixed (or so I heard) and there is no single player mode, so pick up a copy and play this game while you can.  Currently, there are only ever about 60 peeps playing at any given time and it probably won't be too much longer before this game dies all together.  It will be a sad day indeed when that occurs but I'm glad to have had this expereience while it lasted.
Again, get it while you can - it's pretty cheap even without a sale : )

Here are just a few reasons to give
a chance:
Gameplay - This title is a physics-heavy game that utilizes the three previously stated tools-each obtained progressively through the game’s story- to allow the environment to be altered, and to, subsequently, allow for progression. Though not all of it is, a large part of the environment is destructible, allowing the player to create varying ways in which to solve puzzles and proceed to the next portion of the game. In fact, so much of this game is able to be manipulated that it is highly possible to discover multiple solutions to a single problem, which adds to the replayability of this relatively short title. The control scheme for this title is quite simple, with the standard W, A, S, and D movement layout providing movement, the Space Bar acting as Tiny’s jump button, and all three of the gadgets being accessible by utilizing the mouse; moving the mouse aims the reticle, LMB activates the cutting tool, MMB allows rockets to be placed on objects-with another click of MMB, once attached, to send the mass flying within the rocket’s trajectory-, and RMB connects the grappling hook to a target. The cutting tool takes a bit of getting used to, but is extremely fun to utilize after a short time of learning.
Humorous Dialogue - Both Tiny and Big share not only a physical rivalry but a verbal one. Speech is erected through text bubbles and is acted out through voices that are jabbering gibberish, but with tones unique to each character. Even Tiny’s radio lends notable dialogue to situations while lending a hand with hints and sounding like someone is constantly changing the station. Combined with its cell-shaded graphics, this game’s approach to conversation is both minimalistic and highly enjoyable.
Collectables and Secrets - You can definitely see the developers’ sense of humor within
collectibles system. The most prominent pickups in the game are known as Boring Stones, and pretty much describe how, in general, objects such as these are tossed into games as extra content to add to the replayability; it is quite a silly satire.
There are other secrets
but I will allow you to figure out what and where they are throughout the landscape.
TL:DR - I must admit that I was skeptical about purchasing this title due to its completion time, but the overall feel of the game entranced me into reviewing levels I had already cleared just to retain the same sense of prior enjoyment, just to experience this game’s overworld, conversations, secrets, and themes. Admittedly,
is one of my favorite physics-based adventures, and I have been secretly awaiting a sequel though I know this aspiration is highly unlikely at the given moment. Thanks for reading.

Without external influence, I'd like to personally assert that Homefront feels to me like THQ's answer to Activision's Call of Duty. You can bet your dollar that Homefront boasts a very similar action oriented campaign and multiplayer littered with perks and kill streaks.
However, Homefront isn't complacent with just lifting the best features from its competitor; it bears intention to improve them. While THQ's efforts are appreciated, these additions are not as polished as one would hope.
Starting with its 4-5 hour campaign, the plot here is more emotionally driven. Death is vividly depicted but its repercussions, unfortunately, not fully explored. The characters are multi-dimensional enough to be unique, but play too small a role.
The multiplayer is a blend of Call of Duty and Battlefield, mixing fast paced firefights with vehicles. If you've played either of the aforementioned franchises, then you've played Homefront.
Homefront isn't bad, but neither is it great.
Grade: B-

This War of Mine, released by 11-bit Studios in November 2014, is a survival strategy game based on the civilians’ lives during a devastating civil war. The players' goal is to survive to the next day, and ultimately the end of the war, by utilizing the materials found by scavenging to craft the bare necessities for survival. With gameplay somewhat similar to The Sims, players are responsible for their characters’ health and mentality. The game ends with the announcement of a ceasefire around Day 30-40.
During the day, it is too dangerous to go out, you must stay at your shelter and do what needs to be done. The first day is spent scavenging through the rubble left behind by the previous owners to find anything useful. Once you have acquired enough materials, you can go downstairs to your tool bench and craft things you’ll need either now or later on in the game. (TIP: While beds are important, yes, wait on them until you’ve got weapons—from the metal station—and a stove. Those are more important, since you can sleep on the floor.)
When you make crafting stations (metal, herbal, plant) you are given the ability to upgrade them for more options or better efficiency. You should definitely upgrade the original craft bench first, because it gives you better basic crafting options, such as ‘board-up,’ which protect your shelter better from intruders.
At night, your players deem it safe to go outside. You can send one player out into the night to a location to search for anything you may need. If you’re in desperate need of something in particular, certain places have more of certain things. While scavenging, you will find many things you’ll need, such as materials and wood, but you’ll also find many non-necessities. Things that aren’t necessary to survive, like cigarettes or coffee. These can stay in your inventory and be used by your characters to make them happy, or can be traded for something more useful.
During the game, your characters will quite often react to things around them, either negatively or positively, based on the nature of the event. If you save someone’s life, they’ll be content. If you kill someone or steal, they’ll gain a ‘sad’, ‘depressed’, or ‘broken’ moodlet. Once you reach the ‘broken’ status, that character will do nothing but sleep and eat, if given food. They won’t move on command. To fix this, you must have another character ‘talk’ to them in order to bring up their spirits.
There are many different characters in the game, each of which has different abilities. Each character has a backpack that, when out scavenging, can hold a certain amount of items. If you have less than 4 characters, you may get a random special event from a new character asking to join you. The maximum amount of characters you can have is 4.
While this game is an extremely fun strategy game, it is also a reminder to us of the horrors of war – not just for the soldiers, but for the innocent civilians and families.

Writing this review after finishing my first game (Emancipation Victory). I'm really compelled to throw in my two cents this time. Unllike most games I have where I really don't care about the end product as much. Why I cared so much about this particular title and franchise? I been buying and playing civ since the start and other sid meiers games since Activision (late 90's).
If you've played civ before, you'll find the game much like any of the civ's you've played in the past. The graphics are sharper, colors more vibrant, gives it that "new game" feel. Once you start playing; you'll find some new additions. Nothing innovative or ground breaking. Concepts all veteran players will be familiar with. The AI is nothing more than a bot; Building and moving units in a predictable fashion. You'll recieve harrassing pop-ups from the AI as you make your way thru the game. The AI lacks indepth understanding and regretfully relies soley on it's metagame leverage over the player rather than actually being clever.
Even the ending was not even worth the time. No mini movie showing your amazing victory, just a picture and short narrative that you won the game. Honestly that was a deal breaker for me. In this age of gaming an ending so uninspiring, so lack luster, doesn't belong on a main stream title like civ. Every aspect of this game is borderline subpar, all the way to the very end.
In short; The game "looks" good. Painfully mediocre at best. The game is marketed as "new" but, it plays much like an older game with some updates. I had that feeling before I bought the game; that's why I waited for it to go on sale at 40% off. I like civ but, if this is the pinnacle of a franchise of over 20 years then I think it's time to buy into some other developers that are really trying to "Wow" the market with exciting "new" ideas. In some respects this title is worse than civ5 and offers less of a fun experience but, it looks "new" and I know for many players that means a lot.
Firaxis seems to be content on riding the wave of mediocrity, relying on its' seniority to stay in the main stream market. I was really hoping for more from this new title and just very disappointed.
As of this post; There is a bug which does not allow city "Health" gain from tile improvements or building purchases which effects the AI more because the player has the ability to "think" where as the AI just follows an over simplified algorithm.

It's not terrible, but ultimately playing it isn't a very fulfilling experience.
Gameplay consists of exploring an abandoned house, spamming your E key hoping to find the item you need to complete the puzzle you're confronted with. Some of these items are easily spotted and even have icons suggesting they can be used, while others don't, for whatever reason. Providing you find the right items though, the puzzles won't test you in the slightest. Saving, however, proved to be challenging.
Visually, the game looks pretty decent. If you've ever played a Unity horror game from Gamejolt or Itch.io, chances are you'll know what to expect. Audio is okay, with some basic ambient noises and sound fx adding a little extra creepiness to the experience.
Is the game scary?
Not especially. Don't listen to that "No screamers" bit in the description.
Completing the game will probably take you around 20-40 minutes, after which you'll probably regret becoming in any way invested.
I've paid for far worse, but overall, I still wouldn't recommend this unless you've really run out of other games to play.

The gameplay itself is standard fair. Go here, find an item, use the item on object and receive spooks. The atmosphere is average again for a horror game, very dark, and the flashlight doesn't help a great deal. The 'batteries' for it to me seem mostly useless, because it's such a short game, the batteries only last for like 5 minutes. Would suggest using batteries like this for much longer games.
The spooks mainly come from the atmosphere and anticipation of things lurking in the darkness, but I would like to warn people, while the game description states it doesn't have 'screamers', it DOES have jumpscares. They don't happen often and are placed pretty well at the end of atmospheric segments.
The story is almost non-existent, with there only being a brief mention at the start of the game. You never really find out what happened and why. Would advise to add more story elements to the next game.
There are a few bugs. The first is that 2 crucial items (the cup and leaky pipe in the bathroom) do not have a cog icon indicating they can be used. The second is the flashlight having a black splodge in the centre, but the developers have said they will fix this in an update.

So I bought this game on sale a couple weeks ago and read lots of mixed reviews all over the place. I decided to pick it up not only because I am racing fan in general but also because I love Ferrari.
So here is my take on the game.
The graphics in my opinion are staggering. The amount of detail put into the cars themselves in this game are beyond anything Ive seen in most racing games. Not only has every level of intricate detail been placed outside the car, but the interior is where it shines as well. Having sat in several Ferraris, its amazing to see every dial and vent modeled in 3D with shadows and texture. Reflections and detail ripple off the cars. The racing circuits themselves are just as good. Possibly due to my hardware, but I have not seen any graphics problems or anomalies whilst racing.
From the cars Ive ran so far with, the sound is on par. Each engine has a different subtle tone between cars that helps with the realism.
The actual controls of the game, at first, seem something to be desired. I picked up an Xbox 360 controller before I bought this game, and I planned on using that from the get go. That being said, I ask you this question: How many high performance (300+ HP) cars have you driven lately? If you can imagine the amount of power these Ferraris generate, you will soon learn that the actual physics of the cars are actually quite good. While not perfect in any real sense, after several laps I was able to properly handle the car and start pushing lap times.
The AI is ok. Ive raced better. But it works and still makes for an enjoyable race.
Thier is no car customization other than paint colors. Ferrari wanted you to race the car how they designed it. Fine with me.
And to finish my review off, yes this does use GFWL, which may in the future be removed, however, it didnt ruin the game for me nor take away the beauty of the Italian made sports cars.
Recommended for people who enjoy racing or Ferraris in general. B+ rating.

Technically, I haven't played this game for very long and I'm not near finishing it (I think), I saw plenty of the galaxy and the ships to be able to review this game. So, let's get right to it.
Basically you're a space cowboy, thrown deep into space and
.
You fly around, do quests, build relations with factions, acquire credits, ships and new parts.
There's a main storyline, but it's NOT breathtaking and you probably won't follow it anyways.
You can use a controller or mouse and keyboard. I personally used the second option.
You fly around using QE + WSAD keys, block incoming damage using SPACE, switch weapons with numerical keys and aim and fire with your mouse.
The game controls alright, you need to remember about weapon ranges when aiming and firing, maybe it's slightly disappointing you can only move in a 2D plane unlike your opponents (!), but your weapons have a slight autoaim to make up for that, so you don't feel too much pain because of it.
You fly around the stations in star systems, do randomly generated quests that scale with the system's "level" and apparently how wealthy and strong you are, pew pew quite a bit, mine, loot, buy, sell and trade various minerals and equipment, where there's just enough of said elements to make for a decent variety.
Some missions are way too easy, some downright impossible, but you can eventually find something for yourself.
The game didn't take me away, but I come back to it every now and then. It has this charm about itself.
The game looks fine. It doesn't explode with colors nor does it shock you with its photorealism, but it does look like a fairly new game, you won't look away in disgust, maybe I could complain about all ships looking exactly like stock models, no real differentiation between different factions so you can occassionally dumbfire at allies or neutrals.
Also it's hard to attack and defend in battles where there's a lot of stuff flying around, but I'll let that slide.
One thing I didn't like was the lack of the feeling of power behind every shot of broadside cannons. This game needs it.
The game is optimized just OK - I have a medium-class computer and it never even stuttered. Seriously, good job devs.
Sound effects are nice, maybe they could be a bit more intense just like the graphics, especially when you're using your most powerful guns. They are pretty good, though.
The dialogues are copy-and-paste, all the same except for the main plot, repetitive and annoying after some time.
Also apparently all human spacers are Southern Americans and Aussies. Interesting.
The music is fantastic and fits the theme of space cowboy adventures perfectly, but, like pretty much everything else in this game, it gets repetitive and you may want to use your own soundtrack for this game later on.
This is where it gets tricky. That's because I haven't explored the entire game yet. From what I've seen though, I'm only a few ships away from the most powerful destroyer in the game and about halfway in loadout, so I'll try to be credible.
Systems are built differently, with different kinds of stations and factions controlling them, also with a different amount and kind of randomly generated events, so that's a pretty good job well done.
There's technically quite a few kinds of weapons, but after looking at it for a while, there's a few weapons superior to others (lasers and missiles namely) and a flak cannon or dumbfire missiles for secondary weapons are pretty much the only ones that make sense - for defense or for offense respectively. So it's kind of boring.
I'm heavily disappointed about being unable to have a small, powerful ship, because the strongest destroyer can just kill off a smaller ship in one strike from the broadside cannons. No way to manually avoid and a lot is limited by ship's size.
So, how would I rate this game?
On one hand, it's magical. It sucks you in as you start and you're guaranteed to come back to this game many times.
It's pretty decent on the technical side, it's definitely not a ripoff and the optimization was wonderful for me.
On the other hand, it can get really repetitive, boring, and eventually turn into a grind.
Grinding is one of those things I absolutely HATE in most cases, but I'm yet to hate it here, so... Here it goes.
Take the grade with a bit of salt, because I'm giving it credit for the "magic" I felt. Buy it on sale, probably.

Finally beat the game after 32 hours. Not bad for a 10$ game (on sale.)
I'd rate it a solid 7-10
Pros:
Solid Soundtrack - Honestly this may be the best part about the game, it really gives you the feeling of being on the frontier fringes of space, especially getting into scraps with pirates and crime syndicates and other degenerates (provided you aren't already working for them and taking on the militia.)
The Ships - You start out with a barebones tiny 2 guns ship. From there you work your way up the ladder, selling it off along with whatever credits you have towards larger more heavily armed and armored vessels. The ship I ended the game with was roughly 10x the size of my starting one, with so many laser cannons and turrets I felt like I was at a light show.
The Combat - The travel and controls are two dimensional for your ship, but that doesn't mean there aren't plenty of options to choose from here. From long range low recharge broadside cannons and pulse turrets to short range lasers and mine-launchers. Swarm missiles and Shieldbuster Rockets, and even an offensive deflector shield made to ram other ships. Your shields and hull will protect you in four different directions, and parts of the ship can be damaged if enemy weapons penetrate the shields to your hull. You can also hire a mercenary fighter pilot to accompany your battleship for as long as they can survive (though your combat ability will vastly outstrip theirs around 3/4's of the way through the game.)
Cons:
Grindfest - The most glaring issue I had with this game was definitely the amount of time it takes to make money in the earlier to mid parts of the game. New ships and components can be quite expensive, doubling in price for each tier up to the mk.6 parts. Also, if you aren't careful to be sure to upgrade your defenses before your weapons you can find yourself vaporized much faster than your weapons can destroy the other groups of ships coming after you.
The Story - Not a whole lot going on here. You get called to the♥♥♥♥♥end of the galaxy in the middle of nowhere by your aunt who leaves her rust bucket of a ship with a bartender to give to you when you show up, only to learn that she's missing, and you're sent off to find her. I won't spoil the rest of the story that follows, but suffice to say it isn't terribly exciting.
----
All in all a decent game.
