To start this off- I'm a racing simulation fanatic mainly focused on the multiplayer aspects of things.
Also my system is so-so (look at bottom page) and since my racing wheel disintegrated I'm bound to my Xbox controller,
so I lay an great eye on the steering tweaking options since.
All this only, was mainly focused in this review! Enjoy!
In my respect this game is mainly for all non arcade racers out there.
I couldn't believe that arcade racers would rate this over Need for Speed Most Wanted (1)/ Underground. ;)
This is not an arcady game- it's a game for players trying to perfect their driving skills!
The greatest strengs of this game are clearly it's very convincing driving model and
it's variety of Ferrari cars from the beginning of their
career as a racing car manufacturer, to what they are now.
I use a Xbox controller and the steering works fine but the steering customisation options (there are quite a few)
don't provide you with the in my respect perfect setup I'm used to from Grid (1).
It is ok to drive but for me it's bit a pain having to fling my left thumbstick around ever so slightly not to oversteer or force it in one direction not to understeer depending on the vehicles speed.
You can turn the speed regulation off,
but unfortunately the steering vector is bound to a
(beginning of a sine wave)-inclination-vector so you have the same problem with over and understeering
and there is no way to change that. :(
The selection of tracks isn't bad and they are all very authentic, but let's the demanding players a bit down.
Me the most out of the non implemented Nürnburgring! :(
Atleast the great Nordschleife is there.
I haven't tested the single player extesively but it seemes to be pretty standard for a racing simulation.
All the cars and tracks you sure DO want for multiplayer, you actually have to unlock in the single player camplaign.
For all you multiplayer-racing-geeks!! Here's the download-link to all the cars and tracks:
You only have to complete the first mission in first place and then you got them!
The multiplayer is quite straight forward and bound to the games for windows live service.
You can change all needed settings for the race except for driving the track backwards
and you can't drive at night. You can't let it rain either!
It's also a shame, that you can't get damadged in multiplayer wich is actually a nice feature when you drive alone!
Also there are some bugs (very rare), that if you drive with certain cars on certain tracks they will just collide with "nothing"
from time to time! xD
The graphics can look very nice.
Performance isn't bad for a Xbox port but I wished there were more options to tweak.
The dynamic reflections are hitting my system quite hard and look ugly at low settings anyway!
The game, for me, is running at 28-60 FPS at the lowest settings in 1600:900- depending on the tracks detaildness.
My System Specs: 2,4 GHz Harddrive, NVIDIA GT 600m (not overclocked) and 8 GB Ram.
I hope I could provide you with an good overview of the games pros and cons.
Cheers!

I wanted so bad to like this game.
I also wanted to give a brief synopsis as to why this game didn't do it for me but that didn't work out, so there's a TL;DR at the end.
I've been a huge fan of everything that Egosoft has done for the last decade, the amount of hours I put into the X series since X2 has probably been the reason my plots for world domination haven't come into affect yet (at least that's my excuse), so when I saw all the concept art and everything promised by egosoft, I was real excited.
I tried this game on release and it WAS as bad as everybody said it was. It was terrible, it crashed non-stop, the AI was painful, but those are the only two things Egosoft have seemed to improve on since release. Against my better judgement, I read the steam reviews and saw everyone saying to "give it another chance. You love egosoft. They love you." And I did. And I regret it. Here's why:
- This whole game is the embodiment of "half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" I will reference the human models and movement, the dialogue, the transience of the dialogue, the plot, the textures, the trading. It was like they took an idea, threw some things together and said to each other "This kind of looks like that! Let's use it!"
- The ship (singular. That's right, you get one ship that has been described from the get go as a "piece of junk" and they're not lying) doesn't feel nice to fly. It's responsive, sure, but it's just not "immersive", a concept that the creators obviously tried very hard with in regards to everything else.... *elbow nudges*
- The menus never stop being confusing. the maps aren't insightful, maybe this one part is immersive in the fact that it looks like somebody designed it and never decided to change it. It's horrible.
- The AI is still mostly terrible, but it's just not terrible enough that when you're not looking, it can do what you asked it to do. When it comes to your ship though, it's not even worth using the autopilot command, because it was obviously designed by Japanese Engineers during World War 2, you're going head-first into whatever it is you'd like to go to.
- Design-wise, the ships look great. This is something I always appreciated about the X-series. They had a wide range of ships, from god awful (Xenon - Teladi) to sleek and sexy (Terran - Terran. (Maybe also the paranid.)) However the textures and aliasing issues let them down if you ever want to admire them. My system is more than capable, so don't let there be confusion there. I have a team of several hamsters working around the clock to make sure I can boost my graphics as much as I want, but the game was having too many issues with this. Your co-pilot's (Who is so unlikable I literally forgot her name on purpose) hair was either having some graphical issues, or it was super cool and futuristic and could change between red highlights to jet-jet-black to white, all in the space of several miliseconds.
- The sound design is awful. Awful. This was something Egosoft didn't pay too much attention to previously, as many of the looped sounds were 2-3 seconds long and it was obvious they were just looped samples, but it wasn't obvious enough to bug me. Now in stations, there are many more of them, and you hear them all the time, and the transition is so obvious Steve Reich would be disgusted. The music in the highways bugs me the most, and oh boy, let's talk about the highways.
- One of the things I liked about the X games was that they were at your own pace. If you wanted fast paced, you could have that (kind of), if you wanted to slow it down and be a trader, you could do that as well. But with the removal of the time accelerator, this absolutely awful "Boost-in-exchange-for-shields" addition and the highways, it was like they were trying to make the game more interesting all the time, but again, it was done in a severely half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥fashion, so none of it is fun, none of it is immersive and it makes you feel like an idiot when you drop out of the highway because your mouse was a centimeter from the center of your HUD. It's a bad minigame, with no obvious parameters for collisions with other ships, the lighting from the systems your travelling through often obscuring whatever it is that is in front of you. Of all the things I didn't like in this game, I didn't like these the most. My best example of this would be audiosurf, except the music you're listening to is start menu music from a low-budget game from 1998 that lasts 3 seconds, looping over and over but not even perfectly, so the tempo is off, and you can't really see the bricks you're meant to hit and not meant to hit, and your rent is late again and your parents really want you to visit for the weekend.
- The human models haven't been upgraded since X2. Remember, when you first meet Saya Kho onboard the Express and you were like "WOAH, what the F**K is that thing!", well that's what they're still like now. The textures have barely even been upgraded, the movement is so non-human it's actually unnerving, the "guards" that you see inside stations have weapons that look like they cost 1.49 in your nearest pound shop. The dialogue is abysmal, everyone is talking like they are trying to record an automated message for EA customer support, a lot of it makes no sense in regards to where it came from and why they said it, much like EA customer support. Maybe this is art, and Egosoft are trying to describe a future far from now, in which the masses have been silenced and free will has been an illusion for so long, humans aren't even good at feigning it anymore... Probably not though.
And that's as brief as I could make this rant. Wow.
Look... Don't buy this game. I believe as a community that still cares about good space Sims, if we all collectively believe that this never existed, there's still hope.
Egosoft, if you ever get around to reading this, please just let us go back to the way things were. I miss you.
TL;DR: Not bad. 7/10

is a fairly simple game: you play as either a dinosaur or a human, and the goal is simply to be on the winning team. Each round can be around 20-30 minutes, and you have to use your skills in order to kill as many enemies as possible. It can be quite fast paced and sometimes stressful, but always fun regardless whether you play as a dinosaur or human.
It's often on sale, and I'd recommend buying it then. The game is good for killing an hour or so of your time, but there really isn't anything more to
other than maiming your opponents and the amount of maps is fairly small, so perhaps it's not a game one should pay full price for (there isn't a lot of content).
Be aware that there often is a significant amount of lag regardless of your ping, and that does take away from the fun. But the lag isn't always there and it's sufferable. Anecdote:  One time I managed to lag severely while launching a jump attack as a Raptor, and somehow went flying across the entire map and into a cliff, where I died from the impact. Was going for a new personal record too, so that was a bit irritating... : P
All in all, I do recommend this game for people who enjoy dinosaur games and/or first person shooters.

Dark, gritty, violent, awesome.
The Story of Hatred:
This game has had "haters" (I hate this word-but it works here) since it's inception. People were calling it trash before it was even released and many were asking for it to be banned (so much for living in a free society). After it was released, even MORE people were complaining about how it was "disgusting" and that anyone who played the game was "a psycopath" or just "an edgey neckbeard". The discussion boards of Hatred were/are filled with trolls who try and smear the reputation of Destructive Creations by calling them con artists who made the game seem more violent than it turned out to be and purposely tried to garnish negative attention (even though it was the gaming/local media who made a big deal of the game's violence). The trolls also harass anyone who likes the game and get away with it because the moderators apparently dislike the game as well (I got banned for telling someone to play a "My Little Pony" game if they didn't like Hatred-I was banned for "flaming"-mods =Bronies).  To me, it almost seems like many of the trolls have a more sinister agenda behind their trolling, but I digress. The game itself does have some issues; it isn't perfect by any means, but I feel like the developers are working diligently to address the problems/concerns of the community.
PROS:
+The atmosphere of the game is spot on.
+The audio really adds to the darkness, with pedestrians screaming and pleading for their lives; all set to a dark, atmospheric soundtrack.
+Destruction in Hatred is unlike any game I've played to date.
+A lot of attention to detail in every level of the game.
+Bodies and blood stay the way you left them (and don't seem to affect performance).
+My god the explosions are epic. I often shoot propane/gas tanks just to watch the explosions.
+For an isometric shooter, the controls are nice and easy to pick up (despite what others say)
+The Devs are pumping out updates quickly and fixing the problems this game has. They seem to really care about thier game.
+Hatred isn't easy by any means. The different difficulty levels add replayability.
+One day in the near future, it will have a workshop, which will add to the longevity of the game.
CONS:
-Many machines/gpu's have trouble running this game smoothly.
-Even on high-end rigs like my own, framerates WILL drop, which is never good. (I stay around 50-60 for the most part)
-Minor glitches (which are being worked on)
-The game itself is very short and there isn't much of a backstory (this horse is still being beaten on the discussion board).
-Sometimes the NPCs are pants-on-head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
-There aren't too many guns, but there isn't necessarily a LACK of guns either. Could be more.
Overall, I am pleased with the way this game has turned out. I never expected a deep story or a meaningful ending. Many people have been asking/getting refunds because the game is so short, but I don't understand why they are wanting refunds. Almost the entire game was uploaded to YouTube before it was even out. If they would have done their research, maybe they could have realized that the game was not for them (I'm sure I'll get a ton of thumbs down for saying this, but it needs to be said). This game ISN'T for everyone. I suggest watching YouTube walkthroughs before purchasing.
Verdict: 7.5/10

BS2 brings back the awesome BS gameplay with a few improvements. For starters, the hacking "game" was changed to be more pleasant (thank god), and also you have the equipment to hack from a distance. Like in BS, you can rescue Little Sisters from Big Daddies. However, you now have the option to let her sit on your shoulder and let her harvest ADAM when you come across an appropriate body. During which, inhabitants of Rapture will swarm in to get to your girl and it's your job to keep her safe. This was a welcoming addition and I found it challenging and fun, and The Protector Trials have the same purpose but with limited plasmids and weapons.
While the story wasn't as strong as that of BS1 and BSI, it still showcased a number of gameplay elements that I wish was in the original game, which would have made it perfect. On the other hand, you can't deny the thrill when exploring a new map in Rapture. Splicers are some of the creepiest villains created.
Not only do I highly recommend this title, I do the same for the entire series. Try getting the triple pack on a sale. It will be worth it!

The overwhelmingly positive reviews of this game and a post-apocalyptic setting were very intriguing for me. In fact it's kind of that zombie game you ever wanted, even if there are no zombies. I guess humans are bad enough to make survival in a warzone extremely hard. Many people wrote featuerette-like reviews that are bound to draw you into their feelings when playing the game which can be interesting but those reviews only cover a certain aspect of the game. What counts is the whole package you buy.
I bought the game when I first saw it on sale 50% off and played for about seven hours by the time I'm writing this review. I have to admit I never reached the end of the playthrough but I think I got a pretty good feel of how the game evolves. The binary recommendation system of steam doesn't give you a lot of choice, but please note that
means what it says. It doesn't mean I hated the game and had no enjoyable moments with it at all. It just means that I wouldn't go to my friends and say "go buy this game, it's so awesome!"
At first you get a very distinctive
when playing the game. It kind of combines stealth with those point and click adventures you played back in the early 90s but merges a fighting system into it that actually works pretty well. The developers have thought about what they are doing and executed a solid system that at first seems unintuitive (everything is done with mouse-clicking although you have to react fast at times) but works quite flawlessly in the end.
The art is set in a place between the graphics of Deadlight and Limbo. Colors are scarce and everything is rather dark and depressing, as it should be. The different locations are giving you a feel of dread and desperation which works quite well most of the time. Some are chosen a certain way that lets you just hear the name
and you immediately know that this is probably one of the more dangerous places (but very rewarding if survived).
Which brings me to the atmosphere of the game. It delivers. You are in a warzone and it's supposed to be brutal and unforgiving. You have to make tough choices that might influence or even ruin the lives of others in order to survive yourself. The ambient sounds with the graphics work very well to achieve that and the different locations you can visit are chosen in a way that can touch you on a surprisingly emotional base.
Decisions are hard and you never know how they will pan out. One decision can end someone's life and that's exactly what the game does. But in the end it is a game. I want to go back and reload it if it doesn't work out. You might argue that this would ruin the game's aim. Hard decisions are only hard if you can't go back to fix it and you might be right. But the game's playtime is far to extended to really say "I'll do it correctly next time when I caught up the six hours of this playthrough." Some people would probably feel my wish for saving and going back game-breaking and I can understand that but this is how I felt.
The other issue with the game was for me that you are given some very unlikable male characters with a incredibly bland and discouraging backstory. When one of those characters was dying I felt completely disconnected; not because the war is so bad and turns you into a sociopath but because the characters was only a pawn in my game and it actually would have been easier without him (he survived in the end, though). If I just could create my own characters they would've had a different backstory that happens in my head, that makes me feel a lot more emotionally bound to the characters. But instead you are stuck with what you get, let your character be uninteresting, completely replacable and a white male (as happens with many, many games nowadays).
What put me off the most were some of the weird and nonsensical choices the developers made. For example the crafting system is so
that it totally ruined the experience for me. You get your workbench and then you need to upgrade it with some insane amounts of loot to build new or improved other tables that help you out. Speaking of loot: Your characters have an arbitrary number of inventory slots, just like you remember from your 90's point and click adventures. Those slots are filled with one kind of item. Some stack, some don't. And they stack in different amounts. So you can end up with carrying 20 wooden planks and 4 pieces of scrap metal (which is not nearly enough to do even the first upgrade of your workbench) but you can't go home with a rifle, a pistol, ammo for both, and a roll of toilet paper because that takes more slots. So, the logical thought here for me was "I don't have enough inventory slots, so lets take more people out for scavenging." But, of course, that is also not possible. You can't have a team of two in one scavenging zone and no, you cannot send out two teams to scavenge at different spots in the city. Also, in the end it turned out that those hard choices you make did not matter at all. I robbed someone
of all their food and when I came back a week later they were still very much alive
. I encountered a few more issues like that during my playtime with the game but I think you got the idea.
... the game is a nice idea and has some very strong points in its execution but also some issues that finally made me not like the game. It is supposed to be super atmospheric but at pretty much every turn you make you will find yourself confronted with those small things that rip you out of your immersion and throw you back in a state that makes you question the game's mechanics all the time. And this spoiled my experience with
Add the characters that were unlikeable and hollow in the first place and you lost me. Many people think differently about the game. Maybe they don't get put off by those small details like I did or they are totally fine with it. So please read a bunch of other reviews to get a better idea wether the game is worth the money for you. I just know it wasn't worth it for me.

This is an enjoyable 4X strategy game.  I prefer it to Civ V for the following reasons:
* More dynamic research tree allows genuinely strategic research decisions.
* Streamlined interface provides the information needed, but allows you to focus on strategy rather than a complex UI.
* Sci-Fi setting is interesting both in terms of philosphical lore and aesthetics (although this is a matter of personal taste).
* The core 4X one-more-turn Civ V mechanics are not diminished.
I've only played one full single player game and a couple of multiplayer games, however I've not encountered any technical issues.  The networked mulitplayer seems more stable than Civ 5, as we've not had any crashes as compared to occasional glitches in Civ V, although it may be to early to claim this as more than anecdotal for now.
If you'd like a Sci-Fi take on Civ gameplay in a highly polished and steamlined package that retains the strategic gameplay of the series, this is stronly recommended.  Just remember, if you've got hundreds of hours invested in Civ V you'll have very nuanced expectations of every cause and effect in the game.  This isn't the same game, and that level of nuance and depth of understanding in the mechanics isn't going to be there on your first play through.  What is there, or at least was there for me, is the same strategic, compelling gameplay.

Civilization players be warned:  This game is nothing like classic Civ games!  You will face an incredibly steep learning curve that may cause you to languish while even easy AI rivals outpace you.  This is not helped by the unforgiving nature of the aliens in this game.  Do not confuse them with the easily cleared barbarians of Civilizations past.  They do not scale with technology, since technology is no longer divided into linear ages, but into a complex, interwoven web, and so you can expect to lose an undefended settlement or fresh city immediately to some of the tougher ones.  If you are unlucky, you may have a behemoth land worm or two (with 100 battle power!) spawn near you and prevent you from expanding.  Worse yet, you could be prevented from escaping via the sea if a monstrous sea serpent (also with 100 power) spawns near your coast.  In addition to these frustrations (or perhaps because of them), I felt the game could be a bit bland compared to something like Civ5.
As for positives, I do actually like the settlement system, where deploying a settler doesn't found a new city, but a settlement, which claims itself and one other adjacent tile, then expands its borders over the next few dozen turns until it can work every available adjacent tile, at which point it becomes a city and can defend itself and build things.  It may sound irritating to you, but I actually liked that.  I liked the anomaly excavation concept (though I feel there's no reason to limit scouts to just one excavation per unit), and I liked the mission system, which could give you goals to distract and aid you while working toward victory.  The unit upgrade system is also a good idea, allowing players to apply certain upgrades to all of their units of a particular type, both present and future.  However, I feel that it can really take too long to earn upgrades, and I didn't really get to see much of the system in action as a result.
Do I recommend this game?  I don't know.  If you like Civ5 and are looking for something more challenging, then this may be just what you're looking for.  A multiplayer game with a few friends could also be less irksome than facing a bunch of AIs, since you'd have someone to commiserate with over bad luck, and you could convince your friends to help you (maybe) if the aliens are keeping you penned in.  If you're just looking to play a fun strategy game that maybe doesn't require absolute optimized prioritization, I might recommend Civ5, or better yet, Galactic Civilization II (though buyer beware; the latter of those has no multiplayer!)

First off, I'll say that while I have played pretty much every X game (not through steam) except Albion Prelude, and most other space sim/traders, its been so long I barely remember them. I was very much in the mood for space game, and while I had heard Rebirth came out several years ago I was very disappointed to see linux support dropped. Well its back as of a few months ago! This prompted a near-instant purchase from me, after checking to see if the devs had been working on patching the horrible state the game was in at launch. I'm happy to say they have been working very hard.
This review will NOT attempt to compare X:R with any of the other X games, since its been so long since I've played them. I also won't generally compare it with other similar games in the genre. However I will say that if you are considering getting X vs Elite: Dangerous, I recommend X unless you are okay with an *always*-online game, including for single player. Also, E:D doesn't support linux, which I use exclusively.
Graphics:
I opted into in the 4.0 beta 6 and it runs very well on my linux mint OS with a GTX 970. On ultra with 8xAA, 16xAF, I get 40-60 fps in every area I've been to, including large battles with cap ships. There are occasional (rare) times where the FPS drops to about 2-5 when docking into a station, but a quick hop to the graphics settings and re-selecting ultra fixes it right away, so I'm confident the devs will fix that issue. Obviously I can't speak to the Windows performance, but since it uses the ultra-slow dog known as DX12, YMMV and I suspect it might run worse than the linux version.
Side note - I installed on a linux laptop I have with an intel 5500 and with a little tweaking to lower the settings, the game runs playably, though obviously not near 60 fps. I mention this because the system requirements state you need AMD/Nvidia, but thats not strictly true.
I won't go into much detail, but this game looks absolutely breathtaking. Destroying a major component of a cap ship results in an awesome looking plume of fire and smoke, that while not realistic for space, makes for a really awesome sight. The amount of 'local' station air traffic is awesome, with a very 5th Element / Blade Runner type feel. You can get scanned by cops, and if you're carrying illegal wares for that area, you might need to hit those afterburners quick! It really helps with the overall immersion.
Though I'm sure there will be a few hiccups here and there in such a massive game, so far I have encountered no major bugs, even in the linux beta!
Controls:
The controls with a mouse+kb are very good, so if you're not a "joystick jockey" then you'll still be very much able to enjoy this game. That said, there is joystick support that seems to work well enough, and gamepad support which I don't recommend. The gamepad mappings leave a lot to be desired, especially since to control throttle you must CONSTANTLY have the trigger depressed. This should have been a more traditional left trigger=throttle down, right trigger=throttle up.
I personally have found after playing with all the control options (mouse, joystick, gamepad, steam controller) that a custom binding of the steam controller in non-gamepad mode works best for me. My joystick is showing its age so its just not as precise as it used to be. However if you have a steam controller this game is awesome with it. You can get my steam controller bindings in the 'Community' section, titled "XR Non-Gamepad Bindings".
Sound:
Effects are about as you'd expect for a space sim and serve the purpose, with your gun and laser and computerized voices. The music is generally quite good and the main menu music in particular (can't speak to the DLC) is great. It definitely gets me in the mood for flying. Voice acting is awful, which is typical of X games. Just turn voices off in the beginning and save your ears the trouble. In future X games I hope they drop voice acting to spend more time on launch-day polish, which has always lacked a bit in Egosoft games.
Gameplay:
Alright, so this is of course the meat of the game. I'm about 75% through the main plot missions, and have done a relatively small amount of side missions. The plot isn't half bad, and generally better than most games of this type. The last truly good plot I've seen in games like these was way back in Wing Commander: Privateer (yea I'm old) and its expansion. So that said, its a pretty enjoyable plot overall if you can get past the horrid voice acting or just turn it off. It'll feel a bit like an old JRPG that way.
The plot missions start a bit bland, per most games of this type, but about 40% through you'll start seeing cap ship battles, a prison break thats pretty cool, and get to see a significant portion of the systems and zones.
You can get up and walk around your ship, or dock with stations and walk around them. It can be somewhat rewarding to explore stations in the beginning of the game, and some stations are quite cool to look at and explore, but most use a random selection of about 5 or 6 layouts so it does get a little dull. That said it goes help with immersion if you don't like to do everything via menus like in previous games, so overall its actually a nice addition. You can, as of one of the past patches, just do pretty much everything but black market trading through menus from your ship.
This game does not hold your hand, in fact it probably needs more of a hands-on tutorial to explain how to properly do trading, station building, etc. All X games have suffered from this, but my personal feeling is you should take your time to grow into these games and learn/discover for yourself as much as you can while enjoying the game and environments, so maybe thats what they intend. When you really get stuck, an online video or tutorial is just a quick search away. (Try to find a recent video as Egosoft really has changed this game dramatically since release)
I have a decently upgraded main ship, and 4 'large' ships, some of which do trading missions, and some come with me on combat. Seeing and participating in a large scale combat is just awesome looking. Sadly, stations can't be destroyed, but on the plus side this makes the economy of your game harder to really screw up. Some of the 'generic' auto-generated missions are a bit vague or exploitable, however they are actively patching and improving them.
I have not built a station, but the beauty of a game like this is that you can play the go-it-alone smuggler type, the economic behemoth, the private military force, heavy mining operations or just about any other type of role you might want to play that involves space + ships.
I have about 20 hours of play time so far. Obviously many players and fans of X will say thats not enough for a review because I haven't done X, Y or Z. However thats not true in my opinion. I'm having a blast and have definitely got my money's worth already. Since I am not comparing this to previous X games, thats enough to write a review. Also I haven't noticed any linux reviews, so its important to write one for any linux fans who might want to know how the game runs. That said, I expect I'll be enjoyably playing this for many hundreds of hours more. I can't say that about any other game I've bought in the past 3-5 years.

TD:FRL is much harder than it looks, this game is closer to Forza or Gran Turismo interms of realism. With multiple eras of Ferraris, from classic to modern, and a full campaign for each, as you attempt to accomplish various objectives, such as showing off certain vehicles, win certain races, and so on.
You will be at first, be distracted by eye candy aplenty, then you realize the game has excellent driving models that portrays convincing weight transfer, throttle while turn, drifting, and so on, but also has full driver aids like auto brake, optimum line, and so on. The catch, of course, is you are basically doing the equivalent of GT races and test drives where you need to negotiate chicanes, hard braking turns without spinning the car, hairpins, and so on, often with competition.
Beware that even "easy" is not easy on a track when any sort of cutting across a corner may earn you a warning, and repeated offense will earn you a DNF / DQ (did not finished, disqualified).
Each era as mentioned before, has a lot of vehicles to try. Think the old EA "Porsche Unleashed" and you're not far off, except there is no point to point races, only circuits, and evolution is combined with factory driver, but cut up into multiple eras, each with separate progress.
The main problem is the AI is not very tunable, and with races of only a few laps, any mishap will mean you fail to achieve your goal. Furthermore, some of the missions are next to impossible given the required car. For example, one of the missions I got stuck on was "dodge the simulated debris on track, while still achieve required laptime". There are like six different "debris" sets and they are in the driving line, so you can no longer take optimal line to retain speed, and your car is not exactly a speed demon (but an 1950's UNsporty Ferrari) and I'm always 2 seconds short and I can't find any way to make up the time any more. And that's on EASY. There's also medium and hard with even tighter time requirements.
On the races, I can usually beat out the competition. It's these timed races that got me.
The game is basically GT racing, so braking and precision maneuvering through tight corners and chicanes is expected, and that, I'm not very good at. You may do better.
With dozens of Ferrari vehicles to unlock in career mode, and a dozen tracks to experience, this driving sim really needs a wheel for full enjoyment, and some patience. Don't expect to jump in and master the cars just like that. Ferarris are race cars, and deserve some respect.

Rebel Galaxy is a game with a space setting that locks you in a 2D plane. You can steer right, you can steer left and that's it. Optimization is questionable (1440p, max IQ is using 100% from a GTX 980 with framerate dips into the 30 range), the "story" is paper thin and the ending is abrupt. There are a number of critically well received games that are flat out broken especially with the popularity of early access.  Destructive Creations are also very transparent with the community and have been very quick to release patches for issues some have encountered as well as adding new features.

The Dream Machine is, by far, one of the most complicated adventure games I've ever played.
You play as a man who has just moved with his wife to a new apartment. Something is amiss, however, and soon you learn that you'll have to take it upon yourself to stop a sinister plot where your dreams, and the dreams of all the apartment residents, are being infiltrated by your land lord and his out of control contraption. The graphics are marvelously creepy, being claymation, and the soft ambeint music and horror-like storyline set the scene for a truly challenging adventure that will have you immersed for hours.
Game play wise, I will say that some of the puzzles may be easy to solve in a few minutes, and other may take hours, or even days, depending on your thought process and how you deal with puzzles. There are puzzles for all types of people, so while I certainly don't suggest that you cheat, it's always fun to team up on this game. Some of the game play can get slightly monotonous while you're stuck, which can be frustrating. (But such is the bane of adventure games.) There were also a few times where I thought I was supposed to be trying to solve a puzzle to unlock something, but it wasn't time for that in the story yet. Still, when things become clear, it's easy to sit down and focus on the puzzle intently.
The story line is creepy and unsettling. It is not a full out horror tale, but at times it can be graphic and disturbing. It also moves slowly towards the disturbing, and as you get further into the plot it becomes stranger.
This IS the sort of adventure game where you may need to keep some scrap paper beside you in order to jot down notes and figure things out. If you are not into complicated adventure games, then this is not for you. But if you are, then welcome to The Dream Machine.

(Broken up into pieces because Steam is being whack, everything else is in the comments section)
Apart from this introduction, I will not mention the controversy this title has generated. The game is a top-down shooter about mass murder. If that description does not sit well with you, don't bother with it. Some people seem to be making their minds up based on the themes alone, and this is simply not fair. Hatred, I really wanted to like you. While I unfortunately do not think this is a great game, this is due to design flaws, not what I personally think is tasteful subject matter.
Graphics: A simple style for a simple game. The black and white is complimented by colorful visual effects to either set the stage or distinguish action. It's okay. However, the game runs on Unreal Engine 4, and it shows. If your computer isn't up to spec (ie, NASA supercomputer, because what is optimization), it will look ugly and slow. Also, the game has ragdolls, with all of the eyesores those can entail. The destruction detail is some of the sexiest I've ever seen.
Sound: Rather than go all out edgelord with Linkin Park music, the soundtrack (except for the end credits) is almost entirely composed of slow, pulsating beats with either woodwinds or organs. It sets quite a serious tone. The voice acting is cheesy, but expected.
AI: A combination of basic intelligence, and profound idiocy. At their best, enemies will try to flank you, civilians will pick up fallen weapons and fight back. At their worst, enemies will shoot each other, and civilians will literally line up against flat walls.
Gameplay: A lot of shooting. In some of the levels, the goal is simply to get to the end. For the bigger, more "sandbox" levels, the player is given an initial objective, with a laundry list of other tasks that become uncovered by exploring the map. This is where the game starts to show problems. The shooting works fine on a 2-D basis, but given that the game does not entirely take place on a horizontal plane, aiming can be inaccurate. Most of the time, the camera is fixed at a strange angle that would be fine for more open areas, but the game is more tactical than that. Open areas are suicide, with most enemies constantly pestering me just offscreen. It requires the player to go indoors to avoid gunfire, and due to Not Important's slippery handling, I end up tripping over all sorts of stuff just laying on the ground, and accidentally bouncing grenades off of walls when I believed I had a clear shot. Death will allow the player to use one of a limited set of respawns (which are gained by completing sidequests) that spawn me either on the other side of the map, or right in the middle of a group of enemies.
Of course, if any of that seems unbalanced, just go into crouch mode and see your worries disappear. This turns most of the game into a cakewalk, even on extreme difficulty.
Disappointing.

I was excited for months about this game, having expectations of seeing this game to be somewhat the holy grail of all violence and brutality, hyping itself to be a bloodbath of epic proportions which promises to leave the player grinning a sadistic grin, was this what I recieved? The short and easy answer is definitely not. This game I decided to spend hard earned cash on turned out to be a game which caused disappointment and rage as opposed to something I could release my stress playing.
When I started playing the game I was using a controller instead of a keyboard, even though it supported this I was faced by tedious controlls and awkward gameplay. My most hated problem is that the button Y is used to change weapon, execute victims and switch weapons with weapons on the ground, often leading to my swapping to an unloaded gun during a firefight when I only wanted to execute a victim, not only that but after executing the person I always had to check I had the right gun selected. You cannot even change the button set up.
The game's performance is terrible for my above standard computer, meaning that if you want a smooth running game you have to put up with terrible graphics, there are so many patches that would be needed to make this game enjoyable for me.
There are few pros to this game such as sadistic one liners from the main character, often though sounding cheesy which can spoil the mood of the gameplay. The game has emphesis on violence however the so called 'graphic' nature of the game turns out to be no more graphic than most first gen consoles, and gore fan can get a much more satisfying gore experience from pretty much most 18 rated games instead of seeing low polygon characters with bad gore effects being stabbed and shot into smaller polygons.
I'm sorry developers, but as a player I have not recieved what I was promised from this game, and I feel you can do better. This is the sort of game which could have made a much better first or third person game to show of what is supposed to be a gore fest.

17 hours to see the end of the war. It wasnt an easy road my little family of misfits walked. It was one that left them stretched to their limits many times. Some days barely enough strength to even stand or a will to keep going yet I drove them on like a merciless and maybe in theirs eyes a malevolent force.
It seems a life though at first littered with trouble for the first 19 days, then in a moment of tragedy 2 soldiers cornered Marko who though armed was unable to kill them before he was shot down.
This hit the rest hard. Things got bad fast, supplies started to thin out, the wounds of boris made sending him out risky at best and the only hope seemed a cottage with an old couple Id been avoiding. I was desperate and just hoping maybe they had some medicine, bandages, and food they would trade for a sizable amount of moonshine. Boris carried a knife, boris was wounded, sick, very hungry, and very tired. These old people seemed to have it all and were unwilling to even consider trade. Boris lashed out at the old man who tried to stop the taking of what was so badly needed back at home.
The old man ran then, and hid down in the basement. the old woman ran upstairs. Boris was in a rage then and just wanted the screaming to stop. He lumbered slowly after the old woman who managed to stumble ahead fast enough to get upstairs first and hide in a room at the end of the hall, but eventually Boris found her, and made her stop screaming forever. Eventually he found the old man and let him go join his wife.
The supplies where amazing. 3 days later Boris hung himself. It got real hard after that. Bruno seemed to endure it all even when he was at his limits he kept things going, kept the booze brewing which helped everyone fight off the depression.
And then day 45 the war ended. It was over when it seemed no one was going to make it.
This game is brutal, it will make you feel something almost certainly at least the first time you play through, and the money for playtime for even one play through is fair price.

There is the survival aspect of the game, scavanging for food and materials.  Making makeshift tools and building things to aid in survival. Even that is limited.  Trade and bartering is limited.
Social interaction is also a limitation in the game.  There is almost no interaction between the main charcters, what interaction there is very scripted and repetitive. The game is indeed thought provoking without a doubt, but that does not always make a game good.  I do recommend the game for the social content, there is merit in the game on that. I not recommend the game if you are looking for playability and depth.
I do not regret buying the game, I only wish there was a bit more substance to the game.

The game title says "Hitman", and you play a guy who is bald and everyone calls him "47".
But this bald 47-guy is not the guy that stuck a scissor into the back of a nosey housewife because she wanted to call the police.
This 47-guy is not the 47 that killed a 14 year old girl on her birthday party to get her necklace unwitnessed.
This 47 is not the 47 that shoots a deliveryman for bringing him a letter.
This 47 is not the same 47 who responded to a woman who told him she was likely to get brutally murdered soon: "I am sorry to hear that, has my payment been arranged?".
No no, this 47 is utterly sentimental. He protects little girls - free of charge.
He gets put on his back 2 times only surviving because his idiot enemies  fail to put a bullet into his brains right away.
He is a 47 that is uncapable of keeping his equipment sorted, so he has to start his assignments with whatever he found in the trashbin down the road.
He is a 47 that can stick Sniperifles and Shotguns into his pants (and nobody will notice!), but can only start a contract with one type of weapon.
He is a 47 who's face everyone has seen on TV (or where was it?) already, hence he can dress up all the way he likes - someone is bound to indentify him anyways. Well, unless he wears his standard suit that is.
And last but not least, this is the 47 who can bend time and travel back in time to not-do-what-he-did-before.
I cannot rate this game as a Hitman title because it clearly isn't, so i will rate it as a standalone game:
6/10
Because i see there has been put quite some effort into providing a good game. Interessting map-design, good AI, a decent movement system, it is really not all bad.
But it has a low replayability value, despite the user-created contracts, which play on the same maps with the same mechanics as the storyline missions.
You cannot spawn new characters, you can't even alter the pathing for already existing characters. All you can do is replay the mission, define new targets and ways to kill them, and others may try to do as you did and either beat your score or die trying.
Concerning gameplay you can but say that controls are rather complicated and not well thought out, button confusion for most part. There is no 1st person mode, so you better run through those curtains before you find your view obstructed by them while you get pounded with .45cals from the other side.
No pre-mission gear selection, no blueprints, no layouts, no freedom.
The rating system is a real bummer, spoils all the fun in progress already, unless you don't give a f***.
The graphics are superb and deliver a premium experience with low impact.
So, this is great a firework of eyecandy with a semi-interessting story about some bald guy who accidently got mistaken for Mr Fourty-Seven from Hitman: Blood Money, and now everybody wants a piece of him and he wants the girl.
If you have never played a Hitman title before this could be nice to play before you play Blood Money. Afterwards it is just a huge disappointment.

People like saying that it is bad, but I disagree with that. People like saying that it is a reskin of Civ V, wich I disagree with as well. Beyond Earth has the affinities, the orbital layer, and satellites in general, better spying system (in my opinion), quests, the tech web, new resources which have a large impact on how a game will turn out (i.e. firaxite, floatstone), different units (as opposed to a civilization's special unit in Civ V, the affinity changes more than just a single unit). Aliens might be compared to barbarians, but you can not tame barbarians and have them help fight with you. The multiple special abilities you may pick from is a nice little feature to slightly impact gameplay, the trade system with foreign cities and outposts is good too. And when people say that it is a reskin of Civ V, its a Civ game. Did you want something else? I agree that the colors are dull, but other than that I would say that Civilization: Beyond Earth is a good game.

At first glance, Betrayer looks pretty awesome. The first hour or so, it was pretty entertaining. The graphics are stark, morose and creepy (very befitting the story). The story and setting start out very compelling. The soundtrack is subtle. The gameplay relies on stealth-based combat.
Unfortunately, most of this begins to wear thin the more you play. The graphics eventually become a strain on the eyes, as you try to squint and find a flash of red in the repetative black and white landscape (which can be confusing, as the enemies are usually red, but so are certain small plants/flowers). The soundtrack becomes dull, as all you hear is the sound of the wind and the odd growl from the monsters roaming the map. The combat is repetative and boring, widly going from one-shot easy kills to mobs that kill you in a few hits. The weapons are limited to bow, crossbow, pistol, musket, rifle and melee (with sub-weapons like tomahawk and bomb), but are very clunky to use (rotating between them should be smooth, but turns out awkward and sometimes doesn't work at all) and the variety within said weapons is small. The gameplay gets boring, very fast.
The setting gets dull as you notice there is very little difference between the zones. Trees, long grass, and the odd small fort/camp. The stealth mechanic is pretty bad, as you are caught between walking (the enemies see you easily), running (the enemies see you very easily) and sneaking (the enemies shouldn't see you, but mostly do unless you're at a far distance).
Overall, it felt like this could have been a great game, but just missed its mark.

Tl;Dr - I'd give X Rebirth an 8 out of 10. It's an incredibly fun, diverse game with plenty of things to do. The Steam reviews do not represent the game in its current state.
Let me start by saying this to prospective buyers; X Rebirth is NOT X4. It's a game set in the X universe, and aspired to be a new game entirely - Something which I think it has done very, very well.
You can only fly one ship. This ship is virtually your own Millennium Falcon - It's unique, incredibly powerful, and quite customizable, and is basically a few different ships in one package. If you were able to fly multiple types of ships, you'd probably go for this one every time.
Now, onto the review.
You'll notice that X Rebirth has a very low score on Steam. Don't judge a book by its cover - Most of these scores were given around the time of v1.0, or were given by people who don't read up on a game before they buy it.
X Rebirth 1.0 was a shoddy mess, virtually an early beta of a game with clunky mechanics, bad voice acting, and more glitches than you could possibly imagine. Most people dropped X Rebirth straight off the bat, gave it a bad review, and never looked back.
Not long after that, however, 2.0 came out and completely revolutionized the game. Everything was streamlined and most of the problems fixed, and the game became more or less playable, and even pretty enjoyable. A few patches later and the game was pretty much how you'd expect a game to be at launch, with hundreds upon hundreds of hours of content (If you're a creative person) and lots of ways to make your empire what you want it to be - If you want an empire at all, that is.
The story was honestly not that compelling, but there's plenty of reasons to play it as it confers unique bonuses on certain systems that free play simply would not, such as more diverse economies in certain systems.
3.0 rolled around at the end of 2014, only a year after the game's release, and set the bar higher than before. The game became much, much more fun, now with a total of 5 systems to explore (Note that each system has multiple sectors, each of which is bigger than a system from previous X games) as well as dozens of factions to meet, hundreds of ships and stations to build and use, and wares to mine, manufacture, and trade.
X Rebirth today is an incredibly fun game. A single save could take hundreds of hours of your time as you build yourself an empire in a system. You could start a new game and take a completely different route, giving you hundreds more hours of gameplay as you make a name for yourself elsewhere. The sky's the limit with your choices in X Rebirth.
While there are still a few glitches and bad mechanics to the game, most of it has been smoothed out. With the upcoming Home of Light DLC, the world is set to almost double in size and have many new factions to play with.
If you're looking for X4, don't bother with X Rebirth. If you're looking for a new and fun space business and combat sim that'll provide hours of fun, then X Rebirth is the game for you.

I dislike game consoles, but in this game, you can for once see their potential to have a positive effect for PC gamers:  Consoles force Developers to develop an intelligent control scheme, that works with just a few keys, but still requires skill.
This beats the use of countless different keys other common space flight sims require, which do make things tedious sometimes. In WoW, I was forced to write macros, cause I just didn't have enough quickly reachable keys on my keyboard.
In Rebel Galaxy, the control scheme is mostly excellent, a few smallish Problems not withstanding, like your ship drifting by containers and by the time you reach and hold the 'E' key to tractor it aboard, the container often got deselected by your ship's slow movement and you end up warping off, instead of grabbing the loot.  Combining too many functions into one key *can* become a problem.  Like when you are trying to warp, but you got hailed by someone, now that same 'E' key will start an unwanted conversation instead of warping off to save your skin.
But beyond those two high level niggles, the UI and keyboard scheme used are a charm in this game, allowing you to play it very naturally after a very short time. What also helps is, that there is a subtle tutorial that pops in during the first few missions, teaching you the right keys in the right situation, done in such a way, that you never forget or have to look up those keys a second time.
At first, I was a bit concerned about 6dof missing, but it quickly turned out that this is so well designed, you don't really miss the 6dof.
Game play is such, that if you even half like it, you won't stop playing any time soon, once you started.
Its not a huge game as yet, but the core is so well done, it could stand being extended for many more stories and iterations and I'd keep coming back. As it is now, it is certainly fair value for the money, it took me about 40 hours to play it through, and that was without even getting near having the best possible ships and equipment possible.
In a way this makes it the opposite of Elite: Where Elite has vast empty spaces and billions of systems, it boils down to being not that much fun, with Braben being satisfied that its the same as the original Elite: a pure, highly repetitive grind.
Rebel Galaxy on the other hand may not be as huge as that, but it sure meets the primary purpose of a game far better than Elite:  To be really fun.
I haven't bothered to write any reviews on Steam yet, but this game deserves one more toast from a long time space game fan :)

TL:DR? A great game, but not in the same way as the others. Still worth a playthrough. Just play the first Bioshock first, and expect this to be a slightly different experience. Also, I've heard that the Minerva's Den DLC is fantastic, even from people who don't like this game.
Bioshock 2, the black sheep of the series. It is a wonderful game, but not quite in the same way as the other two. While the other Bioshocks excel in atmosphere and world-building, that is where this one is rather weak. The only noteworthy addition, universe-wise, is the fleshing-out done with characters and locations mentioned in the first game. The game's real strangth, particularly when compared to the first Bioshock, is the mechanics. Hacking is now more fluid, as is plasmid use. Gene tonics are no longer separated into types. Weapons all have a third, "ultimate" upgrade. There is a new level to the moral choice system, and (later in the game at least) this one is a bit more ambiguous than you would expect, and has interesting implications at the end. You can now adopt little sisters and protect them as they gather adam. All of this (apart from the moral choice thing) results in a mechanic-driven Bioshock, at least in the first half of the game. And honestly, this gets old pretty quickly. It's a whole lot of "I gotta stand here and kill people who are attacking me for a period of time." But, as the game goes on, more interesting elements emerge. The game escalates well from a level-based explore, loot, and kill stuff-athon like the first game, to the same thing but with a new, more interesting enemy type and mildly creative abilities, but also with a nice story pull. While I did not like this game coming from Bioshock 1, coming back to it later I really can't find much to hate about it. It's just a little different, under the surface.
Just don't expect to finish a playthrough without crashing every other session.

Hatred features a protagonist/antagonist (depending on your point of view) hell bent on murdering everyone in his vicinity and dying a "violent death."  Personally, I love these types of games, and I've been watching Hatred for awhile, so I figured why not light $20 on fire and give it a shot.  I know next to nothing about the technical aspects of video games, so below are a few of my observations.
It's a top down twin stick shooter (isometric if you want to be fancy).  The camera does a fairly decent job of keeping up with your character, but every so often I find myself getting shot...and getting shot....and getting shot from seemingly invisible foes.  There is a 'mini map' (it shows the location of enemies and nothing else) that alerted me to the fact that these incorrigible civvies have armed themselves and had begun shooting me from off screen, as have the police, military, and swat units.  Frankly, I found that a little annoying, since I couldn't see them and they could see me.  I began the practice of randomly spraying off screen in their direction, wasting my precious little buddies on walls/doors/cars, and not on those pesky humans.
The targeting system, in my opinion, works fine.  I play with an Xbox 360 controller so I hold down LT and it 'lengthens' my point of aim.  Think of it as a zoom, since that also takes focus off of your character.  Not that great when you're getting mobbed by half the population.  I swear these people are more murderous than I am.  If they see a weapon you can bet your left nut that they'll pick it up and start blasting away...at you.  I'm shocked that no one else harbors my disdain for humanity, no one else wished to pick up the flag and join my mission.  A shame really.  In any case, I haven't had too much of a problem with the aiming system.  While it can be a hassle for the above reason, it's alright for the most part.
Weapon variety is another thing Hatred could benefit from.  There are only 10 (maybe?) weapons in the whole game and they fall into 6 categories: special, handgun, grenades, shotgun, smg, and rifle.  In the first category you have the rocket launcher and flamethrower.  The rocket launcher is just that, it launches an explosive projectile towards whatever you're aiming at.  Typically the target(s) will either explode...or explode with a red mist.  The flamethrower lights things on fire, as a flamethrower should.  Just make sure you keep it pointed in a safe direction, too often I found myself gleefully hosing victims only to find a pillar in the way...and myself on fire.  The handgun is, you guessed it, a handgun.  Point at victims, pull trigger, hopefully watch victim hobble away in pain.  If you missed, then keep pulling trigger until desired effect is reached or you're out of ammo.  I've only found one handgun throughout the game so far, and I'm around 4/5 hours in.  The grenades come in three flavors - boom (standard), burn (molotov), and flash (flash bang).  Boom grenade goes boom when thrown at stuff (walls, doors, people, cars, etc.).  Again, be wary of walls, pillars, and other obstructions.  Boom grenade doesn't discern between friend and foe.  Burn does just that, it burns aything it lands on.  Same warnings apply, although the radius is rather small, especially if the contents don't burst on someone.  Flash grenade blinds/stuns targets.  The effects last 2-3 seconds and you better be behind something when it explodes or you're going to be blinded as well.  If that happens, the cleanser becomes the cleansee if you know what I mean.  The shotgun is a pump action, takes FOREVER to reload, and has a short effective range...meaning if you don't have the shotgun firmly planted in someones ribs it's likely not going to kill them in the first shot.  DO. NOT. USE. IT.  I know I know, I too was drawn to the pull of the shotgun, but alas, after I mutilated...I mean cleansed, a scant few people I found myself on the wrong side of the law, and the ground.  Throughout my play time I found two smg's, one used by SWAT, and the other used by the russian mafia.  Both function the same, except the SWAT one has a blinding light that I use to let someone know I'm aiming at them.  This way they have a fighting chance.  Unless of course they're a bum lounging around in the sewers, then they're perfectly alright sitting there waiting to be executed.  I only discovered one rifle thus far, and it's used by the military.  Basically has the same characteristics as the smg's, but a higher damage rate.
I also seem to find myself cleansing the same people a little too often.  Some of the character models look really similar for civilians, police, swat, and military units.  It didn't bother me personally, since most of the time their facial features were being stomped on repeatedly or shot off.
The AI is no joke.  On the second level I was skipping to the first objective with my trusty handgun and people started yelling, screaming, and running before I had cleansed anyone or anything.  Old bart started fleeing the gas station when I was approaching the wall he was standing behind.  Now, unless Bart is superhuman, I'm not entirely sure how he knew I wanted to put a bullet in his head before I was even visible.  Jokes on him since I blew up the entire gas station, specifically the pumps, while he was standing right next to them.  Died like the punk he was.
The instant someone obtains a weapon they turn into Robocop.  Meaning they don't miss, at least not on 'Hard' difficulty (there was easy/hard/extreme to choose from), which I guess makes sense, since it makes the game pretty damn hard.  Literally anyone can pick up a weapon and start shooting.  I thought that was pretty neat and realistic until I walked into a firearm convention.  My God.  Everyone turned and looked at me, I looked at them, they looked at me, I pointed my gun at them, they pointed their weapons at me...I ran, they all fired...I kept running, they chased and continued firing.  Now at this point the police also got involved.  I managed to reach an apartment complex and hid in the bathroom, but they knew...they all knew.  I've never seen so many explosions and so much destruction.  In the end I came out on top, mainly because they all wanted the glory and decided to attack via the one entrance...they entered one by one.  It was close though.  One last helpful hint...if you hear sirens make sure you're inside, I thought I was cool and could take a police cruiser on, I stood right in front of that house taunting them to come at me.  Welp, they called my bluff, ran me over and dragged me until I was dead.
If I had to rate this game on a scale of 1-10 I'd give it around a 7.  Hope you enjoyed reading through my journey with Hatred, and I do hope to see you out on the streets cleansing with me. :)

I have not played the older Hitman games so I don't know how they compare to this one, but I can say that I very much enjoyed this one. The game is very well polished with a large variety of ways to play through missions and even create your own to a limited degree. For a shooter it has a substantial amount of replayability which is always a good thing.
While I did enjoy the game, it's still not perfect. The controls can be clunky at times and the multipurpose context sensitive buttons mean that occasionally you'll activate the item next to you instead of grabbing the guard as he comes around the corner or repeatedly pick up the wrong item in the stack of guns in front of you.
Switching weapons can also be a bit clunky at times and blocks the whole screen which is annoying when you're quickly trying to dispatch several guards in different ways.
Sometimes people will see you do things through walls which gets annoying very quickly, not to mention their insane peripheral vision. Also, people with like disguises spot you way too quickly and Agent 47 for all his skills still hasn't learned the simple art of covering his face when in disguise unless you use his special ability meter.
The checkpoint system is and always has been annoying when you have to repeatedly replay an annoying section. Adding insult to injury, the enemies respawn when reverting to a checkpoint (even ones you killed before activating the checkpoint).
While not really a con, I did feel like much of the story was contrived and most of the bad guys were over the top caricatures. It definitely has a slight Japanese feel to the writing which is understandable given the publisher but occasionally went too far IMHO.
Despite those things, I still very much enjoyed the game and can easily recommend it, even at the regular not on sale price.

More please of Saints row 4 and this time set in hell and make the main characters Gat and Kinzie. Please. Well comments out of the way ill will now review Gat out of Hell. I will go over it in a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.
Pro:
The game looks good. The color and world definantly looks like what a fictional representation of hell may look like. They even combined aspects of hell to how steelport looks like in both saints row 3 and 4.
Shooting enemies are very nice even in hell. There are 20 guns but each look and feel unique and there are the 7 deadly sins adaptation in the shape of guns which is pretty cool. Greed, sloth, lust, .ect. They all represent the sins properly and like how greed grants more money per kills with it's jackpot skill or how lust causes enemies to be passifist with hearts above their heads and they dance.
Con:
Its saints row 4 but painted hell colored. I know i said that already but it is pretty lazy and looses points on making a more unique world that doesnt feel like a copy paste level design. Yes it has added items like sharp rocks and lava but still the structure is steelport at its base.
Representations from famous and infamous people in history is kinda lazy. Why is shakspear in hell? What is the deal with blackbeard? Sure it makes more sense with him but it is odd how they have a mixture of fictional, realistic, and oddly placed people as helpers in hell. It would be a good opportunity to revist old villians of saints row in the game in hell or all historical villans but it was just an odd choice or selection of characters to choose from. Mainly it felt more Assassin's creed like by saying "hey we have historical figures in our game...we do our history homework " but even this game doesnt do that just either.
Cars have been more useless to use and horrible to drive. Cars look ok to a degree but when you think of it with the super powers you can avoid the need to drive in the game entirely. Thats not too bad but with the added bonus that cars are very light and doing some challenges are just unbareable to do. It just adds to the frustration one can have when trying to drive a car. Motorcycle on the other hand are still ok to drive, they are not too bad but cars have to be the worst in all the saint row games I personally played. They get stuck very easily.
Hitboxes of ganky is very very off. All the enemies have a well fit hitbox where shooting is never the issue but when fighting ganky... all that goes right out the window. Shooting anywear on the head provides no hit feedback so the only way that I could do damage was to shoot him in the chest.
Gun upgrades is horribly skewed. The first upgrade price is good being $100 but after that it jumps straight to little over $6k. Thats a big jump. Now if it was those 7 deadly sin guns being pricey to upgrade then i wouldnt mind but every single gun from starting handgun to any 7 deadly sin gun has a pricey upgrade ammount. It is a way to keep players staying in the game grinding to upgrade all guns if they wanted because grinding is sooo much fun in a game like this. Money was never an issue in other saint row games like 3 or 4 with it auto pay system.
Conclusion:
After many hours in Gat out of Hell it was very apparent that the game was not fun. Yes it had its normal Saints row humor but I didnt enjoy the story, I didnt enjoy the driving, Flying was a pain till you maxed it out, gun upgrading is a major grind, many challenges are very specific like the arch combo one where you have to shock an enemy from another AI to work on that challenge. The issue with that is enemies do not clump up together often. They normal are spread out enough so it makes things a pain to do. All and all i can not reccomend the game because it does not add more to what Saints row was but it is just saints row painted in hell but much much boring and tedius to play.

HITMAN: ABSOLUTION REVIEW
BY LUKE REILLY For a game built upon the concept of slipping by unnoticed, Hitman: Absolution is certainly doing the opposite. It’s standing conspicuously amongst today’s fad-driven modern shooters and me-too multiplayer hopefuls, middle fingers extended. A slow-paced, single-player focused sneak ’em up, Absolution looms in stark opposition to many of the most pervading trends in gaming today. It cares not for the overly delicate, their minds rendered dull and flabby after years of being prodded through corridors blasting anything that breathes. Absolution delights in letting players skulk through it expending few bullets at all. It’s a game that wants to let you think for yourself.A game that wants to remind you that trial and error done right equals satisfaction, not frustration.
For those of you counting at home it’s been 2368 days since Hitman: Blood Money was released, give or take. That’s a long time between drinks. It’s nearly six-and-a-half years. In video game terms that’s somewhere in the Cretaceous Period. In actual fact the besuited Agent 47 and his barcoded dome have spent the vast bulk of this generation on the sideline. Hitman: Absolution has been a long time coming, a fact fans are acutely aware of.The pressure to deliver, then, is high. Blood Money may be a dinosaur in some respects but it remains a cult favourite adored by its faithful fans. Six-and-a-half years on the team at Io Interactive must ship a successor to it worthy of the wait.The good news is, they have.Above everything, Absolution is a game that wants you to experiment with it. It refuses to be rushed through, rewarding brains over brawn. It wants you to spend time inside it, methodically picking your way around and discovering morbid new ways to snuff out your unfortunate marks. Like Blood Money before it, your targets here can be executed in a host of ever-so-slightly sickeningly different ways. Returning Hitman fans won’t settle for a simple bullet to the back of the head; they’ll immediately be on the lookout for the tell-tale signs of a classic Hitman kill opportunity. Some of them are more subtle than others but, like Blood Money, they’re all there, waiting to be discovered. A couple of the game’s kills are more tightly choreographed for dramatic effect, complete with a brief cutscene of your deserved victim sucking in their last breaths, but most of the game’s kills – two dozen of them at least – are traditional Hitman fare. How you take them out is in your hands. This is a slow-paced, measured experience. This is not Medal of Duty: Modern Warfighter Ops. Impatient action junkies need not apply.The way Absolution itself plays is very much a refined version of what Io attempted with its previous effort, but gone are most of the quirks Hitman diehards were happy to overlook in Blood Money. 47 feels far more connected to the environment rather than skating about on it, and successfully sneaking up on a target from behind with your signature fibre wire is no longer quite as fickle an exercise. It’s all a lot more organic and a lot less stiff.Furthermore Absolution adds a host of additional abilities for 47. 47’s limited use sedatives, for instance, are no longer necessary because of his close-quarters combat skills. Sneak up on an enemy or NPC unawares and you can grab them and either subdue or kill them with your bare hands. It’s just like Blood Money, where you could simply take people as a human shield and then knock them cold with the butt of your pistol when your syringes ran dry, only without all that rigmarole (although, of course, you can still do that too).There’s a cover system that allows you to properly exchange fire with enemies when things go pear-shaped, rather than being stuck out in the open desperately strafing left and right. When you’re playing as you should, stealthily and patiently, the cover system is even more useful, allowing you to spring from behind it as enemies pass by to quietly choke them out, or snap their necks. You can also fake surrender too, disarming your would-be captor and taking him hostage.There have been tweaks to the shooting system too. Point Shooting, which is a slo-mo power-up that functions not unlike a similar power-up in Splinter Cell Conviction, works fine but Hitman veterans will almost certainly never use it outside the couple of instances it’s required throughout the game. Rabid Hitman fans simply won’t be doing the levels of indiscriminate killing that would warrant the use of Point Shooting. You can’t get Silent Assassin ratings by mowing down scores of henchmen in slow-motion. Better is Precision Shot, which allows you to gently squeeze the trigger to steady your aim before actually firing. It feels very natural; it’s a hugely better solution than the normal “click-here-to-hold-your-breath” malarkey.Then there’s Instinct Mode, which is basically 47’s intuition represented visually. Instinct Mode remains a true bone of contention for some but at its most fundamental level this replaces the previous, god-like minimap. 47 can sense nearby enemies and you can note where they are in relation to him. How you use it beyond that is really up to you. New Hitman players can use it as a crutch, noting enemy patrol paths or objects of interest. Veterans can simply refer to it sparingly or dial it down entirely. On the higher of the game’s five difficulty settings it’s automatically neutered anyway.On the topic of difficulty settings, there are five – and they cover the whole spectrum. Easy is exceedingly so, and Purist is insane. The sweet spot for a first play through is probably Normal or Hard. Enemy reaction times are quite forgiving in Normal and the game will tolerate some sloppiness on your part at the expense of realism, but it’s a good setting to build up an understanding of the levels. Hard ramps things up. It’s interesting to note that enemy NPCs aren’t just sharper on higher difficulties; there are also more of them. Depending on your approach you may well find your undetected route through a level on Normal completely thwarted by an added patrol on Hard.When things do go sour the adjustments to how enemies react to your presence is also welcome. If you’re spotted and you can contain the situation by subduing or killing all nearby witnesses before they inform others an alert won’t be raised. This is a refreshing change from Blood Money, where one foul up would dispatch every enemy on the map against you like heat-seeking missiles.Absolution looks good. There’s arguably a bit too much lighting bloom, particularly when harsh light begins to glint off 47’s cue ball bonce, but it’s not going to be something that’ll have you dropkicking the disc down your driveway in disgust. It’s darker and grittier than Hitman titles past but the visuals shouldn’t raise many complaints. It looks its best at its busiest; when you’re threading your way through the game’s thick crowds. It’s these moments when you’re keenly aware you’re playing something a little different. The levels are nicely dressed and the cutscenes are well-produced; it’s a solid effort all around.It sounds great too.
There are 20 levels but many are broken up into a series of stages. The key difference between this and Blood Money is the levels are segmented. Instead of one big level, say, like the Heaven and Hell Club, levels in Absolution are often completed in discrete chunks. X Rebirth. Lets get something clear, this is a vastly different direction from X3:TC/AP. Only three systems that you can visit, but this game does several things that the previous games do not.
1: Space is big.
With the previous games, each system could easily be crossed in a minute or two before reaching jumpgates. In this particular game, each region is massive. The stations are huge and modular, can fight back, and can be precision disabled instead of outright destroyed easily. You can find ships by the hundreds, making space feel less empty. Speaking of stations...
2: Improving infrastructure is no small deal.
In the last game, all you needed to do to build a station is buy a prefab set, hire or buy a ship large enough to carry the parts, and just plop it down anywhere you like. Here, you can't just build anywhere you like, which is more realistic. Plus, once you plce down a blueprint, you have to obtain all the materials needed to build the structure. In addition, after you build the station, you can expand on it further using the same methods. Every station is going to be dependant on others for one thing or another, you can't just build a megaplex that takes care of itself. Unfortunately, this leads to some problems in the storyline.
3: You can't do everything yourself.
You only have one ship, and its more a fighter then a cargo ship. Granted, this is a bit of a downer as being able to fly any ship you like was one of the more enjoyable parts of prior games. Fleets are also fairly small and mostly freighters instead of fleets of destroyers. Managing your fleets isn't simple, and too clunky for my tastes.
4: The economy...
Is a joke. Trading isn't easy and can't be automated, and isn't profitible in the end. Your best bet is to turn to piracy/bounty hunting and jack freighters. There hasn't been any other decent source of money.
In the end, you can't build up to be a force that matches the major governments. If you dive into the lore, the limited number of systems makes sense, and is a bit worrying if you really think about this. This is mostly a very clunky game that has been too long in development and doesn't nearly match the standards of todays games. Maybe if it was released back in 2007...
