Even with the much-derided 1.3 patch, Primal Carnage is still a solid and straightforward asymmetrical multiplayer game that's well worth the low price of admission.
Primal Carnage is split between two separate styles of play: the human team is controlled from a first-person perspective with a focus on shooting and technology; the other team controls dinosaurs in third-person whose attacks center around stealth, ambushing and conspicuous amounts of slashing and biting. You'd think such a setup would compromise one or the other, but that's not the case, for the most part.
As with many multiplayer games, Primal utilizes a class system, each character with their own unique abilities and attacks. Somewhat like Team Fortress 2, if less symmetrical. On the human team, a fair bit of effort is given to make each class feel interesting and different. Weapons include conventional guns like pistols, shotguns and rifles, but the game mixes it up with interesting special equipment such as nets, tranq darts, flares and flamethrowers. The gunplay itself is rather loose and doesn't feel up to the high standards set by other multiplayer games. Nevertheless, the variety in the weapons makes playing as the humans an interesting gameplay experience, particularly when alone...
Of course, the selling point here is the dinosaurs, how do they control? Like the human team, there are five classes of various shapes and sizes, each with a primary (usually bite) and (usually) secondary attack. They also each have a special roar ability, which gives them temporary boosts and abilities such as faster attacks, health boosts and enemy spotting. Also like the humans, they all feel unique and generally fun to play as, thanks in no small part to the rather ludicrous ragdoll system which turns dead characters into orbiting devices. Movement with the larger lads can feel cumbersome, but you soon learn to adapt to the control differences between the classes. The best moments, of course, are those that involve waiting and stalking lone human players as they bumble about the forest until waiting for the correct moment to strike. A large chunk of the game is spent at the centre of incomprehensible carnage, but these moments of cat-and-mouse are no doubt where the game truly shines, creating moments of tension for both players
However, there are a couple of mechanical problems that bear worth mentioning here. Due to changes made in the 1.3 patch, the Novaraptor class's secondary ability, the pounce, was left in a somewhat buggy state. It seems to be a sporadic issue, but sometimes attempting to leap on an unsuspecting pleb from the bushes can instead launch you halfway across the map. It's not a game-breaking issue, but it can be rather frustrating. Aside from this, glitches are common. Most are minor and simply involve visual quirks, like humans lying on the ground screaming in terror at a raptor that ripping them apart from twenty feet away, presumably with some kind of prehistoric telekinesis. However, game crashes do occur. I haven't suffered from too many of them, but they are present.
Aside from that, the game runs fairly well even on lower-end systems. It's not the best-looking game in the world, but the modelling and environmental work is still pretty good for an indie game that's now hitting its third year. Some maps are more taxing though, tanking the framerate even on my GTX 770 when the visuals get busy. Again, not a big problem, but worth noting.
One last important thing everyone should bear in mind before purchasing this game. Due to complicated behind-the-scenes happenings, this game is no longer being updated. Instead, the new developers have released the long-awaited 2.0 update as a separate game titled "Primal Carnage: Extinction". I cannot comment on the state of this game as I have not played it yet. If you do commit to the original Primal Carnage, be mindful that it will likely never see another update. In my estimation, the game is stable enough to not warrant any concerns in the near future.
At the moment, the population is still pretty reasonable. Servers can get quiet at some times during the day, but there are plenty of players milling about online in the evenings.
If you're into dinosaur games or mindless corny action, then Primal Carnage has got you covered: it's a bone-crunchingly good time once you get a handle on it and never gets old. It ain't the deepest or most expansive dinosaur game out there, but it's still a darned fine one. If you see it on sale, then it's an absolute steal!

Grandpa's Leftovers is one of those titles that combines tried and tested, existing platformer gameplay mechanics but with its own take, then soaks it in style or charm and dash of intelligence to produce something new, unique, fun, and with plenty of character. The developers could've very easily went the artistic approach with this, and put its playstyle on a pedestal and chased after game awards with a deeper story or writing about a real world problem or story, but instead it keeps things silly and delightful with immature but not crude or stupid comic-style humour and characters which will probably make you smile once or twice while having fun platforming.
The twin elements of fantastic mechanics and a smooth, visually impressive engine marry together and make for unique gameplay in an interesting world and really made this title stand out for me as something pretty unique. The other thing that bolsters it and brings it up another level is the great writing, cool characters and silly story.
There's a childish comic-book theme throughout, and things like the visual pop-out text elements and the creature movements and asset designs all help add to a child-like adventure.
The biggest complaint against this title is the short play length and it clocks in at an average of just 2-4 hours for the story. However, the wonderful nature of the mechanics means that you can solve any level in unpredictable strange new ways. That, and the addition of simple but fun achievements and extras mean replaying this title is as much fun as the first play, and Completionists can expect a good 10+ hours of playthrough. If you're not in a rush or like to explore, the play time shouldn't be a huge problem for you.
There are also some issues with the lack of precision in the controls. For a game about manipulating the environment to your advantage, it's frustrating to run into situations where you've sliced a rock or pillar at a slightly different angle than you wanted due to the lack of precision allowed, then find yourself unable to progress as expected. The problems become more apparent during boss fights where you're pressured to keep up with what's happening on screen while trying to remain precise and can end up being a stressful annoyance.

Shortly after his son Tim Schafer launched him into space, Sid Meier began work on his most ambitious project to date: Civilization: Beyond Earth. How this idea came to him was fairly obvious. What's notable about this game is that programming is nearly impossible to perform in freefall. Without the force of gravity to aid the finger in pushing keys on the keyboard, the strain in typing anything is enormous. Sid Meier had to spend the first 4 years of this 4.043-year game's development cycle learning how to do one-fingered upside-down hand-standing pushups, not unlike the time half of Lieutenant Riker was stuck on Nervala IV. This is ironic because Tim Schafer was similarly created from Sid Meier in a teleportation accident (documented in the film Half-Life: Blue Shift). So while Tim was trying to drum up support for his game Broken Rage (which would later come into a legal dispute over its name with id software), Sid was hard at work improving his skills. Once he was ready, Sid spent the next 15 days patching his game Alpha Centuri until it was Civilization: Beyond Earth: a documentary of his life in space. Thankfully, the game won him the awards of best game written in space, worst game written in space, fastest game development cycle in space and an honorary mention in Gabe Newell magazine for being almost as good of a software developer as Gabe Newell according to Gabe Newell, and so he was allowed to return to Earth. He flipped Tim off on his way down.

Here's a surefire way to ensure your stealth game is DOA: Make running and gunning EASIER than the actual stealth. While previous Hitman games all but forced you to keep a low profile and approach levels creatively, the path of the Silent Assassin has become sadly optional in this outing. Due to the dim-witted AI, all you need to do is find a bottleneck and keep the trigger pulled as enemy after hapless enemy keeps pouring in, regardless of how many of their buddies they've just seen gunned down in front of their eyes. Adding to the overall disappointment is an irritating departure from the series' traditional contracts format, in favor of story-based missions that more often than not see Agent 47 merely progress from point A to B in order to trigger the next cutscene. If you're not a hardcore fan of the series, I recommend garotting this game and dumping it in the nearest skip.

This game is pretty good, definitely give it a go, if you like psychological horror.
Good:
+ Concept
+ Voice acting
+ Support
The voice acting is very well done and the author of the short story voices the antagonist, AM.  The story itself is well-written and in my opinion stands well on its own, that is there is no need read the short story(though it's very very very extremely so so superbly smart and also cool so maybe read it?).  The game's story is quite different from the short story, though it takes some of the environmental ideas of it (read notes for further information). Also this game is still being patched and improved on after all this time, at least people care about it, maybe you should too?
May Need some Improvement:
1/2 Pace
1/2 Decisions
Some small pacing issues, not so much in the scenarios themselves (in my perspective) but outside of them. Some more interactions with AM in between scenarios would have sufficed to give it a bit more continuity between scenarios, though this is a big nitpick and as a result I wouldn't weigh this very highly.   There are quite a few approaches to solving scenarios that can be taken, though many either break the scenario or they are paths that lead to utlimately the same result. Forgiving this there are multiple endings, which aren't bad and there are various ways to see a scenario unfold. All and all not that bad and certainly the different approaches are all interesting. Definitely a lot of ways to play through a scenario.
Cons:
- Pixel regions
In certain parts of the game the pixel regions you need to click on to go to another area are a bit obscured and slightly unintuitive.
Notes: The game takes a different approach than the short story does, the characters were essentially entirely rewritten (names preserved) and given new characteriztions. This includes new back stories, and some personality changes (Ellen especially so). So if you are a fan of the short story, you should note that it is not the same pace nor does it provide the same personality. The game did keep some aspects of the short story characterization and makes reference to certain short story aspects in character scenarios. All in all, the preservation of the short story, wasn't bad in my opinion.
Tl;dr some of the lore and some character design is seen being intact .

Simply put, Betrayer is stunningly beautiful and hauntingly mysterious! It's use of black and white, emphasizing the color red, gives it a unique look not seen too often in games and when paired with the frequent breezes, swaying vegetation and nature sounds truly make the experience surreal.
The selection of weapons in pretty impressive for a budget game and there are even charms you can find, that when equipped, will enhance your movement speed, HP and other attributes.  Both the charms and weapons (muskets, rifles, crossbows, short/longbows, etc.; it takes place in colonial times) have varying degrees of strength depending on the type, such as crude, quality and exceptional. There is a light and dark world you must trek through in order to solve the mystery of what's going on in the game and in particular, with the Maiden in Red.  There are collectibles such as chests and letter scraps  and gifts to find and also clues that will allow you to solve other, lesser mysteries involving ghosts you encounter along the way.  There are also a decent number of enemy types, such as skeletons, spider=like crustacean things (yeah, no idea what these things are but they're cool), undead Spaniards, phantoms (skull/deer=headed ghosts....don't ask about the deer heads, freaked me out first time i saw them, thinking it was the Wendigo or something coming after me...) and burning, undead Native American warriors. You can even unlock destinations and quick travel between them, as well as upgrade how many times you can heal. You even have tomahawks and explosives to throw, and like arrows, the tomahawks can be retrieved from fallen enemies which is very nice.
Keep in mind this is a budget game, so the amount of content the developers put into Betrayer for only $20 is truly impressive.  I know this was certainly one gaming experience I won't soon forget. I highly recommend buying this game, even if it's not on sale.  Enjoy!!
